### BOOK ONE

...it is declined in the plural as both masculine and feminine.
**גדילים** <term>Gedilim: Tassels or twisted cords</term> phylacteries of garments, or cords in the fringes. Deuteronomy 22: "You shall make cords in the fringes." <note>original: "Funiculos in fimbriis facies"</note>

**גדע** <term>Gada: To break or cut off</term> He broke; he cut off. Psalm 75: "And I will break all the horns of the sinners." And Jeremiah 48: "The horn of Moab is cut off." <note>The Latin text cites Jeremiah 47, but the verse regarding Moab's horn is found in chapter 48.</note>

**גדף** <term>Gadaf: To revile or blaspheme</term> He despised; he reproached; he blasphemed. Zephaniah 2: "I have heard the reproach of Moab, and the blasphemies of the children of Ammon."

**גדר** <term>Gadar: To wall in or enclose</term> He circumscribed; he hedged; he enclosed; he built around; he surrounded with a wall. Lamentations 3: "He built around against me." Likewise: "he enclosed my ways with stones." From this comes the noun **גדר** <term>Geder: A wall or fence</term> A hedge, fold, stone wall, or wall. As in Numbers 22: regarding that which we have translated as "in the narrowness of two stone walls by which the vineyards were surrounded," the Hebrews read "a hedge on this side and a hedge on that side." It is found in both the masculine and feminine gender. First, in Psalm 80: "Why have you destroyed its stone wall?" Second, in Psalm 89: "You have destroyed all its hedges." Among logicians, this word signifies a "definition," because it terminates and circumscribes the thing defined. <note>The author is drawing a parallel between a physical wall and a logical definition that "fences in" the meaning of a word.</note>

**גדיש** <term>Gadish: A stack of grain</term> A heap of sheaves or produce in the stalks. As in Exodus 22: "If a fire breaks out and finds thorns and catches the heaps of grain."

**גבול** <term>Gevul: A boundary or territory</term> This. As in Ezekiel 47: "This is the boundary in which you shall possess the land." And it is said in place of **זבול** <gloss>Zevul: a dwelling</gloss> according to Rabbi Kimhi <note>David Kimhi, a famous 12th-13th century grammarian and commentator</note> in his commentaries on Ezekiel, by the substitution of the letter *Zayin* for *Gimel* according to the **אטבח** <term>Atbash: A system of letter substitution</term> custom, of whose secret and elegant alphabet practice it is fully treated in the book by Joseph "Caton" <note>Referring to Joseph Gikatilla, a 13th-century Kabbalist</note> titled *The Garden of Nuts*. <note>The Hebrew title is Ginat Egoz.</note>

**גהה** <term>Gahah: To heal or relieve</term> He was medicated; he healed; he made to cease; he laid down; he loosened. As in Hosea 5: "Nor can he loosen the bond from you," which the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Bible</note> translated as "he will make to cease," and Jonathan the Chaldean <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel, to whom the Aramaic Targum (paraphrase) of the Prophets is attributed</note> explains: "he will not make the scourge rest from you."

**גהר** <term>Gahar: To stretch out or prostrate</term> He prostrated; he inclined toward the earth; prone upon the belly. As in 1 Kings...

THE BOOK

**1 Kings 18.** And he bowed down to the ground and put his face between his knees. <note>original: "1 Regum 18"</note>

**גו** <note>Hebrew: Gev</note> **Inside** or **middle**. As in Job 30, in place of what we have: *those snatching these things from the valleys*; the Hebrews read: *they shall be expelled from within* or *from the inside*. And it takes the letter *he* at the end. As in Job 20: *Drawn out and coming out from its sheath*, for that which ought to be translated as: *from the interior* or *from the inside* or *from the middle*. For where **מתוך** <note>Hebrew: mi-tok; meaning "from the midst"</note> is placed in the Hebrew—that is, *from the middle*—there the Chaldean <term>Chaldean: Aramaic, often referring to the Targum translations of the Bible</term> translator placed **מגו** <note>Aramaic: miggo; meaning "from within"</note>. Numbers 16: *Separate yourselves from the midst of the congregation.* See Onkelos <note>Onkelos was a famous 2nd-century convert to Judaism who authored the standard Aramaic translation of the Torah</note> in that place.

**גו** <note>Hebrew: Gav</note> **Back** or **body**. As in Isaiah 50: *I gave my body to those who strike.* And it is translated as "back" in Proverbs 10: *And a rod is for the back of him who lacks heart.* This is because of the similarity in the pronunciation of the letters *vav* and *beth* <note>The Hebrew letters Vav (ו) and Bet (ב) often represented similar "v" or "b" sounds in various traditions</note>, as mentioned above. So also in Nehemiah 9: *And they cast your law behind their backs.* And it has a plural form, **גויות** <note>Hebrew: Geviyot</note>, of the feminine gender, as at the end of the same chapter: *And they have dominion over our bodies.* This more correctly descends from **גוה** <note>Hebrew: Gevah</note>, as seen below.

**גוב** <note>Hebrew: Guv</note> **Cage** or **gathering**. As in Nahum 3, meaning "to gather," like a *gathering of locusts*.

**גובי** <note>Hebrew: Govai</note> **Locust**. Amos 7: *And behold, the creator of the locust.* According to the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>, it is a *bruchus* <note>A type of wingless locust or beetle</note>.

**גוד** <note>Hebrew: Gud</note> **He plundered** or **raided**. Genesis 49: *Gad, a troop shall raid him.* <note>This is a wordplay on the name Gad in Jacob's blessing</note>. It is the same as **גדד** <note>Hebrew: G-D-D</note>, which we treated above.

**גויה** <note>Hebrew: Geviyah</note> **Corpse** or **body**. As in Judges 14: *But he did not want to indicate that he had taken the honey from the body of the lion.* It is perhaps drawn from **גוה** <note>Hebrew: Gevah</note>, which is derived from the word **גו** <note>Hebrew: Gev</note> by adding the aspiration of the letter *he*. Similarly in Daniel 10: *And his body was like chrysolite.* <note>A yellowish-green gemstone</note> It is spoken as if it were **גופת** <note>Hebrew: Gufat; body</note>.

**גוז** <note>Hebrew: Gaz</note> **It flew**. Numbers 11: in place of what our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> has: *a wind going out from the Lord brought quails across the sea*, the Hebrews read: *And a spirit went forth from the Lord, and made quails fly from the sea.* And although it is written without the letter *vav* in that place, the <term>Qamets: A Hebrew vowel mark indicating a long 'a' sound</term> is placed to supplement it.

**גוזל** <note>Hebrew: Gozal</note> **Educator**; one who leads something out from potential into action. Also **protector**. In Psalm 71: *You are my protector.* <note>In modern Hebrew, this word usually refers to a fledgling or young bird, but the author here connects it to the idea of bringing forth or guarding</note>.

-># BOOK ONE<-

**To push forth, to lead out, or to extract.** <note>original: *giach* (גִּיחַ)</note> As in Psalm 22: "For you are he who **extracted** me from the womb." It is also used as a <term>transitive verb</term> <note>A verb that carries action toward an object.</note> as in Job 40: "Though the Jordan should flow into his mouth," which means "that he should cause the Jordan to be **drawn out** into his mouth," where the Hebrew word is used. Some say the river of paradise, the **Gihon**, took its name from this, because it is led out to water the garden. This was also the name of a pool in Jerusalem, which is called **Siloam**. It also signifies to groan and to be anxious, as in Micah 4: "Be in pain and labor to **groan forth**," perhaps because it also "draws out" tears.

**A people or a nation.** <note>original: *goy* (גּוֹי)</note> Both terms are used for the same word in Deuteronomy 4: "Nor is there any other **nation** so great," and again, "For what other **people** is so renowned?" The Hebrews now call those who are not Israelites **Goyim**, meaning <term>ethnics</term> <note>From the Greek 'ethnos,' referring to non-Jewish nations; gentiles.</note> and gentiles. This follows Joel 1: "For a **nation** has come up over my land," although Jonathan the Chaldean <note>Refers to the Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the prophets.</note> translated it as "people."

**To exult.** <note>original: *gil* (גִּיל)</note> Isaiah 65: "And I will **exult** in Jerusalem, and rejoice in my people." More fittingly in Proverbs 23: "The father of the righteous **exults** with joy." Although the common translation <note>The Latin Vulgate.</note> of Psalm 22 says, "He hoped in the Lord, let him rescue him," and Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the primary translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> translates it as "He fled to the Lord," it is more correctly: "He **exulted** in the Lord." There is another transitive form in the aforementioned chapter of Isaiah: "But you shall rejoice and **exult**." From this comes the noun **exultation** a little later: "Behold, I create Jerusalem as an **exultation**." It is also found with an <term>apocope</term> <note>The loss of a sound or letter at the end of a word.</note> of the final breathing sound in Hosea 9: "Do not rejoice, O Israel, unto **exultation** like the peoples."

**To be consumed, to expire, to perish, or to die.** <note>original: *gava* (גָּוַע)</note> Genesis 49: "And he **died** and was gathered to his people." And in Numbers 17: "Behold, we are **consumed**, we all perish." From this comes the name for one **suffering in their final moments**, as in Psalm 88: "I am poor and in **labors** from my youth." Where Jerome, in his Psalter translated from the Hebrew truth, renders it as "**wretched** from my youth," we can explain this as "failing," "expiring," "weary," or "gaping open."

**A body, a corpse,** <note>original: *guph* (גּוּף)</note> and that material person which surrounds every individual human being. In Exodus 21, in place of what our translation has as "With whatever garment he entered, with such shall he go out," the Hebrew reads: "If he entered with his **body**, he shall go out with his **body**." They explain it thus: "If he entered in his own **person** and not with another person <note>Likely referring to entering service without a wife or family.</note>." Onkelos the Chaldean <note>Refers to the Targum Onkelos, the authoritative Aramaic translation of the Torah.</note>...

...expressing the sense rather than the word, translates it thus: "If he entered alone, let him also leave alone." Nicholas of Lyra <note>A prominent Franciscan teacher and influential biblical commentator of the 14th century</note> thinks this name signifies "cloth," but he offers no proof for his claim. But the Chaldean translation of Jonathan <note>original: "translatio chaldaica Ionathę," referring to the Targum Jonathan, an Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> certainly shows us the property of this word; for it uses גופא <note>Hebrew: *gufa*, meaning "body" or "corpse"</note> for "corpse" or "body." As in the first book of Kings, chapter 31: "And they took the corpse of Saul and the corpse of his sons." And the Hebrew masters commonly use the present word for "body" in the sense of a physical substance, as Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>Maimonides (1135–1204), a preeminent Jewish philosopher and scholar</note> does in the first book of *The Guide for the Perplexed*, chapter 49, where he teaches that many words are said of the Creator, from which—if the words were understood in their bare literal sense—someone might think that the Creator was גויה <note>Hebrew: *gviyah*</note>, that is, a living body.

גור <note>Hebrew root: *Gur*</note> **He dwelt**, as a stranger or a tenant. Psalm 15: "Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle?" and Isaiah 16: "My fugitives shall dwell with you." It also signifies "he lived as a foreigner." Genesis 26: "And live as a foreigner in this land." From which comes:

גר <note>Hebrew: *Ger*</note> **Stranger**, newcomer, or tenant. Leviticus 18: "And of the strangers who live among you," and in the plural גרים <note>Hebrew: *Gerim*</note> in Isaiah 5: "Strangers shall eat." From this are derived other words which signify a dwelling, a meeting place, or a habitation. In Psalm 55: "For wickedness is in their dwellings," which they explain as "in their meeting places."

גור <note>Hebrew root: *Gur*</note> **He feared**, he trembled, or he was afraid. Job chapter 3: "And what I feared has happened to me." From this comes מגור <note>Hebrew: *Magor*</note> fear or dread, as in Jeremiah chapter 6: "Because the sword of the enemy and dread are all around." Thus they read this verse in Deuteronomy 32: "If I did not fear the wrath of the enemies," for which we read <note>The Latin Vulgate translation</note>, "But on account of the wrath of the enemies I delayed." Others, however, read it from אגורה <note>Hebrew: *Agurah*</note>, that is, from the word for "collection," in this way: "If the wrath of the enemies had not been collected and increased." We spoke of this word above under the letter *aleph*.

גור <note>Hebrew root: *Gur*</note> **He increased**, he brought forth, or he gathered. Habakkuk chapter 1: "He drew it in his dragnet and gathered it in his net." Regardless of what our translation says, or even the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note>. For so David Kimhi <note>Radak (1160–1235), a celebrated Jewish grammarian and commentator</note>, the greatest critic of words among the Hebrews, explains in his commentaries on the Twelve <note>The Twelve Minor Prophets of the Old Testament</note>. In this way, some understand Hosea chapter 10: "The inhabitants of Samaria worshipped the calves of Beth-aven," for which others read "they feared."

-># FIRST BOOK<-

...others gathered, others brought. <term>Jonathan the Chaldean</term><note>Referring to the Targum of Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> says "they caused to ascend." The <term>Seventy</term><note>The Septuagint (LXX), the earliest Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> remained [with their reading]. I would say "they brought," which fits both the historical context and the idiom of the language.

**גור** [gur] — A young animal or a cub. As in Genesis 49: "Judah is a lion’s **whelp**."

**מגורה** [megurah] — A granary, or any place where produce is stored. <term>Jerome</term><note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the primary translator of the Latin Vulgate.</note> investigated the specific property of this word more wisely and reasonably, saying it signifies the "husk" or "casing" of the grain, in his *Commentary on the Twelve Prophets*, where we read in Haggai chapter 2: "Is the seed yet in the **husk**?" The Seventy, however, translated it as "threshing floor."

**גוש** [gush] — A clod or a small portion of mud. Jerome translated it as "filth." Job 7: "My flesh is clothed with rot and **clods** of dust."

**גז** [gaz] — He sheared. Genesis 31: "At that time Laban had gone to **shear** his sheep." And in 1 Samuel 25: "I have heard that your shepherds were **shearing** your flocks." It is also found as a single syllable through <term>apocope</term><note>A linguistic term for the loss of one or more sounds from the end of a word.</note> of the final letter in Job chapter 1, where we read "and with a shaved head," the <term>Hebrew truth</term><note>original: "veritas," a term often used by scholars to refer to the original Hebrew text as the ultimate authority over translations.</note> has "and he **shaved** his head." Also in Amos chapter 7: "After the king’s **mowings** [shearings]."

**גזבר** [gizbar] — A treasurer or guardian of the public chest. Ezra 7: "To all the **keepers** of the public chest."

**גזה** [gezah] and **גז** [gez] — A fleece. Psalm 72: "He shall descend like rain upon the **fleece**." And Judges 6: "I will put this **fleece** of wool on the floor."

**גזית** [gazit] — Smoothed, cut, scraped, and polished; used in reference to stones in 1 Chronicles 22: "To cut and polish **stones**." Jerome translated it as "square stones" in Lamentations 3: "He has blocked my ways with **square stones**."

**גזל** [gazal] — He snatched, extorted by force, or plundered. As in Leviticus 6: "or has **extorted** something by force." And it follows: "he shall restore all that he wished to obtain through fraud," where the Hebrew truth has: "he shall restore the **plunder** which he plundered," or what he obtained through false accusation, etc.

**גוזל** [gozal] — A young bird, which Jerome translated as "dove" in Genesis 15: "A turtle-dove also and a **pigeon**." But it is also used for other species, such as in Deuteronomy 32: "As the eagle enticing its **young** to fly."

**גזם** [gazam] — A caterpillar; a worm born in garden herbs. Joel 1: "That which the **caterpillar** left..."

**גזר** <note>original: "Gazar"</note> **He cut off. He severed. He cut into. He ordained. He arranged. He established.** Habakkuk 3: *The flock shall be cut off from the fold.* Psalm 88: The daily reading has: *and they are repulsed from your hand*, but Jerome, in his psalter based on the <term>Hebrew truth</term> <note>Jerome’s "Hebraica veritas" refers to his translation directly from the original Hebrew rather than the Greek Septuagint</note>, more correctly says: *who are cut off from your hand.* And 4 Kings 6: *When they had come to the Jordan, they were cutting wood.* From this comes a verbal noun as in Genesis 15: *And a lamp of fire passing between those divisions.* This word is translated differently in Lamentations 4: *Waters flowed over my head; I said, "I am perished."* which the Hebrews explain as "I was predestined and ordained for this." **גחון** <note>original: "Gachon"</note> **Belly.** We read "breast" in Leviticus 11: *whatever goes upon its breast*, and Genesis 3: *Upon your breast shall you go.* But <term>Onkelos the Chaldean</term> <note>A famous 2nd-century convert who translated the Torah into Aramaic</note> translated it more properly as *belly*, with which we agree.

->FIRST<-

...broken by a great valley. It is also found without the letter *aleph*, as in Joshua 8: "There was a valley between them." It takes a plural form in the feminine manner, as in Ezekiel 6: "To the mountains and hills, to the crags and valleys." And in chapter 35 of the same: "On your hills and in your valleys" גיאיתיך <note>original: "ge'ayoteykha"</note>. In this word, there is often a variation of the *yod* itself, sometimes placed before the *aleph* and sometimes after it; for it takes the place of the "h" breathing sound <note>the aspiration</note> that this vocabulary occasionally assumes, which authors treat in the art of grammar.

**Sinew.** <note>Hebrew: גִּיד (Gid)</note> As in Genesis 32: "For which reason the children of Israel do not eat the sinew that shrank." And in the plural in Job 10: "And with sinews you have bound me together."
**Staff, cord, sinew, or strap.** As in Isaiah 48: "Your neck is an iron sinew."

**Peer, contemporary, [or peer].** <note>Hebrew: גִּיל (Gil). The Latin OCR "coquis" (cooks) is likely a transcription error for "coetaneis" (contemporaries), which matches the biblical context of Daniel 1:10</note> Daniel 1: "Above the rest of the young men, your peers."

**He closed.** <note>Hebrew: גִּיר (Gir), though contextually linked here to the act of shutting</note> As in Nehemiah 7: "And while they were still standing by, the gates were shut and barred." In place of which the true reading is: "Let them shut the doors."

**Chalk** <note>Hebrew: גִּיר (Gir)</note> or a crust made of stones crushed into dust, suitable for a wall or floor. Some wish it to signify mortar made of lime with which walls are smoothed. Regarding these tiny stones reduced to dust, we read in Isaiah 27: "And this is all the fruit, that his sin may be taken away: when he shall have made all the stones of the altar like crushed lime-stones." The Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translated it thus: "When he shall have made all the stones of the altars crushed like fine dust."

**He turned, moved, rolled, or rotated.** <note>Hebrew: גָּלַל (Galal)</note> Genesis 29: "And let us move the stone from the mouth of the well." And Genesis 43 <note>OCR says 24, but the text "roll a false accusation upon us" refers to Genesis 43:18</note>: "That he may roll a false accusation upon us." And Psalm 37: "Reveal your way to the Lord"—meaning "roll" or "move your way toward the Lord." Some explain "reveal" as "open" because of certain authorities where that meaning fits well, but those words are derived from *Galah* <note>גלה - to reveal or uncover</note> as will be shown below. For example, Psalm 119: "Open my eyes," and Numbers 22: "Immediately the Lord opened the eyes of Balaam." Nevertheless, it can also apply to the eyes that they move and turn because of their roundness and rolling motion. Hence *Galili* <note>גְּלִילֵי - cylinders or rings</note> are called rolling wheels, which Jerome <note>The translator of the Latin Vulgate</note> translated from "roundness" as "turned" in Song of Songs 5: "My hands are as if turned [in a lathe]." Others say "golden rings." In another place, it is interpreted as "rings" in Esther 1: "Which were inserted into ivory rings." Others translate it as "spheres."

# BOOK

**And anything round.** Whence גלגל <note>original: *galgal*</note> **Sphere, circle, wheel.** By this name the heaven is called, as in Psalm 77: *The voice of your thunder was in the wheel.* <note>original Latin: "Vox tonitrui tui in rota." Modern translations often render this as "whirlwind," but the author emphasizes the circular root.</note> From this comes the proper name **Galgala** <note>Gilgal</note> in Joshua 10. This word is also sometimes found with a single letter *l*, as in the same chapter of Joshua: *Roll great stones to the mouth of the cave.* <note>original Latin: "voluite saxa ingētia ad os putei."</note> And from "rolling" comes מגלה <note>original: *megillah*</note> **Scroll, small book, letter, writing, or document.** This is because the ancients were accustomed to **roll** their papers, not fold them—a custom that is still seen among people in the East. Hence that passage in Zechariah 5: *And behold, a flying scroll.*

גלל <note>original: *galal*</note> **Chaff or dung.** As in Ezekiel 4: *And you shall cover it with the dung that comes out of a man.* And in Zephaniah 1, used in the plural: *And their bodies like dung.*

גלל <note>original: *gillul*</note> **Idol.** So called because of its stench and abomination, as in Deuteronomy 29: *Abominations and filth, that is, idols.* Or, it is said to come from **shining marble**, like ivory, because that is the material from which idols are manufactured.

גלגלת <note>original: *gulgoleth*</note> **Skull, the bone of the head, Calvary, or simply the head.** As in Exodus 16: *A gomor* <note>a dry measure of about 2 liters</note> *for every head.* We pronounce the location of this word's corrupted form as **Golgotha**, intending to say "the place of the skull." We would read this more correctly as *Golgaltha* in Matthew 27: *And they came to the place called Golgotha.* In Hebrew it is *gulgoleth*, but in Syriac <note>Aramaic</note> it is *gulgaltha*.

גל <note>original: *gal*</note> **A heap of stones.** Genesis 31: *Bring stones; and they took stones and made a heap.* And in the plural גלים <note>original: *gallim*</note> in Hosea 12: *Their altars are like heaps.*

גל <note>original: *gal*</note> **A vortex, a spring, or an eruption of a fountain**, because of the circular motion it makes as if bubbling up in a ring. Song of Solomon 4: *A sealed fountain.* In the plural גלות <note>original: *gulloth*</note> **fountains or vortices**, from the action of turning, circling, and moving. These are translated by Jerome as **irrigation** or **watered places** in Joshua 15 and Judges 1: *So Caleb gave her the upper springs and the lower springs.* <note>original Latin: "irriguum superius et irriguum inferius."</note> Whence it is written in Amos 5: *And judgment shall be revealed like water*, which the Hebrews explain as: it shall go away, it shall move, it shall roll down like water. This comes from the root גלל <note>original: *galal*</note>, as indicated by the *patah* vowel point.

גלי <note>original: *gallê*</note> **Storms, waves, and whirlpools**, named for the circles and globes of water into which they turn—

...as in Jonah chapter 2: "All your billows and your waves have passed over me." <note>original: "Omnes gurgites tui et fluctus tui super me transierūt." This quote refers to the Hebrew root גל (gal), meaning wave or heap.</note>
[Hebrew root: גל or גלה] **Small basin.** A round vessel like a washbasin. Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into Latin</note> translated this as "lamp" in Zechariah chapter 4: "one on the right of the lamp and one on the left."
[Hebrew root: גליל] **Boundary.** A limit, region, end, or border. Our translation <note>the Latin Vulgate</note> follows this, and the Seventy Translators <note>the Septuagint, the ancient Greek version of the Old Testament</note> translated it as **Galilee**. Isaiah chapter 9: "The way of the sea across the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles." Matthew the Evangelist agrees with this, perhaps because the Greeks had already adopted the translation of the Seventy. However, the Hebrew scholars and Symmachus <note>an early translator of the Old Testament into Greek</note> translate it as "boundary" or "border." Jonathan the Chaldean <note>referring to the Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic paraphrase of the Bible</note> explains it as "cities near the nations," which is the same as "the border of the nations." In the plural form in Joshua chapter 13: "All the districts <note>original: "galilęa"</note> of the Philistines," which the Hebrew scholars explain as "all the borders of the Palestinians" or "the total limits of the Philistines." It comes from the word [Hebrew: גלילה - *gelilah*], which Jerome—imitating Aquila <note>a 2nd-century translator known for his literalism</note>—translated as a "mound of sand" or "gravel," as if it were derived from the word for "heap" [Hebrew: גל - *gal*]. Thus in Ezekiel chapter 47: "These waters which go out to the eastern mounds of sand." But in my opinion, Symmachus translated it much better in this passage as "boundary," following the Hebrew interpretation, although others argue it is a proper name of a specific place.
[Hebrew root: גלל] **Grace.** Consideration, because of, or on account of. Genesis chapter 12: "And may my soul live on account of your grace." <note>original: "ob gratiam tui"</note>
[Hebrew root: גלב] **Barber.** A leather-worker or parchment-maker. Ezekiel chapter 5: "Take a sharp sword for shaving hair." They are also called clerks, librarians, scribes, and senators [Hebrew: גלבים - *gallabim*].
[Hebrew root: גלד] **Skin.** As in Job chapter 16: "I have sewn sackcloth over my skin."
[Hebrew root: גלמוד] **Solitary.** Bereft or abandoned. Job chapter 3: "Let that night be solitary."
[Hebrew root: גלע] **He confounded.** Or he mixed. The reflexive form <term>Hithpael<gloss>a Hebrew verb form indicating intensive or reflexive action</gloss></term> is read in Proverbs chapter 17: "He who lets out water is the head of quarrels, and before he suffers slander he abandons judgment." ...translated after the same word in chapter eighteen: *At all times he will be reproachable.* <note>original Latin: "Omni tempore erit exprobrabilis"</note> Indeed, I marvel at this translation, as I do at many others.

**גָּלַשׁ** <note>transliterated: *galash*</note> *To pluck or shear.* In the Song of Songs, chapter four, in place of what we read as "which have ascended from Mount Gilead," <note>Referring to the description of a lover's hair like a flock of goats.</note> the Hebrews explain it as: "your hair is like a flock of goats that have been shorn." From this, a shaved or bald head is called **גָּלוּשׁ** <note>transliterated: *galush*</note>.

**גַּם** <note>transliterated: *gam*</note> *Also, too, and.* Genesis 31: *And he sold us and also ate up our price.* The <term>Hebrew Truth<note>A scholarly term (*Hebraica Veritas*) referring to the original Hebrew text as the most reliable source, contrasted with later translations.</note></term> has: *and he also ate our price.* This word is frequently used in the speech of Pharaoh when, after the death of the firstborn, he sent away the children of Israel, saying in Exodus 12: *Rise up, go out from among my people, both you and the children of Israel.* And further down: *Take also your sheep and herds as you asked, and departing, bless me also.* But the translator everywhere rendered it simply as "and." It signifies "and" specifically when it is repeated multiple times from the beginning of a sentence, such as "both pious and prudent."

**גָּמָא** <note>transliterated: *gama*</note> *To drink quickly or swallow greedily.* Genesis 24: *Give me a little water to drink,* <note>original Latin: "pauxillum aquae mihi ad bibendum praebe"</note> meaning: "make me gulp down or swallow a little water from the jar."

**גֹּמֶא** <note>transliterated: *gome*</note> *Rush, reed, or cane.* Papyrus, from which very light boats are hollowed out. Exodus, chapter two: *She took a basket of reeds.* This is the same thing called **גֶּמִי** <note>transliterated: *gemi*</note> in the common speech of the teachers.

**גֹּמֶד** <note>transliterated: *gomed*</note> *The measure of the palm of a hand,* or a fist. Others explain it as a cubit or an ell. It is first translated in Judges 3: *who made himself a two-edged sword having a hilt in the middle the length of a palm.* The <term>Pygmies<note>A legendary race of tiny people described in classical and medieval literature; the author derives their name from this Hebrew measure of a small hand-span.</note></term> are named from this word because of their tiny stature. Ezekiel 27: *but also the Pygmies who were in your towers.*

**גַּמָּה** <note>transliterated: *gammah*</note> *Against or opposite.* This is used in Habakkuk 1. However, our translation <note>Likely referring to the Latin Vulgate.</note> which we read omitted this word, saying: *their faces are a burning wind,* when it ought to be read: *from opposite their faces.* Hence, the <term>Seventy<note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note></term> interpreted it more correctly: *destruction shall come upon those resisting opposite their faces.* And <term>Jonathan the Chaldean<note>Referring to the Targum of Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary.</note></term> translated it as **מַקְבִּיל** <note>transliterated: *makbil*</note>, that is **נֶגֶד** <note>transliterated: *neged*</note>, which signifies "against." I mention this because there are some who mistakenly think it signifies "aspect," "countenance," or "form."

# FIRST BOOK

**גמל [Gamal] — He repaid, paid in full, recompensed, or returned.**
As in Psalm 116: "Return, my soul, into your rest, because the Lord has dealt well with you." For this passage, the "Hebrew truth" <note>original: "hebraica ueritas"; a term used by scholars like Jerome to refer to the original Hebrew text as opposed to translations</note> has, according to the testimony of Jerome: "because the Lord has repaid you." And in Psalm 119: "Deal bountifully with your servant." From this, they derive the word for "recompense" or "turn," which is **גמול [Gemul]**.

**גמל [Gamal] — He weaned.**
As in Genesis 21: "The boy grew therefore, and was weaned." And in Hosea chapter 1: "And she weaned her who was 'Without Mercy.'" <note>Referring to the symbolic name of the prophet's daughter, Lo-Ruhamah.</note>

**גמל [Gamal] — Camel.**
As in Deuteronomy chapter 14: "The camel, the hare, and the <term>rock-badger</term> <note>original Greek: "χοιρογύλιον" (choirogryllion); a small mammal often identified as a hyrax.</note>."

**גמץ [Gamat] — A pit.**
Ecclesiastes chapter 10: "He who digs a pit shall fall into it." It is also written with the letters <term>vav</term> and a <term>dagesh</term> <note>Hebrew grammatical marks used for vowels and emphasis</note> point.

**גמר [Gamar] — He finished, failed, or was completed.**
As in Psalm 12: "Save me, O Lord, for the holy man has failed."

**גן [Gan] — A garden.**
As in Genesis 2: "Now the Lord God had planted a paradise of pleasure from the beginning." <note>The Latin "a principio" follows the Vulgate translation; modern versions often say "in the east."</note> And in the Song of Solomon chapter 4: "My sister is a garden enclosed." The plural is **גנים [Gannim]**, as in the same book: "A fountain of gardens." It is also found in the feminine gender, both in the singular and the plural. As in Isaiah 1: "Like a garden without water," and a little earlier: "You shall be embarrassed by the gardens you had chosen." And in Song of Solomon chapter 6, it is found with a <term>hireck</term> <note>a Hebrew vowel mark representing the 'ee' sound</note> where it is written as **גנת [Ginat]**: "I went down into the garden of nuts."

**גנן [Ganan] — He protected.**
As in Isaiah 37: "And I will protect this city so that I may save it." In this instance, a <term>dagesh</term> point is placed where the letter <term>nun</term> was removed. <note>A technical note on Hebrew morphology where one letter is absorbed into another, indicated by a dot.</note> For it is read in its full form in chapter 31 of the same book: "protecting and delivering, passing over and saving." There, the "heavy" and "defective" verb <term>yagen</term> [יגן] is also used: "So shall the Lord of hosts protect Jerusalem." From this comes the name **מגן [Magen]**, meaning "protection," "shield," "buckler," or "small shield." Song of Solomon chapter 4: "A thousand shields hang from it." It is declined in both the masculine and feminine forms.

**מגנת [Maginat] — A covering.**
Others translate this as "a fragment" or "a loss"; others as "a shield" or "protection." Lamentations 3: "You will give them a shield of the heart, which is your labor." <note>This refers to a difficult phrase often interpreted as "sorrow of heart" or "a covering/veil over the heart."</note> From this comes the verbal form in Hosea 11: "I will protect you, Israel."

**גנב [Ganav] — He stole, or he took away by stealth.**
Genesis 31: "Why have you stolen my gods?"

**גרם** <note>Hebrew root: G-R-M</note> **Bone.** Proverbs 17: "A sorrowful spirit dries up the bones." From this is derived the term "bony," meaning strong and powerful. Genesis 49: "Issachar is a strong donkey."
**גרם** **A summit or a step of ascent.** This is translated in various ways. 4 Kings 9 <note>In modern Bibles, 2 Kings 9:13</note>: "And each one, taking his cloak, placed it under his feet in the likeness of a tribunal." The Hebrew is read thus: "And each took his garment and placed it under him at the step of ascent." For it signifies the step of the sun on a clock, which we call a *solarium* <note>original: "solarium"; a sundial</note> in Latin. It is a stone raised in a public square inscribed with the marks of the hours, from which a rod extends which we call a <term>gnomon</term> <note>The part of a sundial that casts the shadow</note> in Greek, and a *stilus* in Latin. To that height the men of Gilead promoted their king, Jehu, by laying down their garments upon which he ascended to the sundial stone. On this point, David Kimhi <note>A famous 12th-century Hebrew grammarian and biblical commentator</note> in his commentaries on the four <note>likely referring to the Former Prophets</note> explains the "step of ascent" as the highest step of that stone, following the Chaldean translation <note>Chaldean refers to Aramaic; here specifically the Targum, an Aramaic paraphrase of the Bible</note>. For Jonathan the Chaldean translated it as <gloss>at the step of the clock</gloss> <note>original Aramaic: "על דרג שעיא"</note>—that is, at the step of the sundial or the nail in the wall that demonstrates the linear shadow. Others explain it differently; see the commentaries on this verse in Song of Songs 2: "My dove in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the wall."
**גרם** **He dislocated; he broke.** As in Numbers 24: "And they shall break their bones."
**גרן** **A granary,** but more correctly a **threshing floor.** 2 Kings 24: To whom David said, "That I may buy the threshing floor from you." And 1 Kings 22: "And they plunder the threshing floors." For in the East, they keep their granaries at the threshing floors; therefore, one term is often used for the other.
**גרס** **He overwhelmed; he crushed; he broke; he ground down.** As in Psalm 119, in the *Gimel* section <note>Psalm 119 is an acrostic; this verse begins with the third letter, Gimel</note>: "My soul has desired to long..." where the Hebrew reads: "My soul is **broken** with longing," or "crushed," or rather "overwhelmed by a multitude of desires." The word is used in a heavy sense in Lamentations 3: "He has broken my teeth with gravel." You will find this written not only with the letter *Samekh* [ס], but sometimes with the letter *Sin* [ש]. As in Leviticus 2: "And you shall break it in the manner of coarse meal," which is written with six points <note>referring to vowel or diacritical markings</note> **גרש**. From this comes **מגרשה** <note>Gershah</note>, meaning **meal**—that is, something demolished, pounded, and worn down, much like <term>ador</term> <note>A type of ancient grain, often translated as spelt or emmer</note>.

**G-R-A** <term>גרע|Gara</term> To diminish. As in Deuteronomy 4: "You shall not add to the word, nor shall you take away from it" <note>original: "Non addetis ad uerbum. nec auferetis ex eo"</note>, that is, you shall not diminish it. Its passive form is found in Numbers 9: "Why are we defrauded <note>original: "fraudarur"</note> so that we are not able to offer an offering?" In place of that, it should be read as "Why are we diminished?"—meaning, we are made worse.

**E-G-R-O-P-H** <term>אגרוף|Egroph</term> Fist. Exodus 21: "And if one man strikes another with a stone or with his fist." <note>original: "Et percusserit alter proximum suum lapide uel pugno"</note> This word uses the <term>prothesis|the addition of a letter at the beginning of a word</term> of the letter *Aleph*.

**M-A-G-R-E-P-H-O-T-H** <term>מגרפות|Magrephoth</term> The dung of the stalls. As in Joel 1: "The beasts have rotted in their dung." <note>original: "Computruerunt iumenta in stercore eorū"</note> The <term>Septuagint|The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</term> translation has "in their mangers." Some among the Hebrews translate this as "vessels," suggesting they rot from mold. But <term>Rabbi David Kimhi|A famous 12th-century Hebrew grammarian and scholar</term> says in his commentary on the Twelve <note>referring to the Twelve Minor Prophets of the Bible</note> that this word signifies motes of dust.

**G-R-S-H** <term>גרש|Garash</term> He cast away, expelled, or rejected. Genesis 4: "Behold, you drive me out today from the face of the earth." <note>original: "Ecce eiicis me hodie a facie terrę"</note> And Jonah 2: "And I said, I am cast out from the sight of your eyes."

**G-E-R-E-S-H** <term>גרש|Geresh</term> Maturity, budding, the shoots of fruit-bearing trees, or the outgrowth of fruits. It is named from the "expelling" or pushing out of fruit from the trees from month to month. Thus, Deuteronomy 33: "For the choice fruits <note>original: "pomis"</note> produced by the sun and moon."

**M-I-G-R-A-S-H** <term>מגרש|Migrash</term> Suburb or pasture land. As in Numbers 35: "And the suburbs shall be for the cattle." So also in Ezekiel 48.

**M-I-G-R-A-S-H-A** and **G-E-R-E-S-H** <term>מגרשה et גרש</term> We have spoken about these words above under the entry for the word <term>G-R-S|גרס - Garas, meaning to crush or grind</term>.

**G-A-S-H-A-S-H** <term>גשש|Gashash</term> He felt, touched, or groped. As in Isaiah 59: "We grope for the wall like the blind, and we touch it as if we had no eyes." <note>original: "Palpauimus sicut cęci parietem. & quasi absq; oculis attrectauimus"</note> This is the same as the word *Mashash* <term>משש|to feel or grope</term>.

**G-E-S-H-E-M** <term>גשם|Geshem</term> Rain or a heavy shower. As in Isaiah 55: "As the rain and snow come down from heaven." From this root comes the verb and participle in Jeremiah 14: "Are there any among the idols of the nations that can cause rain?" The Syrians <note>referring to speakers of Aramaic/Syriac</note> also use this same word, and the Hebrew masters use it alongside them to mean "body," as <term>Rabbi Moses|Moses Maimonides, the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher</term>...

# BOOK

The Egyptian <note>A reference to the Jewish philosopher Moses Maimonides, often called "Moses the Egyptian" in the Renaissance</note> in the first book of the *Guide for the Perplexed*, chapter 49, when treating the subject of angels, says that they are not **geshamim** <note>Hebrew: *geshamim*</note>, that is, bodies. He mostly uses that word within the category of continuous quantity; hence they say that a **geshem** <note>Hebrew: *geshem*</note> is a thing which possesses length, width, and depth. We read this in the *Art of Logic* by the wise philosopher **Abenrusd** <note>Ibn Rushd, known in the West as Averroes</note>, who among us—due to an ignorance of Greek letters—is called **Averroes**. This happened because of a certain similarity between the characters *nu* and *rho*, and the entanglement of *sigma* with *tau*. For it is written in Greek as **Abenrois** <note>original: αβενροις</note>, meaning Abenrust, which our ancestors, being unskilled in languages, read as **Averroys**, just as they are mistaken in many other matters. I myself possess a specific work on logic by the same philosopher, written in Hebrew letters.

**Gath** <note>Hebrew: *Gat*</note>: A hand-mill; a winepress. **Judges 6**: "And when Gideon his son was threshing and cleaning the grain in the winepress." And in **Joel 3**: "Come and go down, for the winepress is full." And in the plural, **Gattot** <note>Hebrew: *Gattot*</note>, **Nehemiah 13**: "In those days I saw in Judah people treading winepresses on the Sabbath." The inscription of the eighth Psalm alludes to this: "To the victory upon the **Gittith**" <note>The term *Gittith* likely refers to a musical instrument or a melody originating from the city of Gath</note>. For the eminent teachers of the Hebrews say that David composed this psalm when he was among the winepresses of the Philistines—although **Aben Ezra** <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a prominent medieval Sephardic scholar</note> disagrees with this view.

**Galah** <note>Hebrew: *Galah*</note>: He migrated; he departed; he exulted. Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible</note> translated it as "it was transferred." **1 Kings 4** <note>Today cited as 1 Samuel 4:21</note>: "The glory of the Lord was transferred from Israel." Its transitive form is used in **1 Chronicles 9**: "And they were transferred into Babylon." And in **Isaiah 5**: "Therefore my people were led away captive." Thus **Galah** can mean he wandered or exulted, as in **Amos 5**: "Because Gilgal shall be led away captive." The Hebrews explain this as "by expelling, he shall be repelled." Jerome interpreted this as "he took away" in **Joshua 5**: "Today I have taken away the reproach of Egypt from you"—that is, "I have made it migrate." From this, **Galut** <note>Hebrew: *Galut*</note> is translated as "migration" or "exile" in the last part of **Obadiah**: "And the migration of this host of the children of Israel," meaning their expulsion.

**Galah**: He opened; he revealed; he uncovered; he laid bare. **Amos 3**: "Because he does not do..." <note>The text cuts off here; the full verse is "Surely the Lord God does nothing, unless He reveals His secret to His servants the prophets"</note>

**m** Breast, teat. Song of Songs 1: "For your **breasts** are better than wine." <note>original Latin: "quia meliora sunt ubera tua uino"</note>

**דאב** He panted, grieved, languished, or was weakened. Psalm 88: "My eyes **languished** because of poverty." **דבב** He denounced, stirred up a report, defamed, spread rumors, or caused to speak. Song of Songs 7: where our translation <note>the Latin Vulgate</note> has, "For his lips and teeth to **ruminate**," the *Hebrew Truth* reads: "making the ancient things **speak**." Perhaps the scribe erred, writing "to ruminate" (*ruminandum*) instead of "to spread rumors" (*rumigerandum*), that is, to make a report. This can be used in both a just and an unjust sense. For at first, Joseph truly reported his brothers in Genesis 37: "And he accused his brothers before his father of a most wicked crime," where the *Hebrew Truth* reads: "And Joseph made their **bad report** come to their father." Secondly, however, those who were with Caleb falsely defamed the land of Canaan in Numbers 13: "And they disparaged the land they had seen," where the Hebrew scripture reads: "They caused an **infamy** of the land they had seen to go out." Thus a report, whether true or false, is called **דבה**, which I find the Seventy <note>the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> sometimes translated as *psogon* <note>original Greek: "blame" or "reproach"</note>, that is—

**Reproach.** <note>Latin: vituperium</note> Psalm 31: *For I have heard the reproach of many.* Jerome, in his psalter translated "from the Hebrew truth," <note>Jerome’s phrase for the original Hebrew text as opposed to the Greek Septuagint</note> interprets it as "reproach."
דבא <note>Hebrew root: D-B-A</note> **Old Age.** According to our translation <note>the Latin Vulgate</note> in Deuteronomy 33: *Iron and brass are your shoes; as the days of your youth, so also your old age.* The Hebrews read it this way: *And as your days, so is your strength.* Onkelos the Chaldean <note>referring to Targum Onkelos, an ancient Aramaic translation of the Torah</note> translated it thus: *Strong as iron and brass, and as the days of your youth is your power.* For this reason, the Hebrews explain this blessing as: *You shall be strong and robust in the days of your old age, just as in the days of your youth.*

דבלה <note>Hebrew root: D-B-L-H</note> **Dried Fig**—that is, a cake of figs. As in Isaiah 38: *And Isaiah commanded that they should take a mass of figs.* <note>Reference to the poultice used to heal King Hezekiah</note>

דבק <note>Hebrew root: D-B-Q</note> **He Adhered.** As in Genesis 2: *For which reason a man shall leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave to his wife.* It is also found ending with the vowel *zere* <note>a Hebrew vowel mark</note>, as in 2 Kings 3: *Nevertheless, he clung to the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin.* It is also used as a transitive verb <note>an action performed on an object</note> in Ezekiel 29: *And I will fasten the fish of your rivers to your scales,* in the sense of "I will make them adhere." It sometimes signifies "to pursue," as in Jeremiah 42: *And the famine for which you are anxious shall cleave to you,* that is, it shall pursue or overtake you.

דבר <note>Hebrew root: D-B-R</note> **Thing.** As in 2 Kings 5: *And if the prophet had told you a great thing.* It also signifies **Word**, as in Esther 7: *The word had not yet gone out of the king's mouth.* From this comes the active form which means "to speak," as in Amos 3: *Hear the word that the Lord has spoken.* And the phrases <note>Hebrew: 'al dibrat</note> or <note>Hebrew: 'al dabar</note> are used in place of "because of," "for the sake of," "concerning," or "about" something. As in Ecclesiastes 3: *I said in my heart concerning the sons of men.* It is also translated as "according to the order," as in Psalm 110: *According to the order of Melchizedek.* And in Exodus 8, regarding the matter <note>literally "response"</note> of the frogs. A "circuit of words" <note>an idiom for a formal accusation</note> refers to a criminal investigation, as in Deuteronomy 22: *He lays a very bad name upon her,* that is, the disgrace of a criminal inquiry.

דבר <note>Hebrew root: D-B-R</note> **Plague.** Pestilence or contagion. As in Exodus 5: *Lest perhaps plague or sword should fall upon us.* From this is derived the transitive verb which means "to kill," as in Psalm 18: *And you subdue the peoples under me,* which the Hebrews explain as: *And you kill or destroy the peoples under me.*

מדבר <note>Hebrew root: M-D-B-R</note> **Desert.** Solitude or wasteland. As in Exodus 19: *On this day they came into the wilderness of Sinai.*

**דָּבָר** <note>Transliteration: Davar</note> Instinct, inclination, guidance, custom, or manner. Genesis 31:18: *“And he took all his livestock and his flocks,”* where in place of the Hebrew word **מִקְנֶה** <note>Miqneh: livestock/property</note>, <term>Onkelos</term> <note>The famous 2nd-century translator of the Torah into Aramaic</note> uses **דָּבָר**. From this, one may recognize the specific property of the term, from which some believe the preceding name for the "desert" or "wilderness" <note>Hebrew: Midbar</note> originated, because cattle are led there for the sake of grazing.

**דֹּבְרוֹת** <note>Transliteration: Dovrot</note> Rafts. As in 1 Kings 5:9: *“And I will prepare them into rafts.”*

**דְּבוֹרָה** <note>Transliteration: Devorah</note> A bee. As in Isaiah 7:18: *“And for the bee which is in the land of Assyria.”* And in the masculine plural, as in Judges 14:8: *“And behold, a swarm of bees in the mouth of the lion.”*

**דְּבִיר** <note>Transliteration: Devir</note> An <term>Adytum</term> <note>A Latin term for the innermost, most sacred part of a temple</note>; that is, the more secret place of the temple from which oracles are brought forth. It is also taken to mean the "oracle" itself. As in 1 Kings 6:19: *“The oracle in the midst of the house,”* and a little earlier: *“around the circuit of the temple and the oracle.”*

**דְּבַשׁ** <note>Transliteration: Devash</note> Honey. As in Exodus 3:8: *“To a land flowing with milk and honey.”*

**דַּבֶּשֶׁת** <note>Transliteration: Dabbeshet</note> The hump of camels, upon which one sits as if in a saddle. Isaiah 30:6: *“And upon the hump of camels, their treasures.”*

**דָּגָה** <note>Transliteration: Dagah (as a verb)</note> To be multiplied, or to grow. Genesis 48:16: *“And let them grow into a multitude upon the earth.”*

**דָּגָה** <note>Transliteration: Dagah (as a noun)</note> A fish. As in Isaiah 50:2: *“Their fish will rot for lack of water.”* The monosyllabic masculine form **דָּג** <note>Transliteration: Dag</note> also signifies a fish. Jeremiah 16:16: *“Behold, I will send many fishermen, says the Lord, and they shall fish them.”*

**דֶּגֶל** <note>Transliteration: Degel</note> A sign of an army, a banner, or any insignia. THE FIRST [SECTION]

And in the name of our God we shall be magnified <note>original Latin: *magnificabimur*</note>. For so the Greek translation <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek version of the Old Testament</note> has it. But it erred in spelling, thinking the word itself was derived from *gadol* <note>Hebrew for "great"</note>, when it actually arises from *dagal* <note>Hebrew for "to raise a banner"</note>. Thus Jerome, in his Psalter based on the Hebrew Truth <note>Jerome’s *Hebraica Veritas* refers to his translation of the Old Testament directly from Hebrew into Latin, rather than from the Greek</note>, attempted to translate it more correctly, saying: "And in the name of our God we shall lead the dances." I would think it might be more properly said: "In the name of our God we shall be distinguished and notable, or noble."

**Grain.** <note>Hebrew: *Dagan*</note> As in 2 Chronicles 32: "Storehouses also for grain, wine, and oil."

**Brooded or cherished.** <note>Hebrew: *Dagar*</note> As birds are accustomed to sit upon eggs. Jeremiah 17: "The partridge broods, though she did not hatch them."

**He went forward.** <note>Hebrew: *Dadah*</note> He moved a little and gently; likewise, he walked or progressed with a soft step. Jerome translated this in various ways. For in Isaiah 38, he took it to mean "reflection": "I will reflect upon all my years to you in the bitterness of my soul." That is, according to the Hebrews: "I will cause to progress" or "I will move all my years toward bitterness." For it is transitive to the third degree; hence the letter *Daleth* is marked with a *Dagesh* point <note>A grammatical dot in a Hebrew letter indicating it is doubled</note> due to the absence of the letter *Tav*. The Seventy <note>The translators of the Septuagint</note> translated it into Greek as we read "wonderful" in Psalm 41: "In the place of the wonderful tabernacle." But I believe that the similarity of the letters *Resh* and *Daleth* caused this variation, as often happens elsewhere. For Jerome, in his Psalter from the Hebrew Truth, interprets it differently: "I will be silent even unto the house of God." The Jews explain it as "I will walk with them" or "I will make them proceed even unto the house of God." And in Isaiah 10: "Madmenah has moved away." Moreover, it has much in common with [Hebrew characters] <note>likely *nadad*</note>, that is, "he moved." Isaiah 10: "And there was none that moved a wing."

**Gold.** <note>Hebrew: *Dahab*</note> Through the relationship of the letter *Daleth* with *Zayin*, it is as if it were *Zahab* <note>The standard Hebrew word for gold</note>; for in the Chaldean language <note>Aramaic</note>, gold is called *Dehab*. See Onkelos <note>The author of the Targum Onkelos, an influential Aramaic translation of the Torah</note> on Genesis 2: "where gold is born, and the gold of that land is the best." Furthermore, from this word is derived the term <term>dahevah</term> <note>meaning tributary gold</note>, "tributary gold," by which we acknowledge lordship. According to the translation we read in Isaiah 14: "How has the oppressor ceased? How has the tribute rested?"

**דודאי** <note>original: *duda'im*</note> **Mandrake flowers.** As in Song of Songs 7: "The mandrakes gave out a scent." And Genesis 30: "He found mandrakes which he gave to his mother Leah," and later, "unless you also take my son's mandrakes."

**דוה** <note>original: *davah*</note> **Suffering, aching, or mourning.** As in Lamentations 1: "Spent with sorrow all day long." It is especially used regarding one suffering a "flow" <note>Referring to a discharge of blood</note>, like **דוי** <note>original: *davuy*</note> as in Leviticus 15: "This is the law of her who suffers a flow of blood," etc., "and who is separated during her menstrual times." Sometimes the letter *he* [ה] is changed to *yod* [י], as in Lamentations 1: "And my mourning heart." From this comes the nouns for pain, sorrow, suffering, and distress, as in Job 6: "Now they are my food out of distress." Sometimes it takes a *mem* [מ] at the beginning, as **מדוי** <note>original: *madvey*</note>, meaning infirmity or suffering, as in Deuteronomy 7: "The Lord will take away from you every languor and the infirmities of Egypt." It also signifies **מדוי** as garments, as in 2 Kings 10: "And he cut their garments in the middle." We will see this further under the word *mad*.

**דוח** <note>original: *dachah*</note> **Cast out, pushed, overturned, supplanted, or thrust down.** As in Psalm 35, where instead of the reading "and the angel of the Lord squeezing them," Jerome more correctly translated in his psalter from the <term>Hebrew Truth<note>The *Hebraica Veritas* refers to Saint Jerome's translation of the Old Testament directly from Hebrew sources rather than the Greek Septuagint.</note></term>: "And let the angel of the Lord drive them away." And Psalm 118: "I was pushed and overturned so that I might fall." Jerome puts it thus: "I was driven by a push so that I might fall." And Psalm 140: "Who thought to supplant my steps." And Psalm 147, where we read: "he will gather the dispersed of Israel," Jerome translated better from the Hebrew truth: "He will gather the outcasts of Israel." Likewise, with the change of the letter *vav* [ו] into *yod* [י], **דוח** <note>original: *duach* / *diach*</note> means **Washed**, as in Isaiah 4: "And he shall have washed the blood of Jerusalem from the midst of it."

**דוך** <note>original: *duch*</note> **Ground, shook, or shattered.** From this comes **מדוכה** <note>original: *meduchah*</note>, a mortar. Numbers 11: "He broke it with a mill or ground it in a mortar."

**דום** <note>original: *dum*</note> **Was quiet or silent.** As in Leviticus 10: "Hearing which, Aaron was silent." From this comes **דומה** <note>original: *dumah*</note>: **A cavern, a grave, or the underworld.** As in Psalm 94: "My soul would have almost dwelt in the underworld." This is perhaps derived from the word for silence, as Virgil says in the sixth book of the *Aeneid*: "Ye gods who rule the spirits, and silent shades, and Chaos and Phlegethon, places silent in the vast night." Likewise in Jeremiah 47: "Rest and be silent."

# BOOK

¶ **דון** (*Dun*) — **He strove, disputed, litigated, contended in judgment, or judged.** As in Genesis 6: where we read, "My spirit shall not remain in man forever," the Hebrew truth <note>original: "hebraica veritas" — a common Renaissance term for the original Hebrew text of the Bible, as opposed to the Latin Vulgate translation.</note>—according to Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the most influential medieval Jewish commentator.</note> and Lyra <note>Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349), a Franciscan whose literal-sense commentaries were highly respected by both Catholics and later Reformers.</note>—holds that it says "my spirit shall not **dispute** <note>original: "disceptabit"</note> forever." This can be understood from the Aramaic <note>original: "chaldaica" — referring to the Targum, the Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> explanation: "The corrupt generation shall not be raised up to contend before me forever."
But Rabbi Judah <note>Likely Judah ben David Hayyuj, a pioneer of scientific Hebrew grammar around the year 1000.</note> thinks this very word is derived from **נדן** (*Nadan*) in this passage, which means a **sheath**. For example, in 1 Chronicles 21: "The Lord commanded the angel, and he returned his sword into its **sheath**." This would be an instance of <term>apheresis|the grammatical loss of one or more sounds or letters from the beginning of a word</term>, as if the Lord were saying, "My spirit shall not be sheathed <note>i.e., contained or housed</note> in man." Paul of Burgos <note>original: "Burgensis" (c. 1351–1435), a Jewish convert who became a Bishop; his "Additions" to Nicholas of Lyra’s work were standard scholarly reading.</note> follows this view in his additions, even though a certain **bold little brother** <note>original: "frater audaculus" — a disparaging reference to a contemporary monk or friar who had criticized the author’s humanist scholarship.</note>—who understands neither Hebrew nor Greek, as is often the case—reproaches this explanation quite rashly. However, I am not arguing about the meaning as a theologian, but about the words as a grammarian.
Likewise, its derivatives signify contention and a kind of judicial arguing. As in 2 Samuel 19: "And all the people **were contending** across all the tribes of Israel," that is, they were arguing through certain contentious means. Jonathan the Aramaic translator <note>Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation of the Prophets.</note> seems to prove this when he explains "he contended" as "he clarified" or "he justified." From this, by <term>catasyncope|the shortening of a word by removing a letter from the middle</term>, we get **Dan**, the son of Jacob and the handmaid Bilhah, after whom one of the twelve tribes is named. Genesis 30: "The Lord has **judged** me," etc., and therefore he called his name Dan. And in Genesis 49: "Dan shall **judge** his people." And according to daily custom, by changing the letter *vav* into a *yod*, we get **דיין** (*Dayyan*), which means a **judge**. As in Psalm 68: "Father of orphans and **judge** of widows," from the verb **דון** (*Dun*), that is, "he judged." As in Psalm 72: "He shall judge your people in justice." Similarly in Ecclesiastes 6: "And he cannot contend in judgment against one stronger than himself." From this comes:

¶ **מדון** (*Madon*) — **Contention, lawsuit, or strife.** As in Proverbs 15: "A wrathful man provokes **strife**." Also from the same book, chapter 16: "A perverse man stirs up **lawsuits**." And chapter 21: "than with a **litigious** woman." Also in the same: "than with a **quarrelsome** woman," that is, one full of lawsuits or strife.

¶ **מדינה** (*Medinah*) — **Province or governorship.** As in Esther 1: "Over 127 **provinces**." It is named this way from the power of judging, because a governor <note>original: "praeses"</note> is a judge of judges.

¶ **דין** (*Din*) — **Rigor or judgment.** A noun derived from the verb above. As in Job 35.

# FIRST BOOK

Regarding the passage we read: *Judge before him and wait for him.* <note>Job 35:14</note> Many of the Hebrews interpret this as "Judgment before him," or "vengeance," or "rigor." This word is frequently used in this sense among the Hebrew masters, especially the Cabalists <note>Followers of Kabbalah, a Jewish mystical tradition that explores the hidden meanings of the Torah.</note>. From this comes the teaching regarding the angels' places of vengeance and mercy, as can be seen in the scholarly notes concerning the *Tree of the Ten Numerations* <term>Tree of the Ten Numerations: Also known as the Sephirot, these represent the ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah through which the Divine is revealed.</term>. From this source, the illustrious Giovanni Pico della Mirandola <note>A famous Italian Renaissance philosopher (1463–1494) known for his "900 Theses" and his interest in combining Kabbalah with Christian philosophy.</note>, the most noble philosopher of our age, translated the properties of clemency and judgment in his *Cabalistic Conclusions*. Jerome <note>The 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> also translated this term as "the cause," specifically the case being argued in a trial, as in Job 36: *Your cause has been judged like that of the wicked,* taking "cause" and "judgment" together. For this, the Hebrews read: *You have completed the judgment of the wicked,* etc.

**דוש (Dush) — He rejoiced.** As in Job 41, regarding the passage we read: *And want precedes his face.* The Hebrews interpret this as: *And sorrow shall rejoice before him,* or *pain shall dance before him.* Truly, I do not wonder at the translation as much as I do at our commentator Nicholas of Lyra <note>A 14th-century Franciscan whose literal commentaries on the Bible were highly influential.</note>, who almost always passes over these points superficially—perhaps because he deferred so much honor to the holy doctors of the past. But I praise the sentiment of Aristotle: *Plato is my friend, but truth is a greater friend.* <note>original: "Amicus Plato maior amica ueritas." A famous proverb suggesting that objective truth must come before personal loyalty.</note>

**דור (Dur) — He endured; he dwelt; he inhabited.** As in Psalm 84: *...than to dwell in the tents of sinners.* For the Chaldean <term>Chaldean: In this context, it refers to the Aramaic language used in the Targums (ancient Jewish translations and paraphrases of the Bible).</term> exposition translates this word as "to inhabit."

**דור (Dur) — A heap.** Ezekiel 24: *Also arrange a heap of bones under it.* From this comes **מדורה** (*medurah*), that is, a funeral pyre or a bonfire, as in the same chapter: *Woe to the bloody city, for which I will make a great pyre.*

**דור (Dor) — An age; duration; a generation.** As in Ecclesiastes 1: *A generation passes away, and a generation comes.* It is declined in the plural in both the masculine and feminine gender. It is perhaps derived from the first verb mentioned above, suggesting that the time a person inhabits or endures in this world constitutes their "generation" or "age."

**דוש (Dush) — He threshed.** Micah 4: *Arise and thresh, daughter of Zion.* And Isaiah 25: *And Moab shall be threshed under him as straw is threshed in a wagon.* From this comes:

**דיש (Dayish) — Threshing.** Leviticus 26: *The threshing shall reach unto the vintage.*

**דישון (Dishon) — Pygarg.** <note>A white-rumped antelope or mountain goat mentioned in the Bible.</note> An animal mentioned in Deuteronomy 14: *The pygarg, the oryx.* Others call it a "unicorn," because Onkelos the Chaldean <note>A famous 2nd-century convert who authored the leading Aramaic translation of the Torah.</note> translated it as **רימא** (*re'ema*).

# THE FIRST

He has crushed my life to the earth. <note>original: *Confregit in terra uitam meā*</note> That is, he wore it down. And Psalm 34: "And he will save the humble in spirit." Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> says more accurately: "And he will save those crushed in spirit." And sometimes a *vau* <note>the Hebrew letter ו</note> is found placed in the stead of an *aleph* <note>the Hebrew letter א</note>.

**דכא** [Daka] Crushed, shattered, humbled. As in Psalm 51: "A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise." And in the same: "And the humbled bones shall rejoice." It signifies the same thing as the word above.

**דך** [Dakh] Destitute, helpless, poor. Psalm 9: "And the Lord became a refuge for the poor." Its synonyms are **רש** [Rash], **עני** [Ani], **אביון** [Evyon], **דל** [Dal], and **מסכן** [Misken]. <note>These are various Hebrew terms for poverty, ranging from 'impoverished' to 'socially oppressed'.</note>

**דוכיפת** [Dukhiphat] A wild cock, or according to our translation <note>referring to the Latin Vulgate</note>, a hoopoe. As in Leviticus 11: "The hoopoe also, and the bat."

**דלל** [Dalal] Exhausted, thinned out, dried up. Isaiah 19: "The streams of the rivers shall be thinned and dried up."

**דל** [Dal] Miserable, poor, helpless, as above. And Leviticus 14: "But if he is poor and his hand cannot find what was mentioned." It is declined in the masculine and feminine with added endings. From this comes **דלות** [Dalut], a collective noun meaning "poverty," just as *iuuentus* <note>Latin for 'youth' or 'the youth' collectively</note> is used among the Latins. As in the last chapter of 2 Kings: "And of the poor of the land he left the vinedressers and husbandmen." Where in Hebrew it is placed collectively: "and of the poverty of the land," that is, of the assembly of the poor.

**דלית** [Dalyat] Locks of hair, tresses. As in Song of Songs 7: "And the hair of your head is like the king's purple."

**דלג** [Dalag] Leapt over, danced. Song of Songs 2: "Behold, he comes leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills." And Isaiah 35: "Then the lame man shall leap like a deer."

**דלה** [Dalah] Drew water. Exodus 2: "Moreover, he also drew water with us." And a little before: "Who had come to draw water."

**דלי** [Dli] A bucket. As in Isaiah 40: "Behold, the nations are like a drop in a bucket."

**דלף** [Dalaf] Raised up, lifted. Isaiah 38: "My eyes have grown thin." For which the Hebrews explain: "My eyes were raised up," according to David Kimhi <note>A famous 12th-century Medieval Jewish rabbi and grammarian known as Radak.</note> in his commentary.

# FIRST

**Genesis 19.** "Lot went out to them, closing the door behind him." The word for door <term>Delet <note>Hebrew: דלת</note></term> is declined in the plural with both masculine and feminine endings. It is also found in a shortened form in **Psalm 141**: "Set a door of restraint over my lips," which Saint Jerome translated as: "Keep the poverty of my lips." <note>The Hebrew root for "door" (delet) is visually similar to the word for "poor" (dal), leading to different interpretive traditions in early Latin translations.</note>

**Dam** <note>Hebrew: דם</note> Blood. As in **Genesis 9**: "Whoever sheds human blood, his blood shall be shed." According to the Hebrew tradition, it is used in the plural in **Genesis 4**; where our common version says, "The voice of your brother's blood cries out to me," they read it as: "The voice of your brother's *bloods* cry out to me" in the plural number. However, Onkelos the Chaldean <note>Onkelos was a famous convert and scholar who produced an influential Aramaic translation (Targum) of the Torah in the 2nd century.</note> translated it in the singular, just as we do. It is commonly translated as singular among us in places where the Hebrew uses the plural, such as **Zechariah 9**: "And I will take away his blood from his mouth." This plural form is used unless it signifies a capital crime or the penalty of death, as in **Psalm 51**: "Deliver me from bloods," meaning from the punishment of blood <note>original: "a poena sanguinis"</note>. It is also used in the singular, which Jerome interpreted as "guilt" in **Numbers 35**: "He who kills him shall be without guilt." Likewise, it appears in the plural in **Deuteronomy 19**: "Lest you be guilty of blood," which reads word-for-word in Hebrew: "and bloods shall be upon you," meaning the final punishment or the penalty of blood. **Dam** also signifies red wine, as in **Deuteronomy 32**: "And they drank the purest blood of the grape."

**Damam** <note>Hebrew: דמם</note> He rested, was silent, or waited. **Lamentations 3**: "It is good to wait in silence for the salvation of the Lord." And **Psalm 107**: "He stilled the storm into a breeze," which Jerome translated as: "He will set the whirlwind into tranquility," meaning silence or rest. Similarly in **Joshua 10**, where our version says: "Sun, do not move against Gibeon," the Hebrews read: "Sun, be still (or be silent, or wait) against Gibeon." Then it follows: "And it stood," that is, it rested. From this comes what we read in **Psalm 62**: "Shall not my soul be subject to God?" Jerome, in his translation from the "Hebraic Truth" <note>Jerome’s *Hebraica Veritas* refers to his pioneering work translating the Bible directly from the original Hebrew rather than the Greek Septuagint.</note>, rendered it: "Nevertheless, my soul is silent toward God," and further down: "Nevertheless, be subject to God, my soul," or more accurately according to Jerome: "Nevertheless, be silent toward God, my soul."

**Damah** <note>Hebrew: דמה</note> He likened, or was made similar. As in **Psalm 144**: "Man is made like a vanity." And **Ezekiel 31**: "To whom are you made similar in your greatness?" From this comes **Demut** <note>Hebrew: דמות</note>, meaning likeness. **Genesis 1**: "Let us make man in our image..."

# **BOOK**

...our image, according to our likeness. The specific property of this word Moses the Egyptian <note>The famous Jewish philosopher Moses Maimonides (1135–1204)</note> explained in the first book of the *Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: "libro perplexorum"</note>. It also signifies: he cut off, he cast out, he demolished, he devastated, he restrained, he consumed, he finished. 

In Hosea 10: "Samaria made its king pass away," where the translation of the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> is better, namely: "Samaria cast out its king." And in the eleventh chapter of the same book, where we read: "As in the morning the king passed, he passed away," the Seventy have: "In the morning the king was cast out." 

Which many indeed translate differently in many places. As in Hosea 4: "In the night I made your mother silent," <note>original: "Nocte tacere feci matrem tuam"</note> for which the Seventy have: "I made your mother like the night." The Hebrews <note>Referring here to Jewish grammarians or the Hebrew text tradition</note> explain it as: "I restrained your congregation." 

Thus in Zephaniah 1: "All the people of Canaan have become silent." The Seventy: "All the people of Canaan have been likened." The Hebrews explain it as: "He was cut off, destroyed, and devastated," as David Kimhi <note>Rabbi David Kimhi (c. 1160–1235), also known as Radak, a preeminent medieval Hebrew grammarian and commentator</note> says in his commentaries on the Twelve <note>The Twelve Minor Prophets of the Old Testament</note>.

->THE FIRST<-

**דונג** Wax. As in Micah 1[:4]: "Like wax before the face of fire." <note>original Latin: *Sicut cera a facie ignis*</note>

**דעך** Crushed, extinguished, or consumed. Proverbs 20[:20]: "Whoever curses his father and mother, his lamp will be extinguished in the midst of darkness." And Isaiah 43[:17]: "They are crushed; they are extinguished like a wick." <note>original Latin: *quasi linum*, referring to the flax used in a lamp wick</note> And regarding what is found in Psalm 118[:12]: "They surrounded me like bees; they blazed like fire among thorns." Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible</note> translated this as: "They were extinguished like a fire of thorns." The Hebrews read: "they are consumed and scattered."

**דפי** Reproach, fault, slander, or offense. As in Psalm 50[:20]: "And against your mother's son you set a scandal." Jerome translated this as "reproach." <note>original Latin: *opprobrium*</note>

**דפק** He knocked. Song of Songs 5[:2]: "The voice of my beloved knocking." And Genesis 33[:13]: "If I drive them too hard in walking, they will die in one day." More accurately: "And if they are beaten [driven] for one day, they will die."

**דקק** He thinned, refined, broke into pieces, or crushed. As in Exodus 32[:20]: "He burned it and ground it down." And Isaiah 29[:5]: "And it shall be like fine dust." And Psalm 18[:42]: "I will destroy them like the mud of the streets." Jerome: "I will cast them out." The Hebrews [translate it as]: "I will make them thin" or "I will crush them." Some Hebrews, by an error of the similarity between the letters *vav* and *resh* <note>In the Hebrew alphabet, ו (vav) and ר (resh) look very similar and are often confused by scribes</note>, say: "I will empty them out."

**דק** Having a thin film over the pupil of the eye, which Jerome translated as "bleary-eyed." <note>original Latin: *lippus*</note> Leviticus 21[:20]: "If he be hunchbacked or bleary-eyed."

**דוק** Skin, membrane, hide, or a spider's web. Jerome translated this as "nothing." Isaiah 40[:22]: "Who stretches out the heavens like nothing." <term>Lyra</term> <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a famous medieval Bible scholar</note> explains it as a "web." The Hebrews [explain it as] a "curtain" or "skins."

**דק** Tiny, thin, or dust, on account of its refinement. As in Isaiah 40[:15]: "Behold, the islands are like tiny dust."

**דיק** A war engine, which they call a <term>bombard</term> <note>an early type of cannon</note>, because it crushes and breaks down walls. Jerome translated this as "fortification." Ezekiel 26[:8]: "And he shall surround you with fortifications."

**דקר** He pierced through, transfixed, or stabbed. Zechariah 12[:10]: "And they shall look upon me whom they have pierced." And Numbers 25[:8]: "And he pierced both of them together, namely the man and the woman."

**דר** A precious stone. As in Esther 1[:6]: "Upon a pavement of emerald..."

...and paved with stone. They say it shines like the midday sun, from which it takes its name. For *Darom* <term>דרום: South or Midday</term> signifies the south.

**Freedom** <term>דרור: Deror</term>. Release. Leviticus 25: "And you shall proclaim a release to all the inhabitants of your land." <note>Leviticus 25:10. This refers to the Jubilee year when debts were forgiven and slaves freed.</note> From this, that which is free is called *Deror*. As in Exodus 30: "Take for yourself the primary spices of choice myrrh," <note>Exodus 30:23</note> that is, myrrh that flows freely and of its own accord, rather than from a cut made in the bark. <note>original: "non demum inciso cortice"</note> Because of this, a certain bird is called *Deror* <term>דרור: Swallow</term>, which some call a swallow, because it nests freely among humans even in their houses without any fear. This is the opinion of Paul of Burgos in his additions to Psalm 84. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> translates this as "trygona," meaning a turtledove; but Jerome <note>The 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate.</note> translates it simply as "bird," using the general category for the specific species.

**Abhorrence** <term>דראון: Diraon</term>. Disgrace. Daniel 12: "Others to everlasting shame and contempt." <note>Daniel 12:2</note> Some, deceived by the spelling, translated this as "that they may see forever."

Song of Songs 2: "In the hollows of the wall." <note>Song of Songs 2:14</note> And in Ezekiel 38 he translated it as "hedges": "The hedges and every wall shall fall." <note>Ezekiel 38:20</note> But later in his commentaries, correcting himself, he explains it as "fortifications," which resonates more correctly with the Hebrew idiom. Lyra <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a prominent medieval commentator.</note> says "fortresses," which Jonathan the Chaldean <note>Refers to the Targum, the Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Bible.</note> called *magdalaia* <note>original: "magdalaia," meaning towers.</note>. However, according to Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the famous 11th-century French rabbi.</note>, these are upright stones that overhang as if they appear ready to fall. Onkelos the Chaldean <note>The author of the standard Aramaic translation of the Torah.</note> names steps as *dragin* in Exodus 20: "You shall not go up by steps." <note>Exodus 20:26</note>

**Thistle** <term>דרדר: Dardar</term>. Briar, thorn, or thistle. Genesis 3: "Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you." <note>Genesis 3:18; part of the curse following the Fall of Man.</note>

**Treading** <term>דרך: Darakh</term> <note>The OCR text reads דדך, a printer's error for דרך.</note>. He stepped, went, trod, or walked. It also signifies "directed," that is, he made one walk correctly, as in Psalm 25: "He directed..."
