->FIRST<-

[...they shall not sound] in their throat <note>The text begins mid-sentence, referring to Psalm 115:7 regarding the silence of idols</note>. This was not correctly translated by the "Seventy" <note>The Septuagint, the influential Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> who rendered it in Greek as φωνήσουσιν <note>original: "phonisusin" — they shall cry out</note>. According to the properties of the Greek language, it should have said "they will not cry out," "speak," or "make melody." However, Jerome translates more suitably from the "Hebrew Truth" <note>Jerome’s term for the original Hebrew text</note> as: *They shall not make a sound in their throat.* We can explain this as "they shall not hold discourse." From this, the Hebrews encompass logic, rhetoric, and poetics under a single technical term, **Higgayon** (הגיון), which is, as Cicero says in his *Topics*, "the art of discourse" or even "the shaping of melodies or sounds." Jerome translated this as "meditation" in Psalm 19: *And let the meditation of my heart be always in your sight.* Also in Isaiah 59: *We have spoken words of lies from the heart.* And in the same chapter: *We shall groan like moaning doves*; for the voice of doves and turtledoves is called a "groan." It is also found with a doubled letter *gimel* in Psalm 39: *In my meditation a fire shall break out.*

**הגה** [Hagah] He took away; he removed. As in Isaiah 27, where we read: *He meditated in his harsh spirit in the day of heat,* the learned masters of the Hebrews read it as: *He removed the fruit in his harsh wind during the days of the east wind.* From this comes that passage in Proverbs 25: *Take away the dross from the silver* and *Take away the wicked from the presence of the king.*

**הגינה** [Haginah] Direct; prepared. According to Rabbi Jonah <note>Jonah ibn Janah, a famous 11th-century Hebrew grammarian</note>. As in Ezekiel 42, regarding the passage we read as: *Which way was before the separate vestibule by the way of the east as one enters.* The Hebrew masters read it thus: *The door at the head of the way, directly across from the outer wall*; that is, a way directly toward the orchard or enclosure for those entering from the east. Our commentator Lyra <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a prominent medieval Franciscan exegete</note>, along with many other interpreters, did not look accurately at the property of the word in this place. For he explains it as a "closing of an arrangement," thinking that **Haginah** (הגינה) here is the same as **Neginah** (נגינה), a musical instrument. He calls this an "organ" in the title of the fourth Psalm: *To the victory, on the organs, a Psalm of David.* He uses a long paraphrase to color over the error of just one word. Nevertheless, even Jerome confesses that he does not know that chapter because of the obscurity of the translations, citing that saying of Socrates: *This I know: that I know nothing.*

**THE BOOK**

<term>Hed [הד]</term> Sound or noise, and more accurately resonance or an echo. This is the source of that passage in Ezekiel 7: "The day of slaughter is near, and not the glory of the mountains." <note>original Latin: "Prope est dies occisionis et non gloriae montium"</note> 
Symmachus <note>An ancient translator of the Old Testament into Greek</note> translated it as: "The day of haste is near, and not of delay." 
The Septuagint <note>The influential Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> renders it: "The day has approached, not with confusion nor with pains." 
Theodotion <note>Another early Greek biblical translator</note> however, wrote: "The day of famine is near, not the glory of the mountains." 
But those skilled in this specific language <note>Hebrew</note> interpret it thus: "The day of crying out, wailing, or mourning is near, and not the echo or sound of the mountains." For such is the artificial and not true sound of men, which tries to imitate our voice among the highest mountains. 
From this comes <term>Hedad [הידד]</term>, that is, a shout or noise, which Jerome translated as a <term>rhythmic shout</term> <note>original Latin: "celeuma," a Greek-derived word for a rhythmic call used by rowers or laborers</note>. 
Jeremiah 25: "A rhythmic shout shall be sung out, as if by those treading grapes." 
For so it is commonly said, although among the Greeks it should regularly be written as *celeusma* with an 's' in the middle. A *celeusma* is the shout of sailors and their mutual encouragement to one another, as found in Martial: "You guide the happy oars to the rhythmic shout." <note>original Latin: "Laetos rigitis ad celeusma remos"</note> 
Jerome also translated the same word elsewhere as the voice of those treading grapes, as in Isaiah 16: "The voice of the treaders has rushed in; I have taken away the voice of the treaders."

<term>Hadah [הדה]</term> He placed, extended, stretched out, or sent. As in Isaiah 11: "And into the cave of the basilisk <note>a mythical serpent</note>, the child who has been weaned shall reach out his hand." 
Sometimes these first syllables are found to change into the letter *Yod* [י] according to the teaching of Rabbi Judah, who explains the said sentence this way: "And into the cave of the basilisk the weaned child, in sending, shall send," or "in placing, shall place." Similarly in Lamentations 3: "And they placed a stone upon me." We shall speak of this further below under the letter *Yod*.

<term>Hadak [הדך]</term> He trampled or crushed. As in Job 40: "And crush the wicked in their place."

<term>Hadom [הדום]</term> Footstool. Isaiah 66: "The earth is the footstool of my feet." And Psalm 110: "Until I make your enemies your footstool."

<term>Hadas [הדס]</term> Myrtle. As in Nehemiah 8: "Myrtle leaves and palm branches." And Isaiah 55: "In place of the nettle, the myrtle shall grow."

<term>Hadaf [הדף]</term> He struck, drove forth, or impelled. Numbers 35: "If anyone has pushed a man out of hatred." And elsewhere Jerome translated it as "destroyed" <note>original Latin: "delevit"</note>, interpreting the sense of the passage rather than translating word-for-word. Deuteronomy 6: "That he might destroy all your enemies before you."

<term>Hadar [הדר]</term> He decorated, glorified, or honored. Leviticus 19: "And honor..."

**הוה** (*Havvah*): Corruption, perversity. <term>Jerome</term> <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century scholar and translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> translated this as "desire," perhaps thinking it came from the root *avah* [אוה] which we discussed above. For example, in Micah 7: "And the great man spoke the desire of his soul." However, he translated it differently in Psalm 38 according to the <note>original: "hebraica ueritate"</note> "Hebrew truth" <note>Jerome's term for the original Hebrew text as opposed to later translations.</note>: "And those seeking evils against me spoke snares." **הוי** (*Hoy*): Woe. As in Jeremiah 22: "Woe brother and woe sister! They shall not lament him: Woe lord and woe noble!" It is also found without the letter *iod*, as seen above. Jerome, in his commentary on Isaiah 29, writes that this <term>interjection</term> <note>A word used to express emotion.</note> is sometimes used in the <term>vocative case</term> <note>The grammatical case used for addressing someone directly.</note>.

**הון** (*Hon*): An abundance of riches. Proverbs 13: "He is as a poor man though he is in much wealth." A little further down, it is translated as "substance," as in "hastened substance shall be diminished." It also signifies "enough" or "sufficiency." Proverbs 30: "The fourth thing which never says 'it is enough,'" and "the fire truly never says 'it is enough.'"

**הון** (*Hun*): He slumbered. Jerome used a <term>circumlocution</term> <note>Using many words where fewer would do.</note> for this word in Isaiah 56: "Seeing vain things, sleeping, and loving dreams." And the Septuagint puts it thus: "Dreaming, loving the bed, slumbering."

**הי** (*Hi*): Woe, alas; a voice of sorrow. As in Ezekiel 2: "And there were written in it lamentations and a song and woe."

**היא** (*Hi*): This, that, she. It is often used as a participle or the substantive verb "to be." As in Genesis 12: "Why did you not indicate to me that she was your wife?"

**היה** (*Hayah*): He was, it was. Genesis 10: "He was a mighty one before the Lord." This is the substantive verb <note>The verb "to be".</note>.

**היה** (*Hayah/Hahah*): He corrupted, destroyed, annihilated; and in the passive, it vanished, perished, or fled. Daniel 2: "And his sleep fled from him."

**איך** <note>original Hebrew: *Eich*</note> **How.** 1 Chronicles 13: *How can I bring the ark of God to me?* And the letter *he* is changed into *aleph* <note>original: "conuertit he in aleph"</note>; regarding this word I have spoken above under the first letter.

Deuteronomy 7: *And he will kill them until he utterly destroys them,* where the final *mem* is not part of the substance of the word, but is a plural relative pronoun <note>the suffix meaning "them"</note>. In the aforementioned sentence you will find its verbal noun.

**הים** <note>original Hebrew: *Hamah*</note> **He cried out.** He roared; he disturbed; he moved; he made a tumult; he made rumors; he spread reports impetuously. As in Psalm 55 <note>Psalm 55:2 in the Latin Vulgate, 55:3 in English bibles</note>, for which we read: *I was saddened in my exercise and I was disturbed,* the Hebrew truth <note>original: "hebraica ueritas"; a scholarly term for the original Hebrew text</note> has: *I will lament in my speech and I will make a tumult.* Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate Bible</note>, changing the future to the past tense, translated it thus: *I was humbled in my meditation and disturbed.* And in Ruth 1, where the translator used a paraphrase <note>original: "perifrasticos circumlocutus"</note> for this word, saying: *When they had entered the city, a swift report spread among them all.* However, the Hebrew reads: *And it happened when they came into Bethlehem, the whole city was stirred up because of them, and they said: Is this Naomi?*

**הין** <note>original Hebrew: *Hun*</note> **He willed.** He was ready. As in Deuteronomy 1: *And when you were girded with weapons to go up into the mountain,* for which the Hebrews read: *You willed to ascend the mountain,* or *you were ready to ascend.*

**הין** <note>original Hebrew: *Hin*</note> **A measure of liquids.** As in Exodus 29: *And a fourth part of a hin.*

**היכל** <note>original Hebrew: *Heikhal*</note> **A palace.** A royal court; the house of the Lord; which the Greeks call *kyriakin* <note>original: "kyriakin", from the Greek for "belonging to the Lord"</note>, the Germans call *kyrchen* <note>original: "kyrchen"; modern German: "Kirchen", English: "churches"</note>, and the Latins call a *templum* [temple]. 1 Kings 6: *And there was a porch before the temple,* and other similar things there. However, a *yod* is often added after the *he* by <term>prothesis: the addition of a letter or sound to the beginning of a word</term>, and it becomes four letters; but here it is only a two-syllable word. It is declined in the plural in both the masculine and feminine. And note that the Lord, through Jeremiah, uttered this name three times. Jeremiah 7: *Do not trust in lying words, saying: The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord is this.* For the Holy Spirit says nothing in vain.

**הכר** <note>original Hebrew: *Hakar*</note> **He overwhelmed.** He amazed; he led into wonder or into an alienation of the mind; he made someone stunned. This is what Jerome interprets as *oppressed.* Job 19: *And you are not ashamed, oppressing me.*

**THE BOOK**

[Hebrew: הלל] **He praised.** He spoke praise. As in Psalm 119: *Seven times a day I have spoken praise to you.* And Psalm 150: *Let every spirit praise the Lord,* where he places [Hebrew: תהלל]; <note>original: "tehallel"</note> from this comes **Alleluia**. It consists of two words: *hallelu*, which is a verb in the plural imperative mood <note>meaning "you all praise"</note>, and *ia*, which is one of the divine names and signifies God or the Lord. And as the most blessed Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential early Christian theologian</note> correctly teaches in *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, in the chapter on the sacred unction: **Alleluia** means "Praise the Lord." Both Greeks and Latins, however, have been accustomed to write this word without an aspiration <note>the "h" sound</note> both at the beginning and at the end. This is because among us, only Hebrew words written with the letter *Heth*—which indicates a *dasian* <note>Greek term for a "rough breathing" or strong "h" sound</note>, that is, a strong aspiration—are written with an 'h'. Others that have a *psilen* <note>Greek term for a "smooth breathing" or lack of "h" sound</note>, meaning those written with the letter *He*, lack aspiration in our usage. Therefore, while the Hebrews say *halleluiah*, we write *alleluia*.

[Hebrew: הלל] **He was insane.** He acted wickedly. Psalm 75: *I said to the wicked, do not act wickedly.* Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible</note> translated this as: *I said to those acting wickedly: Do not act wickedly.* Others explain it as: *to the foolish, do not act foolishly or stupidly,* following the paradox of Cicero: *All fools are insane.* From this comes insanity, folly, and error [Hebrew: הוללות] <note>original: "holelut"</note> as in Ecclesiastes 7: *And that I might know the impiety of the fool, and the error of the imprudent.* And in chapter 10 of the same book: *The beginning of his words is folly, and the end of his talk is the worst error.* Because of the similarity of the letters in both this verb and the one above <note>the root for "praise" and "madness" is spelled the same way: H-L-L</note>, a variety of interpretations often occurs. For example, in Psalm 102: *And those who were praising me swore against me.* Jerome translates it: *The exulting swore by me.* Our Hebrew scholars translate it: *Those insulting me or making a fool of me swore against me.* Hence that passage in Nahum 2: *The chariots were thrown into confusion in the paths.* In place of which the seventy translators <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translated: *The chariots shall be confounded,* instead of *they shall be driven wickedly,* that is, the chariots shall be led.

[Hebrew: הלל] **It shone.** It gave light. Job 29: *When his lamp shone over my head,* where only one letter *L* is placed, strengthened by a *dagesh* and a *hireq* <note>technical terms for Hebrew vowel and pronunciation dots</note> in the first letter. For it is the function of the *dagesh* to fill in missing parts, which is discussed more fully in the art of grammar. And in Isaiah 13: *For the stars of heaven and their splendor shall not spread their light.* Regarding this, see above under the word [Hebrew: אהל] <note>Ohel</note>.

[Hebrew: הלאה] **Across. Beyond.** Amos 5: *And I will make you go into exile beyond Damas[cus].*

They say this word comes from מסס <note>original: "masas"</note> through the <term>prothesis: addition of a letter at the start</term> of the aspirated *he*, and the <term>apocope: the loss of a sound at the end of a word</term> of the doubling, so that in the following word the *yod* and *mem* are markers of the plural number. # BOOK

And in Psalm 51 <note>original: "ps.li."; in the Vulgate this is Psalm 50:8</note>: **For behold, you have loved the truth.** And this word <note>original: "הנה" (hinnēh)</note> takes an aspiration at the end, as in Isaiah 23 <note>Note: The text cites Isaiah 23, but the quote "Ecce dies veniunt" (Behold, the days are coming) is more commonly found in Jeremiah 23:5 or 31:31.</note>: **Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord.** It also serves for pronouns, just as *eccum* <note>look at him</note> and *ellum* <note>look at that one</note> are used among the Latins.

**Behold** <note>original: "הנה" (hinnēh)</note>: Now or here; it refers to the present either in place or in time. Both meanings are found together in our translation of Genesis 15: **But in the fourth generation they shall return here, for the iniquities of the Amorites are not yet full even to the present time.**

**Behold / They** <note>original: "הן" (hēn)</note>: A pronoun of the feminine gender, plural number, and third person. For example, in Numbers 27, in place of what we read as: **And let them succeed him in inheritance,** the <term>Hebrew Truth</term> <note>original: "hebraica ueritas"; a term used by scholars like St. Jerome to refer to the original Hebrew text</note> has: **And you shall cause the inheritance of their father to pass to them.** Through <term>paragogue</term> <note>the addition of a letter to the end of a word</note> it also receives a *he* at the end <note>original: "הנה" (hinnāh)</note>, meaning "themselves" or "those women," as in the first chapter of Exodus: **For they themselves have the knowledge of midwifery.**

**Hush** <note>original: "הס" (has)</note>: He was silent; he held his peace. Amos 6: **Be silent, and do not remember the name of the Lord.** A transitive form is derived from it in Numbers 13: **Amidst these things, Caleb, restraining the murmuring**—that is, he made them be silent.

**Turned** <note>original: "הפך" (haphak)</note>: He subverted, turned, or converted. Lamentations 3: **Only against me has he turned and turned again his hand.** It is sometimes translated as "changed," as in Leviticus 13: **And the hairs changed into a white color,** that is, turned. From this is derived **turning** <note>original: "מתהפכת" (mithhappeketh)</note>, meaning versatile or revolving. Genesis 3: **And a flaming and turning sword.** This applies to other derivatives as well.

**Stocks** <note>original: "מהפכת" (mahpeketh)</note>: Fetters, chains, stocks, a prison, or a house of captives. Jeremiah 29: **That you might put him in the stocks and in prison.**

**Chariot** <note>original: "הצן" (hotzen)</note>: A four-horse carriage or chariot; specifically, it refers to the equipment for transport. Ezekiel 23: **And they shall come upon you equipped with chariot and wheel.** Or, according to some, it refers to the "equipping of an army."

**Mountain** <note>original: "הר" (har)</note>: A mountain, as in Genesis 13 <note>likely Genesis 14:6</note>: **In the mountains of Seir even to the plains.** And Psalm 50: **The cattle on the mountains and the oxen.** Through <term>apocope</term> <note>the loss of a sound or letter at the end of a word</note> it is frequently found as <note>original: "הר" (har)</note>, as in Psalm 24 <note>original: "ps xxiij"</note>: **Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord?** It is found in both masculine and feminine gender in Amos 1: **Because he has ripped up the pregnant women of Gilead.** Some of the Hebrews interpret this as: **Because they have split the mountains of Gilead.**

<meta>This page continues a lexicon or dictionary of Hebrew terms, focusing on the letter Vav and its grammatical and lexical uses in the Bible.</meta>

->BOOK<-

->In the name of the four-lettered name <note>original: "εν ονοματι τω τετραγραμματω" — referring to the Tetragrammaton, the sacred four-letter name of God in Hebrew (YHWH).</note> ו<-

**ו** The letter of the alphabet. It is also a joining word <term>conjunction: a word used to connect clauses or sentences</term> signifying **and**. As in Genesis 1: "In the beginning God created the heaven **and** the earth." Sometimes, however, it is not a joining word, because it does not connect one thing to another. As in Genesis 22: where we read, "On the third day, lifting up his eyes, he saw the place from afar," the Hebrew truth <note>The "Hebraica Veritas" was a term used by scholars like Jerome to refer to the original Hebrew text of the Bible as the ultimate authority.</note> has: "On the third day **and** Abraham lifted up his eyes." But in this way, it converts the future into the past and vice-versa. This occurs at the beginnings of books, specifically: Leviticus: "**And** he called Moses." Numbers: "**And** the Lord spoke to Moses." Joshua: "**And** it came to pass after the death of Moses." Judges: "**And** it came to pass after the death of Joshua." Ruth: "**And** it came to pass in the days of the judge of judges." Likewise Samuel: "**And** there was one man." Likewise Kings: "**And** king David had grown old." Likewise Ezra: "**And** in the first year of Cyrus." Likewise at the beginning of Esther: "**And** it came to pass in the days of Ahasuerus." Likewise Ezekiel: "**And** it came to pass in the thirtieth year." Likewise Jonah: "**And** the word of the Lord came to pass." In all these instances, the letter **vav** is placed at the start of the books when it connects to nothing. But the verb, which by its own conjugation would otherwise have been in the future tense, is made into the past tense by this method. Similarly, in reverse, a **vav** placed before a past-tense verb makes it future tense. As in Exodus 25: "**And they shall make** me a sanctuary," and in the following chapters 26 and 27, in the words "**you shall make**" (singular) and "**you shall make**" (plural), and throughout Holy Scripture in many places, as can be seen in the art of grammar.

**וו** The hooked head of something, shaped like the letter **vav**. As in Exodus 26: "Whose **heads** shall be of gold and bases of bronze." And in the same, chapter 27: "**And their heads** with their silver engravings."

**והב** A mass <note>original: "moles"</note>. Numbers 21: regarding what we read as: "As he did in the Red Sea, so he will do in the valleys of Arnon," the Hebrews translate word-for-word thus: "**From the mass** in the sea even unto the valleys of Arnon." This translation pleases Master Solomon the Frenchman <note>This refers to Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, 1040–1105), the preeminent medieval French commentator on the Torah and Talmud.</note> in his commentaries on the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible.</note>. He thinks this word is spoken as if it were **יהב**, that is, a "mass" or "burden." As in Psalm 55: "Cast your **care** upon the Lord"—more correctly, your **mass** (or burden).

**ושתי** The proper name of the Queen. Esther, chapter one: "**Vashti** the queen also gave a feast."

# FIRST
<margin>Wolf</margin>
1 **Wolf.** As in Isaiah eleven: "And the wolf shall dwell with the lamb." <note>original: Isaiah 11:6</note>

**Fly.** <note>Hebrew: *Zevuv*</note> Isaiah seven: "The Lord shall hiss for the fly that is in the uttermost part of the rivers of Egypt." <note>original: Isaiah 7:18</note>

**Dowry.** <note>Hebrew: *Zavad*</note> A gift or a legal portion. Genesis thirty: "God has endowed me with a good dowry." From this, the verb is derived as seen in the same verse. <note>original: Genesis 30:20</note>

**He sacrificed.** <note>Hebrew: *Zavach*</note> He offered up, or he killed. Psalm fifty: "Offer unto God a sacrifice of praise." <note>Psalm 50 in the Vulgate is Psalm 51 in modern Bibles.</note> And First Kings one: "And Elkanah sacrificed." <note>The author refers to 1 Samuel 1:4 using the older "First Kings" naming convention.</note> From this comes the noun for **sacrifice** marked with a <term>segol</term> <note>A Hebrew vowel marking three dots like an inverted triangle, indicating an 'e' sound.</note>; likewise other derivatives which you will find while reading the Bible. From this, the place upon which one sacrifices is called a <term>mizbeach</term>, that is, an altar or shrine. Genesis eight: "Noah built an altar to the Lord."

**He dwelt together.** <note>Hebrew: *Zaval*</note> As in Genesis thirty: in place of what we usually read—"Even this time my husband will be with me"—the <term>Hebrew truth</term> <note>A phrase used by Renaissance scholars to refer to the original Hebrew text of the Bible as opposed to the Latin translation.</note> has: "This time my husband will dwell with me." From this comes <term>zevul</term>, that is, a dwelling place, as in Third Kings eight: "Building, I have built a house: your dwelling place." <note>1 Kings 8:13 in modern Bibles.</note> And it sometimes receives a 'he' [ה] aspiration at the end, as in Habakkuk three: "The sun and moon stood still in their dwelling place."

**Husk.** <note>Hebrew: *Zag*</note> A small husk or the outer skin of grapes. Numbers six: "Anything that can come from the vineyard, from the dried grape to the stone, they shall not eat." For which the Hebrew text reads: "Of all that is made from the vine of wine, from the stones to the husk or skin of the grape, he shall not eat." <note>original: Numbers 6:4</note>

**This.** <note>Hebrew: *Zeh*</note> He, that, this. As in Psalm twenty-three, according to Jerome’s translation from the Hebrew: "Who is this king of glory?" and further: "Who is he, this king of glory?" <note>Psalm 24:8-10 in modern Bibles.</note> In the masculine, it is written with a <term>segol</term> vowel as above; in the feminine, however, it is written with a <term>holem</term> <note>A Hebrew vowel mark indicating an 'o' sound.</note>. As in Ecclesiastes two: in place of what we read—"And I said to joy: why are you fruitlessly deceived?"—the Hebrew truth has: "And to joy: what does *this* [feminine] do?" <note>Ecclesiastes 2:2</note> And it is sometimes written with a final 'vau' [ו] instead of a 'he' [ה], becoming *zo* [זו], as in Psalm one hundred thirty-two: "And these my testimonies that I shall teach them." It is used for both singular and plural and all genders, as in Exodus fifteen: "the people whom [this/that] you have redeemed." This indeed is the masculine form, but it appears as feminine in Psalm one hundred forty-two: "In *this* way in which I walked." Now in the plural number, Psalm sixty-two: "These two things have I heard." Likewise, the 'vau' is changed into an 'aleph' [א], and the feminine ending 'thau' [ת] is added, and it is called *zot* [זאת].

# BOOK

**Gold** <note>Hebrew: *Zahab*; Latin: *Aurum*</note>. 2 Kings 7 <note>In the historical Vulgate, 1 and 2 Kings are referred to as 3 and 4 Kings</note>: "And they took from there silver and gold." 

And because nothing in our world is purer than gold, it therefore also signifies purity and clarity. As in Job 37: "From the north comes gold," <note>original Latin: *Ab aquilone aurum venit*</note> which means the clarity or purity of the air. For it is thus translated from the Hebrew: "From the north, clarity is brought; before God is venerable beauty." And **Abraham Ibn Ezra** <note>a celebrated 12th-century Spanish-Jewish scholar and astronomer</note> understands this passage to mean the splendor of the heavens, since its appearance resembles gold, and the splendor of the sky is revealed from the northern region. This is supported by **Aristotle** in the second book of his *Meteorology*, where he says a **bright wind** <note>original Greek: πνεῦμα λαμπρόν (*pneuma lampron*)</note> blows from the north. It is established by him that these are the **Etesian winds** <note>strong, cool Mediterranean winds that blow from the north in summer</note>, which are called "delicate" by sailors. From this, he also writes in the same book that a serenity occurs which he calls **windlessness** <note>original Greek: νηνεμία (*nēnēmia*)</note>, as if it were lacking wind and storm.

**To Defile** <note>Hebrew: *Zaham*; Latin: *Inquinavit*</note>. To make abominable and nauseating. Job 33: "Bread becomes loathsome to him in his life." <note>This refers to the loss of appetite during suffering or illness</note>

**To Warn** <note>Hebrew: *Zahar*; Latin: *Praemonuit*</note>. He cautioned or warned beforehand.

¶ **זָוִית [Zavit]** Edge, corner; which Jerome translated as "horn" in Zechariah 9: "And like the horns of the altar." And in Psalm 144 <note>original: "ps.cxliij"; the Vulgate numbering differs from modern Bibles</note> where we read: "Their daughters are arranged," Jerome, in his psalter translated according to the "Hebrew truth" <note>original: "hebraica ueritate"; Jerome’s term for his translation directly from Hebrew rather than the Greek Septuagint</note>, more correctly interprets it as: "Our daughters like decorated corners."

¶ **מְזוּזָה [Mezuzah]** Lintel, doorpost, or threshold; formed by adding the letter *mem* at the beginning and *he* at the end. In Deuteronomy 6: "And you shall write them on the threshold <note>Usually translated as doorpost</note> and the gates of your house." It is named thus from the idea of "lifting up" or "sublimity."

¶ **זָלַל [Zalal]** He despised or scorned. As in Lamentations 1: "All who glorified her have despised her." It is also found with a doubled *lamed* at the end, as in Jeremiah 15: "And if you separate the precious from the vile," where the word **זוֹלֵל [zolel]** is used.

¶ **זָן [Zan]** A kind of grain; from which comes **מָזוֹן [mazon]**, meaning food or nourishment. As in Genesis 45: "And as many she-asses carrying wheat, bread, and food for the journey." Here, the text implies they were carrying "flour or food or pottage," so that the full meaning is: "asses carrying wheat and bread and sustenance for his father for the journey," for this is how the Hebrew presents it.

¶ **זַן [Zan]** Kinds, genus, or species. For Rabbi Jonah <note>Rabbi Jonah ibn Janah, a famous 11th-century Hebrew grammarian and lexicographer</note> explains this verse of Psalm 144 in this way, where we read: "Their storehouses are full, overflowing from this to that." He reads it as: "Our corners are full, bringing forth from kind to kind." He proves his interpretation through the Aramaic translation <note>original: "translationem chaldaicam"; 'Chaldean' was a common historical term for Aramaic</note>; for wherever we read in Genesis 1 "according to its kind" <term>le-mino</term>, Onkelos <note>The author of the standard Aramaic translation of the Torah</note> translated it as *liznohi*. Others explain it as "year," saying "yielding from year to year," as if the word were a corrupted form of **זְמָן [zeman]** (time/season).

¶ **זוֹנָה [Zonah]** A harlot. As in Joshua 2: "They entered the house of a woman who was a harlot." Others interpret this as an "innkeeper" or "provisioner" <note>original: "lixa"</note> who runs here and there to gather food. Thus Jonathan the Aramaic translator renders it as "innkeeper" <note>original: "cauponā"</note>. Similarly, Rabbi Jonah explained this passage in Joel 3: "And they have placed a boy in a brothel," interpreting it as: "And they handed the boy over to a tavern/inn," where the text uses **בַּזּוֹנָה [ba-zonah]**.

¶ **זַיִן [Zayin]** Weapons or tools. This is found with a prefix *aleph* as **אָזֵן [azen]** and signifies a tool for digging and burying, which is called a spade. Jerome uses the diminutive form "small stake" in Deuteronomy 23: "You shall have a place outside the camp to which you may go for the requirements of nature, carrying a small stake..." <note>The text ends mid-sentence</note>

**THE BOOK**

...drops falling upon the earth. Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> translated it thus: "As drops bedewing the earth."

**זַרְזִיר** <note>original: *Zarzir*</note> A hunting dog of wondrous speed. It is called *Laelaps* by Ovid in the third book of his *Metamorphoses*, named after the speed of the wind; according to this custom, the Germans also call that dog "the wind" <note>original: *uentum*; referring to the *Windhund* or Greyhound</note> and the French call it a "harrier" <note>original: *leporarium*; literally a dog for chasing hares</note> because it hunts hares. Others think it is a starling bird. Jerome translates it as "rooster" in Proverbs 30: "A rooster girded about its loins." But Lyra <note>Nicholas of Lyra, an influential Franciscan biblical commentator of the Middle Ages.</note> says it does not mean a rooster, though he does not say what it actually is. Others write that it is a leopard, because it is slender around the loins and yet strong. Because this is Solomon’s prophecy warning us of things to come, the words are therefore uncertain to the uninitiated to whom these mysteries are presented.

**זָרַח** <note>original: *Zarach*</note> To rise or dawn. As in Isaiah 60: "And the glory of the Lord has risen upon you." From this comes the verbal noun for "rising" <note>original: *ortus*; in Hebrew, *Mizrach*</note> which receives the letter *mem* at the beginning, as in Psalm 112: "From the rising of the sun even to its setting." Sometimes it takes the letter *aleph* at the beginning, and thus signifies a native-born person and anything original to a place, as if "risen" from that spot. As in Leviticus 19: "But let the stranger who dwells among you be as a native-born person <note>original: *indigena*</note> among you."

**אֶזְרָח** <note>original: *Ezrach*</note> A green tree, always fresh, which some think is the laurel. Psalm 37: "I have seen the wicked highly exalted and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon." More correctly: "like the laurel."

**זֶרֶם** <note>original: *Zerem*</note> Force, wave, storm, or a powerful rain. Isaiah 32: "A man shall be as one who is hidden from the wind and hides himself from the storm." And Job 24: "Whom the rains of the mountains soak." The Hebrews read this as: "They shall be moistened by the streams or waves of the mountains." But Jonathan the Chaldean <note>Refers to the Targum Jonathan, an Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible.</note> thought it meant a powerful rain fallen from the clouds. Where we read in Habakkuk 3: "the surge of waters passed by." In another place, Ezekiel 23 understands a foul stench of "feminine rain" <note>The author is likely interpreting a Hebrew euphemism for bodily discharge or seminal emission mentioned in this chapter.</note> by this name: "As the flow of horses is their flow."

**זָרַע** <note>original: *Zara*</note> He planted, he sowed, or he seeded. Judges 6: "And whenever Israel had sown." From this comes the participial noun **זָרוּעַ** <note>original: *Zarua*</note> meaning something seeded, planted, or sown. Psalm 97: instead of what we read, "Light has risen for the just," the Hebrews have, "Light is sown <note>original: *Lux seminata est*</note> for the just." From this comes "seed." Genesis 1: **מַזְרִיעַ זֶרַע** <note>original: *Mazria Zera*</note> that is, "seeding seed," for which we read "bringing forth seed." And Numbers 24: "And his seed shall be in many waters," which refers to his offspring, namely his children.

# BOOK

[Hebrew: חח] <note>Transliterated as 'Chach'</note> [Hebrew: בטס כלי המזלג] <note>original: "A plate or vessel for a fork/hook"</note>
A hook, a brooch, or a bracelet, as in Exodus 35: **Bracelets and earrings**, etc. It is called a *fibula* <note>a decorative clasp or brooch</note> because of its similarity to a thorn, for the pins—or "thorns"—by which garments are fastened pass through a ring or circle. Indeed, "thorn" is named [Hebrew: חוח] <note>Choach</note> in Song of Solomon 2: **As a lily among thorns.** From this, the ring that carries a pin within itself took its name. Because of this, they often translate it as a "circle" or "ring," as in Isaiah 37: **I will put a ring in your nose.** Here, the letter *yod* is added at the end through <term>paragoge: the addition of a letter to the end of a word without changing its meaning</term>, as is common in many other words. It is read in the plural in Ezekiel 29, where we have: **And I will put a bridle in your jaws**, but there the Hebrew reads: **And I will put clasps (or hooks) in your jaws.** It also takes the letter *vav* through <term>epenthesis: the insertion of a letter into the middle of a word</term>, which signifies both a thorn and a clasp, as mentioned above. And in Job 40: **Or will you bore through his jaw with a bracelet?** which the Hebrew translates more accurately as: **you will bore through with a thorn.**

[Hebrew: חבב] <note>Chabab</note> He loved vehemently. Deuteronomy 33: **He loved the people.**

[Hebrew: חבא] <note>Chaba</note> He hid. As in Job 24: where we read, "They have oppressed the gentle of the earth," the Hebrew has: **They are hidden together.** This is correctly used in Job 5: **You shall be hidden from the scourge of the tongue**, and in 2 Kings 6: **Who hid her son.** However, the letter *aleph* is sometimes changed into a *he*, and conversely, *he* into *aleph*. Regarding this, see David Kimhi <note>A celebrated 12th-century Hebrew grammarian and rabbi from Provence</note> in the first book of the *Art of Grammar*, where he wrote a specific chapter on this verb and its grammatical properties. From this comes the noun for "a hiding place" [Hebrew: חביון] <note>Chabyon</note> in Habakkuk 3: where we have, "There was his strength hidden," the Hebrew reads: **And there was the hiding place of his power.**

[Hebrew: מחבת] <note>Machabat</note> A pan in which dough is fried. According to Rabbi Solomon <note>Known as Rashi, the most influential medieval commentator on the Torah and Talmud</note>, it was a specific instrument in the Sanctuary in which the unleavened offerings were cooked in oil. Leviticus 2: where we read "griddle"—**If your sacrifice be from the griddle**—the Hebrew there reads "pan." Jerome <note>The 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into the Latin Vulgate</note> translated it as "frying pan." Ezekiel 4: **And take for yourself an iron frying pan**, where it is understood as a smoothing tool similar to a pan used to smooth walls. To this, the Chaldaic <note>Aramaic</note> translations of both Jonathan and Onkelos <note>Authors of the Targums, ancient Aramaic paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible</note> agree. It is also found without the letter *mem* in the book of Chronicles.

->### THE FIRST<-

**חבט** <term>Chabat: To beat out, thresh, or cleanse.</term> *Judges 6*: "When Gideon his son beat out and cleansed the grain." <note>original Latin: *Excussit. purgauit.*</note> However, Jerome <note>The 4th-century translator of the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> translated this differently elsewhere. *Deuteronomy 24*: "If you gather the fruits of the olive trees," instead of "if you beat them out." So too in *Ruth 2*: "Beating and threshing with a rod."

**חבל** <term>Chabal (Legal): To seize from a debtor, to take as a pledge, or to pawn.</term> *Deuteronomy 24*: "You shall not take the lower and upper millstone as a pledge." He translates it more significantly as "taken away for a pledge" in *Job 24*: "They took away the widow's ox as a pledge." From this comes the noun **חבל** <gloss>pledge</gloss>. *Ezekiel 33*: "And if that wicked man restores the pledge."

**חבל** <term>Chabal (Destruction): To corrupt, devastate, demolish, scatter, destroy, or rot.</term> *Ecclesiastes 4*: "Lest he scatter all the works of your hands." *Isaiah 13*: "To destroy the whole land." And *Song of Solomon 2*: "Which demolish the vineyards." Our translation <note>referring to the Vulgate Latin Bible</note> in the book of *Nehemiah* was led astray by the similarity of the sound and translated it as "vanity." This is because "vanity" is written with the letter *He* [ה] and not with *Heth* [ח]. <note>The Hebrew roots for "vanity" (Habel) and "corrupt" (Chabal) sound similar but start with different letters.</note> For where it ought to say, "we have sinned, we are defiled by filth" or "we are rotted" or "corrupted before you," you will find this same meaning in *Isaiah 10*: "And the yoke shall rot away because of the oil." Yet, in *Nehemiah 1*, it was placed as: "We have sinned, we are led away by vanity." However, one can find a better example in *Micah 2*: "Because of its uncleanness, it shall be corrupted with a most grievous rot," where both the verb and the noun are used together.

**חבל** <term>Chabal (Binding): To measure or divide by lot; to bind, entangle, or snare.</term> *Proverbs 13*: "He binds himself for the future." From this comes the words for a measuring line, a rule, a perch, a rope, or a snare. *Zechariah 2*: "A measuring line." And *Amos 7*: "And your land shall be measured by a line." And *Isaiah 33*: "And all its ropes shall not be broken." And *Ezekiel 27*: "Which were wrapped and bound with ropes."

**חבל** <term>Chabal (Birthing): To be in labor, or to give birth.</term> *Psalm 7*: "Behold, he is in labor with injustice." From this comes the noun for birth, **חבל**. *Isaiah 66*: "Before her labor came." And in the eighth chapter of the *Song of Solomon*, where we have the text: "There your mother was corrupted, there she who bore you was violated," the Hebrews instead read: "There she was commanded to be in labor." <note>The translator is highlighting a discrepancy between the Latin Vulgate's "corrupted/violated" and the Hebrew "travailed/brought forth."</note> This is the same noun as **חבל** <gloss>Pain or Sorrow</gloss>, perhaps so called from the act of giving birth. *Isaiah 13*: "Twistings and pains..."

**חָגַג [Chagag]** He danced for joy, feasted, celebrated, or kept a holiday. Here, the word **חָג [Chag]** signifies holidays, solemnity, and feasts.

**חָגָא [Chaga]** Dread or trembling. Isaiah 19: "And the land of Judah shall be a dread to the Egyptians."

**חָגָב [Chagav]** A wingless locust; others say a locust. Our translation translates it variedly: specifically using "wingless locust" for "locust" and vice versa. <note>The author is noting inconsistencies in the Latin Vulgate's translation of different types of insects.</note> Leviticus 11: "and the locust according to its kind," where shortly before for **אַרְבֶּה [Arbeh]** it used "wingless locust." Yet most frequently it translates this as "locust." Exodus 10 indicates these are different animals. Joel 1: "The wingless locust has eaten the residue of the locust." However, Rabbi David Kimhi <note>A famous 12th-century Hebrew grammarian and biblical commentator from Narbonne.</note> determines in his *Book of Roots* that "locust" is the genus and "wingless locust" is a specific species. Some say this word also signifies the loins, the back, or the rear parts of a person. Ecclesiastes 12: "The locust shall be made fat," which they explain as "the back shall be burdened."

**חֲגָו [Chagav]** A cleft, a crack, an opening, or a cavern. Song of Songs 2: "My dove in the [clefts of the rock]..."

**חטם** <note>Hebrew root: H-T-M</note> To block, to close, to stop up; which <term>Jerome<note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the primary translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note></term> interprets as "to bridle." Isaiah 48: "And by my praise I will bridle you." However, the Hebrews explain this as referring to fury, anger, and great-heartedness, which the breath of the nostrils indicates. **חי** <note>Hebrew root: H-Y</note> Life. Genesis 23: "And Sarah lived," <note>original: "Vixit aut̃ Sara"</note> which the Hebrews read as: "The lives of Sarah herself were one hundred and twenty-seven years." From this comes the adverb of swearing: Numbers 14: "As I live, and the whole earth shall be filled with the glory of the Lord." And in the same way, 1 Kings 25: "As the Lord lives and as your soul lives." <meta>This page continues the lexicographical analysis of Hebrew roots starting with the letter Het, focusing on terms related to physical substances (egg whites, stones, flint), architectural features (windows), and verbs of change or piercing.</meta>

# FIRST

...[to] stand, because what is tasted brings death; though none of these words are found in the Hebrew, nor even in the following verse. Instead, the truth of the matter is this: "Is there any flavor in the white of the yolk?" <note>original Latin: "albo uitelli." This refers to Job 6:6, a notoriously difficult verse to translate. The author is correcting a Latin version using the Hebrew text.</note> This "white" is explained by the excellent physician Rabbi Isaac <note>Likely referring to Isaac Israeli the Elder, a famous 10th-century physician and philosopher.</note> as the thick spit or phlegm of the egg, which is so tasteless it makes us feel nauseous. For the Jewish masters are accustomed to say of the egg: "The white <note>original: חֶלְבּוֹן (*helbon*)</note> is on the outside, the yolk <note>original: חֶלְמוֹן (*helmon*)</note> is on the inside." From this, some believe the stone *achlamah* <note>original: אַחְלָמָה; usually translated as amethyst</note> is named, which was discussed under the letter Aleph. This stone is the third in the third row or order of the Breastplate of Judgment <term>Breastplate of Judgment: a ceremonial breastpiece worn by the High Priest of Israel, set with twelve stones representing the twelve tribes</term>, as seen in Exodus 28: "In the third [row], a ligure, an agate, and an amethyst."

**Flint** <note>original: חַלָּמִישׁ (*hallamish*)</note>. A flint-stone, a rock, a strong and hard stone. Deuteronomy 8: "Who brought forth streams from the hardest rock." Here, through the figure of <term>hendiadys: a rhetorical device where two words are used to express one complex idea (literally "one through two")</term>, the same thing is expressed with two words, as if he were to say "a flinty rock." Isaiah encompasses this in a single word in chapter 50: "Therefore I have set my face like the hardest rock."

**Window** <note>original: חַלּוֹן (*hallon*)</note>. Jeremiah 22: "Who opens windows for himself."

**Passed by** <note>original: חָלַף (*halaph*)</note>. It passed through, it changed. Song of Songs 2: "The rain is over and gone." And Job 9: "They have passed by like ships." And Psalm 90: "In the morning it passes by like grass; in the morning it flourishes and passes by." From this comes the <term>transitive verb: a verb that acts upon an object</term> as in Genesis 35: "And change your garments." And Psalm 102: "And like a cloak you shall change them, and they shall be changed." From this are derived "changeable garments" and other terms signifying alteration and renewal.

**For** <note>original: חֵלֶף (*heleph*)</note>. So called from the exchange or substitution of one thing for another. Numbers 18: "Because it is the reward for the service in which you serve." According to Jewish grammarians, it should be written with six points <note>referring to the Hebrew vowel system; the word uses two 'Segol' vowels, which each consist of three dots</note>.

**Cut into** <note>original: חָלַף (*halaph*)</note>. It struck, it pierced, it bored through. Judges 5: "And piercing through his temple with strength." And Job 20: "He shall flee from the iron weapon, and the bronze bow shall rush upon him," for which the truth of the Hebrew has: "And the bronze bow shall strike him."

**Knife** <note>original: מַחְלָף (*machlaph*)</note>. As in Ezra 1: "Twenty-nine knives." So named from the act of cutting, as mentioned above.

# THE BOOK

**Curls** or **locks of hair** <note>original: מַחְלְפוֹת, *machlephot*</note>. From Judges chapter sixteen: "If you weave the seven locks of my head into the web."

**He divided** <note>original: חָלַץ, *chalatz*</note>. It means to be partitioned and distinguished; he withdrew or was removed. From Hosea chapter five: "And they will not find him; he has been removed from them."

**He drew out** <note>original: חָלַץ, *chalatz*</note>. Also to bare, loosen, or show. From Lamentations chapter four: "But even the jackals <note>original: *Lamiae*, a term sometimes used for sea monsters or nocturnal creatures</note> bared the breast."

**He pulled out** <note>original: חָלַץ, *chalatz*</note>. To take away, set down, or take off. As in Deuteronomy chapter twenty-five: "She shall pull the sandal off his foot." And Leviticus chapter fourteen: "He shall command that they pull out the stones in which the leprosy is found." From this is derived the term <term>vestes mutatoriae: formal garments or "changeable suits of apparel" that one puts on after taking off and laying aside their previous clothes</term>. As in Zechariah chapter three: "And I will clothe you with rich robes."

**He rescued** <note>original: חָלַץ, *chalatz*</note>. To deliver. From Proverbs chapter eleven: "The righteous is delivered from trouble." And Psalm 107: "That your beloved may be delivered." And Psalm six: "Turn, O Lord, and rescue my soul."

**BOOK**

Aristotle, in his book *On the Sense and the Sensible*, calls a certain type "drimea" <note>original: *drimea*; from the Greek *drimeia*, meaning sharp, pungent, or acrid</note>, which is to say somewhat harsh to the taste. Regarding this, Numbers 6 says: "Vinegar from wine and from any other drink," etc. I would translate this word for word as: "The harshness of wine and the harshness of strong drink he shall not drink." For what follows—"and whatever the grape expresses"—is not part of the original text. He intended "strong drink" <note>original: *sicera*; a term for fermented beverages other than wine</note> to be understood as every drink that is not wine but can still intoxicate. Ulpian <note>A famous Roman jurist</note> called this *citromum* or beer <note>original: *ceruisia*</note>. To season this, they use hops <note>original: *lupulo*</note>, which causes fermentation and sharpens the taste. Hence, in Psalm 72 it says, "because my heart was inflamed." Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate</note> would have more correctly translated this as "because my heart was embittered" rather than the version he produced in his Psalter based on the "Hebrew truth" <note>original: *hebraica ueritate*; a term used to describe the original Hebrew text of the Bible</note>.

חָמֵץ <gloss>Violent, Unjust, Harmful.</gloss> Psalm 71: "From the hand of those acting against the law and the unjust." From this, they explain the passage in Amos 4, "And sacrifice praise from leavened bread," in a different way; namely: "And burn incense from violence." For thus Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic paraphrase of the Prophets</note> translated it into Chaldaic. "Praise," or according to Aquila <note>A 2nd-century scholar who produced a literal Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note>, "thanksgiving."

חֹמֶץ <gloss>Vinegar.</gloss> Psalm 69: "And in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink."

חָמוּץ <gloss>Dyed, colored.</gloss> Isaiah 63: "With dyed garments from Bozrah." This the seventy translators <note>The Septuagint</note> turned as "with tawny garments from Bosor."

...[me]ri <note>The end of a word meaning "pure" or "undiluted."</note>, that is, of the excellent kind. And in Deuteronomy 32: "And they drank the purest <note>original: *meracissimum*</note> blood of the grape." And in Isaiah 27: "In that day, a vineyard of pure wine."

**חמר** <note>Hebrew: *Chamar*</note> Cement made from a mixture of lime and sand; also clay or bitumen <note>A naturally occurring petroleum substance used as mortar in antiquity.</note> with which things are joined, pitched, or soldered together. Genesis 11: "They had brick for stone, and bitumen for cement." Likewise, Genesis 14: "Many pits of bitumen." It also means mud. Exodus 1: "In the hard labor of mud and brick." From this comes the verb which, because of its similarity to mud, signifies to disturb or to swell up. Psalm 46: "Their waters roared and were troubled." Jerome, in his translation from the "Hebrew Truth" <note>Jerome’s *Hebraica Veritas*, his direct translation from Hebrew rather than the Greek Septuagint.</note>, rendered it: "With its whirlpools roaring and swelling." This word is doubled according to the custom of the Hebrew language, as in Job 16: "My face is swollen from weeping." And in Lamentations 1: "My belly is troubled," though more correctly: "My bowels are swollen."

**חמר** <note>Hebrew: *Chomer*</note> A *corus* or *modius* <note>Ancient units of dry volume; a "homer" is roughly 220 liters.</note>. Hosea 3: "A homer of barley and a half-homer of barley." Ezekiel 45: "That the *bath* <note>A liquid measure</note> may contain the tenth part of a homer, and the *ephah* <note>A dry measure</note> the tenth part of a homer."

**חומר** <note>Hebrew: *Chomer*</note> An accumulation. This refers to how waves subside into themselves, as often happens in the open sea. Habakkuk 3: where it is said, "In the mud of many waters," the Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> translated it as "Disturbing many waters." But the Hebrew masters explain it as a gathering from the settling of waves into themselves. This agrees with what is read in Psalm 33: "Gathering the waters of the sea as if in a goatskin." Jonathan <note>Refers to the Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic paraphrase of the Bible.</note> also suggests such a heap brooding within itself in his Chaldaic <note>Aramaic</note> translation.

**חמר** <note>Hebrew: *Chamar*</note> A heap or mound. Exodus 8: "And they gathered them together into immense heaps" <note>Referring to the plague of frogs.</note>.

**חמור** <note>Hebrew: *Chamor*</note> A donkey; so named from the heaps and packs it carries. 1 Kings 16: "Jesse therefore took a donkey [laden] with bread." In the Hebrew, the word "full" is missing; it says "a donkey of bread" or "a pack of bread." And in Judges 15: "With the jawbone of a donkey, with the jawbone of the colt of donkeys, I have destroyed them." The Hebrew masters interpret this as: "With the jawbone of a donkey that heaps up mounds <note>A play on words between 'donkey' (*chamor*) and 'heap' (*chomer*).</note>, or gathering heaps, with the jawbone of a donkey I have struck" (or according to other books, "slain") "a thousand men." This meaning is clear from the Chaldaic translation. And in 4 Kings 6: "A donkey's head [was sold] for eighty pieces of silver." From this, they think the word **יחמור** <note>Hebrew: *Yachmur*</note> is derived, meaning a wild ox or a fallow deer. Deuteronomy 14.

# FIRST BOOK

<term>Hama</term> <note>Hebrew: חֵמָה - chemah; meaning heat, rage, or poison</note>, which we discussed above. According to that passage in Deuteronomy 32: "The venom of dragons is their wine," <note>original Latin: "Fel draconum uinum eorum"</note> Jerome, in his commentaries on Hosea, translated it as: "The fury of dragons is their wine," which others think is more correctly rendered as: "the cup of dragons is their wine." Theodotion <note>An early translator of the Hebrew Bible into Greek</note> translated the word in Habakkuk above as "outpouring"; the Fifth Edition <note>An anonymous Greek version of the Old Testament</note> as "the overthrow of anger"; Aquila as "the sending forth of fury"; another edition as "whirlwind"; and another as "turbid madness." 

But the most learned Rabbi Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>A celebrated 12th-century Spanish-Jewish scholar</note> explains it as referring to one who lifts the cup and makes his neighbor drunk with wine from your vessel. This is according to the word as it is read in the same way in Hosea 7: "The princes began to rage from wine." Both he and David Kimhi <note>A famous medieval rabbi and grammarian from Provence</note> describe this as a "wineskin" or "flask" of wine—that is, one full of wine. His father, Joseph Kimhi, understands this verse as referring to prelates, who are called "princes" when they are sober; but after they begin to be filled from the flask full of wine, they are called "scoffers." There are also many among the Hebrews who translate the said word as "anger" and "fury," similar to the verse in Job 21: "And he shall drink of the fury of the Almighty."

[Hebrew: חנן] **To be gracious**, to grant by grace, or to have mercy. Exodus 33: "And I will have mercy on whom I will," or more correctly: "I will have mercy on whom I will show mercy." <note>The text notes a grammatical shortening (apocope) of the final letter 'nun'</note>. However, it is read in its full form in Genesis 33: "Which God has graciously given to your servant," and in Psalm 119: "And be merciful to me according to your law." For this, Jerome in his Psalter writes: "And grant me your law." Likewise in Judges 21: "Have mercy on them."

[Hebrew: חן] **Grace**. Exodus 12: "The Lord gave the people grace." This is found in Job with an added 'yod' <note>an 'epenthesis' or insertion of a letter</note>, as also frequently happens in other words. From this comes:

[Hebrew: חנינה] **Mercy**, grace, or piety. I do not know why our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> reads "rest" in Jeremiah 16: "You shall serve strange gods there day and night, who will not give you rest." For the prophet intends to say: "who will not show you mercy." Indeed, the Chaldaic <note>Aramaic Targum</note> translation renders this as *rahanim*, which means "clemency." From this are derived many prayerful forms, such as:

[Hebrew: תחנה] **Clemency**, grace, or mercy. Joshua 11: "And that they might not earn any clemency." Some also interpret this as "prayer" or "supplication," as in 1 Kings 8: "Have regard for the prayer of your servant and for his supplications," and in what follows.

# BOOK

**Supplication** <note>Hebrew: *Tachnun* (תחנון). Signifies a prayer for mercy or an entreaty.</note> **Entreaty. Petition. Prayer. Supplication.**
From **Proverbs 18**: *The poor man speaks with entreaties.* <note>original Latin: "Cum obsecrationibus loquitur pauper."</note> This occurs in the singular masculine form, as in **Psalm 130**: *To the voice of my supplication.* But it is also used in the plural masculine, as in **Zechariah 12**: *The spirit of grace and of prayers.* <note>original: "Spiritū gratię et precū."</note> It also appears in the feminine plural, as in **Psalm 86**: *And attend to the voice of my supplication.* From this root come various forms of derivative words which you will encounter while reading the Bible, such as that in **Deuteronomy 4**: *And I entreated the Lord,* <note>original: "Precatusq; sum dominū."</note> that is, I sought a gift freely given.

**In vain.** <note>Hebrew: *Chinnam* (חנם).</note> **Freely. Pointlessly. Without cause.**
**Psalm 35**: *Since they have hidden the destruction of their net for me without cause; they have reproached my soul pointlessly.* <note>original: "Quoniā gratis absconderunt mihi interitū laquei sui."</note> This is formed by <term>paragoge</term> <note>A grammatical term referring to the addition of a letter or syllable to the end of a word.</note> from the word for "grace" <note>Hebrew: *Chen* (חן).</note>, signifying something done out of favor and without expectation of reward.

**He encamped.** <note>Hebrew: *Chanah* (חנה).</note> **He overcame. He took by storm. He prevailed. He remained. He dwelled.**
As in **Isaiah 29**: *Woe to Ariel, to Ariel, the city which David took by storm,* <note>original: "Vę ariel ariel ciuitas quā expugnauit Dauid."</note> which **Jonathan the Chaldean** <note>Refers to the Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible.</note> interprets thus: *Alas, the altar, the altar of the sons of the city which David overcame,* or *in which David prevailed.* **Symmachus** <note>A 2nd-century translator of the Old Testament into Greek.</note> translated this as "camp," and **Theodotion** <note>Another early Greek translator of the Hebrew Bible.</note> as "circumvallation" <note>A fortification or surrounding wall.</note>. **Jerome** <note>Saint Jerome, the primary translator of the Latin Vulgate.</note> relates that "a certain most learned man of the Hebrews," as he puts it, explained it as "a dwelling place." Everyone abounds in their own sense of the word. For they translated the same word in **Zechariah 9** differently; for where we read: *And I will encircle my house with those who serve as soldiers for me,* the **Septuagint** <note>The early Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> translation has: *And I will place an elevation in my house.*
From this is derived **Encampment** <note>Hebrew: *Machaneh* (מחנה).</note>, that is, a surrounding wall, a troop, or a camping ground. It is of common gender in both the singular and the plural. **Genesis 32**: *The other troop which remains shall be saved.* Here it is in the singular masculine. Also in the same chapter: *If Esau comes to one troop.* Here it is in the singular feminine. Also in the plural masculine in the same place: *And he called the name of that place Mahanaim,* that is, "Camps." Also in the plural feminine in the same place: *He divided the people who were with him, etc., into two troops.* There is also another form of this noun which is read in **2 Kings 6** <note>The text says "4 Kings 6" following the naming conventions of the Latin Vulgate, where 1 & 2 Samuel and 1 & 2 Kings are titled 1, 2, 3, & 4 Kings.</note>: *In such and such a place let us place ambushes.* More accurately, word-for-word, it says: *In an unknown and hidden place are my dwellings.* From this we read in **Judges 19**: **Lodgings** <note>Hebrew: *Chanot* (חנות).</note>, that is, dwellings or habitations for spending the night.

**Spear.** <note>Hebrew: *Chanit* (חנית).</note> **Lance. Spear.**
**1 Samuel 26**: *Behold the king’s spear.* And **2 Samuel 23**: *It is he who lifted his spear.* In the plural, it is of both masculine and feminine gender.

**פג** [PG] It budded, or any tree produced unripe fruit. As in Song of Solomon 2: "The fig tree has brought forth its green figs." <note>original: "grossos"</note> And in Arabic, they name wheat <note>original: "hintin"</note> from the act of germinating, which in Hebrew they call <note>original: "hitkon"</note>.

**חנט** [HNT] It seasoned with spices, which our people call "embalmed." This is usually done to the bodies of the dead so they may last for a long time without decay. Genesis 50: "To season their father with spices." And it follows: "to those carrying out the orders," which is more accurately translated: "And the physicians of Israel seasoned [Jacob] with spices."

**חנמל** [HNML] Hoarfrost. As in Psalm 78: "And their sycamore trees with hoarfrost." Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate</note> translates this as "cold," but the Hebrews say it is a species of hail.

**חנך** [HNK] It imbued, initiated, domesticated, and trained from the first basics. Proverbs 22: regarding the passage usually read as "it is a proverb: a youth according to his way," the Hebrews have it: "To train a child," or "to imbue a youth according to his way." That is, the first exercises of children should follow their natural disposition—little by little, as much as their tenderness can bear. From this, the home-born slaves and domestics of a person are called <term>chanichim <note>Hebrew: חניכים; meaning those trained or accustomed</note></term>, meaning those accustomed to and imbued with the laws of the house. As in Genesis 14: "He numbered his trained servants."

**חנך** [HNK] It initiated, dedicated, consecrated. Deuteronomy 20: "Who is the man who has built a house and has not dedicated it?" Rabbi Jonah <note>likely Jonah ibn Janah, the influential medieval Hebrew grammarian and lexicographer</note> derives the meaning of this word from the one above. From this comes the noun "dedication," as in the title of Psalm 30: "A psalm of song at the dedication of the house of David."

**חנף** [HNP] It acted hypocritically, seduced, transgressed, showed partiality, or polluted. Our translation <note>referring to the Latin Vulgate</note> reads this way in Jeremiah 23: "For both prophet and priest are polluted." Where the Aramaic translation of Jonathan <note>The Targum Jonathan, an Aramaic paraphrase of the Prophets</note> has: "they have committed a theft of their law," meaning that while they hold the words of the law, they abuse the intent of the law (which belongs to God), pretending one thing while doing another. Therefore, our translation renders the noun <term>chanef <note>Hebrew: חנף</note></term> as "hypocrite" in Isaiah 9: "Because everyone is a hypocrite and an evildoer." In the following chapter of the same book, it is translated as "deceitful": "Against a deceitful nation..."

**חצה** [H-Ts-H] He separated; partitioned; divided; halved. Numbers 31: "From the middle portion of the children of Israel which he had separated." From this, various words are derived according to the rules of grammar.

**חצן** [H-Ts-N] The lap; the bosom. Others explain it as the forearms or arms, just as we read in Isaiah 49: "And they shall bring their sons in their arms," which the Seventy <note>the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translated as "in their bosom."

**חצר** [H-Ts-R] A village; a courtyard. Ezekiel 10: "And the courtyard was filled with splendor."

**Charar** (חָרַר) <note>original: "charar"</note>: It burned with heat, it was incensed, it was parched. **Job 30**: *And my bones were parched before the heat.* <note>The author notes a grammatical shift here involving the shortening of the letter Resh and the addition of the letter He.</note> And in **2 Kings 22**: *Because he was angry with him*; Jonathan also translated it this way in the Chaldean <note>The "Chaldean" refers to the Aramaic Targum, a Jewish translation and commentary</note>. Likewise in **Jeremiah 6**: *The bellows failed in the fire*—meaning it was consumed or scorched. From this comes:
**Charer** or **Charerah** (חָרֵר / חֲרֵרָה): Dry or dryness. **Jeremiah 17**: *But he shall dwell in dryness in the desert.* And note that sometimes the first letter is doubled, as in **Deuteronomy 28**: *With burning and heat.* This word **Charchur** (חַרְחֻר) refers to a burning disease or fever.

**Charav** (חָרַב) <note>original: "charav"</note>: It was dried up. **Genesis 8**: *And he saw that the surface of the earth was dried up*, which Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible</note> translated as "emptied out." **Job 14**: *And the river, being emptied, shall dry up.* From this comes a "heavy" verb form <note>likely referring to the Hiphil or causative grammatical stem</note>, which our translation explains as "to lead to a desert." **Nahum 1**: *And you lead all the rivers to a desert.* From this comes the name **Charavah** (חָרָבָה), meaning dry land. **Exodus 14**: *And he turned the sea into dry land.* From this is derived that adjective in **Proverbs 17**: *Better is a dry morsel.* And **Leviticus 7**: *Whether it be sprinkled with oil or be dry.* And another noun, **Chorev** (חֹרֶב), meaning dryness or drought. **Judges 6**: *And in all the land there was dryness.* And **Isaiah 25**: *As with heat under a parching cloud* <note>The text breaks off here</note>

**חרגל [Chargol]** A winged species having four feet, whose hind legs are longer. **חרג [Charag]** Girded. Bound. Contracted. Constrained. **2 Samuel 22**: *And they shall be constrained in their distress.* This is read as **חרד [Charad]** through a transposition of letters <term>metathesis: the rearranging of letters or sounds in a word</term>. **Psalm 18**: *And they limped away from their paths,* which we discussed above.

**חרד [Charad]** He was terrified. He trembled. He was stunned, or rather, he shuddered with horror. **Isaiah 29**: *And they shall be stunned and fear before the movement of the hand of the Lord.* And **1 Samuel 13**: *And all the people who followed him were terrified.* And **1 Kings 1**: *They were terrified and rose up.*

**חרד [Charad]** He took care. He labored. He served diligently. **2 Kings 4**: *Behold, you have served us diligently in all things.* The Hebrews and Jonathan the Chaldean <note>referring to the Targum Jonathan, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Bible</note> translate it this way: *Behold, you have provided for us all of this provision.* Here a verbal noun is also found by adding the letter *He* (ה) at the end.

**חרד [Charad]** He moved himself because of sudden terror. Jerome translated this as "to be afraid," and in another place as "to fly away." **Hosea 11**: *And the children of the sea shall be afraid.* Also a little further down: *And they shall fly away like a bird out of Egypt.*

**חרה [Charah]** He was incensed. He was angry. **Zechariah 10**: *My anger was kindled against the shepherds.* From this comes the noun in **Psalm 69**: *And the fury of your anger shall overtake them.* From this comes the passive form, "he became angry," for which our translation <note>the Vulgate</note> has "he fought." **Song of Solomon 1**: *My mother’s sons fought against me.* According to the custom of the idiom, it is pronounced with the letter *He* (ה) cut off <term>apocope: the loss of one or more sounds from the end of a word</term>. **Psalm 37**: *Do not be envious.* And in the passive in **Jeremiah 6**: *The bellows failed in the fire,* that is, the bellows were scorched or burned up.

**חרוז [Charuz]** A necklace. A jewel. What they call a collar. **Song of Solomon 1**: *Your neck is like jewels.* It is a stringing together of gems or precious stones on a single thread which they tie around the neck, according to the Hebrew masters.

**חרטם [Chartom]** An enchanter. A soothsayer. **Exodus 32.** <note>This refers to the story of the Golden Calf.</note> **And he fashioned it by a casting work.** <note>original Latin: "Formavitque opere fusorio"</note> which is explained elsewhere in this way: **And he fashioned it with a graving tool or a stylus.** <note>original Latin: "Et formavit ipsum pugillari seu stilo." <term>Charak</term> <note>original Hebrew: חרך</note> He branded, scorched, or marked. Because of this, I believe Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the translator of the Latin Vulgate.</note> translated it as "to find" in **Proverbs 12**: **The deceitful man shall not find gain.** <note>original Latin: "Non inveniet fraudulentus lucrum"</note>

Instead, he singes and burns the very tips of the wings so that it cannot easily fly away from his hands. However, a deceitful man will not prosper so much that a captured bird remains in his hands long enough for him to brand it; rather, it will fly away from the hands of the deceitful hunter before the cauterizing marks of branding [can be applied]. <meta>This page continues a philological examination of Hebrew roots, specifically focusing on the root "Charutz" (חרוץ) and its various meanings in Biblical texts, likely following a previous entry on words beginning with the letter "Cheth."</meta>

->FIRST<-

"And the substance of man shall be the price of gold." <note>original: "Et substantia hominis erit auri precium." This discusses Proverbs 12:27.</note> The Hebrews explain this to mean that the dignity found in the abundance of a man’s riches is integrity and virtue itself. For this reason, they translate it thus: "And the substance of a worthy man is just," or conversely, "And the substance of an honest man is worthy." Our translator <note>likely referring to the Latin Vulgate</note> varied this. For shortly after in the same thirteenth chapter, he translates "diligent" <note>original Latin: *operantem*</note> as: "But the soul of those who work shall be made fat." Rabbi Jonah <note>Ibn Janah, a 11th-century Hebrew grammarian and lexicographer</note> explains the word as deriving from "gold" in this way: "The soul of those who store up treasures shall be enriched."

**CHARUTZ** <note>Hebrew: חרוץ</note> *Decision* or *Council*, according to the translations of Aquila, Symmachus, and the Fifth Edition <note>referring to various Greek versions of the Old Testament used by scholars to compare meanings</note>. From this, our translation of Joel 3 reads: "Multitudes, multitudes in the valley of concision <note>original: *concisionis*, meaning a 'cutting off' or 'decision'</note>, for the day of the Lord is near in the valley of concision." This can agree with the previous interpretation. For a proven, upright, and just man levels his work to precision, so that he does not wander outside the boundaries of virtue; and he does this through diligent, guiding reason, which we call "judgment." Therefore, both the Hebrews and the Seventy Interpreters <note>the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> and Theodotion translated the aforementioned sentence of Joel thus: "In the valley of judgment," because the day of the Lord is near in the valley of judgment or "definition." Hence we read in Isaiah 10: "A shortened consummation"—that is, one decided and defined—"shall overflow with justice." There, the passive form is used: "the Lord God of hosts shall make an abbreviation in the midst of all the earth." This is used in the same way in Isaiah 28, which the Seventy translated as "abbreviated things."

**CHARUTZ** <note>Hebrew: חרוץ</note> *A toothed club, a saw, a flail, a rod, a threshing sledge,* or a *staff* with which harvested grain is beaten out. Isaiah 28: "For the black cumin shall not be threshed with saws." The Seventy translate this as: "For black cumin shall not be cleaned with harshness." And in Isaiah 41: "I have placed you like a threshing wagon." The Seventy translate this as: "Behold, I have made you like the new wheels of a wagon in the manner of iron teeth." See with what words they describe the instrument of this name, according to the custom of threshing grain specific to each region. It is called by some a *tribula* <term>threshing sledge: a heavy wooden board studded with flint or iron teeth, dragged over grain to separate the kernels from the husks</term>, named either from "wearing away" or from the "clattering" of the wagon. Amos 1: "Because they have threshed Gilead with iron threshing sledges."

**CHARUTZ** <note>Hebrew: חרוץ</note> *Fortifications* or *walls*. Daniel 9: "The street and the walls shall be built." Walls are called this because of their resemblance to toothed iron <note>referring to the jagged, "toothed" appearance of defensive battlements</note>.

**CHARTZAN** <note>Hebrew: חרצן</note> *A grape-stone* or the small seed of a grape. Numbers 6: "From the dried grape to the grape-stone." For which the Hebrews have: "From the seeds to the skin," as we read above under the letter *Zain* <note>indicating this dictionary is organized alphabetically by Hebrew letters</note>.

**CHARITZEI** <note>Hebrew: חריצי</note> *Cheese molds* or portions. As in 1 Samuel 17: "And these ten little molds of cheese you shall carry." The Hebrews explain this as: "These ten cheeses made of milk you shall carry." Jonathan the Chaldean <note>referring to the Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and paraphrase</note> translated it this way.

**חרש** <term>Charash: Plowed</term>. Psalm 129: in place of what we have—"The sinners have built upon my back"—the Hebrews read, and Jerome also translated it this way in his psalter: "The plowers plowed upon my neck." and Deuteronomy 22: "You shall not plow with an ox and a donkey together." From this comes the noun for a plow or plowing. Exodus 34: "On the seventh day you shall stop plowing and reaping." For which the Hebrews have: "On the seventh day you shall rest from plowing and from harvest." Similarly, 1 Samuel 8: "And the plowers of their fields," that is, of their farming. The passive form of this verb is used in Micah 3: "Zion shall be plowed like a field."

**<term>Hashman</term>** <note>Hebrew: חשמן</note> A great and excellent man, like some kind of envoy or ambassador. Psalm 68: "Envoys shall come out of Egypt." <note>original Latin: "Venient legati ex Aegypto"</note>

**<term>Hashaf</term>** <note>Hebrew: חשף</note> To lay bare, manifest, or uncover. Isaiah 47: "Uncover your shoulder." <note>original Latin: "Discooperi humerum tuum"</note> And in Joel 1: "Stripping, he despoiled it," which is more correctly read as: "Stripping, he made it bare." <note>original Latin: "Nudans nudauit eam"</note>

**<term>Hashaf</term>** <note>Hebrew: חשף</note> To take away, carry off, or draw out. Isaiah 30: "Or that a little water may be drawn from the pit." <note>original Latin: "Aut hauriatur parum aquę de fouea"</note> Rabbi David Kimhi <note>A renowned 12th-century Hebrew grammarian and philosopher from Provence, often called 'Radak'</note> writes in his *Book of Roots* that this authority should be understood as referring to a pit that holds so little water that when it is removed and drawn out, the bottom of the cistern is bared and uncovered. Thus, this second meaning arises from the first.

**<term>Hashif</term>** <note>Hebrew: חשיף</note> A small flock. 1 Kings 20 <note>referenced as 3 Kings in the source, following the Vulgate numbering</note>: "Like two small flocks of goats." <note>original Latin: "Quasi duo parui greges caprarū"</note>

**<term>Hashaq</term>** <note>Hebrew: חשק</note> To desire greatly, to be pleased with, to cling lovingly to, or to love. Genesis 34: "The soul of my son Shechem has clung to your daughter." <note>original Latin: "Sichē filij mei adhesit anima sua filię uestrę"</note> And in Deuteronomy 7: "It was not because you surpassed all nations in number that the Lord was joined to you"—that is, He was pleased with you or lovingly clung to you. From this comes what is read in Exodus 38: "And he overlaid them with silver"; the Hebrews read this as "and he joined, girded, or surrounded them," as if saying that he had bound them together, according to Onkelos the Chaldean <note>referring to the Targum Onkelos, the authoritative Aramaic translation of the Torah</note>. And in Isaiah 38, where we read: "But you have delivered my soul that it should not perish," the Hebrew scholars explain it as: "But you have desired my soul away from the pit of rot." According to David Kimhi in his commentaries, this is understood as: "But you have clung to me to defend my soul from the pit of corruption."

**<term>Hashuq</term>** <note>Hebrew: חשוק</note> A spoke of a wheel. 1 Kings 7: "And the axles and the spokes..." <note>original Latin: "Et axes et radij"</note>

<term>Malachi 2</term> <note>original: "lachię.ij."</note>. And he was in awe before my name. **חתה** [Hatah] He cherished, sustained, or gathered. As in <term>Proverbs 25</term>: For you shall gather <note>original: "congregabis"</note> coals upon his head, that is, you shall warm or cherish him. Our translation <note>Likely referring to the Latin Vulgate.</note> thinks it is a certain receptacle for ashes where the snuffed lamp-wicks are extinguished.
