**חתת** [Hatath] He cut, wrote down, determined, established, and abbreviated, as scribes and notaries are accustomed to seal for the future memory of a matter. Concerning this, <term>Horace</term> says in his *Art of Poetry*: "to engrave laws on wood." <term>Daniel 9</term>: Seventy weeks are shortened <note>or "decreed"</note> upon your people and upon your holy city.

**חתל** [Hatal] He swaddled, wrapped, or bound around. <term>Ezekiel 30</term>: That it might be bound with cloths and swaddled with linens.

**חתם** [Hatam] He ratified, confirmed, marked, or sealed. <term>Jeremiah 32</term>: I wrote in the book and sealed it. And in <term>Song of Songs 4</term>: A garden enclosed, a fountain sealed, that is, made firm. <term>Jerome</term> <note>The 4th-century saint responsible for the Vulgate translation of the Bible.</note> translated it as if he closed it under a seal. <term>Job 9</term>: And he shuts up the stars as if under a seal. From this comes the noun for a sign, a mark, or a seal. <term>Song of Songs 8</term>: Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm. <term>David Kimhi</term> explains this: just as one who wears a signet ring on his finger never lets it go at any time, so I ask that you place me as a seal upon your heart so that I may never depart from your memory.

-># SECOND BOOK<-

The Hebrew experts explain that passage in Genesis 16, **"because the Lord has heard your affliction,"** in this way: it means that the Lord has heard your cry.
<term>Anah</term> <note>Hebrew: ענה</note>—To afflict or to humble. As in Psalm 35: **"I humbled my soul with fasting."** Likewise in Psalm 116: **"But I was humbled exceedingly,"** and in Zechariah 10: **"they shall be afflicted because they have no shepherd."** So too in Isaiah 31: **"He will not shrink from their voice nor be afraid of their multitude"**—or more accurately: **"he will not be humbled by their multitude."** For this reason, the seventy translators <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translated that verse which reads in Psalm 119, **"Before I was humbled I went astray,"** more correctly than Jerome, who translated it as: **"Before I heard, I was ignorant."** <note>Jerome produced the Latin Vulgate; the author here argues the Greek version captures the Hebrew "humility" root better than Jerome's "hearing" translation.</note> From this comes the adjective for **humbled, lowly, needy, destitute, or afflicted.** Ezekiel 16: **"And they did not stretch out a hand to the needy and the poor."** And Psalm 70: **"But I am needy and poor."** And in the plural in Isaiah 41: **"The needy and the poor seek water,"** and Psalm 12: **"Because of the misery of the destitute."** From this also comes the noun for **humility.** Psalm 22: **"For he has not despised nor disdained the prayer of the poor."** More accurately: **"The affliction or the humility of the poor person,"** or of the afflicted or lowly one. For in the same Psalm it is interpreted thus: **"And from the horns of the unicorns, my humility."** <note>In modern translations, "unicorns" is usually rendered as "wild oxen."</note> Similarly in the same Psalm: **"The poor shall eat and be satisfied."** Also Zechariah 9: **"Poor, and riding upon a donkey."** All these terms signify a certain depression, poverty, and humility of spirit, but also **labor, business, and occupation** as well. Ecclesiastes 1: **"This miserable occupation God has given to the sons of men to be occupied in,"** that is, this business for them to labor in. Likewise in chapter 3 of the same book: **"All his days are full of sorrows and hardships."** In Hebrew it reads: **"Because all his days are sorrowful, and his business is wrath or indignation."** From this comes <term>Lema'an</term> <note>Hebrew: למען</note>, which means the **motivating cause** for which a whole business exists. Psalm 51: **"That you may be justified in your words,"** that is, "because of this" or "for that reason you will be justified." It signifies "on account of." So in Proverbs 16: **"The Lord has made all things for himself,"** that is, for his own purpose or business.

<term>Ma'anah</term> <note>Hebrew: מענה</note>—A **yoke** of land <note>A unit of area</note> that a pair of oxen can plow in a day. 1 Kings 14 <note>Commonly 1 Samuel 14 in modern Bibles</note>, where our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> describes this word through a roundabout phrase when it says: **"In the middle part of an acre which a pair of oxen is accustomed to plow in a day."** In Hebrew, however, it is read much more briefly as: **"As if in the middle of a yoke of a pair of the field,"** that is, of two oxen in the field. # BOOK ע <note>The letter Ayin</note>

David Kimhi <note>A famous 12th-13th century Jewish grammarian and biblical commentator</note> writes in his *Book of Roots* <note>original: *Sefer HaShorashim*</note> that it is called a furrow.

**עבות** <note>Abot</note> **The traces of a plow.** This is the transverse yoke to which the oxen are tied. Hosea 10: *When they shall be chastised for their two iniquities.* However, the Hebrew is more truly read as: *The peoples shall be gathered over them, binding them to their two yokes.* For in this place it does not signify "iniquities," since according to true <term>orthography: the conventional spelling system of a language</term>, after the letter *Ayin*, a *Vav* should not be written here, but rather a *Yod* in its place, and nonetheless it should be marked with a *Holem* <note>A Hebrew vowel mark representing an 'o' sound</note>.

**ענו** <note>Anav</note> **Gentle, mild, kind.** Numbers 12: *For Moses was a man most gentle above all men.* Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to Rashi, the preeminent medieval French rabbi and commentator</note> explains this as humble and tolerant, or patient. And in the plural in Proverbs 16: *It is better to be humbled with the gentle.*

**ענף** <note>Anaf</note> **Leafy branch, bough.** Our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> renders it as "shoot." Malachi 4: *Which shall leave them neither root nor shoot.* But more correctly the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> has it thus: *Neither root nor branch shall be left to them.* Likewise in Leviticus 23: *And the branches of thick leafy trees.*

**ענק** <note>Anaq</note> **A necklace or torque**, specifically a piece of jewelry for the neck hanging around the throat. Song of Songs 4: *And with one hair of your neck*, which should be read: *And with one necklace of your neck.* This is sufficiently indicated by that verse in Proverbs 1: *And a necklace for your neck*, where the masculine plural is used; it is also sometimes declined in the feminine. As in Judges 8: *And besides the golden necklaces around the necks of the camels.* But that which is read in Deuteronomy 15: *You shall give him provision* <note>original: *viaticum*</note>, should be understood according to the property of the language—that is, *decorating, you shall decorate him*, namely with some honorary gift. Rabbi Solomon writes that some explain it thus: *Loading, you shall load him*, namely with gifts, which the rest of the Jews follow.

**ענש** <note>Anash</note> **To shake out, to strike, to fine, to levy, to condemn with a monetary penalty.** Deuteronomy 22: *Condemning them moreover to a hundred shekels of silver.* And 2 Chronicles 36: *And he fined the land a hundred talents.* From this comes the noun for a fine, a levy, or forced labor. 2 Kings 23: *And he imposed a fine on the land of a hundred talents.* And the adjective in Amos 2: *They drank the wine of the condemned.*

**עסס** <note>Asas</note> **To suppress, to trample underfoot, to tread, to crush, to compel.** Malachi 4: *And you shall tread down the wicked.* Or according to the Septuagint: *And you shall trample the unjust.* Others read: *And you shall compel.*

**עסיס** <note>Asis</note> **Must** <term>Must: freshly crushed fruit juice, usually grapes, that contains the skins, seeds, and stems</term>, **dye, or a sweet drink recently pressed.** Joel 1: *Those who drink...*

# SECOND

<note>This heading likely refers to the second book or major division of the volume.</note>

...you shall drink wine in sweetness. And from the same: <note>original: "Stillabunt montes dulcedinem"</note> "The mountains shall drip sweetness." <note>Joel 3:18</note> And in the Song of Songs, chapter 8: "And the must of my pomegranates."

**ענף** <term>Branch</term>. A leafy bough. Our translation <note>referring to the Latin Vulgate</note> improperly renders this as "rock" in Psalm 104: "From the midst of the rocks they shall give their voices." More truly, it should be: "From the midst of the leaves or branches they shall give their voice." Hence, Jerome, translating more accurately, says: "From the midst of the groves they shall give their voice." Some of the Hebrews explain it as "from the midst of the sons of the tree." <note>A Hebrew idiom for branches.</note>

**עופל** <term>Fortification</term>. A citadel, fortress, bulwark, or resistance. Micah, chapter 4: "And you, O cloudy tower of the flock, daughter of Zion," that is: "the fortress of the daughter of Zion." And in Isaiah 32: "Darkness and groping have come upon the caves." From these authorities, you may understand that our translation <note>the Vulgate</note> thinks this name signifies "gloom" or "darkness." But this is not accepted by the Hebrews, especially the learned ones. For **Rabbi Solomon** <note>Rashi, the famous 11th-century commentator</note> explains that verse which reads in Numbers 14: "But they, being darkened, went up," as: "they were fortified and strengthened for ascending." And **Rabbi David Kimhi** <note>Radak, a medieval grammarian and philosopher</note> agrees in his *Book of Roots*, saying that they lifted up their hearts and were encouraged. From this comes that which is read in Habakkuk 2: "Behold, he who is unbelieving, his soul will not be right in himself." They read it thus: "Behold the resistance, contention, or rashness." And **Jonathan the Chaldean** <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase</note> interprets it as "malignity" or "impiety." Rabbi David Kimhi says it means "pride" and "elation of heart," like an elevated and high bulwark.

**עפר** <term>Dust</term>. Genesis 2: "The Lord God therefore formed man from the mud of the earth." More correctly: "the dust of the earth." And Job 28: "Iron is taken from the earth." More truly: "from the dust." Just as in Deuteronomy 9: "Reducing it entirely into dust." In summary, this word has four meanings, which are: **dust**, **mud**, **earth**, or the **world**. From this we read the verb "to pulverize" or "to dust." In 2 Samuel 7: "And sprinkling the earth." <note>Referring to throwing dust on one's head in mourning or penance.</note>

**עפר** <term>Young Hart</term>. Song of Songs 2: "My beloved is like a goat and a young hart of the stags." And in chapter 4: "Your two breasts are like two young harts."

**עופרת** <term>Lead</term>. Jeremiah 6: "The lead is consumed." And in Zechariah, chapter 5: "And behold, a talent of lead was carried."

**עץ** <term>Wood</term> or tree. Genesis 1: "And a fruit-bearing tree making fruit according to its kind." And in Hosea 4: "My people consult their wood." <note>A reference to consulting wooden idols or divining rods.</note>

**עצב** <note>Root: Atzab</note> Worried. Strove. Irritated. Saddened. Disturbed. Provoked to anger. Corrected/Reproved. And **Genesis 6**: *And it touched the grief of his heart.* And in the same, **chapter 3**: *I will multiply your hardships/miseries.* All of these signify labor, pain, and worry. From this comes that passage in **Ecclesiastes 10** <note>The source incorrectly cites "Canticoꝝ" (Song of Songs) 10; the verse regarding "moving stones" is Ecclesiastes 10:9.</note>: *He who moves stones shall be afflicted by them.* And **Genesis 3**: *In pain you shall bring forth children.* It is written then with <term>six points</term> <note>A reference to Hebrew vowel markings (nikkud), specifically the Segol vowel, which distinguishes this noun form.</note> as in **Proverbs 10**: *And affliction shall not be joined with it.* It also signifies to work out with great care/worry. **Job 10**: *Your hands have made me.*

**עצב** <note>Root: Etzeb</note> Money; and the substance of honors. **Isaiah 58**: *And you demand [payment from] all your debtors.* Which **Rabbi David Kimhi** <note>A famous medieval grammarian and commentator known as Radak (1160–1235).</note> explains in his commentaries thus: *And you demand your money.* They are called by this name perhaps from the worry and hardship <note>original: "erumna"</note> associated with them.

**עצב** <note>Root: Itzab</note> A carved image. An idol. A likeness. A statue. From the act of shaping or making. **Hosea 4**: *Ephraim is a partaker of idols.* And **Psalm 106**: *Which they sacrificed to the carved images of Canaan.*

**עציב** <note>Root: Atzib</note> With the consonant *Mem* prefixed <note>This likely refers to a related noun form like 'Ma'atzevad'.</note>, it signifies an instrument of an ironsmith. **Isaiah 44**: *The ironsmith worked with a file.* **Rabbi Solomon** <note>Commonly known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval French commentator.</note> writes here that it is one of the tools of the blowers, or of the blowing-forge <note>i.e., a bellows or smelting tool</note>.

**עצה** <note>Root: Atzah</note> The backbone or spine. **Leviticus 3**: *And the whole tail with the kidneys.* In Hebrew thus: *And the whole tail, taken away close to the spine.*

**עצל** <note>Root: Atzel</note> Lazy. Idle. **Proverbs 6**: *Go to the ant, O sluggard.* And in **chapter 31** of the same book: *And she does not eat the bread of idleness.*

**עצם** <note>Root: Atzam</note> Was strong. Strengthened. Was brave. Prevailed. **Daniel 11**: *And he shall overcome with a small people.* And **Genesis 26** <note>The source cites Genesis 6, but this quote is from Genesis 26:16.</note>: *Since you have become much mightier than us.* And **Psalm 38**: *But my enemies live and are strengthened.*

**עצם** <note>Root: Etzem</note> Bone. **Genesis 2**: *This is now bone of my bones.* And **Psalm 102**: *My bone has cleaved to my flesh.* And it is declined in the plural in both the masculine and the feminine. **Ezekiel 37**: *And the bones came together, each bone to its joint.* In the masculine, however, it is thus in **Ecclesiastes 11**: *And by what reason the bones are joined together in the womb of a pregnant woman.* The word is perhaps derived from "strength" and "fortitude."

**עצם** <note>Root: Etzem</note> Substance. Body. Appearance. **Lamentations 4**: *Ruddier than ivory...*

->**BOOK**<-

Call the assembly. <note>original: "Vocate cœtum"</note> And if there are other interpretations, such as the festivities in which the people gather for the purpose of choosing a king, and so forth.

**עקב** <term>Aqab</term> <note>Hebrew root for "heel" or "to supplant."</note> He supplanted. Jeremiah 9: *Every brother will utterly supplant.* And Genesis 27: *He has supplanted me these two times.* <note>A reference to Jacob (Ya'akov), whose name is derived from this root, taking Esau's birthright and blessing.</note> From this comes the adjective; Hosea 6: *Suppplanted with blood.* Also the noun for "heel," "track," or "sole of the foot." Job 18: *The sole of his foot shall be held in a snare.* And Genesis 3: *You shall lie in wait for his heel.* And "from the heel" signifies "backwards." It is declined as both masculine and feminine; masculine as in Song of Solomon 1: *Go forth after the tracks of your flocks.* Feminine as in Psalm 77: *And your tracks shall not be known.* It also signifies the "heel," "limit," "end," and "extremity" metaphorically, because the sole is the lowest/final part of the body. In those cases, it is written with "five points" <note>This refers to the Hebrew vowel system (nikkud); specifically the combination of vowels like Tsere and Segol that change the word's grammatical function.</note> as in Psalm 119: *I have inclined my heart to perform your justifications forever because of the reward.* It is written thus in Hebrew: *forever, to the end* <note>original: "לעולם עקב" (le'olam aqeb)</note>, that is, to the "heel" or end of the age. This word also metaphorically signifies the "reward of labor," because that is the end of the labor. Deuteronomy 7: *If after you have heard these judgments...* in Hebrew it is: *and there shall be a reward if you hear these judgments,* etc. That is, the "end." Our translation <note>Likely referring to the Latin Vulgate.</note> often interprets this as "retribution." Psalm 19: *In keeping them there is great reward.* It also signifies "on account of" or "because," since according to the philosophers, all things are done for the sake of the "end" <note>Referring to the Aristotelian "final cause" or purpose of an action.</note>. Numbers 14: *My servant Caleb, who was full of another spirit and followed me, I will bring in.* In the "Hebrew truth" <note>A common scholarly term for the original Hebrew Masoretic text.</note>, the word-for-word reading is: *And my servant Caleb, because* <note>original: "propterea qp"</note> *there was another spirit with him, he fulfilled [his walk] after me, and I will bring him in.*

**עקד** <term>Aqad</term> <note>Hebrew root for "to bind."</note> He bound; he tied. Genesis 22: *And when he had bound Isaac his son.* <note>This refers to the "Akudah" or the Binding of Isaac.</note> From this is named the place where shepherds are accustomed to tie sheep by joining the front and back legs together, or the place where sheep are shorn. It is then written with "five points," that is, by way of the *Tsere* and *Segol* vowels. 1 Kings 10: *When he had come to the shepherds' cabin.* From this, such "bound" sheep take their name, as in Genesis 30: *Spotted and variegated and sprinkled with diverse colors.*

**מעקה** <term>Ma'aqeh</term> <note>Hebrew for "parapet" or "railing."</note> A railing which is fixed in front of buildings so that nothing can fall from there. Our translation <note>The Vulgate.</note> considers it to mean a "wall." Deuteronomy 22: *When you build a new house, you shall make a wall for the roof round about, lest you pour...* <note>The text ends mid-sentence at the bottom of the page.</note>

...[so that] blood is not brought upon your house, and you become guilty if another person slips and falls headlong. <note>Original Latin: "datur sanguis in domo tua et sis reus labente alio et in praeceps ruente." This is the conclusion of a scriptural citation regarding building a parapet on a roof to prevent accidents.</note>

**עָקַל** (*Aqal*) He perverts. Its passive verbal noun is commonly used. Habakkuk 1: "Therefore perverse, <note>original: "perversum"</note> or unjust, or twisted judgment goes forth."

**עֲקַלָּתוֹן** (*Aqallathon*) Twisted, perverse, or a winding snake. Isaiah 27: "And upon Leviathan the twisted serpent."

**עֲקַלְקַלָּה** (*Aqalqallah*) Perverse, devious, unjust, or twisted. Judges 5: "By devious paths." <note>original: "per calles devios"</note>

**עָקַר** (*Aqar*) He uprooted, eradicated, or plucked out. Ecclesiastes 3: "A time to plant and a time to pluck up." And Zephaniah 2: "And Ekron shall be uprooted." Because of this, the Hebrew teachers call the root letters of words **עִקָּר** <term>Ikkar (meaning "root" or "essence")</term>, as Rabbi Moses Kimchi <note>A famous 12th-century Hebrew grammarian from Spain.</note> says in his grammar in the chapter on letters, as if they are the sinews of words. Likewise in Joshua 11: "He hamstrung their horses." <note>The Latin "subnervavit" literally means "to cut the sinews," echoing the "nerve/sinew" metaphor for roots.</note>

**עָקָר** (*Aqar*) Impotent, sterile. Psalm 113: "Who makes the sterile woman dwell in the house." This is also spoken of a man in the masculine form. It is thought to be called this because it is as if something has been uprooted, eradicated, or plucked out from them by which they could have produced offspring.

**עַקְרָב** (*Aqrab*) A scorpion. Numbers 34: "By the Ascent of the Scorpions." And Deuteronomy 8: "The scorpion and the parching serpent." <note>original: "dipsas," a legendary snake whose bite caused uncontrollable thirst.</note>

**עִקֵּשׁ** (*Iqqesh*) Perverse. Deuteronomy 32: "A perverse and crooked generation." Also in 2 Samuel 22: "And with the perverse, you will be perverted." From this comes the verb in Micah 3: "And you pervert all things that are straight."

**עֲרִירִי** (*Ariri*) Bereaved, childless, or one who has no children. Genesis 15: "I go childless." And in the plural in Leviticus 20: "They shall die childless." Also a little later in the same chapter: "They shall be without children."

**עַרְעָר** (*Ar'ar*) A species of tree growing in desert places; some think it is the juniper. Because of its lowliness and its tangled nature, they say it signifies the captivity of the Hebrews. They apply the verse from Psalm 102 to this: "He has regarded the prayer of the lowly." Others believe this word signifies tamarisks. <note>original: "myricae"</note> Jeremiah 17: "For he shall be like a tamarisk in the desert."

...Like willows by flowing waters. <note>original Latin: *Quasi salices iuxta fluentes aquas*</note>

**To cry out** <note>Hebrew: *Arag* (ערג)</note>, as is the specific nature of a deer. Our translation renders this as **to long for**. *Psalm 42*: "As the deer longs for the water springs, so my soul longs for you, O God."

**A line of plantings** <note>Hebrew: *Arugah* (ערוגה)</note>. Our translation renders this as **a small garden bed**. *Song of Solomon, chapter 5*: "His cheeks are like beds of spices." And in the plural in *Ezekiel, chapter 17*: "That it might water it from the beds of its growth."

**Wild Ass** <note>Hebrew: *Arod* (ערוד)</note>. That is, a wild donkey <note>original Greek: *onos agrios*</note>. *Job, chapter 39*: "And who loosened the bonds of the wild ass?" It is an animal intermediate between a mule and a donkey.

**To uncover** or **to strip** <note>Hebrew: *Arah* (ערה)</note>. According to our translation in *Isaiah, chapter 22*: "And the shield stripped the wall." But some of the Hebrew scholars say "the shield **clings** to the wall." Others say that *Kir* <note>Hebrew: *Qir*, meaning "wall"</note> becomes the name of a city of the King of the Assyrians, as in *Isaiah, chapter 15*: "And its inhabitants, being shielded, uncovered their shields." This is how Rabbi David Kimhi <note>A celebrated 12th-century grammarian and biblical commentator</note> records it in his commentaries on Isaiah. Likewise in *Leviticus, chapter 20*: "She herself has opened the fountain of her blood." And regarding what we read in *Habakkuk, chapter 3*: "Rousing, you will rouse your bow," the masters of the language attribute it to this word, explaining it thus: "In baring, you will bare your bow."

**To pour out**, **to empty**, or **to clear out** <note>Hebrew root: *Arah* (ערה), a secondary sense</note>. *Isaiah, chapter 53*: "Because he delivered his soul unto death," that is, he poured it out. So also in *Genesis, chapter 24*: "And pouring out her jar into the troughs." In this sense, they understand the verse in *Lamentations, chapter 4*: "You shall be drunk and made naked," which they read as "**you shall be emptied**." For it is the custom of drunkards to empty themselves by pouring out wine from within. And *Psalm 137*: "Who say: empty it, empty it, even to its foundation." From this comes the word for **shame** <note>Hebrew: *Ervah*</note>, which our translation renders as **filth** or **nakedness**, specifically referring to the private parts of a person, as in *Leviticus, chapter 18* nearly throughout. Thus, it signifies filth, abomination, and the detestation of any thing.

**To be joined** or **to adhere** <note>Hebrew root: *Arah* (ערה), a third sense</note>. *Isaiah, chapter 22*: "And the shield stripped the wall," for which the Hebrews read, "and the shield adhered to the wall." From this is derived:

**Herbs and grasses** <note>Hebrew: *Ariyot* (עריות)</note> which adhere to the soil with tiny roots. Whence things are said both "to take root" and "to adhere by the roots." Our translation interprets this from the previous word in *Isaiah, chapter 19*: "The riverbed shall be bared."

Genesis 34: *Nor give our sister to an uncircumcised man.* Word for word: *We cannot do this thing, giving our sister to a man who has a foreskin.* And Genesis 17: *An uncircumcised male whose flesh of his foreskin has not been circumcised.* However, it is said of any man who possesses a hardened heart, or disordered and clumsy lips and ears, that he is "uncircumcised." ...interpreted. <note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing an entry from the previous page.</note> Not that "to gnaw" or "to eat" is signified, but rather **to flee** and **to put to flight**. **ערש** **Bed. Cot.** Deuteronomy 3: "And his iron bed is shown." And Psalm 41: "The Lord will bring help to him upon his bed of pain." And Song of Songs 1: "Our little bed is flowery." And sometimes it changes the letter *shin* into *samech* <note>a phonetic shift between two similar "s" sounds in Hebrew</note>, as in Psalm 6: "I will water my couch with my tears."

**עשש** **Moth. Worm.** By the <term>apocope</term> <note>the loss of a sound at the end of a word</note> of the last letter. Isaiah 50: "The moth shall eat them." From this arises the verb in Psalm 6: "My eye is troubled by fury, corroded and darkened," as if covered by the glass of a lantern. Similarly, Psalm 31: "My eye is troubled in anger, my soul and my belly." Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible</note> translated it everywhere as "it grew dim." But what about the bones? Since it follows "and my bones are troubled," where the same word is used.

**עשב** **Herb.** Genesis 1: "Let the earth bring forth green herb and bearing seed according to its kind." And in the same [book], chapter 3: "And you shall eat the herb of the earth." And it is written with five points <note>referring to the Hebrew vowel markings</note> and is also declined in the feminine gender, as in Proverbs 27: "And the hay is gathered from the mountains," that is, the herb of the mountains. And the letter *shin* is pronounced with a <term>dagesh</term> <note>a dot in a Hebrew letter indicating it should be emphasized or doubled</note> for the sake of euphony <note>to make the word sound more pleasing</note>.

**עשה** **Prepared. Made. Adapted.** Lamentations 2: "The Lord has done what he purposed." From this comes the passive verb in Ecclesiastes 1 regarding "all things that are done under the sun." It should have been translated: "which were made under the sun." And a little above: "What is it that was made? That very thing which is to be made." And Deuteronomy 21: "And she shall trim her nails." More truly thus: "And she shall adapt her nails." -># SECOND<-

**PEAH** <note>Hebrew: *pe’ah* — corner, side, or edge</note>
Boundary, limit, side, a small angular part. Exodus 26: "Therefore twenty shall be on the **southern side**," and below: "And on the **second side** which turns toward the north." And in the same book, chapter 25: "And you shall place them in **four corners**." From this arises the word that signifies—according to my teacher Jacob Jehiel—to scatter through the corners of the world. Deuteronomy 32: "And I said, where are they?" which, according to the property of the language, should be read thus: "I said I will scatter them through the corners or sides of the world." According to the first meaning, they understand that verse of Leviticus 19: "**Neither shall you round off your hair**," that is, the ends or corners of your head. Likewise in the same place: "**Nor shall you shave your beard**," or more correctly: "Neither shall you destroy the end of your beard." And thus it signifies the curls of the head or beard.

**PA'AR** <note>Hebrew: *pa’ar* — to glorify, beautify, or boast</note> Glory and magnificence <note>original Greek: *kai megaloprepeia*</note>. Isaiah 61: "**And I would give them a crown instead of ashes**," for which the seventy interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> more correctly translated "**glory instead of ashes**." It is found at the end with a double 'r' in Nahum chapter 2. From this comes the verb "**to glory**," as in Exodus 8: "**Appoint for me when I shall pray for you**," for which Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Shlomo Yitzhaki, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the foundational medieval French commentator on the Torah and Talmud</note> explains as "**glory against me**"—that is: "may you have that glory so that you may choose the time for yourself, which glory I ought to have had, namely, that the choice should be mine." So correctly in Judges 7: "**Lest Israel glory against me**." Similarly in Isaiah 10: "**Shall the axe glory against him who cuts with it?**" From this, under another form, comes the noun "glory" in Psalm 89: "**For you are the glory of their strength**," that is, magnificence <note>original Greek: *megaloprepeia*</note>, and thus it is one of the ten enumerations in the Kabbalah <note>The *Sefirot*, or the ten divine attributes/emanations in Jewish mysticism</note>. It is also found to signify a "branch."

**PAG** <note>Hebrew: *pag* — early or unripe fig</note> An immature fig, also called a green fig. Song of Songs 2: "**The fig tree has brought forth its early figs**."

**PIGUL** <note>Hebrew: *pigul* — something foul, especially sacrificial meat that has become ritually unclean</note> Profaned, execrable, abominable. For thus Rabbi Solomon explains Leviticus 19: "**It shall be profane and guilty of impiety**," that is, execrable, abominable, and profaned. Thus in Ezekiel 4: "**And no unclean meat has entered into my mouth**," that is, cursed and profaned.

**PAGA** <note>Hebrew: *paga* — to encounter, reach, or entreat</note> He met, he encountered, he prayed, he entreated, he interceded. Genesis 32.

As in Joshua 9: *And they did not ask the mouth of the Lord.* From this it is manifest that in the cited verse of Exodus, it should not be written "of man" <note>genitive case</note> as if governed by the noun "mouth," but "for man" in the dative case, as it is governed by the verb "made." **<term>Napach</term>** <note>Hebrew: נפח. This root generally refers to the act of blowing or breathing.</note> **He breathed** or **blew**. **SECOND**

**פוקה** <note>original: "Pukah"</note> A stumbling block and a groaning of the heart. From the First Book of Kings, chapter 25 <note>Modern 1 Samuel 25:31</note>: "This shall not be a cause of grief <note>original: "singultum," literally a sobbing or hiccup</note> to you." From this comes the meaning of wavering and the loosening of the limbs. Nahum, chapter 2: "And the knees shake <note>original: "dissolutio geniculorum," a loosening of the knees</note>."

**פוק** <note>original: "Puq"</note> He brought forth, drew out, or obtained. Proverbs, chapter 18: "And he shall draw favor <note>original: "iocunditatem," meaning pleasantness or delight</note> from the Lord," which is to say, he shall derive his will from God.

**פור** <note>original: "Pur"</note> He fell. From this comes the transitive verb meaning "he caused to fall," "he made void," "he dissolved," or "he scattered." Psalm 33: "The Lord scatters the counsels of the nations," or according to <term>Jerome</term> <note>The 4th-century translator of the Vulgate Bible</note>, "he dissolves their counsels." Genesis 17: "Because he has made my covenant void." And in another form with the letter 'Res' doubled, it is found in Psalm 74, which we read as: "By your power you established the sea." But Jerome more correctly translates it as: <margin>you crushed</margin> "You shattered." The word is also found doubled upon itself as **פרפר** <note>original: "Parpar"</note> in Job, chapter 16: "I was once wealthy, but suddenly I was broken to pieces." More accurately, word for word, it is: "I was wealthy and he broke" or "scattered" or "oppressed me." For from the word for "oppressing," **פורח** <note>original: "Purah"</note> signifies a winepress. Isaiah 63: "I have trodden the winepress alone."

**פור** <note>original: "Pur"</note> A lot. Esther, chapter 3: "The lot was cast into the urn." Indeed, this "lot" was called "Pur," not the urn itself, as the text later clearly states: "And he cast <term>Phur</term>," which in our language is translated as "lot." And it follows: "From that time these days were called <term>Purim</term>," that is, the "Days of Lots," because the "Pur"—that is, the lot—had been cast into the urn.

**פוש** <note>original: "Push"</note> It increased, it abounded, or it was spread out. Habakkuk, chapter 1: "And his horsemen shall spread out." And in Malachi, chapter 4, where our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> holds: "And you shall leap like calves from the herd," the Hebrews more correctly read it as: "And you shall grow like calves at the stall." They believe that from this verb is named the greatest of rivers, the **Pishon**, which Jerome—witnessed in his book *Hebrew Questions*—believes to be the **Ganges**, on account of its increase and overflowing. For into it, as <term>Pliny</term> <note>Roman naturalist and author</note> notes in the fifth book of his *Natural History*, nineteen rivers are said to flow. But <term>Rabbi Solomon</term> <note>Also known as Rashi, a famed 11th-century Jewish scholar</note> writes that it is the **Nile**, for it frequently floods nearly all of Egypt, especially when the sun is in the sign of Cancer. It was formerly called the "Melo," as <term>Seneca</term> <note>Roman philosopher</note> wrote concerning the geography of India, and it is one of the largest rivers in the whole world, though its source is unknown.

As Lucan says in book 10: Nature has not revealed the secret of your source to anyone; nor has it been permitted for peoples to see you, O Nile, when you are small. <note>original Latin: "Arcanum natura caput non prodidit ulli: Nec licuit populis paruum te Nile uidere." This quote from the Roman poet Lucan refers to the mystery of the Nile River's headwaters, comparing the hidden things of nature to the mysteries of language or scripture.</note>

**פות** <note>The Hebrew root *POTH*</note> **The hinge** of a door. 1 Kings 7: "And the hinges of the doors of the inner house."

**פזז** <note>The Hebrew root *PAZAZ*</note> **He grew strong**; he was fortified and strengthened. Genesis 49: "And the bonds of his arms and hands were dissolved." <note>This verse describes the strength of Joseph.</note> Rabbi Solomon <note>Solomon ben Isaac (1040–1105), better known as Rashi, the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> seems to want to explain this sentence based on the following word which signifies gold, so that it might be understood as: "And the arms of your hands shall be gilded by the hands of the mighty one of Jacob," that is, by the Lord who is the strong one, who is the God of Jacob. Others, however, such as Rabbi David Kimhi <note>A famous 12th-century Hebrew grammarian and philosopher from Provence.</note>, read it this way: "And the arms of your hands shall be strengthened." See also 2 Samuel 6: "Leaping and singing before the Lord," or more correctly, "acting manfully and strongly and leaping before the Lord."

**פז** <note>The Hebrew root *PAZ*</note> **Refined gold**, which has been perfectly purified. Psalm 21: "You have placed a crown of precious stone on his head," which Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420), the translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> much more correctly renders thus: "You shall place a crown of refined gold on his head." And 1 Kings 10: "And he clothed it with gold that was very yellow," that is, with golden gold, which is to say, most pure, namely of the highest value. He is playing on the word above. And here the letter *mem* is prefixed to the word "sons," but sometimes the letter *aleph* is prefixed in its place with the same meaning, as in Daniel 10: "And his loins were girded with refined gold."

**פזר** <note>The Hebrew root *PAZAR*</note> **He dispersed**, scattered, or squandered. Psalm 52: "Since God has scattered the bones of those who please men." And Jeremiah 50: "Israel is a scattered flock." And Psalm 141: "Our bones are scattered near hell."

**פחד** <note>The Hebrew root *PACHAD*</note> **He feared**, dreaded, was afraid, or terrified. Isaiah 33: "The sinners in Zion are terrified." And Psalm 14: "There they trembled with fear." The following half-verse, according to ancient volumes, should be pierced with an obelisk <note>An 'obelisk' (÷) was a scholar's mark used in ancient manuscripts to denote text that was considered doubtful, fake, or corrupted.</note> <margin>the same</margin>. So also the three preceding verses in the same Psalm, from the one that begins, "Their throat is an open sepulcher," <margin>these verses are not found</margin> until the one that ends, "before their eyes," are not found there in the Hebrew, nor even in the Greek among reliable copies <margin>such as "their throat is an open sepulcher"</margin>. For which reason, I wonder that Nicholas of Lyra <note>A Franciscan teacher (c. 1270–1349) whose literal commentary on the Bible was highly influential.</note> commented on that passage. I praise more highly the "Burgensian" <note>Paul of Burgos (c. 1351–1435), a Jewish convert to Christianity who wrote famous "Additions" to Lyra’s work, correcting him on Hebrew matters.</note> who did not pass over it so cursorily, but mentions that note in his golden and precious additions. Jerome, in his Psalter translated from the "Hebrew truth" <note>The phrase 'Hebraica veritas' was used by Jerome to describe the original Hebrew text of the Old Testament.</note>, also did not include them. Likewise Hosea 3: "And they shall fear before the Lord and His goodness." From this comes the nouns fear, dread, stupor, and fright.

**[Hebrew: פלל / Palal]** He performed what was owed: he did what is right. He pronounced the law. He executed justice. He judged. In the First Book of Kings <note>original: i. Regum; now known as 1 Samuel</note>, chapter 2, we read: *If a man sins against another man, God can be appeased for him; but if a man sins against God, who shall pray for him?* There, those learned in the Hebrew language interpret it thus: *If a man sins against a man, a judge shall judge him; but if a man sins against the Lord, who shall appoint a judge for him?* <note>The author is highlighting a translation difference: where the Latin Vulgate says "pray," the Hebrew context implies "judge."</note> And here, remember what I taught you above: that the word *Elohim* can signify a "judge," while the *Tetragrammaton* <term>Tetragrammaton: the four-letter sacred name of God (YHWH)</term> refers only to God. Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204)</note> determines this more extensively in the second chapter of the first book of his *Guide for the Perplexed*.

These points contribute to the understanding of the verse of the prophet Eli cited above. For the first—that is, our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note>—does not seem to agree with Saint James, who says: *Is any among you sick? Let him bring in the priests of the church, and let them pray over him... and the prayer of faith shall save the sick man... and if he be in sins, they shall be forgiven him.* <note>James 5:14-15</note> Therefore, even one who has sinned against God can have others who pray for him, and through that prayer, his sins shall be forgiven.

Likewise, we read in Psalm 106 according to our translation: *Phinehas stood up and appeased, and the slaughter ceased.* <note>Psalm 106:30; original: "placauit"</note> In that context, it is certain that Phinehas did not use any prayer to God, but rather a single execution of justice, as is written in Numbers, chapter 25. Therefore, this word cannot be transferred to mean "prayer" or "appeasement through supplication," but must refer to the "rigor of judgment" and the "execution of justice." Jonathan the Chaldean <note>referring to the Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase</note> expressly approves this in the verse mentioned above from the First Book of Kings, chapter 2. From this comes the name in Job, chapter 31: *for this is a crime and a very great iniquity.* More correctly, it should be: *this is an iniquity to be rigorously judged.* It also receives the letter *yod* through epenthesis <term>epenthesis: the addition of a letter or sound to the middle of a word</term>.

However, a word of this kind in the *Hithpael* conjugation <term>Hithpael: a Hebrew verb form that often indicates reflexive action (doing something to oneself) or intense action</term> also signifies "to pray" and "to ask." As in Genesis, chapter 20: *And he shall pray for you, because he is a prophet.* And further down: *And while Abraham prayed, God healed Abimelech.* From this comes the noun for "prayer," as in the title of the ninetieth Psalm: *A prayer of Moses, the man of God.* And in the Fourth Book of Kings <note>2 Kings</note>, chapter 20: *I have heard your prayer.* This is derived from the higher meaning: for he who prays to God asks that God might judge him according to His mercy, and not look upon the multitude of evils he has committed.

**[Hebrew: פלא / Pala]** It was unknown, hidden, concealed, or a secret. Deuteronomy, chapter 17: *If you perceive a judgment to be difficult and ambiguous for you...* which Onkelos <note>The author of the Targum Onkelos, an Aramaic translation of the Torah</note>, according to some books, translated into the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> as: *When a matter is to be clarified or explained by you.* But other Hebrew books translate...

<meta>This page continues a linguistic analysis of Hebrew roots, specifically focusing on terms related to "hiddenness," "secrecy," and "miracles." The author, Johannes Reuchlin (referred to here by his Greek pseudonym Capnion), is comparing Hebrew scripture with Aramaic (Chaldean) and Greek translations.</meta>

->BOOK<-

They hold the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> version better in this way: *When something is hidden or covered from you.* And so Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the famous 11th-century Jewish scholar</note> explains that little verse of Deuteronomy 30: *This commandment which I command you today is not above you.* More properly, word for word, it is: *because that commandment which I command you today is not hidden nor separated from you,* where the present verb is placed. From this comes the expression for one whose name is not brought forth: **Peloni** <note>original: פלוני</note>, that is, "such and such a man" or "such and such a woman," or someone known to us, or "a certain person." 

In Ruth 4: *Sit here,* calling him by his name—which is read corruptly, for the truth of it is this: *Sit here, someone who is widowed* <note>original: *aliquis uiduus*</note>, as if he were saying, "Sit here, man of widowhood." And this word retains the same meaning that it has among the Greeks as **ho deina** <note>original: ὁ δεῖνα</note>, that is, "a certain one," namely someone whose name I do not wish to bring forth. Although others think this word can be declined, saying in the nominative **ho deinas** <note>original: ὁ δεῖνασ</note>, I nevertheless find **ho deina** in Philostratus’s *Life of Apollonius*, book 3. And in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 26: *Go into the city to a certain man* <note>original: τον δεινα - ton deina</note>.

From that which is secret and unknown is also derived the word that follows: **Pela** <note>original: פלא</note>, meaning "miraculous," "wonderful," "a miracle," or "extraordinary." In Exodus 15: *Doing wonders,* that is, performing a miracle. And in the plural in the first chapter of Lamentations: *She has been brought down violently.* More correctly: *And he made miracles small.* And in the feminine form, as in Psalm 119: *Your testimonies are wonderful.* And in Isaiah 9: *And his name shall be called Wonderful,* for "miraculous" or "extraordinary," as we have written more clearly in our **Capnion** <note>Reuchlin refers to himself by his scholarly name, likely citing his earlier work 'De Rudimentis Hebraicis'</note>. 

From this comes the transitive verb in Psalm 17: *Make your mercies wonderful,* where in certain Hebrew books the letter *aleph* is changed into *he*, especially in recently printed ones; and although in some old parchments I have it written with an *aleph*, I also possess another very ancient parchment volume in which it is found with a final aspirated *he* in place of the *aleph*. And in Psalm 31: *Because he has made his mercy wonderful to me.* The letter *nun* is also placed before this name, as in Psalm 105: *Remember his wonders.* Sometimes the letter *mem* is also placed before it, as in Job 37: *Great and perfect knowledge.* 

And from the word above is derived that which is read in Numbers, chapter 6: *When they make a vow to be sanctified and wish to consecrate themselves to the Lord.* Which word, translated word for word, is: *A man or a woman, when they have hidden themselves, segregated themselves, or concealed themselves to vow the vow of a Nazirite* <note>A person who took a vow of holiness involving abstaining from wine and not cutting their hair</note> or a monk. And thus, in the manner of the word above, it signifies "segregation."

פלך <term>Pelekh: A spindle or a district.</term> It signifies a woman’s spindle. 2 Samuel 3: "And one who holds a spindle and falls by the sword." פלס <term>Peles: A scale or a straight path.</term> A rule of weight. That is, the iron indicating the balance, which is called a "tongue" or a leveling-tool. The Hebrews [read] thus: "The straight gait of the just you shall weigh or balance."

[Hebrew: פִּנָּה <note>original: pinnah</note>] **Corner**. Proverbs 7: *He passes through the street near the corner.* And a little further down: *Lurking near every corner.* In the feminine plural, Job 1: *And it struck the four corners of the house.* But in the masculine gender, Zechariah 14: *Even unto the gate of the corners.* And Psalm 118: *He has become the head of the corner.* Because the corners of a house are strong, therefore a fortress and a robust tower are called by this word. Zephaniah 1, where we read, "over the fortified cities and over the high corners," the Hebrews understand "over the fortified cities and over the tallest towers." And so Rabbi David Kimhi <note>A famous 12th-century grammarian and commentator often cited by Christian scholars</note> explains in his commentaries on the Twelve <note>referring to the twelve "Minor Prophets" of the Old Testament</note>.

[Hebrew: פְּנִינִים <note>original: peninim</note>] **Pearls, gems, precious little stones**. Our translation <note>referring to the Latin Vulgate</note> (I know not why) turns this into "ancient ivory" in Lamentations 4: *Redder than ancient ivory*, meaning they shine with a beauty more than gems. Some understand it this way: more than corals.

[Hebrew: פַּנַּג <note>original: pannag</note>] **A proper name of a place in the land of Israel**, where the best wheat grows—namely, Minnith <note>original: adminith</note>, which the book of Judges mentions in chapter 11, for those traveling from Pannag. Ezekiel 27: *Judah and the land of Israel themselves were your merchants; they set forth in your markets the first wheat, balsam, honey, oil, and resin.* Rabbi Joseph ben Gorion <note>The purported author of the 'Josippon,' a history of the Jews popular in the Middle Ages</note> explained it as an ointment of balsam which is found to be best in Jericho; hence the city also received its name from its most sweet scent <note>The Hebrew name for Jericho, Yericho, is related to the word 're’ach,' meaning scent</note>. Jerome <note>The 4th-century translator of the Vulgate Bible</note>, in the verse cited, writes that Symmachus and Theodotion <note>Translators of the Bible into Greek</note> carried this word over exactly as it is placed among the Hebrews as "Agla," for which the Septuagint <note>The earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> used "ointments," and he himself translated as "balsam."

[Hebrew: פָּנָה <note>original: panah</note>] **Turns, looks at, regards, notices**. Deuteronomy 31: *Because he followed alien gods*; for which the Hebrew truth <note>original: "veritas hebraica," a scholar's term for the original Hebrew text</note> has it: *Because he turned toward alien gods.* And Jeremiah 2: *They turned their back to me and not their face.* Ezekiel 36: *Because behold, I am for you and I will turn to you.* And in the same, chapter 43: *Its steps, however, turned toward the east.* And another noun from the same, chapter 44: *Which looked toward the east.* And in the same, chapter 11: *Which looks toward the rising of the sun.* And in the same, chapter 9: *Which looks toward the north*, that is, which causes one to look.

[Hebrew: פָּנַי <note>original: panai</note>] **Face or countenance**, because it looks here and there. Genesis 16: *I flee from the face of Sarai my mistress.* It also receives the letters *mem* and *lamed* at the beginning <note>The author is noting how the word changes with prefixes, like 'from' (mi-) or 'to' (li-)</note>. ...before the face of the God of Jacob. And Psalm 17: *From your presence let my judgment come forth.* <note>original: "De uultu tuo iudiciū meum prodeat." The author is discussing the various ways "face" or "presence" is rendered in the Bible.</note> From there: *to the face, in the face, in the sight of, before the face*; all of which we translate as *in the presence of*. For example, Genesis 25: *He died in the presence of all his brothers*; and such a phrase is understood as meaning *while all his brothers were still living*. Sometimes it receives only the letter <term>lamed</term> <note>the Hebrew letter ל, used as a prefix meaning "to" or "for"</note> at the beginning without the <term>mem</term> <note>the Hebrew letter מ, often used as a prefix meaning "from"</note>; and it signifies *before*. Psalm 72: *His name endures before the sun.* From this comes the name *interior* and *inner*, as if it were *more forward* [or *in front*]. This is said of the inner temple which was before the oracle. 1 Kings 6: *And he placed the cherubim in the midst of the inner temple.* However, regarding what is written in Psalm 45: *All the glory of the king’s daughter is from within*, it should be understood as being fixed in the countenance [or face]. In this case, the final <term>he</term> <note>the Hebrew letter ה</note> is a <term>paragoge</term> <note>an extra letter added to the end of a word for emphasis or poetic meter</note>. Because the anger of a man is discerned in his face, it therefore also signifies "anger." As in Psalm 33: *The face of the Lord is against those who do evil*, that is, the anger of the Lord.

**פנה** <note>Hebrew root: Panah</note> He cleared out, or emptied. It is written with a <term>dagesh</term> <note>a grammatical point/dot in Hebrew used to indicate a "hard" sound or a doubled consonant</note>. Genesis 24: *I have prepared the house and a place for your camels.* It is more correctly rendered: *I have cleared out the house.* And Zephaniah 3: *He has turned away your enemies.* That is, according to <term>Rabbi David Kimhi</term> <note>Known as Radak (1160–1235), a famous medieval grammarian and biblical commentator</note> in his commentary on the Twelve [Minor Prophets]: *He has cleared out your enemy.* For it is in the singular number, and he cleared him out so thoroughly that he should no longer be in your land. For this, he cites the verse quoted above.

**פנק** <note>Hebrew root: Panaq</note> He indulged—if it were permissible to speak this way in Latin—he fed delicately, or nourished in luxuries. Proverbs 29: *He who delicately brings up his servant from childhood.*

**פס** <note>Hebrew root: Pas</note> A thread or yarn of various colors. Genesis 37: *And he made him a multi-colored tunic.* <note>The "coat of many colors" given to Joseph</note> That is, one made of many threads of different colors. The word <term>polymita</term> <note>multi-colored or embroidered</note> is composed of *poly*, meaning "many," and *mitos*, meaning "thread" or "yarn." It is not as our <term>Lyra</term> <note>Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349), a Franciscan teacher whose biblical commentaries were highly influential</note> derived it from a "plurality of drops" [or spots]. Whether that tunic was made of silk or not cannot be determined by any man from the text. Rabbi David Kimhi, in his *Book of Roots*, says that the cloth of that tunic was woven from multicolored threads, each of which had its own specific appearance. Therefore, the truth of the Scripture is this: *And he made him a tunic of multicolored threads.*

**פסת** <note>Hebrew root: Pissat</note> A cake or a small pastry. Psalm 72: for that which we read as *There shall be a firmament on the earth on the tops of the mountains*, the Hebrew truth holds: *There shall be a small cake of grain.* Rabbi David Kimhi explains it as a "particle of grain." Here, Nicholas of Lyra thought it was a scribe’s error, who wrote *firmamentum* [firmament] instead of *frumentum* [grain]. I, however, am of the opinion that it happened through a fault...

As in 1 Kings 13: *And Saul mustered the people*, <note>original: "Et recensuit Saul populum"</note> meaning he numbered them. Likewise in Numbers 1: *You shall number them by their companies*. It also signifies to command, as in Ezra 1: *And he himself commanded me to build him a house*. According to Dioscorides <note>An ancient Greek physician and botanist</note> in his fourth book on medicinal woods, it is called the *wild gourd* by the Romans, and by others it is named *dog fungus*. It is sharply bitter, as the same author writes; hence it follows in the cited passage of 2 Kings 4: *And there was no longer any bitterness in the pot*. There is also another species fit for food which is called the *colokyntha*, <note>original: "colokyntha"</note> about which Dioscorides writes in his second book. Many think it is so named from the previous word due to its shape and oblong roundness.

# **BOOK**

...firstly. "Increase and multiply" <note>Genesis 1:28</note>. Likewise in Psalm 128: "Your wife is like a fruitful vine," meaning one that bears fruit. Likewise in Genesis 1: "A fruit-bearing tree making fruit," that is, a wood producing fruit. Therefore, from this [root], it also signifies fruit. Amos 9: "They shall make gardens and eat the fruit of them." And in the first Psalm: "Which shall give its fruit in its season." It is sometimes found written with an *aleph* in the middle through <term>epenthesis</term> <note>original: "catepenthesin"; a grammatical term for adding a letter into the middle of a word.</note>.

**פרז** [PRZ] — An open village without a wall and without fortification. Zechariah 2: "Jerusalem shall be inhabited without walls." You will find this in both the masculine and feminine gender. Esther 9: "But those Jews who lived in towns that were not walled and in villages." For those who live without a wall are called **פרזים** [*perazim*] and villages that are not fortified or walled are called **פרזות** [*perazot*].

**פרח** [PRCh] — To flower or germinate. Numbers 17: "It was found that the rod of Aaron in the house of Levi had germinated," meaning it had flowered. And in Song of Songs 6: "If the vines had flowered." And in Psalm 92: "The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree." And in the same: "They shall flourish in the courts of the house of our God." It is also used figuratively in Leviticus 13: "But if the leprosy should break out [flower], spreading in the skin." Ezekiel 7: "The rod has flowered, pride has germinated." Because this word is also applied to the raising of young birds and flight, it therefore signifies "flying away" as well. Ezekiel 13: "Behold, I am against your pillows with which you catch flying souls," for the <term>Targum</term> <note>An ancient Aramaic translation and commentary of the Hebrew Bible.</note> explains this word as "to fly." From this, young birds [chicks] are called **אפרחים** [*ephrochim*]. Deuteronomy 22: "And the mother sitting upon the young [chicks] or the eggs."

**פרט** [PRT] — Berries or individual grains of grapes, according to <note>original: "rabi Salomonem"</note> Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to Rashi, the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator (1040–1105).</note>. Leviticus 19: "Neither shall you gather the clusters and the fallen grains in your vineyard."

**פרט** [PRT] — To particularize or articulate, as is done on musical instruments with a varied touch. Amos 6: "Who sing to the sound of the lute." Hence, in the arts, they are called "particulars."

**פרך** [PRK] — Cruelty and rigor. Exodus 1: "And in all the service in which they were oppressed in the works of the earth." In Hebrew it is thus: "And in all the ministry in the field and all their service of those who served them in cruelty or rigor." And a little earlier where it is read: "And they afflicted them, mocking them," the Hebrew reads thus: "And the Egyptians made the children of Israel serve in cruelty, rigor, and savagery."

**Para** <note>original: "פרע"</note> **He uncovered/stripped/made idle.** Exodus 32. "Moses, seeing the people were naked [exposed]." For Aaron had stripped them; that is, he had uncovered them. **[פתשגן - *patshégen*]** <note>original: "Exemplar. copia ſcripturę. ſummarium. inſtructio."</note> **Copy.** A copy of a writing. A summary or instruction. **Esther 3**: "The summary of the letters was this."

**[פתה - *patah*]** <note>original: "Induxit. lactauit. affecit."</note> **He led.** He enticed or affected. **Hosea 2**: "Because of this, behold, I will entice her." This word is similar to, and effectively the same as, the previous verb.

**[פתה - *patah*]** <note>original: "Dilatauit."</note> **He enlarged.** **Genesis 9**: "May God enlarge Japheth."

**[פתח - *patach*]** <note>original: "Aperuit. incepit."</note> **He opened.** He began. **Psalm 78**: "And he opened the doors of heaven." Likewise in **2 Kings 9**: "And you shall open the door and flee." And in **Judges 3**: "And seeing that no one opened [it]." From this the word for "key" is derived, as in that same passage: "They took the key and, opening, they found their lord." From this also comes "closure" or "enclosure." <note>original: "clauſura uel clauſtrum"</note> **Micah 7**: "Keep the doors of your mouth." It also signifies "to loosen." **Isaiah 20**: "Loosen the sackcloth from your loins." It also signifies "to show." **Psalm 37**: "The sinners have unsheathed the sword," <note>original: "Gladium euaginauerunt"</note> that is, they showed it. So too in **Song of Songs 7**: "If the flowers bring forth fruit," <note>original: "Si flores fructum parturiunt"</note> that is, if the still-unripe grapes show themselves. And from the act of "opening" is derived the word for gate, door, or entrance. **Numbers 10**: "The whole crowd will be gathered to you at the entrance of the tabernacle of the covenant." It is written thus with the first letter having a <term>Segol</term> <note>A Hebrew vowel mark indicating a short 'e' sound.</note>.

**[פתל - *patal*]** <note>original: "Subuertit. et ſecundum quoſdam addidit. adiunxit. affixit."</note> **He subverted.** And according to some, he added, joined, or fastened. **Genesis 30**: "The Lord has compared <note>The Latin 'Comparauit' here refers to the wrestling or competition between Rachel and Leah.</note> me with my sister." But <note>Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349) was a Franciscan whose literal-sense commentaries on the Bible were standard for centuries.</note> **Nicholas of Lyra**, the standard commentator of our Bible, wrote that in Hebrew it is held thus: "By the addition of God, I have been added with my sister." Others, however, say: "By the subversion of God, I have been subverted with my sister." For she [Rachel] was not yet to be compared with her sister [Leah], who had personally borne three sons, while the sister [Rachel] had only two, not from herself but from a servant. This word certainly signifies a certain "twisting" or "perversion," as in **Proverbs 8**: "There is nothing crooked or perverse in them." Likewise in **Psalm 18**: "With the perverse, you will be perverse."

**[פתיל - *pathil*]** <note>original: "Filum duplicatum."</note> **A doubled thread.** **Judges 16**: "As if one were to break a thread of flax."

**[פתן - *pethen*]** <note>original: "Serpens peſſimus. aſpis."</note> **A most evil serpent.** An asp. **Isaiah 11**: "And the infant shall delight over the hole of the asp." And **Psalm 58**: "Like the deaf asp." And in the plural in **Job 20**: "He shall suck the head of asps."

BOOK 2

-><term>Tze’elim</term> [צאל]<- <margin>[Hebrew script in margin]</margin>
A grove or a certain kind of shrub. Our translation <note>The author refers to the Latin Vulgate, the standard Bible of the time</note> renders this as **shadow**. Job 40: *He sleeps under the shadow in the secret of the reed and in moist places*; that is, he sleeps under the shrubbery. From this it follows: *there the shadows protect his shadow*, meaning the shrubs protect his shadow. This is an **antiphrasis** <note>A figure of speech where a word is used in a sense opposite to its actual meaning, suggesting the Behemoth is so large that even "shadows" are overshadowed by him</note>, because there is no tree so high that it could cover his shadow.

-><term>Tzav</term> [צב]<-
A covering, a lid, or a roof. Numbers 7: *Six covered wagons with twelve oxen*; as if to say, six wagons, each with its own covering, and twelve oxen. **Onkelos** <note>A famous 2nd-century convert to Judaism known for his Aramaic translation of the Torah</note> explains this in Aramaic <note>original: "chaldaice"</note> as: *six wagons individually covered*. However, the **Jerusalem Targum** <note>A collection of Aramaic translations and expansions of the Hebrew Bible</note> translates it this way: *Six yoked wagons*, as if to say six pairs of beasts. Likewise, it is the name of a certain unclean animal which we call a **crocodile**. Leviticus 11: *The weasel, and the mouse, and the crocodile*; others name it a **toad**.

-><term>Tzaba</term> [צבא]<-
He served in the army, he trained, he waged war, or he fought. As in Zechariah 14: *All the nations that fought against Jerusalem*. And in Numbers 31: *And when they had fought against the Midianites*. From this comes **fight**, **army**, or **military service**, as in the same place cited above: *He said, arm men from among yourselves for the fight*, and in Numbers 1: *All who were able to go forth to war*. Sometimes the Hebrew letter **aleph** [א] is found changed into **he** [ה] <note>A technical linguistic observation about how Hebrew roots can shift their spelling in different biblical books</note>, as in Zechariah 9: *And I will surround my house with those who serve me*. From this comes **militia** or **host**. Isaiah 24: *On that day the Lord will visit the host of heaven on high*. It is declined in the plural in both genders. In the masculine, Psalm 103: *Bless the Lord, all his hosts*. In the feminine gender, Psalm 24: *The Lord of hosts, he is the king of glory*.

-><term>Tzaba</term> [צבא]<-
An appointed time, or a destined limit. Job 7: *The life of man upon earth is a warfare* <note>original: "Militia"</note>; which according to **Rabbi Solomon** <note>Known as Rashi (1040–1105), the most influential medieval Jewish commentator</note> and other Jews should be read: *is there not an appointed time for man upon the earth?*

-><term>Tzavah</term> [צבה]<-
It swelled, it grew large, it was puffed up, or it burst with swelling. Numbers 5: *And may your swelling womb be torn asunder*; and below: *And with a swelling womb may the thigh rot*; and also in the same: *And with an inflated belly the thigh shall rot*.

# THE SECOND BOOK

**<term>צבי (Tzvi)</term>** A fawn, a roe deer, or a gazelle. <note>original: "Hinnulus.capreolus seu caprea"</note> From Deuteronomy 14: "The deer and the **gazelle**." And from Song of Songs 4: "Like two fawns, twins of a **gazelle**." And likewise in chapter 2: "My beloved is like a **gazelle** or a young stag." Sometimes the letter *aleph* is used in the middle instead of the letter *yod*. Song of Songs 3: "I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the **gazelles** and the stags of the fields."

**<term>צבי (Tzvi)</term>** Excellence, pleasantness, pleasure, beauty, and distinction. <note>original: "Præcipuum.iocundũ.beneplacens.decorũ et egregiũ"</note> From Ezekiel 20: "Which is the **most distinguished** among all lands." And again: "The **excellent** land of all." And Isaiah 28: "In that day the Lord of hosts will be a crown of glory," which Jonathan <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel, the purported author of the Aramaic Targum</note> translates into Aramaic <note>original: "chaldaice"</note> as: "In that time the Messiah of the Lord of hosts shall be a crown of joy." From this, the Land of Israel is called by that name—that is, "pleasing," "beautiful," and "distinguished" to God. Therefore, where we read in Daniel 8: "And it grew great toward the south, toward the east, and toward the **fortress**," <note>The Latin Vulgate uses "fortitudinem" (fortress/strength)</note> the masters of the Hebrew language read it as "toward the south, toward the east, and toward the **Land of Israel**." To support this, I cite Rabbi Levi ben Gershom <note>A famous 14th-century philosopher and commentator also known as Gersonides</note> in his commentaries on Daniel, who writes: "And it grew great toward the south, this refers to the King of Egypt; and toward the east, this refers to the land of the Persians; and toward the land of **צבי (Tzvi)**, this refers to the Land of Israel." Thus he concludes.

**<term>צבט (Tzabat)</term>** He seized or gathered together. Ruth 2: "And he **gathered** parched grain for her." This means that Boaz reached out at the table and took from the bundles of roasted grain—that is, grain dried by fire, which is afterwards cooked in a broth—and he set before Ruth the Moabite her portion.

**<term>צבע (Tzava)</term>** To discolor or dye. <note>original: "Discolorauit"</note> From this comes "speckled" or "variegated." Jeremiah 12: "Is my heritage to me like a **speckled** bird?" They say, however, that this is a bird hated by all other birds; for this reason, it is always bloodstained and splattered with the marks of wounds. From this, that which we read in Judges 5 is explained: "**Garments of various colors** were handed over as spoils," <note>original: "fissaræ"</note> meaning spoils splattered with bloodstained marks. From this:
**<term>אצבע (Etzba)</term>** A finger. Exodus 8: "This is the **finger** of God." And Numbers 19: "And dipping his **finger** in its blood."

**<term>צבר (Tzabar)</term>** He collected or heaped up. Job 27: "If he **heaps up** silver like dust." Likewise Habakkuk 1: "And he shall **heap up** a mound and capture it." From this, a "heap" <note>original: "aceruus"</note> is named.

**צד** <term>Side</term> <note>original: "Latus"</note>. Isaiah 60: *And your sons shall rise from your side.* And Psalm 91: *A thousand shall fall at your side.* A <term>dagesh</term> <note>a grammatical dot placed in a Hebrew letter to indicate doubling or emphasis</note> is placed in these to show the rejection of another letter *daleth*. In the plural, Exodus 25: *Six branches shall come out of its sides: three from one side and three from the other side.*

**צדה** <term>Watched</term> or <term>lay in wait</term> <note>original: "Speculatus est; insidiatus est"</note>. Exodus 21: *But if he did not lie in wait.* And 1 Samuel 24: *But you lie in wait for my soul to take it,* meaning you watch so that you may take my life. From this comes the noun in Numbers 35: *Or if he threw anything at him by lying in wait.* There is also another passive verb of this form which means to be desolated and devastated. Zephaniah 3: *Their cities are desolated,* that is, they are devastated.

**צדק** <term>Justified</term> <note>original: "Iustificauit"</note>. Psalm 51: *That you might be justified in your words,* meaning, for this reason you will justify in your words. It is used transitively in Proverbs 17: *And he who justifies the wicked.* And in the passive, Psalm 143: *Because no living thing shall be justified in your sight.* From this comes "just." Genesis 6: *Noah was a just man.* And in the plural, 1 Kings 2: *Because he killed two men more just and better than himself.* From this is derived both "justice" and "justification," and many other terms.

**צהב** <term>Golden-colored</term> <note>original: "Auricolorauit"</note>. Leviticus 13: *And the hair is yellow and thinner than usual,* standing for "and the hair is golden-colored," as if it were derived from **זהב** <note>original: "zahav"</note>, which means "gold."

**צהל** <term>Rejoiced</term>, <term>whinnied</term>, <term>exulted</term>, or <term>danced for joy</term> <note>original: "Iubilauit; hinniuit; exultauit; tripudiauit"</note>. Isaiah 12: *Exult and praise, inhabitant of Zion.* And Esther 8: *And the whole city exulted and was glad.* In Hebrew it is: *And the city of Susa exulted and was glad.* And Isaiah 23: *They shall whinny from the sea,* that is, from the waters.

**צהר** <term>A window</term> that receives the light of day in a house. Genesis 6: *You shall make a window in the ark.* From this comes **צהרים** <note>original: "tsohorayim"</note>, meaning "midday" or "noon," when the sun pours out light in the middle of the sky. Genesis 43: *Because today the men are going to eat with me at noon.*

**יצהר** <term>Oil</term> <note>original: "Oleum"</note>. 2 Chronicles 32: *Storehouses also for grain, wine, and oil.* From this comes a verb which means to press out oil in the oil-presses, as if one were permitted to say "to oil-make." Job 24: *Among their heaps they spent the noon,* <note>original: "meridiati sunt"</note> where the translator looked back to the previous word <note>the translator of the Vulgate Bible likely confused the word for "oil" with the word for "noon" due to their shared root</note>. And Zechariah 4: *These are...*

**צאן** A flock of any kind of cattle or sheep. Jeremiah 50:6: *My people have been a lost flock.* <note>original Latin: "Grex perditium factus est populus meus."</note> In this instance, the word is written with the letter *aleph* in place of a *vau*, which also sounds like a vowel; but elsewhere it is written without the *aleph* and without the *vau* by a shortening of the word <term>syncopen</term>. Psalm 8:7: *All sheep and oxen.* <note>original Latin: "Oues et boues uniuersas."</note> I must admit, however, that at the end a soft breathing sound is attached <note>original: "κατα παραγωγηv" (kata paragogen) — a Greek grammatical term meaning "by derivation" or the addition of a letter to the end of a word.</note>, though this is rare.

**צור** He surrounded; he besieged; he attacked; he built against; he invaded. <meta>This page continues a lexical study of Hebrew roots beginning with the letter Tsade, focusing on their various meanings in Biblical contexts and philosophical applications.</meta>

SECOND [BOOK]

**צור** <note>Hebrew root: *Tsur*</note> He enclosed, he bound, he tied in a knot. From Deuteronomy 14: "And you shall turn it into a price <note>original: "in precium rediges"</note> and carry it in your hand and go to the place." This phrase is more correctly read word-for-word as: "And you shall give it in money, and you shall **bind** or **enclose** the silver in your hand and go to the place." Similarly, from 2 Kings 5: "And he **bound** <note>original: "ligauit"</note> two talents of silver in two bags."

**צור** <note>Hebrew root: *Tsur*</note> A rock, a flint, a stone. From Exodus 17: "Behold, I will stand there before you upon the **rock** of Horeb, and you shall strike the **rock**." It appears in the masculine plural in Nahum 1: "And the **rocks** <note>original: "petrę"</note> are broken down by him." It appears in the feminine plural in Job 28: "He cuts out a river among the **rocks**." From this is derived the concept of "strong" and "strength." From Isaiah 26: "Trust in the Lord forever, in the Lord God, the **strong one** <note>original: "forti"</note> for eternity." And from 1 Samuel 2: "And there is none **strong** like our God."

**צר** <note>Hebrew root: *Tsar*</note> This is used metaphorically for the **Moon**. From Isaiah 5: "And behold, the darkness of tribulation and the light is darkened in its gloom," which the Hebrews read as: "And behold, the darkness of the **moon** <note>original: "lunę"</note> and the sun is darkened in its gloom."

**צור** <note>Hebrew root: *Tsur*</note> An edge or sharpness. From Psalm 89: "You have turned away the help of his sword," which is more correctly translated: "You have turned back or blunted the **edge** <note>original: "aciem"</note> of his sword."

**צרה** <note>Hebrew root: *Tsarah*</note> He formed, he fashioned, he made. From Exodus 32: "And he **fashioned** <note>original: "formauit"</note> it with a carving tool." And from Isaiah 44: "He who created you, Jacob, and **fashioned** you, Israel." From this, the Hebrew philosophers derive the word for <term>form</term> <note>The philosophical concept of "Form" vs "Matter"</note>, as found in the work of Moses the Egyptian <note>The famous philosopher Maimonides</note> in the second volume, first chapter of his *Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: "libri perplexorum"</note>.

**צואר** <note>Hebrew word: *Tsavvar*</note> The neck. From Genesis 41: "And he put a gold chain around his **neck**." And from Genesis 34: "And clasping his **neck**." Because the neck moves here and there, to the right and the left, we often use the plural form of this name even for a single person. As in Genesis 45: "And when he had fallen in embrace upon the **neck** <note>original: "collum," though the Hebrew is plural</note> of Benjamin." And further down: "He also likewise wept upon his **neck**." In these places, "neck" is written in the plural; sometimes it takes the letter *nun* and loses the letter *aleph*, as in Song of Songs 4: "And with one chain of your **neck**."

**צחת** <note>Hebrew root: *Tsachach*</note> Dryness or aridity. From Ezekiel 24: "He poured it out upon a very **clear** rock," and further: "I have set her blood upon a very **clear** rock, that it should not be covered." In all these places, the true meaning is: "upon a **dry**, waterless, and arid rock." So too in Isaiah 5: "And its multitude is **parched** with thirst."

# BOOK

**צח [Tsach]** Clear, bright, or shining. Lamentations 4: "Brighter than milk." And Song of Songs chapter five: "My beloved is white and ruddy." In the feminine plural, it signifies words that are polished, elegant, and shining.

**צחן [Tsachan]** Rot or stench. Joel 2: "And his stench shall rise because he acted proudly."

**צחק [Tsachaq]** He played or laughed. Genesis 18: "Hearing this, Sarah laughed." And below: "Why did Sarah laugh?" And again: "Sarah denied it, saying, 'I did not laugh.'" And Exodus 32: "And they rose up to play."

**צחר [Tsachar]** Shining or bright. Judges 5: "You who ride upon shining asses."

**צי [Tsi]** A ship. Isaiah 33: "No galley with oars shall pass over it."
And in the plural, Numbers 24: "They shall come in triremes <note>Ancient warships with three banks of oars</note> from Italy; they shall overcome the Assyrians and lay waste to the Hebrews, and at the last they themselves shall also perish." Here, I would have you take keen notice of the Chaldaic translation <note>The Aramaic Targum, a traditional Jewish translation/paraphrase</note>, which suggests that the Romans will torment the Hebrews, but in the end, they too will perish.
And Isaiah 33: "And they shall meet with satyrs <note>original: "onocentauris," mythical creatures half-man and half-donkey</note>." I do not know why our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> rendered it this way, but the proper nature of the language holds it so. "And ships shall reach the islands." According to my teacher Jehiel <note>likely Jehiel ben Jekuthiel Anav, a noted 13th-century Jewish scholar</note>, it also signifies solitude and dryness.

**ציון [Tsion]** A sign, a marker, or a monument. Ezekiel 39: "They shall set up a marker <note>original: "titulum"</note> beside it until the buriers have entombed them." It also signifies dryness when the first letter is written with a *qamets* <note>a Hebrew vowel mark indicating an "a" sound</note>. Isaiah 25: "Like heat in a thirsty land, or even in a wasteland."

**ציץ [Tsits]** It blossomed or flourished. Ezekiel 7: "The rod has blossomed; pride has budded." And Psalm 72: "And they shall flourish out of the city like grass." And Numbers 17: "And with swelling buds, the flowers had broken forth." This is more accurately read word-for-word as: "And behold, the rod of Aaron for the house of Levi had budded; the leaves were brought forth, and the flower blossomed." All these, according to the proper nature of the Hebrew language, signify the prominence and visibility of the swelling nodes on trees that first produce flowers and then fruit. From this, it signifies by extension to be evident, to look out, or to stand out. As in Song of Songs 2: "Peering through the lattices." Likewise, Psalm 132: "But upon him shall my sanctification flourish," that is, his crown shall appear or stand out.

**[Hebrew: צלה]** To roast, which our translation <note>Likely referring to the Latin Vulgate</note> interprets as "cooked." Isaiah 44: "He cooked the pottage and was satisfied." More accurately: "He roasted the roast." And Exodus 12: "They shall eat the meat only when roasted with fire."

**[Hebrew: צלח]** To prosper. Jeremiah 12: "Why does the way of the wicked prosper?"

And in Psalm 1: *And all whatsoever he shall do shall always prosper.* <note>original: "Et omnia quẽcumq̃ faciet semper prosperabuntur"</note> And in 1 Chronicles 22: *May the Lord be with you and may you prosper.* And in Psalm 118: *O Lord, grant good prosperity.* From this comes another word which is not far from that one in meaning; for it signifies "to pass through with prosperity," as in 2 Kings 19: *And breaking through the Jordan, they passed through the fords before the king.*
