**צלע** <term>Rib</term> <note>Hebrew: *Tzela*</note>. Side. Genesis 2: *And the Lord God built the rib which he had taken from Adam.* And in the plural in the same place: *He took one of his ribs.* And because the ribs of a living creature are on both sides, it also signifies the right or left <term>side</term>. Exodus 26: *And set the lampstand against the table on the south side of the tabernacle.*

**צלע** <term>He limped</term> <note>Hebrew: *Tzala*</note>. Genesis 32: *But he himself limped on his foot.* From this comes <term>fracture</term>, as when someone has broken a leg. Psalm 38: *But I am prepared for scourges.* <note>original Latin: "Ego aut̃ in flagella paratussum"</note> Jerome <note>The translator of the Vulgate Bible</note> translates this as "wounds," while the Hebrews translate it as "destruction" and "fracture."

**צמת** <term>Band</term> <note>Hebrew: *Tzammah*</note>. A headband or veil with which we bind the hair or curls. Song of Solomon 4: *Besides that which lies hidden within.* And Isaiah 47: *Uncover your shame,* for which it is more correctly: *Open your binding.*

**To Thirst** <note>Hebrew root: צמא (Tsama)</note>. ->BOOK<-

...most. Numbers 33:55: "And spears in your sides." The Hebrews translate this word as **thorn** or **small spike**. <note>original Latin: "spinam seu spiculum"</note> Joshua 24:12: "And stakes in your eyes."

**צנצנת** A **vial**, **pitcher**, or a **vessel** made of clay, earth, or glass, which has a wide belly and a narrow mouth. Onkelos <note>A famous 2nd-century translator of the Torah into Aramaic</note> calls this in the Chaldean [Aramaic] language *zeluhith*, meaning a **pitcher**. Exodus 16:33: "Take one vessel and put manna there."

**צנח** He **descended** or **turned aside**, as when someone wishes to dismount from a horse. Judges 4:21: "Striking it with a hammer, she drove it through his brain into the ground." More accurately: "And she made it descend into the earth." <note>This refers to the story of Jael and Sisera</note>

**צנע** He **humbled** himself or **stayed in hiding**. Proverbs 11:2: "But where there is humility, there is also wisdom."

**צנף** He **clothed**, **wrapped around**, or **bound**. Leviticus 16:4: "He shall place a linen miter upon his head." From this root you get the name for a **miter**, which we call a **turban**, **headband**, or rather a **fillet** or **head-band**. <note>The author lists several synonyms for head coverings: "tiaram, vittam, uel potius teniam seu fasciam capitalem"</note> Ezekiel 21:26: "Remove the miter, take off the crown." Thus far the word is found with the consonant prefix *mem* and the ending letter *thau*; it is also found with the same meaning without those letters, as in Zechariah 3:5: "Place a clean miter upon his head," and "they placed a clean miter upon his head."

**צנק** **Shackles**, **fetters**, a **bond**, or a **prison**. Jeremiah 29:26: "That you might put him in the stocks and in the prison."

**צנור** A **pipe** or **channel** through which water is diverted from the roof of houses into a cistern <note>original: "castellum"</note>; some call this a **floodgate**, others an **impluvium** [rainwater basin]. Psalm 42:7: "At the voice of your floodgates." <note>original Latin: "cataractarum"</note>

**צנתר** An **outlet** or **nasal channel**. According to Jerome <note>The 4th-century translator of the Vulgate Bible</note>, this is called *myxoter* in Greek <note>original Greek: μυξωτηρ</note>, meaning the passage through which the excess fluids of the head flow down. According to the Greek scholar Suidas, these are like the "beaks" or "spouts" of the nostrils. For this reason, our translation of Zechariah 4:12 renders it: "Which are beside the two golden beaks."

**צעצע** A **metalworker**, **bronze-caster**, or **sculptor**. 2 Chronicles 3:10: "Two cherubim of sculptural work," meaning "made by sculptors."

**צעד** He **walked**, and as if **stepping**, he **processed**. Proverbs 30:29: "There are three things that walk well." Genesis 49:22: "The daughters ran about over the wall," that is, they walked over it. To make the Hebrew expression congruent, it is understood as: "Each of the daughters walked..."

<meta>This page continues a lexicographical entry for Hebrew roots beginning with the letter Tsade (צ), specifically focusing on verbs and nouns related to movement, clothing, and size. It maintains continuity with the previous discussion of "stepping" or "walking."</meta>

# BOOK

...was. For it is a verb in the singular number. And in Habakkuk 3: "In your anger you will tread upon the earth" <note>original Latin: *In fremitu conculcabis terram*</note>. From this comes "walking" and "stepping," as in Psalm 18: "You have widened my steps under me" <note>original Latin: *dilatasti gressus meos subtus me*</note>. It is found, however, with an *aleph* at the beginning and a *he* at the end, and according to our translation, it signifies a *periscelis* <note>An anklet or leg-band</note>. Numbers 31: "Anklets and bracelets" <note>original Latin: *Periscelides et armillas*</note>. This comes from the Greek *peri* <note>original: περι</note> meaning "around" and *skelos* <note>original: σκελος</note> meaning "leg"—almost like a leg-ornament for around the shins. Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek historical encyclopedia</note> writes that these are women’s undergarments. Rabbi David Kimhi <note>A famous medieval Jewish grammarian and commentator</note> explains this word as an ornament for the arm, as if "stepping" upon the arm; however, he asserts that it is the same as the ornament that runs from the shin to the foot. He notes that the first is found written with an *aleph*, but the second without an *aleph*.

**צעד** <note>Hebrew root: Ts-A-D</note> He runs about. It refers to wandering from place to place. Jeremiah 2: "Under every leafy tree you lay down as a harlot"—that is, you wandered about. To this Virgil alludes: "And she flees to the willows, and wishes to be seen beforehand" <note>A quote from Virgil's *Eclogues* 3.65, comparing the biblical wandering to a playful or deceptive flight</note>. And in Jeremiah 48: "And I will send to him those who tilt [vessels], and they shall empty him" <note>The Latin *stratores* usually refers to those who spread or level, but in this biblical context, it refers to those who decant wine jars by tilting them</note>.

**צען** <note>Hebrew root: Ts-A-N</note> He moved or transferred. Isaiah 33: "A tabernacle that can never be moved" <note>original Latin: *Tabernaculum quod nequaquam transferri poterit*</note>.

**צעף** <note>Hebrew root: Ts-A-P</note> A woman's garment; a veil. Our translation renders this as a *theristrum* <note>A light summer veil or shawl</note> in Genesis 38: "Who, having laid aside her widow's garments, took up a veil" <note>original Latin: *theristrum*</note>. As Suidas writes, a *theristrum* is a summer garment; it is also called a *theristrion*. The translation would more correctly have said *Calyptra*—that is, a linen cloth with which women veil their heads. For the Hebrew text reads thus, word for word: "And she removed the garments of her widowhood and was covered with a *calyptra* <note>head-veil</note>, fine linen, or a cloak."

**צעק** <note>Hebrew root: Ts-A-Q</note> He cried out. Lamentations 2: "Their heart cried out to the Lord" <note>original Latin: *Clamauit cor eorum ad dominum*</note>. And Psalm 107: "And they cried out to the Lord when they were in trouble." From this comes the noun "cry." Genesis 27: "And he bellowed with a great cry." It is more correctly: "And he cried with a great cry." It has the same meaning as the word written with the letter *zayin* <note>Referring to the root זעק (Za-A-Q), which also means to cry out</note>.

**צער** <note>Hebrew root: Ts-A-R</note> To make small; to belittle. Job 14: "Whether his sons be noble or ignoble, he does not understand." In Hebrew, this reads: "His sons are honored, and he does not know; they are diminished <note>made small</note>, and he does not perceive them." From this comes "Junior," "moderate," "lesser," or "small." Job 8: "Though your beginnings were small." More correctly: "And your beginning shall be small or moderate." And without the letter *mem*, as in Micah 5: "And you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, are small among the thousands of Judah." And Job 32: "I am younger in years." And other similar derivatives.

**<term>צפצף</term>** (Tsaf-tsaf): He chattered, muttered, chirped, or whispered. <note>original: "Garriuit.mussitauit.ganniuit.suggessit."</note> As in Isaiah 29[:4]: *And your speech shall mutter from the ground.* And in Isaiah 10[:14]: *And there was no one who moved a wing or opened their mouth or chirped* <note>original: "ganniret"</note> instead of "chattered" <note>original: "garriret"</note>.

**<term>צפד</term>** (Tsafad): It adhered or clung. Lamentations 4[:8]: *Their skin adhered to their bones; it withered and became like wood.*

**<term>צפה</term>** (Tsafah): A watchman or observer. <note>original: "Speculator.contemplator."</note> Ezekiel 3[:17]: *I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel*—that is, an overseer. <note>The author uses the Latin "episcopum," the root of "bishop," to describe the role of a spiritual overseer.</note> From this comes the verb in Psalm 5[:3]: *In the morning I will stand before you and I will see.* Regarding this, Jerome, in his "Hebrew Truth," <note>Jerome’s *Hebreica Veritas* was his effort to translate the Old Testament directly from Hebrew rather than Greek.</note> more accurately translates: *In the morning I will be prepared for you and I will contemplate.* Likewise in Nahum 2[:1]: *Watch the way.* It also signifies a place from which one sees from a distance, which we call a "watchtower" <note>original: "speculam"</note>, as found in the books of Samuel.

**<term>צפה</term>** (Tsafah): He overlaid or covered. Exodus 25[:11]: *And you shall overlay it with the purest gold, inside and out.* More accurately: *And you shall cover it with pure gold.* Likewise in Exodus 38[:17]: *Which he also clothed in silver*—that is, overlayed.

**<term>צפחת</term>** (Tsafachat): A jar, a bowl, a cup, a shallow dish, or a small vessel. <note>The author lists several Latin synonyms: "Cantharus.cymbium.scyphus.patera.uasculum."</note> 1 Kings <note>modern 1 Samuel</note> 26[:12]: *So David took the spear and the jar of water.*

**<term>צפיחית</term>** (Tsepichit): Sugar, or according to others, sprinkled flour. Exodus 16[:31]: *And its taste was like flour with honey.* In Hebrew: *And its flavor was like sugar in honey.* Others say it is like a dough seasoned with honey; and so it seems Rabbi Solomon <note>This refers to Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo itzhaki), the famous medieval commentator.</note> understands it.

**<term>צפון</term>** (Tsafon): The North, or the North wind. Song of Solomon 4[:16]: *Awake, O North wind, and come, O South wind.* In Greek it is *borrhas*, which we call *boreas*.

**<term>צפן</term>** (Tsafan): He hid or preserved. Song of Solomon 7[:13]: *New and old, my beloved, I have kept for you.* And Psalm 31[:19]: *Which you have hidden for those who fear you*—that is, reserved. And Job 14[:13]: *Who might grant me that you might hide me in the grave* <note>original: "inferno"</note>—that is, reserve me. From this comes "hidden thing" or "secret" or "hoard." Ezekiel 7[:22]: *And they shall violate my secret place.*

Another similar kind. Isaiah 14: "For from the root of the snake shall come forth a basilisk" <note>original: "regulus," literally 'little king,' a common medieval name for the mythical basilisk or a venomous serpent</note>. **צפע** [Tzefa] Dung, manure, excrement, or filth. Ezekiel 4: "Behold, I have given you cow dung instead of human excrement." And through the *paragoge* <note>a grammatical addition of a letter to the end of a word</note> of the feminine *he* <note>the Hebrew letter ה</note>, it signifies progeny, as well as children, sons, or grandsons.

**צרר** [Tzarar] He disturbed, provoked, troubled, or acted as an adversary. Numbers 33: "And they shall harass you in the land where you dwell." Many words are derived from this, such as in Psalm 118: "Out of my distress I called upon the Lord." Likewise in Psalm 116: "The perils of hell found me; I found trouble and sorrow."

**Tsarar** <note>original Hebrew: צרר</note> Bound. Proverbs 30: "Who has bound the waters as if in a garment?" ->SECOND<-

<term>Tsirah</term> <note>original: צרעה; traditionally a hornet or wasp</note>. The name of a winged reptile that kills men with its sight. <note>The author here conflates the hornet with mythical creatures like the cockatrice or basilisk.</note> So writes Rabbi David Kimhi in his *Book of Roots*. Our translation renders it as **hornets**. Exodus 23: "Sending hornets ahead who will drive out the Hivite and the Canaanite."

<term>Tsaraph</term> <note>original: צרף</note>. He refined; he purified metals. Jeremiah 6: "The refiner refined in vain," that is, he refined the metals. From this comes the word for a goldsmith or silversmith; a refiner or worker in gold. Judges 17: "And he gave them to the silversmith to make a carved image from them." And Isaiah 40: "Or the goldsmith shall shape it with gold, and the silversmith with silver plates." From this comes the verbal noun in Psalm 18: "The words of the Lord are tested by fire." In Hebrew, it is: "The word of the Lord is purified and boiled down," namely, just as a metalworker refines gold. All derived words signify testing, purging, solidity, and firmness.

<term>Zarphath</term> <note>original: צרפת</note>. Gaul, which is now called **France**. In the final part of Obadiah: "And the exile of this army of the children of Israel, which is among the Canaanites, as far as Zarephath." Now, Zarephath is a city of the Sidonians. 1 Kings 17: "Arise and go to Zarephath of the Sidonians." But in that instance, it is written with a final "h" <note>the Hebrew letter He (ה)</note> aspiration. In the cited passage of Obadiah, however, it is written without the "h." It signifies Western France according to Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator</note> and our own Lyra <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a Franciscan scholar influential in the Middle Ages</note>. Rabbi David the Spaniard <note>David Kimhi</note> lists the meaning of this word among the western kingdoms or regions near Germany with his own interpretation, saying: "**Zarphath**, which is France." This is the common usage for all Jews.

<term>Tsfardea</term> <note>original: צפרדע</note>. A frog. Exodus 8: "And Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt and the frogs came up." More accurately: "And the **frog** came up," in the singular number. It appears in the plural a little earlier: "And bring up frogs upon the land of Egypt."

Numbers 25: "He went in after the Israelite man into the brothel." <note>original: "lupanar"</note>

**קבל** He undertook; he received; he accepted; he chose. Esther 4: "Which
she would not accept." And in the same, chapter 9: "And the Jews undertook." And Proverbs 19:
"Hear counsel and receive instruction." And 1 Chronicles 21: "Choose what you
will," though it is more correctly: "accept for yourself." From this is derived the word *Cabala* <note>Kabbalah</note>, that is, "reception," according to
Rabbi David Kimhi in the *Book of Roots*. <note>David Kimhi (c. 1160–1235) was a leading medieval Jewish grammarian and commentator.</note> From this, our seekers of hidden things
name the Cabalistic art the "science of reception," for the reason that it has been derived down to us 
through the successive reception from one person to another.

->THE SECOND BOOK<-

As was clearly shown by the most noble philosopher of our age, Giovanni Pico <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494) was a famous Italian Renaissance philosopher known for his "900 Theses" and his attempt to harmonize Christianity with Platonism and Jewish Kabbalah.</note>, Count of the Holy Roman Empire, Lord of Mirandola and Concordia, in his *Apology* written against the slanderers of his conclusions, specifically in the fifth question. From this art <note>The "art" refers to Kabbalah, a form of Jewish mysticism.</note> many think secret operations arise. Indeed, there was never a secret operation that was not called good by some and evil by others, especially by the ignorant. Thus, the magicians of Pharaoh despised the staff of Moses; thus, the Pharisees slandered the miracles of Christ. Therefore, it is no wonder if the ancient Greeks—who could never reach such perfection in <term>Kabbalistic science</term> <note>A mystical method of interpreting Hebrew scripture.</note>—seeing these secret operations, named the art itself "deceptive." This is found in Aristophanes’ comedy *The Frogs*, where Hercules says: *And not to be a trickster, as you also think* <note>original Greek: "κ μη κoβαλλαγεσιν ωσ και σοι δοκει". The author is highlighting a linguistic pun between the Greek word for trickery (kobala) and Kabbalah.</note>. But with God's help, we shall later inform those whom we find toiling over our readings in the Hebrew language about this very art.

**בלו** <note>original Hebrew: *Belu*</note> — In turn for. Ezra 4: "Therefore, we are mindful of the salt which we have eaten in the palace." Word for word, it is: "Therefore, for every exchange of the salt of the palace which we have scattered." And below: "If that city is rebuilt and its walls restored, you will have no possession beyond the river." More correctly: "In that turn, there shall be no portion for you beyond the river."

**קבע** <note>original Hebrew: *Qaba*</note> — He seized, snatched, shook, extorted, or committed injury or violence. Malachi 3: "Shall a man afflict God? For you afflict me." And you said, "In what do we afflict you?" Which the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> translated as "if he supplants." <term>Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion</term> <note>Translators of the Hebrew Bible into Greek in the 2nd century AD.</note> rendered it as "if he defrauds." The Chaldean translation of Jonathan has: "if a man plunders before a judge." The common Jewish explanation, according to our Lyra <note>Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349), a Franciscan whose Bible commentaries were standard for centuries.</note>, is: "Shall a man do violence to God? For you do violence to me." For the Scripture speaks of God as if he were a man whose goods are taken by force. All its derivatives signify robbery, violence, and injury.

**קובע** <note>original Hebrew: *Qoba*</note> — Helmet; armor for the head. 1 Samuel 17: "And he placed a bronze helmet upon his head." In certain printed books, this word is found written with the letter *Kaph* (כ), but in the most ancient volumes, it is written with *Qoph* (ק). For I possess volumes of many years' age in which this word is written with *Qoph* in this passage; however, in one of those same ancient...

# **BOOK**

...is most closely joined a little note which the Hebrews call *Masorah* <note>original: "massarah"; the body of traditional notes on the text of the Hebrew Bible</note> and the Greeks call a *Scholion* <note>original: "scholion"; a brief explanatory comment or margin note</note>, which speaks briefly thus: not through the letter *Qoph* <note>original: "quf"</note> like the others, but through *Kaph* <note>original: "caf"</note>. Whence I think the younger scholars were moved to print it with a *Kaph* even in this place. But in Ezekiel it is also placed with a *Qoph*. Ezekiel 23: "They shall arm themselves against you on every side with breastplate, shield, and helmet." Because of these two places, you will find it written with a *Kaph* in other instances; and although the spelling is different, the meaning remains the same.

**קבעת** <term>Dregs</term> <note>Hebrew: *Kaba'at*</note>. Our translation <note>referring to the Latin Vulgate</note> rendered it as "the bottom of the vessel." Isaiah 51: "Even to the bottom of the cup of slumber you have drunk." And further down: "The bottom of the cup of my indignation." That is, the dregs, according to David the Spaniard <note>original: "Dauid hispanum"; referring to David Kimhi (c. 1160–1235), a famous medieval Hebrew grammarian and baker from Spain/France</note>.

**קבץ** <term>Gathered together</term> <note>Hebrew: *Kabatz*</note>. He collected, assembled, multiplied. Genesis 41: for that which we read as "the harvests were reduced to sheaves and gathered into the granaries of Egypt," the Hebrew truth <note>original: "ueritas hebraica"; a Renaissance term for the original Hebrew text as opposed to translations</note> has it thus: "And he collected all the food of the seven years which were in the land of Egypt." Likewise in Joel 2: "Gather the elders together."

**קבר** <term>Interred</term> <note>Hebrew: *Kabar*</note>. He buried. Genesis 23: "And so Abraham buried Sarah his wife." And Genesis 49: "Bury me with my fathers." And further down: "There they buried him and Sarah his wife." And Deuteronomy 34: "And he buried him in a valley of the land of Moab." From this comes the name "sepulcher" <note>original: "sepulchrum"</note> in the same place a little further down: "And no man knew his sepulcher."

**קדד** <term>Bowed down</term> <note>Hebrew: *Kadad*</note>. 1 Kings 24: "And David, bowing himself face down to the earth, worshipped." And Genesis 24: "The man bowed himself and worshipped the Lord." It signifies, therefore, to lower the crown of the head to the ground. Whence, when doubled, it signifies the crown of the head: **קדקד** <note>Hebrew: *Kodkod*</note>. Deuteronomy 33: "And upon the crown of the head of the Nazirite among his brothers."

**קדח** <term>Kindled</term> <note>Hebrew: *Kadach*</note>. He set on fire, glowed, burned, scorched. Deuteronomy 32: "A fire is kindled in my wrath." Likewise in Jeremiah 15: "Because a fire is kindled in my wrath." From this, "fever" <note>original: "febris"</note> is named from "burning heat" <note>original: "feruore"</note>. Deuteronomy 28: "The Lord shall strike you with want, fever, and cold." It signifies both a "sacred fire" <note>likely referring to the skin disease erysipelas</note> and a carbuncle, etc.

**קדם** <term>Anteriors</term> <note>Hebrew: *Kadam*</note>. Earlier, before, in front. Isaiah 22: "Which boasted from former days in its antiquity." More correctly thus: "From days before was its priority." Because...

->SECOND [PART]<-

Truly, the eastern region is called "anterior" <note>meaning 'the front' or 'that which comes before'</note> just as the western region is "posterior" <note>the back</note>. For this reason, it is understood as the East, as in Numbers 23: *From the mountains of the east.* Likewise, the winds are called "oriental" [eastern], as in Exodus 14: *With a violent wind blowing*; <note>original: "Flante uento uehemẽti"</note> or more correctly thus: *with an east wind.* It also stands for eternity, which is "anterior" to all things, as in Deuteronomy 33: *From the top of the ancient hills.* <note>original: "De uertice collium ęthernorum"</note> By this same name, the ancients and our ancestors of old are called, as in Psalm 77: *I have considered the days of old,* and in the last chapter of Micah: *From the days of antiquity.* From this comes the verb <term>qadam</term> <note>original OCR: "oriř"; the author is discussing the Hebrew root Q-D-M meaning 'to be before' or 'east'</note>: to place before, to propose, to anticipate, or to stand before. Our translation <note>referring to the Latin Vulgate</note> rendered this as "to offer" in Micah 6: *With what worthy thing shall I offer to the Lord?* More correctly it should be: *In what shall I stand before* or *what shall I present, O Lord?* Many other words are derived from this same source.

<term>קדר</term> <note>Q-D-R (Qadar)</note> It grew dark; he darkened; it was blackened or obscured. Micah 3: *And the day shall be darkened over them.* And Jeremiah 4: *The earth shall mourn and the heavens shall grieve;* <note>original: "mœrebunt"</note> or more correctly: *the heavens shall be obscured* or *grow dark.* Similarly in Joel 2: *The sun and the moon are darkened.* Metaphorically, this signifies humility, depression, grief, or sadness, because those who suffer such things lose their bright color and are blackened, as in Job 30: *I went mourning without heat.* <note>The author links the physical darkening of the skin in illness or grief to the Hebrew root for darkness.</note>

<term>קדש</term> <note>Q-D-SH (Qadash)</note> He initiated; he consecrated; he sanctified. Exodus 29: *And you shall consecrate them and their garments.* And in Exodus 20: *He blessed the seventh day and sanctified it.* And Exodus 13: *Sanctify unto me every firstborn.* Because that which is consecrated or sanctified is separated from common use and the dealings of the common people, such things are also called "separated," "unclean," or "polluted" in this manner: as in Haggai 2: *If a man carries sanctified flesh in the fold of his garment,* that is, profaned or polluted. <note>The author is explaining the concept of 'taboo'—that things set apart for God are 'sacred' and cannot be touched by the common, making them 'untouchable' in both a holy and a defiled sense.</note> Thus among the Latins, the word *sacrum* [sacred] signifies both the holy and also the "execrated" or "abject," as in Virgil: *The accursed hunger for gold.* <note>original: "Auri sacra fames" from the Aeneid, where 'sacra' means 'cursed' or 'holy' depending on context.</note> From this comes "sanctuary," "sanctification," "holy," etc. This present word also signifies to celebrate, to keep a feast, to prepare, to institute, and to solemnize. Jeremiah 6: *Sanctify war against her,* that is, institute or prepare for it.

<term>קדש</term> <note>Q-D-SH (Qadesh)</note> A whoremonger; a fornicator; a male prostitute. Deuteronomy 23: *There shall be no harlot among the daughters of Israel, nor a whoremonger among the sons of Israel.* Thus, by the addition of the feminine ending <note>referring to the 'He' suffix</note> it also signifies a female fornicator or a harlot.

<term>קהה</term> <note>Q-H-H (Qahah)</note> It is blunted; he dulled or beat back. Ecclesiastes 10: *If the iron be blunt...*

**GATHERED** <note>Hebrew root: *Qahal*</note> He gathered together. He held an assembly. He stirred up. He preached. In the **First Book of Chronicles, chapter 15**: "David gathered all Israel." And in **Numbers, chapter 16**: "And when they had stood against Moses and Aaron." It is more correctly translated this way: "And they were *gathered together* against Moses and Aaron." From this comes the noun for a congregation, an assembly, a gathering of people, or a church. As in the same passage: "Why are you lifted up above the people of the Lord?" More correctly: "Why are you lifted up above the *congregation* or *assembly* or *meeting* of the Lord?" From this comes "the Preacher." In **Ecclesiastes, chapter 1**: "The words of the Preacher," <note>original: "Ecclesiastis"</note> that is, of the one who speaks to an assembly, or as we say now, the <term>preacher</term> <note>original: "prędicatoris"; referring to the contemporary office of a sermon-giver.</note>.

**WAITED** <note>Hebrew root: *Qavah*</note> He sustained. He waited for. He hoped. In **Psalm 40**: "Waiting, I have waited for the Lord" <note>This is the literal Hebrew idiom for "I waited patiently."</note>. From this come nouns and participles. In **Psalm 37**: "But those who wait for the Lord, they shall inherit the land." And in **Jeremiah, chapter 14**: "We have sinned against You, O Hope of Israel." And in **Isaiah, chapter 5**: "He expected that it would produce grapes." From this comes the words for "hope" and "expectation." In **Job, chapter 5**: "And there shall be hope for the needy."

**COLLECTED** <note>Hebrew root: *Qavah* (a second meaning)</note> He gathered together. In **Genesis, chapter 1**: "Let the waters that are under the heavens be gathered together into one place." From this comes the noun, as seen a little further below: "The gatherings of waters He called seas."

**LINE** <note>Hebrew root: *Qav*</note> A rule. A standard. A line. A directory. A plumb line. In **Job, chapter 38**: "Or who stretched the line upon it?" In **Zechariah, chapter 1**: "And a plumb line shall be stretched out over Jerusalem." And in the **First Book of Kings, chapter 7**, our translation <note>The author refers to the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> has "small cord" <note>original: "resticulam"</note> thus: "And a small cord of thirty cubits encircled it," that is, a thread, a belt, or a mason's rule. And because one builds using those measuring guides, for that reason such a word is applied to building and architecture. In **Psalm 19**: "Their sound went out into all the earth"; but it is more correctly "their norm," "direction," "rule," "building," or "architecture." <note>The author is correcting a famous translation choice where the Hebrew word for "measuring line" was translated as "voice" or "sound" in ancient Greek and Latin versions.</note>

**LOATHED** <note>Hebrew root: *Qut*</note> He felt disgust. In **Psalm 119**: "I saw the transgressors and was wasting away"; more correctly, "and I loathed them." Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Bible.</note> seems to sufficiently approve this interpretation in **Psalm 95**, where [Marginal note: offended for forty years] we read: "For forty years I was offended by this generation." Jerome interprets it as: "For forty years this generation was displeasing to me," as if he were saying, "I loathed the generation." This is clearer in **Job, chapter 10**: "My soul is weary of my life," or "It loathes my life."

**LITTLE** <note>Hebrew root: *Qat*</note> Almost little, or a small amount. A very little. A tiny bit. In **Ezekiel, chapter 16**: "A very little less than almost."

**VOICE** <note>Hebrew root: *Qol*</note> Voice. In **Genesis, chapter 27**: "The voice indeed is the voice of Jacob." And frequently in **Exodus, chapter 19**.

->SECOND<-

**[Line / Measuring Line]** <note>original: "קו" (Qav)</note> The name arises from that which signifies a web. Isaiah 59:5: *The spider’s webs.* It is spelled with the letters *vau* and *shurek* <note>vau and shurek are Hebrew grammatical terms for specific vowel sounds</note>. It also signifies cold. Genesis 8:22: *Cold and heat.*

**[To Snare / To Gather]** <note>original: "קוש" (Qosh)</note> To draw near; it is fitting. Zephaniah 2:1: *Gather yourselves together, yea, gather together, O nation not desired.* In the first word, the letter *shin* is doubled; in the second, it is not doubled, but receives a *dagges* <note>A dot placed in a Hebrew letter to indicate a stronger or doubled sound</note> in its place. Others translate this as "search out" or "inquire." However, Jonathan the Chaldean <note>Referring to the Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation of the Bible</note> interprets it in Aramaic as *gather together* and *draw near.*

**[To Loathe / To Disturb]** <note>original: "קוט" (Qut)</note> To strike; to affect with trouble; to disturb. Job 10:1: *My soul is weary of my life.* More correctly: *My soul is disturbed in my life.*

**[Destruction / Sickness]** <note>original: "קטב" (Qeteb)</note> A sickness befalling a person and striking them. Deuteronomy 32:24: *And birds shall devour them with a most bitter bite.* The Jerusalem Targum <note>An ancient Aramaic translation and commentary</note> explains this as "cutting off." The "masters of secrets" <note>A reference to Kabbalists, Jewish mystics</note> well know what this word properly designates in the Art of Kabbalah, and they know its use, which is supported by the verse in Psalm 91:6: *From the arrow that flieth by day, from the business that walketh in darkness, from the assault and the noonday demon.* On this, Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator</note>, the ordinary commentator of the Jews, writes that these are the names of demons, among which this present name is placed. Just as in Isaiah 28:2: *The force of hail, a destroying tempest.*

**[To Slay / To Kill]** <note>original: "קטל" (Qatal)</note> To kill; to slay. Job 24:14: *He kills the needy and the poor.* And Job 2 <note>Though cited as Job 2, the author is likely referencing Daniel 2:13</note>: *The wise men were being slain, and they sought Daniel and his companions so that they might perish.* From this comes the word for "slayer" and "slaughter" or "killing," as in Obadiah 1:9: *That man may be cut off from Mount Esau because of the slaughter.*

**[To be Small / To be Diminished]** <note>original: "קטן" (Qatan)</note> I have been diminished; I have been made small. Genesis 32:10: *I am smaller than all your mercies.* From this comes the word for "small" and "little child." Job 3:19: *The small and the great are there.* And Isaiah 11:6: *And a little child shall lead them.* And Psalm 114 <note>Psalm 115:13 in modern numbering</note>: *The small with the greater.*

**[To Pluck / To Cut Off]** <note>original: "קטף" (Qatap)</note> To mutilate; to cut; to tear away; to pluck. Ezekiel 17:4: *He tore away the top of its twigs.* In Hebrew: *He plucked the head of its plantings.* And Job 8:12: *While it is yet in its flower, it is not plucked by the hand.* This is the passive form.

**[To Burn Incense / To Sacrifice]** <note>original: "קטר" (Qatar)</note> To smoke; to burn; to sacrifice; to offer as a burnt offering; to evaporate. Amos 4:5: *And sacrifice a thank-offering with leaven.* Leviticus 2:2: *And the priest shall burn them upon the altar.* And Song of Solomon 3:6: *Like a pillar of smoke from the spices of myrrh and...*

<meta>This page continues a lexical or encyclopedic study of Biblical Hebrew terms, likely from a Renaissance-era dictionary or commentary. It focuses on the philology of incense, vapors, and specific plants mentioned in the Bible.</meta>

# BOOK

**Of incense** <note>original Latin: *thuris*</note>. That is, a fumigation or incense of myrrh and frankincense. From this comes the name **suffumigation** <note>the act of "smoking out" or burning incense</note>, which the Greeks call *incense* <note>original Greek: *thymiama*</note>. Thus, in Deuteronomy 33: "They shall put incense in your wrath." From this also comes the word for "vapor," which our translation interprets as **hot embers** <note>original Latin: *favillam*</note>. Genesis 19: "And he saw the embers rising from the earth like the smoke of a furnace." Our Hebrew scholars read it this way: "And he looked, and behold, the vapor of the earth rose like the vapor of a furnace." But we translate it more correctly: "The smoke of the earth like the smoke of a furnace." So too in Psalm 119: "I have become like a wineskin in the frost." I would have thought this was an error of the scribe, who might have written **frost** <note>Latin: *pruinam*</note> when he intended to write **coals** <note>Latin: *pruna*</note>, except that I see in the Greek it is written as *frost* <note>original Greek: *pachne*</note>. Therefore, it was an error of the translator who turned this into the Greek language. This little verse is said of a person's skin, that it is wrinkled and dry, just as if a wineskin were hung in the smoke. Therefore it should be understood thus: "I have become like a wineskin in the smoke." But certainly the Greek interpreter varied the same word out of hesitation; for in Psalm 148, he translates it as "crystal," which Jerome <note>The 4th-century translator of the Vulgate Bible</note> turns into "ice." "Fire, hail, snow, ice." In truth, according to the properties of the Hebrew language, it signifies here a vapor rising from the earth in the likeness of smoke, on the authority of <term>Rabbi David Kimhi</term> <note>A famous medieval Hebrew grammarian and lexicographer, 1160–1235</note> in his *Book of Roots*. From this word, by using the prefix *mem*, the word for **censer** or **incense-burner** <note>Latin: *thuribulum* or *acerra*</note> is derived. Ezekiel 8: "And each one had a censer in his hand." And just as an altar is named from the incense-burner because of the fumigation of the sacrifice, so this Hebrew word is used for an **altar**. As in 2 Chronicles 30: "Overturning all the altars on which incense was burned to idols."

**קיקיון** <note>Hebrew: *Kikayon*</note> The proper name of a fast-growing tree, frequently used in the speech of the Talmudists. But its diminutive form, *kikaion*, is used in the Book of Jonah, which Jerome translates as **ivy**. For this, he was rebuked by learned men whom he himself calls "Gourd-ites" <note>Latin: *cucurbitarios*; a jab at those who insisted the plant was a gourd</note>, because they thought it was more correctly translated as **gourd**. Jonah 4: "And the Lord God prepared an ivy." But Jerome himself writes in his commentaries that the Latin language does not have a name for this species of tree. It grows most frequently in Palestine, having broad leaves like a vine-shoot. It spreads out like a branch; if you plant it, it quickly rises into a tree. And within a few days, what you saw as a herb, you now look up at as a small tree. These are the words of Jerome. In the Punic or Arabic language, it is called **elkeroa** <note>The castor oil plant, *Ricinus communis*</note>.

**קיר** <note>Hebrew: *Kir*</note> **Wall**. Leviticus 1: "He shall cause the blood to run down upon the base of the altar." More correctly thus: "Let its blood be sprinkled against the **wall** of the altar." And 1 Samuel 19: "And Saul sought to strike David..."

# BOOK

**קלת (Qallat)** **Cauldron**. Formed by the <term>paragoge</term> <note>A linguistic term for adding a letter to the end of a word; original: "per paragogen thau in fine"</note> of the letter **thau** [Tav] at the end. Our translation [the Vulgate] renders this as **pot** in Micah 3: "Just as in a kettle and like meat in the middle of a pot." Jonathan <note>referring to Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary of the Hebrew Bible</note> translates this into Aramaic as *cadra*, which we call a **cauldron**.

**קלט (Qalat)** **Closed** or **Joined**. This refers to when the cleft in an animal’s hoof grows together, resembling the hoof of a horse or mule; in such a case, the animal itself is called **joined**. Leviticus 22: "An ox or sheep with an ear or tail cut off." It is more accurately rendered as: "An ox or sheep with separated or **joined** limbs." This describes a condition where a limb that should be single splits into two, or where two limbs that should be separate grow together into one. From this word, the place of refuge called an **asylum** takes its name, because fugitives "grow together" and find common shelter there. Numbers 35: "And the assembly shall restore him to the city of refuge to which he had fled." And a little earlier: "Designate which cities shall be for the protection of fugitives."

**קלס (Qalas)** **Derision**, **mocking**, or **ridicule**. Psalm 44: "A mocking and deri-" <note>The text breaks off here at the end of the page; original: "Subfannationē et deri-"</note>

<meta>This page continues the lexical analysis of Hebrew roots, specifically focusing on terms beginning with the letter 'Qoph' (ק) and 'Tav' (ת), following previous discussions of property and measurements.</meta>

# THE BOOK

From this [root], all acquired "goods" are named, namely immovable, movable, and self-moving, such as cattle and livestock. Concerning **movable goods**, it is written in Genesis 13: *And he was very rich in possessions of gold and silver,* that is, in acquired goods. Concerning **self-moving goods**, Genesis 26: *And he had possessions of sheep and herds.* Concerning **immovable goods**, Jeremiah 32: *And fields shall be possessed.*

**קנה** [Calamus/Reed]. Isaiah 19: *The reed and the rush shall wither.* And because in the East they make staffs from cane or reed with which they measure quantities, it is therefore used as a metaphor for a **measure**. Ezekiel 40: *And a measuring reed was in its midst.* This is just as we use the terms "ell" <note>original: "ulnam," a unit of measurement based on the length of the forearm</note> or "arm." From this is also derived the term for the transverse bar from which weights are hung on either side, which our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> renders as a **scale** <note>original: "statheram"</note>. Isaiah 46: *And weigh out silver with a scale.* It also signifies **aromatic cane**. Exodus 30: *Similarly, of aromatic cane, two hundred and fifty shekels.*

**קנמון** [Cinnamon]. Exodus 30: *And of cinnamon half so much.* And Song of Solomon 4: *Pipe and cinnamon,* where it translates "cane" <note>original: "cannam"</note> as "pipe" <note>original: "fistulam," likely referring to the hollow, tube-like shape of cinnamon bark</note>.

**קטף** [He cut off, plucked, or stripped]. Ezekiel 17: *And he shall strip off its fruit and it shall wither.*

**קסם** [He practiced magic, divined, or acted as a soothsayer]. Ezekiel 13: *And you shall no longer divine divinations.* And 1 Samuel 28: *Divine for me by a spirit* <note>original: "in pythone," a reference to the Pythian spirit or a familiar spirit</note>. And all words derived from this signify the prediction of the future.

**קסת** [Inkhorn]. Ezekiel 9: *And the writer’s inkhorn was at his loins.* Others say it signifies a tablet and a writing-case; for so the Targum <note>An ancient Aramaic paraphrase/translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> explains it as *pinax*, which is *pinax* in Greek and *tabula* [tablet] in Latin.

**קעקע** [Stigmatization/Branding]. Leviticus 19: *Nor shall you make any figures or marks upon yourselves.* By this, some believe the art of **geomancy** <term>geomancy: a method of divination that interprets markings on the ground or the patterns formed by tossed soil or stones</term> is forbidden, about which Rabbi Judah Alharizi <note>A celebrated medieval Spanish-Jewish poet and translator (1165–1225)</note> and many others have written.

**תקע** [He drove away or moved]. Genesis 32: *He touched the nerve of his thigh,* that is, he moved the hip from its place of connection and dislocated it. Thus Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the foundational medieval commentator on the Torah and Talmud</note> explains it, and he cites the verse from Jeremiah 6: *Lest my soul depart from...*

**קערה** <note>Hebrew: Ka’arah</note> **A small dish or platter.** What our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> renders as a *vinegar-vessel*. **Numbers 7**: "A silver vessel weighing one hundred and thirty shekels." And **Exodus 37**: "The vessels, the bowls, and the cups."

**קפא** <note>Hebrew: Kafa</note> **It congealed; it thickened.** Our translation renders it as *gathered*. **Exodus 15**: "The depths were gathered <note>original: "congregatę"</note> in the midst of the sea." More correctly in **Job 10**: "And did you not curdle me like cheese?" **Zephaniah 1**: "The men settled on their dregs," that is, congealed and thickening upon their own dregs.

**קפד** <note>Hebrew: Kafad</note> **He cut off; he severed.** **Isaiah 38**: "My life is cut off as if by a weaver." In this same form, it names an animal that inhabits deserted places, which some wish to be a bird and others a reptile. Our translation renders it as *hedgehog* <note>original: "ericium"</note>. **Isaiah 34**: "The bittern <note>original: "onocrotalus"</note>, the hedgehog, and the ibis." Similarly in **Zephaniah 2**: "The bittern and the hedgehog." It is written at the end with a *cholam* <note>a Hebrew vowel mark representing an 'o' sound</note>.

**קפוז** <note>Hebrew: Kafuz</note> **This signifies the same as the preceding word**, whether a hedgehog or another animal. It is placed in the same chapter, **Isaiah 34**: "There the hedgehog had its nest." However, some printed books have *kiphod* there, but the older ones more correctly have *kaphon*.

**קפץ** <note>Hebrew: Kafats</note> **He closed; he shut up; he restrained; he contracted.** **Psalm 77**: "Or will he in his anger shut up his mercies?" And **Job 5**: "But iniquity shuts its mouth," that is, it concludes and restrains. And **Deuteronomy 15**: "Neither shall you close your hand, but you shall open it to the poor." And **Isaiah 52**: "Over him kings shall shut their mouths," that is, they shall close them. In the same word form, it signifies **to leap across**. **Song of Songs 2**: "Leaping across the hills."

**קצץ** <note>Hebrew: Katsats</note> **He cut off; he lopped off; he mutilated.** **Deuteronomy 25**: "You shall cut off her hand, nor shall you be moved by any pity for her." And **Exodus 39**: "And he beat it into thin threads," that is, he cut the threads. From this comes "end" and "boundary." **Genesis 6**: "The end of all flesh has come," that is, the lopping off. This sometimes takes a *nun* through <term>epenthesis</term> <note>the addition of a letter in the middle of a word for pronunciation</note> because one *tsade* is dropped; and when the letter *nun* is not present and there isn't a second *tsade*, a <term>dagesh</term> <note>a dot in the middle of a Hebrew letter indicating it should be doubled or hardened</note> is added to mark the omission.

**קצב** <note>Hebrew: Katsav</note> **He limited; he designated; he cut off; he carved; he severed.** **2 Kings 6**. <note>original: "iiij. Regum" — In the older numbering used here, 1 and 2 Kings are referred to as 3 and 4 Kings.</note>

# BOOK 2

"He cut off the wood and threw it there." <note>original: "Precidit ergo lignum et misit illuc" — 2 Kings 6:6</note>. This means he cut and leveled it so that it would be a handle for the axe. Similarly, in 1 Kings 6:25: "Both cherubim were of one measure and one workmanship." In Hebrew, it is: "One measure and one cutting <note>original: 'precisio'</note> for the two cherubim." He later translated this "cutting," changing the sense of the word, as "sculpture." 1 Kings 7:37: "And with a similar measure and sculpture," meaning "shape" or "cutting." It is also translated as the extreme or final limit. Jonah 2:7: "I went down to the lowest points <note>original: 'extrema'</note> of the mountains." From the idea of leveling through cutting, the Song of Songs 4:2 says: "Like a flock of shorn sheep," meaning precisely leveled or equally shorn.

**קצץ** [Katsats] **To cut down, cut off, or mutilate.** Habakkuk 2:10: "You have cut down many peoples." More correctly: "by cutting down peoples," for the word is a gerund. From this comes "mutilated" or "cut off and truncated." Proverbs 26:6: "Lame in the feet and drinking iniquity." From this also comes "end," "corner," or "extremity." Exodus 25:19: "Let there be one cherub on one side and another on the other." In Hebrew: "And let the faces of the cherub be one from this end <note>original: 'extremitate'</note> and one from that end." It appears in the masculine in Psalm 65:5: "The hope of all the ends of the earth." And in the feminine in the same Psalm: "And those who inhabit the boundaries shall fear." Various translators have rendered this differently; for "boundary" or "extremity," they have used "summit." Deuteronomy 4:32: "From one end of heaven to its other end." It also has another meaning: to be weary or nauseated. Numbers 21:5: "Our soul now loathes <note>original: 'nauseat'</note> that very light food." Here Rabbi Solomon <note>A reference to Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo itzhaki), the medieval commentator.</note> explains this word through what was written slightly earlier: "And the people began to be weary of the journey."

**קצח** [Ketsach] **Black cumin, fennel flower, or gith.** <note>term: Gith: An archaic name for Nigella sativa (black cumin), often used in early botanical and biblical texts.</note> Isaiah 28:25: "He shall sow the gith and scatter the cumin." And further on: "For the gith shall not be threshed with iron tools." And again: "But the gith shall be beaten out with a rod."

**קצין** [Katsin] **Captain, prince, or lord.** Isaiah 3:7: "Do not appoint me a leader of the people."

**קצע** [Katsa] **To scrape off or shave away.** Leviticus 14:41: "He shall cause the house to be scraped within, all around." When combined with the preposition *mem* <note>The Hebrew letter 'm' (מ) used as a prefix</note>, it signifies "a corner." Nehemiah 3:20: "After him Baruch the son of Zabbai built a second measure from the corner <note>original: 'angulo'</note> to the door of the house." And 2 Chronicles 26:9: "Above the corner gate." And Ezekiel 46:21: "By the four corners of the court," etc. It also signifies—through the addition of the letters *he* and *yod* <note>Referring to the Hebrew word 'Ketziot'</note>—a certain spice which we call cassia. Psalm 45:8: "Myrrh and stacte and cassia."

...did not call his brother. And in Psalm 99: <note>original: "Inuocabant dominum & ipse exaudiebat eos"</note> "They called upon the Lord and he heard them." From this comes the verbal noun. Isaiah 45: "I am the Lord who calls your name, the God of Israel." From this, men who are renowned, great, and most excellent leaders are so named. Numbers 26: "These are Dathan and Abiron, the leaders of the people." It also means to cry out. Psalm 34: "This poor man cried out." It also means to encounter or meet. Isaiah 31: "When a multitude of shepherds meets him." This can also be understood from the previous meaning: "When a multitude of shepherds shouts at him," and the following speech indicates this: "he will not be afraid of their voice." Our translation <note>The author likely refers to the Latin Vulgate</note> adds another meaning in Proverbs 27: "And he pours out the oil of his right hand." 

It has another meaning as well: to happen, occur, or befall. Genesis 42: "Lest perhaps he should suffer any evil on the journey"—that is, lest death should happen to him. Thus also in Jeremiah 13: "Why have these things come upon me?" It is sometimes written with the letter *he* at the end instead of *aleph*. 1 Samuel 6: <note>original: "i. Regum. vi." - In older systems, the books of Samuel and Kings were often grouped as 1-4 Kings.</note> "But it happened by chance." And in Ecclesiastes 9: "Because the same things happen to all"; in Hebrew it is: "one event for all." It is also found with an *aleph* and without a *he* at the end, as in Deuteronomy 25: "How he met you on the road." 

Jewish logicians often use that name for one of the five <term>Porphyrian predicables</term> <note>The five concepts—genus, species, difference, property, and accident—used to classify how we describe subjects in logic.</note> which they have in translation from <term>Abenrost</term> <note>The Arabic philosopher Ibn Rushd, known in the Latin West as Averroes (1126–1198).</note>, who is called Averroes by us. They form the word for "accident" <note>Hebrew: *mikreh*</note> by adding a *mem* at the beginning and a *he* at the end. 

Likewise, it means to read. Nehemiah 8: "And he read in it openly in the square." And further down: "and they read in the book of the law of God distinctly." From this comes the verbal noun "reader." Habakkuk 2: "That he who reads in it may run"—that is, the one reading or the reader.

**קרב** <note>Hebrew root Q-R-B: to draw near</note> He approached, touched, or reached; he drew near, used periphrastically. Exodus 14: "So that they could not approach one another the whole night long." More correctly in Hebrew, word for word, it is: "And this one did not approach that one all night." And Exodus 32: "And when he had approached the camp." And Isaiah 8: "I approached the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son." 

In these cases, they are <term>intransitive verbs</term> <note>verbs that do not take a direct object</note>. They also become transitive and mean "I cause to approach"—that is, "I offer." Leviticus 1: "A man among you who shall offer a sacrifice." From this comes "offering," "offertory," and "victim." Leviticus 2: "When a soul shall offer an offering." And this is called <term>corban</term> <note>Hebrew: *korban*, a gift or sacrifice dedicated to God.</note>; hence we read in Matthew 27: "It is not lawful to put them into the *corbanas*"—that is, the treasury or offering-box where gifts are placed. 

From this also comes the word "near." Isaiah 55: "Call upon him while he is near." Likewise Psalm 145: "The Lord is near to all who call upon him." And from this root is named anything that is intimate and within our vitals, as in Psalm 103: "And all that is within..."

->SECOND [PART/BOOK]<-

...are [within] me. And what is in the midst of it. Numbers 15: *He shall perish from among his people.* <note>original: "Peribit de populo suo"</note> More correctly: *from the midst of his people.* Likewise, the word for "close" or "neighbor." Psalm 15: *And he did not accept a reproach against his neighbors*—or "fellows." Or, according to Jerome, *over his kin.* It is said to come from "approaching" <note>original: "propinquando"</note>, as in when someone joins hands to fight in battle. Psalm 144: *Who teaches my hands for battle.* <note>The author is connecting the Hebrew root Q-R-B (קרב), which means both "to draw near" and "battle/warfare."</note>

**קרדם** <note>Qardom</note> **Axe**. Psalm 74: *They cut down with axes.* And Judges 9: *Having seized an axe.*

**קרה** <note>Qarah</note> **To board over.** To roof with beams, panel houses, or build. 2 Chronicles 34: *For the roofing of the houses.* Likewise in the Song of Songs 1: *Our paneled ceilings are of cypress.* From this word, some derive the name for a "city" <note>Hebrew: Qiryah</note> through the insertion of the letter *yod*. Proverbs 11: *In the prosperity of the righteous the city shall rejoice.* In the same meaning, the *he* is sometimes changed to a *tav* and the *yod* is missing; hence the Chaldeans <note>referring to Aramaic speakers</note> call a city *kartha*. Job 29: *When I went out to the gate of the city.* See also above under the letter *ayin* followed by *resh*.

**קרח** <note>Qarach</note> **To make bald.** Micah 1: *Make yourself bald and shave for the children of your delight.* Ezekiel 29: *Every head was made bald.* From this comes the noun **baldness**. Ezekiel 27: *And they shall shave a baldness upon you,* where an *aleph* is used instead of a *he*. When written with the vowel *segol*, it also signifies **crystal** or **ice**. Ezekiel 1: *And the likeness over the heads of the living creatures of the firmament was as the appearance of terrible crystal.* And according to Nicholas of Lyra <note>A prolific 14th-century Franciscan biblical scholar</note>, it means **ice**. For Jerome wrote in his commentaries that water constricted by frost is called "crystal" in the Greek language. This is also confirmed by the dictionary they call the *Great Etymologicum*.

**קרם** <note>Qaram</note> **Covered with leather.** To clothe with skin; to cover with hide. Ezekiel 37: *And I will stretch skin over you.* From this, the word **membrane** <note>original: "membrana"; used for skin or parchment</note> is derived.

**קרן** <note>Qeren</note> **Horn**. Daniel 8: *The great horn was broken.* This word is used in both the singular and plural. As a verb, it also means **to radiate** and **to shine**. Exodus 34: *Who saw that the face of Moses as he came out was horned.* <note>The Latin Vulgate famously translated the Hebrew "shone" as "horned" (cornutam) due to the similarity of the words for "horn" and "ray of light."</note> More correctly, word for word from the Hebrew: *And the children of Israel saw the face of Moses, that the skin of Moses' face shone.*

**קרס** <note>qaras</note> He fell or collapsed to the ground. Isaiah 46: *Bel is broken, Nebo is crushed* <note>original Latin: "Confractus est Bel contritus est Nebo"</note>; that is to say, the two idols of the Babylonians were thrown down to the earth. It also signifies a circle, a ring, or a clasp <note>or "fibula"</note> with which curtains are connected to one another. Exodus 26: *You shall make fifty clasps.*

**קרסל** <note>qarsal</note> The ankle. This is the joint where the foot and the lower leg are joined. 2 Samuel 22: *And my ankles did not fail.*

**קרע** <note>qara</note> He broke, split, or tore. 1 Samuel 15: *The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today.* And Judges 11: *He tore his clothes.* And in the passive voice in 1 Kings 13: *The altar also was split.* A similar phrase is read in Psalm 35: *They were torn and not cut to the heart* <note>original Latin: "Dissipati sunt nec compuncti"</note>. Jerome translates this as *Tearing and not keeping silent*, but our Hebrew scholars explain it as: *If they are torn apart, they do not bleed.* It also signifies "to open." Jeremiah 22: *Who opens windows for himself.*

**קרקע** <note>qarqa</note> Bottom, foundation, or floor. Numbers 5: *And a little dust from the floor.* And Amos 9: *If they hide themselves from my eyes at the bottom of the sea.*

**קרקר** <note>qarqar</note> He demolished or pierced through. Isaiah 22: *Searching the walls.* And Numbers 24: *And he shall lay waste to all the sons of Seth*; that is, he will cause them to fall. See more on this above under the word **קיר** <note>kir</note>.

**קרץ** <note>qaratz</note> A shaper, cutter, sculptor, or imitator. Jeremiah 46: *An imitator from the north will come to her.* From this comes the word in Job 33: *And I also was formed from the same clay.* It also signifies winking with the eyes, or making a sign with the tongue, or nodding with the face. Psalm 35: *They wink with their eyes.* Proverbs 6: *He winks with his eyes, shuffles with his feet.* And in the tenth chapter of the same book: *He who winks with the eye will cause trouble, etc.*

**קרש** <note>qeresh</note> A board or plank. Exodus 26: *Make the standing boards of the tabernacle of acacia wood* <note>original Latin: "lignis setim"</note>; and so on through the text, in both the singular and the plural. Ezekiel 27: *And they made your benches of Indian ivory*; or more correctly, *your planking.*

**קשש** <note>qashash</note> He gathered or collected. Exodus 5: *And the people were scattered throughout all the land of Egypt to gather stubble.* And a little earlier: *They go and gather straw for themselves.* From this comes **קש** <note>qash</note>, meaning straw that has been broken down and crushed.

<meta>This page appears to be part of a Hebrew-Latin philological dictionary or biblical commentary, focusing on words beginning with the Hebrew letter 'Qoph'. It continues an analysis of currency terms and transitions into roots related to binding, weaponry, and armor.</meta>

->BOOK<-

...he had pitched his tents from the children of Hamor, the father of Shechem, for a hundred lambs. <note>original: "centum agnis"; referring to Genesis 33:19</note> Here, Lyra <note>Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349) was a hugely influential Franciscan teacher and biblical commentator whose knowledge of Hebrew was rare for his time.</note> writes that our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate, the standard Bible of the Middle Ages.</note> is lacking in this instance. For the Hebrews translate this as a hundred <term>obols</term> <note>An obol was a small ancient coin; the author is debating whether the biblical text refers to a unit of currency or actual livestock.</note>. And he speaks truly. Similarly, in the final chapter of Job, where our version has: "And they each gave him one sheep," the Hebrews read "one coin" or "one obol."

**[קשר — Q-Sh-R]** United, bound together, tied, knotted. Deuteronomy 6: "And you shall bind them as a sign upon your hand." The passive form of this word is used in 1 Samuel 18: "And the soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David," meaning it was bound. From this comes "binding together," "conspiracy," or "league." Isaiah 8: "Do not say 'conspiracy,' for all that this people speaks of is conspiracy." For this reason, our translation rendered it as "rebellion" in Amos 7: "Amos has rebelled against you," meaning he formed a league or conspired. Likewise, in 2 Samuel 15: "The conspiracy was strong and the people flocked together." From this root, the sheep that are born around the time of March are called by this name because they are "stronger." <note>The author connects the Hebrew root for "binding" to "strength" or "firmness."</note> Genesis 30: "And those of the first season belonged to Jacob."

**[קשת — Q-Sh-Th]** A bow. 1 Samuel 2: "The bow of the mighty is overcome," and Genesis 9: "I will set my bow in the clouds," and later: "My bow shall appear in the clouds." In the feminine plural, Psalm 37: "And let their bows be broken." From this comes "crossbowman" or "archer." Genesis 21: "A young archer," though it literally means "master of the bow."

**[קשקשת — Q-Sh-Q-Sh-Th]** A scale. Leviticus 11: "Everything that has fins and scales." It is declined in the feminine plural in Ezekiel 29: "All the fish shall stick to your scales." From the likeness of scales, an iron tunic is made, which they call a <term>coat of mail</term> <note>original: "lorica"; a piece of armor covering the torso, made here of overlapping metal plates resembling fish scales.</note> of scales or "scaled armor." 1 Samuel 17: "And he was clothed in a scaled coat of mail." This word is declined in the plural with the ending "-im."

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical or thematic dictionary of Hebrew roots, likely following a section on words beginning with the letter 'Resh'. It focuses on the roots related to seeing, rain, wild animals (unicorns/rhinoceroses), and the concept of the "head."</meta>

# SECOND [PART]

<note>original Hebrew: ראה (Ra'ah)</note> **To see.** <note>original Hebrew: יורה (Yoreh)</note> **Early rain / Teacher.**

He looked or saw. In Lamentations: *Because he saw the nations.* In Psalm 34: *He saw all the sons of men.* And in Genesis 37: *Go and see if all things are prosperous.* From this comes the sense of "to look askance" <note>original Latin: invidere</note> or "to look down upon." In Psalm 22: *They indeed considered and looked upon me.* On this point, the Hebrew scholars say: *They looked and envied me,* or *They saw and despised me.* From this, many metaphorical terms are derived, such as "mirror" <note>original Latin: speculum</note> in Exodus 38: *From the mirrors of the women.* From this also comes the word for "early rain" in Deuteronomy 11: *He will give the rain of your land, the early and the late.* You may form other derivatives from this verb according to grammatical rules, as you will find them in great abundance when reading the Hebrew Bible.

This same form has another meaning: "a goiter" or "a vesicle of the throat." In Leviticus 1: *The vesicle of the throat.* <note>The author refers to the "crop" of a bird, part of the sacrificial laws.</note> It has another meaning that is obscene, shameful, or foul. Our translation <note>The Vulgate</note> renders this as "an example" in Nahum 3: *And I will set you as an example.* However, the Hebrew scholars translate it as: *I will set you as a thing of filth or foulness.*

It is also the name of a bird which our translation calls the *ixon* <note>original Greek/Latin: ixon; likely referring to a type of vulture or hawk</note>, an animal unknown to us. However, the Hebrew scholars interpret it as a "vulture." According to Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Shlomo Yitzhaki, known as Rashi, a preeminent medieval French commentator</note>, it is a bird so named because it sees more clearly than others due to the sharpness of its sight. Deuteronomy 14: *The ixon, the vulture, and the kite.*

<note>original Hebrew: ראם (Re’em)</note> **Rhinoceros or unicorn.** Deuteronomy 33: *His horns are the horns of a rhinoceros.* It appears to Tortellius <note>Giovanni Tortelli, a 15th-century Italian humanist and orthographer</note> that the unicorn and the rhinoceros are different animals. Perotto <note>Niccolò Perotti, author of the 'Cornu Copiae,' a massive 15th-century commentary on Martial</note> says the same in his *Cornu Copiae*, for the former carries its horn on its forehead, while the latter carries it on its nose. However, our translation uses the terms interchangeably. Psalm 92: *My horn shall be exalted like that of the unicorn.* Sometimes the letter *aleph* is dropped and replaced by the letter *yod* with the same meaning. Job 39: *Will the rhinoceros be willing to serve you?* Perhaps it is from this animal that precious garments woven from its hair are named, which our translation renders as "silk." Ezekiel 27: *Fine linen and silk.*

<note>original Hebrew: ראש (Rosh)</note> **Head.** Leviticus 1: *Namely, the head and all things that adhere to the liver.* From this, it metaphorically signifies a summit, a peak, the top, or the first. Genesis 28: *And its top touched the heavens.* Song of Solomon 4: *With all the chief ointments.* From this, great princes and captains are named. Micah 3: *Hear, you [heads of Jacob]...*

**רבב** <note>Hebrew root: R-B-B</note> **It has increased and multiplied; it grew.** Psalm 69: *They are multiplied more than the hairs of my head.* <note>original: "Multiplicati sunt super capillos capitis mei"</note> And Genesis 1: *Increase and multiply.* From this comes the meaning of **much** or **great.** Jonah 4: *Great mercies.* And Psalm 47: *The city of the great king.* And Psalm 3: *Lord, how they are increased who trouble me, many rise up against me, many say,* etc. It also signifies **enough** or **it suffices.** 1 Chronicles 21: *It is enough now; stay your hand.* And Numbers 16: *Let it suffice you, for all the multitude is holy.* It also signifies **ten thousand** in calculation. Deuteronomy 32: *And two would put ten thousand to flight, and twice as many.* Nehemiah 7: *Twenty thousand drachmas of gold.* From this same verb, a preeminent man who is honored and a master of great counsel is called a **rab**, whom our translation calls a **defender.** <note>original Latin: "propugnatorem"</note> Isaiah 19: *And he shall send them a savior and a defender who shall deliver them.* From the sense of "multiplication," they also use this word for **drops** or **showers of rain**, using a double "beth" <note>referring to the Hebrew spelling</note>. Micah 5: *And as the drops upon the grass.* Another meaning is **to shoot** or **to draw a bow.** Genesis 49: *They provoked him and quarreled,* for which the Hebrew says: *they embittered him and shot at him.* <note>The author is noting a difference between the Latin Vulgate "quarreled" and the Hebrew "shot arrows."</note>

**רבד** <note>Hebrew root: R-B-D</note> **A collar** or **an ornament around the throat.** Ezekiel 16: *And a collar around your neck.* It is also applied to other ornaments that are hung up, as in Proverbs 7: *I have woven my bed with cords,* <note>original: "Intexui funibus lectulum meū"</note> which the Hebrew expresses as: *I have adorned my bed with ornaments.*

**רבה** <note>Hebrew root: R-B-H</note> **He increased; he multiplied.** Deuteronomy 30: *And you shall live and be multiplied.* And more clearly in Genesis 35: *Grow and multiply.* From this comes a "weighty" verb form through the addition <note>term: prothesis (the addition of a sound at the beginning of a word)</note> of the "h" sound. Genesis 3: *I will multiply your sorrows.* And Isaiah 9: *You have multiplied the nation.* From this comes the reading in Psalm 130: *With him is plenteous redemption.* From this also comes **multiplication.** Proverbs 29: *In the multiplication of the wicked, crimes will be multiplied.* And Isaiah 9: *His empire shall be multiplied;* more correctly, using the preposition "mem" and the article: *for the multiplying of his empire.* It also signifies **often.** Psalm 129: *Often have they fought against me.* Another meaning is an **archer** <note>term: balistarius (specifically one who uses a stone-thrower or large crossbow)</note> directing a bow. Genesis 21: *And the youth became an archer.* From its primary meaning [of multitude], they believe the word **arbeh** is derived, that is, **a locust.** Exodus 10: *Stretch out your hand over the land of Egypt for the locust.*

**רבך** <note>Hebrew root: R-B-K</note> **He fried; he scorched.** Leviticus 6: *Which, sprinkled with oil in a frying pan, is fried.*

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical exploration of Hebrew roots, specifically focusing on the letter Resh (R). It follows the previous page's format of providing Latin equivalents and biblical citations to explain Hebrew vocabulary.</meta>

->SECOND [BOOK]<-

**[Hebrew: רבע] Square. quadrangular.** Exodus 27. Five cubits in length and just as many in width, that is, a square <note>original: "quadrum"</note>. Which in Hebrew, word for word, is: the altar shall be square. From this comes the numeral **four**, by the addition of the letter *aleph*. <note>The author uses the term "cata pthesin" to describe the grammatical addition of a letter at the beginning of the word *Arba* (four).</note> Exodus 22: And **four** sheep for one sheep. From this is derived the **fourth part**. Leviticus 23: A **fourth part** of a *hin* <note>A 'hin' was an ancient Hebrew unit of liquid measure, roughly 4 to 6 liters.</note>, and so on for the ordinal numbers. I do not know what our translation <note>Likely referring to the Latin Vulgate.</note> intended to say in Numbers 23: *And to know the stock of Israel*, since no word here signifies "stock" <note>original: "stirpem"</note>. It is more correctly rendered thus: *Who has counted the dust of Jacob, and the number of the **fourth part** of Israel?*

**[Hebrew: רבץ] He lay down. he reclined.** Isaiah 11: And the leopard shall **lie down** with the kid. And Genesis 49: Resting, you **lay down** like a lion. In Hebrew it is: He shall **recline** on his knee. And Canticles 1: Where you **rest** <note>original: "cudes," likely a variant or error for "cubes"</note> at midday. And Isaiah 13: Neither shall the shepherds **rest** there, but wild beasts shall **rest** there.

**[Hebrew: רבק] He fattened. he made thick.** Amos 6: And calves from the midst of the herd. More correctly: From the midst of the **fattening** or the **stall**. For it signifies a place where animals are stuffed or fattened. We are taught to speak this way by Marcus Cato in his work *On Agriculture* <note>Cato the Elder (234–149 BCE) wrote the oldest surviving work of Latin prose; the author is comparing biblical Hebrew agricultural terms to classical Latin ones.</note>.

**[Hebrew: רגב] Gravel. mud. clod.** Job 38: And the **clods** were joined together. And in Job 21: The **gravel** of the Cocytus <note>In the Vulgate, "Cocytus" (a river of the underworld) is used to translate a Hebrew word for "valley."</note> was sweet. Rabbi Jonah <note>Ibn Janah, a famous 11th-century Hebrew grammarian and lexicographer.</note> said that these are places of marshy filth where the dust soaks up standing water.

<margin>†</margin>
**[Hebrew: רגז] He disturbed. he moved. he trembled. he disquieted. he saddened.** Jerome translated this as *he was angry*. Psalm 4: **Be angry** and do not sin. And Proverbs 29: Whether he **is angry** or he laughs. And Joel 2: Let all the inhabitants of the land **be disturbed**. And 2 Kings 18: The king was therefore **saddened**. And Habakkuk 3: The skins of the land of Midian **were troubled**. Rabbi Salomon <note>Rashi (Solomon ben Isaac), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> explains this as "to be moved" in Psalm 4, but in Genesis 45, regarding the phrase *Do not **be angry** on the way*, he explains it as "do not quarrel." And there, Onkelos <note>The author of the famous Aramaic translation (Targum) of the Torah.</note> renders it in Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> as "do not strive." Jonathan the Chaldean <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel, traditionally credited with the Aramaic translation of the Prophets.</note>, however, interprets it as "to tremble" in 2 Kings 22, where we read: *the foundations of the mountains were shaken*. The Hebrews have *the foundations of the heavens*, but in Psalm 18, in a similar passage, it is written *foundations of the mountains*. Thus Jonathan explains the verse cited above in Chaldean: The foundations of the heavens **[Hebrew: רגזו]**, that is, **they trembled**. Although later, when it is read *because he was angry with them*, Jonathan himself translates that same passage using our word for anger. All the meanings of this word tend toward a commotion of anger, or fear, or terror.

## <term>Ruth [רות]</term> <note>original: "רות" - This entry discusses a root associated with trembling or being broken.</note>

**He trembled.** **He was moved.** **He set in motion.** **It was broken.** Ezekiel, chapter forty-seven <note>Ezekiel 47:12</note>: *And its leaves for medicine.* More correctly: *for motion*—meaning for taking away and repairing **infirmity, wounds, and fractures**; that is, that it might restore the wound. From which we read in Job, chapter twenty-six <note>Job 26:11</note>: *The pillars of heaven tremble*—namely, they are to be broken—where it signifies motion. Likewise, in the second book of Kings <note>Known in modern English Bibles as 2 Samuel 24:16</note>, chapter twenty-four: *Let your hand cease,* meaning "let your hand be moved away."

Let us run.*

Word for word it says: *As they were emptying their sacks, behold, each man’s bundle was in his sack.* And in Psalm 2: *And the peoples meditated on vain things.* And in Ecclesiastes 11: *If the clouds are full, they will pour out rain upon the earth,* that is, they will empty themselves. And in the first chapter of the Song of Solomon: *Your name is oil poured out,* that is, emptied. However, in that instance, the name is an adjective written with the <term>prefix thau</term> <note>the Hebrew letter 'Tav' (ת)</note>, notwithstanding that the last syllable is marked with a <term>pathach</term> <note>a Hebrew vowel sign indicating an 'a' sound</note>. Another meaning is to **unsheath**. Leviticus 26: *And I will unsheath the sword after you.* In this sense, it signifies preparing weapons and drawing them out for battle.

**ריר** <note>Hebrew root: R-Y-R</note> **It stood; it flowed.** Leviticus 15: *If a foul moisture has clung to his flesh and thickened.* Here, the translator has again turned away from the literal words to follow "the little flowers of speech" <note>an idiomatic way of saying the translator was being overly poetic or stylistic rather than literal</note>. Instead of that gushing moisture, we read "spittle" in 1 Samuel 21: *And his spittle flowed down into his beard.*

**רכך** <note>Hebrew root: R-K-K</note> **Thinned; softened; made gentle; made tender.** Psalm 55: *His words were made softer than oil,* that is, they were made into tender words. From this comes "tender" and "very young." Genesis 18: *A very tender and good calf.* And in Proverbs 4: *Tender and only-begotten.* And Genesis 29: *And Leah had weak eyes.* He ought to have said "tender eyes." And again the verb in Deuteronomy 20: *Let not your heart be afraid,* or more correctly, "let it not grow soft," which is to say, let your heart not be softened. And so it is with other derived words.

**רכב** <note>Hebrew root: R-K-B</note> **Carried; rode; was borne or brought.** In the <term>third conjugation</term> <note>referring to the Hebrew Hiphil or causative verb form</note>, it means "he sat upon." Numbers 22: *Am I not your beast, upon which you have always been accustomed to sit?* instead of "upon which you have ridden." From this come the nouns for **cavalry**, **chariot**, and every kind of **vehicle**. Song of Solomon 1: *In the chariots of Pharaoh.* From this, the one who is carried is called a "rider." Exodus 15: *The horse and the rider.* And Psalm 68: *Who ascends above the heaven.* Many things are said figuratively...

[Hebrew: רכל] **To trade.** <note>Hebrew: *rakhal*</note> He traded, or bought and sold. Ezekiel 17: "He placed it in a city of merchants." And Nehemiah 13: "The merchants and sellers of all kinds of goods remained outside Jerusalem." It is also used for a spice-dealer, a dealer in pigments, a perfumer, or an apothecary. Song of Solomon 3: "Of all the powders of the merchant." It has another meaning: a fraudulent whisperer <note>a slanderer</note> or an informer. Leviticus 19: "You shall not be a slanderer nor a whisperer among the people." And Proverbs 11: "He who walks fraudulently."

[Hebrew: רכס] **A very high mountain** <note>Hebrew: *rakhas*</note>, or the height of mountains. Isaiah 40: "And the rough places [shall become] plain ways." From this is derived a verb meaning to raise or to draw upward, or to strengthen. Exodus 28: "And let the breastplate be bound by its rings with the rings of the shoulder-piece <note>the *ephod*</note>." More accurately, word-for-word, the verb means: "And they shall raise or draw up the breastplate from its rings to the rings of the ephod—specifically, to that which will be above it."

[Hebrew: רכש] **A certain very swift animal** <note>Hebrew: *rekesh*</note> suited for carrying or riding. Some think these are mules, others a type of camel, and others dromedaries. Our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> has "couriers" <note>original: *veredarios*</note>. Esther 8: "And [letters] were sent by couriers who hurried through all the provinces." But the translator, again following a rhetorical style for the sake of oratorical ornament, leaves out the specific words; for in Hebrew it reads: "And letters were sent by the hand of runners on horses, riding the swiftest horses, dromedaries, and the offspring of mules." <note>The author is pointing out that the Latin simplifies several specific terms for animals into the general word "couriers."</note> And again in Micah 1: "The noise of the chariot of amazement to the inhabitant of Lachish." I do not know what the translator intended to say, but in Hebrew it is read: "Bind the chariot to the swiftest horse, you who dwell in Lachish." It has another meaning: the entire substance of goods possessed by a person, generally, whether in immovable things <note>real estate</note> or movable and self-moving things <note>livestock</note>. Genesis 14: "Give me the souls, take the rest for yourself," <note>original: *da mihi animas cetera tolle tibi*</note> which means "give me the people, and take the substance of the goods for yourself." Thus it signifies opulence and riches.

[Hebrew: רמם] **He exalted** <note>Hebrew: *ramam*</note>, or he raised up. Job 22: "And may he raise [him] above the summit of the stars." More accurately: "And behold the peak of the stars, that they are exalted or raised up." And Ezekiel 10: "And the glory of the Lord was lifted up above the cherubim." From this comes the name in Psalm 112: "The Lord is high above all nations." And thus in another meaning... <note>The text cuts off here at the bottom of the page.</note>
