-># SECOND [SECTION]<-

**Pomegranate** or the fruit of the pomegranate tree. <note>original: *punicum siue pomum granatum*</note> In the fourth chapter of the **Song of Songs**: *Like a fragment of a pomegranate.* It has another meaning: **worm**. In **Job 21**: *And the worm shall cover them.* In another place it is interpreted as **moth**. In **Isaiah 14**: *Under thee shall the moth be strewn.* Another meaning is **fraud** and **deceit**. In **Proverbs 26**: *So is the man that deceitfully hurts his friend.* And in **Hosea 7**: *Like a deceitful bow.* Another meaning is **to throw** or **to hurl**. In **Exodus 15**: *The horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea.* For this reason, some explain the preceding verse in **Hosea** as referring to a bow used for hurling arrows.

**רמח** (Romach): **Lance**. **Dagger**. **Spear**. In **Numbers 25**: *And having seized the dagger, he went in after the man.* And in **Jeremiah 46**: *Polish the spears.*

**רמך** (Ramach): A **large mule** born from a mare. In **Esther 8**: *Couriers,* etc., where it is more correctly said: *Young mules, the foals of mares.*

**רמס** (Ramas): **He trampled**. In **Psalm 91**: *Thou shalt tread upon the lion and the dragon.* And in **Ezekiel 26**: *He shall trample all your streets.* And it is found spelled with a *sin* [ש] at the end instead of a *samech* [ס], having nearly the same meaning. <note>The author is noting a variation in Hebrew spelling that does not change the core meaning.</note> **Genesis 7**: *And all flesh was consumed that moved upon the earth.* From this comes **to creep**, **to crawl**, and **reptile**, and other derivatives.

**רנן** (Ranan): **He rejoiced**. **He was cheered**. **He was witty**. **He was glad**. **He spoke craftily**. Because a man reveals himself in sarcasms, jokes, and crafty sayings, I believe our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> interpreted "to be opened" as being "loosened into jokes." In **Isaiah 35**: *And the tongue of the dumb shall be opened.* <note>The author argues this "opening" of the tongue implies a burst of joyful speech.</note> Likewise in **Psalm 51**: *My tongue shall sing of thy justice.* In **Zechariah 2**: *Praise and rejoice, O daughter of Zion.* More correctly according to the Septuagint: <note>The Greek Old Testament</note> *Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Zion.* All derivatives signify **vocal joy** and a **shout of gladness**. It has another meaning: an **owl** or another nocturnal bird that cries "huhu." Our translation renders it as **ostrich**. In **Job 39**: *The wing of the ostrich.*

**רנב** (Arnev): With the prefix *aleph* [א] and the suffix *thau* [ת], it signifies a **hare**. <note>The Hebrew word for hare is 'Arnevet'.</note> In **Deuteronomy 14**: *The camel, the hare, and the rock-badger.* Our faulty books <note>Corrupted manuscript copies of the Latin Bible</note> have "chirogrillum" [hedgehog/shrew-mouse].

**רסס** (Rasas): **Droplet**. **Drop**. In the fifth chapter of the **Song of Songs**: *And my locks with the drops of the night,* that is, with droplets. For this is how the Targum <note>The Aramaic translation/commentary of the Bible</note> explains it. Another meaning is a **crack** or **fissure**. In **Amos 6**: *And he shall strike the great house with breaches.* For the word "ruins" <note>Latin: *ruinis*</note> is a mistake in the text.

->[Hebrew: רסן <note>original: resen</note>] Bridle, muzzle. Isaiah 30: "And a bridle of error which was in the jaws of the peoples." And Psalm 32: "With bit and bridle."<-

->[Hebrew: רעב <note>original: ra’av</note>] To hunger. Psalm 34: "The rich lacked and suffered hunger." And Isaiah 49: "They shall not hunger nor thirst." From this comes the noun <note>meaning "famine"</note> in Genesis 41: "And in all the world the famine prevailed."<-

->[Hebrew: רעד <note>original: ra’ad</note>] To tremble. Psalm 104: "Who looks upon the earth and makes it tremble." From this comes the noun <note>meaning "trembling"</note> in Exodus 15: "Trembling took hold of the mighty men of Moab."<-

->[Hebrew: רעה <note>original: ra’ah</note>] To pasture; he ruled in a flock, namely as a shepherd. Jeremiah 50: "And Carmel and Bashan shall be pastured." And Isaiah 5: "And the lambs shall be fed according to their order." From this comes the noun <note>meaning "shepherd" or "ruler"</note> in Psalm 23: "The Lord rules me <note>Latin: regit me</note> and I shall want for nothing," which Jerome translates much more correctly in this way: "The Lord is my shepherd." And Song of Solomon 1: "Where you pasture..." and below: "And pasture your kids beside the tents of the shepherds." At times, through a certain linguistic liberty, the plural letter *mem* is dropped <note>changing the word from plural to a form that looks singular</note>, as in Isaiah 38: "Like the tent of shepherds," though it can still be interpreted as "like the tent of a shepherd," so that the final *yod* stands in place of the letter *he*, as occurs in grammar. From this come "pasture" and other derivatives.<-

Another meaning of this root is to labor in vain, to consume fruitlessly, to afflict, or weariness. Ecclesiastes 1: "Vanity and affliction of spirit," and further on: "Labor and affliction of spirit," that is, the wasting away of the spirit. Likewise in Hosea 12: "Ephraim feeds on the wind," or more correctly: "Ephraim fruitlessly consumes the wind," because he is neither helped nor nourished by it.

Another meaning is "friend." Leviticus 19: "You shall love your friend as yourself." Similarly, a female friend, as in Song of Solomon 2: "My friend, my beautiful one."

Another meaning is "will" or "thought." Psalm 139: "You have understood my thoughts from afar."

Another meaning is to shatter, to crush, or to break into pieces. Jeremiah 2: "They have defiled you even to the crown of your head," but <term>Nicholas of Lyra <note>A prominent 14th-century Franciscan bibical exegete known for his focus on the literal sense of scripture.</note></term> more correctly interprets this as "they have broken you." To this similar meaning, certain Hebrew scholars explain the verse in Job 24: "He feeds the barren woman who does not bear" in this way: "He shatters and breaks the barren woman who does not bear and does not do good to the widow." However, <term>Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note></term> explains this as referring to two widows: one who has children is in need and hungers, while the other who has no children is fed and rejoices. Also Micah 5: "And they shall feed the land of Assyria with the sword," or more correctly in this way: "And they shall break or shatter the land of Assyria with the sword."

->SECOND<-

**RE’AL** <note>Hebrew: רעל; primarily meaning to shake or quiver</note> Trembling, groaning, or tumult. Our translation <note>The author refers to the Latin Vulgate</note> translates it in various ways as "intoxication," "remorse," or "slumber." In Zechariah 12: *The threshold of intoxication for all peoples* <note>original: "Superliminare crapulae omnibus populis"</note>, for which the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> has: *The thresholds which are moved* <note>original: "Superliminaria quae moventur"</note>. I understand this to mean "those which tremble." And in Nahum 2: *And the drivers are put to sleep* <note>original: "Et agitatores consopiti sunt"</note>, for which the Septuagint has: *they shall fear*. And in Psalm 60: *You have made us drink the wine of remorse* <note>original: "Potasti nos vino compunctionis"</note>, for which Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate</note> provides: *numbing wine*. But the true property of this word is to groan and tremble. It has another meaning as a headdress adorned with jewels. In Isaiah 3: *Bracelets and headbands and veils*. The Hebrew masters say these are women's veils with which Easterners are accustomed to cover their heads so that their faces are not seen.

**RA’AM** <note>Hebrew: רעם; primarily associated with thunder or agitation</note> It was in tumult, it was indignant, it rages, it shook, it trembled. In Ezekiel 27: *They shook their faces* <note>original: "Motaverunt vultus"</note>, not "they changed" as some faulty manuscripts have it; it is as if he were saying they detested it indignantly, arising from that motion of tumult and trembling. Our translations have adapted this word to refer to thunder. In 1 Chronicles 16: *Let the sea thunder and its fullness* <note>original: "Tonet mare et plenitudo eius"</note>, instead of "let it tremble." For thundering belongs not to Neptune but to Jupiter <note>The author uses classical Roman gods to illustrate the distinction between the sea shaking and the heavens thundering</note>. Likewise in 2 Samuel 22: *The Lord shall thunder from heaven*, and Psalm 18 similarly. From this comes the noun in Job 26: *Who can gaze upon the thunder of his greatness?* He should rather have said "lightning," for thunder is not seen. But the Hebrews more correctly say: *And who shall understand the tumult or indignation of his strength?*

**RA’ANAN** <note>Hebrew: רענן; meaning to be green or flourish</note> It was flourishing, it was green. It does not occur frequently in use except by the doubling of the final *nun* <note>The Hebrew letter 'n'</note>. In the first chapter of the Song of Songs: *Our bed is flowery*, covered in greenery. From this comes the noun in Psalm 52: *But I am like a fruitful olive tree*, for which Jerome more correctly translates in his own Psalter: *like a green olive tree*.

**RA’APH** <note>Hebrew: רעף; meaning to trickle or distil</note> It dripped, it dewed. In Proverbs 3: *And the clouds are thickened with dew* (more correctly thus: *And the clouds shall drip dew*). And in Psalm 65: *And your fields shall be filled with abundance, the beauties of the desert shall grow fat*. But Jerome more correctly translates: *They shall be dewed with fatness* <note>original: "rorabuntur pinguedine"</note>, that is, they shall drip.

**RA’ATS** <note>Hebrew: רעץ; meaning to shatter or break</note> It wore down, it crushed, it scattered, it shattered, it destroyed. In Exodus 15: *Your right hand has struck the enemy*, that is, shattered and destroyed him. In Judges 10: *And they were afflicted and vehemently oppressed*, that is, worn down, scattered, and shattered.

**[Root: RA-ASH]** <note>Hebrew: רעש</note> **He shook; he moved violently; he trembled.** Ezekiel 38: "And the fish of the sea **shall shake** at my presence." And in the same book, chapter 26: "The islands **shall be moved**." It is also used as a transitive verb in Job 39: "Can you **make him leap** <note>original Latin: "fufcitabis", meaning to rouse or stir up</note> like a locust?"—meaning "will you move him?" However, whenever this word is found to signify increase and multiplication, it occurs through a metathesis <note>a transposition of letters within a word</note> of the letters.

**[Root: RA-FA]** <note>Hebrew: רפא</note> **He restored; he made whole; he healed; he cured.** Isaiah 6: "And let him return, and **I will heal** him." Jeremiah 17: "**Heal** me, O Lord, and I shall be healed." And Genesis 20: "And God **healed** Abimelech." From this comes the words for **physicians** and **perfumers**. Genesis 50: "And he commanded his servants, the **physicians**, to embalm his father with spices." From this also comes the noun for **medicine** or **health**, etc. Jeremiah 46: "In vain do you multiply **medicines**; there shall be no **health** for you." Sometimes the letter *aleph* is changed into a *he* and signifies the same thing, as in Jeremiah 3: "Be converted, you returning children, and **I will heal** your rebellions," although in many books, both printed and manuscript, it is found written in that same place with an *aleph*. Nevertheless, in corrected books, a <term>Masorah</term> <note>traditional Hebrew marginal notes regarding the correct spelling of the Biblical text</note> is added which indicates it should be written there with an *h*. Likewise, 2 Chronicles 7: "And **I will heal** their land," that is, I will restore it. 

Another meaning is **giants** or **mighty men**. Deuteronomy 2: "**Giants** like the Anakim." Another meaning is **the dead**. Psalm 88: "Or shall **physicians** raise them up and they shall praise you?"—for which Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate</note> writes: "and the **giants** shall rise again." But it is more correctly translated: "or shall the **dead** rise again and praise you?" Likewise, Proverbs 21: "The man who wanders from the way of doctrine shall remain in the assembly of **giants**." It is more correctly: "He shall dwell in the congregation of the **dead**."

**[Root: RA-FAD]** <note>Hebrew: רפד</note> **He paved; he spread out.** Job 41: "And he shall **spread** gold for himself like mud." More correctly: "He **spreads** gold upon the mud." From this comes the noun in Song of Songs 3: "A golden **support**" <note>original Latin: "reclinatorium"</note> for "a golden **bed**." Another meaning is **to comfort** or **to sustain**. Song of Songs 2: "**Sustain** me with apples."

**[Root: RA-FAH]** <note>Hebrew: רפה</note> **He settled; he rested.** Judges 8: "When he had spoken this, their spirit **rested**." Jonathan the Chaldean <note>referring to the Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation</note> also explains it this way. From this comes the noun for **powerless**, **infirm**, and **weak**, because such a person rests easily. Numbers 13: "Whether they be strong or **weak**." It is read in the passive in Exodus 5: "For they are **idle** <note>original: "vacant", meaning empty or at leisure</note> and therefore they cry out"—as if one might say, "they are making themselves quiet." Sometimes an *aleph* is found in place of the final *he*, as in Ecclesiastes 10: "For **healing** <note>original: "curatio"</note> will cause the greatest sins to cease." More correctly: "**Weakness** allows great sins to sink in." It signifies—

signifies to let down, deposit, or leave. 2 Kings 24: "Stay your hand." <note>original: "Contine manum tuam"</note> More correctly: "Make your hand rest," or rather, "Let your hand go."

[Hebrew: רפס] Walked, ran, or proceeded. <note>Hebrew root: R-P-S</note> Psalm 68: "That they may exclude those who are tested with silver." The translations of this word are varied and obscure. <meta>This page continues the alphabetical lexicon of Hebrew roots, focusing on the letter Resh (R). It follows the previous entries by providing a headword, its primary meaning in Latin (here translated to English), and various scriptural examples where the word or its derivatives appear, often commenting on the choices made by the Latin translator (Saint Jerome).</meta>

->BOOK<-

**רצח** [Ratsach] He killed. Deuteronomy 4: "Whoever shall kill his neighbor unintentionally." <note>original: *Qui occiderit nolens proximum suum*</note> From this comes "killer" or "murderer," as seen in that passage and in Deuteronomy 19: "He who has fled because of homicide, and this shall be the law for the murderer."

**רצע** [Ratsa] He pierced. Exodus 21: "And he shall pierce his ear with an awl" <note>term: *subula* — a small pointed tool for piercing holes in leather or skin</note> or a piercing instrument. Thus you have both the verb and the noun.

**רצף** [Ratseph] A live coal from a glowing ember, which our translation calls a "pebble" <note>original: *calculum*</note>. Isaiah 6: "And in his hand was a coal which he had taken with tongs from the altar." And 1 Kings 19: "And behold, at his head was bread baked under the ashes." More correctly: "A cake of coals." Another meaning is "pavement." Ezekiel 40: "And the pavement was laid with stone in the court." And Esther 1: "Upon a pavement of emerald and Parian stone." From this comes the verb "he covered the middle with love"; more correctly: "Internally it is paved with love." <note>This refers to the description of Solomon's chariot in Song of Solomon 3:10</note>

**רק** [Raq] Surely, certainly, nevertheless, only, perhaps. Deuteronomy 3: "For only Og the king of Bashan..." Psalm 32: "Nevertheless, in the flood of many waters..." And Isaiah 28: "Only the vexation alone shall give understanding to the hearing." And Genesis 20: "Perhaps the fear of God is not in this place." And thus its meaning is understood in various ways according to how it is applied to each sentence, just like other significant particles.

**רקק** [Raqaq] Consumed, exhausted, thin, wretched, lean. Genesis 41: "And behold, seven other cows followed them that were so lean." And so on, where again the translator acts more as an orator than an interpreter <note>The author suggests the Latin translator used more poetic or descriptive language rather than a strictly literal word-for-word translation</note>. And from "thinness" come "wafers," "thin cakes," or "thin pastries." Exodus 29: "Also unleavened wafers smeared with oil." Another meaning is the "temples of the head"; our translation has "cheeks" <note>original: *gena*</note> because the flesh is thin there. Song of Solomon 4: "Like a fragment of a pomegranate, so are your cheeks." Another meaning is "to spit," "spittle," or "saliva." Deuteronomy 25: "And she shall spit in his face." And Leviticus 15: "If a man of this kind shall cast his saliva." And Job 30: "And they do not fear to spit in my face." And Job 7: "Until I swallow my saliva."

**רקב** [Raqab] It has rotted. Isaiah 40: "The craftsman chooses wood that will not rot." And Proverbs 10: "And the name of the wicked shall rot." And from this the noun "rottenness" or "decay." Job 13: "And they are consumed like rottenness." And Job 41: "And he considers iron as straw, and brass as rotten wood."

**רקד** [Raqad] He leaped, he danced, he exulted. Psalm 114: "The mountains skipped like..."

...study. Since there is within our souls—from where, I do not know—an ingrained desire for great variety, it follows that the proverb "the commonplace becomes cheap" <note>original: *uilescit quotidianum*; a sentiment similar to "familiarity breeds contempt"</note> is often on our lips. It will therefore be necessary for the ancient dignity of the Holy Scriptures to be restored to a new appearance, one hitherto unknown to the Latin-speaking world. 

By casting aside the excessive familiarity of our daily readings, we may grasp for ourselves—not without a certain wonder for this recent and unheard-of field of study—a new and native style of expression within the Divine Scripture, just as the very mouth of God spoke it. For the common boredom felt toward all translations is only removed when the Bible of the Old Testament can be both read and understood by our people in its original tongue—that is, in Hebrew. This should be done in no other way and by no other manner than that which its primary foundation, established by the supreme Creator of all things, requires. 

This clearly cannot happen if we do not first, with eager effort, willingly pursue the proper meaning of Hebrew words and the true nature of the language <term>source of all theology: a common Renaissance idea that Hebrew was the "primordial" language of God and the purest source of divine truth</term> from which the fountain of all theology gushes forth. ->BOOK ONE.<-

Our ancestors avoided this task, which in my opinion is nearly infinite, or perhaps they thought it beneath their dignity. They likely felt that by leaving behind the highest disciplines of divine and human affairs, they would be turning themselves into mere schoolmasters of childish elements. I, however, feeling pity for such holy letters <note>The author refers here to the Hebrew alphabet and the study of the Bible in its original language</note>, grieved that in my time students have lacked knowledge of the Hebrew language for so long. Therefore, favoring their natural talent, I have dared—perhaps with excessive boldness—to be the first of all to place such a heavy weight upon my shoulders, and at the same time to offer myself to the bites of barking critics (would that they were only Jewish critics!). 

Nor did I consider it foreign to the dignity of a learned man to stoop to these elementary associations, following the example of Aurelius Opilius <note>A Roman scholar mentioned by Suetonius who moved from philosophy to grammar</note>, who did not disdain to study philosophy first, then the art of rhetoric, and finally grammar. Suetonius Tranquillus testifies to the same regarding Ateius Praetextatus the philologist. A similar thing is said of Valerius Cato, who was called the "Latin Siren." I confess, therefore, that concerning the system of letters, these are the studies of boys; and yet I have now advanced so far that some consider me partly a philosopher and partly a lawyer. 

This is mostly for these reasons: first, because of what we published under the name of **Capnio** <note>Johannes Reuchlin’s scholarly pseudonym, a Greek translation of his German name meaning "Little Smoke"</note> concerning *The Mirific Word* <note>original: "De Verbo Mirifico," Reuchlin's famous 1494 book on the Kabbalah and the power of the divine name</note>, from which they are persuaded that something approaching true philosophy can be drawn. Second, because for many years now I have held the dignity of the Triumvirate <note>A high judicial and administrative position in the Swabian League, a powerful association of cities and nobles in Southern Germany</note> over the most brave Swabians—attained not through ambition, but by pure election—and they see that I have kept that honor unshaken and sacred to this day. 

Nonetheless, I am not at all ashamed of this elementary art <note>The "elementary art" refers to the basic grammar and alphabet of Hebrew</note>. Since my very early youth, it has been my practice and habit to join "playful" disciplines <note>In this context, grammar and linguistics were seen as "play" compared to the "serious" work of law or theology</note> with great contemplations, always teaching while learning—if not teaching the greatest men, then at least the lowliest. For after my eighteenth year, when I began the literary studies of Priscian of Caesarea <note>A famous 6th-century Latin grammarian whose work was a staple of medieval education</note> in the school of Paris, I compiled a dictionary two years later among the people of Basel <note>original: "Rauracos," the Latin name for the region of Basel, Switzerland</note> which I called the *Breviloquus* <note>The "Concise Speaker," a popular Latin dictionary Reuchlin compiled in the 1470s</note>. 

At that same time and in that same place, Basel on the Rhine, I learned the Greek language under Andronicus Contoblacas, a Greek by nation. Four years later, I first sowed the seeds of that language among the Gauls at Genabum (which they now call Orléans). There, over a long period, I also devoted myself to Civil Law and was decorated by the doctors with the honor of the **Papinianists** <note>A title for advanced law students who had reached the study of the works of the Roman jurist Papinian</note> in the Year of Our Lord 1479. 

See, my brother, with what great care I have led my life! For the entire sum <note>original: "stipem," a small coin or contribution</note> that I spent on learning, I acquired by teaching. For at the same time, I both learned the laws of the Latins and taught the precepts of the Greeks, concerning which I then [wrote] a Greek grammar...

# BOOK.

I wrote a work whose title was *Little Education* <note>original: "μικροπαιδεία" (Mikropaideia)</note>, that is, a "Small Curriculum." A year after that, I lectured publicly among the people of Poitiers <note>The Latin "pictonibus" refers to the inhabitants of Poitiers, France</note> in Aquitaine, Gaul, and there I earned a Chair in Civil Law. Returning from there to Swabia, and having taken a wife, I assumed the insignia of a Doctor, practicing public law cases before tribunals and judges. And when the renowned prince Eberhard the Bearded <note>original: "Eberhardus Probus." Eberhard V was the first Duke of Württemberg and a significant patron of Reuchlin</note>—he who was later, at the most splendid Diet of Worms <note>original: "Vangionũ Comitiis"</note> by Maximilian I, King of the Romans, appointed the first Duke of the Württembergers by the unanimous consent of the Empire—sent me on an embassy to the most Serene Emperor Frederick III. I was also a Councilor among his nobles. Then, during that embassy, I found a Jew who was both learned and literate named Jacob ben Jehiel Loans; by imperial generosity, he was both a Doctor of Medicine and a Knight of the Golden Spur <note>original: "Equitem auratum." Loans was the court physician to Emperor Frederick III and Reuchlin's first Hebrew teacher</note>. He was the first who taught me the Hebrew letters faithfully, more than can be described. Later, however, as an envoy to Rome to Pope Alexander VI, I sought out the remaining rules of that language from a Jew of Cesena, namely Obadiah, son of Jacob Sforno <note>Obadiah ben Jacob Sforno was a famous Italian Jewish commentator and philosopher</note>, who very kindly instructed me in Hebrew every day during the entire time of the embassy, not without the payment of a significant fee.

I write this to you, my dear brother <note>Likely addressing his brother Dionysius, or perhaps the "learned brother" in a broader sense</note>, so that you may notice and frequently reflect in your mind with how much labor, time, and expense I obtained only the beginnings of the Hebrew language, which I now hand over to you in a much richer form than I received them. For I alone composed a Hebrew dictionary with much sharp study, along with other exercises which you may see with both your eyes and mind. Indeed, I have remembered the miserable misfortunes of the Jews in our time, who, driven not only from the borders of Spain <note>A reference to the 1492 expulsion of Jews from Spain</note> but also from our own Germany, are forced to seek other dwellings for themselves and turn toward the Hagarenes <note>A term used for the Ottoman Empire or Islamic lands, referring to the descendants of Hagar</note>. Because of this, it is likely that the Hebrew language might eventually cease and vanish among us, to the great ruin of Sacred Scripture. I decided within myself to lay the first foundations in this book for handing down the skill of the Hebrew language to Christians, in accordance with the sacred constitution of Pope Clement V concerning teachers <note>Refers to the decree of the Council of Vienne (1311), which mandated the teaching of Hebrew, Arabic, and Aramaic at major universities</note>. Since it appears that no one among the Latins <note>Western Christian scholars</note> has done this before me, I hope to gain from it no small favor and, among posterity, a praise that will not die away, free from envy. 

Therefore, with God's help, I will complete the whole work in three volumes. The first will be concerning letters, syllables, and words up to those terms beginning with the letter K. The second will be concerning words beginning from L until the end of the vocabulary. The third will be concerning the art of grammar and its practice. The title of this book is *On the Rudiments of Hebrew* <note>original: "de rudimentis hebraicis"</note>, because I have composed these volumes not for those already learned, but for the unpolished and those yet to be instructed.

In the same way, whatever things are written in Hebrew take their path from right to left. On the leaves themselves, however, whatever is written in Latin is read from left to right in the Latin manner. You will note these things as diligently as possible. We now proceed to the elements and the letters themselves.

<meta>This page serves as the introduction to the first book of the treatise, establishing the philosophical definitions of language and the fundamental differences between the Hebrew and Latin writing systems.</meta>

->**BOOK ONE**<-

...they enter into the name of a word, but by their own suitability, they provide the application of the voice to the vocal instruments. Now you can see that what the Stagirite philosopher <note>Aristotle, who was born in Stageira.</note> wrote in the third volume of his book *On the Heavens* is true: an element is that into which other bodies are divided, whether it exists potentially or in actuality. From this, following the opinion of Priscian <note>A famous 6th-century Latin grammarian.</note>, they have called letters by the name "elements," because when joined together, they compose the literal voice as if it were a kind of body. All the letters of the alphabet enter into syllables only by their potential, but they enter into voices by their actual effect and <term>entelechy</term> <note>original: "entelechia"; a Greek philosophical term meaning the realization or complete activation of a potential.</note>. It is as if the letters were colors and the points <note>vowel marks</note> were the light.

Therefore, so that I do not stray entirely from the path accustomed to by Latin speakers—enabling our people to learn foreign things more easily—I have chosen to divide the Hebrew elements into two parts. For we shall call some "letters" and others "voices." The letters are the signs of the alphabet. The voices are the added points <note>In Hebrew, vowels are often indicated by small dots or "points" around the consonants.</note>. Do not be surprised that these things are foreign and unheard of; for it is necessary for you to be instructed in Hebrew differently than in either Greek or Latin, since the speech of the Hebrews is distinct from theirs.

Indeed, according to the opinion of Ammonius the Peripatetic <note>A philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note> in his commentary on Aristotle's *On Interpretation*: since any nation uses its own specific sounds, it also adopts particular marks for letters—not natural marks, but established ones—which are held in place according to the requirements of its own language. This is most clearly seen in that nation which, as Cicero maintained in his speech *For Lucius Flaccus*, has always been opposed to Roman customs; consequently, they even seem to write in a manner contrary to the Romans. For the Latins write from the left to the right, but the Jews write from the right to the left. And just as the Egyptians boast that they write more "right-handedly" than the Greeks (according to Herodotus in the book titled *Euterpe*), so the Jews lead the pen to the right. They consider the Latins to lead it to the left, which they think resembles the way one scatters stones or seeds.

There is also the convenient fact that the letters **Beth**, **Caph**, **Lamed**, **Phe**, and **Quf**—that is, **B**, **C**, **L**, **P**, and **Q**—are drawn by the Latins and Jews with their shapes mirrored or turned toward each other. Thus, you may easily believe that in this book of *Rudiments*, there will often be a need for foreign and unaccustomed instructions.

->### BOOK<-

Of letters, some are vowels and some are consonants. They call those **Vowels** which are suited to be brought forth from the deepest part of the lungs by a simple opening of the mouth, relying especially on the support of the soul <note>The author uses *animi*, referring to the breath or "vital spirit" used in speaking</note>. Vowels are said to be more suitable for expressing the voice because they use no external instrument except only a variation of the breath. Thus, although they are <term>letters</term> <note>original Hebrew: אותיות (*otiyot*)</note>, they nevertheless possess a "home": *He* and *Heth* in the chest <note>Latin: *precordiis*, the region around the heart and diaphragm</note>; *Ayin* in the throat; *Aleph* and *Yod* in the hollow of the mouth; *Vav* in the open mouth. From these arise two "aspirations": the **Smooth**, like *He*, and the **Strong**, like *Heth*, just as with the <term>rough and smooth breathings</term> <note>original Greek: *Dasia* and *Psile*</note> among the Greeks. Certain diphthongs also arise. For *Aleph* and *Vav*, and similarly *Ayin* and *Vav*, make an *o* or *u* sound. *Aleph* and *Yod* signify *i* or *e*. *Vav* at the end of a word without a <term>Holam</term> <note>the dot representing an 'o' sound</note> or <term>Shurek</term> <note>the dot representing a 'u' sound</note> signifies the <term>Aeolic digamma</term> <note>an ancient Greek letter 'F' that functioned like a 'w' or 'v'</note> and makes a diphthong like *af* or *ef*, just as with the Greek *au* (αυ) and *eu* (ευ). Similarly, *Yod* at the end without a vowel point makes a diphthong by mixing the *i* sound with the preceding point, as will be shown more extensively below. And just as with the Latins *i* and *u* are sometimes vowels and sometimes consonants, so it is with *Vav* and *Yod* in the Hebrew language. They are **Consonants** when they use the service of the palate and lips. They are **Vowels** when they are expressed solely by the opening of the mouth. When they are counted among the consonants, they are taken either for a single consonant or a double one, entirely according to the teaching of Priscian of Caesarea <note>A famous 6th-century Latin grammarian</note> in the first book of the *Art of Grammar*. Consonants are letters which, when joined to sounds, require the aid of "instruments" in pronunciation. These instruments are the lips, the tongue, the teeth, and the palate.

Among the consonants, some are "dual-formed" and others are "uniform." Those are called **Dual-formed** which possess two characters under one name, and they are five in number: *Kaph*, *Mem*, *Nun*, *Pe*, and *Tsade*. These shapes, which we see placed in the alphabetical row, are called the **Principal** ones: כ מ נ פ צ. These should be placed at the beginning of words or only in the middle, and never at the end. However, these are called the **Terminal** shapes: ך ם ן ף ץ, which are found placed only at the end of words—with only one verse excepted: the ninth chapter of Isaiah, "His empire shall be multiplied" <note>In Isaiah 9:7, the Hebrew word *le-marbeh* (למרבה) is written with a "closed" or final Mem (ם) in the middle of the word, which is a famous scribal anomaly</note>, where a terminal *Mem* begins a word. This mystery requires a deeper investigation than what pertains to the grammarian. All the remaining letters are **Uniform**, because they are written everywhere with one and only one type of character. There is also another division of the twenty-two letters. For of them, eleven are **Substantial** <note>Also known as "radical" letters that form the root of a word</note> only, and the remaining eleven are at the same time **Accidental** <note>Also known as "servile" letters used for grammatical prefixes or suffixes</note>. Substantial letters are those which only pri...

<meta>This page continues the technical introduction to Hebrew grammar, moving from the basic alphabet to the functional categorization of letters and the rules of pronunciation (phonology).</meta>

->**FIRST [BOOK]**<-

...primitive <note>original: "mitiua" (primitive/radical)</note> [letters] of words, they denote them as חטסמרגזועצדק <note>Chet, Tet, Samekh, Mem, Resh, Gimel, Zayin, Vav, Ayin, Tsadi, Dalet, Qof</note>. Accidental letters <note>Also known as "servile" letters; these are used for grammatical prefixes, suffixes, and inflections rather than being part of the root word.</note>, however, are those which simultaneously indicate grammatical changes and inflections, as well as the formation of derivative words; according to **Rabbi Moses Kimhi**, these are את כנחמשליבו. But **Rabbi Moses ben Gabirol** collects them as follows: אני שלמה כותב <note>original Hebrew: "I, Solomon, am writing." This is a famous mnemonic device used to remember the servile letters.</note>. Some of the accidental letters are usually only placed at the beginning of words, such as אלבט; others, however, are found both at the beginning and at the end, such as תבנהיום. Likewise, some of the consonants are accustomed to take on a double mode of pronunciation; for they can be pronounced either softly or strongly. There are six of these: בגדכפרת <note>The "Begadkefat" letters: Beth, Gimel, Dalet, Kaph, Pe, and Tav.</note>. When they are uttered with a certain softness and a light breath, then either a lying <term>virgula</term> <note>a small horizontal line</note> is placed above them, which is called <term>raphe</term> <note>from the Hebrew for "weak" or "soft"</note>—like this: ֿ —or certainly, even if it is not placed above, it is nevertheless understood to be there. In this state, *Beth* [ב] is pronounced in the place of the consonant *V*. *Caph* [כ] in the place of the Greek letter *Chi* [χ], which for us has the value of *ch*. Likewise, *Pe* [פ] in the place of *Phi* [φ], which is equivalent to *F* or *ph*. Similarly, *Thau* [ת] in the place of *Theta* [θ], which for the Latins is equivalent to *th*; it produces a lisping tongue in Hebrew pronunciation. For if you see the *raphe* line lying above the *Thau*, you must place your tongue between your upper and lower teeth while hissing, and emit a sound such as geese are accustomed to do when they are moved with anger toward revenge. On the other hand, if the listed letters are marked with a dot placed in the "belly" <note>the middle of the character</note>—which dot is called <term>Dagesh</term>—then they are pronounced more strongly and harshly, and no longer flowingly. For the *Dagesh* point strengthens the letters so much that often a single letter is considered as if it were doubled. There are two, however, which receive neither *Dagesh* nor *raphe*, namely *Tet* [ט] and *Qof* [ק]. Furthermore, the second-to-last letter, *Sin* [ש], is also pronounced in two ways. For if a point is placed above it on the left side [שׂ], it expresses the sound of *sigma* or an *s* with a sharp hiss. But if the same point is placed on the right side [שׁ], then it will emit the sound of powerful water falling with force from high rocks and foaming; for this reason, I shall hereafter call it, for the sake of brevity, the "Right-hand Sin" or the "foaming" or "lathering s," to signify the sound of foaming water. We imitate this sound when we join the upper and lower teeth directly together while withdrawing the tongue from the teeth. The Germans try to signify this sound through *sch*, the Italians through *sci*, and the French through *x* or *ch*. Hence, Italy writes the letter *sin* as *scin*; Celtic Gaul as *xin* or *chin*; and Swabia <note>representing German speakers</note> as *schin*. In whatever way you write it, understand it to be thick, foaming, and broad.

->## ON VOWELS<-
<note>original: "DE VOCIBVS." In this grammatical context, "vocibus" (voices) refers specifically to vowel sounds.</note>

<margin>n</margin> Now, let us turn our hand to the second part of the elements, which we have called "voices." According to Aristotle in the second book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "de Anima"</note>, a voice is the striking of air—breathed out by the soul—against the windpipe <term>windpipe: the "arteria," referring here to the larynx and trachea where vocal sound originates</term> within the vocal organs. This occurs in five ways among the Latins, but in ten ways among the Hebrews. For the Latins have the signs for their voices <note>vowels</note> inserted among the other letters of the alphabet. The Hebrews, however, only have vowel letters as a matter of habit within the alphabet; they placed the actual voices <note>vowel points or niqqud</note> outside the sequence of the alphabet. 

Therefore, among the Hebrews, a "vowel" <note>vocalis</note> is one thing, and a "voice" <note>vox</note> is another. A vowel is a letter that is first suited to go forth into a sound of the windpipe, using the varieties of its own "dwellings" <note>the specific positions of the mouth, throat, or tongue</note>. But voices are points <term>points: the Hebrew vowel markings known as niqqud, which are dots and lines placed around consonants</term> attached to the letters, which open the gap of the mouth according to the diversity of the letters. So that you may more clearly understand the voices of the Hebrews, I shall proceed according to the Latin vowels: A, E, I, O, U, of which each...

Next comes the fourth vowel, **O**, which is simply to be enunciated with a round mouth. In its place, the Hebrews place a single dot above the letter, and it is called <term>Holem</term> <note>The standard Hebrew vowel mark for 'o'.</note>. It must be pronounced correctly and subtly, as in the words "add," "benevolent," or "underhanded." In that same region of the mouth, a certain sound is usually found that falls between **O** and **A**, being a middle point between them, though it approaches the sound of **O** more closely than the <term>Qamets</term> <note>A long 'a' sound in Hebrew.</note> mentioned above. For this reason, it is called <term>Hatef Qamets</term> <note>A "reduced" or very short 'o' sound.</note>. However, those who do not distinguish sounds clearly tend to always pronounce it as a standard **O**, as in the name **Chedorlaomer**, king of the Elamites. It is written beneath the letter with the shape of a *Qamets* preceded by two vertical dots standing side by side, like this: [Hebrew character with Hatef Qamets vowel mark]. The fifth vowel of the Romans is **U**. To represent this sound, the letter *Vav* is usually used with a dot included in its belly, like this: [Hebrew character Vav with Shureq vowel mark], and it is called <term>Shureq</term>. Beside it is a "collection of the lips" <note>A phonetic description of rounding the lips for the 'u' sound.</note>, which is written with three dots arranged like a staircase or steps following one another, like this: [Hebrew Qibbuts vowel mark], and it is named <term>Qibbuts</term>. It has the sound that the letter **U** has among the French, specifically with a blending of the vowel **I**. It is a middle sound between **U** and **I**, such as the ancient Greeks gave to their letter *Upsilon*. Originally, they used to place the mark of the vowel **I** inside the belly of the **U**, like this: [Greek letter upsilon with internal mark]. Later, removing it, they attached it underneath like this: [Greek letter upsilon], as seen in the word *harpy*.

We have described the nine clear sounds of the Hebrews. There remains another sound—dull, blunt, and so thin that it is either scarcely heard or not heard at all. It is called <term>Sheva</term>. It is written similarly to the *Hatef* shown above, with two dots placed vertically one under the other, like this: [Hebrew Sheva vowel mark]. Hence, it is sometimes called by the name *Hatef*. For example, in the word "compress" <note>original Latin: "comprimo"</note> or the name **Amraphel**: if you close your lips on the letter **M**, you cannot proceed to the next syllable unless you open your mouth again. That tiny sound that arises from the opening of the lips, however slight or short it may be, is called *Sheva*, as if you were pronouncing it "com-primo" or "Am-raphel." Indeed, it is an indistinct sound which, due to its thinness, can hardly be perceived by the senses. Furthermore, the <term>Hatef</term> <note>meaning "rapid" or "stolen"</note> mentioned above is placed before three vowels: *Pataħ*, *Qamets*, and *Segol*. They are called <term>Hatef Pataħ</term>, <term>Hatef Qamets</term>, and <term>Hatef Segol</term>—meaning rapid and swift—and they indicate a shortened sound. Occasionally, a dot is placed in a final letter *He*, which signifies a pronominal relationship <note>The "Mapiq," indicating that the 'H' is a consonant meaning "her."</note> and is called <term>Mapiq</term>, but this has nothing to do with pronunciation.

The sibilant <term>Samech</term> (ס) and left-side <term>Sin</term> (שׂ) are pronounced like the [Greek] *sigma* or the Roman *s* with a thin and sharp sound. The sibilant right-side <term>Shin</term> (שׁ) is made with the teeth directly joined and the tongue pulled back from them, like the sound of rushing water. The sibilant <term>Thau</term> (ת) is made with the tongue inserted between the upper and lower teeth and with a lisping mouth. The sibilant <term>Caph</term> (כ) when aspirated—that is, with a <term>raphe</term> <gloss>a horizontal line</gloss> placed above it—is made by applying the root of the tongue to the uvula of the throat, expressing a breath just as the Greeks are accustomed to doing with the letter *chi*. The pronunciation of the letter <term>Ayin</term> (ע) arises in the depth of the throat, just as <term>Aleph</term> (א) does in the hollow of the mouth.

There are ten vowel points. **A** is *pathah* ( ַ ) and *qamets* ( ָ ). **E** is *tsere* ( ֵ ) and **I** is *hiriq* ( ִ ) placed below. **O** is *holam* ( ֹ ) placed above and *hataf-qamets* ( ֳ ). **V** is *shureq* ( וּ ) and *qibbuts* ( ֻ ). A thin and dull sound is the *sheva* ( ְ ). Compound points are *hataf-pathah* ( ֲ ), *hataf-qamets* ( ֳ ), and *hataf-segol* ( ֱ ).

The **Dagesh** ( ּ ) in the belly of a letter is "strong"; in the middle of a word, it doubles the letter.
The **Raphe** ( ֿ ) above a letter indicates it should be aspirated with a soft breath.
A single point ( ּ ) is sometimes placed in a final *he* (הּ); it signifies the relationship of one thing to another and is called **mappiq**.

From these alphabets and points <term>vowel markings</term> construct syllables in this way: *aleph* with *patha* is *a*; *beth* with *patha* is *ba*; *gimel* with *patha* is *ga*; *daleth* with *camez* is *do*; *he* with *camez* is *ho*; *vau* with *zere* is *ve*; *zain* with *zere* is *ze*; *heth* with *segol* is *he*; *teth* with *segol* is *te*; *iod* with *segol* is *ie*; *caph* with *holem* is *co*; *lamed* with *holem* is *lo*; *mem* with *holem* is *mo*; *nun* with *hatefcamez* is *no*; *samech* with *hatef camez* is *so*; *aleph* and *vau* with *surek* is *u*; *ain* and *vau* with *surek* is *u*; *ain* with *kibuz* is *u*; *pe* with *kibuz* is *pu*; *sade* with *kibuz* is *zu*; *qof* with *kibuz* is *qu*; *sin* with *scheua* is *sh*; *taf* with *seua* is *th*.

So that an easier path to further things may lie open to you, it will first be necessary to test your strengths, to prepare your mouth and pen, and to press on continually so that after gaining knowledge of the elements and the science of syllables, you may arrive at the pronunciation of words. This will happen if you first exercise yourself diligently in the connection of many syllables. Just as they say Demosthenes—by placing little stones in his mouth—repeated the Greek letter *rho* (which because of a defect of the tongue he was unable to pronounce for a long time) with unwearied zeal and immense labor many times and often, until at last from long practice nothing stood in the way of him speaking that *rho*. When this had occurred, he is said to have exclaimed in Greek words: "I have found the spoken rho" <note>original: "eurika to rho reroreumenō"</note>, to show that "dogged labor conquers all" <note>original: "labor improbus omnia vincit," a famous quote from Virgil’s Georgics</note>. Let us return, therefore, to the syllables and test what they produce when joined together. For example, if you say *aleph* with *patha* and *beth*, there arises *ab*; *beth* with *patha* and *gimel* makes *bag*; *gimel* with *patha* and *daleth* makes *gad*; *he* with *patha* and *sdain* makes *hasd*.

I note this here so that you may keep it accurately in your memory, since you heard in the summary of the elements that there is a double *z*. One is very soft, which is called *zain*; and so that the lightness and softness of its pronunciation may be clear, I have written *sdain* for you in place of *zain*. Hieronymus <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible</note> did this before me; for when he had to write the Book of *Ezra* using the letter *zain*, he wrote it as *Esdras*—that is, using *sd* for *zain*. The other *z* is harsh and is called *zade* <note>Tsade</note>, which is pronounced like *ts*, as in *ezem*—pronounced as if it were *etsem*—or *ez* as if it were *ets*. Remember, therefore, that you have two *z* sounds, namely *zain* and *zade*; one soft, the other hard. You have two *s* sounds, namely *samech* and *sin*; two *t* sounds, *thau* and *teth*; and even softer than both of these is *d*, that is *daleth*. For this reason, many people even hiss the letter *daleth* slightly, and where we say *iod*, they say *ius*. Likewise, there are *qof* and *caf*, and softer than both of these is *gimel*. There are two aspirations, *he* and *heth*, of which the first breathes out gently, while the second pants forth strongly. There are two *a* sounds, namely *aleph* and *ain*, of which the first is formed in the mouth and the second in the throat. Let me remember all these things often, so that I may more faithfully...

<meta>This page continues the technical instruction on Hebrew grammar, transitioning from basic syllable pronunciation to the specific rules of diphthongs. It connects Hebrew phonology with familiar Latin and Greek linguistic structures.</meta>

->FIRST<-

Keep this in memory, for it will be very useful for pronouncing syllables. Added to this is the knowledge of diphthongs, the explanation of which we have reserved until now. For without these, you will read neither syllables nor words correctly. A **diphthong** is a monosyllabic utterance of two sounds mixed under a single point <note>The author uses "point" likely to refer to a single vocal beat or a specific grammatical mark</note>. Some diphthongs are called **proper**, while others are called **improper**.

There are six proper diphthongs: **af, ef, if, ai, ei, oi**.
1. The first diphthong is **af**: as in *thaf* <note>original: "thaf"</note>, thus [Hebrew: תו] from Ezekiel 9: "Mark a *thau* <note>The Hebrew letter Tav</note> upon the foreheads of the men."
Similarly [Hebrew: עשו] *Esaf* <note>original: "Esaf"</note> from Genesis 25: "And his name was called Esau."
2. The second is **ef**: as in *Kislef*, which is November, thus [Hebrew: כסליו] from Zechariah 7: "on the fourth [day] of the ninth month, which is Casleu."
3. The third is **if**: as in *zif*, which is April, thus [Hebrew: זיו] from 1 Kings 6: "In the fourth year, in the month of Ziv."
And although the Romans say *au, ei, iu* for these, the Greeks imitate the Hebrews in this. For example, when they say *Autocraton* for *autocrator* <note>original: "autocrator"</note>, meaning **emperor**; *Efangelion* for *euangelion*, meaning **Gospel**; *Ifgenios* for *Eugenios*, meaning **bearded** <note>The author likely associates the name Eugenios with "barbatus" (bearded) here, though it traditionally means "well-born"</note>. However, in this place the **F** should sound softly and not strongly, like the old Aeolic **digamma** <term>digamma: an ancient Greek letter (Ϝ) that sounded like a 'w' or 'v'</term>, for which the Latins found the consonant **v** (according to Priscian in Book 1), which today can still be called the Aeolic digamma.

4. The fourth proper diphthong is **ai**: just as in Latin with Virgil: "They were pouring bowls of wine in the middle of the *aulai* <note>archaic Latin for 'hall'</note>." So also in Hebrew *hai* [Hebrew: חי] meaning **living**. Psalm 42: "My soul thirsts for God, the strong, living [God]." Or *ai* with the *camez* <term>qamets: a Hebrew vowel mark usually indicating a long 'a' sound</term> as in [Hebrew: שדי] from Isaiah.
5. The fifth diphthong is **ei**: as in *heil* [Hebrew: חיל] meaning **wealth** or **abundance**. Job 20: "according to the multitude of his inventions." Just as the Latins do; Terence in *Andria*: "Alas [*Hei*], I was afraid of Chrysis."
6. The sixth diphthong is **oi**: as in *hoi* [Hebrew: הוי] meaning **woe**. Jeremiah 22: "Woe, brother! and Woe, sister!" which the Latins end in *e*, like *hoe*. Horace in the Odes: "Alas, *hoe*, spare the book."

The others are called **improper diphthongs**. For although they are written with two vowels under one syllable, there is no mixing of multiple sounds in the pronunciation itself; rather, only one sound is heard. There are three improper diphthongs:
**I**, as in [Hebrew: אלי] or [Hebrew: עלי]
**O**, as in [Hebrew: אלו] or [Hebrew: עלו]
**U**, as in [Hebrew: אלו] or [Hebrew: עלו]
Let these few things about diphthongs suffice for the unrefined <note>The author uses "rudibus" to refer to students or beginners</note>.

**BOOK.**

**ON PRONOUNCING OR NOT PRONOUNCING**

<margin>1</margin> In forming syllables, however, certain vowels are pronounced, while others are not. For whichever letters have one of the **vowel points** <note>Hebrew uses a system of dots and lines called *nikkud* to indicate vowel sounds, as the alphabet consists only of consonants.</note>, those are pronounced according to the sound of the point attached to them. The two aspirates <note>Breathy sounds produced in the throat: the letters *He* and *Heth*.</note> at the end of a syllable are excepted when a **sheva** <note>term: sheva; a mark indicating a very short vowel sound or no vowel at all.</note> is noted under them. An example of the letter **he** is found in 4 Kings 10 <note>original: "iiij. Re. x."; refers to modern 2 Kings 10:9</note>: וַהֲרָגָנוּ <note>original: *vaharaganu*</note>—that is, **and I killed him.** <note>The Hebrew text provided actually means "and he killed us," but the author translates the Latin as "interfeci eum" (I killed him).</note> An example of the letter **heth** is in Isaiah 53: וְנֶחְמְדֵהוּ <note>original: *vanechmedehu*</note>—that is, **and we desired him.** This is because they are not pronounced unless another vowel follows.

But those letters which have no point, even if they are written, are nevertheless not pronounced; instead, the syllable itself takes its sound from the vowel point preceding the letter in that same syllable. The final **yod** <note>The letter *iod* or *yod*.</note> is an exception in three specific cases. First, when a **diphthong** <note>Two vowel sounds joined in one syllable.</note> is broken up by **diaeresis** <note>The separation of two vowels into distinct syllables.</note> as in גּוֹי <note>original: *goy*; nation</note>; then the diaeresis creates the two-syllable sound **oi**. The second case is when it follows a **shurek** <note>term: shurek; a vowel point for the "u" sound.</note> such as תָּלוּי <note>original: *taluy*</note>, a three-syllable word meaning **suspended.**

The third case is when **yod** is added as a pronoun to signify "myself," such as פָּנַי <note>original: *panay*</note>, a three-syllable word meaning **my face.** In these three cases, the final vowel **yod**, although it is not pointed, is nonetheless pronounced with its natural sound, namely **I**. In other cases, however, the rule remains, which may be explained more clearly by taking the first word of the Bible as an example, which is בְּרֵאשִׁית <note>original: *bereshit*; "In the beginning"</note>.

**Bereshit.** In this word, you see two vowel letters, namely **aleph** and **yod**. For if you were to take the **aleph** out of the word, you would nonetheless read it as **Bereshit**, because the point called **tzere** <note>term: tzere; a vowel point for a long "e" sound.</note> sits under the consonant **resh**. Therefore, since **resh** and **tzere** make the sound **re**, we see that the **aleph** does not necessarily add to the sound of **re**. The same judgment must be made regarding the vowel letter **yod**. If it were not written, the consonant **shin** and the point **hireq** <note>term: hireq; a vowel point for the "i" sound.</note> would no less make the sound **shi**, and with the **tav** <note>thau</note> joined, it would become **shit**, and thus **Bereshit**. This should be considered carefully not only in the middle of words, but even more strongly at the end. For the second word of the Bible, בָּרָא <note>original: *bara*</note>, that is, **he created**, consists of **beth** and **qamets** <note>term: qamets; a vowel point for the "a" sound.</note>, making **ba**, and **resh** with **qamets**, making **ra**, where the **aleph** rests and is silent, even though it is written. There are times when two vowel letters at the end of a word are silent, no matter how much they are written, such as הִיא <note>original: *hi*</note>, that is, **this one** <note>usually "she" in Hebrew</note>. For the letter **he** and the point **hireq** make **hi**, and the rest are silent. This also must be especially noted: the vowel **he**, the mark of aspiration, is never pronounced at the end of words, even if...

...written. Similarly with the letter *heth*. For the function of those letters at the end of words is to add a breath to each point, and to adapt it as either a rough or smooth breathing, even though in writing the letters *he* and *heth* differ. <note>original: "he & heth". These are the Hebrew letters ה (He) and ח (Heth).</note> For a terminal *he* is never pointed. But a terminal *heth* sometimes has a point <note>A vowel mark</note> placed beneath it, such as [Hebrew: רוּחַ] which is pronounced **Ruah** and not *ruha*. <note>original: "Ruah et non ruha". This refers to the "Pattach Ganuach," a unique rule where a vowel is pronounced before the final consonant.</note> This is truly worthy of note.

Indeed, it must not be forgotten what I said regarding the terminal *heth*. For if another letter follows it, so that the *heth* begins another syllable, it places its breath in the earlier order, such as [Hebrew: רוּחִי] which means **my spirit** <note>original: "ruhi"</note> and [Hebrew: רוּחוֹ] meaning **his spirit**. <note>original: "ruho"</note> But when the letter creates a final syllable for itself, then the sound of the point placed beneath precedes the breath, and a strong breath follows the very utterance of the vocal sound.

Furthermore, you should not be unaware of the usage customarily observed regarding the <term>Sheva</term> <note>A Hebrew diacritic ( ְ ) consisting of two vertical dots that can represent a very short 'e' sound or no sound at all.</note> point. It is accustomed to sometimes be pronounced and sometimes not. Regarding "connected" <note>consonant clusters</note> consonants, those living beyond the Alps <note>Italians and Spaniards</note> follow one custom, while those on this side of the Alps <note>Germans</note> follow another. There are indeed "connected" pairs according to the doctrine of <note>Priscian was a famous Roman grammarian whose 6th-century works were the standard for medieval linguistic study.</note> Priscian at the end of the first book of the *Art of Grammar*: **BD, GD, CT, PT, MN, SB, SC, SL, SM, SP, ST**.

And among the Hebrews, just as one judges the letter *s*, so must one judge the letter *z*. Also, all <term>mutes</term> <note>Consonants produced by stopping the flow of air, like p, b, t, d.</note> precede the three <term>liquids</term> <note>Smooth, flowing consonant sounds like l, n, r.</note> individually: specifically **l, n, r**; but only **c, d, g, t** can be placed before **m**. At the end of a word, however, all liquids are found before **s**, but only three precede **x** (or **cs**): namely **l, n, r**. Likewise, triple capital clusters can stick together: **scr, str, spr**; and similarly **scl, stl, spl**. When they are at the end, the liquid comes first, then the mute, and the *s* third.

Having considered this accurately, it must be noted that whenever the **Sheva** point is written beneath connected consonants, among the Germans it is usually quiet and silent. Among the Italians and Spaniards, however, it is slightly moved and whispered, as if you hear a very thin *e* sound underneath. We experience this in the aforementioned beginning of the Bible, [Hebrew: בְּרֵאשִׁית] <note>Bereshit ("In the beginning")</note> where the mute and liquid are connected. Therefore, the **Sheva** under the letter *beth* is not pronounced by the Germans; for they say **Bresith** <note>original: "bresith"</note> just as the Latins say *brevis*. Let us take the beginning of the second book of the Bible <note>The Book of Exodus</note>, where the second word is found to be [Hebrew: שְׁמוֹת] <note>Shemot ("Names")</note> where **sm** are the connected letters. Therefore, the **Sheva** point is quiet and silent on this side of the mountains (that is, in Germany). But it is whispered beyond the mountains; for the Germans say **Smoth**, while the Italians and Spaniards say **Semoth**, with the first syllable being <term>Iambic</term> <note>A short-long rhythm</note> and very shortened. Similar cases are [Hebrew: סְפָרַד] meaning **Spain** <note>original: "Hispanus"</note> and [Hebrew: צְפַנְיָה] <note>The name Zephaniah</note>.

At the end of syllables as well as words, whether there are several consonants or only one, the Sheva is always silent. An example is the name **Belshazzar** <note>original Hebrew: בֵּלְטְשַׁצַּר (*Baltschazer*)</note> from Daniel, chapter 4: Daniel, whose name was Belshazzar. It has three syllables, and the first syllable ends in two consonants, *l* <note>Lamed</note> and *t* <note>Teth</note>, each of which is written with a Sheva. Nevertheless, the sound of a vowel is not read; rather, the power of both consonants serves the <term>Pathach<note>A Hebrew vowel sign representing the "a" sound.</note></term> vowel marked under the letter *Beth*. Therefore, it is read as "balt." 

Another example of the rule at the end of a word where the Sheva points are similarly silent is the name of **Artaxerxes** in Ezra, chapter 7, which is written **Artaxerxes** <note>original Hebrew: אַרְתַּחְשַׁשְׂתָּא (*Arthahschasst*) </note> and read as *Arthahschasst*. You should think no differently regarding a single consonant that ends either a syllable or a word; the Sheva point noted under it is not pronounced but remains silent. For example: **Libneh** <note>original Hebrew: לִבְנֶה</note>, the name of a tree, which is pronounced *libne*. Also, **Issachar** <note>original: יִשָּׂשכָר (*issaschar*)</note>, which we read as *Isachar*. 

This rule concerning the middle of a word has two particularly memorable exceptions which it is best not to be ignorant of. 

**The First Exception:** When two consonants are placed sequentially in the middle of a word, and the first one contains a <term>Dagesh<note>A dot placed inside a Hebrew letter to indicate it should be doubled or hardened.</note></term> and a Sheva is written beneath it. In that case, the consonant is pronounced strongly as if it were doubled because of the Dagesh (as was shown above), and the Sheva is pronounced in its usual way, very briefly. For example: **Sisera** <note>original Hebrew: סִיסְרָא</note>, which is read as the three-syllable *Sissera*, from Judges, chapter 4. In the case of <note>original: "Ezra illo scriba"</note> Ezra that scribe, the name is two syllables because the letter <term>zain (the Hebrew letter 'Z')</term> does not contain a <term>dagesh (a dot within a letter indicating it should be doubled or hardened)</term>. The second exception is: when one and the same consonant is doubled in the middle of a word—that is, placed twice in succession—then if the first consonant is marked with a <term>sheva (a vowel sign indicating a very short 'e' or a vocalized pause)</term>, that <term>sheva</term> is regularly pronounced. For example, הַלְלוּיָהּ **Hallelujah**. For if the <term>sheva</term> were not pronounced, then the context would cause it to be spoken as **Alluia**, a word of three syllables; but as it stands, it is four syllables, meaning <note>original: "laudate deum"</note> "praise the Lord." Let these things be said regarding the <term>sheva</term> of consonants. However, when a vowel follows after the consonant under which a <term>sheva</term> is written, then the <term>sheva</term> is always pronounced, as in תְּאֵנָה *theena* <note>original: "ficus"</note> **fig tree**, and יִשְׁמְעוּ <note>original: "audient"</note> **they will hear**. Also קְחוּ *kechu* <note>original: "Sumite"</note> **take**, from chapter 42 of the same book, which is a two-syllable word; and so it is with other similar cases.

It is also very pleasing to bring up here that point regarding the <term>qamets (a vowel sign usually sounding like 'ah')</term> which practice has taught us more than formal rules. For as often as two <term>qamets</term> follow one another, the latter inclines toward the pronunciation of the vowel **o**; or, as is the custom for many, the first sounds like a proper **o** and the second like an oblique **a**. This occurs equally in monosyllables, especially those ending in the letter <term>lamed (the letter 'L')</term>, and in those words where the preceding letter is written with a <term>qamets</term> and the following with a <term>sheva</term>. This is also observed by some in multi-syllable words when the last syllable is written with a <term>qamets</term> and is followed by a one-syllable word. All these are contained in these examples:

->Bo Ethmoch Adom Chol Hochma<-
->בּוֹ אֶתְמֹךְ אָדֹם כֹּל חָכְמָה<-

The last of these is interpreted as <note>original: "suscipiam eum"</note> "**I will uphold him**" in Isaiah 42. But truly, at the outset, everyone must be reminded that I am not writing for the learned, but for the unrefined, who <note>An allusion to 1 Corinthians 3:2 and Hebrews 5:12.</note> have **need of milk, not solid food**. Therefore, I promise rules only for reading, not for writing. In this book of rudiments, I will teach you at least this one thing: how to read what is written, not how to write what is to be read. For if it were otherwise, I would certainly produce many proofs of my talent and method, which, God willing, I shall not omit later, once I perceive that you have stepped beyond the elementary boundaries and desire higher things.

# BOOK

## ON THE ART OF PRACTICAL INSTRUCTION
After so many and such varied rules regarding the basic elements and syllables, I believe it will be especially useful—indeed, almost necessary for the skill of reading—to bring forward certain selected words. These should be words that are not entirely foreign to your ears, yet are not without difficulty in their understanding and pronunciation, so that you may train your mouth and breath to them. For it often happens that things which are completely foreign, and which wander from the well-trodden path of speech according to the idiom <term>idiom: the specific character or "way" of a language</term> of this language, turn away the mind of the Neophyte <term>neophyte: a beginner or person newly starting a study</term> with terror or despair at the very beginning—especially in a study that has not yet been clarified in our own language. On the contrary, it happens that one who applies effort and expense to the beginnings of an art is particularly unwilling to sweat over common and entirely trite matters for the sake of attaining the "praise of virtue," which is always occupied with difficult tasks. Therefore, I thought it fitting to set before those being instructed the noble lineage of the Virgin Mary. Students have often heard this lineage pronounced in the church on feast days, albeit unlearnedly, yet it is not so commonly chanted that one does not need to strive with all one's strength to correctly assemble the syllables. Therefore, store this matter in your deepest senses; it is no small thing.

The name **Adam** <note>original Hebrew: אָדָם</note> has two syllables. The letter *Aleph* with a *Qamets* <note>A Hebrew vowel mark, usually representing a long "a" sound.</note> creates an "oblique a"; therefore, that syllable is to be pronounced with a middle sound between "a" and "o." The second syllable is the letter *Dalet* with a similar *Qamets*, making the sound "da"; and with the *Mem* joined, it becomes "dam," and the whole word becomes **Adam**. 

However, because two *Qamets* marks follow one another, the latter sound shifts toward an "o" sound, which is why they say "**Adom**." The *Mem* at the end is closed, and it is not similar to the version of that letter found in the standard alphabet row, because it is one of the five **terminal letters** <term>Final forms (Sophit): In Hebrew, five letters (Kaf, Mem, Nun, Pe, and Tsadi) change their shape when they appear at the end of a word.</term> which must only be placed at the end of a word. 

**Seth** <note>original Hebrew: שֵׁת</note> is a monosyllabic name. Its first consonant is called the "right-hand Shin," that is, a "hissing Shin" <note>original Latin: "schin spumosum," literally "foamy" or "frothy," referring to the sibilant shushing sound.</note>; the second consonant is...

**THE BOOK**

The softened <term>tav</term> <note>original: "thau raphatu," referring to the Hebrew letter Tav without a dagesh (dot)</note>, that is, a lisping and hissing *tav*. Therefore I speak thus: <term>shin</term> with <term>tsere</term> <note>a vowel mark for a long 'e' sound</note> makes *she*. Join the hissing *tav* and it becomes *Sheth* <note>Seth</note>. I cannot express this hissing sound in our script except by placing a horizontal line underneath the letter. אֱנוֹשׁ <note>Enosh</note> has two syllables. The first, <term>aleph</term> with <term>chateph segol</term> <note>a composite vowel for a very brief 'e'</note>, makes a slanting and short *e* because of the <term>chateph</term>. That syllable generates a guttural sound, a shortened *en*. The second, <term>nun</term> with <term>vav cholem</term> <note>the letter Nun combined with the vowel for 'o'</note>, becomes *no*. Join the right-handed and foaming <term>shin</term> <note>referring to the letter ש</note> and so arises *nosh*. Combine the individual parts and it becomes *Enosh*. קֵינָן <note>Kenan</note> has two syllables. The first, <term>qof</term> with <term>tsere</term>, makes *ke*, to which is joined a <term>yod</term> as a diphthong—which is the fifth in number—and it becomes *kei*. The second, <term>nun</term> with <term>qamets</term> <note>a vowel usually for a long 'a'</note>, makes a slanting *na*; by adding another <term>nun</term> (that is, the letter *n*), it becomes *nan*. Combine the individual parts and it becomes *Keinan*. Note, however, that the final *nun* has a different shape than the preceding one, because it is one of the five terminal consonants noted above. מַהֲלַלְאֵל <note>Mahalaleel</note> has five syllables. The first, <term>mem</term> with <term>patah</term> <note>a vowel for 'a'</note>, makes a straight *ma*. The second, <term>he</term> with <term>chateph patah</term>, makes a lightly shortened *ha* because of the <term>chateph</term>. The third, <term>lamed</term> with <term>patah</term>, is *la*. The fourth, <term>lamed</term> with <term>sheva</term> <note>a very brief vowel or syllable divider</note>, mutters a sudden *e*; it is pronounced and is not silent because when a pointed vowel follows, the *sheva* is always pronounced, as was clear in the previous chapter. The fifth, <term>aleph</term> with <term>tsere</term>, makes a straight *e*; by subjoining <term>lamed</term> (that is, *l*), it will be *el*. Combine the individual parts and it becomes *Mahalaleel*. יֶרֶד <note>Jared</note> has two syllables. The first, <term>yod</term> with <term>qamets</term> <note>The text specifies 'camez', though 'segol' is standard for Jared; it produces a 'ya' sound here</note>, makes a slanting *ia*. Here, <term>yod</term> is a consonant; for although it is a vowel by nature, its use here is as a consonant. And regularly, <term>yod</term> at the beginning of a syllable is always an active consonant; remember this, student. The second, <term>resh</term> with <term>segol</term> <note>a short 'e' vowel</note>, makes a thick or slanting *re*, to which subjoining <term>dalet</term> (that is, *d*) results in *red*. Combine the individual parts and it becomes *Iared*. חֲנוֹךְ <note>Hanoch/Enoch</note> has two syllables. The first, <term>het</term> with <term>chateph patah</term>, makes a straight and short *ha*. It is "straight" because of the <term>patah</term> and "short" because of the <term>chateph</term>. It must be pronounced with a strong and panting breath, because it is a <term>dasia</term> <note>from Greek 'dasys', meaning a rough breathing or aspiration</note> and a strong aspiration. When this is transferred to Latin, it ought to be written by us with an *h*. For the other aspiration, namely the <term>psile</term> <note>from Greek 'psilos', a smooth breathing</note>, is not written among the Latins, but only the vowel itself which it aspirates. The second, <term>nun</term> with <term>vav cholem</term>, makes *no*; with the softened <term>caph</term> added (that is, *ch*), it will be *noch*. Combine the individual parts and it becomes *Hanoch*. Note that the long <term>caph</term> <note>the final form ך</note> does not have a shape similar to the one placed in the alphabet sequence, because it is one of the five terminal letters.

**Rehoboam** [Hebrew: רחבעם] has four syllables. The first, *resh* with *sheva*, murmurs the voice and is not silent because a vowel follows; let it therefore be a "sudden" *re*. Put the parts together and it becomes **Rehafeam** or **Rehoboam**.

**Abijah** [Hebrew: אביה] has three syllables. The first, *aleph* with *ḥatef pataḥ* <term>ḥatef pataḥ: an extremely short 'a' sound</term>, makes a short and "upright" *a*. Collect the whole and it becomes **Avijah**.

**Asa** [Hebrew: אסא] has two syllables. The first, *aleph* with *pataḥ*, makes an "upright" *a*. The second, *samekh* with *qamets*, makes an "oblique" *sa* with a sharp hissing sound. To this is joined an *aleph* which is not pronounced because it is not dotted.

**Jehoshaphat** [Hebrew: יהושפט] has four syllables. The first, *yod* with *sheva*, murmurs the voice and is brought forth because a vowel follows. Because the <term>iod</term> contains a <term>dagesh</term> <note>A dot inside a letter that doubles its sound.</note>, it serves as a double letter on both sides. <term>Iechoniah (Jeconiah)</term> <note>original: "יכניה"</note> has three syllables. The second, <term>caph</term> with <term>raphe</term> <note>A mark indicating a soft pronunciation.</note> and <term>hatef-qametz</term> <note>A very short "o" sound.</note>, makes *cho*, which sounds together with the <term>nun</term>. The third, <term>iod</term> with <term>qametz</term>, makes a broad *ia*, to which is joined at the end a <term>he</term> with a gentle and imperceptible breath that is not read. Combine them now and it becomes *Iechoniah*—the one conquered in Babylon, who is also called <term>Iehoiachin</term>, the son of <term>Iehoiakim</term>, son of <term>Josiah</term>.

<term>Schealthiel (Shealtiel)</term> <note>original: "שאלתיאל"</note> has four syllables. The first, <term>shin</term> with a dot on the right and a <term>shva</term>, mutters a hissing sound. The <term>shva</term> is pronounced because a vowel follows it. The second, <term>aleph</term> with <term>pataḥ</term> <note>A vowel mark for a short "a" sound.</note>, makes a straight *a*, which sounds with the <term>lamed</term> and a <term>shva</term> that is not voiced, thus becoming *al*. The third, <term>tav</term> with <term>dagesh</term> and <term>hirik</term>, becomes a hard and solid *thi*. The fourth, <term>aleph</term> with <term>tsere</term> <note>A vowel mark for a long "e" sound.</note>, makes a straight *e*, which sounds with the <term>lamed</term> (the letter *l*) and becomes *el*. Combine them and it becomes *Schealthiel*, the father of <term>Phadaia</term> <note>Pedaiah</note> and the grandfather of <term>Zorobabel</term>.

<term>Zerubbauel (Zerubbabel)</term> <note>original: "זרבבל"</note> has four syllables. The first, <term>zayin</term> with <term>shva</term>, makes a sudden sound with a thin whistle. It is voiced because the <term>zayin</term> and <term>resh</term> are not connected. The second, <term>resh</term> with <term>qibbutz</term> <note>A vowel mark for the "u" sound.</note>, makes *ru*. The third, <term>beth</term> with <term>dagesh</term> and <term>qametz</term>, makes a solid and broad *ba*. The fourth, <term>beth</term> with <term>raphe</term>—which is the <term>Aeolic digamma</term> <note>A Greek letter (Ϝ) used by scholars to represent the 'v' or 'w' sound; here, it explains the soft 'b' sounding like 'v'.</note>—and <term>segol</term> <note>A vowel mark for a short "e" sound.</note> make *ve*. When <term>lamed</term> (*l*) is added, it becomes *vel*. Combine the individual parts and it becomes *Zerubbauel*, the son of <term>Phadaia</term> and the grandson of <term>Salathiel</term>.

<term>Rescha (Resha)</term> <note>original: "רשע"</note> has two syllables. The first, <term>resh</term> with <term>segol</term>, makes a broad *re*. The second, <term>shin</term> with a dot on the right and <term>qametz</term>, makes a broad and hissing *sha*, to which is joined the guttural <term>ayin</term>. This letter indicates nothing other than a movement of the throat; no other sound is produced because it is not pointed with a vowel. Combine them and it becomes *Rescha*, who is also named <term>Messollam</term> <note>Meshullam</note>.

<term>Iohanan (Johanan)</term> <note>original: "יוחנן"</note> has three syllables. The first, <term>iod</term> with <term>vav</term> and <term>holem</term>, is *io*. The second, <term>heth</term> with <term>qametz</term>, is a broad and breathed *ha*. The third, <term>nun</term> with <term>qametz</term>...
