->...<- the oblique *na*, to which add a final *nun* and it will be *nan*. Combine the individual parts and it becomes *Iohanon*. יהוחנן <note>The Hebrew name Yohanan, or John</note> has three syllables. The first, *iod* with a silent *sheva* <term>sheva: a Hebrew vowel sign indicating a very short or absent vowel sound</term>, softens the voice and is uttered with a very brief throat-clearing sound. It is not entirely silent, for a vowel follows. The second, *he* with *vav-shurek* <term>shurek: a vowel mark producing a 'u' sound</term>, makes *hu* with a gentle aspiration. The third, *daleth* <note>The text here describes the name "Yehuda" despite the Hebrew heading for "Yohanan"</note> with *kametz* <term>kametz: a long 'a' vowel sound</term> makes the oblique *da*. To this is added a *he* of such thin breath that it cannot be perceived; thus it is not pronounced because it is not pointed with a vowel. Collect the whole and it becomes *Iehuda*, called Hircanus the first. יוסף <note>Joseph</note> has two syllables. The first, *iod* with *vav-holem* <term>holem: a vowel mark producing an 'o' sound</term>, makes *io*. The second, *samech* with *tsere* <term>tsere: a vowel mark producing an 'e' sound</term>, makes the upright *se*. To this is joined a final *phe*, that is, an *f*, and it will be *seph*. For *caph* and *phe* are always aspirated at the end of a word, even if a *raphe* <term>raphe: a horizontal line over a Hebrew letter indicating a soft pronunciation</term> is not placed over them. Note this well. Combine the parts and it becomes *Ioseph*, who is called the first.

שמעי <note>Shimei or Shimai</note> has two syllables. The first, a right-side *sin* <note>The letter Shin</note> and a *mem* with *kametz*, make the oblique and foaming *schma*; for the *sheva* under the *sin* is not read, because the *sin* and *mem* are joined together. The second, *ayin* with *hiriq* <term>hiriq: a vowel mark producing an 'i' sound</term>, makes *i*, to which the vowel *iod* is added so that it becomes an improper diphthong. Collect the whole and it becomes *schmai*, which those from beyond the mountains <note>original: "ultra montani"; likely referring to Northern Europeans/Germans</note> call *semai*. מתתיה <note>Matthathiah or Matthew</note> has three syllables. The first, *mem* with *patah* <term>patah: a short 'a' vowel sound</term>, makes *ma*. But because the following *thau* contains a *dagesh* <term>dagesh: a dot in a letter indicating it should be doubled or hardened</term> in its belly, it sounds as if doubled, partly harmonizing with the first syllable to make *math*. The second, a solid *thau* and a *patah*, make *tha*. With this, another *thau* with a *raphe* harmonizes to make *thath* with a final hissing sound; for the *sheva* is not pronounced because it is at the end with a following consonant. The third, *iod* with *kametz*, makes the oblique *ia*. To this is joined a *he* of thin spirit, but it is not pronounced because it is not pointed. Combine the parts and it becomes *matthathiah*. מאות <note>Maoth</note> has two syllables. The first, *mem* with *kametz*, makes the oblique *ma*. The second, *aleph* with *vav-holem*, makes an improper diphthong *o*. If a *thaf* with *raphe* harmonizes with this, it becomes *oth* with a final hiss. Connect them and it becomes *maoth*. נגיד <note>Nagid, meaning "leader" or "prince"</note> has two syllables. The first, *nun* with *patah*, makes the upright *na*. The second, *gimel* with *hiriq*, makes *gi*, and it adds the vowel *iod* which is not pronounced there because it is not pointed. With this, the *daleth* (that is, *de*) harmonizes, and it will be *gid*. Collect them and it becomes *nagid*. חסדי <note>Hesdi</note> has two syllables. The first, *heth* with *segol* <term>segol: a vowel mark producing an 'e' sound</term>, makes the oblique and breathy *he*. With this, the *samech* (that is, *s*) harmonizes and becomes *hes*, for the *sheva* is not pronounced.

# FIRST BOOK

->אָב [Father]<-

**Father** is written with the vowel *qamets* <term>qamets: a Hebrew vowel mark indicating a long 'a' sound, used here to show the word in its independent form</term> when denoting honor and care. Ezekiel 22: "In you they have treated **father and mother** with contempt." However, it is written with the vowel *pathach* <term>pathach: a Hebrew vowel mark indicating a short 'a' sound</term> when joined to another word, as in Genesis 17: "**Father** of many nations." It also receives the letter *yod* at the end as an addition <term>paragogen: the addition of a letter to the end of a word that does not change its basic meaning</term> and is spoken as *Avi* in Genesis 10: "**Father** of all the children of Heber." In the plural, it is declined like feminine names—**Avot**—as in Numbers 36: <note>The text cites Numbers 37, but this passage regarding the daughters of Zelophehad is found in chapter 36.</note> "The leaders of the **fathers** of the families of Gilead approached." By this name, it also signifies an elder, a lord, an author, and a teacher. It is also found in Daniel as *Avich*, meaning "**your father**." See the teacher Paul, Bishop of Burgos <note>Paul of Burgos (c. 1351–1435) was a Jewish convert to Christianity and a prominent biblical scholar whose "Additions" to Nicholas of Lyra's work were widely read.</note>, in his addition to the second Psalm.

->אֵב [Shoot]<-

**Shoot**, green wood, a vine branch, or a sprout. It is found with the shortening of the last letter <note>original: "apocopen"</note> and the doubling of the letter 'b' with a *dagesh* <term>dagesh: a dot placed inside a Hebrew letter to indicate it should be pronounced more strongly or doubled</term> in the plural form in the sixth chapter of the Song of Songs: "I went down into the nut orchard to see the <gloss>fresh shoots</gloss>," meaning the lovely shoots or the green and fruitful wood, which Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD) produced the Vulgate, the standard Latin Bible translation of the Middle Ages.</note> translated as "fruits" <note>original: "poma"</note>.

->אָבִיב [Spring/Ear of Grain]<-

**An ear of grain** with the new fruits of wheat or barley, roasted by fire. This word alludes to the "sprout" or "shoot" mentioned above, as the ear bears fruit in that same likeness. From this, the month of new fruits—which we call July but the Hebrews call the month of **Aviv** or **Av**—takes its name. <note>The author's synchronization of Hebrew months with the Julian calendar (July) reflects medieval or early modern attempts to align biblical time with their own, though Aviv traditionally corresponds to March/April.</note>

->אָבַד [Perished]<-

**He perished**. Isaiah 57: "The righteous man **perished**." And in the first Psalm: "The way of the wicked **shall perish**."

->אָבָה [Willed]<-

**He willed** or desired. Deuteronomy 23: <note>The text cites chapter 22, but the quote is from 23:5.</note> "And the Lord your God **would not** hear Balaam." From this is derived the following word:

->אֶבְיוֹנָה [Desire]<-

**Desire** or pleasure. It is formed by dropping the last letter of the root, because one who lacks the fulfillment of desire is called a "pauper."

->אֶבְיוֹן [Poor]<-

**Poor** or needy. As in Psalm 70: "But I am needy and **poor**."

->**BOOK**<-

**Eglaim** <note>Hebrew: אגלים</note> A proper name of a place mentioned in Isaiah. <note>Isaiah 15:8</note>

**Agam** <note>Hebrew: אגם</note> A pond, ditch, or lake, as in Psalm 106: <note>Modern numbering: Psalm 107:35</note> "He turned the desert into a **pool** of water." In the plural, the root letter 'm' is strengthened by a *dagesh* <term>dagesh: a dot placed in a Hebrew letter to indicate it is doubled or emphasized</term>, becoming **agamim**.

**Agmon** <note>Hebrew: אגמון</note> An iron ring or hook, as in Job 40: <note>Modern numbering: Job 41:2</note> "Can you put a **ring** through his nose?"

**Agmon** <note>Hebrew: אגמון</note> A cauldron or bronze pot that hangs over a hearth, which we call a "boiler," though others translate it as a "pot," as in Job 41: <note>Job 41:20</note> "Like a heated and boiling **pot**." This should be understood as: "From his nostrils (or mine) smoke shall go forth like a boiling pot and cauldron."

**Agmon** <note>Hebrew: אגmon</note> A bulrush or reed, derived from the word *gome* <note>original: גמא</note> used in Isaiah 35: <note>Isaiah 35:7</note> "the greenness of the reed and **rush**," which the Hebrew teachers call **agmon**.

**Agan** <note>Hebrew: אגן</note> A bowl or basin, as in Exodus 24: <note>Exodus 24:6</note> "And so Moses took half of the blood and put it in **basins**." It takes the form **aganot** in the plural, and in the singular **agan**, as in Song of Solomon 7: <note>Song of Solomon 7:2</note> "Your navel is a rounded **bowl**."

**Agaph** <note>Hebrew: אגף</note> The wing of an army; Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible</note> translates it as "troop," as in Ezekiel 17: <note>Ezekiel 17:21</note> "And all his fugitives with all his **troop** shall fall by the sword." It is called **agaph** as if it were **kanaph**. <term>kanaph: the standard Hebrew word for 'wing'</term>

**Agartale** <note>Hebrew: אגרטלי</note> Basins for washing hands. Jerome translated these as "vials" or "bowls." In Ezra 1: <note>Ezra 1:9</note> "Thirty gold **vials**."

**Agar** <note>Hebrew: אגר</note> To gather or collect, as in Deuteronomy 28: <note>Deuteronomy 28:39</note> "And you shall not drink the wine nor **gather** [the grapes] from it."

**Letter** <term>Hebrew: אגרת; *Iggeret*</term>, as in Nehemiah 6[:5]. *And he had a letter in his hand.* It is perhaps derived from the word above <note>Likely referring to a root meaning to collect or gather</note> and named for "collecting," because in a letter many affairs and many words are gathered together. In the plural form, <term>Hebrew: אגרות; *Iggerot*</term>, as in 2 Chronicles 30[:1]: *And he wrote letters to Ephraim and Manasseh.*

**Coin** <term>Hebrew: אגורת; *Agorath*</term>, as in 1 Samuel 2[:36]: *And he may offer a silver coin and a loaf of bread.*

**To be Sorrowful** <term>Hebrew: אדב; *Adab*</term>. He is sad, afflicted, weakened, sorrowful, and consumed by grief. This occurs through the transposition <note>original: "per conuersionem," referring to the linguistic phenomenon of metathesis where letters swap places</note> of the word <term>Hebrew: דאב; *Da'ab*</term>, which signifies the same thing. As in Psalm 88[:9], where it is said *my eyes languished because of poverty.* The Hebrew truth <note>original: "veritas," a term often used by scholars to refer to the original Hebrew text as opposed to the Latin Vulgate</note> holds that *my eye is weakened by affliction* or *consumed by grief.*

**To be Red** <term>Hebrew: אדם; *Adam*</term>. To glow or redden. As in Lamentations 4[:7]: *Ruddier than ancient ivory*—which is more accurately translated as *they glowed in brilliance or appearance more than gold, or coral, or pearl.* From this comes the verbal noun for **Glowing** or **Reddened** <term>Hebrew: מאדם; *Me’adam*</term>, like fire, as in Nahum 2[:3]: *The shield of his mighty men is ignited.* In another passage, Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate</note> translates this as *dyed red.* In the plural, <term>Hebrew: מאדמים; *Me’adamim*</term>, in Exodus 25[:5]: *and ram skins dyed red,* or rather *glowing.* From this comes the noun of quality **Ruddy** <term>Hebrew: אדום; *Adom*</term> or **Red**, as in the Song of Songs 5[:10]: *My beloved is white and ruddy.* From this, Esau is called **Edom** in Genesis 25, which is why his name was called Edom. It is often doubled as <term>Hebrew: אדמדם; *Adamdam*</term>, meaning **Reddish** or **Bright Red**, as in Leviticus 13[:49]: *A woolen or linen garment which has the leprosy in the warp or the woof, or indeed a skin or anything made of skin, if it has a white or reddish mark.*

**ADAMAH** <note>Hebrew: אֲדָמָה</note> Soil. Reddish earth. As in Genesis 6: "And when men began to multiply upon the earth." From which "man" <note>Latin: *homo*</note> is named.

Regarding the second, it is written in Malachi 1: "And if I am a Lord, where is my fear?" In which place it is put in the Hebrew plural, "Lords." The Hebrews say this is done out of reverence for the Divine Majesty. Some distinguish this name when it is secular <note>prophanum</note> from when it is sacred through the use of the vowel points <term>qamets</term> and <term>patah</term>. It should be known that the four-syllable *Adonai* is always sacred and never secular.

# THE FIRST.

**Adon** <note>Hebrew: אדן</note> A <term>peristyle</term> <note>original: "Peristillium"; a courtyard or porch surrounded by columns</note>, an auxiliary column, or a base, as in Exodus 38: "A hundred bases were made from a hundred talents, a talent for each base." It also signifies "great" in Ezekiel 17: "and it shall become a great cedar." Likewise, in the feminine form without the letter *yod*, **adderet** <note>Hebrew: אדרת</note>, it signifies "large," as in the same chapter: "that it might become a large vine." **Adar** <note>Hebrew: אדר</note> The month of February <note>Adar is the twelfth month of the Hebrew calendar, usually overlapping with February and March</note>, as in Esther 9: "Therefore, in the twelfth month, which we have already said is called Adar."

**Adarkon** <note>Hebrew: אדרכון</note> A <term>solidus</term> <note>A gold coin; in the biblical context, this refers to the Persian daric</note> in Ezra 8: "And twenty gold bowls, which were worth a thousand gold coins."

**Ahav** <note>Hebrew: אהב</note> He loved, as in Genesis 37: "Now Israel loved Joseph." It also signifies "the beloved," as in the same chapter: "I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and the deer of the field, that you do not stir up or awaken the beloved." Look for other similar instances in the same book.

**Ahah** <note>Hebrew: אהה</note> The voice of one crying out in pain, in Joel 1: "Alas for the day! For the day of the Lord is near." And in Jeremiah 1: "Ah, Lord, I do not know how to speak."

As in Leviticus 1: "But if the offering to the Lord be of birds, for a burnt sacrifice, of turtledoves <note>original: "turturibus"</note> or <note>original: "vel"</note> of young pigeons." In that passage, our printed edition <note>the contemporary Latin Vulgate Bible</note> has "and" instead of "or," but it is incorrect.

# BOOK

This word <term>na’vah (נאוה)</term> is also often used for **it pleases**; likewise for **it is fitting**. As in Proverbs 26: "As snow in summer and rain in harvest, so glory is **unbecoming** for a fool." <note>original Latin: "indecens"</note> This word is expressed thus: glory does not befit a fool, or it does not please, or it is not beautiful or decorous for a fool. Derivatives and nouns from this root are often found with the omission of the letters *aleph* or *vav*, which one may learn from the art of grammar.

<term>Och (אוח)</term> signifies a certain beast of a monstrous kind. However, the interpreters have been unable to find anything certain regarding what name it might be called among the Latins or what its nature might be. In Isaiah 13, where it is written: "But wild beasts shall rest there, and their houses shall be filled with *Ohim*." <note>The plural form of Och</note> Jerome translated this as **dragons** <note>original: "draconibus"</note>; Aquila as **typhons** <note>original: "typhonibus," referring to mythical giants or whirlwinds</note>. Symmachus left the word without translation as *ohim*, as did Jonathan the Chaldean <note>Referring to the Targum, the Aramaic translation of the Hebrew Bible</note>, who, according to the custom of the Chaldeans, changed the *m* into *n*, saying *ohin*. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> and Theodotion translated it as **cries** or **sounds**. Others call them **Martichoras** <note>A legendary creature similar to a manticore, with the head of a human and the body of a lion</note>, and the barbarians call them **martens** <note>original: "Marder," the German word for the animal</note>. Many of the Hebrew scholars say they are **sea-cats** <note>original: "feles marinos," a term often used in this period to describe monkeys or marmosets</note>; my own teacher explained them as **cercopes** <note>Monkey-like forest creatures from Greek mythology</note>. Nicholas of Lyra <note>A famous 14th-century Franciscan administrative and biblical scholar</note> thinks they are **large birds** that love solitude. Such a great diversity of opinions confesses an ignorance of this name <term>Och (אוח)</term>.

# FIRST

The **Chaldean translation** <note>The Aramaic Targum</note> shows that the Hebrew word **אולם** <note>ulam</note> is translated as **but** <note>original Latin: *p ברם* (beram)</note> as in Numbers 14, where it is read: *As I live, the glory of the Lord shall fill the whole earth.* The **Hebrew truth** <note>A common term for the original Hebrew Masoretic text</note> has: *and truly I live.*

**אולם** <note>ulam</note>: Palace, vestibule, or porch. As in 1 Kings 6: *And the porch was before the temple, twenty cubits long.*

**און** <note>on / aven</note>: Virtue, strength, injustice, pain, mourning, sad, or murmuring. As in Job 18: *The steps of his strength shall be narrowed.* And in the same book, chapter 20: *His children shall be worn out by poverty, and his hands shall restore his sorrow to him.* Also below in chapter 21: *God shall keep the father's sorrow for his children.* **Jerome** <note>The 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate</note> wished to embrace all these meanings at once when, in Numbers 11, he translated the word **מתאוננים** <note>mit’on’nim</note> as *the murmur of the people grieving over their labor.* It is specifically placed for a "murmur" in Lamentations 3: *Why has a living man murmured?*

**און** <note>aven</note>: Iniquity or vanity. Isaiah 32: *And his heart will work iniquity,* for which the **LXX** <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> understands "vain things."

As in Exodus 5: *The overseers of the works also were urgent,* that is, they compelled them by hastening, where the word **אצים** <note>atzim</note> is used. And **אץ** <note>atz</note> signifies "he hastened," as in Joshua 10: *So the sun stood in the midst of heaven and did not hasten.* All meanings of this kind pertain to haste, impulse, oppression, and tribulation.

**אור** <note>or</note>: It shone, from the verb *to shine*. Next, in the same verse mentioned, **אור** <note>or</note> is placed, meaning "light" or "brightness." 96. **His lightnings shone upon the world.** <note>original: "Alluxerunt fulgura eius orbi terre," quoting Psalm 97:4</note> According to the rules of grammar, this means "they made lightnings to shine upon the world." The word "of the earth" <note>Latin: "terre"</note> is not placed there; if we were able to express this in proper Latin, we would certainly explain it more precisely as "they light-made" <note>The author suggests a literal but non-standard Latin term "lucificaverunt" to capture the active sense of creating light</note>, or let us at least say "they illuminated." From this comes the word **light** <note>Hebrew: אור, 'or'</note>, meaning "let it make to shine," or "let it illuminate," as in Psalm 67: **May he illuminate his face upon us.** <note>Psalm 67:1</note> From this also comes **luminary** <note>Hebrew: מאור, 'ma'or'</note> and its feminine plural form **luminaries** <note>Hebrew: מאורות, 'ma'orot'</note> as in Genesis 1: **And God made two great lights.** <note>Genesis 1:16</note>

However, the word **light** <note>Hebrew: אור, 'or'</note> is also declined in the masculine as **lights** <note>Hebrew: אורים, 'orim'</note>; it is also found as **radiance** <note>Hebrew: אורה, 'orah'</note> as in Esther 8: **To the Jews a new light seemed to arise.** <note>Esther 8:16</note>

**Ur** <note>Hebrew: אור</note> of the Chaldeans is a valley, or the proper name of a place. Many, in order to make it agree with the previous word for light, have said it refers to the "purification" <term>lustratio; a ritual washing or illuminating ceremony</term> of the Chaldeans which they performed for their gods. For we use the word "to purify" <note>Latin: "lustrare"</note> to mean "to illuminate," as Virgil says: **The following dawn was illuminating the lands with the lamp of Phoebus.** <note>Virgil, Aeneid, Book 4, line 6</note> Thus, the same word can signify both: the location of the valley in Chaldea in which Haran was born, as it is written in Genesis 11: **And Haran died before Terah his father in the land of his birth in** <note>Genesis 11:28; the text cuts off mid-sentence at the end of the page</note>

# BOOK

In the translation of certain Hebrew words: "one does not redeem; let each redeem" or "let every man redeem." This is so that <term>eth</term> <note>original: "את"</note> stands for <term>one</term> <note>original: "אחד"</note>, just as in other places the letter <term>Chet</term> <note>original: "ח"</note> is put for <term>He</term> <note>original: "ה"</note>. From this comes <term>together</term> <note>original: "יחד"</note> meaning "into one," and it sometimes takes the letter <term>Yod</term> at the end, as in <term>with me</term> <note>original: "אתי"</note>, as seen in Genesis 14: "The brother of Eshcol and the brother of Aner."

**Sister** <note>original: "אחות," transliterated as "achot"</note>. As in the Song of Solomon 8: "Our sister is small and she has no breasts." In the plural, **sisters** <note>original: "אחיות," transliterated as "achayot"</note>, as noted in the grammar.

**One** <note>original: "אחד," transliterated as "echad"</note>. As in Ezekiel 37: "And one king shall be ruling over them all... and my servant David shall be king over them, and there shall be one shepherd for them all."
**Few** <note>original: "אחדים," the plural of "one"</note>. As in Genesis 29: "And those days seemed to him but a few because of the greatness of his love." According to this meaning, many things are derived from it.

**Meadow** <note>original: "אחו," transliterated as "achu"</note>. A meadow of hay, or sedge. As in Job 8: "Can the papyrus grow green without moisture, or the meadow-grass grow without water?"

**He seized** <note>original: "אחז," transliterated as "achaz"</note>. He held. As in Exodus 15: "Pangs—otherwise 'tremblings'—seized the inhabitants of Philistia." Hence, in the participial form in Song of Solomon 3: "All holding swords." And in the same chapter: "I held him," that is, "I seized him." Likewise, in the second chapter of the same book: "Catch for us the foxes." From this comes:

**Possession** <note>original: "אחוזה," transliterated as "achuzah"</note>. That is, a seizing, a possession, the right of using and enjoying, or an inheritance. As in Genesis 23: "Give me the right of a burial place among you." and in chapter 47 of the same book: "Joseph gave his father and his brothers a possession in Egypt."

**Oh that** <note>original: "אחלי," transliterated as "achalai"</note>. Power or faculty. Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into the Latin Vulgate</note> translated it as "If only" in Psalm 119: "If only my ways were directed." Some say "my desire," others "my prayer." The Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translated it in Greek as *ophelon* <note>original: "οφελον"</note>, which we say comes from the word for "useful," as if to say "it is useful for..." And in 2 Kings 5: "If only my lord had been [with the prophet]," where <term>achalai</term> is placed. It is a word of entreaty using the prefix <term>Aleph</term>; for without it, the root signifies to ask, to pray, and to beseech. As in Exodus 32: "Moses besought the Lord his God," where <term>yachal</term> <note>original: "יחל"</note> is used. Jonathan the Chaldean <note>Referring to the Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary</note> explains this as "my good lord."

<meta>This page appears to be from a 16th-century Hebrew-Latin lexicon, likely intended for scholars of the Reformation era who were returning to the "original" languages of the Bible. It covers words beginning with the Hebrew letter Aleph, moving from 'Amethyst' to 'Thorn/Bramble.'</meta>

->THE FIRST<-

**Amethyst** <note>original: *Amethystus*</note>. As in Exodus 28: in the third row, a ligure, an agate, and an **amethyst** <note>original: *אַחְלָמָה* / *achlamah*</note>. Others interpret this as crystal.

**Another** or **other** <note>original: *אַחֵר* / *acher*</note>. As in Psalm 109: And let **another** take his office.

**After** <note>original: *אַחַר* / *achar*</note>. In Ezra 7: Now **after** these words. From this, many words are derived, such as **the end** <note>original: *אַחֲרִית* / *acharit*</note>, meaning the last, the latest, the furthest, or the conclusion. In Deuteronomy 32: Oh, that they were wise and understood this, and would consider their **latter end**.

**Backward** or **behind** <note>original: *אֲחֹרַנִּית* / *achorannit*</note>. As in Genesis 9: And walking **backward**, they covered the nakedness of their father.

**The last ones** <note>original: *אַחֲרֹנִים* / *acharonim*</note>. In Genesis 33: Leah and her children in the second place, and Rachel and Joseph in **the last**.

**Delayed** <note>original: *אָחַר* / *achar*</note>. As in Deuteronomy 23: When you make a vow to the Lord your God, you shall not **delay** to pay it.

**Leader** <note>original: *אֲחַשְׁדַּרְפְּנֵי* / *achashdarpenim*</note>. As in Ezra 8: To the satraps <term>Satrap: a provincial governor in the ancient Persian Empire</term> who were in the king’s presence and to the **leaders**. Similarly in Esther 3.

**Mules** <note>original: *הָאֲחֲשְׁתְּרָנִים* / *ha-achashteranim*</note> born from a horse and tamed wild asses, according to Pliny in Book 8, Chapter 44. They are swift in running, which is why Jerome translated the word as **swift couriers**. As in Esther 8: And the **swift couriers** went out, carrying the messages.

**Turned aside** or **tracked** <note>original: *אָט* / *at*</note>. As in Hosea 11: And I **bent down** to him so that he might eat—as if to say, "I guided my footsteps toward him." From this, in Genesis 33, it is written: And I will follow **little by little** in his footsteps. There, the word is written as "to my pace" <note>original: *לְאִטִּי* / *le-itti*</note>, using a <term>paragogic yod: an extra letter 'yod' added to the end of a word for emphasis or style in ancient Hebrew</term>. Its nature is to signify "step-by-step," "slowly," or "at least."

**Thorn** <note>original: *אָטָד* / *atad*</note>, a bramble or a type of spine that some call a thistle. In the last chapter of Genesis: When the inhabitants of the land of Canaan saw [it]... though the words are shortened in our common translation <note>The author is referring to the Latin Vulgate</note>. It ought to be read: "And the inhabitant of the land of Canaan saw the mourning at the **threshing floor of Atad**."

# BOOK

...which he placed a little further up when he said, "and they came to the threshing floor of Atad, which is situated across the Jordan." According to the Hebrews, and as witnessed by Nicholas of Lyra <note>Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349) was a Franciscan teacher and one of the most influential biblical exegetes of the Middle Ages.</note>, **Atad** is not a proper name in this context. Rather, this threshing floor was hedged in with thorns, which is why it is called the "area of thorns." I find in the third chapter of Genesis, in the Aramaic translation of Onkelos <note>The Targum Onkelos is the primary Aramaic translation (Targum) of the Torah.</note>, that he used this word where the Hebrew text has "thorns and thistles shall it sprout for you." The Aramaic Onkelos translated "thistles" as *atadin* in the plural. Elsewhere, our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate.</note> renders it as "buckthorn" in Psalm 58: "Before your thorns could feel the buckthorn."

**אטם** [Atam]: To hide, close, obstruct, or stop up. As in Isaiah 33: "He who stops his ears lest he hear of blood." *Atum* means hidden or closed, as in Ezekiel 40: "And there were slanted windows in the chambers," which Jonathan the Aramaic translator <note>Targum Jonathan, the traditional Aramaic translation of the Prophets.</note> rendered as "hidden windows," and the translation of the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> has "concealed windows."

**אטון** [Atun]: A rope or a border of a garment. Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Bible into Latin.</note> translated this as "tapestry" in Proverbs 7: "I have woven my bed with cords; I have spread it with painted tapestries from Egypt." Strictly speaking, it refers to a cord or a sash.

**אטר** [Atar]: To bind, press, close, or stop up. As in Psalm 69: "Let not the deep swallow me up, nor the pit press its mouth over me." For he who said, "and let not the pit *crown* its mouth over me," translated poorly. This word is written with the letter *Aleph* (א), whereas the word for "crown" is written with the letter *Ayin* (ע) <note>The author is correcting a common error where translators confused two similar-sounding Hebrew roots.</note>.

**אי** [Ai]: Where. As in Genesis 4: "Where is Abel your brother?" It is a question regarding a location. Sometimes it receives the letter *H* at the end, such as:

**איה** [Ayah]: Where. Genesis 18: "Where is Sarah your wife?" From this same word are derived *Eikah* (how/where) and *Eiphah* (where).

**אי** [I]: Island. As in Isaiah 20: "And the inhabitant of this island shall say." And in the plural, *Iyim*, as in Jeremiah 2: "Pass over to the islands of Kittim," or in Ezekiel 26: "And the islands in the sea shall be troubled." Additionally, **אי** is often used for "not" <note>a negative particle</note> by dropping the letter *Nun* <note>A grammatical process called apocope, where the word 'Ain' (nothing/not) is shortened.</note>, as in Proverbs 31.

->### BOOK ONE<-

...after the verse: "It is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to give wine" <note>Proverbs 31:4</note>. And there follows what our translation <note>The translator refers to the Vulgate, the standard Latin Bible of the time</note> does not have: "and for princes let there not be strong drink or drunkenness."

**אי** **Woe**, as in Ecclesiastes 10: "Woe to you, O land, whose king is a child."

**אילו** **Woe**, as in Ecclesiastes 4: "Woe to the one who is alone when he falls." It is a compound formed from **אי** <note>meaning "woe"</note> and **לו** <note>meaning "to him"</note>.

**איה** **Vulture**, as in Leviticus 11: "The kite and the vulture according to its kind."

**איב** **He acted as an enemy**, as in Exodus 23: "I will be an enemy to your enemies." From this comes **אויב**—**enemy**, as in 1 Samuel 18: "And Saul became an enemy to David." Also **איבה**—**enmity**, as in Genesis 3: "And I will put enmity between you and the woman."

**איד** **Affliction, destruction, calamity, ruin.** Proverbs 1: "I also will laugh at your ruin." And Psalm 17: "They confronted me in ☞ the day of my affliction."

**איד** **Mist** <note>original: vapor</note>. Which our translation calls a "fountain" in Genesis 2: "But a fountain rose up from the earth," but others interpret it as a "cloud," just as Onkelos the Chaldean <note>Onkelos was a famous 2nd-century scholar who produced the standard Aramaic translation (Targum) of the Torah</note> translated it.

**איך** **How**, as in Genesis 39: "How then can I do this evil thing?" This is sometimes said through a <term>paragoge</term> <note>The addition of a letter or sound to the end of a word without changing its meaning</note> of the breathing sound "h" as **איכה**, as in Lamentations 1: "How does the city sit solitary?" It is also sometimes written with a doubled letter 'k' <note>the Hebrew letter Caph</note> as **איככה**, as in Song of Solomon 5: "I have stripped off my robe; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?"

**איכה** **Where**, derived from **אי**, as in Song of Solomon 1: "Where you pasture, where you rest your flock at noon."

**איל** **Lord, helper, strong, powerful, robust.** Ezekiel 17: "But he shall also take the mighty of the land."

->BOOK<-

**STRENGTH.** Robustness. Virtue. Help. Power. <note>original Latin: "Fortitudo. robur. uirtus. auxiliū. poteſtas."</note> As in Psalm 22: "But you, O Lord, do not remove your help far from me." From this comes **EL**, meaning strong, as in Exodus 15: "Who is like you among the strong, O Lord?" It is also used for the most powerful God, as in Genesis 33: "He called upon the most powerful God of Israel."

**OAK** or **TEREBINTH.** <note>The Hebrew terms "Elah" and "Elon" refer to large trees, often translated as oak or terebinth.</note> A tree. An oak. As in Judges 9: "And they appointed Abimelech king by the oak that stood in Shechem." And where the Hebrew text uses the word for tree in a general sense (**ETZ**), the Chaldean <note>Referring to the Aramaic Targum, an ancient translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> explains it as **ILAN**, meaning a tree or wood.

**RAM.** <note>original Latin: "Aries."</note> Genesis 22: "And he saw behind his back a ram." And in the plural: Psalm 29: "Bring to the Lord the sons of rams."

**DEER** or **STAG.** <note>original Latin: "Ceruus."</note> As in Psalm 42: "As the deer longs [for flowing streams]." Similarly also **AYALAH** <note>The feminine form, "doe."</note> in Genesis 49: "Naphtali is a doe let loose." It is also used in the plural in Song of Songs 2: "I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and the deer of the fields." This noun is of common gender, for the feminine form is used in Jeremiah 14: "the doe in the field gave birth," namely **AYALET**.

**THRESHOLD.** The front of a building, a facade, or the surrounding structure of the thresholds, or the margin of windows. Regarding the various interpretations of this word, see Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the scholar responsible for the Latin Vulgate Bible; his commentaries were standard reference works in the Renaissance.</note> in his commentaries on Ezekiel 40, where you will find the variations **Eyl**, **Eylei**, **Eylim**, and **Eylav** used for the facade, the lintel, the posts, or the threshold. **EYLAMMAH** and **EYLAMMOT** refer to the margins of the windows.

**IF.** <note>original Latin: "Si."</note> As in Esther 7: "And would that we were sold as male and female slaves," used in the sense of "if only we were sold," etc.

->FIRST<-

**איום** Dreadful and terrible, as in Habakkuk 1: <note>Habakkuk 1:7</note> "he is dreadful and terrible." The feminine form is **איומה**, Song of Songs 6: "terrible as an army with banners."

**אימה** Terror or horror, a noun as in Genesis 15: "And a great and dark horror fell upon him."

**אימים** These are giant peoples, Deuteronomy 2. Finally, the Moabites call them Emim, and it is said they are so named from "terror," <note>The Hebrew root for Emim is related to the word for terror or dread.</note> because they are dreadful and fearsome to look upon.

**אין** Derived from **אי**, this is a question of place, such as "from where?" <note>original: "me-ayin"</note> as in Genesis 29: "Brothers, where are you from?"

**אין** No or not, as in Genesis 28: "This is nothing else but the house of God." The compound form is also found as **ואין**, meaning "and not," "nor," or "neither," as in Jeremiah 30:

"Alas! For that day is great, and there is none like it." And similarly **כאין**, meaning "almost" or "nearly," as in Psalm 72: <note>In modern numbering, this is Psalm 73:2</note> "my steps had nearly slipped."

**איפה** A dry measure <note>A dry volume measure often translated as an 'ephah,' roughly 22 liters.</note>, as in Leviticus 19: "and a just ephah." It is also written without the letter *yod*, as in Leviticus 5: "the tenth part of an ephah of fine flour."

**איפה** Where, as in Job 38: "Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?"

**איפוא** Where, Genesis 27: "Who, where, is he that just now brought me the venison he had taken?" This is a particle used without a middle conjunction, meaning "who, where," similar to Habakkuk 3: <note>The text mistakenly cites Habakkuk 2.</note> "Sun and moon stood still," rather than "sun *and* moon."

**איפוא** Now, or here; Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> explained it as "hereafter" in Genesis 27: "And for you, my son, what shall I do hereafter?" You will also find it written with only the letter *vav* in Job 17: **ואיפו איפו**, "where now then is my hope?"

**איש** Man, as in "Blessed is the man who has not walked," and "Blessed is the man who fears the Lord." And in the plural **אישים**, Isaiah 53: "the lowest of men." Its feminine form is written without the letter *yod* and ends with the letter *he*:

**אשה** Woman, as in Genesis 2: "She shall be called 'man-ess' <note>original: "virago." Jerome coined this term in the Latin Vulgate to preserve the wordplay: in Hebrew, man is *Ish* and woman is *Ishah*.</note> because she was taken out of man." For the translator wanted a derivative term...

-># BOOK<-

...in Latin to seek from a man what would suit a woman, just as we have been accustomed to do in the Hebrew language. It is also said "Woman" <note>original: "Ishah" (אִשָּׁה)</note> and in the plural "Women" <note>original: "Ishot" (אִישׁוֹת)</note>. For what is found as "Women" <note>original: "Nashim" (נָשִׁים)</note>, that is, ladies, is derived from "Mankind" <note>original: "Enosh" (אֱנוֹשׁ)</note>.

**Man** <note>original: "Ish" (אִישׁ)</note> Each one, or anyone, or whoever. As in Exodus 25, where we read: "spreading their wings and covering the oracle, and they shall look at one another with faces turned." There, the Hebrew Truth <note>The "Hebrew Truth" (Hebraica Veritas) was a term used by scholars like Jerome to refer to the original Hebrew text of the Bible as the ultimate authority.</note> has: "and they shall be spreading their wings above, in turn entwining their wings over the mercy seat, and their faces shall be each one <note>original: "Ish"</note> toward his brother." In the same sense, it is also used in the feminine gender as "Woman" <note>original: "Ishah" (אִשָּׁה)</note>, as in chapter 26 of the same book, where we read: "five curtains shall be joined to one another." There, the Hebrew Truth has: "five curtains shall be joined each one <note>original: "Ishah," literally "a woman"</note> to her sister."

**Man** <note>original: "Ish" (אִישׁ)</note> A hero, a great man, a head, and a leader. As in Judges 7: "This is nothing else but the sword of Gideon the son of Joash, a man of Israel." For it is incorrectly read as "Israelites," but rather "man of Israel," meaning the head of Israel. And in 1 Samuel 26: "Are you not a man?"

**Man** <note>original: "Ish" (אִישׁ)</note> A patrician and noble man. Whereas "Man" <note>original: "Adam" (אֵדָם)</note> refers to a common man from the populace. As in Psalm 49, where we read: "Whatever earth-born and sons of men." The Hebrew Truth has: "both sons of the common people and sons of the noble," which is "sons of Ish" <note>original: "Ish" (אִישׁ)</note>.

**Little Man** <note>original: "Ishon" (אִישׁוֹן)</note> The black image in the pupil of the eye; it is taken to mean the pupil itself. As in Psalm 17: "Guard me as the pupil of the eye." Some wish to say that this is the form of diminutives <note>A diminutive is a word form that implies smallness or endearment, like "booklet" or "duckling."</note> among the Hebrews, specifically the ending "-on" <note>original: "וֹן"</note>.

**Enduring** <note>original: "Eitan" (אֵיתָן)</note> Hard, strong, robust. As in Numbers 24: "Your dwelling is indeed robust." And in Deuteronomy 21, the translator paraphrased that expression, saying: "and they shall lead her to a rough and stony valley," using that for "strong and hard."

**Enduring** <note>original: "Eitan" (אֵיתָן)</note> The name of a riverbed. As in Psalm 74: "You dried up the rivers of Ethan."

Jerome, following the former meaning, translated this as "strong rivers."

->FIRST<-

Nicolaus de Lyra <note>A 14th-century Franciscan scholar famous for his "Literal Commentary" on the Bible, which drew heavily on Hebrew traditions.</note> says that it is a proper name for a desert, but he looked at the spelling carelessly and incautiously; for it signifies a station of the Israelites in the desert. It is written at the end with the letter *mem* <note>The Hebrew letter ם</note>, as in Numbers 33: "From Succoth they came to Etham, which is at the furthest edges of the wilderness." However, when it is the proper name for the bed of the Jordan [river], as it is here, it is written with a *nun* <note>The Hebrew letter ן</note> at the end. In Exodus 14, the bed of the sea is also noted by the same word where it is read: "And when Moses had stretched out his hand against the sea, it returned at the first dawn to its prior place," that is, to its accustomed bed.

אך <term>Ak</term>: But. Yet. Nevertheless. Or. Indeed. Certainly. Also. At least. As in Exodus 10: "But now forgive my sin also this time." And Genesis 29: "Indeed you are my bone and my flesh." It also signifies "how" or "as," such as in Psalm 73: "How good is God to Israel." It is also composed with רק <term>Rak</term> (meaning "nevertheless") so that it becomes רק אך <term>Rak Ak</term>, meaning "only" or "just." As in Numbers 12: "Has the Lord spoken only through Moses?"

אכל <term>Akhal</term>: He ate. As in Deuteronomy 8: "So that when you have eaten and are full."

אכל <term>Okhel</term>: Food or sustenance. As in Genesis 42: "From the land of Canaan so that we may buy the necessities for sustenance."

אכל <term>Akhal</term>: Devoured. Consumed. Burned up. As in 2 Kings 1: "Let fire descend from heaven and devour you." And Exodus 3: "And he saw that the bush burned and was not consumed." And Deuteronomy 4: "The Lord your God is a consuming fire."

אכלת <term>Okhlah</term> <note>Literally "food" or "fuel," but here used for the "devouring" action of a blade.</note>: The edge of the sword. As in Jeremiah 46: "The sword shall devour and be satisfied." Otherwise translated as "the edge of the sword shall be satisfied." In the same way, מאכלת <term>Ma'akhelet</term> is a knife used for sacrificing, named as such because of its sharpness.

אכן <term>Akhen</term>: Indeed. Certainly. Therefore. However. Truly. As in Psalm 82 <note>original: "ps. lxxii"; the text cites Psalm 72, but the quote is from Psalm 82:7.</note>: "But you shall die like men."

אכף <term>Akhaf</term>: He inclined. Bent. Curved. Turned aside. Compelled. As in Proverbs 16: "The soul of the laborer labors for himself because his mouth has compelled him to it." And it signifies the same as כפף <term>Khafaf</term>, as in Psalm 146: "The Lord raises up those who are cast down," which the Hebrew scholars explain as "those who are bent or bowed over."

->BOOK<-

**אכר** [Akhar]. Farmer or plowman. As in Jeremiah, book 51 <note>original: "li.Et collidam" referring to Jeremiah 51:23</note>: "And I will break in pieces with you the farmer and his team of oxen."

**אל** [Al]. No or Not. As in Psalm 121: "He will not allow your foot to be moved." It signifies the same thing as "not." The following are similar: **לא** [Lo]; **אין** [Ayin]; **אל** [Al]; **בל** [Bal]; **בלי** [Beli]; **בלתי** [Bilti], all of which signify negation. According to some, **אל** [Al] is also placed for **על** [Al], meaning "above" or "against," as in 1 Samuel 27: "Against the south of Judah." However, when written with the <term>segol</term> <note>A Hebrew vowel mark indicating an "e" sound</note> we translate it as "to," as in "and the Lord said to Moses" in Exodus 10, and so in other places. It also signifies "is it not?" or "whether?" when written with the <term>pathah</term> <note>A Hebrew vowel mark indicating an "a" sound</note> as in 1 Samuel 27: "Against whom have you made a raid today?" for which it is written as a question, "Have you not made a raid today?"

**אל** [El]. God. As in Psalm 50: "The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken." It also means strong. Exodus 15: "Who is like you among the strong, O Lord?" and Psalm 42: "to the living strong [God]," which we read incorrectly as "to the fountain" <note>original: "ad fontem." The translator notes a common error in the Latin Vulgate where 'El' (strong/God) was mistaken for 'Ayin' (fountain)</note>; for even the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translated it as *ischyron* <note>original Greek: "ischyron," meaning "strong"</note>.

**אלא** [Ela]. However; but; only; except; solely; besides.

**אליל** [Elil]. Nothing; a thing of no importance; a vain idol; a demon. Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator who produced the Latin Vulgate</note> translated this as "perverse dogma," as in Job 13: "First showing you to be fabricators of lies and cultivators of perverse dogmas." In the plural, **אלילים** [Elilim], idols or demons, as in Leviticus 19: "Do not turn to idols, nor make for yourselves gods of cast metal." It is perhaps derived from **אל** [Al], meaning "not," because there is no good in them.

**אל גביש** [El-gabish]. Hail. As in Ezekiel 13: "And I will give very great stones," in place of "hailstones."

**אללי** [Alalai]. An exclamation of one grieving, wailing, or lamenting. As in Micah 7: "Woe to me!" It is named for the sound of wailing, as in Jeremiah 48: "Wail and cry out," and shortly after, "therefore I will wail over Moab," where it is used in the first person of the future tense: **אייליל** [Ayalil].

**אלי** [Eli]. Strongly. Jerome translated it as "vehemently," as in Job 4: "And they rejoice..."

**אלה** <term>Alah: To swear or take an oath</term>. As in Judges 17: "The eleven hundred pieces of silver that you set aside and concerning which I heard you swear." <note>The OCR reads Judges 7, but the text refers to the story of Micah in Judges 17:2.</note>

**אלה** <term>Alah: A curse or an oath</term>. As in Genesis 26: "Let there be an oath between us and let us make a covenant." And in the plural **אלות** (Aloth), meaning curses or maledictions, as in Deuteronomy 30: "But the Lord will turn all these curses upon your enemies." From this comes **תאלה** (Ta'alah), meaning labor or fatigue, as in Lamentations 3: "You will give them a shield of the heart, your sorrow." <note>The Latin 'labor' here refers to the 'sorrow' or 'anguish' of the heart mentioned in Lamentations 3:65.</note>

**אלי** <term>Eli: To lament or wail</term>. As in Joel 1: "Lament like a virgin girded with sackcloth." For thus Jonathan the Chaldean <note>Jonathan the Chaldean refers to the Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible.</note> translated this mourning, using the word **אליא** (Elya) for it in Ezekiel 19: "And you, take up a lament for the princes of Israel."

**אליה** <term>Alyah: The fat tail of a sheep</term>. As in Leviticus 3: "The fat and the entire tail with the kidneys."

**אלה** <term>Allah: A tree</term>. Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into the Latin Vulgate.</note> translated this as "terebinth" in Genesis 35: "But he buried them under the terebinth which is near the city of Shechem." <note>The OCR says Genesis 25, but this event occurs in Genesis 35:4.</note> This same word was later translated as "oak" in the last chapter of Joshua: "And he took a very large stone and placed it under the oak which was in the sanctuary of the Lord." Some interpret this as a linden tree; others, however, interpret it as a "threshold" according to Jonathan the Chaldean, who translates it as **אילון** (Ailon), which is the threshold of a door, as we said above regarding the word **איל** (Ayil).

**אלילים** <term>Elilim: Idols</term>. The gods of the nations. As in Isaiah 1: "For they shall be confounded by the idols to which they sacrificed."

**אולי** <term>Ulai: A proper name</term>. The name of a spring from which the river Ulai rises, as we showed above in that entry; it is seen more clearly in Daniel 8.

**אולי** <term>Ulai: A particle</term>. An indeclinable part of speech which we saw above. It sometimes means "unless," as in Numbers 22: "And unless the donkey had turned aside from the way." This is found in many other places. However, a little earlier in the same chapter, it signifies an affirmative condition: "If somehow I might be able to fight and drive him out."

->**BOOK**<-

**אלי** "Hark!" <note>original: *Heus*</note>—a composite word used for calling someone, made from **אל** <note>original: *el*</note>, meaning "to," and the letter *yod*, which signifies "me." It essentially means "hither to me." For example, in Exodus 32: *If anyone is the Lord's, let him be joined to me.* It is as if he said, "Who is the Lord's? Hark, come here!" and thus it should be properly read in that way.

**אל** "To" or "Toward." This was mentioned above, as in: *The Lord spoke to Moses.*

**אל** This term sometimes signifies "of" or "from." For example, in Genesis 41: *And all the provinces came into Egypt to buy food from Joseph.* <note>original: *a Ioseph*</note> It also signifies "against," "toward," or "facing." For example, in 1 Samuel 26: *Who are you who cries out toward (or against) the king?* For David was not shouting *to* the king, but toward Abner. It also frequently signifies "in," designating not only movement toward a place but sometimes being within a place. For example, in 1 Samuel 17: *And David put his hand into his pouch*—here it indicates movement to a place—*and struck the Philistine in the forehead*—here it indicates the location. Or, according to the Hebrews, *he struck him upon the forehead*, for it also signifies "upon" or "over." As **Rabbi Kimhi** <note>David Kimhi (1160–1235), a famous medieval Jewish grammarian and biblical commentator.</note> says in his commentaries on the four books: <note>The "four books" likely refers to the Former Prophets (Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings).</note> in 1 Samuel 3: *All that I have spoken over his house.* It also signifies "before" or "in the presence of." Therefore, you may interpret it in various ways for the sake of the sentence’s clarity, such as: *bury me with my fathers in the double cave.* In Genesis 49, **אל** is placed twice: first for "with" and second for "in."

**אלוה** God. As in Habakkuk 3: *God will come from the south.*

**אלהי** God. As in Exodus 3: *The God of the Hebrews has called us.*

**אלהים** God. As in Genesis 1: *In the beginning God created heaven and earth.* According to **Jerome** in his letter to Marcella <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the translator of the Latin Vulgate; Marcella was a noble Roman woman and his student.</note>, this word is of "common number," meaning that the one God is called by this name, but so are many. It is like the word **שמים** <note>original: *shammayim*</note>, which means "heaven" and "heavens," or like the names of cities in our language such as Athens or Thebes <note>Latin *Athenae* and *Thebae* are plural in form but refer to single cities.</note>. According to **Moses the Egyptian** <note>Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher, often called "Moses Aegyptius" in Latin texts.</note> in the first book of the *Guide for the Perplexed*, this name is applied to God, to angels, and to men worthy of admiration. It is also found referring to idols and judges. Where we read in Exodus 21: *His master shall bring him to the gods and he shall be brought to the door*, the Hebrews interpret "gods" as "judges." The Aramaic <note>original: *chaldaica*</note> translation also has: *his master shall lead him to the judge.*

**אלח / נאלח** To grow rancid; to be made corrupt and useless. As in Job 15: *How much more abominable and useless is man.* And in Psalm 14: *All have turned aside...*

**אָלַם** <note>Hebrew root: 'alam</note> He bound sheaves, or gathered bundles. From this comes **אֲלֻמָּה** <note>'alummah</note>, a bundle or sheaf, as in Genesis 37: "And behold, we were binding sheaves." Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the primary translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> renders this more properly in Latin as: "I thought we were binding sheaves in the field." The word is also used in the feminine with the same meaning in the same passage as **אַלְמָה** <note>'almah</note> and in the plural as **אֲלֻמּוֹת** <note>'alumot</note>.

**אֻלָם** <note>'ulam</note> Certainly, or surely. An emphatic particle, as in Psalm 58: "If you indeed speak righteousness." <note>original Latin: "Si vere utique iusticiam loquimini"</note>

**אֵלֶם אֵלֶם** <note>'elem</note> Mute or silent. As found in the title of Psalm 56: "To the victory, regarding the silent dove." <note>original Latin: "Ad victoriam super columba muta"</note> David Kimhi <note>A famous medieval Jewish grammarian and commentator (1160–1235), also known as Radak.</note> explains this as "the dove of the palace." It is also found in Exodus 4: "Or who made the mute man?"

**אַלְמָן** <note>'alman</note> Widowed or forsaken. As in Jeremiah 51: "For Israel and Judah have not been widowed by the Lord their God."

**אַלְמָנָה** <note>'almanah</note> A widow. As in Genesis 38: "Stay as a widow in your father’s house until Shelah grows up."

**אַלְמָנוּת** <note>'almanut</note> Widowhood. As in Isaiah 54: "And you shall no longer remember the reproach of your widowhood."

**אַלּוֹן** <note>'allon</note> A type of tree which is interpreted as an oak. As in Hosea 4: "Under the oak, the poplar, and the terebinth." There you will also find the meaning of **אֵלָה** <note>'elah, a terebinth or pistachio tree</note> as was shown above. From this comes the plural **אַלּוֹנִים** <note>'allonim</note> in Ezekiel 27: "Oaks of Bashan." And **אַלּוֹנֵי** <note>'allonei</note>, which also signifies oak groves or plains planted with trees in an orderly fashion. For this reason, Jerome translated it as "valley" in Genesis 18: "And the Lord appeared to him in the valley of Mamre." <note>original Latin: "in convalle Mamre"</note> It is as if he were saying: "in the field," or "in the plain," where the thickets or oak groves of Mamre were situated.

**אֶלֶף** <note>'eleph</note> A thousand. As in Numbers 31: "Let a thousand men be chosen from each tribe." And the plural **אֲלָפִים** <note>'alaphim</note> as in Exodus 18, where we read: "Appoint from them leaders of thou—" <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence at the bottom of the page.</note>

# BOOK ONE

**אֻמָּה** <note>original: "ummah"</note> or **אֻמּוֹת** <note>original: "ummot"</note> **People, tribe, lineage.** As in Numbers 25, where our translation <note>The author refers here to the Latin Vulgate, the standard Bible of the time.</note> says "the most noble prince of the Midianites," the Hebrew reading has "head of the people’s families of the Midianites." And in Genesis 25: "Twelve princes of their tribes," where the plural number is formed from **אֻמָּה**. But the plural of the other form is **אֻמִּים** <note>original: "ummim"</note> as in Psalm 117: "Praise him, all you peoples."

**אַמָּה** <note>original: "ammah"</note> **Cubit, a measure.** As in Genesis chapter six: "And with a cubit you shall finish its top." <note>Referring to the construction of Noah's Ark.</note>

**אַמָּה** <note>original: "ammah"</note> **Forefront, post, or lintel.** As in Isaiah 6: "And the lintels of the hinges were moved."

**אָמָה** <note>original: "amah"</note> **Handmaid.** Genesis 21: "Cast out this handmaid and her son." <note>Abraham speaking of Hagar and Ishmael.</note>

**אַמְתַּחַת** <note>original: "amtachat"</note> **Sack.** As in Genesis 42: "Fill their sacks with grain as much as they can hold, and put each man’s money in the top of the sack."

**אָמֵן** <note>original: "amen"</note> **Let it be true.** Derived from the word for "truth" above. As in Deuteronomy 27: "And all the people shall say, amen." And in Jeremiah 11: "And I answered and said, amen, O Lord."

**אֱמֶת** <note>original: "emet"</note> **True, truth, or verity.** As in Jeremiah 10: "But the Lord God is the true God; he is the living God." And Psalm 51: "For behold, you have loved the truth."

**אָמַל** <note>original: "amal"</note> **He failed, was feeble, or was weak.** Often the "l" is doubled as **אֻמְלַל** <note>original: "umlal"</note> as in Nehemiah chapter four: "What are these feeble Jews doing?" And for **אֻמְלַל** in Isaiah 16, Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into Latin.</note> translated it as "deserted," because the suburbs of Heshbon are deserted—meaning they have failed. However, he translates the same word differently in Psalm 6: "Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak." Its feminine form is found in Jeremiah 15: "She who has borne seven has grown feeble."

**אָמְנָם** <note>original: "omnam"</note> **Truly.** As in Genesis 18: "Shall I truly bear a child, who am an old woman?"

**הֶאֱמִין** <note>original: "he’emin"</note> **He believed it as true.** As in Genesis 15: "Abraham believed God." And Psalm 116: "I believed, therefore I have spoken," where the form **הֶאֱמַנְתִּי** <note>original: "he’emanti" - the first-person "I believed."</note> is used.

# THE BOOK

**Amen** <note>original Hebrew: *āmēn*</note> or **Emun** <note>original Hebrew: *ēmūn*</note>
Faith, trust, or belief. As in Deuteronomy 32: "For they are a perverse generation, and unfaithful children." <note>original Latin: *infideles filij*</note> Where the Hebrew text has "children in whom there is no faith," the Hebrew scholars explain this to mean "truth." It also signifies an adjective meaning "faithful," as in Proverbs 20: "Many men are called merciful, but who shall find a faithful man?" It is as if one were to explain it as "a man of beliefs," if grammar would permit such a phrase. From this comes **Ne'eman** <note>original Hebrew: *ne’emān*</note> meaning "faithful," in Numbers 12: "My servant Moses, who is faithful in all my house." It also signifies something firm.

**Emunah** <note>original Hebrew: *ĕmūnāh*</note>
Truth. As in Psalm 36: "And your truth reaches even to the clouds."

**Aman** <note>original Hebrew: *āmān*</note>
A craftsman or artisan. As in Canticles 7: "Which were fashioned by the hand of an artisan."

**Omen** <note>original Hebrew: *ōmēn*</note> or **Amon** <note>original Hebrew: *āmōn*</note>
A foster-child or nurturer. As in Esther 2: "Who was the nurturer of Hadassah, the daughter of his brother."

**Amatz** <note>original Hebrew: *āmaṣ*</note>
He prevailed, was encouraged, and was strengthened. As in Psalm 142: "Deliver me from my pursuers, for they have grown strong against me." And in Joshua 1: "Be strengthened and be robust," for the word **amatz**.

**Amotz** <note>original Hebrew: *āmōṣ*</note>
A reddish or fox-like color. As in Zechariah 6: "And in the fourth chariot, dappled and strong horses." For this last word <note>referring to "strong" / *fortes*</note>, the Hebrew scholars explain it as "brightly reddening."

**Amar** <note>original Hebrew: *āmar*</note>
He said. As in Isaiah 66: "Thus said the Lord God." Many words are derived from this.

**Imrah** <note>original Hebrew: *imrāh*</note>
A word, speech, or utterance. As in Psalm 12: "The utterances of the Lord are pure utterances," <note>original: *eloquia casta*</note> meaning the speeches of God are pure speeches. Similarly, **Omer** <note>original Hebrew: *ōmer*</note> as in Psalm 138: "For they have heard the words of your mouth."

**Amir** <note>original Hebrew: *āmīr*</note>
The tip of a branch; a shoot at the summit of a tree, which is properly called a "switch" or "rod." As in Isaiah 17: "And as the shaking of an olive tree, two or three olives at the top of a branch."

**He'emir** <note>original Hebrew: *he’emīr*</note>
He magnified, exalted, chose, loved beforehand, or praised. As in Deuteronomy 26: "The Lord has chosen you today," and slightly above, "You have chosen the Lord today." From this, some explain that passage in Isaiah 3: **Tzadik imru** <note>original Hebrew: *ṣaddīq imrū*</note>—"Choose, praise, and love the righteous man, because he is good"—deriving it from **amirah**, meaning praise or love.

-># THE FIRST<-

Where we have "say to the righteous that it is well," <note>original: "dicite iuſto quoniam bene" — a reference to Isaiah 3:10</note> "with us" is better, as is clear through the **Chaldaic translation**. <term>Chaldaic: An older term for Aramaic, specifically the Targum (Aramaic translations of the Bible) used to clarify difficult Hebrew passages.</term>

**אמש** (*Emesh*) **Yesterday**, or last night. As in Genesis 31: "But the God of your father spoke to me **yesterday**."

**אן** (*An*) and **אנה** (*Anah*) **Whither** or **Where**. As in Psalm 139: "**Whither** shall I go from your spirit and **whither** shall I flee from your face?" and in the Song of Songs 5: "**Whither** has your beloved gone?"

**אנא** (*Anna*) **O**, a particle of beseeching. As in Psalm 118: "**O** Lord, save me; **o** Lord, grant prosperity."

**אנה** (*Anah*) This word also signifies "**o**" like the one above, although that is written with an *aleph* at the end and this one with a *he*. As in Psalm 116: "**O** Lord, deliver my soul," and further down, "**O** Lord, for I am your servant." These are interpreted whenever one says "**I beseech you**." As in Exodus 32: "**I beseech you**, this people has committed a very great sin."

**אנה** (*Anah*) **Lamented**, from the verb to mourn. He was saddened and sorrowful. As in Isaiah 3: "And her gates shall **lament and mourn**."

**אנה** (*Anah*) **Caused to happen**. He allowed it to fall by chance; he delivered it by fortune. As in Exodus 21: "But if he did not lie in wait, but God **delivered** him into his hands."

**אני** (*Ani*) **I**. As in Genesis 15: "**I** am the Lord who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans."

**אני** (*Oni*) **Ship**. As in Isaiah 33: "No **galley** with oars shall pass over it." It is also called a **fleet**. As in 1 Kings 9: "King Solomon also built a **fleet**."

**אניה** (*Oniyyah*) Also signifies a **ship**. As in Jonah 1: "And he found a **ship** going to Tarshish."

**אנח** (*Anach*) **Sighed** or **groaned**. In Jonah 1: <note>The text cites Jonah 1, but the verse "Why did the animal groan?" is actually from Joel 1:18.</note> "Why did the animal **groan**?"

**אנחנו** (*Anachnu*) **We**. As in Psalm 20: "They are brought low and fallen, but **we** are risen..."

FIRST

**אנש** He suffered pain. He bore it with difficulty. He despaired. In the second book of Kings <note>modern 2 Samuel</note>, chapter 12: "And the Lord struck the child that Uriah’s wife bore to David, and he was struck with a desperate illness." From this comes **אנוש** <term>Enosh: a scourge, pain, or despair</term>. Many authorities believe that "man" is named after affliction so that the nations may know they are merely men (Psalm 9).

**אסם** A larder. A repository for grain. A storehouse. As in Deuteronomy 28: "The Lord will send a blessing upon your storehouses."

**אסון** Death. As in Exodus 21: "But if death follows, he shall give a life for a life."

**אסף** He gathered back. He withdrew. He assembled. As in Genesis 30: "God has taken away my reproach," <note>original: "Abstulit deus opprobriū meum"</note> that is, he withdrew it. And Jeremiah 10: "Gather up your confusion from the earth." The future tense of this word is found in Micah 2: "I will surely assemble all of you, O Jacob," where he uses the construction **אסף אאסף**. Likewise, it means he completed, finished, or ended. From this comes **סוף** <term>Soph: the end</term>. As in the final chapter of Ecclesiastes: "Let us all hear the end of the matter." However, it seems to have a different root, as will be seen below under the letter Samech.

**אסר** He bound. He tied up. As in the fourth book of Kings <note>modern 2 Kings</note>, chapter 23: "And Pharaoh Necho bound him in Riblah." From this comes **אסיר** <term>Asir: one who is bound, a prisoner</term>. As in Genesis 39: "And he delivered Joseph into the prison where the king's prisoners were kept," used for **אסורים**, those who are bound. And sometimes the letter Aleph is dropped from the beginning of the word, as in Ecclesiastes 4: "For out of prison and chains one sometimes comes to a kingdom," where **הסורים** is placed instead of **האסורים**.

**אף** Also. Likewise. As in Leviticus 26: "I also will do these things to you." And indeed, still, furthermore. And in Psalm 96: "For indeed you have corrected the world, which shall not be moved." And whenever **כי** <note>the Hebrew word "ki," often meaning "because" or "that"</note> is added to it, it signifies "altogether," "therefore," or "how much more." As in the third book of Kings <note>modern 1 Kings</note>, chapter 8: "How much more this house which I have built for you." And Genesis 3: "Why did God command you that you should not eat of every tree?"—that is, "Is it altogether true that God commanded you?" Onkelos <note>A famous 2nd-century translator of the Torah into Aramaic</note> explains it as "truly" or as a question, as if he were saying, "Is it true?"

->THE FIRST<-

**אפס** <note>Root: *A-P-S*</note> *It has ceased, it has failed, it is finished,* as in Genesis 47: "Why should we die before you, since our money **fails**?" From this comes the verbal noun **אפס** meaning *deficiency* or *failure*, as in Proverbs 26: "When the wood **fails**, the fire is extinguished."
**אפס** *Except that, nevertheless, but,* as in Numbers 13: "**But** the inhabitants are very strong and the cities are great." Sometimes it is placed for *not* or *none*, as in Isaiah 45: "Because beside me there is **no** God." The scripture says this either because He is not [another], or because there is **none** beside me. It also signifies the end of anything, when nothing of it remains beyond that point, as in Psalm 67: "May God, our God, bless us; may God bless us, and let all the **ends** of the earth fear Him."

**אפע** <note>Root: *A-P-'*</note> That which is **not**, and **nothing**, as in Isaiah 41: "Behold, you are from **nothing**, and your work is from that which is **not**."

**אפעה** <note>Root: *A-P-E-H*</note> **Viper**, as in Isaiah 30: "The **viper** and the flying serpent," which is a species of snake.

**אפק** <note>Root: *A-P-Q*</note> *He restrained himself, he dissembled, he changed his face, or feigned his expression,* as in Genesis 43: "And having washed his face, coming out, he **restrained himself**." And in Esther 5: "And having **restrained** his anger, he returned to his house." It also signifies *to be strengthened* and *to bear oneself bravely*.

**אפיק** <note>Root: *A-P-I-Q*</note> *Inundation, wave, a strong flow, a torrent.* The Septuagint <note>original: "lxx", referring to the 70 scholars who translated the Greek Old Testament</note> translated **אפיקי** as *fountain* or *spring*, as in Psalm 18: "And the **fountains** of waters appeared." This is what Jerome <note>The 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate</note> interpreted from the Hebrew truth as: "And the **outpourings** of waters appeared." And in Job 6: "Like a **torrent** that passes swiftly in the valleys." It also signifies *strong*, as seen above in Job 12, where we have: "And those who are oppressed he relieves," but there the Hebrews read: "And the **bonds** of the strong he loosens." There are some who explain this as the belts of their chains, for it also signifies a **bond**.

**אפר** <note>Root: *A-P-R*</note> **Ash**, Genesis 18: "Since I am but dust and **ashes**." This is called by another name, **דשן** <note>Root: *D-Sh-N*</note>, in Leviticus 6: "And he shall take up the **ashes** which the devouring fire has burned."

**אפר** <note>Root: *A-P-R*</note> **Veil**, *covering*, 1 Kings 20: "And he changed [his appearance] by the sprinkling of **dust**," through which he changed the **veil** over his eyes. This is by metathesis <note>the transposition of letters</note> from **פאר** <note>Root: *P-A-R*, usually meaning a headdress or ornament</note>.

<note>original: "LIBER"</note>
that is, the band of Ezekiel 44. <note>original: "vitta"</note> Linen bands. From this comes the Hebrew word [Hebrew: אפריון] <note>Appiryon; usually translated as a palanquin or carriage</note> as in Song of Songs 3: a Tabernacle veiled with curtains.

[Hebrew: אופיר] <note>Ophir</note> was the son of Joktan from the lineage of Shem, whose kinsmen lived in the East, as mentioned in Genesis 10. When the lands and islands were divided according to the families of the sons of Noah, Joktan and his children possessed the most fertile river of India, the Ganges, and the land closest to it, the richest of all. His two sons, Ophir and Havilah, were allotted the most abundant gold mines. For this reason, those regions took their names from those two lords and owners, Ophir and Havilah. As in Genesis 2: "The name of one is Pishon; it is the one that circles the entire land of Havilah, where gold is born, and the gold of that land is the best." Regarding the other, it is written in 1 Kings 9: "And Hiram sent in that fleet his servants, sailors and those knowledgeable of the sea, with the servants of Solomon. When they had come to Ophir, they took from there four hundred and twenty talents of gold and brought it to King Solomon." We call that gold from Ophir <term>obrizum</term> <note>pure or refined gold</note>, as Jerome testifies in his commentary on Jeremiah 10, as if it were "ophirizum."

[Hebrew: אצל] <note>Atzal</note> Swift. [Hebrew: אצל] He left behind, or he designated. Jerome explained it as "reserved." Genesis 27: "Have you not reserved a blessing for me also?" <note>Referring to Esau's plea to Isaac</note> as if he were saying, "Have you not kept a blessing with you for me?" This is how the Hebrews explain it. Also in Ecclesiastes 2: "And everything that my eyes desired, I did not deny them," where the <term>Hebrew truth</term> <note>original: "veritas"; a common term for the original Hebrew text</note> has "I did not release or leave [anything] from them." Many translate this as "I separated" or "I divided," as in Numbers 11: "And I will take away from your spirit and hand it over to them," and further down, "taking away from the spirit," etc.

[Hebrew: אצל] <note>Etzel</note> Near, or next to. As in Leviticus 6: "And you shall place it next to the altar, and he shall be stripped of his former garments." And in the feminine form [Hebrew: אצלה] in Genesis 39, where we read "and he refused the debauchery," the Hebrew truth has: "and he did not listen to her to lie near her when she was with him." <note>Referring to Joseph and Potiphar's wife</note>

[Hebrew: אציל] <note>Atzil</note> Someone from the leaders and honored nobles; a magistrate. As in Exodus 24: "Nor did He lay His hand upon those of the children of Israel who had withdrawn far away," for which the Hebrews read: "and upon the nobles or honored ones of the children of Israel He did not lay His hand." With this agrees the Chaldean translation of <term>Onkelos</term> <note>An authoritative 2nd-century Aramaic translation (Targum) of the Torah</note>, which translated it as [Hebrew: רברבי] <note>Ravrevay</note>, meaning magistrates, lords, great ones, or honored ones.

Our translation <note>referring to the Latin Vulgate</note> considers it to be a <term>tragelaphum</term> <note>original Latin: "tragelaphum," a mythical "goat-stag" or a rare species of mountain goat</note>. It is also found with a single <term>resh</term> <note>the Hebrew letter ר</note> as in **Numbers 22**: "Come now therefore and curse this people for me," where an *he* <note>the letter ה</note> is placed at the end; it also appears without the *he* further down in the same chapter: "for I know that he whom you bless is blessed, and he upon whom you heap a curse is cursed," where it is written as <term>ארה ואר</term> <note>original: "ara v'ar"</note>, meaning "cursing, he shall be cursed."

From this also comes **יארב** <note>Hebrew: *ye'erov*, "he will lie in wait"</note> a little further down in the same chapter. The name for the thing itself is **אורב** <note>Hebrew: *orev*</note> and in the plural **ארבות** <note>Hebrew: *arubot*</note>, a lookout point from which we watch while lying in wait. It is also used for a window or the floodgates of heaven. As in **Genesis 7**: "And the floodgates of heaven were opened." And **Isaiah 60**: "And like doves to their windows." Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Bible into Latin</note> translated this as a "smoke-hole" in **Hosea 13**: "And like smoke from a chimney," meaning from the opening or window of a chimney.

**ארג** <note>Hebrew root: *arag*</note> He wove, entwined, or braided. As in **Judges 16**: "If," he said, "you braid the seven locks of my head with the web."

**ארג** <note>Hebrew: *ereg*</note> A web, a braid, or a weaving. As in the same chapter of **Judges** mentioned above.

**ארגמן** <note>Hebrew: *argaman*</note> Purple. As in **Exodus 25**: "Blue, and purple, and scarlet."

**ארגז** <note>Hebrew: *argaz*</note> A small box or chest. As in **1 Samuel 6**: "You shall put it in a box at its side."

**אורג** <note>Hebrew: *oreg*</note> A weaver. As in **1 Samuel 17**: "The shaft of his spear was like a weavers’ beam." Many other words are derived from this.

->FIRST<-

**Arzim** <note>Hebrew: ארזים</note> for **charuzim** <note>Hebrew: חרוזים</note>: **Necklaces** or **Jewelry**, as seen below under the letter *heth*.
**Orach** <note>Hebrew: ארח</note>: **Path** or **Way**, as in Job 16: "And I walk the path by which I shall not return." From the verb *arach*, meaning he began a journey; hence *oreach*, a **guest** or **traveler**; hence *orchah*, a **company** or **caravan**, and *aruchah*, a **portion** <note>original Latin: *Portio*; usually referring to a meal allowance</note>.
**Arach** <note>Hebrew: ארך</note>: **He prolonged**, as in Deuteronomy 6: "That your days may be prolonged."
**Arech**: **Slow** or **long**, as in Psalm 103: "The Lord is merciful and gracious, slow to anger" — or **long-suffering** <note>original Latin: *longanimis*</note> — "and of great mercy."
**Aruchah** <note>Hebrew: ארוכה</note>: **Healing** or **repair**, as in Nehemiah 4: "Because the scar of the wall of Jerusalem was closed up," which the Hebrews read as "the **healing** or **repair** had come to the walls of Jerusalem."
**Aram** <note>Hebrew: ארם</note>: **Syrian**, as in 2 Kings 10: "They hired the Syrian of Rehob." It also signifies **Syria**, which is twofold according to Strabo in book 16: he names **Coelosyria** <note>meaning "Hollow Syria"</note> and the land of rivers, called in Greek **Mesopotamia** <note>original Greek: *Mesopotamia*</note> because it is situated in the middle between two rivers, the Euphrates and the Tigris, as Pliny notes in book 5. The other is **Syrophoenicia**, which is full of merchants, for Mesopotamia delights in farmers and livestock; hence the Scripture mentions two Syrias in 1 Chronicles 19: "They sent a thousand talents of silver to hire for themselves from *Aram Naharaim*," that is, **Syrian Mesopotamia**, "and from *Aram Maacha*," that is, **Syrophoenicia**.
**Armon** <note>Hebrew: ארמון</note>: **House, palace, hearth, household gods, or inner chamber**, as in 1 Kings 16: "He entered the palace and burned the royal house over himself." And the plural **armonot** <note>Hebrew: ארמונות</note> as in Jeremiah 6: "Arise, and let us go up by night, and let us destroy her houses," where the *holem* <note>a Hebrew vowel mark</note> is dropped because of the connected reading; in this word, the aspiration of the letter *he* is also found in place of the letter *aleph*, as in Amos 4: "And you shall be cast out into **Harmona**," says the Lord, which Symmachus translated as **Armenia**, and the Seventy <note>the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament</note> as **Mount Remmon**. Aquila translated it as **Mount Armona**, Theodotion as **Mount Mona**, and the fifth edition as a **high mountain**. Lyra <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a famous medieval Bible commentator</note> says it is the name of a distant region beyond the land of the Assyrians.
**Oren** <note>Hebrew: ארן</note>: A **type of tree**, which some call a **cedar** and others a **pine**. Isaiah 44: "He planted a pine which the rain nourished."
