<meta>This page continues the alphabetical dictionary or concordance of Hebrew terms, likely from a Renaissance-era Christian Hebraist text. It focuses on the various uses of the particle 'et', the pronoun 'you', and the verb 'to come'.</meta>

# FIRST

The Almighty will bless you. In that passage, the Hebrew text has: *from the God of your father and from Shaddai*—that is, from the Almighty <note>original: "à deo patris tui et a Sadai hoc est ab omnipotente"</note>—where the word *et* <note>אֵת</note> is placed similarly to Genesis 41, where we read, "nor was there anyone who could interpret," but the truth of the text holds: "and there was no interpreter from among them for Pharaoh." It also signifies the preposition "with," as in Genesis 43: "When he had seen them and Benjamin together with them." Also a little later: "for they are to eat with me today at noon." Sometimes it is used in place of the <term>dative marker</term> <note>originally: "lamed articulo datiuo"; the Hebrew letter 'Lamed' usually indicates 'to' or 'for'</note>, as in Leviticus 16: "And when he has killed the goat for the sin of the people, he shall bring its blood within the veil as was commanded concerning the blood of the calf." Where the Hebrew reads: "He shall bring its blood within the veil, and shall do to that blood as he did to the blood of the calf." It also signifies "in" or "to," as in Psalm 78: "And his spirit was not faithful with God," which they interpret as "in God," where *et* <note>אֶת</note> is used. And with a final *yod* <note>the letter י</note> and the first syllable strengthened by a <term>dagesh</term> <note>a grammatical dot used to double a consonant sound</note>, it is found as an exhortation meaning "hey, come with me," as in the fourth chapter of the Song of Songs: "Come from Lebanon, my bride, come from Lebanon."

**אֵת** <note>Plowshares</note> Iron tools or instruments with which the earth is broken. Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Bible into Latin</note> translated this as "plows" in Joel 3: "Beat your plows into swords." Some think they are mattocks with which we dig the earth, or hoes.

**אַתָּה** <note>You</note>. The pronoun of the second person singular. As in Deuteronomy 5: "And you shall speak to us, and we, hearing, shall do it." And in the plural **אַתֶּם**, as in Genesis 42: "You are spies." And this pronoun sometimes takes a *he* <note>the letter ה</note> at the end, as in Psalm 6: "And you, Lord, how long?" Yet the feminine form never does this, but is always found without the *he*, contrary to the usual custom of other nouns.

**אָתָה** <note>He came</note>. As in Isaiah 21: "Morning comes and also the night." And Job 3: "Because the fear which I feared has come upon me." And you will find it sometimes with the initial *aleph* <note>the letter א</note> missing, and the final *he* changed to an *aleph* at the end, as in Deuteronomy 33: "who came with the leaders of the people and performed the justice of the Lord." And the final *he* is sometimes changed into a *yod*, as in Isaiah 56: "all you beasts of the field, come to devour." Similarly, the initial *aleph* is sometimes changed into a *he*, as in Isaiah 21: "Meeting the thirsty, bring water," meaning "make water come."

**אָתוֹן** <note>Female donkey</note>. Numbers 22: "And having saddled the donkey, he set out." It is also written with a *vav* <note>the letter ו</note> after the *tav* <note>the letter ת</note>, as you will find quite often in that same chapter: "And when the donkey saw the angel."

It is frequently found with the second letter *daleth* dropped.

<meta>This page continues a Hebrew-Latin dictionary or philological study, focusing on roots starting with the letter Bet (ב). ...it is enough for you that God has separated you. And below: "Separate yourselves from the midst of this congregation." <note>This refers to the rebellion of Korah in Numbers 16, where the root בדל (badal) is used for "separation."</note>

**בדל** <term>Cartilage</term> or the outer edge of the ear. As in Amos 3: "Just as a shepherd rescues two legs or the <term>tip of an ear</term> from the mouth of a lion." <note>Original Latin: *extremum auriculę*.</note>

**בדיל** Tin or <term>litharge</term>. <note>Litharge is a secondary mineral, often lead oxide, produced during the refining of silver.</note> Zechariah 4: "And they shall see the tin stone in the hand of Zerubbabel."

**בדלח** Bdellium, which according to Priscian <note>Priscian was a famous 6th-century Latin grammarian whose works remained standard for centuries.</note> in his first book is a type of stone. As in Genesis 2: "And there is found bdellium and the onyx stone." There are some who translate "bdellium" as a <term>carbuncle</term> <note>A generic name for a red gemstone, such as a garnet or ruby.</note>, as witnessed by Jerome in his *Hebrew Questions*.

**בדק** He examined; he mended; he restored cracks and fissures. As in 2 Chronicles 34: "To restore the temple and mend whatever was weak." From this comes **בדק**, a crack, fissure, or ruin, and everything that needs restoring. As in 2 Kings 12: "And let them restore the <term>repairs</term> of the house <note>Original Latin: *sarta tecta*, a legal phrase meaning "buildings in good repair."</note> if he sees anything necessary for restoration."

**בהו** The privation of matter or a void. As in Genesis 1: "But the earth was empty and void." <note>Original Latin: *inanis & uacua*.</note> Onkelos <note>The author of the Targum Onkelos, the influential Aramaic translation of the Torah.</note> also translated it this way in the Chaldean language. But the more excellent Hebrew masters write that **בהו** refers to a thing lacking all form, which is <term>prime matter</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "prime matter" is the most basic substance of the universe before it receives any specific form.</note>; and **בהו** is the aptitude for having, or the desire that moves prime matter toward every natural form, as Aristotle determined in the first book of his *Physics*.

**בהט** Emerald, or another certain stone from the listed gems. Esther 1: "Upon a pavement layered with emerald and Parian stone." <note>Parian stone refers to high-quality white marble from the Greek island of Paros.</note> Certain Hebrews say it is a type of marble.

**בהל** He disturbed, terrified, shuddered, or was stunned. Jerome translated it as "he was troubled" in 1 Kings 28: "And so that woman went in to Saul, for he was greatly troubled." Where the Hebrews read: "And she saw that he trembled or was stunned," or more truly, that "he was greatly astonished." Similarly in Psalm 6: "And my soul is greatly troubled." And at the end: "Let them blush and be vehemently troubled," that is, let them be terrified.

# THE FIRST BOOK

**[Hebrew: בהל]** <note>bahal</note> He hurried much too quickly, he rushed forward rashly, he rushed in violently <note>original Latin: *irruit condtatus*, likely a typographical error for *concitatus* meaning 'stirred up' or 'violently'</note>, and he overwhelmed without consideration. Ecclesiastes 4: *Do not speak anything rashly.* And from the same book, chapter 7: *Do not be quick to anger.* Esther 6: *And they forced him to go quickly to the banquet the queen had prepared.*

**[Hebrew: בהלה]** <note>behalah</note> Terror, disturbance. Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the primary translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> translated this as "quickly." Leviticus 26: *I will visit you quickly in poverty,* etc., as if it were said: *I will set terror over you.* Therefore, it signifies both.

**[Hebrew: בהמה]** <note>behemah</note> Beast, animal. As in Deuteronomy 14: *This is the animal that you ought to eat.*

**[Hebrew: בהן]** <note>bohen</note> The thumb or the big toe, as in Leviticus 14: *And upon the thumbs of his hand and his right foot.* It is preferably declined in the feminine form by adding the letter *vav*: **[Hebrew: בהונות]** <note>behonot</note>.

**[Hebrew: בהק]** <note>bohaq</note> A freckle, or a malignant whiteness of the skin. Jerome translated this as a "white-colored spot" in Leviticus 13: *Let him know it is not leprosy but a white-colored spot and the man is clean.* Others interpret this as a freckle <note>original: *lentiginem*</note>.

**[Hebrew: בהר]** <note>bahar</note> It shone or was bright white. Leviticus 13: *A man or woman in whose skin a brightness appears.* From this comes **[Hebrew: בהיר]** <note>bahir</note> meaning lucid, or white as snow.

**[Hebrew: בוא]** <note>bo</note> He came, as in Psalm 36: *Let not the foot of the proud come to me.* This is often found without the letter *vav* as **[Hebrew: בא]** <note>ba</note>, such as in 1 Samuel 4: *And the Philistines were afraid, saying: God has come into the camp.* From this comes **[Hebrew: תבואת]** <note>tevuat</note> which means produce or income. As in 2 Kings 8: *Restore to her all that was hers and all the income of the fields.* Its derivatives and compounds vary in a wonderful way through many rules of grammar, both in their abundance and lack of letters <note>A reference to "defective" and "full" spellings in Hebrew grammar, where vowel-pointing letters like *vav* are sometimes omitted in the text.</note>.

**[Hebrew: בוז]** <note>buz</note> He reproached, looked down upon, or despised. As in Proverbs 23: *Do not speak in the ears of the foolish, because they despise the teaching of your speech.* This is often found through the <term>syncopation: the shortening of a word by omitting a letter from the middle</term> of the letter *vav* as **[Hebrew: בז]** <note>baz</note>, such as in Proverbs 1: *Fools despise wisdom and instruction.* And it is written more clearly in Zechariah 4: *For who...*

# BOOK

...he despised the days of small things <note>original Latin: "despexit dies parvos," likely referencing Zechariah 4:10</note>. And in Malachi 2: "Therefore I have also made you **contemptible**," where the word *nibzim* <note>Hebrew: נבזים</note> is placed.

**בוך** [BWK] **To ensnare.** From this comes *nabokh* <note>Hebrew: נבוך</note>: he was perplexed, he wandered out of the way, he was confused and doubtful. Esther 3: where the [Latin] translator rendered the text as "and all the Jews who were in the city were weeping," the Hebrew truth <note>original: "hebraica veritas," a common term for the original Hebrew text among Renaissance scholars</note> has: "and the city of Susa was **perplexed**." It is also found with a missing letter *vav*, where a *shurek* <term>shurek: a Hebrew vowel mark representing a "u" sound</term> point is pronounced instead, in Exodus 14. Where we read "they are entangled in the land," the word *nebukhim* <note>Hebrew: נבכים</note> is placed there, meaning wandering, ensnared, doubtful, or confused.

**בול** [BWL] **A trunk** or wooden stake. Isaiah 44: "I shall fall down before the **trunk** of a tree." According to Master Jonah <note>Rabbi Jonah ibn Janah, a celebrated 11th-century Hebrew grammarian and lexicographer</note>, it is a species of wood, so that it is an appositive construction: "A stake of wood," as if he were to say "I shall worship the wooden stake," just as one might say "the dusty earth" or "the rainy shower."

**בול** [BWL] **A shrub** or shoot, which Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible</note> translated as "grass." Job 40: "Hence the mountains bring forth **grass**." However, it signifies everything that the earth produces, such as fruits, shrubs, and branches, and likewise anything else that is halfway between grass and wood. The word *yebul* <note>Hebrew: יבול</note> is similar, as in Psalm 67: "The earth gave its **fruit**."

**בול** [BWL] **The month of October.** As in 1 Kings 6 <note>original: "iii. Regum," following the older numbering where 1 and 2 Samuel were 1 and 2 Kings</note>: "And in the eleventh year, in the month of **Bul**—which is the eighth month—the house was finished." Some of the Hebrews say the month is named after *mabul* <note>Hebrew: מבול</note>, meaning "flood" (from Genesis 6: "Behold, I will bring the waters of the flood upon the earth"), because that month abounds in rain.

**בוס** [BWS] **He ruined**, trampled, defiled, or brought to nothing. As in Psalm 60: "And he himself shall bring to nothing those who trouble us." Jerome, in his translation from the Hebrew, interprets this as "he will trample." From this comes the verbal noun in Zechariah 10: "And they shall be as mighty men, **trampling** the mire of the streets in battle." It drops the letter *sin* [s], as in Amos 5: "Therefore, because you have plundered the poor."

**בוץ** [BWTZ] **Linen**, which Jerome interprets as *byssus* <term>byssus: an extremely fine and costly fabric, often translated as "fine linen," used for royal or priestly garments</term>. Esther 1: "Supported by cords of **fine linen** and purple."

**בוק** [BWQ] **He emptied out** or scattered. As in Nahum 2: "She is **emptied**, and torn, and rent." And with the last letter doubled, *boqeq* <note>Hebrew: בוקק</note>: he devastated or emptied.

->**THE FIRST BOOK**<-

**בוק** <note>Hebrew root: *buq*, meaning to empty or scatter</note> **He scattered.** Isaiah 24: *Behold, the Lord has scattered the earth.* And a little further below: *The earth shall be scattered with scattering.* <note>original Latin: "Dissipatione dissipabitur terra"</note>

**בולק** <note>Hebrew root: *bolaq*</note> **He laid waste; he stripped.** As in the place mentioned above, Isaiah 24: *And he shall strip it.*

**בור** <note>Hebrew root: *bor*</note> **A pit; a cistern.** As in Genesis 37: *And they cast him into an old cistern which had no water.* It differs from the word **באר** <note>Hebrew: *be'er*, usually a well</note> in that the latter is made by the hand of a craftsman, while this one <term>bor</term> exists by the guidance of nature. It also signifies a prison, as in Genesis 41: *Immediately, by the king's command, they brought Joseph out of the prison <note>original Latin: "carcere"</note> and shaved him.* It also signifies a grave or a pit, which Jerome translated as "lake" <note>original Latin: "lacum"</note> in Psalm 28: *And I shall be like those descending into the lake,* that is, the grave, according to the Hebrews. It also signifies uncultivated land, reduced to a wilderness and a deserted place.

**בוש** <note>Hebrew root: *bush*</note> **He was confounded; he blushed.** As in Psalm 71: *When they are confounded and put to shame <note>original Latin: "confusi fuerint & reueriti"</note> who seek my harm.* And above in Psalm 70: *Let them be confounded and put to shame who seek my soul.*

**בושה** <note>Hebrew root: *bushah*</note> **Reproach; modesty; confusion.** As in Psalm 89: *You have covered him with confusion.* Sometimes it receives the letter 'nun' through <term>epenthesis</term> <note>the addition of a letter in the middle of a word</note>, and is written as:

**בשנה** <note>Hebrew: *boshnah*</note> **Modesty; confusion.** As in Hosea 10: *Confusion shall seize Ephraim and he shall be confounded.* From this comes the <term>transitive hiphil</term> <note>a causative verb form in Hebrew</note> **הביש** <note>Hebrew: *habish*</note>, as in Psalm 53: *They are confounded because God has despised them.* From this comes **מביש** <note>Hebrew: *mabish*</note>, that is, "making confusion" or "causing shame." Proverbs 10: *And rot in his bones is she who conducts herself in ways worthy of confusion,* that is, she causes shame.

**בזז** <note>Hebrew root: *bazaz*</note> **He seized; he plundered.** As in Isaiah 24: *The earth shall be utterly emptied with emptying, and utterly plundered with plundering.* And when the last letter is doubled, it is found lacking the letter 'vav' as **בז** <note>Hebrew: *baz*</note>, meaning **he plundered or tore away**, as in Ezekiel 39: *And they shall plunder those to whom they had been a prey.* And it is sometimes pronounced with an <term>apocope</term> <note>the loss of a sound at the end of a word</note> of a single letter 'zain'. From this comes the verbal noun **ביז** <note>Hebrew: *biz*</note>, meaning **plunder**, as in Esther 9: *They did not wish to take plunder from their goods.*

**בזה** <note>Hebrew root: *bazah*</note> **He despised; he held cheap; he scorned.** As in Numbers 15: *Because he despised the word of the Lord...*

...for he has despised the word of the Lord. <note>original Latin: "bum [verbum] enim domini contempfit". This is the conclusion of an entry from the previous page, likely the root *bazah* (בזה), meaning "to despise."</note>
**בזא** <term>Baza: To plunder or despoil</term>. He plundered, he despoiled, he seized, as in Isaiah chapter eighteen: *Rivers have plundered his land.* For we showed above that **בז** <note>Baz</note> is found by <term>apocope</term> <note>the loss of one or more sounds at the end of a word</note>, but even then it adds the letter *he* [ה], and it is said as **בזה** <note>Bazah</note> with the same meaning of plundering; this aspiration [the 'h' sound] is indeed often changed into an *aleph* [א], as it is here.
**בזק** <term>Bazaq: A flash or spark</term>. Sparkling, flashing, lightning, as in Ezekiel chapter one: *And the living creatures went and returned like the appearance of flashing lightning.* It is spoken as if it were **ב-רק** <note>Baraq</note>, which means the same thing. It is also a place name, in Judges chapter one: *And they found Adonibezek in Bezek.*
**בזר** <term>Bazar: To scatter</term>. He dispersed, just as **פזר** <note>Pazar</note> means he scattered, as in Psalm 147: *He scatters the mist like ashes,* and in Joel chapter three: *Whom they have dispersed among the nations.*
**בחל** <term>Bachal: To loathe</term>. He shuddered, he abominated, he grew weary, as in Zechariah chapter eleven; in place of what we read <note>referring to the Latin Vulgate translation</note>, "for indeed their soul varied toward me," the Hebrew scholars explain it as "felt nausea" or "abhorred."
**בחן** <term>Bachan: To test or examine</term>. He proved, he tempted <note>in the sense of testing for quality</note>, Zechariah chapter 13: *And I will test them as gold is tested,* and Ezekiel chapter 21: *Clap your hands upon your thigh because it has been tested.*
**בחון** <term>Bachon: A watchtower or stronghold</term>. A citadel, a fortress, a tower, a bulwark; it can also refer to "every strongest person" when speaking figuratively, as in Isaiah chapter 23: *They have led away his strong ones into captivity.*
**בחר** <term>Bachar: To choose</term>. He chose, as in Psalm 135: *For the Lord has chosen Jacob for himself,* and Judges chapter five: *The Lord will choose new things.*
**בחור** <term>Bachur: A young man</term>. An adolescent, a warlike youth, a chosen man, a strong boy. In 2 Samuel <note>originally cited as 2 Kings</note> chapter six: *And David again gathered all the chosen men of Israel.* From this comes the nouns for "adolescence" and "youth," as in Ecclesiastes chapter 11: *Rejoice, therefore, young man, in your youth and in the days of your young manhood.*
**בחיר** <term>Bachir: The chosen one</term>. Chosen, as in Psalm 89: *I have made a covenant with my chosen ones.*

**בטא** <note>Bata</note> He spoke rashly or uttered. As in Leviticus 5: "A soul that shall swear and utter with its lips." In the verbal noun, the letter *aleph* changes into the letter *he*.

**בטח** <note>Batach</note> He trusted. As in Psalm 28: "In him my heart has trusted." This word has many and very diverse variations of derivatives, which one ought to seek from the art of grammar and the use of books.

**בטל** <note>Batal</note> He was idle or at leisure. As in Ecclesiastes 12: "And the grinders shall be idle because they are few in number."

**בטן** <note>Beten</note> Belly. As in Proverbs 13: "But the belly of the wicked is insatiable."

**בטנים** <note>Botnim</note> Pine nuts. Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate Bible</note> translated this as the fruit of the Terebinth tree, as in Genesis 43: "Of storax and terebinth and almonds." In the Jerusalem Targum <note>an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary of the Hebrew Bible</note>, it is taken to mean aromatic oil.

**ביב** <note>Bib</note> Hollow, empty, or void. Exodus 27: "You shall make it not solid, but empty and hollow on the inside."

**בין** <note>Bin</note> He understood. At the end of Daniel: "And I heard and I did not understand."

**בינה** <note>Binah</note> Understanding. Although Jerome translates it differently in various places. For in Proverbs 4, he interpreted it as "prudence": "Hear, O children, the discipline of a father, and attend that you may know prudence." And in chapter 30 of the same book, he translated it as "wisdom": "I am the most foolish of men, and the wisdom of men is not with me." From this comes **הבין** <note>Havin</note>, that is, "to understand," as in Proverbs 14: "The wisdom of the clever man is to understand his way." From this comes **נבון** <note>Navon</note>, as in the same book: "And the learning of the prudent is easy." From this comes **תבונה** <note>Tevunah</note>, that is, "understanding," which they have also translated sometimes as "prudence" and sometimes as "wisdom," as in Psalm 147: "And of his wisdom there is no number." And so it is for other derivatives. In the exposition of all these, the Cabalists <note>Jewish mystics who studied the hidden, esoteric meanings of the Torah</note> speak more precisely when they write about the "fifty gates of understanding," not of prudence, nor wisdom, nor knowledge or science. They show that there are many differences between wisdom and understanding, for one pertains to judgment and the other to grace, as these are treated more clearly in the "Tree of the Ten Numerations" <note>The Sefirot, or the ten attributes in Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals itself</note> and at the end of Job 28.

**בין** <note>Beyn</note> Between. As in Genesis 1, where we read: "And he divided the waters which were under..."

->BOOK<-

...the firmament, etc. There the Hebrew scripture has: "And he made a distinction between the waters which are under the firmament, and between the waters which are above the firmament." <note>Genesis 1:7; the author is noting the repetition of the Hebrew word for "between" (ben)</note> Similarly, where it follows: "And let it divide the day and the night," <note>Genesis 1:14</note> there it is read in Hebrew: "to make a distinction between the day and between the night." The word *binot* <note>Hebrew: בינות, a variant or plural form of the word for "between"</note> is also found, as in Ezekiel 10: "And fill your hand with coals of fire, which are between the cherubim." It sometimes takes prepositions, and occasionally articles; but it is also found to be declined by numbers <note>meaning it can appear in plural or construct forms</note>.

**Eggs** <note>Hebrew: *beitzim* (ביצים)</note>. As in Deuteronomy 22: "And the mother sitting upon the young or the eggs." Its singular form is rarely read in the Sacred Scriptures. However, in other books <note>referring to post-biblical Rabbinic literature</note>, we find the irregular form *beitza* <note>Hebrew: ביצה</note>, which is also the title given to a specific book <note>The Talmudic tractate *Beitzah*, which deals with laws for festival days</note>.

**Pit**, **cistern**, or **well**. Much like the word *be'er* <note>Hebrew: באר, the more common word for a well</note>. In Jeremiah 6: "As a cistern keeps its water cold."

**Palace**, **royal residence**, or **dwelling**. This is what Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate)</note> translated as "the beginning of the kingdom." In Esther 1: "The city of Susa was the beginning of his kingdom," <note>original Latin: "Susan ciuitas regni eius exordium fuit"</note> that is, the palace and residence. It has a plural form, *biraniyot* <note>Hebrew: בירניות</note>.

**House**. As in Exodus 12: "For there was not a house in which there did not lie someone dead." It also signifies a lineage or stock <note>a "house" in the sense of a family dynasty</note>, as in Deuteronomy 25: "Thus shall it be done to the man who does not build up his brother's house." Likewise, it can mean a nest or any kind of dwelling, as in Psalm 84: "For even the sparrow has found herself a house."

**Within** or **inside**. As in Genesis 6: "And you shall smear it with pitch inside and out." And in Ezekiel 1: "Like the appearance of fire inside all around it."

**Palace** or **hall**. As in Esther 7. Instead of what we read—"Who, when he had returned from the garden planted with trees and had entered the place of the banquet"—the Hebrews read: "And the king returned from the garden of the palace to the house of the banquet."

# THE FIRST BOOK

**בכא** <note>original: "Baka"</note> A type of tree which some call a mulberry, but Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD) was the primary translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> called a pear tree. In the second book of Kings, chapter five: <note>In the Latin Vulgate, 1 and 2 Samuel are titled 1 and 2 Kings. This refers to 2 Samuel 5:23-24 in modern Bibles.</note> "And you shall come upon them opposite the pear trees. And when you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the pear trees."

**בכה** <note>original: "Bakah"</note> He wept. As in Hosea, chapter twelve: "He wept and entreated him." And sometimes it is written without the final letter *He* <note>The Hebrew letter ה</note> as in Genesis, chapter fifty: "He fell upon his father's face, and wept over him, and kissed him." From this comes the verbal noun **בכי** <note>original: "Bekhi"</note> meaning weeping. As in Psalm thirty: "Weeping may endure for a night." It is also called **בכות** <note>original: "Bakhut"</note> and sometimes **בכות** <note>original: "Bakhot"</note>. As in Genesis 35: "And the name of that place was called the Oak of Weeping." From this the source of rivers is also derived, following the likeness of abundant tears.

**בכור** <note>original: "Bekhor"</note> Firstborn. In Psalm eighty-nine: "I will make him my firstborn." It is declined irregularly in the plural as **בכורות** <note>original: "Bekhorot"</note> or **בכורי** <note>original: "Bekhorei"</note>. It also signifies **בכר מות** <note>original: "Bekhor Mavet," literally "Firstborn of Death"</note>, an Angel or a power of wealth <term>Mammon: a term for wealth or material greed, here personified</term> appointed to death, whom Jerome called "the firstborn death." As in Job, chapter eighteen: "Let the firstborn death consume his arms." Rabbi Joseph <note>Likely referring to Joseph Kara or another medieval Jewish commentator.</note> thinks this refers to a lethal disease followed by death. Lyra <note>Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349), an influential Franciscan teacher and biblical commentator.</note> understands it as a premature death that precedes a natural death.

**בכורי** <note>original: "Bikkurei"</note> Firstfruits. As in Exodus, chapter thirty-four: "The firstfruits of the produce of your land you shall offer in the house of the Lord your God."

**בל** <note>original: "Bal"</note> Not or lest. As in Psalm sixteen: "Because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved." It takes the letter *Yod* at the end, as in **בלי** <note>original: "Beli"</note> meaning "not," in the second book of Kings, chapter one: "The shield of Saul, as though it had not been anointed with oil." Again, it takes the letter *Mem* at the beginning, as in **מבלי** <note>original: "Mibeli"</note> meaning "not" or "without." In Job, chapter four: "The tiger perished because it had no prey." From this comes **לבלתי** <note>original: "Lebilti"</note> meaning "only," "not," or "except." As in Leviticus 20; and **מבלעדי** <note>original: "Mibaladei"</note> and **מבלתי** <note>original: "Mibilti"</note> and others which signify a negation like "unless," "except," or "without." As in Psalm eighteen: "For who is God except the Lord, or who is God except our God?"

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical exploration of Hebrew roots, specifically focusing on terms beginning with the letter Bet (ב). The previous pages likely covered earlier "B" roots, and this page moves from 'Belial' through words related to 'mixing' and 'strengthening.'</meta>

->**BOOK**<-

**בליעל** <note>Hebrew: *Belial*</note> **Evil. Iniquity.** As in Psalm 41: *They have established an iniquitous word against me.* <note>original: "Verbum iniquum constituerunt aduersum me"</note> From this comes the name of the demon who is the father of all evil, as in Nahum 1: *And he shall no longer continue to pass through you, Belial.* <note>original: "Et non adiiciet ultra ut pertranseat in te belial"</note> Thus, those who are from the father, the devil, are called the "sons of Belial," as in Judges 19: *The men of that city, sons of Belial, arrived.* The Chaldaic translation <note>The Aramaic "Targum," a common interpretive translation used in the Middle Ages.</note> explains this as "sons of malice." Some Hebrews believe it is a compound word from **בלי** <note>*Beli* - "without"</note> and **על** <note>*Ol* - "yoke"</note> because it does not allow our mind to be carried upward.

**בלל** <note>Hebrew: *Balal*</note> **He mingled. He confused.** As in Genesis 11: *Because there the language of the whole earth was confused.* <note>original: "Quia ibi confusum est labium uniuerse terre"</note> Which in Hebrew is read: *Because there the Lord mingled or confused the language of the whole earth.* And by changing the final letter into a Hebrew "H" aspiration, it is placed in the same chapter a little earlier as **נבלה** <note>Hebrew: *Navlah*</note> meaning "let us confuse their tongue there." From this they wish to derive **בלילה** <note>Hebrew: *Belilah*</note> meaning "mixed thing," which Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into the Latin Vulgate.</note> translated as "sprinkled" or "tempered" in Leviticus 2: *Fine flour mixed with oil and without leaven.* Dyers use this word to mean "to stain" or "to dye." From this comes **תבל** <note>Hebrew: *Tebel*</note> meaning "confusion" or "wickedness," as in Leviticus 20: *If anyone sleeps with his daughter-in-law, let both die, because they have committed a crime.* <note>original: "scelus operati sunt" — Here *tebel* is interpreted as a "confusion" of natural order.</note> From this comes **תבלול** <note>Hebrew: *Tebalul*</note> that is, a spot in the eye, which Jerome named "albugo" <note>A white medicinal spot or film over the eye.</note> in Leviticus 21: *If you have a white spot in your eye.* It is so called from **בלבל** <note>Hebrew: *Balbal*</note> that is, from a "confusion" of the pupil in the eye. From which also **בבל** <note>Hebrew: *Babel*</note> **Babylonia** was named, as if it were "Balbel" [Confusion]. Hence:

**בליל** <note>Hebrew: *Belil*</note> **Fodder for beasts,** mixed from various things like hay, straw, and chaff. It is so called from the "confusion" or mixing of different things. Jerome called this *migma* in Greek—you will not find a Latin word for it—meaning "a mixture." Isaiah 30: *They shall eat mixed fodder <term>migma</term> just as it has been winnowed on the floor.* <note>The author notes that there is no direct Latin equivalent for this specific type of animal mash, so he uses the Greek-derived term.</note>

**בלג** <note>Hebrew: *Balag*</note> **He is content. He persisted firmly. He prevailed. He was strengthened and comforted.** Although Jerome intended it to mean "torments of pain" in Job 9: *When I say I will by no means speak thus; I change my face, and I am tortured by pain.* Where the text places **אבליגה** <note>Hebrew: *Abligah*</note> which the Hebrews explain as: *If I say I will forget my complaint, I will set aside my anger and be comforted <gloss>strengthened</gloss>.*

**בלם** [B-L-M] He tightened, closed, blocked, bound, or bridled. As in Psalm 32: "Bind their jaws with bit and bridle," that is, for the purpose of restraining or tightening, for thus we read **לבלום** <note>The infinitive form "to restrain."</note>.

**בלס** [B-L-S] He examined or sought. Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the primary translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> translated this in the book of the prophet Amos as "pinching" <note>original: *vellicauit*</note>, as in Amos 7: "But I am a herdsman, nipping sycamore figs." **בלע** [B-L-`] He engulfed, swallowed down, or devoured. As in Exodus 7: "But Aaron’s rod devoured their rods." From this comes the verbal noun **בלע**, which Jerome, in our daily reading of the Psalter, translated as "ruin" <note>original: *precipitatio*, literally "a headlong fall" or "destruction."</note>, although the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> better renders it as *catapontismos*, which means "drowning" or, more properly, "engulfing" or "absorption." In Psalm 52: "You have loved all words of ruin, O deceitful tongue." The Greeks, however, translate it: "You have loved all words of swallowing, O deceitful tongue." Saint Jerome, translating this same verse more accurately according to the "Hebrew Truth" <note>original: *hebraica veritate*, a term Jerome used for the original Hebrew text as opposed to translations.</note>, interprets it thus: "You have loved all words for devouring, O deceitful tongue."

**<term>Ba’ar</term>** <note>original: בער</note>: He consumed, molested, injured, grazed, or tore out. As in Exodus 22: *If anyone should damage a field or a vineyard.*

...as in Numbers 16: "But if the Lord performs a new thing." <note>original: "Sin autem nouam rem fecerit dominus." The Hebrew root implied is B-R-A, meaning to create.</note>
**בריא** [Bari]: **Firm, healthy, fat, or thick.** As in Judges 3: "Now Eglon was a very fat man." You will find derivatives of this as you read; often, through the omission of the letter *aleph* at the end, you will find it written as **בריה** [Beryah], as in Ezekiel 34: "Behold, I myself will judge between the fat sheep and the lean sheep."
**ברבור** [Barbur]: **Poultry, or a fatted bird.** As in 1 Kings 4: "Besides the hunting of stags, roebucks, and buffaloes, and fatted birds." Where it is written **ברבורים אבוסים** [barburim abusim], that is, "fatted birds from the stalls," meaning those kept in a stable.
**ברד** [Barad]: **Hail.** As in Exodus 9: "Behold, tomorrow at this very hour I will rain down a great deal of hail." From this comes the verb **ברד** [barad] with a <term>qamets</term> <note>A long 'a' vowel sound.</note> on the first syllable and a <term>patah</term> <note>A short 'a' vowel sound.</note> on the second. <margin>4</margin>
**ברדים** [Berudim]: **Sprinkled with points or spots,** as in Genesis 31: "Streaked, speckled, and spotted."
**ברה** [Barah]: **He chose.** As in 1 Samuel 17: "Choose a man from among yourselves."
**ברה** [Barah]: **He dined, or he ate.** 2 Samuel 13: "Let me eat from her hand." From this are derived the verbal nouns in Psalm 69: "They gave me gall for my food," and 2 Samuel 13: "Bring the food into the inner chamber, that I may eat from your hand." Some believe this explains the verse in Genesis 47: "And it was springtime." <note>This likely refers to Genesis 48:7. The author is discussing the term 'kivrath-eretz', which relates to distance or grazing land.</note> Where, according to the <term>Hebrew truth</term> <note>original: "hebraicam ueritatem" — a common Scholarly term for the original Hebrew text as opposed to the Latin Vulgate translation.</note> it should be read "when the field was already like pasture." This is a parenthetical point that the translator expressed by paraphrasing with other words, saying: "For it was springtime."
**ברזל** [Barzel]: **Iron.** Psalm 105: "Iron entered into his soul."
**ברח** [Barach]: **He fled.** As in 2 Samuel 13: "Moreover, Absalom fled and went away." It also means to frame with beams or to shut, as seen below.
**בריח** [Beriach]: **A bolt, spear, beam, or bar.** As in Exodus 26: regarding what we read as "and of the same number for the western side," followed by "which shall be passed through the middle of the boards." The Hebrew original says: "And the beam passing through the middle of the boards, bolting them together from end to end." It also signifies a lock or a bar, as in Job 38: "And I placed a bar (that is, a bolt) and doors."

### FIRST [BOOK]

**ברך** [Barak] **He blessed.** As in Psalm 118: *Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. We have blessed you from the house of the Lord.* <note>original: "Benedictus qui uenit in nomiē dñi. Benediximus uobis de domo dñi."</note> Likewise, **He greeted.** As in Genesis 47: *Who, in blessing him...* <note>original: "Qui benedicēs illi."</note> for which the <term>Hebrew Truth</term> <note>The "Hebraica Veritas" was a term used by scholars like St. Jerome to refer to the authentic Hebrew text as opposed to later translations.</note> has: *And Jacob greeted Pharaoh.* Likewise, **He bent his knees.** As in Psalm 95 according to the Hebrew Truth: *Come, let us worship, let us bow down, let us bend our knees.* And Genesis 24: *And when he had made the camels kneel down.*

**ברך** [Barak] **He blasphemed, rebuked, reproached, or cursed.** As in 1 Kings 21, regarding what we read as: *Naboth blessed God and the king* <note>original: "Benedixit Naboth deū et regē."</note>—for which reason they led him outside the city and killed him with stones. The Hebrews translated this as: *he blasphemed.* And the <term>Chaldean translation</term> <note>Referring to the Targum, an Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> of Jonathan has <gloss>גדיף</gloss>, which means *he despised.* Whence <term>Nicholas of Lyra</term> <note>A famous 14th-century Franciscan scholar known for his literal interpretations of the Bible.</note> explains "blessed" as "cursed." Similarly, in Job 2: *Bless God and die*—the Hebrews explain this as: *Rebuke and reproach God.* <note>This is a classic example of a "contrapuntal" meaning in Hebrew, where a word is used as a polite euphemism for its opposite.</note>

**ברכה** [Berakhah] **A gift or a present.** Genesis 33: *And receive the blessing that I have brought to you*—which means, *receive the gift which was brought to you.*

**ברכים** [Berakhayim] or **ברכי** [Berakhei] **Knees.** As in Deuteronomy 28: *May the Lord strike you with the worst sores on the knees and on the legs.*

**ברכה** [Berekhah] **A fountain, a nursery, a pond, or a pool.** As in the seventh chapter of the Song of Songs: *Your eyes are like the pools in Heshbon.*

**ברם** [Berom] **A type of very precious garment.** Others think it is a small chest for precious jewels. Jerome translated it as "precious treasure." Ezekiel 27: *Your merchants themselves dealt in many ways with bundles of blue cloth, embroidered work, and chests of precious treasures* <note>original: "gazarūq; preciosarū."</note>—where the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> interpreted it as "chosen treasures."

**ברק** [Baraq] **Radiance, lightning, a flash, or a spark.** 2 Samuel 22: *He sent out his arrows and scattered them; lightning, and he consumed them.* It also signifies a stone of that kind.

**ברקנים** [Barqanim] **A certain species of thorns**, which our translation calls "thistles." <note>original: "tribulos."</note> Judges 8: *And when I return victorious in peace, I will tear your flesh with the thorns and thistles of the desert.*

**ברש** [Berosh] **A certain tree from which spears are made.** Jerome translated it as **fir**, others as **cedar**. Isaiah 55: *Instead of the briar, the fir tree shall come up.* And in the 60th chapter of the same book: *The fir tree, the box tree, and the pine tree together.*

[Hebrew: ברושים] <note>transliteration: *beroshim*</note> Projectiles, spears, weapons, javelins, arrows; because these shafts are made from the tree named previously <note>referring to the fir or cypress</note> on account of its great height. Jerome, however, translated it as *charioteers*, and the Septuagint <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> rendered it as *horsemen* in Nahum 2[:3]: *And the charioteers were lulled to sleep.* The Septuagint reads it as: *And the horsemen trembled in their ranks.* For they wished to follow, as much as they were able, the Chaldaic translation <term>Targum</term> of Jonathan, who explains it as *exalted ones* and *nobles* and *masters of armies*. I myself would call them *lancers* or *artillery-men*.

[Hebrew: בשל] <note>transliteration: *bashal*</note> It has ripened. As in Joel 3[:13]: *Put in the sickles, because the harvest has ripened.*

[Hebrew: בשל] <note>transliteration: *bashal*</note> To cook or boil. As in Exodus 12[:9]: *You shall not eat any of it raw, nor boiled in water.* And in Ezekiel 24[:5]: *And its bones were boiled in its midst.*

# FIRST BOOK

...the feet upon the mountains of him who brings tidings and proclaims peace, who brings tidings of good. <note>original Latin: "montes pedes annunciantis et predicantis pacem, annunciātis bonū," quoting Nahum 1:15 or Isaiah 52:7</note> Here is placed his name **Messenger** <note>Hebrew: *mevasser* (מבשר)</note>, an evangelist or bearer of news, who in common parlance is called an "ambassador." From this comes **Good News** <note>Hebrew: *besorah* (בשורה)</note>, meaning a reward or payment for a message delivered, as in 2 Samuel 4: "To whom I should have given a reward for his news." <note>The author cites "2 Kings 4" following the Vulgate numbering, where 1 and 2 Samuel are titled 1 and 2 Kings.</note>

**Desolation** <note>Hebrew: *batah* (בתה)</note>. Empty, deserted, or laid waste. As in Isaiah 5: "And I will lay it waste."

**Bath** <note>Hebrew: *bat* (בת)</note>. This is a measure for liquids, which Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the primary translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible</note>, alluding to the name, translated as "bathum" in Ezekiel 45: "You shall have a just balance, a just ephah, and a just bath."

**Virgin** <note>Hebrew: *betulah* (בתולה)</note>. As in Genesis 24: "And the girl was very beautiful, a virgin unknown to any man." And in the plural **Virgins** <note>Hebrew: *betulot* (בתולות)</note>, as in Amos 8: "In that day the beautiful virgins shall faint." For the masculine plural forms <note>Hebrew: *betulim* (בתולים) and *betuli* (בתולי)</note> signify physical integrity or the signs of virginity. As in Deuteronomy 22, saying: "I did not find your daughter a virgin"—whereas we ought to read it as: "I did not find in your daughter the tokens of incorruption or integrity; and these are the signs of my daughter's virginity."

**To Pierce** <note>Hebrew: *bataq* (בתק)</note>. He pierced through, killed, or slaughtered. Ezekiel 16: "And they shall slaughter you with their swords."

**To Separate** <note>Hebrew: *batar* (בתר)</note>. He separated, parted, or divided. As in Genesis 15: "But the birds he did not divide."

**Part** <note>Hebrew: *beter* (בתר)</note>. A part, division, separation, portion, or partition. As in Genesis 15, as mentioned above: "And he laid each piece over against the other." And in the Song of Songs 2: "Be like a roe, my beloved, or a young stag upon the mountains of Bether." In this passage, certain ignorant writers have put an "L" for an "R," writing *Bethel*; but the Hebrews read it as "the mountains of partition" or "separation."

->THE BOOK<-

<insert>Handwritten Hebrew notes: ggg l-din algan</insert> <note>These scribbles appear to be pen trials or a student's mnemonic notes, possibly referencing a legal context ("l'din"), though they are largely informal.</note>

### גג <term>Gag (Roof)</term>
**A roof.** As in Psalm 102: *I have become like a solitary sparrow on the roof.* It declines irregularly according to the feminine gender in the plural, גגות (*gagot*), as in Zephaniah 1: *And those who worship the host of heaven upon the roofs.*

### גאה <term>Ga’ah (To be exalted)</term>
**He was elated, elevated, and exalted; he ruled and was gloriously magnified.** It is used intransitively. As in Exodus 15: *Let us sing to the Lord, for he is gloriously magnified.* This phrase is read literally word-for-word as: *In triumphing he has triumphed,* or *In ruling he has ruled.* In Isaiah 16, it signifies arrogance and pride: *We have heard of the pride of Moab, he is very proud; his pride and his arrogance, etc.* From this comes גאוה (*ga'avah*), meaning pride.

### גאון <term>Ga’on (Majesty/Excellence)</term>
**Majesty.** Jerome, in his commentaries on the Twelve Prophets, says this word signifies the rushing and sound of running water. In Zechariah 11, where the Greek Septuagint translation says: *The voice of the roaring lions because the rushing of the Jordan is distressed,* our translation <note>original: "nostra," referring to the Latin Vulgate used by the Church</note> more correctly reads: *The voice of the roaring lions because the pride of the Jordan is laid waste.* This is also attested by the Chaldean translation of Jonathan <note>The Targum Jonathan, an Aramaic paraphrase of the Bible</note>, which explains it as "the height of the Jordan."

### גאל <term>Ga’al (To redeem or To defile)</term>
**He ransomed or redeemed.** As in Isaiah 48: *Say, the Lord has redeemed his servant Jacob.* From this, you will find גאולה (*ge’ulah*, redemption) and גאל (*go’el*, redeemer) and many other derivatives in Leviticus 25, signifying ransoming, redemption, and liberation.
Likewise, it signifies **to foul, defile, mar, or obscure.** As in Job 3: *Let darkness and the shadow of death obscure it.* It also means to **pollute**, as in Daniel 1: *But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not be polluted.*

### גב <term>Gav (Back/Summit)</term>
**A summit, back, height, or top.** As in Psalm 129: *Sinners have built upon my back.* It also signifies the **eyebrow**. In Leviticus 14, on the seventh day: *He shall shave the hair of his head, his beard, and his eyebrows.* Sometimes the letter *nun* is added <note>creating the form "Gevnun"</note>, as in Psalm 68, where we read: *A curdled mountain.* In that passage, Jerome, in his Psalter translated from the "Hebrew Verity" <note>Jerome’s translation directly from the Hebrew text rather than the Greek</note>, more correctly translated it as "a high mountain." Some, conversely, explain it as a humble and hilly mountain—that is, "hunchbacked"—and thus it derives from the following word:

### גבן <term>Giben (Hunchbacked)</term>
**Humped or hunchbacked**, perhaps drawn from the idea of the "height of the back." For so Jerome translated Leviticus 21: *If he has a broken foot, or hand, or if he is hunchbacked, or bleary-eyed.* Although the Jerusalem Targum <note>The Aramaic translation of the Torah</note> understands this word to refer to those in whom the hairs of the eyebrows grow so long they cover the eyes, which the Jews now commonly follow in their explanation.

...be placed גבר <term>Gever: a man or a rooster</term> and with the robust one, he is perfect.
**גבר** <note>original: "Gallus gallinaceus"</note> A poultry rooster. Isaiah 22: "Just as the rooster is carried away." Jerome affirms in his commentaries that he learned this interpretation from his Jewish teacher.

**גביש** <term>Gavish: crystal or precious stone</term> A precious stone. Job 28, where our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> says: "High and eminent things shall not be mentioned." In that place, the Hebrew truth <note>A common Renaissance term for the original Hebrew Masoretic text</note> identifies these two most precious stones, which are rarely used, saying: "Ramoth and Gabish shall not be mentioned." In comparison to the Hebrew, that entire Latin phrasing should be marked with an obelisk <note>A symbol used by scholars to indicate that a passage is doubtful or should be removed</note>. This error happened to the translator here because of carelessness and negligence regarding orthography <note>spelling</note>, which has often deceived many, as is evident in various places.

**גד** <term>Gad: coriander</term> Coriander. As in Numbers 11: "Now the manna was like coriander seed."

**גד** <term>Gad: Fortune</term> The goddess Fortune. As in Isaiah 65: "You who set a table for Fortune." Rabbi Moses Cohen <note>Likely the 11th-century scholar Moses ibn Chiquitilla</note> says that this refers to the planet Jupiter, and that Jupiter is called by this name in the language of Kedar—that is, Arabic. Rabbi David Kimhi, in his commentaries on Isaiah, also explains it as a star.

**גדד** <term>Gadad: to crowd or gather</term> He gathered an army, he girded himself for battle, or he prepared himself. As in Genesis 49: "Gad, being girded, shall fight before him, and he himself shall be girded from behind." Jerome, in his *Book of Hebrew Questions*, translates this verse as: "Gad the raider shall raid him, and he himself shall raid the heel." Nevertheless, in that same place, he explains *Gedud* as "girded" and "prepared." I would supplement the meaning with "cohort" <note>a military unit</note>. As in 2 Kings 22: "For in you I will run girded." Similarly, Rabbi Solomon the Frenchman <note>The famous commentator Rashi</note> explains the word in the previous passage as *chalutz*, which means "prepared" or "expedited." We read of such soldiers as "raiders" <note>original: "latrunculos," literally small thieves or skirmishers</note>. As in 2 Kings 24: "And the Lord sent against him raiders of the Chaldeans, and raiders of Syria, and raiders of Moab, and raiders of the children of Ammon." In those instances, the word **גדודי** <note>Gedudei: troops/bands</note> is always used. Jonathan the Chaldean <note>Referring to the Targum Jonathan, an Aramaic translation</note> explains it as **משריתא** <note>mashrita</note>, meaning a military expedition.

**גדר** <note>The context suggests this may be a variant or error for 'gadad' in the sense of cutting</note> He tore to pieces, he lacerated, he flayed, or he scratched. Jeremiah 47: "How long will you cut yourself?"

**גדי** <note>Hebrew: *Gedi*</note> **Kid.** As in Genesis 38: "But Judah sent the kid of the goats by his shepherd." and Judges 15: "And he brought him a kid of the goats." It is declined in the plural in both genders: in the masculine, as in Genesis 27: "Bring me two of the best kids"; and in the feminine, as in the first chapter of the Song of Songs: "And feed your kids beside the tents of the shepherds."

**גדות** <note>Hebrew: *Gedot*</note> **Shores** or **banks.** As in Joshua 3: "The Jordan had filled the banks of its channel during the time of the harvest."

**גדל** <note>Hebrew: *Gadal*</note> **He magnified; he was great; he was made magnificent.** As in Psalm 104: "O Lord my God, you are exceedingly magnified." and 1 Chronicles 29: "The Lord therefore magnified Solomon." and Genesis 41: regarding that which we read as "only by one throne of the kingdom shall I precede you," the word-for-word reading from the Hebrew is: "only the throne will I magnify above yours" or "above you." And Genesis 25: regarding that which our translation reads as "when they were grown up," the <term>Hebrew Truth</term> <note>original: *hebraica ueritas*; a term used by scholars to refer to the original Hebrew text as the ultimate authority</note> has: "And the boys were magnified," that is, they grew. In this and similar words, the <term>dagesh</term> point <note>a dot inside a Hebrew letter used to indicate a "heavy" or doubled sound</note> is always preserved. From this comes **גדול** <note>Hebrew: *Gadol*</note> **Great.** Exodus 11: "And Moses was a very great man." All words of this sort signify magnificence, honor, beauty, stature, strength, and power. Ezekiel 16: "And she committed fornication with the sons of Egypt, your neighbors of great flesh," where **גדלי** <note>Hebrew: *Gidlei*</note> is placed.

**גדל** <note>Hebrew: *Godel*</note> **Magnitude** or **Greatness.** A substantive noun. As in Deuteronomy 5: "Behold, the Lord our God has shown us his majesty and his greatness." and sometimes it is written with the first letter having the <term>shurek</term> point <note>original: *puncto surek*; a Hebrew vowel mark representing the "u" sound</note>, as in the last Psalm [150]: "Praise him according to the multitude of his greatness." And sometimes it takes the letter *he* at the end with a *shurek* in the penultimate syllable, as in Psalm 145: "And of his greatness there is no end." You will find all things derived from this signify an excellence of quality or quantity.

טבור <note>Hebrew: *Tabbur*</note> **Navel.** The middle part of the belly. טוח <note>Hebrew: *Tuach*</note> **He coated.** He plastered, smoothed, polished, or obscured. 1 Chronicles 29: "To overlay the walls of the temple." In Hebrew it says: "To smooth and polish or plaster the walls of the temple," namely with gold and silver, just as elsewhere it is done with mud or cement. Leviticus 14: "To smear the house with other mud." This is written with a contraction of the letter *vav*; however, the passive gerund soon follows in its full form, which our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate, the standard Bible of the time.</note> expresses through a roundabout phrase. In building, it means to cover the cracks between stones or the entire wall, hiding them with a certain coating. Hence in Psalm 51, it is written: "In the hidden and secret parts of wisdom you shall teach me." For this, our translation reads: "The uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom you have made manifest to me." Others read: "In the dullness and closed-up places <note>original: "ebetudinibus et obturato"</note>, you shall teach me wisdom."

**טור** <term>Tur: A row, arrangement, order, verse, or linear progression.</term> <note>Exodus 28:17</note> *You shall set in it four rows of stones; in the first row there shall be a sardius stone.* In the <term>Chaldaic</term> <note>Aramaic</note> language, however, this word signifies very high mountains, which we call "bulls" because of their high peaks. As in <note>Daniel 2:35</note>: *It became a great mountain and filled the whole earth.*

**טוש** <term>Tush: He hastened, he flew.</term> <note>Job 9:26</note> *Like an eagle flying to its prey.*

**טוח** <term>Tuach: He stretched, he threw.</term> This is an unusual word, from which—according to Rabbi Ionan—the doubled <term>dagesh</term> <note>a grammatical emphasis in Hebrew</note> conjugations are derived. From this comes the passage in <note>Genesis 21:16</note>: *As far as a bow can shoot.* Here the noun is used in the plural for "shots" or "strikes." From this also comes *tohoth*, meaning "intentions."

**טחן** <term>Tachan: He ground [at a mill].</term> <note>Numbers 11:8</note> *He crushed it with a millstone.* And in <note>Judges 16:21</note>: *And they made him grind while shut in the prison.* Here a verbal noun is used, which the <term>Hebrew Truth</term> <note>original: "veritas hebraica" — a common Renaissance term for the original Hebrew text of the Bible</note> reads as: *And he was a grinder [or miller] in the house of the prisoners.* Also in <note>Ecclesiastes 12:3</note>: *And the grinders shall be idle.* This is more correctly said of the stones themselves: *And the millstones shall be vacant.* In the same chapter <note>Ecclesiastes 12:4</note>: *In the lowliness of the voice of the mill.* Because male and female servants were put into the mill-house to grind perpetually, the word is used metaphorically for serving or "beating." <note>Job 31:10</note> *Let my wife be another man's harlot.* Word for word, following the image of a pounding mill, this is translated: *Let my wife grind for [or serve] another.* It is used here in a passive sense, as if Job were saying: "let her be threshed by another," that is, "let her be sexually handled by others."

**טחור** <term>Tachor: An infirmity of the anus which they call 'figs.'</term> <note>Hemorrhoids</note> Our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> describes this disease circuitously in <note>1 Samuel 5:6</note>: *And their protruding secret parts rotted.* And further on: *They were struck in the more secret part of the buttocks.*

**טוטפת** <term>Totafot: A frontal ornament.</term> This is what the Jews place on their heads in the place of a crown so they may be reminded of God's precepts. Concerning these kinds of ornaments, it is written in <note>Deuteronomy 6:8</note>: *And they shall be and shall move between your eyes.* In the Chaldaic <note>Aramaic</note> language they are called *tefillin*, a name now in more daily use among the Hebrews than the other. They have a knot at the back of the head which forms the shape of a cross, because all the precepts of God are fulfilled in the Cross. As God says: *He who does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me.*

**Soil, mud, or mire.** <note>Hebrew: *ṭiṭ* (טִיט); original Latin: "Humus. lutum. cœnū."</note> As found in Psalm 69: "Deliver me out of the mire, so that I do not sink." And Habakkuk 2: "And heaps up thick clay against himself," where this name is composed of two roots.

**Threw or sent.** <note>Hebrew: *ṭil* (טִיל)</note> In Jonah 1: "But the Lord sent a great wind," and later, "Take me up and cast me into the sea," and again, "And they took up Jonah and cast him into the sea." From this comes the doubled form **threw away or carried off** <note>Hebrew: *ṭilṭel* (טִלְטֵל)</note>. Isaiah 22: "Behold, the Lord will cause you to be carried away, just as a rooster is carried away." <note>This verse is traditionally difficult to translate; the author follows a contemporary interpretation comparing the exile of a person to the way a bird is tossed.</note>

**Habitation, dwelling, or residence.** <note>Hebrew: *ṭir* (טִיר)</note> Psalm 69: "Let their habitation be desolate," which Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate.</note> translated as "their dwelling." In another way, Rabbi David Kimhi <note>A famous 12th-century Jewish grammarian and commentator, often called the Radak.</note> says in his *Book of Roots* that it signifies planks or walls. He cites Song of Songs 8: "If she is a wall, we will build upon it silver planks," which we read as "we will build upon it silver battlements." Others think this word is derived from the term for "order," <note>Hebrew: *ṭur* (טוּר)</note> because of the squareness and order of the stones with which stone planks are constructed.

**Covered or roofed.** <note>Hebrew: *ṭalal* (טָלַל)</note> Nehemiah 3: "He built it and covered it." From this, those living under the shade of a tree are said to be covered by the tree, as in Daniel 4: "The beasts of the field dwelt under it," meaning they were covered and sheltered beneath it.

**Dew.** <note>Hebrew: *ṭal* (טַל)</note> Song of Songs 5: "For my head is filled with dew."

**Spotted or speckled.** <note>Hebrew: *ṭalu'a* (טָלוּא)</note> Genesis 30: "Whatever is reddish and spotted or variegated, among the sheep as well as the goats, shall be my wages." For this reason, regarding what is read in Ezekiel 16, "You made for yourself high places patched together here and there," Symmachus <note>An early translator of the Old Testament into Greek.</note> more correctly interprets this as "multicolored high places"—that is, idols. They are said to be "patched together" from various colors, just as when old things are mended with new pieces. So also in Joshua 9: "And wine skins, torn and mended," meaning they were of many colors or patched.

**Lamb.** <note>Hebrew: *ṭaleh* (טָלֶה)</note> Isaiah 65: "The wolf and the lamb shall feed together." The Hebrew commentators explain this as a reference to peace, similar to what is read in Isaiah 11: "The wolf shall dwell with the lamb." Jonathan <note>Referring to the Targum of Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> interpreted both passages with a similar word in Chaldaic <note>Aramaic</note>. The grammarians say the final letter *he* is not a mark of gender, but part of the substance of the word itself, created by a change from the letter *aleph*.

This is explained by David Kimhi <note>A famous medieval Jewish grammarian and commentator</note>: *According to a small measure you have measured my days, because a thousand years in your eyes are like yesterday.* And Lamentations 2: *Little ones to the measure of a palm.* From this comes the verb "measured," "increased," and "reared." In the same passage of Lamentations as above: *Those whom I reared and nourished.*
<term>מטפחת</term> <note>Mitpachat</note> A woman’s garment, which we in Latin call a *plaga* <note>wrap</note> or *rica* <note>ritual veil</note>. It is the linen cloth with which women cover themselves, which Jerome translated as a "cloak" <note>original: "pallium"</note> in Ruth 3: *Spread out,* he said, *your cloak with which you are covered.* But he also translates it as "linens" in Isaiah 3: *And the linens, and the needles, and the mirrors,* similar to a towel or napkin. Many explain it this way: A veil or a mantle.
<term>טפל</term> <note>Taphal</note> Composed, joined, or fastened. Although our common translation <note>the Vulgate</note> reads "multiplied" in Psalm 119: *The iniquity of the proud has been multiplied over me.* Regarding this, our Jerome, in his Psalter translated from the "Hebrew Truth," more correctly reads: *The proud were applying a lie to me,* that is, they composed a falsehood against me. According to Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the preeminent medieval commentator</note>, "fabricators" should be read instead of "composers"...

**טפסר** <term>Taphsar: Prefect, prince, or governor.</term> **Jeremiah 51:27**: "Appoint a captain against her," which our <note>The author refers to Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349), a Franciscan teacher whose literal commentary on the Bible was highly influential.</note> Lyra explains as "an army." But <note>Paul of Burgos (c. 1351–1435), a Jewish convert to Christianity and a noted Hebraist who often critiqued Lyra’s work.</note> Paul of Burgos, who was far more learned in the Hebrew language than he, translated it much more correctly as "leader and captain." Thus, by changing the <term>vowel point</term> from *hirek* to *patha*, it signifies the same in **Nahum 3:17**: "And your prefects are like locusts upon locusts." Perhaps because of carelessness and negligence, our translator interpreted this as "little ones" due to the similarity to the word *taph* <note>original: "thaph," referring to the Hebrew word for children or little ones.</note>, which we discussed above.

**טפש** <term>Taphash: To thicken, to dull, or to blunt.</term> For which our common translation reads "curdled." **Psalm 119:70**: "Their heart is curdled like milk." But <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate.</note> Jerome says better: "Their heart is thickened like fat."

**טרד** <term>Tarad: To be assiduous, to continue, or to perpetuate.</term> **Proverbs 27:15**: "A leaking roof on a cold day," for which the Hebrews read: "A heavy, assiduous, and continuous downpour or dripping on a day of impetuous rain." Hence, they are accustomed to name an assiduous laborer or a diligent head of a household *tarda* <note>original: "טרדא"</note> in his perpetual constancy.

**טרה** <term>Tarah: To rot.</term> From this comes *tariyah* <note>original: "טריה"</note>: rotten, poisonous, and that which wastes away with the stench of the ground. **Judges 15:15**: "Seizing a jawbone of an ass that was lying there," he meant to say, of course, "that was rotting."

**טרח** <term>Tarach: To labor to the point of exhaustion.</term> From this is that which is read in **Deuteronomy 1:12**: "Your business, your weight, and your quarrels," as if he were saying, "your labor and exhaustion."

**טרם** <term>Terem: Before.</term> **Genesis 2:5**: "Before it sprang up in the earth." And **Isaiah 65:24**: "And it shall be that before they call, I will hear."

**טרף** <term>Taraph: To tear, to seize, to snatch, or to plunder.</term> **Deuteronomy 33:20**: "And he seized the arm and the crown of the head." And **Psalm 7:2**: "Lest at any time he seize my soul like a lion." And **Genesis 37:33**: "Tearing, he has torn Joseph," for which we read: "A beast has devoured Joseph." From this comes the noun *terefah* <note>original: "טרפה"</note>: torn prey, a capture, or plunder; which Jerome translated as "captured by a beast." **Leviticus 22:8**: "That which dies of itself or is captured by a beast they shall not eat." This is found elsewhere without the final aspiration, written with six points <note>referring to Hebrew vowel pointing</note>. **Genesis 49:9**: "From the prey, my son, you have gone up."

**טרף** <term>Tereph: A sprout or a branch torn from the trunk.</term> **Ezekiel 17:9**: "And it shall wither all the shoots of its growth."

And as we wrote under the letter *He* <note>referring to a previous section of this dictionary</note>, by the exchange of the letter *Yod* for *He*, it is read similarly; hence it is thought that the word signifying praise and confession arises from this root: as in Psalm 136: "Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good," and Genesis 49: "Judah, your brothers shall praise you."

**<term>Yada‘</term>** <note>Hebrew: ידע</note> He knew; he perceived. 1 Samuel 3: "Now Samuel did not yet know the Lord." Genesis 4: "And Adam knew his wife." Psalm 76: "In Judah God is known." ->**BOOK ONE**<-

**יום [Yom] Day.** <note>original: "Dies"</note> This term is sometimes found referring to the "artificial day" during which the sun shines above our horizon, as in Genesis 1: *And God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night.* At other times, it refers to the "natural day" of twenty-four hours, as in the following passage: *And the evening and the morning were the first day.* Sometimes the final letter *Mem* is doubled, and it is pronounced *Yomam*, as in Psalm 1: *And in his law he shall meditate day and night.* Sometimes a *Yod* is placed between two *Mems*, and it is pronounced as the three-syllable *Yomaim*, which signifies two days or a "two-day period." Sometimes it is pronounced in the plural as *Yomim* (two syllables), meaning "many days." Often, the letter *Vav* is removed through <term>syncope</term> <note>the loss of a sound or letter from the middle of a word</note>, as in Genesis 3: *And you shall eat of the earth all the days of your life.*

**יון [Yaven] Mud**, mire, filth, or dung. <note>original: "Lutum, coenum, stercus"</note> As in Psalm 40: *And from the dregs of the mud.* Jerome, in his Psalter translated from the "Hebrew Verity," <note>Jerome’s "Hebraica Veritas" refers to his effort to translate the Old Testament directly from Hebrew rather than the Greek Septuagint</note> translated this more accurately as *from the mud of the mire.*

**יונה [Yonah] Dove.** <note>original: "Columbus"</note> The feminine form *Yonah* is commonly used, as in Genesis 8: *And he sent out a dove, which did not return.* In the plural, however, it is declined in the masculine, as in the first chapter of the Song of Songs: *Your eyes are those of doves.*

**יון [Yavan] Greece.** <note>original: "Grecia"</note> So named after the Ionians. As in Isaiah 66: *Into Italy and Greece, to the distant islands.* Jonathan the Chaldean <note>Referring to the Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary</note> uses this as a name for a specific region. Jerome, in his book of *Hebrew Questions*, says: *Javan refers to the Ionians, who are also the Greeks, which is where the Ionian Sea gets its name.*

**יזם [Yazam] Thought** or considered. <note>original: "Cogitauit, considerauit"</note> As in Genesis 11: *Neither will they desist from their thoughts.* It is more correctly translated as: *And now nothing will be restrained from them which they have imagined to do.* This is also how Onkelos <note>The author of the Targum Onkelos, the primary Aramaic translation of the Torah</note> explains it. This word is one and the same as the root *Z-M-M* [זמם].

**זמם [Zamam] Armed**, adorned, or prepared. <note>original: "Armauit, phalerauit, apparauit"</note> As in Jeremiah 5: *They were as fed horses in the morning, everyone neighing after his neighbor's wife.* Regarding this, the Hebrews read: *Horses armed with reins, adorned or prepared, and driven.* Rabbi Jacob ben Eleazar derives this word from *mazon*, meaning nourishment—as if to say "well-fed horses." Others derive it from the "reins" or "bridle" mentioned by Jerome in 1 Kings 22: *And they washed the reins according to the word of the Lord.*

**יזע [Yeza] Sweat.** <note>original: "Sudor"</note> Used metaphorically for labor. As in Ezekiel 44: *And they shall not gird themselves with anything that causes sweat.* From this, by <term>metathesis</term> <note>the transposition of sounds or letters in a word</note>, comes *Zeah* [זעה], meaning sweat, which also often lacks the letter *Yod*, as in Genesis 3: *In the sweat of your face.*

**יחד [Yachad] Together** or as one. <note>original: "Simul, in unum"</note> As in Psalm 49: *The rich and the poor together.* It sometimes receives a <term>paragoge</term> <note>an extra letter added to the end of a word for emphasis or grammatical form</note> as if indicating a plurality, *Yachdau* [יחדיו], as in Jeremiah 31: *The young men and...*

...old men together. <note>original: "senes simul"</note> It seems to many that this word is derived from **Echad** <note>Hebrew: אחד; original: "vnus"</note>, which signifies "one," about which we spoke above. From there comes **Yachid** <note>Hebrew: יחיד</note>, meaning unique or "only one." In Psalm 25: "Because I am unique and poor."

**Yachal** <note>Hebrew: יחל</note> — He waited. Genesis 8: "He waited moreover yet another seven days." And below: "And he stayed nonetheless yet other seven days." Its passive form takes the letter "vau" <note>the Hebrew letter Vav</note> in the first syllable: **Vayichal** <note>Hebrew: ויוחל</note> in Ezekiel 19: "When she saw that she was weakened and her expectation <term>hope</term> had perished." For which the <term>Idonei</term> <note>Literally "the fit ones," likely referring to the Septuagint translators or a specific scholarly tradition</note> read: "And he saw that as he waited, the hope of himself perished." This passage Rabbi David Kimhi <note>A celebrated 12th-13th century Jewish grammarian and commentator from Narbonne</note> explains thus: "When he now stood for many days in expectation, behold, the hope of himself perished"—this refers to the hope that was held concerning him. From here comes the intensive verb <term>original: "verbũ graue"; refers to the Hiphil or "heavy" Hebrew verb stem</term> **Hochal** <note>Hebrew: הוחל</note> in Psalm 130, regarding that which we read: "My soul has sustained in his word; my soul has hoped in the Lord." More correctly, the Hebrew truth <note>original: "hebraica veritas"; a scholarly term for the original Hebrew text</note> has it: "My soul sustained, and for his word I have waited." For what is read in Jeremiah 4—"My belly, my belly, I am in pain"—is not from this root, but is derived from the word **Chyl** <note>Hebrew: חיל</note>, which refers to trembling or writhing, of which we spoke above.

**Yacham** <note>Hebrew: יחם</note> — He warmed, and metaphorically, he conceived. Ecclesiastes 4 <note>The text cites Chapter 2, but the quote is from 4:11</note>: "How can one be warm?" Genesis 30: "And they should conceive in their sight." Likewise: "so that in their contemplation they might conceive." And above, according to the Hebrew truth: "And the sheep conceived before the rods." And Psalm 51: "Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins did my mother conceive me," although Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate</note> in his Psalter translates it as: "my mother gave birth to me."

**Yachaph** <note>Hebrew: יחף</note> — Barefoot. Isaiah 20: "And he did so, walking naked and barefoot."

**Yachash** <note>Hebrew: יחש</note> — Distinguished, noble, or of high birth; so called from lineage, nobility, and distinguished ancestry. 1 Chronicles 4: "This is their habitation and the distribution of their seats." For which the Hebrew truth reads: "These are their seats and their nobility <note>or "genealogy"</note> to them." Likewise in chapter 5 of the same book: "And he was not reckoned in the first-born." For which the Hebrew truth reads: "And not the nobility <term>genealogy</term> for the first-born."

**Yatab** <note>Hebrew: יטב</note> — It pleased. 2 Kings 3: "And all that the king did pleased them." And Joshua 22: "And the word pleased all those who heard it." And some wish for this verb to be deduced from **Tob** <note>Hebrew: טוב</note>, which signifies "good," as if everything that appears good should please. But the grammarians write that this word itself is among the first...

### FIRST BOOK

The Chaldean <note>Refers to the Aramaic Targum, a translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible.</note> explains it: "destroying him in a pleasing destruction."

**Wine** <note>original: "יַיִן" (yayin)</note>. Numbers 15: "And wine for a drink offering," and further down: "And wine for libations to be poured." In the plural number, it is declined as a feminine noun.

**He rebuked** <note>original: "יָכַח" (yakach)</note>, or corrected. Genesis 31: "God looked and rebuked [him] yesterday." And Psalm 50: "I will rebuke you and set [it] before your face." And Proverbs 28: "He who rebukes a man will afterward find favor."

**He was able** <note>original: "יָכֹל" (yakal)</note>. Genesis 45: "Joseph could no longer restrain himself." And Numbers 14: "Because we shall be able to overcome it." From this, the Hebrew masters <note>scholars and grammarians</note> name the course of water flowing quickly in a channel, which can be forded, a <term>brook</term> <note>original: "מִיכָל" (mikhal)</note>, though by a very strained derivation; for it has no other word similar to it. It is placed in 2 Samuel 17 <note>original: "ii. Regum." In the Latin Vulgate, 1 & 2 Samuel were titled 1 & 2 Kings.</note>, where our translation used a peculiar <term>circumlocution</term> <note>a roundabout way of speaking</note>, saying: "they crossed over quickly, having tasted a little water." The <term>Hebrew truth</term> <note>original: "hebraica ueritas," a term used by scholars like Jerome to refer to the original Hebrew text</note> reads it thus: "they crossed the ford of the water or the river." This is supported by Jonathan the Chaldean <note>The Targum of Jonathan ben Uzziel</note>, who explains this passage simply in the Aramaic language as: "they crossed the Jordan."

**He shook** <note>original: "יָכַת" (yakat)</note>, broke into pieces, or demolished. Numbers 14: "Striking them and breaking them in pieces." To this, Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval French rabbi and commentator.</note> cites its first-person form from Deuteronomy 9: "And breaking it all into pieces, reducing it even to dust." Onkelos the Chaldean <note>Author of the Targum Onkelos</note> alludes to this, explaining this word in Aramaic as "he grew weary."

**A cry of pain** <note>original: "יָלַל" (yalal)</note>, a shout, wailing, or howling. Our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> rendered it as "horror" in Deuteronomy 32: "In a place of horror and vast solitude." In Zephaniah 1: "A voice of crying from the Fish Gate and a howling from the Second Quarter." From this root, a gerund form is also found through the <term>aphesis</term> <note>the loss of a short unaccented vowel or letter at the beginning of a word</note> of the letter *yod* [ללת] and the lack of one *lamed*; for it should properly be written with three *l*'s, but one is dropped for the sake of <term>euphony</term> <note>the quality of being pleasing to the ear</note>. In 1 Samuel 4: "she was pregnant and near to giving birth," which many Hebrew masters like Moses, the brother of Kihi <note>Likely referring to the Kimhi family of grammarians</note>, and others interpret with this meaning: "And his daughter-in-law, the wife of Phinehas, being pregnant, was wailing." They explain this as the days of pain and crying for the birth approaching. Others, however, with whom our [Latin] translation agrees, think it is placed there through the <term>syncope</term> <note>the omission of sounds or letters from the middle of a word</note> of the letter *daleth*. This is supported by the translation of Jonathan, who says: "the wife of Phinehas, pressing on to give birth." Zechariah 11: "Howl, fir tree; howl, oaks of Bashan," and further: "A voice of the howling of shepherds," not as the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> translated: "A voice of the mourning of shepherds."

**ילק** <note>Hebrew: *yelek*</note> **A type of locust,** which our translation <note>Referring to the Latin Vulgate.</note> renders as a **cankerworm**. <note>original: *bruchum*</note> **Nahum** [chapter 3]: "The **cankerworm** has spread its wings and flown away." For from the location of Jerusalem, this Great Sea [is the west].

**ימין** <note>Hebrew: *Yamin*</note> The right hand. Genesis 24: "Whether I go to the right or to the left."
