**יונק** <term>Yoneq: to suckle or a nursing child</term> refers to milk, as in Isaiah 11: "The infant shall play by the breast." From this come the terms for **sucklings** and **nurses**, according to various grammatical forms. Because of their tenderness, we also call young plants by this name. Job 15: "The flame shall dry up his branches," which the Hebrew scholars explain as: "the flame will dry up the root that sucks up moisture."

**יסד** <term>Yasad: he founded</term>. Psalm 103 <note>Protestant Psalm 104:5</note>: "He founded the earth upon its own stability," and later: "In the place which you have founded for them." From this comes the adjective in Isaiah 28: "Behold, I lay a stone in Zion, a tested stone, a precious corner stone, a **foundation well-founded**." In that passage, the word is placed twice: *musad* <note>original: מוסד</note> first as a noun, then as a participle. However, we usually read: "Behold, I will send in the foundations, etc." From this comes the passive verb *nosad* <note>original: נוסד</note>, meaning it was **founded**, **strengthened**, or **established**. Psalm 2: "The kings of the earth stood up and the princes were **established and founded** together," where we usually read: "and the princes convened as one." Others interpret this as "they took counsel" from *sod* <note>original: סוד</note>, meaning a secret council; hence, Jerome in his translation of the Psalter used the term "they discussed."

**יסך** <term>Yasak: he poured, smeared, or anointed</term>. Exodus 30: "The flesh of man shall not be anointed with it."

**יסף** <term>Yasaf: he gathered, added, or increased</term>. Genesis 38: "And he **did not add** further to know her," <note>Referring to Judah and Tamar</note> whereas we read: "nevertheless, he did not know her again." It also takes the letter *vav* <note>a Hebrew prefix meaning 'and'</note> as in Genesis 30: "The Lord added to me another son." Sometimes it even takes the letter *aleph* instead of *vav*, as in Exodus 4: "And they gathered all the elders of the children of Israel," and Isaiah 8: "And the Lord added to speak to me."

**יסר** <term>Yasar: he instructed or disciplined</term>. Proverbs 9: "He who instructs a mocker." Hosea 7: "And I instructed." From this comes *musar* <note>original: מוסר</note>, meaning **instruction** or **discipline**, as both are evident in Proverbs 1: "To know wisdom and discipline, to receive the instruction of doctrine." It is also used to mean **chastisement** and **correction**, as in Jeremiah 31: "You have chastised me, O Lord, and I was instructed."

**יעד** <term>Ya'ad: he met, appointed, covenanted, testified, promised, or betrothed</term>. Exodus 21: "But if he has betrothed her to his son," and a little earlier: "whom he did not betroth," for which we read: "to whom she was not delivered." The passive form is found in Exodus 25, where we have: "From there I will command and speak to you," but the Hebrew reads: "And I will **testify** to you there and speak with you." From this derivation come **pacts**, **appointments**, **treaties**, and **solemnities**.

# THE FIRST BOOK

**יעה** He cleaned or purified. <note>original: "Purgauit, depurauit"</note> Our translation <note>The "translation" refers to the Latin Vulgate Bible, the standard version used in the West for centuries.</note> interprets this as "overthrew."
**Isaiah 28[:17]**: *And hail shall sweep away the hope of lies.* The Hebrews explain it this way: *And hail—that is, the enemy—shall clean, remove, and take away the protection of lies.* From this comes **יעי**, meaning the "shovels" or "brooms" with which houses are cleaned and impurities are removed. These are sometimes made from the feathered wings of geese, and sometimes from pig bristles bound together into a single bundle. The translation we read renders this as "three-pronged forks" or "hooks."
**Numbers 4[:14]**: *All the vessels used in its ministry, that is, the fire-receptacles, the flesh-hooks, the three-pronged forks, and the shovels.* <note>The author is comparing how the same Hebrew root for "cleaning" or "sweeping" is applied to different temple tools.</note>

**יער** <note>The author identifies this as meaning "Barbarous," though it is likely a variation of related roots.</note> Barbarous, dull, strong, brutish. It is as if by <term>metathesis</term> <note>Metathesis is a linguistic term for when sounds or letters in a word are rearranged.</note> it comes from **ערי**, where the letter *yod* is added, meaning "vigor" or "strength."
**Isaiah 12[:2]**: *Because the Lord is my strength and my praise.* Thus, they called strong and stout men "barbarous" and "ignorant," according to the common proverb: *Rarely are short men humble; rarely are tall men wise.* From this comes **לעז**, meaning "ignorant" or "barbarous."
**Isaiah 33[:19]**: *You shall not see an ignorant people,* that is, a people of a foreign tongue and barbarous. Because of the easy transition between the letters *nun* and *lamed*, we say it has the same meaning in:
**Psalm 114[:1]**: *When Israel went out of Egypt, the house of Jacob from a barbarous people.*

**עטה** He wrapped or clothed. As in **Psalm 104[:2]**: *Wrapped in light as with a garment,* that is, "Putting on light like a clothing." This is indeed the more correct way to translate it. And in **Isaiah 59[:17]**: *He was covered as if with a cloak of zeal.* I would read it as: "He covered or clothed himself with zeal as if with a cloak."

**יעל** He helped or profited.
**Habakkuk 2[:18]**: *What does the carved image profit, because its maker has carved it?* And **Isaiah 30[:5]**: *Who could not profit them, they were of no help.*

**יען** Because, for that reason, on account of, instead of. As in **Leviticus 26[:43]**: *Because they rejected my judgments.* In that passage, the Hebrew text places the same word twice because of the intensity of the threats, as if to say, "specifically and in return for the fact that they rejected my judgments."

**יענה** and **יען** The Ostrich <note>original: "Struthio"</note> in the feminine gender.
**Leviticus 11[:16]**: *The ostrich, and the owl, and the gull.*
**Isaiah 13[:21]**: *And ostriches shall dwell there.*
In the masculine gender, in **Lamentations 4[:3]**: *Like the ostriches in the desert.*

**עיף** <note>original: "Ayaph"</note> **He failed, grew weary, was tired, or was exhausted.** Habakkuk 2: *And the nations shall fail in vanity* <note>original: "Et gentes in vacuum deficient"</note>—used here in place of "they have failed." And Isaiah 40: *And they shall not fail nor labor.* Also: *He who gives power to the weary.* And in the same chapter: *The youths shall fail and be weary.* From this comes the adjective "tired." 2 Samuel 16: *Wine for any who fail on the road to drink,* which reads word-for-word as: *And wine for the tired man in the desert to drink.* From this, they consider the saying in Daniel 9: *Behold the man Gabriel, whom I had seen in the vision at the beginning, flying swiftly, touched me.* In this passage, certain teachers have translated the Hebrew phrase <gloss>מועף ביעף — mu’aph bi’aph</gloss> according to our Latin translation as "flying with flight," as if to say "flying quickly." They do not derive this from our present word, but from **עוף** <note>original: "uph"</note>, that is, "to fly," which is discussed further down under its own letter. This is the opinion held by **Rabbi David Kimhi** in his *Book of Roots*, where he explains the passage: *Gabriel, whom I saw in the vision at the beginning when he was flying from above, then I saw that he was approaching me.* But **Rabbi Levi ben Gershom**—who, according to the testimony of **Paul of Burgos** in his *Examination*, is commonly called **Master Leo de Banolis** <note>A renowned 14th-century philosopher and astronomer also known as Gersonides</note>—interprets these words of Daniel in his commentaries on the same prophet as being expressly derived from our present word: *Gabriel, whom I had seen from the beginning, reached me wearied with fatigue.* If we were to follow both opinions, we would say: *Gabriel touched me, either exhausted from flying or flying with fatigue.*

**תועפות** <note>original: "To'aphot"</note> **Might or strength.** Numbers 23: *Whose strength is like that of a rhinoceros*—or a unicorn.

**יעץ** <note>original: "Ya'atz"</note> **He decreed, thought, concluded by consultation, or established.** Isaiah 23: *Who has planned this against Tyre?* and later: *The Lord of hosts has purposed this.* And in chapter 14: *The Lord of hosts has decreed,* and earlier: *This is the counsel that I have thought over all the earth.* From this comes **Counselor**, one who has the authority to issue a decree and interpose their influence in a council, much like the two **Consuls** of the Romans. Isaiah 9: *Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God.* In legal terms, such a person is called a <term>silentiarius</term> <note>A high-ranking court official in the late Roman/Byzantine Empire trusted with the most private matters</note>, to whom the highest secrets are entrusted. Because of this, the most ancient of the Hebrew sages forbade passing on the secrets of the Law except to a <gloss>ליועץ חכם — l'yoetz hacham</gloss>, that is, a **wise counselor**. From this also comes "counsel." Psalm 1: *Blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the ungodly.* <note>The author notes a grammatical "apheresis of the letter Iod" here.</note>

**יער** [Ya’ar] — **Honeycomb.** <note>In Hebrew, this word can mean both a forest and a honeycomb.</note> [Song of] Songs, 5: "I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey."

**יפה** [Ya-fah] — This means **to be made beautiful** or **to become beautiful**. As in [Song of] Songs, 7: "How beautiful are your steps," where if the Latin usage allowed, it should have been read: "how much your movements have become beautiful." Also in the same book: "how beautiful you are and graceful." Its passive form is used in Ezekiel 31: "He was most beautiful in his greatness," <note>original: "Erat pulcherrimus in magnitudine sua"</note> meaning "he was made" or "he became" beautiful. This word is found doubled to signify excellent beauty: Psalm 45: "Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men," meaning "you were very, very beautiful." It is also found in a shortened form <term>apocope|the loss of one or more sounds or letters from the end of a word</term> in Ezekiel 28: "Upon the beauty of your wisdom."

**יפח** [Ya-pach] — **He meditated within himself**, and arranged within himself, or established and ordered with himself. I find various translations for this. Jerome, <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible</note> in Habakkuk chapter 2, says "it appeared," for so we read: "And it will appear in the end and will not lie." There, the <term>Septuagint|the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, often abbreviated as LXX</term> translated it as: "And it will rise in the end." Many others translate it as: "And it will speak at the end." For so the most learned grammarian **Rabbi David Kimchi** <note>A famous medieval Jewish commentator and grammarian (1160–1235), also known as Radak</note> explains it in his commentaries on the Twelve [Minor Prophets]. And the same author suggests in his *Book of Roots* that this word signifies meditating on something within oneself, and preparing or arranging it with oneself by whispering or murmuring. The <term>Chaldean translation|The Targum, an Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</term> of Jonathan agrees with this. From this comes what we read in Psalm 12: "I will act confidently in it." Also what they translated in Proverbs 14: "A deceitful witness brings forth a lie," where it is everywhere explained by the Hebrews as "he speaks" or "he said."

**יפע** [Ya-pha] — **He illuminated**, clarified, or purified. From this, with the letter *he* [ה] or *tav* [ת] added at the end, comes: **illumination, appearance, beauty, or purity.** Ezekiel 28: "And they shall defile your beauty." And Deuteronomy 33 uses a derived word: "He appeared from Mount Paran," which Onkelos <note>The reputed author of the famous Aramaic translation of the Torah</note> explains in Chaldean as: "He appeared in majesty upon Mount Paran." In another place, our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note>—I do not know why—translated it as "helped." Job 10: "And you help the counsel of the wicked," which the Hebrews say means "you illuminate."

**יפת** [Ya-phat] — With the prefix *mem* and the vowel *holem* [forming *Mofet*]: **a sign of some future thing** which we call a **portent** or **prodigy**. Psalm 71: "I have become as a portent to many." And Deuteronomy 6: "And he performed signs and great portents," in the masculine gender.

"The expectation of the nations," <note>original: *yakehat* (יקהת); a word from Jacob's blessing of Judah in Genesis 49:10</note> that is, "expectation." # BOOK

Regarding that passage in Psalm 130: *For with you is forgiveness, and because of your law* <note>original: "Quia apud te propiciatio est et propter legem tuam." This is the Vulgate version of Psalm 130:4.</note>. Concerning this, Jerome, in his Psalter according to the Hebrew truth <note>Jerome’s "Hebraica Veritas" was his effort to translate the Old Testament directly from Hebrew rather than the Greek Septuagint.</note>, writes: *with you is forgiveness because you are awesome.* A disagreement among translations occurs in this place because of this word: **תורה** <note>T-W-R-H</note>. If it is viewed written without vowel points, it can be read as *Torah*, which signifies **Law**. If, however, it is pointed as it ought to be—namely with the vowels *hiric*, *qamets*, and *tsere*—it signifies our word **that you may be feared** <note>The author is discussing the Hebrew root Y-R-A (to fear) versus the word Torah (Law). Modern scholarship reads the verse as "that you may be feared."</note>. Thus the reading should be: *For with you is forgiveness, so that you may be feared.* 

It is possible, therefore, that the seventy interpreters <note>The "LXX" or Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> were negligent regarding that word, translating the Hebrew term *Torah* into the Greek tongue as *nomon* (that is, **law**) instead of the word *onoma* (that is, **name**) <note>The author is suggesting a scribal confusion between the Greek words for 'law' and 'name'.</note>. For it is now commonly read in Greek: *Because of your name I have waited for you, O Lord.* In this, a double error of both <note>Likely referring to the Septuagint and the older Latin translations based on it.</note> is discovered. The truth of the matter, however, is this: *because with you is forgiveness, so that you may be feared.* All the Hebrews read it this way. This is testified to, following his own Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note>, by our Lyra <note>Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349), a Franciscan whose influential Bible commentaries relied heavily on Jewish interpretation.</note> and Paul of Burgos <note>A Jewish convert to Christianity (c. 1351–1435) who wrote "Additions" to Lyra’s work.</note>. Jerome’s aforementioned translation also agrees. The writers and commentators of that passage explain it thus: Joseph Kimhi, Abraham ibn Ezra, and Solomon the Gaul <note>Another name for Rashi.</note>.

**נורא** <note>N-W-R-A</note> **Distant.** In Isaiah 21, where we have *from a horrible land*. The Jewish masters read it as *from a distant land*, namely that of the Medes and Persians, according to the opinion of Rabbi Jonah <note>Jonah ibn Janah, a famous 11th-century Hebrew grammarian.</note>. This is because men are accustomed to fear things that are foreign and distant when they do not know their manners and customs; for this reason, another translation has *from a hostile land*. For whatever is usually derived from that root signifies **terror**, **trembling**, **fear**, and **horror**.

**ירד** <note>Y-R-D</note> **He descended.** In Exodus 19: *Because the Lord had descended upon it.* It is also found sometimes with the <term>aphaeresis</term> <note>The loss of a letter or sound at the beginning of a word.</note> of the letter *yod*, as in Judges 19, where instead of what we read as *and the day was changing into night*, the Hebrew truth has: *And the day had descended greatly.* Rabbi David <note>David Kimhi, also known as Radak (1160–1235).</note> explains this in his commentaries on the four <note>Likely referring to the "Earlier Prophets" (Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings).</note> as: *it had descended toward evening.* From this comes a second, transitive verb, which our scholars translate as **to lead down** or **to humble**. In Lamentations 2: *Let tears run down like a torrent* (that is, make them descend). From this, some think the word **מורד** <note>M-W-R-D</note> is derived, meaning **projecting**, **hanging down**, or as if **sloping**. In 1 Kings 7: *Like wreaths of brass hanging down*, which they explain as stretched out or expanded.

**ירה** <note>Y-R-H</note> **He sent** or **threw.** Exodus 15: *Pharaoh’s chariots and his army...*

<term>ירך</term> **Thigh** or **femur**. Genesis 32: "he touched the nerve of his thigh." And regarding Israel: "who withered in the thigh of Jacob." And in the same book, chapter 24: "Put your hand under my thigh." It is also used in the plural according to the masculine ending in Exodus, chapter 28: "From the loins even unto the thighs."

<term>ירך</term> **The base of a lampstand** or the **shaft** from which the branches of the lampstand proceed. Exodus 25: "Its shaft and its branches."

<term>ירך</term> and <term>ירכה</term> **Side**, **border**, or **region**. Leviticus 1: "At the side of the altar that looks toward the north," where it is placed in the masculine form. However, it also takes a feminine terminal letter with the same meaning, as in Genesis 49: "reaching even unto Sidon," where the original Hebrew text <note>original: "hebraica veritas," a common term for the Hebrew source text</note> has it: "and its side or region reaches even unto Sidon."

<term>ירע</term> **Exasperated**, **acted wickedly**, or **acted craftily and hatefully**. Deuteronomy 15: "Neither shall you act craftily in any way in relieving his needs." Isaiah 15: "Because of this the armed men of Moab shall wail, his soul shall wail to itself," where it signifies the cry and wailing of imminent sorrow for a man under two forms of spelling, both with the letter *yod* and without it. For thus Jonathan <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel, the purported author of the Aramaic Targum</note> translated it into Aramaic: "the armed men of Moab wail, wailing or crying out for his soul." We signify, therefore, by this word someone acting unwillingly and sighing with a broken, dismayed, somewhat sad, and embittered spirit.

<term>יריעה</term> **Veil**, **curtain**, or **covering**. And because curtains of this kind were sometimes accustomed to be made from skins, our translation <note>referring to the Latin Vulgate</note> often translated "skins" instead of "curtain" or "veil." As in Psalm 104: "Stretching out the heaven like a skin," where it would be more correctly said: "Stretching out the heaven like a curtain." And similarly in the Song of Songs 1: "As the skins of Solomon," that is, like the curtains of his bed. Otherwise and more truly, our translation has it in Exodus 26: "You shall make eleven curtains of goat hair," where the original Hebrew text reads: "And you shall make curtains or coverings of goats," that is, made of goat hair, for the tent over the tabernacle; "with eleven curtains you shall make them."

<term>ירק</term> **To spit**. Numbers 12: "If her father had but spit in her face." Similarly in Deuteronomy 25: "And she shall spit in his face."

<term>ירק</term> **Vegetable**, **green herb**, or **any sprouting thing**. Genesis 9: "Even as the green herbs have I delivered all things to you." And in 2 Kings 19: "As the green herb on the housetops." Similarly in Deuteronomy 11 we read where, after the seed is cast, the waters are said to be irrigated in the manner of gardens. But the original Hebrew text says: "where you shall sow your seed and shall water it in your turn as..." <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence.</note>

<meta>This page continues a Hebrew-Latin dictionary, likely focusing on roots starting with the letter Yod. The previous entry (partially visible) discussed the root for "green."</meta>

->FIRST<-

...as a garden of herbs. From this comes the adjective **green** or **flourishing**. Job 39: "And he searches out every **green thing**."

<term>Yerakrak</term> <note>original Hebrew: ירקרק</note> Discharge-colored, yellow, or whitish. Leviticus 13: "If it has been infected with a white or **reddish** spot." Because that yellowness tends somewhat toward the color of gold, they believe that from this is derived the term for the mildew of crops and vines, <term>Yerkon</term> <note>original Hebrew: ירקון</note>. Haggai 2: "With a scorching wind and with **mildew**." Similarly in Amos 4: "I struck you with a scorching wind and with **mildew**."

<term>Yarash</term> <note>original Hebrew: ירש</note> To **possess**, to **inherit**, or to acquire by succession. Jeremiah 49: "Are there no sons in Israel? Or has he no heir? Why then has Milcom **possessed** Gad by inheritance?" and a little later it follows: "And Israel shall **possess** those who possessed him." And 1 Chronicles 28: "That you may **possess** the good land." Numbers 13: "Let us go up and **possess** the land." Sometimes it is found with a missing *yod* at the beginning due to <term>catapheresis</term> <note>a grammatical term for the dropping of an initial letter</note>, as in 1 Kings 21: "Arise, **possess** the vineyard of Naboth." From this comes the verbal noun "inheritance." Psalm 61: "You have given an **inheritance** to those who fear your name." From this also comes a "heavy" <note>intensive or causative</note> verb which signifies to expel, to delete, to consume, or to devastate. Deuteronomy 4: "To **destroy** the nations." Job 13: "And you wish to **consume** me for the sins of my youth." and Numbers 14: "I will strike them with pestilence and **consume** them." From this comes the noun "possessor," one who possesses. At the end of Obadiah: "And the house of Jacob shall **possess** those who had possessed them," that is, their **possessors**, otherwise translated as "inheritances" or "heirs," which Saint Jerome indicates in his book of explanations on Obadiah with these words: "And the house of Jacob the supplanter shall **possess** those who had possessed them by **inheritance**." It also signifies in another way "to make poor." 1 Kings 2: "The Lord **makes poor** and makes rich." And Proverbs 30: "Lest, compelled by **poverty**, I steal," because it should be read, "Lest I be **made poor** and steal." From this comes **poor** and **poverty** when written without the *yod* at the beginning. Psalm 82: "Vindicate the humble and the **poor**."

<term>Yashish</term> <note>original Hebrew: ישש</note> An ancient man of many days. Job 15: "Both the gray-haired and the **aged** are among us," where the word is placed in the singular number in Hebrew. This word signifies "old" in a sense more than "aged" but less than "ancient," as if "long-lived." And it can arise from the word <term>Yesh</term> <note>original Hebrew: יש</note> which means "is" or "there is." Psalm 7: "If **there is** iniquity in my hands," as if it refers to that which "is" for a long time and lasts long.

**BOOK**

**ישב** <note>transliterated: *yashav*</note> **He sat.** He had a residence. That is to say, **he dwelt.** Genesis chapter thirteen: “Abram sat, or dwelt, in the land of Canaan.” And in the first Psalm: “And in the seat of scoffers he did not sit.” It is sometimes found through the dropping of the first letter <note>apheresis of the letter *yod*</note> or through a rearrangement of letters <note>metathesis</note>. From this root come transitive and intensive verb forms. Psalm 112 <note>Psalm 113 in modern bibles</note>: “Who makes the barren woman dwell in a house.” Ruth chapter 2: “And she did not return to the house even for a moment,” meaning she stayed put. Others interpret it this way: “She who dwells in a modest or small house.” For the same word is similarly interpreted as “dwelling” in Jeremiah chapter 9: “Your dwelling is in the midst of deceit,” as if to say one's **conduct** or way of life. This word is often confused with **שוב** <note>transliterated: *shuv*</note>, which will be placed further down and means **he returned.** Jeremiah 32: “And I will bring them back to this place and make them dwell in safety.”

**יש** <note>transliterated: *yesh*</note> **Is** or **There is.** It is found in a shortened form <note>through apocope, the loss of a final sound</note> in the Second Book of Kings chapter ten <note>2 Kings 10:15</note>: “Is your heart right?” and he answered, “It is.” From this comes **תושיה** <note>transliterated: *tushiyah*</note>, which I find translated in as many different ways as any other word. I am often persuaded that many previous interpreters were just as capable of error as we ourselves are. For our Latin translation reads “equity” in Proverbs chapter 8: “Counsel and equity are mine.” In another place, it is “salvation,” as in chapter 2 of the same book: “He will guard the salvation of the upright.” Likewise, in another place, it is “justice,” as in Isaiah chapter 28: “And he shall magnify justice,” which the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> rendered as “consolation.” But I would say this word properly signifies <term>energy</term> <note>original Greek: *energeia*</note> or **efficacy**—the power by which one drives a work toward actual existence. Our translation seems to hint at this through a roundabout description in Job chapter 5, when it says: “Lest their hands be unable to fulfill what they began,” instead of what the Hebrew actually reads: “And their hands will not perform **efficacy**.” <term>Jonathan the Chaldean</term> <note>referring to the Targum, an Aramaic paraphrase of the Bible attributed to Jonathan ben Uzziel</note> translates this as “wisdom” in Isaiah chapter 28, implying a **deliberation of the soul.** <term>Rabbi David Kimhi</term> <note>a famous 12th-century medieval Jewish scholar and grammarian</note> understands it this way in his commentaries on the twelve prophets regarding Micah chapter 6: “And there will be salvation for all who fear His name.” It is as if the prophet cried out in the city: “Who is the man of wisdom among them? He alone will fear your name in his heart.” For thus the Hebrew reads: “And of wisdom or deliberation,” which means, **a man of wisdom or of a deliberate mind shall fear your name.**

**ישח** <note>transliterated: *yashach*</note> **Humiliation.** A bending or a bowing down. Micah chapter 6: “And your humiliation is in your midst.” From this the verb is derived: **to humble** or **to bend down.**

<meta>This page continues a lexicon or theological dictionary of Hebrew terms, focusing on their etymological roots and how they have been translated into Latin and Greek. It specifically addresses the names of the Savior and the identification of precious stones in the Bible.</meta>

->**THE BOOK**<-

The Lord made his Christ. Whence in Psalm 118 <note>Original: ps.xviij. The text quoted, "Save us, O Lord," is actually from Psalm 118:25. The author may be using a different numbering system or there is a transcription error.</note> it is read: "O Lord, save me, I pray. O Lord, prosper me, I pray." In Hebrew, this is held as *hoshiah na* <note>original: הושיעה נא</note>. In place of this, in our own liturgical sacrifices, we pronounce "Hosanna," due to an ignorance of the holy language. From this also comes "savior." In the third chapter of Judges: "Afterward they cried out to the Lord, who raised up a savior for them." And in Nehemiah chapter 9: "You gave them saviors," in the plural number. And although the most sacred proper name of our Savior is derived from this root, because it takes on so many arrangements of letters, I shall rightly leave its judgment not to grammarians but to the most contemplative of men. I have discussed this at length in my *Capnion* <note>The author refers to Johann Reuchlin, the famous Hebrew scholar whose nickname was "Capnion," the Greek word for "smoke" (a pun on his German name Reuchlin/Rauch).</note>. Truly, this same name could have arisen from the substantive verb *yesh* <note>original: יש; meaning "there is" or "existence"</note>, because Christ Jesus said: "Before Abraham was, I am."

**Jasper** (*Yashepheh*) <note>original: ישפה</note>. Exodus 28. In the fourth row: chrysolite, onyx, and beryl. Where some have translated "jasper" in place of "beryl," for the sound of the word is similar. But our reading is supported by the Chaldean translation <note>The author refers to the Aramaic Targums, which were ancient translations and paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible.</note>; for in place of *yasep*, both Onkelos and Jonathan—both Chaldeans—translated it as *burla*, which our people think is beryl. Indeed, in every language there is such great error in the names of things that, in investigating them, many of the most diligent researchers of my time seem to me to have labored almost in vain. This is because every nation imposes new names on its things in every new age, and even the things themselves change every day along with their names. As Horace says in his *Art of Poetry*: "Thus the old age of words perishes. And many things will be reborn which have now fallen, and those now in honor shall fall." Unless this were the case, all of Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, author of *Natural History*, the Roman encyclopedia of the natural world.</note> would by now be perfectly understood. But even the seventy translators <term>Septuagint</term> and Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion disagree on this name, as Jerome testifies in his commentary on Ezekiel.

**To be Pleasing** (*Yashar*) <note>original: ישר</note>. It was pleasing; it was right. 1 Kings 18: "The word was pleasing in the eyes of David." From this comes the noun *yashar*, meaning "upright" or "right." In the last chapter of Judges: "Each man did what seemed right to himself." And with the <term>cataprothesin</term> <note>A grammatical term here likely referring to a prepositional prefix or a specific Hebrew grammatical construction.</note> of the letter *mem* in the first chapter of the Song of Songs: "The upright love you."

**Nail** (*Yated*) <note>original: יתד</note>. A nail or tent-peg. Judges 4: "And so Jael, the wife of Heber, took a nail." It is declined in the feminine gender in Exodus 27: "Both the pegs of the Tabernacle and of the courtyard."

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical or thematic exploration of Hebrew roots and their biblical applications, following a previous discussion of related linguistic terms. The focus here is on the roots Yatom (orphan) and Yatar (to remain/excel).</meta>

->FIRST<-

...for which the Hebrew is thus: *And all its pegs and all the pegs of the court were of bronze.* <note>original Latin: "Et omnes clauos eius et oēs clauos atrij eneos." This refers to the construction of the Tabernacle in the book of Exodus.</note>

**יתום [Yatom] Orphan.** Psalm 146: *The Lord protects the orphan and the widow.* And Lamentations 5: *We have become orphans without a father.* This is explained as follows: Even if our parents are still living, we have nonetheless become like orphans and wards. The Hebrews <note>The author frequently refers to "the Hebrews" to mean Jewish commentators or the Hebrew grammatical tradition.</note> derive this interpretation from the words that immediately follow: *and our mothers are as widows.* Not truly widows, but *as if* they were.

**יתר [Yatar] To excel; to abound; to remain; to surpass.** Proverbs 2: *And the simple shall remain in it,* for which the Hebrew reading is: *and the upright shall remain in it.* And in chapter 12 of the same book, in place of our version which says: *He who neglects a loss for a friend is just,* the <term>Hebrew Truth [Hebraica Veritas]: a term used by Renaissance scholars to refer to the original Hebrew text of the Bible as the ultimate authority</term> reads: *The just man surpasses his neighbor.* That is, the just man is more excellent and more highly praised than anyone else. One might then ask: Why then do not all follow the way of the just? The wise man answers in the words that follow: *Because the way of the wicked leads them astray.* It always signifies "above," "plus," or "more." For example, in Genesis 49: *The beginning of my sorrow, first in gifts, greatest in power.* <note>This is the blessing of Jacob to his eldest son, Reuben, in the Latin Vulgate translation.</note> In Hebrew, it is read: *The beginning of my strength, superior in offering, superior in strength.* Onkelos <term>Onkelos: the 2nd-century author of the most famous Aramaic translation (Targum) of the Torah</term> explains the sense of the passage rather than the literal word in <term>Chaldaic: an older term for the Aramaic language</term>. He says: *To you were owed three prerogatives: the birthright, the priesthood, and the kingdom.* From this root comes **יתרון [Yitron]**: Superfluity, excess, and abundance, or "more," "further," "greater." Ecclesiastes 3: *What more does a man have from all his labor?* And in chapter 12: *Beyond these, my son, do not seek.* From this also comes the "heavy" word: *Unstable as water, you shall not grow,* meaning you shall not be increased or made greater. There are many other derivations of various forms, such as in Leviticus 2: *And what is left over,* meaning that which remains.

**כאב (K-A-B)** He felt pain. Job 14: "But his flesh upon him shall have pain." From this comes the noun for "one who suffers." Psalm 69: "I am poor and sorrowful." And in Genesis 34, regarding what the Hebrews read as "while they were in pain," our translation uses a paraphrase <note>The translator refers to the "Latin Vulgate" or similar standard version that explains the physical state of the men after circumcision.</note> for when the pain of wounds is most severe. **כבל (K-B-L)** Detention, shackle, bond, or enclosure. Psalm 105: "They humbled his feet in shackles."

**Cabul** (כָּבוּל) <note>original Hebrew: *Kabul*</note> Holding fast, adhesive, muddy, or closed off. As found in 1 Kings 9: "And he called them the land of **Cabul**," meaning a sterile and uncultivated land, as if it were "closed up," where people neither pass through nor stay. Master Nahaman son of Isaac <note>likely referring to the medieval scholar Nachmanides</note> explains this as coming from the depth of the sand in which the feet of those walking are caught and fixed. This is cited by Rabbi David Kimhi <note>a famous medieval grammarian known as Radak</note> in his commentaries on Kings. Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note>, as witnessed by Lyra <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a Christian theologian</note>, believes the land was so named from the "binding" or "tying" of the feet.

**Kabas** (כָּבַס) He washed, dipped, or dyed. Genesis 49: "He washed his robe in wine." Similarly in Numbers 8: "And they shall wash their clothes," and Psalm 51: "Wash me more from my iniquity and cleanse me from my sin." From this comes the word for a <term>fuller</term> <note>a person who cleans and thickens raw wool cloth</note> in Isaiah 7: "In the way of the fuller’s field."

**Kova** (כּוֹבַע) A cap or helmet. Isaiah 59: "And a helmet of salvation on his head." And in 1 Samuel 17: "And he placed a bronze helmet upon his head." It is declined in the masculine gender in Jeremiah 46: "And stand in helmets."

**Kabbir** (כַּבִּיר) Manifold, strong, or great. Job 8: "And the manifold spirit is the speech of your mouth." From this is derived a verb for speaking weightily, as in Job 35: "And without knowledge he multiplies words," essentially meaning he "magnifies" them.

**Kebir** (כְּבִיר) A skin or hide. 1 Samuel 19: "And he placed a hairy goatskin at his head."

**Makber** (מַכְבֵּר) A coverlet, a thick garment, or a covering for beds. It is made from goat hair in the style of animal skins, from which it takes its name. 2 Kings 8: "And he took a coverlet and soaked it in water."

**Kebarah** (כְּבָרָה) A sieve. Amos 9: "As grain is shaken in a sieve."

**Kibrat** (כִּבְרַת) An acre, a <term>stadium</term> <note>an ancient Greek unit of distance, roughly 600 feet</note>, a mile, or a distance of space. Genesis 35: "He came in the springtime to the land which leads to Ephrathah." The <term>Hebrew truth</term> <note>original: "hebraica ueritas," a term used by scholars to refer to the original Hebrew text as the ultimate authority over translations</note> reads: "There was still a stadium of land to go to Ephrathah." Rabbi Solomon explains this using the previous entry, which signifies multitude and greatness, as if to say there had been a "manifold space" of land to reach Ephrathah.

Things that are to come have already been, which in Hebrew he expresses in the singular number.
**כבש** <note>Hebrew: *Kavash*</note> He subdued, he subjected, he brought under his control. From Zechariah chapter 9: *And they shall subdue with sling-stones.* This should be understood according to Rabbi Jonah <note>Rabbi Jonah ibn Janah, an influential 11th-century Hebrew grammarian</note> as: *And they shall subdue their enemies by means of sling-stones,* as if to say the slingers shall capture their enemies. **כבש** <note>Hebrew: *Kevesh*</note> The first step of a climb, or the beginning of a staircase with a wider space, or a footstool. **כבש** <note>Hebrew: *Keves*</note> A lamb. From Isaiah chapter 11: *And the wolf shall dwell with the lamb.* and Numbers chapter 7: *One yearling lamb for a burnt offering.* The word changes from masculine to feminine by adding suffixes.

**ברקת** <note>Hebrew: *Bareket*</note> A precious stone, which some call a "union" or a pearl, and assert that it is white; others say it is crystal; others, such as the wise Abraham <note>likely Abraham ibn Ezra, a prolific 12th-century scholar</note>, say it is a *subata* or dark gem, which our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> calls jasper. **כיון** <note>Kiyyun</note> An idol, which many believe to be Saturn, because Saturn itself is called by this name in the Arabic and Persian languages. **כוס** <note>Kos</note> A genus of hooting bird. Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to the commentator Rashi</note> calls it a "pelican," while others call it the "night-raven" <note>original: "nycticoracem," likely the night-heron</note>. **כור** <note>Kor</note> A measure of grain; a *kor* or a *sextarius* <note>An ancient Roman dry measure</note>. 1 Kings, chapter five: *Twenty thousand kors of wheat as food for his household.*

However, our translation <note>Likely referring to the Latin Vulgate</note> interprets the root as "origin" or "root." Ezekiel, chapter sixteen: *Your root and your birth are of the land of Canaan,* meaning your colony. It is written with the vowel *holem* <note>A Hebrew vowel mark indicating an 'o' sound</note>.

**כוש** <note>Kush</note> The proper name of the son of Ham, from whom Ethiopia is named. Genesis, chapter two: *It encompasses the whole land of Ethiopia.* From this name, "Ethiopians" is derived, as in Jeremiah, chapter thirty-eight: *Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, a eunuch man.* This is spelled with a *yod* at the end, to which another *yod* is often added in derivative forms. As in Amos, chapter nine: *Are you not as the children of the Ethiopians unto me?* Rabbi Kimhi explains this according to the verse in Jeremiah, chapter thirteen: *Can the Ethiopian change his skin?* It is as if he were saying: just as that man cannot change his skin, so you do not wish to change your vices. In this way, King Saul is called an "Ethiopian" in Psalm 7: *Concerning the words of the Ethiopian, the son of Jemini,* because Saul could not change his heart regarding his hatred of King David, even though he had said in 1 Samuel, chapter twenty-six: *Return, my son David, for I will no more do you harm.* Furthermore, David Kimhi writes in his *Book of Roots* that the Ethiopians, Midianites, and Ishmaelites are one and the same. It is also found meaning "bride" <note>original: "sponsa"</note> both in the Septuagint and in the common translation <note>The Vulgate</note> of Isaiah 49: "And you shall clothe yourself with them as a bride."

**כלכל** <note>Hebrew: *Kilkel*</note> He decreed: limited, determined, calculated, or numbered.

as in Genesis 47: *And he nourished them and his father's whole house, providing food to each.* Which could nonetheless be read word-for-word as: *And he established* or *decreed for his father and his brothers and his father's whole house food according to the little ones.* But the reason for this variation was perhaps provided by the translation of Onkelos <note>Onkelos (c. 35–120 AD) was a famous proselyte whose Aramaic translation of the Torah is a standard rabbinic text.</note>, who translated it into Aramaic as *טף* <note>original: "taf"</note>, which among the Babylonians refers to food. It also refers to something "established," specifically through a syncope <note>A linguistic term for the shortening of a word by omitting sounds or letters from the middle.</note> from *טפף* <note>original: "tapap"</note>. Thus, a little earlier in Genesis 45: *And there I will feed you.* For which it could also be read: *And I will establish you there.* It also signifies to sustain or to bear, as in the paraphrase of Jeremiah 20: *Not sustaining the bearing.*

**כלא** <note>original: "kala"</note> **He forbade; he prohibited.** Haggai 1: *Because of this, the heavens above you were prohibited from giving dew, and the earth was prohibited from giving its fruit.* That is, it "avoided" or "withheld." And Numbers 11: *My lord Moses, forbid them.* And Exodus 36: *And so the gifts to be offered ceased.* The word-for-word translation stands thus: *And the people were prohibited from the offering.* And Genesis 8: *And the rains from heaven were restrained.* And Psalm 119: *I have restrained my feet from every evil way.*

**כלא** <note>original: "kela"</note> **Cell; fold; prison; a narrow monastery.** <term>monasterium: The author uses this Latin term to describe a secluded cell or place of confinement, drawing a parallel between a prison cell and a monk’s cell.</term> In the last chapter of Jeremiah: *And he led him out of the house of the prison.* and shortly after: *And he changed his prison garments.* It is found at the end of words sometimes changing the letter *aleph* into *he*, and sometimes adding the aspiration *he*, as I find in the most ancient books in the last chapter of Habakkuk: *The flock shall be cut off from the fold,* where the letter *mem* is also placed at the beginning to indicate it is a noun.

**כלאים** <note>original: "kil'ayim"</note> **Of two species, and mixed or mingled.** This is how Onkelos the Chaldean interprets the end of Leviticus 19, where in one verse the same word is placed three times: *You shall not let your cattle mate with animals of another kind; you shall not sow your field with diverse seed; you shall not wear a garment woven of two types of material.* The word-for-word translation is: *Your beast you shall not cause to crouch in a mixture; your field you shall not sow in a mixture; and a garment of mixture—namely of wool and linen—shall not come upon you.*

**כלב** <note>original: "kelev"</note> **Dog.** 1 Samuel 17: *Am I a dog?* And Exodus 11: *But among all the children of Israel, a dog shall not bark.* <note>The original Latin "mutiet" refers to making a small sound or muttering.</note> And in the plural in Isaiah 56: *Dumb dogs, unable to bark.*

**Cage** <note>original Hebrew: כלוב (kluv)</note> A cage in which fattened fowl and birds are kept, which our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> renders as a "trap." In Jeremiah 5: *Like a trap full of birds.* For this, Jonathan the Chaldean <note>The Aramaic Targum of Jonathan, an ancient Jewish paraphrase of the Bible</note> interprets it as a "house of fattening." David Kimhi <note>A renowned 12th-century medieval Hebrew grammarian and commentator, also known as Radak</note> writes in his *Book of Roots* that it is a receptacle woven from twigs in which birds were customarily kept. Joseph the Spaniard, his father <note>Joseph Kimhi, a grammarian who migrated from Spain to France</note>, says in his commentaries on Jeremiah that it is a place designated for the fattening of fowl. From this comes the passage found in Amos 8: *And behold, a hook of fruits* <note>original Latin: uncinus pomorum</note>, which the Jewish teachers interpret as a basket or hamper filled with fruit. **Ceased** <note>original Hebrew: כלה (kalah)</note> He ceased, failed, or finished. Jeremiah 8: *Summer is finished*, or *summer has ended*. Also in chapter 14: *Their eyes failed because there was no grass.* From this comes a verbal noun with the prefix *mem* <note>Referring to the Hebrew grammatical form where the letter 'mem' is added to the root to create a noun or specific verb form</note> in the same place as above: *I will consume them* <note>original: Ego consumam eos</note>, in the sense of "I am making them fail" or "bringing them to an end."

->FIRST<-

In the Greek language, *posapos* <note>original: "posapos," meaning "of what kind" or "how much"</note> is what we read as "how manifoldly." In Psalm 63: "How manifoldly my flesh longs for you." But the Hebrews speak more correctly: "My flesh has thirsted for you." And so Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Bible into Latin</note> translated it in his Psalter according to the Hebrew truth. However, Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator</note> writes concerning this word that it is not found elsewhere with this meaning.

**כמה** [Kamah] **How many**. As in Psalm 119: "How many are the days of your servant?" The Hebrews use this expression in the <term>categories of quantity</term> <note>Aristotelian philosophical categories used to describe how much of something exists</note>, as is found in Averroes <note>The 12th-century Andalusian philosopher Ibn Rushd</note> in his Hebrew logic.

**כמז** [Kumaz] **A feminine thigh-ornament** usually tied underneath. It is like a woman’s garter adorned with gold and gems, according to the Hebrew masters. Our translation renders it as "necklaces" or "armlets." Numbers 31: "Armlets and necklaces."

**כמון** [Kamon] **Cumin** or vetch, or some such kind of legume. As in Isaiah 28: "He will sow gith <note>black cumin</note> and scatter cumin." Likewise in the same passage: "nor will the cartwheel roll over the cumin."

**מכמן** [Mikman] **Hidden thing** or **treasure**. Daniel 11: "And he shall have power over the treasures of gold and silver."

**כמס** [Kamas] **Laid up**, **stored away**, **hidden**, or **a secret**. Deuteronomy 32: "Are these things not stored up with me?"

**כמר** [Kamar] **He grew warm**. Genesis 43: "Because his heart was moved" <note>literally: his bowels grew warm</note>. Word for word, it should be read as: "Because his mercies grew warm." Rabbi Solomon also explains it this way. This is supported by the last chapter of Lamentations: "Our skins were burned like an oven."

**כמר** [Kemar] **A religious man**, **monk**, or **black-clad temple official**, whom they call a chaplain. Hosea 10: "And its priests exulted over it." And in the first chapter of Zephaniah: "And the names of the temple-priests with the priests."

**מכמר** [Mikmar] **A net**, **snare**, or **lattice**. Psalm 141: "The sinners shall fall into his net." And in Habakkuk 1: "And he gathered them into his net."

**כן** [Ken] **So** or **thus**. Genesis 1: "And it was so." We have spoken about this expression above under the word **כון** [Kun].

**כנים** [Kinnim] **Gnats** or **lice**. Exodus 8: "And let there be gnats throughout all the land of Egypt."

**כנה** [Kennah] **A place of residence**, **base**, or **seat**. Exodus 30: "A bronze basin with its [base]"

->**BOOK ONE**<-

The irregular <term>declension</term><note>The author is discussing 'heteroclite' nouns, which change their pattern of grammatical endings.</note> of this noun is common in gender and number. **Numbers 15**: "Tassels throughout the four corners." And **Deuteronomy 22**: "On the four corners of your cloak." Our translation <note>Likely referring to the Latin Vulgate.</note> renders this as "hem." **Haggai 2**: "In the hem of his garment." This word is used for the edges and sections of garments because unstitched clothes create a shape like wings; it is used similarly for the "ends of the earth." Also in **Isaiah 10**: "And there was no one who moved a wing." <note>original: "pennam"</note> From this comes the verb in **Isaiah 30**: "And he will no longer cause your teacher to fly away from you." <note>The Hebrew root here is 'Kanaf', meaning wing or edge.</note>

**כנור** <note>Hebrew: Kinnor</note> **Lyre.** **Genesis 4**: "He was the father of those playing the lyre and the pipe." <note>original: "cithara et organo"</note> And **Job 30**: "My lyre is turned to mourning." It is declined in the common gender. For it is found in the masculine in **Ezekiel 26**: "And the sound of your lyres shall be heard no more." And it appears in the feminine gender in **1 Kings 10**: "And lyres and harps for the singers." Our translation <note>The Vulgate</note> uses the general term "instruments" <note>original: "organa"</note> in **Psalm 137**: "We hung up our instruments," which Jerome, in his own translation of the Psalter, specifically translated as "lyres."

**כסס** <note>Hebrew: Kasas</note> **He counted, he calculated.** **Exodus 12**: "According to the number of souls who might suffice for eating the lamb." This word is read literally as: "According to the number or the calculation of souls, each of you shall count or calculate according to what he can eat of the lamb." From this comes "calculation," <note>original: "supputatio"</note> with a prefixed *mem* and the final letter removed. **Numbers 31**: "From which six hundred and seventy-five sheep were calculated for the Lord's portion." For which the word-for-word reading is: "And there was a calculation for the Lord from the sheep of six hundred seventy-five." One may see this very word used frequently in that passage.

**כסא** <note>Hebrew: Kisse</note> **Throne, royal seat, chair.** **Jeremiah 17**: "A throne of glory, set on high from the beginning." And **2 Samuel 3**: "And let the throne of David be exalted." And **Isaiah 66**: "Heaven is my seat." Sometimes, however, the letter *aleph* is changed to a *he*, as in **1 Kings 10**, which mentions "six steps"; for which the Hebrew Truth <note>A common Renaissance term for the original Hebrew Masoretic text.</note> has: "six steps to the throne," and it follows: "And the top of the throne was round." Regarding this, Rabbi David Kimhi <note>A famous 12th-century Jewish grammarian and commentator known as 'Radak'.</note> writes in his commentaries on the Book of Kings that in this place "throne" is written twice with the aspiration of the letter *he* in place of *aleph*. However, I find variation in the books, both in manuscript and in print.

**כסה** <note>Hebrew: Kasah</note> **He concealed, hid, covered, or protected.** **Proverbs 12**: "A shrewd man conceals knowledge." And **Numbers 4**: "And they shall cover it again with a veil of violet skins," for which the Hebrew Truth has: "And they shall put upon it a covering of <term>tachash</term> skin." <note>The identity of 'tachash' is a famous mystery; it has been translated as badger, dolphin, or violet-dyed leather.</note> From this comes the noun "covering" or "roofing"...

Ecclesiastes 4: "Better is a handful with rest," which is phrased thus: "Better is a full palm of quiet." And in Isaiah 1, when it says "from the sole of the foot," it ought to be read "from the palm of the foot," that is, from the inner part of the foot. And it is declined irregularly <note>Latin: *heteroclite*</note>; for in the plural number, although according to the rules of others it ought to be a two-syllable word, by usage it becomes three syllables. As in Job 36: "In his hands he hides the light." It is also often used for a "footprint." As in 1 Kings 18: "Behold, a little cloud like a man's footprint." Isaiah 60: "And they shall worship the footprints of your feet." And from its similarity, clouds are often called by this name, as in Lamentations 3: "Let us lift up our hearts with our hands," which the Hebrews translate thus: "Let us lift up our hearts toward the clouds to God in the heavens," as **David Kimhi** witnesses in his *Book of Roots*. Just as it is written in Isaiah 49: "Behold, I have described you in my hands," which **Rabbi Joseph son of Kimhi** and **Rabbi Saadia** <note>Saadia Gaon, a major 10th-century Jewish philosopher and exegete.</note> understand thus: "Behold, I have ordained you above the clouds," although Jonathan agrees with our translation. It also signifies the concave bone in which the thigh turns, which our translation calls a "nerve." <note>Genesis 32:25; modern translations usually render this as the "socket" of the hip.</note> Genesis 32: "He touched the nerve of his thigh." It also signifies a shell, or a bowl, or a spoon, which our translation renders as "a little mortar." Numbers 7: "A little golden mortar weighing ten shekels full of incense." And 2 Chronicles 24: "Also phials and other vessels." More correctly it is called a cup or a vat, and this is of the feminine gender, as is clear from the following: "twelve little golden mortars."

כפה <term>Kapheh: A root meaning to subdue, bend, or extinguish.</term> **He restrained.** He extinguished or restricted. Proverbs 21: "A hidden gift extinguishes anger." Some, like **Rabbi Judah**, explain it according to the verse in Micah 6: "I shall be bowed before the high God," thus: "A gift in secret bends or turns back anger."

כפל <term>Kaphal: A root meaning to double or fold.</term> **He doubled.** Exodus 26: "That you may double the sixth curtain in the front of the roof." Its passive is used in Isaiah 21: "And let the sword be doubled and tripled." From this comes the name "double" or "duplicated," as in Genesis 23: "That he may give me the double cave." <note>Referring to the Cave of Machpelah, the burial place of the Patriarchs.</note>

# FIRST BOOK

<term>כפן (kaphan)</term>: **He hungered** or **perished from famine**. This is how some of the Hebrews interpret this little verse which we read in Ezekiel 17: *“And behold, this vine, as if sending its roots toward it.”* <note>original: "Et ecce uinea iſta quaſi mittēs radices ad eam"</note> They more truly interpret it as: *“Behold, this hungry vine, its roots are above it.”* For the word *caphan*, meaning "famine," is found in Job 5: *“In devastation and famine you shall laugh.”* <note>original: "In uaſtitate & fame ridebis"</note>

<term>כפיס (kaphis)</term>: **A beam** or **paneled ceiling**. Our translation <note>The Vulgate</note> interprets it as the wood that is between the joints of buildings, which they commonly call a "tie-beam." Habakkuk 2 says: *“And the wood that is between the joints of the buildings shall answer.”* The <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament (LXX)</note> translated this as “a beetle <note>original: "scarabeus"</note> speaks from the wood.” **Symmachus** <note>A 2nd-century translator of the Bible into Greek</note> rendered it as “the wooden joint of the building.” **Theodotion** <note>Another 2nd-century Greek translator</note> called it “a wooden ceiling.” So testifies **Jerome** <note>The primary translator of the Latin Vulgate</note> in his "fifth edition," who also writes that he had seen other translations of this verse: one where "a worm speaking in the wood" appears, and another that translated it as *Scolix* <note>Greek for worm</note> speaking from the wood, which is the same thing. But Jerome himself determines in his commentaries on the Minor Prophets that *caphis* signifies the wood placed in the middle of a structure to hold the walls together. Generally, however, the Jews understand it as the shavings of hewn wood.

<term>כפר (kaphar)</term>: **He waterproofed with bitumen** or **pitched**. Genesis 6: *“And you shall smear it with bitumen inside and out,”* <note>referring to Noah's Ark</note> where you will find both the noun and the verb.

<term>כפר (kaphar)</term>: **He expiated**, **appeased**, or **propitiated**. Genesis 32: *“For he said, ‘I will appease him with gifts.’”* From this comes the **Mercy Seat** <note>original: "ppiciatoriū" (propitiatorium), the golden cover of the Ark of the Covenant</note>. Exodus 25: *“You shall also make a Mercy Seat of purest gold.”* And Isaiah 47: *“Which you shall not be able to expiate.”* And Proverbs 16: *“A wise man will appease it.”* From this are named the **Days of Atonement**, which in Hebrew are called *Kipurim* <note>Yom Kippur</note>, just as the season of **Lent** <note>original: "tēpusquadrageſimale"</note> is among us. As in Leviticus 23: *“On the tenth day of this seventh month, the Day of Atonement shall be most celebrated, and you shall afflict your souls in it.”* And it follows: *“Because it is a day of propitiation, that the Lord your God may be appeased toward you.”*

<term>כפר (kaphar)</term>: **A village**. 1 Samuel 6: *“From the walled city even unto the village.”* And Song of Songs 7: *“Let us abide in the villages.”*

<term>כופר (kopher)</term>: **A species of sweet-smelling spice**, which some call **camphor**, others the **henna plant** <note>original: "herbā cyperū"</note>, and others any flowering and sweet-smelling thing. As in Song of Songs 1: *“A cluster of henna is my beloved to me,”* <note>original: "Botrus cypri"</note> almost as if "flowering," which in Greek is called *cypris*. Others read it as "a cluster of cyperus," as follows in Chapter 4 of the same book: *“Cyperus with nard.”*

# THE BOOK

כפיר **Lion cub.** <note>original: "Catulus leonis"</note> Psalm 17: *Like a lion cub dwelling in hidden places.* <note>Psalm 17:12; in many modern Bibles this is Psalm 17, while the Latin Vulgate cites it as 16</note> and plural in Psalm 103: *The lion cubs roaring.* <note>Psalm 104:21</note> In another place, our translation <note>Referring to the Latin Vulgate</note> renders it as "lion," such as in Ezekiel 32: *You are compared to a lion of the nations.* Jonathan the Chaldean <note>A reference to the Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible; "Chaldean" was a common historical term for Aramaic</note> translated the sense of the passage as: *You have become powerful among the people.* From this comes the idea of robustness and strength.

כפור **Hoarfrost.** <note>original: "Pruina"</note> Exodus 16: *There appeared in the wilderness something small and as if crushed by a pestle, in the likeness of hoarfrost upon the earth.* <note>Exodus 16:14, describing the appearance of Manna</note> and Psalm 147, for that which we read as: *He scatters the mist like ashes,* Jerome, following the "Hebrew Truth," <note>term: <term>Hebraica Veritas</term>—Jerome’s principle of translating the Old Testament directly from Hebrew rather than the Greek Septuagint</note> translates much more correctly as: *He scatters the hoarfrost like ashes.*

כפור **Basin or bowl.** <note>original: "Pelvis sive crater"</note> Ezra 8: *And twenty golden bowls.*

כפש **He overturned,** <note>original: "Evertit"</note> that is, he turned the top part to the bottom, such as the head to the place of the feet and vice versa. Lamentations 3: *He fed me with ashes,* <note>Lamentations 3:16</note> which the Jews translate as: *He turned me over in the ashes,* and this usage is not found elsewhere.

כפתר **A cup in the manner of a nut** or a knob, or according to the form of a pomegranate broken open at the top. <note>original: "Sciphus in modum nucis"</note> Exodus 25: *Three cups in the manner of a nut for each branch,* that is, like pomegranates split at the top. In resemblance to these, they use this name for the <term>retinacula cardinum</term> <note>the sockets or pivots of door hinges</note> in which doors turn, because they are shaped like perforated fruits. As in Amos 9: *Strike the hinge,* <note>Amos 9:1</note> that is, the knob in which the hinge turns, upon which birds often nest. Zephaniah 2: *They shall dwell in its thresholds.*

כר **Lamb.** <note>original: "Agnus"</note> Deuteronomy 32: *With the fat of lambs.* and Jeremiah 51: *I will lead them like lambs to the slaughter.* and in the singular in Isaiah 16: *Send the lamb, the ruler of the earth,* which <term>Rabbi Joseph Kimhi</term> <note>A 12th-century Hebrew grammarian and teacher in Narbonne, France</note> explains as: "Send a tribute to King Hezekiah, the ruler of the land, namely a lamb." But Jonathan the Chaldean explains it as referring to the Messiah.

כר **Captain,** <note>original: "Capitaneus"</note> or according to Jonathan the Chaldean, the more powerful among the people. 4 Kings 11: <note>In the older system used here, 1 & 2 Samuel and 1 & 2 Kings were called 1, 2, 3, & 4 Kings. This refers to 2 Kings 11:4.</note> *And he took the centurions and the legions of the Carithi and Pheleti.* <note>The Cherethites and Pelethites, King David's elite royal guard</note> It is also called the *Cari* cohort, as just above: *And taking the centurions and the soldiers.* Jonathan understands these as "powerful men" and "prefects of the cohort"; they understand the same word to mean both the prefect of the cohort and the cohort itself.

כר **Pasture field,** or a place of pastures according to <term>David Kimhi</term> <note>Also known by the acronym Radak, a famous 13th-century rabbi and grammarian whose work was essential to Christian Hebraists</note> in his commentaries on the Major Prophets. Isaiah 30: *It shall graze in your possession in the day...*

->FIRST<-

...there the lamb [will graze] spaciously. More correctly, the Seventy <note>The "Seventy" refers to the Septuagint (LXX), the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> translated it: *And your cattle will graze in that day in a rich and spacious place.* From this, the Hebrew masters explain the verse of Psalm 65, *The rams of the sheep are clothed*, in this way: *The fields of the pastures are clothed with sheep.* As Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), a preeminent medieval Jewish scholar.</note> says: "The fields and pastures are clothed with sheep that come to graze on the grass which the rain causes to sprout."

**כרכר** [KRKR] He danced. He performed a choral dance. 2 Samuel 6: *David danced with all his might before the Lord.* From this, pacing horses moving with a triple gait are called by that name in the feminine gender. The Hebrews, however, use this word to designate camels and other animals suited for transport by which we are carried, which our translation <note>Referring to the Latin Vulgate, the standard Bible of the time.</note> interpreted as "carriages" in Isaiah 66: *And on mules and in carriages.* But more truly they understand these as animals upon which sleeping quarters with awnings are placed, which are called "covered litters" or "sedan chairs," according to the translations of Aquila, the Septuagint, and Symmachus.

**כרר** [KRR] Bedding; a place for beasts of burden to lie down. Genesis 31: *Under the camel’s saddle* <note>original: "stramenta", literally bedding or straw spread out.</note>.

**כרבל** [KRBL] He wrapped; he clothed. As in 1 Chronicles 15: *Moreover, David was clothed in a robe of fine linen*, that is, wrapped in a cloak.

**כרוב** [KRWB] A winged creature [Cherub]. Exodus 25: *Let there be one cherub on one side and another on the other.* And further down: *And the cherubim shall be spreading their wings.* By "cherub," however, Rabbi Abraham ibn Ezra <note>A distinguished Spanish Jewish scholar and philosopher (1089–1167).</note> understands a class of every separate form, such as that of a man or an ox, as seen in the vision of Ezekiel.

**כרה** [KRH] He cut into; he opened; he cut out; he took away or uprooted; he dug. Psalm 7: *He opened a pit and dug it out.* And 1 Samuel 20: *You shall not take away your mercy.* Likewise, *when the Lord shall have uprooted the enemies of David.* And regarding Psalm 40, where we read, *but you have perfected ears for me*, the "Hebrew Truth" <note>original: "hebraica ueritas", a term used by scholars like Jerome to refer to the original Hebrew text as the ultimate authority over translations.</note> according to the testimony of Jerome, has: *but you have pierced ears.* Genesis 50: *In my tomb which I dug for myself.* From this comes the noun for a "digging" or a "mine," as in Zephaniah 2: *And heaps of salt*, which the Hebrews explain as, *And a cutting or a mine of salt.* From this are named the places which are cut out for sheep, which we call "folds," as in Zephaniah 2: *And folds for the flocks.*

**כרה** [KRH] He ordered; he arranged; he prepared, or made ready. As in 2 Kings 6: *A great preparation of food was set before them.* The Hebrews, word for word, more correctly read this as: *And he caused to be prepared for them a great preparation.* In this way also Onkelos <note>A famous convert to Judaism who authored a highly regarded Aramaic translation of the Torah.</note> explains it in Chaldean <note>original: "chaldaice", the term then used for Aramaic.</note> as *atken* <note>Aramaic for "he prepared" or "he established".</note>.

**BOOK**

**כרה** <note>Hebrew root: *karah*</note> **To buy.** As in Deuteronomy 2: "You shall draw and drink purchased water." They read this word-for-word as: "You shall also buy waters and drink them." Wherefore the Hebrews better explain the verse in Hosea 3: "And I bought her for myself for fifteen pieces of silver." In place of this, we <note>original: *nos legimus*; referring to the Latin Vulgate Bible commonly used in the West</note> read: "And I dug for her for myself for fifteen pieces of silver." For even the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> interpreted it as: "And I hired her for myself for fifteen pieces of silver." Nicholas of Lyra <note>A prominent Franciscan teacher and influential Bible commentator (c. 1270–1349)</note> similarly asserts that it is this way in the Hebrew. The fact that the letter *Kaph* is written with a *dagesh* <note>original: *dagges*; a small dot in a Hebrew letter that can change its pronunciation or grammar</note> does not indicate the passive voice, but is placed there for the sake of euphony <note>To make the word sound more pleasant or easier to pronounce</note>. From this comes the noun for "sale" or "price" by prefixing the letter *Mem*. Numbers 20: "We will give what is just"—that is, word-for-word: "I will give their price." And in Amos 2: "They sold the righteous for silver"—that is, concerning their sale. According to the meaning of this word, the verse which we read in Genesis 50: "In my tomb which I dug for myself," is better understood according to the Hebrews; it would be more correctly translated as: "In my tomb which I bought for myself," as is clearer to anyone looking closely.

**כרך** <note>Hebrew root: *karak*</note> **To wrap, clothe, dress, or sew in.** Esther 8: "And clothed in a silk and purple cloak."

**כרכב** <note>Hebrew root: *karkob*</note> **A border, perimeter, or circuit.** Thus Onkelos the Chaldean <note>referring to the Targum Onkelos, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the Torah</note> interprets that which we read in Exodus 27: "Which you shall place under the hearth of the altar," namely, under the circuit of the altar. Nicholas of Lyra also translates it in this way, namely: "which you shall place under the border of the altar."

**כרכם** <note>Hebrew root: *karkom*</note> **Saffron.** Which in Arabic is called *safran*. Song of Songs 4: "Spikenard and saffron."

**כרם** <note>Hebrew root: *kerem*</note> **A vineyard.** Genesis 9: "And he planted a vineyard." And 1 Kings 8: "And he will take the best vineyards and olive groves." And Song of Songs 1: "They made me a keeper of the vineyards, but my own vineyard I have not kept."

**כרמל** <note>Hebrew root: *karmel*</note> **Grain threshed from the ear and early-ripened,** which our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> renders as "pottage from the harvest." Leviticus 23: "And you shall not eat pottage from the harvest." Likewise, **a wooded field.** Isaiah 29: "Lebanon shall be turned into a *carmel*"—that is, high things shall be changed into low things. Likewise, *carmil* signifies the color **crimson**, as in 2 Chronicles 2: "Purple, crimson, and hyacinth [blue]." Likewise, without the letter *Yod*, it signifies **Mount Carmel**. 1 Kings 25: And the possess—

->THE BOOK<-

...because you have fallen in your iniquity. <note>original: "quoniam corruisti in iniquitate tua"</note> Thus also in Isaiah 31: **And the helper shall fall.** <note>original: "Et corruet auxiliator"</note> And in the same book, chapter 59: **We have stumbled at midday as if in the darkness,** <note>original: "Impegimus meridiem quasi in tenebris"</note> and further down in the same chapter: **Because truth has fallen in the street.** <note>original: "Quia corruit in platea veritas"</note> From this comes the word in Psalm 105: **And there was not one feeble person among their tribes.** <note>original: "Et non erat in tribubus eorum infirmus"</note> The passive form of the verb is placed in Zechariah 12: **And he who stumbles in 그날,** <note>original: "Et erit qui offenderit in die illa"</note> that is, he shall be struck or shall have been offended. In Zephaniah 1: **And the ruins of the wicked shall be.** <note>original: "Et ruinae impiorum erunt"</note> Nahum 3: **And they shall fall over their own bodies.** <note>original: "Et corruent in corporibus suis"</note>

From this is derived the noun <term>stumbling block</term> <note>original: "offendiculum"</note> by which someone is harmed either in soul or in body. Isaiah 57: **Take up the stumbling blocks out of the way of my people,** <note>original: "Auferte offendicula de via populi mei"</note> which the Greeks call a *skandalon*. <note>original: "schandalon"</note> And Ezekiel 3: **I will lay a stumbling block before him.** <note>original: "Ponam offendiculum coram eo"</note>

**כשיל** <term>Ax</term>. <note>Hebrew: *Kashil*</note> Psalm 74: **With ax and hatchet they have cast it down.** <note>original: "In securi et ascia deiecerunt eam"</note>

**כשף** <term>To enchant</term> <note>Hebrew: *Kashaph*</note> or to practice magic, or to use sorcery. Deuteronomy 18: **Let there not be a sorcerer,** <note>original: "Ne sit maleficus"</note> under which Latin name three species of evil-doers are contained in the Hebrew. Likewise in Exodus 22: **You shall not suffer sorcerers to live.** <note>original: "Maleficos non patieris vivere"</note> This is placed in the feminine gender in Hebrew, namely thus: **a sorceress shall not live.** <note>original: "malefica non vivat"</note> Upon this, the Hebrew masters <note>The "Magistri Hebraeorum" usually refers to rabbinic commentators like Rashi or Kimhi.</note> write that it is placed in the feminine rather than the masculine because there are more <term>witches</term> <note>original: "lamiarum," referring to female nocturnal demons or witches.</note> than wizards; for this kind of evil-doing is found more frequently in old women and females. It is placed in the masculine plural in Daniel 2: **That the soothsayers, and the magicians, and the sorcerers, and the Chaldeans should be called together.** <note>original: "Ut convocarentur arioli et magi et malefici et chaldaei"</note>

**כשר** <term>To be fitting</term> <note>Hebrew: *Kashar*</note> or suitable. Ecclesiastes 11: **You know not which may more arise,** <note>original: "Nescis quid magis oriatur"</note> for "which may be more fitting." And in Esther 8, for that which our translator has expressed through circumlocution saying: **And my prayer does not seem to be contrary to him,** <note>original: "Et deprecatio mea non ei videtur esse contraria"</note> the Hebrew truth <note>The "Hebraica Veritas" was a common term for the original Hebrew text as opposed to the Vulgate translation.</note> has: **And the thing shall be convenient or fitting before the king;** <note>original: "Et conveniens seu congruens res erit coram rege"</note> as if he were saying "it shall be right or acceptable." Thus, for that which is read in Ecclesiastes 10: **Wisdom shall follow industry,** <note>original: "post industriam sequetur sapientia"</note> the Hebrew truth holds: **And wisdom is an abundant fittingness.** <note>original: "Et abundans congruentia est sapientia"</note> A noun derived from this was interpreted by our translation as "strength" in Psalm 68: **Who leads out the prisoners in strength,** <note>original: "Qui educit vinctos in fortitudine"</note> but the Hebrews more correctly read: **in fitting times.** <note>original: "in congruentiis"</note> Thus writes <term>Rabbi Solomon</term> <note>Rabbi Shlomo Yitzhaki, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator.</note> that God led the children of Israel out of Egypt at the most fitting time for beginning a journey, neither in the heat nor in the cold. And when we read in the last chapter of Proverbs: **She put her hand to strong things,** <note>original: "Manum suam misit ad fortia"</note> the Hebrews explain it: **to right and fitting things.** <note>original: "ad recta et congrua"</note>

**כתת** <term>To beat</term> <note>Hebrew: *Katat*</note> or to crush or compress. Leviticus 22: **Crushed...** <note>The entry continues on the next page.</note>

# FIRST BOOK

...either beaten or cut. It is found with the last letter removed <term>apocope<note>The loss of one or more sounds or letters at the end of a word.</note></term>, as in Joel 3: **Beat your plows into swords**, which would have been more correctly translated as **crush** or **pound**, as in Deuteronomy 9: **And breaking it into pieces**, where the Hebrew text <note>original: "veritas hebraica"</note> stands word-for-word thus: "And your sin which you had made, namely the calf, I took and burnt it in fire, and crushed it by grinding it entirely until it was thinned into dust." Our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate.</note> converts it in a similar way as above in Numbers 14: **Striking them down as far as Hormah**, and Psalm 89: **And I will crush his enemies before his face**, which Jerome also translated similarly in Zechariah 11: **And they shall crush the earth.**

**כתב** <note>Hebrew: *Katav*</note> **He wrote.** Exodus 32: **From your book which you have written.** And Jeremiah 36: **Take the volume of the book and you shall write in it.** And Ezekiel 2: **And there was writing on the front and the back**, for which we read: **And it was written within and without, and written in it were lamentations, etc.** And Psalm 87: **The Lord shall be recounted in the writings of the people.** And with the prepositional letter *Mem*, as in Exodus 32, for that which we read: **The writing of God was also engraved on the tablets**, the Hebrew truth has it thus: **And the writing, the writing of God it was**, which is also found without the *Mem* with the same meaning, as in Esther 3: **This was the sum of the letters**, for which they more truly read: **The instruction of the writing.**

**כתל** <note>Hebrew: *Kotel*</note> **Wall.** As in Song of Songs 2: **He stands behind our wall.**

**כתם** <note>Hebrew: *Ketem*</note> **A mass of gold**, which our translation renders as **the finest gold.** Song of Songs 5: **His head is the finest gold**, which is described in Hebrew by two words, as if one were to say "the most sublime or purest gold," which the ancients called **obrizum** <note>Refined or pure gold.</note> as if it were "Ophir-gold." From this, our translation in Job 31 has: **And I said to the refined gold: you are my confidence.** However, in other places it incorrectly translates this as "color," as in Lamentations 4: **The finest color is changed**, where <term>Nicholas of Lyra<note>A highly influential Franciscan teacher and biblical exegete (c. 1270–1349) known for emphasizing the literal sense of the Bible.</note></term> rightly teaches that in Hebrew it is placed as "a good mass." From this, some wish to derive the title and military dignity of David himself, who was called **Michtam** <note>A term of uncertain meaning found in the headings of several Psalms.</note> as if "gilded," just as we call them **Golden Knights**. This appears in the titles of five Psalms, from Psalm 56 inclusive to Psalm 61 exclusive. Or according to others, **David’s Michtam** means "distinguished" or "marked," for **כתם** also signifies a mark or a sign. It is sometimes taken in a bad sense and interpreted as a **stain**, as in Jeremiah 2: **You are stained in your iniquity before me**, that is, "marked." Just so among the Latins, the word is used both ways.
