**<term>Ketonet</term>** <note>Hebrew: כתנת</note> **Tunic**, shirt, or short cloak; that which the Greeks call a *chiton*. **Genesis 37**: *They stripped him of his long and multicolored tunic.* <note>original: "tunica talari & polymita"</note>

**<term>Kateph</term>** <note>Hebrew: כתף</note> **Shoulder**, shoulder blade, or side. **Zechariah 7**: *They turned a stubborn shoulder.* And **Numbers 7**: *And they carry the burdens on their own shoulders.* This word also signifies the edges of garments around the shoulders, as in **Exodus 28**: *It shall have two edges joined like shoulder-pieces.* <note>The author is likely referring to the ephod of the High Priest.</note>

**<term>Keter</term>** <note>Hebrew: כתר</note> **Crown** or diadem. **Esther 2**: *And he placed the royal diadem on her head.* From the roundness of a crown that encircles the head, a verb is derived which means "to surround" and "to embrace." For example, **Psalm 22**: *Fat bulls have besieged me,* which Jerome translated as *they have walled me in* <note>original: "vallauerunt me"</note>—that is, they have surrounded or "crowned" me.

Also in **Judges 20**, where once again (as often happens elsewhere) the specific words were set aside and only the general sense was translated; for it says: *And so it happened that they were cut down on both sides by the enemies, and there was no rest for the dying.* In contrast, the Hebrew Truth <note>The "Hebrew Truth" (*Hebraica Veritas*) was a term used by scholars to refer to the original Hebrew text as opposed to the Latin Vulgate translation.</note> reads word-for-word: *They surrounded—or embraced—Benjamin and pursued him to the resting place; they trampled him until they were near Gibeah from the rising of the sun.*

And **Habakkuk 1**: *Because the wicked prevails against the righteous.* The Hebrew Truth says: *Because the wicked surrounds the righteous.* It also sometimes signifies "to sustain," "to expect," or "to delay," as in **Job 36**: *Bear with me a little.* <note>original: "Sustine me paululũ"</note>

**<term>Katash</term>** <note>Hebrew: כתש</note> **He pounded** or crushed. **Proverbs 27**: *If you crush a fool in a mortar like grain.* From this comes the term for a "molar tooth," as in **Judges 16**: *And so the Lord opened a molar tooth.* <note>original: "molarem dentem." Modern translations usually refer to the "hollow place" in the jawbone from which water flowed for Samson.</note> From this also comes the "pounded mill" which is called a **mortar** <note>original: "pila"</note>, as in **Zephaniah 1**: *Howl, you inhabitants of the Mortar.*

## **BOOK SECOND**

->**The second book of Johannes Reuchlin of Pforzheim, Doctor of Laws, on the Rudiments of Hebrew, dedicated to his blood brother, the priest Dionysius.**<-

In the first volume, brother Dionysius, we worked diligently to write briefly and clearly concerning the letters, syllables, and those words which begin in their proper order with the first eleven characters of the alphabet. However, because it was not convenient to discuss everything in a single book, it pleased us that you should hear the remaining words treated in this second volume. You will therefore possess a complete and perfect dictionary if you also apply your mind to this book.

<margin>לא</margin> <note>The Hebrew word *Lo*, meaning "Not."</note>
**Not.** As in Psalm 1, verse 1, where it is placed three times. It seems to be spoken through a conversion or *metathesis* <note>original: "metathefin"; a grammatical term for the switching of letters within a word</note> from the word *El* <note>original: "אל"; meaning "God" or "to/towards"</note> as you can see above under the letter *Aleph*. Sometimes an aspirated *He* <note>The letter ה</note> is found at the end instead of an *Aleph* <note>The letter א</note>, as in Deuteronomy 3: "Who is in Rabbath of the children of Ammon," which is more truly read as: "Is he not here in Rabbath of the children of Ammon?" Similarly, when written with a *Vav* and an *Aleph* <note>לוֹא</note> it means "If only" or "Would that." See Isaiah 48 <note>OCR says 47, but likely refers to 48:18</note>. It is also written with a *Vav* but without an *Aleph* <note>לוּ</note>, as in Genesis 17: "Would that Ishmael might live before you."

<margin>לאב</margin> <note>The root *La'ab*.</note>
**It withered.** This is found in a derivative form in Hosea 13: "In the land of solitude," which the masters <note>The "masters" refers to traditional Jewish commentators and grammarians</note> explain as "In the land of thirst," that is, a dry and thirsty land, specifically in the desert. Master Jonas <note>A reference to Jonah ibn Janah (Abū al-Walīd Marwān ibn Janāḥ), a highly influential medieval Hebrew grammarian and lexicographer</note> wrote that the Arabs and Phoenicians call parched and dry places <margin>לאבה</margin> <note>*La'abah*</note>.

<margin>לאה</margin> <note>The root *La'ah*.</note>
**He was exhausted.** Genesis 19: "So that they could not find the door," meaning they were exhausted from trying to find the entrance. Indeed, the entire derivation signifies weariness, weakness, difficulty, labor, and trouble. As in Job 4: "Perhaps you will take it as a trouble." And Malachi 1: "Behold, what a labor." And Micah 6: "In what have I been a trouble to you?" which Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into the Latin Vulgate</note> interprets in his commentaries as: "And with what labor have I pressed you?" But more truly it is: "And in what have I wearied you?"

<margin>לאט</margin> <note>The root *La'at* in its first sense.</note>
**Gradually** or **Gently.** Just as they explain that passage in 2 Samuel 18: "Keep for me the boy Absalom," meaning: "Deal gently for me with the boy Absalom." Although Jonathan the Chaldean <note>Refers to the *Targum Jonathan*, an ancient Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Prophets</note> agrees with our translation.

<margin>לאט</margin> <note>The root *La'at* in its second sense.</note>
**He veiled, covered, hid, wrapped, or concealed.** 2 Samuel 19: Moreover...

...the king covered his head. There are some who think that certain secret magical experiments are named from this word through the omission of the letter *aleph*. Others derive it from לט [*lat*] as in Exodus 7: "And the magicians of the Egyptians did in like manner with their incantations." <note>original: *incantationibus suis*. The author is discussing the Hebrew root for "secrecy" or "enchantment."</note>

לאך **He sent.** But it is found with the prepositional prefix *mem*, as in מלאך [*mal’akh*], a **messenger** or **one who is sent**. Job 1: "A messenger came to Job who said..." and it is the same term that the Greeks call *angelos*, from which our word "angel" is derived. Thus in Sophocles' *Ajax*, Tecmessa speaks: "nor called by *angelis*," that is, by **messengers**. As in Haggai 1: "And Haggai the messenger of the Lord spoke regarding the messengers of the Lord," or more truly, "the messenger of the Lord in the Lord’s embassy or message." And for this reason, a prophet is called *malach* <note>The author is likely referring to the Prophet Malachi, whose name means "My Messenger."</note>—that is, an **angel**—because he is an envoy of God. Numbers 20: "And he sent an angel who brought us out of Egypt," which Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval French rabbi and commentator.</note> and David Kimhi <note>A famous medieval rabbi and grammarian from Narbonne (c. 1160–1235).</note> and others explain as referring to a prophet, namely Moses. Some learned men explain the previous verse of Haggai in this same way. From this, the ministering spirits of God descending to men and ascending to God are so named, as if they were **intermediaries**. Judges 13: "The angel of the Lord likewise ascended in the flame of the altar."

מלאכה **Thing. Substance. Opulence** or **riches. Work.** Genesis 2: "From all his **work** which he had created." And Exodus 36, where our version reads: "Because the offerings were enough and more than enough," the Hebrews have: "And the **wealth** was sufficient for all the work to be done, and even abounding." This is according to the Hebrew masters: the silver and gold and the rest which they offered. Exodus 22: "that he has not put his hand to his neighbor’s **property**"; for it signifies beasts of burden and cattle as well. As in Genesis 33, where our version reads: "And I will follow slowly in the tracks as I see my little ones are able," for which the Hebrews more accurately have: "And I will lead on slowly, according to the pace of the **livestock** <note>The word *mela'khah*, usually "work," here refers to the property or cattle being driven.</note> that is before me, and according to the pace of the children."

מלאכת **Star-cluster. Star.** And it is found with the omission of the letter *aleph* by <term>syncope</term> <note>a grammatical shortening where a letter or sound is dropped from the middle of a word.</note>. Therefore, various people translate it differently. For our translation <note>the Latin Vulgate, the standard Bible of the time.</note> renders it "Queen," as if derived from the name *Melech* [King]. Jeremiah 7: "That they may make cakes for the **Queen of Heaven**," which the Seventy <note>the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> translated as "the host of heaven," as if it refers to all the stars collectively. Jonathan the Chaldean <note>referring to the Targum of Jonathan ben Uzziel, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Bible.</note> also agrees with this, translating it thus: "That they may sacrifice to the planets and the stars of heaven." Rabbi Joseph Kimhi says a great star in the heaven is so called. I, however, think the planets are so called by the <term>prothesis</term> <note>the addition of a letter at the beginning of a word.</note> of the letter *mem*, which are otherwise named without the *mem*...

->The beauty of Carmel and Sharon<-
<note>original: "decor carmeli et saron" (Isaiah 35:2). This likely serves as a poetic subtitle for this section of the dictionary or commentary.</note>

**לָבַשׁ** [He] **Clothed.** <note>Hebrew: *lavash*</note> In the Book of Esther, chapter 6: "He must be clothed in royal robes," where it stands for what the king put on himself. And in Psalm 93: "The Lord is clothed with strength." From this comes the words for "garment," "clothing," and "raiment," etc. <note>original: "uestis et uestimentum et indumentum"</note>

**אַלְגּוּמִּים** With the letter *aleph* prefixed, **algom** signifies a type of precious wood. <note>Hebrew: *algummim*</note> In 2 Chronicles, chapter 9: "The servants of Hiram with the servants of Solomon brought gold from Ophir and **thyine wood** <note>original: "ligna thina"; a fragrant, valuable wood, possibly sandalwood or citrus wood</note>." It is also found in some places as *almog*. Many believe it to be coral.

**לָאָה** [He] **Failed.** <note>Hebrew: *la’ah*</note> To be weary, fatigued, or oppressed. Genesis 47: "And the famine oppressed the land," especially the lands of Egypt and Canaan. The land was fatigued or exhausted according to **Rabbi Solomon** <note>refers to Rashi, the 11th-century Jewish scholar whose commentaries were essential to Renaissance Hebraists</note>. By a repetition of letters, it is found in Proverbs 26: "As a troublemaker is he who shoots arrows," for which it is more accurately rendered: "As one who is fatigued shooting sparks," where this word **כְּמִתְלַהְלֵהּ** is placed. <note>Hebrew: *k’mitlahle’ah*</note>

**לַהַב Flame.** <note>Hebrew: *lahav*</note> Judges 13: "And as the flame ascended." It is declined in the masculine plural in Isaiah 13: "Faces burned [with heat]" for "flaming faces." It is also found in the feminine singular in Numbers 21: "A flame from the town of Sihon." And in the feminine plural in Psalm 105: "A fire burning in their land." **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate</note> in his psalter uses "flaming fire," but the Hebrews more accurately say "a fire of flames."

**לֶהָבָה The edge of a blade** or its splendor; or a polished and sharp blade, like a shining flame. <note>Hebrew: *lehavah*</note> Nahum 3: "And of the flashing sword." The translation of the **Septuagint** <note>original: "lxx"; the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> has "and of the glittering sword." It also signifies the iron head of a spear, as if it were a little tongue of fire shining like a pyramid of flame. In that case, it is used in the feminine gender, as in 1 Samuel 17: "The iron head of his spear."

**לַהַג A saying** or a speech. Our translation <note>the Latin Vulgate</note> has "meditation." Ecclesiastes, the last chapter: "And much study [meditation] is a weariness of the flesh." <note>Hebrew: *lahag*</note>

**לַהַט The edge of a sword.** <note>Hebrew: *lahat*</note> Or, according to **Rabbi Solomon**, a blade that is polished, bright, and shining; as in Genesis 3: "And a flaming, turning sword." From this comes the word for "burning," or a "reflected heat," or a "collection of rays" as if in a concave burning mirror. As in Psalm 104: "And his ministers a burning fire," meaning shining, vibrating, and sparkling like a polished sword.

<term>Lahat</term> <note>Hebrew: להט</note> opposite the sun, or like a concave mirror reflecting rays that burn; from which the word derived from it means to inflame, to set on fire, or to burn. In the final chapter of Malachi: *And the day that comes shall burn them up.* The <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament, often abbreviated as LXX</note> translated this as "and it shall kindle," just as it is read in Deuteronomy 32: *And it shall burn the foundations of the mountains.* It also signifies magical sorceries which are performed through the consecration of a sword, which our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> calls "Egyptian incantations" and "certain secrets." In Exodus 7: *And they also did in like manner with their Egyptian incantations and certain secrets.* <term>Onkelos</term> <note>Author of the famous Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Torah</note> translated this into <term>Chaldean</term> <note>Aramaic</note> as "mutterings," and Rabbi Solomon <note>The famous medieval commentator Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo itzhaki)</note> says that its full form is not found elsewhere in the Bible.

<term>Laham</term> <note>Hebrew: להם</note> He alluded by a nod, or spoke indistinctly. In Proverbs 18: *The words of a double-tongued man are as if simple,* meaning as if of those speaking by a nod or speaking indistinctly; others explain it as if of those who are stunning or striking, through a <term>metathesis</term> <note>reordering</note> of letters: *laham* for *halam* <note>original: "laham pro halam"</note>. For it is written this way in Judges 5: *And she struck Sisera, seeking his head,* though it is more truly translated: *She struck Sisera, piercing his head.*

<term>Lahakah</term> <note>Hebrew: להקה</note> A company, troop, wedge, or congregation. 1 Samuel 19: *When he had seen the company of prophets.* It is used as if by a transformation of the word <term>Kehillah</term> <note>Hebrew: קהלה</note>, which means a church or synagogue.

<term>Lu</term> <note>Hebrew: לו</note> Perhaps, would that, if by chance, lest by chance. Genesis 17: *Would that Ishmael might live before you.* And in the final chapter of Genesis: *Lest by chance he should be mindful of the injury.*

<term>Log</term> <note>Hebrew: לוג</note> This is a small measure, which our translation calls a *sextarium* <note>A Roman unit of volume, roughly a pint</note>. Leviticus 14: *And a sextarium of oil and two turtles.*

<term>Lavah</term> <note>Hebrew: לוה</note> He borrowed, he lent, he practiced usury. Deuteronomy 28: *And you shall lend to many nations, and you shall not take interest from anyone.* And in Psalm 37: *The sinner shall borrow and shall not pay back.*

<term>Lavah</term> <note>Hebrew: לוה</note> He clung to, he accompanied, he joined, or he coupled; which our translation explains as "bringing with oneself." Ecclesiastes 8: *and this alone he shall bring with him from his labor.* And in Genesis 29: *Now at this time my husband will be joined to me.* And in Isaiah 56: *he who clings to the Lord.* From this comes the noun meaning an addition, an accumulation, or an increase. Proverbs 4: *It shall give to your head increases of grace.*

**לח** [L-CH] **Green, fresh, moist.** Ezekiel 17: "And I dried the **green** wood." And Numbers 6: "He shall not eat **fresh** or dried grapes." Likewise in Genesis 30: "**Green** poplar rods," though in the Hebrew text this is written in the singular.

**לח** [L-CH] **Splendor, re-flowering, greenness and vigor, and good facial color.** From the last chapter of Deuteronomy: instead of what we read, "Neither were his teeth moved," <note>A description of Moses at the end of his life.</note> the Hebrews more accurately explain it as: "And his **beauty** had not fled." **לט** [L-T] **Secretly, solitary, hiddenly and with silence.** Judges 4: "And she entered **hiddenly** and with silence." Perhaps this form is due to a missing *aleph* in the middle.

**לוט** [L-W-T] **He wrapped, covered, or hid.** 1 Samuel 21: "It is **wrapped** in a cloak behind the ephod." A transformation between the letters *vav* and *aleph* can be found here, as can be seen above in the word <term>LA’AT</term> <note>original: לאט</note>.

**לוט** [L-W-T] **Aromatic liquid**, which our translation calls <term>stacte</term> <note>A fragrant resinous gum or oil used in incense; the term "stacte" is from the Greek for "distilled."</note>.

This word is often written with a <term>dagesh</term> <note>A small dot placed inside a Hebrew letter to indicate it should be emphasized or doubled.</note> to distinguish it from the entry above.

**[Hebrew: לָחַךְ]** He licked, lapped up, bit off, or gnawed. <note>original: "Lambit. linxit. mordicus carpsit. rosit."</note> Numbers 22: "Thus this people will consume all who dwell in our borders, just as an ox is accustomed to pluck up grass even to the roots." <note>The original Latin transcription uses "desebit," likely a scribal error for "delebit," meaning "will destroy" or "will erase."</note> In this passage, the present word is translated as "to destroy" and "to pluck up even to the roots." Literally, the word sounds like this: "Now the crowd will gnaw away everything around us just as the ox gnaws the grass of the field." Also Psalm 72: "His enemies shall lick the dust." <note>original: "terram lingent" — literally "lick the earth."</note>

**[Hebrew: לָחַם]** He ate. <note>original: "Comedit"</note> Proverbs 23: "Do not eat with an envious man." <note>original: "Ne comedas cum homine invido"</note> In that passage, the text has: "Do not eat the bread of an evil eye." But the noun form of this verb—namely **lehem** <term>Lehem: The standard Hebrew word for bread, though its root implies "consumption" or "feeding" generally.</term>—signifies not only bread but also food or nourishment in general. For example, 1 Samuel 14: when Saul had forbidden **Lehem**—which our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> translates as "bread," though less accurately—Jonathan then broke the rule by dipping [his rod] into a honeycomb. So also in Nehemiah 9: "You also gave them bread from heaven," and it is well known that this refers to manna. From this, it is clear how the passage in Psalm 78 should be explained: "Man ate the bread of angels," meaning their food. Proverbs 23: "When you sit to eat with a prince." It signifies not only bread but also flesh, as in Zephaniah 1: "And their bodies like dung," which the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translated more accurately as: "And their flesh like the dung of oxen." They also explain the verse in Job 20, "He shall rain his war upon him," in this way: "He shall rain upon him in his flesh." It also signifies an offering, as in Leviticus 21: "Yet he shall eat of the breads which are offered in the sanctuary," which the Hebrews and Chaldeans <note>Aramaic-speaking scholars and translators</note> interpret as: "He shall eat the offering of his God from the holy of holies and from the holy things." Onkelos <note>The author of the standard Aramaic paraphrase (Targum) of the Torah</note> translated this as **korban**, which means "offering." Thus, the same word generally signifies everything we eat. Leviticus 22: "He shall be nourished by the foods of his father." It is a general term for all nourishment, as Rabbi Joseph Kimhi <note>A 12th-century Spanish-Jewish grammarian and teacher</note> writes on Jeremiah 11 regarding the verse: "Let us put wood into his bread" <note>This is a difficult idiomatic phrase usually interpreted as "let us destroy the tree with its fruit (or food)."</note>.

**[Hebrew: מִלְחָמָה]** War. <note>original: "Bellũ"</note> It is called this because it is a "consumption" and "devouring" by the sword on the part of both combatants. Exodus 17: "And the war of God shall be against Amalek." And in Exodus 15: "The Lord is a man of war," meaning, according to Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the preeminent medieval French commentator</note>, the author of the battle; or as Onkelos the Chaldean understands it: "Adonai <note>The Lord</note> is the master of victory in battle." From this comes the following verb:

**[Hebrew: לָחַם]** He fought. <note>original: "Pugnauit"</note> Psalm 35: "Fight against those who fight me."

...and to be stammering. Isaiah 32:4: *and the tongue of the stammerers shall speak quickly*. <note>The author is discussing the Hebrew root for stuttering or speaking a foreign language.</note> This involves a metathesis <note>original: "catametathesin" — a Greek grammatical term for the transposition of letters</note> as seen below under the letter *Ayin* before *Lamed*. And in Isaiah 28:11, according to the Septuagint <note>The early Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> interpreters, it refers to the "mockery of lips." Our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate, the standard Bible of the time</note> reads: *For with stammering lips*. It is as if he were saying: "With a stuttering and mocking lip," as in 2 Chronicles 30:10: *They laughed them to scorn and mocked them*.

**לעג** <term>Barbarus</term> <note>original: "לעג" (La'ag) — meaning to mock, deride, or speak unintelligibly</note>. According to the Jews, this term is used for anyone who does not speak the "Holy Tongue"—that is, the Hebrew language. Psalm 114:1: *From a people of strange language*. Concerning this, Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator</note> writes that there is an easy exchange between the letters *Lamed* [L] and *Nun* [N] and vice versa. Moreover, a coarse, robust, and imprudent man is called *noez*, as was explained earlier under the letter *Yod*.

**לעט** <term>Poured</term> <note>original: "לעט" (La'at) — to feed or provide a swallow of food</note>. Genesis 25:30: *Give me some of that red stew, for I am exceedingly faint*. Rabbi Solomon explains it in this way: "And Esau said to Jacob, 'I will open my mouth, and you, I pray, pour this food into it.'" Rabbi David Kimhi <note>Also known as Radak, a celebrated grammarian and commentator from Provence</note> interprets it as: "Please make me eat." Our translation <note>The Vulgate</note> translates the sense of the passage rather than the word itself.

**לענה** <term>Wormwood</term> <note>original: "לענה" (La'anah) — a bitter plant often used as a metaphor for sorrow or judgment</note>. With the addition of a soft breathing *He* at the end, it signifies wormwood. Jeremiah 9:15: *Behold, I will feed this people with wormwood*. And Lamentations 3:15: *He has made me drunk with wormwood*. Also in the same chapter: *Wormwood and gall*.

**לפיד** <term>Lamp</term> <note>original: "לפיד" (Lappid) — a torch or flame</note>. Isaiah 62:1: *As a lamp that burneth*. Others say it refers to a torch or a lit firebrand, or any such burning. This is how Onkelos <note>The author of the famous Aramaic paraphrase (Targum) of the Torah</note> translated it into Aramaic in Exodus 20:18: *And all the people saw the thunderings and the torches*.

**לפת** <term>Embraced</term> <note>original: "לפת" (Lafat) — to twist, grasp, or turn</note>, or "clasped"; he took hold of. Judges 16:29: *And taking hold of the two pillars*. Rabbi David Kimhi explains this word in his commentaries on the "Four" <note>Referring to the Former Prophets: Joshua, Judges, Samuel, and Kings</note> as "he inclined," "he bent," or "he overturned." It is used in the passive voice in Ruth 3:8: *The man was startled and troubled*. For this, the Hebrews read: *He was startled and bent over*. Others read it in the passive as *he was embraced*.

THE BOOK

**Melzar** <note>original: "מלצר"</note> The letter *mem* indicates a steward of the house, a master of the court, or a cellarer, whom the ancient Latins called a *promus* <note>a servant in charge of the larder</note> or a *condus* <note>a storekeeper</note>. In the first chapter of Daniel: *And Daniel said to Malassar.*

**Laqaq** <note>original: "לקק"</note> He licks or lapped. In the twenty-first chapter of the third book of Kings <note>modern 1 Kings 21:19</note>: *In this place where the dogs licked the blood of Naboth, they shall also lick your blood.*

**Laqach** <note>original: "לקח"</note> He took, received, or carried. In the twentieth chapter of Genesis: *Because of the woman whom you have taken.* And in the twenty-seventh chapter of the same: *He took my birthright before and now a second time he has snatched away my blessing.* It is also found with the first letter missing <note>the imperative form "take"</note>. In the twenty-second chapter of Genesis: *Take your son.* And in the fifteenth chapter of the same: *Take for me, he said, a three-year-old heifer.* In other cases, it is a perfect three-letter verb, as in the fifth chapter of Genesis: *Because God took him.* Although in conjugation it loses the primary letter *Lamed* through the <term>Ethan letters</term> <note>the letters Aleph, Taw, He, and Nun used to form future tenses</note>, the letter *Qoph* itself assumes a <term>Dagesh</term> point <note>a grammatical dot used to double a consonant to compensate for a missing letter</note>, as the art of grammar prescribes. From this come nouns and participles, as in the second chapter of Genesis: *Because she was taken from man.*

**Malqachayim** <note>original: "מלקחים"</note> Tongs or forceps. In the sixth chapter of Isaiah: *Which he had taken with tongs from the altar.* It is written in the plural because it consists of two parts; it is also used for lamp-snuffers. In the twenty-fifth chapter of Exodus: *Also the snuffers.*

**Malqoach** <note>original: "מלקוח"</note> Booty, especially regarding cattle and beasts of burden. In the thirty-first chapter of Numbers: *The booty and all that they had captured, both of humans and beasts.* For three words are placed there signifying "prey": the first refers to the captivity of humans; the second to the driving off of beasts; the third to the looting of utensils.

**Malqach** <note>original: "מלקח"</note> The jaw or throat. In Psalm 21 <note>Psalm 22 in modern Bibles</note>: *My tongue has stuck to my jaws.*

**Miqqach** <note>original: "מקח"</note> Merchandise, sale, or something for sale. In the tenth chapter of Nehemiah: *Those who bring in wares and all things for use.*

**Miqqach** <note>original: "מקח"</note> Desire or greed. In the second book of Chronicles, chapter 19: *Nor the desire for gifts* <note>referring to bribery</note>.

**Leqach** <note>original: "לקח"</note> Doctrine, precept, or law. In the twenty-ninth chapter of Isaiah: *And the whisperers shall learn the law,* for which the <term>LXX</term> <note>the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> interpreted as "obedience," and Jonathan the Chaldean <note>referring to the Targum, an Aramaic paraphrase of the Bible</note> interpreted as "precept" or "doctrine." So too in Deuteronomy 32: *May my doctrine drop as the rain.*

## SECOND

**He gathered** <note>original: *לקט* (*leket*)</note>. He collected. Exodus 16: "But on the sixth day they gathered double food." You will find several forms of this word in that same chapter.

**Shepherd’s Bag** <note>original: *ילקוט* (*yalkut*)</note>. A shepherd’s pouch or a sack in which things are collected. 1 Samuel 17: "And he put them into a shepherd’s bag."

**Late Rain** <note>original: *לקש* (*lekesh*)</note>. The second rain or the late-season shower, as in Amos 7: "In the beginning of the sprouting of the late rain; and behold, it was the late rain after the king’s mowings." It also takes the letter *mem* at the beginning <note>forming the word *malkosh*</note>. Deuteronomy 11: "He will give the rain for your land in its season, the early and the late rain." [ornament]

**Kneaded** <note>original: *לשד* (*leshad*)</note>. Something worked and, if one may speak this way, "made into bread." Numbers 11: "With a taste like oily bread." However, the masters of Hebrew explain this same word as meaning "moist" or "fresh."

**Chamber** <note>original: *לשכה* (*lishkah*)</note>. A tavern, a dining room, or a <term>triclinium</term> <note>a formal dining room with three couches used for reclining during meals in the ancient world</note>. 1 Samuel 9: "He brought them into the dining room." And Nehemiah 10: "To the treasury of the house of our God."

**Ligure** <note>original: *לשם* (*leshem*)</note>. A precious stone placed in the third row of the "Breastplate of Judgment," though our translation calls it a <term>ligure</term> <note>a gemstone mentioned in the Bible, possibly zircon or tourmaline</note>. Exodus 28: "In the third row, a ligure, an agate, and an amethyst." Others write that it is a topaz; the Chaldeans call it a "crab stone," while others call it the Lydian stone.

**Tongue** <note>original: *לשון* (*lashon*)</note>. Tongue. Psalm 12: "And the tongue that speaks great things." It also signifies speech. Genesis 10: "Each according to his own language." It also signifies a ray or a geometer’s rod, a land-surveyor’s line, or even a boundary stone (called a <term>limitaris</term>) which is made in the shape of a tongue. Joshua 15: "From the tongue of land that looks toward the south"; likewise "from the tongue of the sea." Among the Hebrew masters, it also signifies an "exposition" <note>an interpretation or explanation of a text</note>, just as the Greeks use the term <term>glossomata</term> and we use "glosses" (a feminine plural noun). Zechariah 8: "Out of all the languages of the nations."

**Garment** <note>original: *לתך* (*letekh*)</note>. With the letter *mem* placed before it and a *he* added at the end <note>forming the word *meltakhah*</note>, it signifies a robe or clothing. 2 Kings 10: "And he said to him who was in charge of the vestry." However, Rabbi David Kimhi writes in his *Book of Roots* <note>a famous 12th-century Hebrew grammar and dictionary</note> that it means a chest...

**מאד** <note>Hebrew root: *me’od*</note> [Handwritten Hebrew notes: <unclear>unclear</unclear>]

Deeply. **Exceedingly.** Genesis 1: *And they were **exceedingly** good.* <note>original: "ualde bona"</note> And Psalm 119: *Do not forsake me **utterly**.* <note>original: "usquequaque"</note> Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the primary translator of the Latin Vulgate</note> translates this more correctly as: *Do not forsake me **too much**.* And Genesis 15: *Your reward is **exceedingly** great.* And Joshua 1: *Be **exceedingly** strong,* that is, powerfully; from which it is understood as validity, strength, might, and power, faculty, or substance. Deuteronomy 6: *And with all your **strength**,* which the Hebrew masters explain as: "Greatly, and with all one’s powers."

**מאה** <note>Hebrew root: *me’ah*</note> **One hundred.** 2 Chronicles 36: *And he fined the land **one hundred** talents of silver.* From this, by changing the final letter *he* [ה] into a *thau* [ת], the adverb for the number **a hundredfold** <note>original: "centies"</note> is signified. Ecclesiastes 8: *A sinner, because he does evil **a hundred times**.* The Hebrew gloss <note>original: "glosa hebraica" — a marginal or interlinear explanation</note> says this means "for a hundred days" or "a hundred years."

**מאום** <note>Hebrew root: *me’um*</note> **Anything,** or **nothing,** or **scarcely anything,** or **the smallest bit.** Numbers 22: *Will I be able to speak **anything** except what God has put in my mouth?* Deuteronomy 13: *And let **nothing** of that cursed thing <term>anathema: something set apart for destruction or banned</term> cling to your hand.* This word often takes the *h* aspiration at the end, but it is also found without it, as in Job 31: *And if a **spot** <note>or "blemish"</note> has clung to my hands,* which some think should be interpreted as "the smallest bit." However, that word is a single syllable, while this one is two syllables, as will be shown below.

**מאן** <note>Hebrew root: *ma’en*</note> **Refused.** He was unwilling. Numbers 22: *Balaam **refused** to come with us.* From this comes the noun for "one who is unwilling." Exodus 10: *But if you resist and **will not** let them go.* This phrasing in Hebrew is read: *Because if you are **unwilling** to release my people.* The substantive verb <note>the verb "to be"</note> is frequently understood or implied here, following the custom of the Hebrews.

**מאס** <note>Hebrew root: *ma’as*</note> **Rejected.** Despised, looked down upon, hated, cast away, or abhorred. Psalm 53: *Because God has **despised** them.* And Isaiah 30: *Because you have **rejected** the word.* And Hosea 4: *Because you have rejected knowledge, I will reject you*—meaning you have despised it.

**מאר** <note>Hebrew root: *ma’ar*</note> **Pricked** or **stung.** Leviticus 13: *It shall be considered a spreading <note>or "infectious"</note> leprosy,* for which the Hebrews read: *it is a **stinging** leprosy,* according to the testimony of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Shlomo Yitzhaki, or Rashi (1040–1105), a famed medieval commentator</note>. Or, according to Nicholas of Lyra <note>A 14th-century Franciscan scholar who emphasized literal and Hebrew-informed biblical interpretation</note>, it means **corrosive.** It is also taken to mean defective or accursed.

**מגד** [Meged] **Delicate. Sweet.** According to Rabbi Solomon <note>original: "rabi Salomonē," referring to the famous Jewish commentator Rashi (1040–1105)</note> in Deuteronomy 33.
In the blessing of Joseph, where this word is often used, it is interpreted as "apples" and "fruits" according to our common translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note>. For we read there of the "apples of heaven," and likewise of the "apples of the fruits of the sun," and "apples of the eternal hills," and the "fruits of the earth." In all these places, the Hebrews read "from the sweetness" or "from the delicate things" or "delights." Also in Song of Songs 4: "With the fruits of apples," which the Hebrews more correctly read as: "With sweet and delicate fruits." The Chaldeans <note>Aramaic speakers</note> call these *magdenin*, from which the same letter *nun* is preserved in the feminine plural, as in Genesis 24: "He also offered gifts to her brothers and mother." Where the Hebrews have: "He offered delicate things," that is, the sweet fruits of the land of Israel. For thus Rabbi Solomon explains the feminine form through the masculine.

**מגל** [Magal] **Sickle.** Joel, the last chapter: "Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe." And Jeremiah 50: "And him who handles the sickle in the time of harvest."

**מגן** [Magan] **Closed. Protected.** Genesis 14: "By whose protection the enemies are in your hands." The Hebrews have it: "He who shut your enemies into your hands." Others say: "He who bound or rebuked," with which the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> translation seems to agree. From this comes "protection" or "shield," as in Genesis 15: "I am your protector." And Deuteronomy 33: "The shield of your help." And Proverbs 4: "A glorious crown shall protect you." And Hosea 11: "I will protect you, Israel."

**מגר** [Magar] **Dragged down. Cast down. Dashed.** Psalm 89: "And you have dashed his throne to the ground." Jerome, in his 'Hebrew Truth' <note>original: "Hebraica veritate," referring to Jerome's translation directly from Hebrew rather than the Greek Septuagint</note>, translates it thus: "And you have dragged down his throne to the earth."

**מד** [Mad] **A garment or linen tunic**, which we call a shirt <note>original: "camisiam"</note>. Leviticus 6: "The priest shall put on his tunic." And Psalm 109: "And he clothed himself with cursing as with a garment." It is declined in the plural in both the masculine and feminine forms.

**מדד** [Madad] **Measured.** Isaiah 40: "Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand?" And Numbers 35: "Which are outside the walls of the cities," where the text of the words is shortened; for the Hebrew letters sound like this: "And you shall measure outside the city the eastern corner, two thousand cubits." And Hosea 1: "As the sand of the sea..."

which is without measure. For which the Hebrews say: *That which shall not be measured.*
<term>Middah</term> <note>Hebrew: מדה</note> Manner and measure. Zechariah, chapter two: *And behold, a measuring line* <note>original: "funiculus mēsurę"</note>, which the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the influential Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> translated as "geometers." From this, it is said of men of tall stature in Numbers, chapter thirteen: *The people whom we saw are of tall stature.* For this, the "truth" <note>The author uses "truth" (veritas) to refer to the original Hebrew text, a common practice among scholars like Jerome.</note> has: *And all the people we saw in it are men of measures*—with "great" being understood. This is also used for inanimate things, such as in Jeremiah, chapter twenty-two: *I will build myself a wide house*, for which the truth has: *I will build myself a house of measures*—with "great" being understood. They also use it to describe a span of space, so that it may be seen that every dimension is named by this word. Joshua, chapter three: *A space of two thousand cubits.*

<term>Medinah</term> <note>Hebrew: מדינה</note> Province, city, straight path, or contention. Esther, chapter one: *Over a hundred and twenty-seven provinces.* And in Judges, chapter five, where we read: *and you who sit in judgment*, the Hebrews explain it as: *And you who sit above the place so named.* For they say it is a proper name for a place, or a path, or a road. A similar reading is found in the book of Joshua. See the rest under the letter *daleth*.

<term>Madua</term> <note>Hebrew: מדוע</note> Why, whether, wherefore, what. Genesis, chapter twenty-six: *Why* <note>original: "Quid"</note> *have you come to me, a man whom you hate?* And Isaiah, chapter five: *wherefore* <note>original: "an. q̃"</note> *I expected that it should produce grapes.* Numbers, chapter sixteen: *Why are you lifted up above the people of the Lord?* Many believe this to be a compound word.

<term>Mah</term> <note>Hebrew: מה</note> What. Esther, chapter five: *What is your petition, that it may be given to you, and for what do you ask?* Exodus, chapter three: *What is his name, what shall I say?* It also signifies "when," as in Psalm seventy-nine: *How long* <note>original: "Vsq̃ quo"</note> *O Lord, will you be angry forever?* And with the letter *lamed* at the beginning <note>Hebrew: למה (Lammah)</note>, it signifies "on account of," as in Exodus, chapter five, where we have: *why have you sent me?* The Hebrews read: *On account of what have you sent me?* It also takes the letter *shin* at the beginning <note>Hebrew: שמה (Shemah)</note>, as in the Song of Songs, chapter one: *Lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions*, in place of "on account of what." It also signifies "how" or "how much," as in Psalm thirty-one: *How great is the abundance of your sweetness!* And Psalm one hundred thirty-three: *Behold how good and how pleasant.* Regarding this, see what the most learned Master Paul, Bishop of Burgos <note>Paul of Burgos (c. 1351–1435) was a Jewish convert to Christianity whose "Additiones" to Nicholas of Lyra's biblical commentaries were highly respected.</note>, wrote more extensively in his second addition to chapter thirty-eight of the prophet Isaiah. And if the letter *caph* is placed before it <note>Hebrew: כמה (Kammah)</note>, it then signifies quantity, as in Genesis, chapter forty-seven: *How many are the days of the years of your life?* It also signifies "how often." Job, chapter twenty-one: *How often is the lamp of the wicked extinguished?*

<note>Hebrew root: M-H-M-H</note> **He neglected, postponed, delayed, or deferred.** Psalm 119: *I am prepared and have not been disturbed.* Jerome, in his psalter, translates this more correctly as: *I hurried and did not neglect.* See also Isaiah 29: *Be stunned and amazed,* where he interpreted "stupor" specifically in the sense of a lingering slowness. <note original: " מוֹט ">**Pole**</note>. A stake, a pole, a bar, a spear, or a staff upon which things are suspended and carried, or moved from one place to another. Numbers 13: *Which two men carried on a pole.* And Numbers 4: *And they shall bring in the bars.*

<note original: " מוֹטָה ">**Yoke**</note>. A yoke for beasts of burden. Our translation <note>The author refers to the Latin Vulgate bible here.</note> uses the word "chain" in Jeremiah 28: *And Hananiah the prophet took the chain from the neck of Jeremiah the prophet and broke it.* The Hebrew masters refer this to a "yoke," so that the phrasing is consistent. Among them, the word *motah* is feminine in gender. According to their reliable authors, it signifies a "phalanx"—a long piece of wood that pierces the yoke where the oxen are placed. Because this is sometimes forked, the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> translate it as "fork" in the passage from Jeremiah mentioned above.

For example, in Psalm 118, where we read: *And in the name of the Lord, for I have been avenged upon them,* the Hebrew text has: *Because I will cut them off, I will sever them, I will cut them down.* With a doubled *lamed* through a paragogic addition <note>A linguistic term for adding a letter to the end of a word for emphasis or rhythm.</note>, as in Psalm 90: *In the evening it falls away and withers,* instead of "it shall be cut down." Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate.</note> translates this as "it is crushed." It appears thus in another form.

<note original: " מוּל ">**Opposite**</note>. Against, across from, before, or in front of. And Deuteronomy 1: *Opposite the Red Sea.* It also sometimes signifies the position of a place, as in 2 Kings 5: *And you shall come upon them from opposite the pear trees.* And Numbers 8: *Facing that part which the lampstand regards.* It is also sometimes written with an *aleph* after the *vav* with the same meaning of a location, as if from a region—for instance, Nehemiah 12: *And the second choir of those giving thanks went from the opposite side,* that is, from the same region.

**BOOK**

According to some Hebrew grammarians, there is sometimes a <term>cataparemptosis</term> <note>A grammatical term for the insertion of a letter into the middle of a word</note> through the insertion of the letter <term>Aleph</term>, which nonetheless remains a monosyllable; for example in Job 31: "If a stain has clung to my hands," which some translate as "ever so little" or "not even the least bit," as is found above.

**דמות** <note>Hebrew: *Demut*, meaning likeness</note> With the prefix *thau* <note>the letter Tav</note> and taking a feminine ending, it signifies a likeness, image, or effigy of things both physical and spiritual. Exodus 20: "Nor any likeness of what is in heaven above or what is on the earth below."

**מוץ** <note>Hebrew: *Mots*, meaning chaff</note> Chaff or that smallest part which is in the ears of grain, such as refuse. From this word, our translators often use "dust," as in Hosea 13: "Like dust carried away by a whirlwind," and Psalm 1: "Like dust which the wind drives away," and Zephaniah 2: "Like the dust of a passing day." Our translation also renders it as "chaff" <note>original: *fauillam*</note> in Job 21: "And like the chaff which the whirlwind scatters."

**מור** <note>Hebrew: *Mor*, meaning myrrh</note> Myrrh. Song of Solomon 1: "A bundle of myrrh is my beloved to me."

**מוש** <note>Hebrew: *Mush*, meaning to cease or depart</note> It ceased, it withdrew, it caused to withdraw—that is, it moved or took away. Zechariah 3: "And I will take away the iniquity of that land," for which the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>original: "lxx"; the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translated as "I will touch." Also Numbers 14: "They did not withdraw from the camps," and Exodus 13: "The pillar never failed." It is sometimes active and sometimes neutral; truly that which is found in Psalm 115: "They have hands and they shall not feel" is derived from a certain following primitive root.

**מות** <note>Hebrew: *Mut*, meaning to die</note> He died; by <term>syncope</term> <note>the loss of a letter or sound from the middle of a word</note>. 1 Samuel 26: "But the Philistines, seeing that he was dead." And Genesis 25: "He died in a good old age." And Ezekiel 28: "And you shall die in the destruction of the slain," which the Septuagint renders: "And you shall die the death of the wounded," where the *mem* is prefixed by <term>cataprothesis</term> <note>a grammatical term for adding a prefix</note>; and what follows, the Septuagint translated better than we did: "You shall die the deaths of the uncircumcised." This word is also found in the words of Isaiah 6: "In the year that King Uzziah died," and Genesis 47: "Why then do we die?" From this comes the transitive "heavy" form <note>Referring to the *Hiphil* or *Piel* verbal stems in Hebrew</note> in 2 Samuel 1: "I killed the Lord’s anointed," and Jeremiah 20: "Because he did not kill me from the womb," that is, put me to death.

**מזג** <note>Hebrew: *Mazag*, meaning to mix or pour</note> He mixed, served as a cupbearer, or poured into cups. Song of Solomon 7: "Never lacking mixed wine."

**מזה** <note>Hebrew root: M-Z-H</note> **Burning of hunger.** According to others, it means **madness**. According to others, a **small swelling or abscess**. From Deuteronomy 32: *They shall be consumed with hunger and birds shall devour them.* <note>original: "Conſumentur fame & deuorabunt eos aues"</note>

**מזח** <note>Hebrew root: M-Z-CH</note> **A fastening.** A binding, a belt, or a girdle. From Isaiah 23: *There is no more girdle for you.* And from Psalm 109: *And the belt with which he is always girded.*

**מזר** <note>Hebrew root: M-Z-R</note> With the letter *mem* placed before it, it becomes **mamzer**, according to Rabbi Jonah <note>Rabbi Jonah ibn Janah, a famous 11th-century grammarian</note>, and it signifies a **bastard** <note>original: "ſpurium"</note>. From Deuteronomy 23: *A mamzer (that is, one born of a prostitute) shall not enter the church.* Some Latin speakers, in error, pronounce this word with an 'n' <note>as "manzer" instead of "mamzer"</note>. Some, however, derive it from the word *zar* <note>meaning 'stranger'</note> mentioned above, saying the two letters *m* were added by <term>prothesis</term> <note>the addition of a sound or letter at the beginning of a word</note>.

**מזרות** <note>Hebrew: Mazzaroth</note> **The Morning Star** <note>original: "Lucifer"</note> or another constellation; so it is called in Job 38: *Can you bring forth the Morning Star in its season?* It is said to be like the word *mazala* <note>meaning constellation or destiny</note> by changing the 'l' <note>lamed</note> into an 'r' <note>resh</note>.

**מחה** <note>Hebrew root: M-CH-H</note> **He took away.** He wiped out or deleted. From Numbers 5: *And he shall blot them out with the most bitter waters.* And Psalm 51: *And blot out all my iniquities.* And Exodus 17: *In wiping out, I will wipe out the memory of Amalek from under heaven.* And in the <term>passive voice</term>, as in Psalm 69: *Let them be blotted out from the book of the living.* And Isaiah 25: *And the Lord God shall take away every tear.* And Isaiah 44: *I have blotted out your iniquities like a cloud.*

**מחה** <note>The same root used in a geographical sense</note> **It sloped.** It reached or was extended. From Numbers 34: *From there it shall reach toward the east to the Sea of Chinnereth* <note>The Sea of Galilee</note>.

**מחה** <note>The same root used for physical action</note> **He clapped.** He struck. Here, the letter *aleph* is sometimes used in place of *he*. As in Isaiah 55: *All the trees of the region shall clap their hands.* And Ezekiel 25: *Because you have clapped with your hand.*

**מחי** <note>Derived from the root meaning to strike</note> **A battering ram.** A wild ass, a ballista, or an engine of war with which walls are struck by throwing a mass of stones. Rabbi Judah and Rabbi Jonah derive this word from the verb above. Ezekiel 26: *And he shall set battering rams against your walls.*

**מחץ** <note>Hebrew root: M-CH-TZ</note> **He pierced through.** He wounded or shattered. Psalm 110: *He has shattered kings in the day of his wrath.* Jerome, in his translation of the Psalms from the <term>Hebrew Truth</term> <note>Jerome’s 'Hebraica Veritas', his translation of the Old Testament directly from Hebrew rather than the Greek Septuagint</note>, interprets this as "he struck." **מחק** [Machaq] He cut off. He took away. He subtracted. He removed. He put aside. And Isaiah 10: "And he is the staff himself."

### SECOND

Active and passive verb. Amos 4[:7]: "And I rained upon one city, and upon another city I rained not: one part was **rained upon**." <note>The author is highlighting the distinction between the active "I rained" and the passive "was rained upon" in the Latin and Hebrew texts.</note>

☞ Who or what. Deuteronomy 20[:5]: "**Who is the man?**" It seeks the substance or identity, sometimes a proper name and sometimes a common noun, of a human being alone. Whence Manoah, seeking the proper name of the substance of the angel speaking with him, said in Judges 13[:17]: "**Who is your name?**" <note>original: "Quis est nomen tuum"</note> For thus it is read in Hebrew, which we translate grammatically as "**What is your name?**" And in 1 Samuel 25[:10]: "**Who is David and who is the son of Jesse?**" Concerning which <term>Rabbi Moses of Gerona</term> <note>Also known as Nachmanides or Ramban, a 13th-century Spanish scholar.</note> says on Genesis 21[:7]: "**Who said to Abraham?**" for which we read, "**Who would have believed, having heard it, that Abraham [would have children]?**" And in common speech, when followed by a relative pronoun, it signifies "he," "she," or "it." Just as <term>Rabbi Moses the Egyptian</term> <note>The famous philosopher Maimonides.</note> says in the preface of the book he titled *The Guide for the Perplexed* <note>Latin: *Dux Neutrorum* or *Monstrator Oberrantium*</note>, namely: "I adjure, by Him who is blessed, every one who shall read [this]." <note>Hebrew: *mi she-kara*, meaning "he who reads."</note> Sometimes a relative pronoun does not follow, and then it signifies "someone," as in Job 5[:1]: "And turn to **someone** among the saints."

☞ Waters. As in Joshua 4[:7]: "**The waters of the Jordan failed.**" There you will also find that word doubled; so also <term>maim</term> <note>Hebrew: *mayim*, the word for water, which always appears in a plural-like form.</note>.

☞ Species, form, genus, or condition. Genesis 1[:12]: "**Producing fruit according to its kind.**" And in the last Psalm [150:4], where we read, "**Praise him with strings,**" the Hebrews have, "**Praise him in manifold condition**" or "**in many ways.**" <note>The author is noting a difference between the Latin Vulgate's "strings" and a Hebrew interpretation relating to the "variety" or "nature" of the praise.</note>

☞ An expressor, a wiper, a provoker, or one who milks. Proverbs 30[:33]: "**He who strongly presses the breasts to draw out milk expresses butter; and he who violently wipes [the nose] elicits blood; and he who provokes angers produces discords.**" There, the word <term>miz</term> <note>Hebrew: *mitz*, meaning pressure or squeezing.</note> is placed three times. My teacher Jacobus Johannes explained it as "expressed juice," as if saying: "Because the **expressed juice** of milk produces butter, and the **expressed juice** of the nose produces blood, and the **expressed juice** of angers produces a quarrel." From this, <term>mitz</term> <note>Hebrew: *mitz*</note> flowed, and <term>mitz</term> <note>Hebrew: *mitz*</note> is milked or expressed moisture.

☞ It perished, it was dissolved, it vanished. In Psalm 73[:8]: "**They have thought and spoken wickedness.**" Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Bible into Latin.</note> translated it as "**they mocked,**" but...

**מלל** [M-L-L] **He spoke or said.** This is frequently used in the Aramaic Targum <note>original: "thargum chaldaicum"</note>. Regarding this, Rabbi Moses of Gerona <note>Nachmanides (1194–1270), a major Spanish Sephardic scholar</note> writes <insert>that</insert> this word **מלל** [M-L-L] signifies either praise or reproach depending on the subject matter. Here it signifies praise, but elsewhere it signifies shame, such as: "Who is Abimelech?" and 1 Samuel chapter 25: "Who is David and who is the son of Jesse?" ...is there any man who would be so trusted, even before Abraham, if he were to announce this miracle to him? Similarly, in Psalm 106: "Who shall speak of the powers of the Lord?" From this comes the name **<term>Millah (מִלָּה)</term>** <note>A Hebrew term for "word" or "speech."</note>, that is: a phrase, a speech, or a word. Psalm 139: "And there is no speech on my tongue." It is also declined in the plural with a masculine termination, sometimes ending with the letter *n*, as in Job 18: "Until what end will you cast about words?" and sometimes with the letter *m*, as in Job 16: "I also could comfort you with speeches." Hebrew grammarians consider this to be one of the parts of speech which we call an indeclinable or "consignificative" part <note>original: "consignificatiuam"; in medieval grammar, this refers to words like prepositions or conjunctions that only have meaning when paired with other words</note>, as will be shown in our work on the art of grammar.

And it is sometimes found without the letter *aleph*, but I also sometimes find the letter *vav* in place of *aleph*. Ezekiel 41: "By the measure of a reed of six cubits' space," which is more correctly the "full" or "filled" measure of the reed. In that passage, certain Hebrew codices <note>ancient manuscript books</note>, both printed and handwritten, contain the *aleph*, but those large and most corrected volumes <note>likely referring to high-quality Masoretic manuscripts used as standards</note> contain the letter *vav* with a *holem* <note>a vowel mark indicating an "o" sound</note> in place of the *aleph*.

**<term>Millo (מִלּוֹא)</term>** Millo, a proper name of an empty space in the city of Jerusalem near the wall that had not yet been built up, which Solomon filled with buildings. 1 Kings 9 <note>The text cites "3 Kings," following the older Vulgate numbering system</note>: "Then he built the Millo." It seems to derive its origin from the verb mentioned above <note>Mala, meaning "to fill"</note>.

**<term>Malach (מָלַח)</term>** He salted, or seasoned with salt. Leviticus 2: "Whatever you offer as a sacrifice, you shall season with salt." From this comes "salt," as found in the same passage.

**<term>Malach (מָלַח)</term>** He devastated; he wore away; he corrupted. It is read in the passive sense in Isaiah 51: "For the heavens shall vanish like smoke." And Psalm 107: "A fruitful land into saltiness," for which the Hebrews read "a fruitful land unto devastation."

**<term>Malluach (מַלּוּחַ)</term>** A certain herb. Job 30: "And they ate herbs." The Hebrew reading is: "And they plucked or tore at herbs that grow wild and are held in contempt." David Kimhi <note>A famous 12th-13th century Jewish rabbi and grammarian</note> writes that the nettle is called by this name.

**ממלח** <note>A form of the root MLCh, meaning salted or seasoned</note> Finely scattered; broken up. In the manner of spice-merchants who mix many finely ground powders together. This is read in Exodus thirty: *Carefully mixed.* <note>Exodus 30:35</note> The Aramaic Translation of Onkelos <note>The Targum Onkelos, a 2nd-century translation of the Torah</note> explains it as "blended." Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Shlomo Yitzhaki, or Rashi, a famous 11th-century French commentator</note> says it refers to a fine grinding, beautifully mixing one substance with another.

**מלח** <note>MLCh</note> A steersman of oars; a sailor; a rower. Ezekiel twenty-seven: *All the ships of the sea and their sailors.* <note>Ezekiel 27:9</note> The Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translated this as "rowers." According to Rabbi Solomon, it is derived from the word above because sailors "mix" the waters with their oars and beat them. Similarly in Jonah 1: *And the sailors were afraid.*

**מלט** <note>MLT</note> He saved, delivered, or rescued. Genesis nineteen: *Save your life.* Also: *nor can I be saved on the mountain.* Also further below: *It is small, and I shall be saved in it.* Also: *Hurry and be saved there.* <note>These references all concern Lot’s escape from the destruction of Sodom in Genesis 19.</note> It also signifies "he escaped." Job one: *And I alone have escaped.*

**מלך** <note>MLK</note> He reigned. Fourth Kings eight <note>In modern Bibles, this is 2 Kings 8:17</note>: *And he reigned eight years in Jerusalem.* And Jeremiah thirty-three: *And a king shall reign.* See there the noun and the verb. From this comes "kingdom" and other such words. First Kings twenty-four <note>Modern 1 Samuel 24:20</note>: *And now I know most certainly that you will reign and will hold the kingdom of Israel in your hand.* The noun uses the letter <term>Mem</term> as a prefix, and the verb uses an inserted <term>Vav</term>. Sometimes it is found written with an <term>Aleph</term> in the middle; be careful there not to think it refers to an "angel," which is written with an <term>Aleph</term>. <note>The author warns the reader not to confuse "Melekh" (king) with "Malakh" (angel), which sound similar but are spelled differently in Hebrew.</note> Second Kings eleven <note>Modern 2 Samuel 11:1</note>: *At the time when kings are accustomed to go out to war.* There is something unique in the Bible here, as the Hebrew annotation suggests.

**מלך** <note>MLK</note> He appointed, consulted, or thought. Nehemiah five: *And my heart thought.* <note>Nehemiah 5:7</note>

**מלך** <note>MLK</note> A demon; Moloch; an idol; the lord of the heavenly form who holds many ranks among the astrologers. Jerome <note>The 4th-century translator of the Vulgate Bible</note> thinks it is Lucifer <note>The Morning Star</note> in his commentaries on Amos chapter five: *And you carried the tabernacle of your Moloch.* <note>Amos 5:26</note> But Rabbi Moses of Gerona <note>The 13th-century scholar Nachmanides, also known as Ramban</note> says on Leviticus twenty: *If anyone gives of his seed to the idol Moloch,* that it is not a proper name of an idol, but generally refers to anything to which sacrifice is made wrongly and profanely instead of to God the Creator. This sacrifice is called <term>idolatry</term> in Greek, and he provides a long teaching on this in the aforementioned place. Others say it is a star; others say it is a birth chart or "selection" <note>A choice of an auspicious time</note> which the Magi <note>Ancient astrologers or wise men</note> call <term>syderation</term> <note>The supposed influence of the stars on human affairs</note>.

[Hebrew: מָלַץ] **He sweetened.** <note>original: *Dulcorauit*</note> Psalm 119: "How sweet are your words to my throat." And Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate</note> says: "How sweet is your speech to my throat." The Hebrews, according to Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi, the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator</note>, interpret it thus: "How sweetened," or "how smooth to my palate are your words." From this comes "eloquence," "eloquent," etc.

[Hebrew: מָלַק] A <term>verb</term> signifying the priestly ritual in the sacrifices of birds to be offered. I cannot express this in a single Latin word. Perhaps the Greeks would say *kinzin* <note>original: *kinzin*; likely a corruption of *knizein*, meaning to nip or prick</note>, that is, to cut, to incise, or to divide. But my teacher, a man from the Jewish people of no small learning, Jacob Jehiel Loans <note>Jacob ben Jehiel Loans was a physician to Emperor Frederick III and taught Hebrew to the humanist Johannes Reuchlin</note>, wishing to express the specific nature of the word, explained it through a longer phrase: *malak* means he cut the neck of the bird with a fingernail during sacrifices. Jerome says this in the first chapter of Leviticus: "And with the head twisted back to the neck and the place of the wound broken open." For this Hebrew phrase—namely *vmalak roso*—the meaning is "and he shall cut its head with a fingernail."

[Hebrew: מִן] **From, of, by, out of.** <note>The Hebrew preposition *Min*</note> Ezekiel 39: "From 그날 [that day] and thereafter." Also Genesis 2: "But a spring rose up *from* the earth." Likewise in chapter 3: "Except that you have eaten *from* the tree of which I commanded you that you should not eat." It also takes a prefix, as in Jeremiah 7: "From age unto age." And it takes a suffix, as in Job 20: "This I know from the beginning, since man was placed." More often it is uttered without the letter *nun*, using only the letter *mem*. Psalm 112: "From this time forth and forevermore."

[Hebrew: מִן] **Not.** For this is how Onkelos the Chaldean <note>Onkelos was a famous convert and author of the Targum Onkelos, the standard Aramaic translation of the Torah</note> translates it in Deuteronomy 33, where we also read: "And let those who hate him *not* rise up."

[Hebrew: מִן] **More, or above, or than.** This is a mark of comparison. As in Proverbs 22: "A good name is better *than* great riches; for good favor is *above* silver and gold." When followed by a consonant, the letter *nun* is dropped by <term>apocope</term> <note>The shortening of a word by omitting the final sound or syllable</note>.

[Hebrew: מִן] This is also written with the letter *yod* [as *Minim*] by others, as noted above. It is a musical stringed instrument according to Rabbi Solomon. As in the last Psalm [Psalm 150]: "Praise him with strings and the organ." <note>The author uses *organo*, which in a Renaissance context refers to any complex musical instrument, often a pipe organ or a series of pipes</note>.

[Hebrew: מָנָה] **He numbered.** 2 Kings 24: "Go, number Israel and Judah." And its <term>gerund</term> form appears in Psalm 90: "To number your right hand, make it known in this way." Here Jerome, better and more correctly than the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>, translated it thus in his Psalter: "So show us that our days may be numbered."

<meta>This page continues the philological analysis of Hebrew roots, specifically those related to the concept of counting, portions, and numbering (M-N-H). It follows a discussion of the deity "Meni" or "Fate" mentioned in Isaiah.</meta>

# THE BOOK

But Rabbi Jonah <note>Rabbi Jonah ibn Janah, a preeminent medieval Hebrew grammarian and lexicographer</note> writes that it is a noun with the article and not a verb. And in Isaiah 65: "I will **number** you for the sword." From this comes the noun for "number," with the *he* [ה] converted into *yod* [י], and sometimes a *nun* [ן] added at the end. In the same chapter of Isaiah: "And you pour out drink offerings upon it," where the text has, "and you fulfill the libation by **number**" <note>original Latin: *numero*; the author is discussing the deity Meni, often associated with Fate or Number</note>, that is, you sacrifice to the seven planets. To this the Septuagint translation <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament, often abbreviated as LXX</note> agrees: "And you fill the cup for the **demon**." From this, the Hebrew grammarians say that it is a general name for the stars. And David Kimhi <note>A famous medieval rabbi and grammarian, often called the Radak</note> writes in his commentaries on Isaiah that it is the name of a star. However, I believe "number" is indicated in this way: that the scripture noted idolaters who follow the philosophy of Pythagoras <note>Pythagoras was an ancient Greek philosopher who believed that numbers were the fundamental reality of the universe</note> by serving **number**, to which the Scripture alludes in its usual manner when it follows in the text: "I will **number** you for the sword."

**מָנֶה** <note>Hebrew: *Maneh*</note> A certain weight which we call a *mna*, a *mina*, or a pound. As in Ezra chapter 2: "Five thousand **minas** of silver," and Nehemiah chapter 7: "And two thousand **minas** of silver."

**מָנָה** <note>Hebrew: *Manah* (verb)</note> He decreed, appointed, or prepared. Daniel chapter 1: "Who **appointed** for you food and drink." And Job chapter 7: "And he **numbered** [appointed] wearisome nights for me," which has not been correctly translated, but should be rendered: "And nights have **prepared** labor for me." And by <term>apocope</term><note>A linguistic term for the dropping of the last letter or syllable of a word</note> in Jonah chapter 2: "And the Lord **prepared** a great fish."

**מָנָה** <note>Hebrew: *Manah* (noun)</note> A part, a lot, a portion, a gift, an office, a debt, a decree, or what pertains. Leviticus chapter 8: "For his **portion** as the Lord had commanded him." And Psalm 63: "They shall be a **portion** for foxes"; for it ought to be read in the singular and not the plural. And Psalm 16: "The Lord is the **portion** of my inheritance and of my cup," which in Hebrew is: "The Lord is the lot of my **portion**." And it is sometimes found with an <term>epenthesis</term><note>The addition of a letter into the middle of a word</note> of the letter *aleph* [א] to signify the turn or lot of the priests. It is also found by apocope as *man*, which we call **manna**, in Exodus chapter 16: "And the house of Israel called its name **man**." Because they did not know by what name to call that food sent from heaven, they wanted to say *man* in a general sense, as if it were a gift; thus Nehemiah chapter 9: "And your **manna** you did not withhold from their mouth."

**מִנְחָה** <note>Hebrew: *Minchah*</note> With the letter *he* [ה] added at the end, it signifies an offering, a sacrifice, a prayer, and an atonement. Leviticus chapter 7: "And every **sacrifice** of fine flour which is baked in the oven." And Psalm 141: "The lifting up of my hands as the evening **sacrifice**." And Ezra chapter 9: "And I sat mourning until the evening **sacrifice**."

SECOND [BOOK]

<term>Mana' [מנע]</term> He removed. He avoided or caused to avoid. He deprived or deposed. 
**Genesis 30**: "Who has deprived you of the fruit of the womb?" 
**Psalm 84**: "He will not withhold good things from those who walk in innocence." 
**Numbers 24**: "God has deprived you of honor."

<term>Manor [מנור]</term> A smooth and elongated piece of wood, like a pole, around which the weaver's warp is wound. Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Bible into Latin</note> calls it a "weaver's beam" <note>original Latin: *liciatorium*</note>. 
**1 Kings 17** <note>In modern Bibles, this is 1 Samuel 17, the story of Goliath</note>: "And the shaft of his spear was like a weaver's beam." 
The final letter should be written as a *resh* <note>the Hebrew letter 'r'</note> according to ancient and corrected books, though in many more recent volumes—and especially in printed ones—I find it written with a *daleth* <note>the Hebrew letter 'd'</note>.

<term>Masas [מסס]</term> It is dissolved. It has vanished. It fled. It perished. 
**Isaiah 10**: Where we read "and he will be a fugitive in terror," the Hebrew says "and he will be as one vanishing and fleeing." Jonathan <note>Referring to the Targum of Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary</note> explains this similarly in Aramaic. 
**Exodus 16**: "And when the sun grew hot, it melted," that is, it vanished. Onkelos the Chaldean <note>Another famous Aramaic translator</note> translates it as "it was dissolved." 
**Joshua 7**: "And the heart of the people was afraid," that is, the heart of the people was dissolved as if melted. 
**Joshua 2**: It is interpreted as "And our heart grew faint."

<term>Mas [מס]</term> Personal service; a tax collection or levy; forced labor <note>original: *angaria*, a term for postal or military requisitioning</note>; tribute; census. 
**1 Kings 5**: "And the levy was thirty thousand men." 
**Lamentations 1**: "The princess of provinces has been made subject to tribute." 
**Genesis 49**: "And he shall be a servant to tribute." 
From this, by adding the letter *he* at the end, comes the word <term>Missah [מסה]</term>, which is an offering made to a superior lord as a required personal service. 
**Deuteronomy 16**: "The spontaneous offering of your hand which you shall offer according to the blessing of your God." 
We Christians have retained this name for our sacrifice up to this time, so that it is called the **Mass** <note>original: *missa*</note> by us, which the Greeks call "liturgy." 
Note, therefore, that "Mass" is neither Greek nor Latin, but Hebrew—just as "Pascha" <note>Passover/Easter</note> is neither Greek nor Latin, but borrowed from the Hebrews, as we shall see in its own entry. This is supported by the Gospel passage where Christ judged concerning the giving of tribute to Caesar. 
**Matthew 22**: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's."

<term>Masah [מסה]</term> He dissolved. He melted. It agrees with the entry above. 
**Joshua 14**: "They dissolved the heart of the people." 
**Psalm 6**: "I will soak my bed with my tears," that is, I will melt it, soften it, or dissolve it.

**מסך <note>MSK</note>** He mixed by pouring out, in the manner of cupbearers. <term>Psalm 102:9</term> <note>original: "ps.cij."</note> *And I mixed my cup with weeping.* <term>Isaiah 19:14</term> *The Lord has mixed a spirit of dizziness in her midst.* So also in <term>Proverbs 9:2</term> *She has mixed her wine,* and in the same place <note>v. 5</note> *Drink the wine which I have mixed.* From this comes the noun written with six points <note>referring to Hebrew vowel markings/niqqud</note>, in <term>Psalm 75:8</term> *Full of the mixture.*

**מסך <note>MSK</note>** A veil, a covering, or an overhead canopy, such as we are accustomed to stretch over the head in beds, which the French call a *sky* <note>original: "celum," referring to a "ciel de lit" or bed canopy</note>. Jerome called it a "tent" from the act of "stretching." <term>Exodus 26:36</term> *You shall make a tent for the entrance of the tabernacle and five columns for the tent.* In another place it is translated in <term>Isaiah 22:8</term> *And the covering of Judah shall be revealed.* Other texts have *And he revealed the covering of Judah,* but the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translated it as *And they shall reveal the gates of Judah.* Certain Hebrews translated it thus: *The dominion of Judah shall go into exile,* or *the tent of Judah shall pass away.* Rabbi Jonah, following the meaning of this word, also explains that passage in <term>Ezekiel 28:13</term> *Every precious stone was your covering,* which Jonathan <note>referring to the Targum Jonathan, an Aramaic translation</note> says means *arranged distinctly upon your garment.* I have found this written elsewhere with the letter *sin* in place of *samech* <note>a linguistic note on the interchangeable nature of two Hebrew letters that both make the "s" sound</note>.

**מסר <note>MSR</note>** He chose, cited, handed over, or delegated. <term>Numbers 31:5</term> *And they gave a thousand from each tribe.* Onkelos <note>the author of the Aramaic Targum Onkelos</note> translates this in <term>Chaldean</term> <note>Aramaic</note> as: *A thousand per tribe were chosen from the soldiers.* From this word, the Hebrew masters say that Moses received the Law from Sinai and "delegated" <note>original: "delegauit"</note> it to Joshua. They call the traditional citations in the Bible the *Masaroth* <note>The Masorah: the tradition of notes and rules for the correct transmission of the Hebrew Bible</note>, which I am accustomed to call "annotations." However, they explain the same word differently later in the same chapter of Numbers <note>31:16</note>: *And they made you trespass against the Lord in the sin of Peor,* which Onkelos translates in Chaldean as: *by failing falsely before the Lord.*

**מעד <note>M'D</note>** He tottered, wavered, or slipped. <term>Psalm 18:36</term> *And my steps have not weakened.* For this, Jerome in his psalter wrote: *And my ankles did not fail.* He translated this same phrase similarly in <term>2 Samuel 22:37</term> *And my ankles did not fail.* The Hebrews translate it: *And my knees did not slip.* And in <term>Psalm 37:31</term> *His steps shall not be tripped,* for which Jerome wrote *his steps shall not fail.* From this comes the adjective in <term>Proverbs 25:19</term> *And a weary foot,* that is, wavering or prone to slipping.

**מעה <note>M'H</note>** Bowels, belly, or intestines. <term>Jeremiah 4:19</term> *My belly, my belly, I am in pain.* And <term>Isaiah 16:11</term> *Upon this my belly [moans] for Moab like [a lyre].*

<term>מצה</term> <note>matsah</note> **Strife**. <note>The author links this to the double cave in 2 Samuel 24—modern 1 Samuel 22—regarding David at the cave of Adullam</note>. <term>מצץ</term> <note>matsats</note> **He sucked**. Our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> has “milked” from the act of milking. Isaiah 66: “That you may milk and flow with delights.” But the seventy interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation</note> more correctly put it this way: “so that after you have sucked, you may be delighted.” See above under the word <term>מץ</term> <note>miz</note>.

<term>מצא</term> <note>matsa</note> **It sufficed** or **he found**. Jeremiah 31: “The people found grace in the desert.” And Proverbs 8: “He who finds me finds life.” From this comes the noun in Psalm 32: “For this every holy person shall pray to you in an opportune time.” Jerome, in his psalter <note>St. Jerome’s translation directly from the Hebrew, rather than the standard Vulgate</note>, more correctly says: “at the time of finding.” Its passive form is found in Isaiah 13: “Everyone who is found shall be killed.”

<term>מצד</term> <note>matsad</note> **Citadel**, tower, fortress, a fortified place, or an impregnable height of rocks. Our translation <note>the Vulgate</note> has “refuge.” Psalm 31: “Since you are my strength and my refuge.” And in the plural in the same: “Into a house of refuge.” And 2 Samuel 5: “David took the stronghold of Zion.”

<term>מצה</term> <note>matsah (a different root from the first entry)</note> **He poured out**, squeezed out, extracted, or drained. Judges 6: “Having squeezed the fleece, he filled the bowl with dew.” In its passive form, Leviticus 1: “Let him cause the blood to drain out at the base of the altar.”

<term>מצח</term> <note>metsach</note> **Forehead**. Exodus 28: “And it shall be upon the miter, hanging over the forehead of the priest.” And Ezekiel 3: “And I have made your forehead harder than their foreheads.”

<term>מצחה</term> <note>mits-hah</note> **Greave** <note>Armor protecting the shin</note>. 1 Samuel 17: “And he had bronze greaves on his legs.”

<term>מצר</term> <note>matsar</note> **Anguish** or a narrow place from which we cannot escape. Lamentations 1: “All her persecutors overtook her between the straits.” Our translation renders this as “perils.” Psalm 116: “And the perils of hell found me.” For which Jerome says: “The fortifications of hell.” Often the letter *mem* is added as a prefix so that the root word appears to be <term>צרה</term> <note>tsarah</note>, which means “tribulation.” As in the same passage: “I found tribulation and sorrow.” Whence that in Psalm 118: “Out of distress I called upon the Lord, and the Lord heard me in a broad place.”

**הַמֵק** <note>Hamek</note> He destroyed. It means to perish, or to cause to waste away and die. Likewise, it melted or was being liquefied.
