a proper name for a demon. Rabbi David Kimhi <note>A renowned medieval Jewish grammarian and scholar (1160–1235) from Provence.</note> explains that passage as referring to intense heat that brings death to men. From this, we can understand that verse in Job 3 more clearly than our usual reading, "let it be enveloped in bitterness," by translating it more accurately as: "and let the demons of the day scorch it." He means the "noonday demon" <note>original: "demonium meridianum," a common medieval reference to a spirit of lethargy or heat-induced illness</note>, which refers to excessive heat and the chills of fever.

**מָרַר** [M-R-R]: **He rebelled, he failed, or he opposed.** Our translation interprets this as "despised" in Exodus 23: "Nor should you think to despise him." For this reason, certain Hebrew scholars explained the verse in Isaiah 38: "I will reflect on all my years in the bitterness of my soul," as meaning "in the rebellion <note>original: "rebellione"</note> of my soul." Alternatively, according to Joseph Kimhi <note>David Kimhi’s father, also a distinguished grammarian.</note>, it means "In the changing of my soul."

**מָרַר** [M-R-R]: **He changed or altered.** Jeremiah 48: "And its scent has not changed."

**תַּמְרוּרִים** [Tamrurim]: **Bitterness**, according to Jerome <note>The 4th-century scholar who produced the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> in his commentaries on Jeremiah. However, Symmachus <note>An ancient translator of the Old Testament into Greek.</note> translates it as "transmutations" or "changes" in the same book, chapter 31: "Set up markers <note>The Hebrew word can mean both bitter things and waymarks/pillars.</note> for yourself." David Kimhi, however, in his work on the prophet Hosea, chapter 12, says: "Ephraim provoked me to anger with his bitterness." He translates "bitterness" here as "statues," "mounds," "heaps," or "piles" in the manner of an altar—these being elevations of stone. From this comes the passage in Daniel 8: "He was emboldened against him." The Hebrew masters explain it this way: "he was elevated over him." Thus, the correct reading would be: "set up markers for yourself; set up altars or statues for yourself." Others have translated this as "mourning" or "weeping." Jeremiah 31: "A voice was heard in Ramah of lamentation, mourning, and weeping," for which the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> reads "lamentation and weeping and mourning." Jonathan the Chaldean <note>Refers to Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Bible.</note> explains it this way: that the prophet Jeremiah weeps because Nebuzaradan inflicted a great slaughter and many deaths from Ramah upon the house of Israel, which wept for Jerusalem itself in bitterness, etc.

**מְרֵרָה** [Mererah]: **Gall.** Job 20: "The gall of asps within him."

**מְרִיא** [Meri]: **Fat cattle**, which we read as "sheep" in Isaiah 11: "The calf and the lion and the sheep shall stay together." This word signifies livestock fattened at home, such as fat sheep and oxen. This is why our translation of 1 Kings 1 reads: "With rams and calves and all fatlings." It also signifies exaltation, sublimity, and elevation, which our translation [continues to the next page...]

For example, Psalm 105: *And he did not provoke his words*; regarding which Jerome, more accurately in his own Psalter, wrote: *And they were not incredulous toward his words*—referring specifically to Moses and Aaron. **Dominion** <note>original Latin: "dominatio"; likely referring to the Hebrew root ממשלה (mem-mem-shin-lah)</note>. Rule and power. Genesis 1: *To rule the day, and likewise to rule the night* <note>original: "Ut preesset diei... ut preesset nocti"</note>, meaning for the dominion of the day and the dominion of the night. It takes the letter *he* or *thau* at the end, and another *mem* at the beginning. Just as in Psalm 145: *And your dominion is throughout all generations* <note>original: "Et dominatio tua in omni generatione"</note>.

**משל** <note>mashal</note> Comparison, likeness, parable, or proverb. Ezekiel 18: *If this parable shall be used by you as a proverb any longer.* From this comes the verbs "to speak in proverbs" or "proverb-makers" <note>original: "prouerbiare & prouerbiantes"</note>, if it were permitted to speak thus in Latin. As in the same chapter of Ezekiel: *What is it that you turn into a parable among yourselves?* <note>original: "parabolam uertitis"</note>, that is, you speak in parables or proverbs. And in the passive sense, as in Psalm 49: *He is compared to the foolish beasts* <note>original: "Comparatus est iumentis insipientibus"</note>, and Psalm 27: *And I shall be likened to those who go down into the pit* <note>original: "assimilabor descendentibus in lacum"</note>.

**ממשק** <note>mimshaq</note> Left behind, deserted, or dry. Zephaniah 2: *A dryness of thorns* <note>original: "Siccitas spinarum"</note>. And Rabbi Joseph, the father of David Kimhi <note>A famous family of medieval Hebrew grammarians and commentators</note>, thinks that the same explanation also fits that verse in Genesis 15 where we read: *And the son of the steward of my house is this Eliezer of Damascus.* He suggests it should be read as "the son of the one left behind," namely, the one to whose hands I have left everything in my house to be managed.

**מתג** <note>metheg</note> A bridle, a halter, or a muzzle. This is how the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translated it in Psalm 32: *With muzzle and bridle bind their jaws.* Now, "muzzle" <note>original: "camus"</note> is taken from the Greeks, whom they call *kimos* <note>Greek: κημός</note>; it is a certain kind of bridle according to Julius Pollux and Suidas <note>Ancient Greek lexicographers</note>. Thus in Proverbs 26: *A whip for the horse and a bridle for the donkey.* Although David Kimhi wishes it to be understood there as a "goad" with which donkeys are pricked.

**מְתֵי** <note>methe</note> A nation, a people, or men. Job 11: *Before you alone shall men keep silence.* And Psalm 17: *O Lord, divide them from the few of the earth.* For which Jerome, in his Psalter <note>Referring to Jerome's "Iuxta Hebraeos" translation directly from the Hebrew</note>, more correctly translates: *From the men of your hand, O Lord, who are dead in the depths.* When joined with a number, it signifies "few," as in Deuteronomy 4: *And you shall remain few in number.* We find this word only in the plural.

**מתום** <note>methom</note> Integrity, health, or wholeness. Psalm 38: *There is no health in my flesh.* Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the preeminent medieval commentator</note> explains "integrity" in both French and German <note>original: "tam gallice quam teutonice"</note>. And in Isaiah 1: *There is no health in it*, that is, according to Jonathan the Chaldean <note>The Targum, an Aramaic paraphrase</note>, either "rest" or "quietness"; or even "integrity" according to other Hebrews, or "firmness," or "good health."

**מתח** <note>mathach</note> He expanded, or stretched out. Isaiah 40: *And he expanded them like a tent to dwell in.*

[Handwritten Hebrew: נא] **Now** <note>Hebrew: *na*. A particle of entreaty or request.</note> A particle used for beseeching, meaning "oh" or "I pray you." Just as the ancients were accustomed to say "I will love you" [if you do this] <note>original: *amabo te*, a Latin idiom for "please"</note> and similar things. Exodus 11: "Speak now to all the people," which is more correctly read as: **"Speak now to the ears of the people." And Numbers 12:** "I beseech you, my lord," and further down: "God, I beseech you, heal her." It also takes an *aleph* at the beginning as *ana*, which signifies the same thing. Psalm 118: "O Lord, save me; O Lord, grant us success." Similarly, it is an adverb of exhortation in Song of Solomon 3: "I will rise and go about the city," meaning "come now, let me rise."

[Handwritten Hebrew: נא] <note>The OCR shows אל (El), but the text describes the city of "No" or "No-Amon," which is Alexandria.</note> **No**, which is in Egypt. For thus Jonathan the Chaldean <note>Refers to the Targum Jonathan, an Aramaic translation and commentary</note> interprets Ezekiel 30: "And I will execute my judgments in Alexandria." Jerome, in his commentaries, says that for some reason he does not know, the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> called it *Diospolis* <note>Greek for "City of Zeus"</note>.

[Handwritten Hebrew: נאד] **A flask or wineskin.** Judges 4: "She opened a wineskin of milk." and Psalm 119: "For I have become like a wineskin in the frost," which ought to be read as "like a wineskin in the vapor of smoke." Indeed, I would wonder at the translation if I did not see that Jerome also translated it this way from the "Hebrew Truth" <note>Jerome’s term for the original Hebrew text</note>. I used to believe it was a scribe's error, who might have written "frost" [*pruina*] instead of "burning coals" [*pruna*]. But when I saw that the Seventy interpreters translated it into Greek as *pachne* [frost], I was of two minds, remembering that passage of Paul to the Romans 14: "Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind." It is declined in the plural in the feminine gender: Joshua 9: "Wineskins of wine, torn," where its adjective is of the masculine gender, as seen further in the same chapter: "We filled new wineskins of wine." And although it is sometimes written with the diphthong <term>aleph and vav</term> <note>meaning the vowel sound 'o' is written out</note> as in the book of Judges cited above, and sometimes with a simple *aleph* as in others, it did not please me to place the *vav* after the *nun* in the alphabetical order as some have tried (as if the *aleph* were an extra letter), but rather I placed it here because, in my opinion, *aleph* is the principal letter, as it is written with a simple *aleph* more frequently than with the diphthong.

[Handwritten Hebrew: נאם] **He spoke, he said, he says, he quoth.** Jeremiah 23: "They take up their tongues and they say: 'He says,'" where according to Jerome "the Lord" is understood, for "the Lord" is not in the actual text. Grammarians write that [נאם] is a noun and signifies "a saying," although we always interpret it as a verb, such as "he says" or "he speaks." From this are named those who are eloquent and prudent in speech [Hebrew: נאמנים], which our translation <note>The Vulgate</note> rendered as "truthful men" from the word *amen*. Job 12: "Changing the lips of the truthful." Others, however, read from this word for speaking as: "Tripping up the lips of the orators" or "the eloquent."

**נאף** <note>original: "Na'af"</note> **He committed adultery; he was unfaithful.** Leviticus 20: "If any man commits adultery with the wife of another and perpetrates adultery with the spouse of his neighbor, let both the adulterer and the adulteress be put to death." **נאק** <note>original: "Na'ak"</note> **He cried out bitterly; he shouted in pain.** Our translation <note>referring to the Latin Vulgate</note> interprets this as **he groaned.** Ezekiel 30: "And they shall groan with the groans of the slain before me," where the Chaldean translation of Jonathan <note>The Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> has: "And he shall roar with a roar." Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator</note> explains this through an equivalent word that signifies a "cry" in Isaiah chapter 5, where it is read: "And behold, a cry."

**נאר** <note>original: "Na'ar"</note> **He cursed and took away glory.** Lamentations 2: "He has cursed his sanctuary." Rabbi Solomon says: "You have made it void." Others, such as Joseph Kimhi <note>a 12th-century Hebrew grammarian and teacher</note>, say: "You have devastated." I would think this word signifies **to make light of**, **to dismiss from the heart**, or **to cast away.** So in Malachi 3: "And you are cursed with poverty."

**נבב** <note>original: "Nabab"</note> **Vain, empty, hollow, or not solid.** Exodus 27: "You shall make it not solid, but empty and hollow on the inside." And Job 11: "A vain man is raised up in pride." See above under the word *bib*. <note>A cross-reference to another entry in this dictionary</note> And Jeremiah 52: "And it was hollow on the inside."

<note>original: "stri.et Ieremię.xxiij."</note> ...of our [Lord]. And in Jeremiah 23: "They prophesy by Baal." From this, the noun "prophet" and the participle "prophesying" and other derivatives are found in the same chapter. And in Deuteronomy 33: "And there arose not a prophet since."

**[Hebrew: נבח] To bark.** Isaiah 56: <note>original: "Canes muti non ualentes latrare"</note> "Dumb dogs, not able to bark."

**[Hebrew: נבט] To gaze, to pay attention, or to see.** Isaiah 5: <note>original: "Aspiciemus in terram"</note> "We shall look toward the earth." According to those learned in grammar and literature, this should be translated as "he will look toward the earth," for the letter *nun* <note>The Hebrew letter נ (N)</note> is substantial <note>A "substantial" or radical letter is part of the root word itself, rather than a prefix or suffix</note> here and not accidental, though it is often missing in other forms. As in Isaiah 51: "Look to the rock from which you were hewn; look to Abraham your father." And Psalm 102: "The Lord looked down from heaven to the earth." And Genesis 19: "Do not look behind your back," which they read word-for-word as: "Do not look behind you."

**[Hebrew: נבל] To wither, to be thinned out or exhausted, to grow pale, or to fall.** Isaiah 40: <note>original: "Cecidit flos"</note> "The flower fell," which others read as "the flower grew pale," but it is better rendered as "withered." Likewise in Isaiah 28: "And to the falling flower." Perhaps this is because they thought the letter *p* had been converted into a *b*, <note>Referring to the phonetic similarity between the Hebrew letters Pe (פ) and Bet (ב)</note> because it signifies the weak, the falling, the empty, and that which lacks strength. which is written as follows: *I will bring yet one more plague upon Pharaoh* <note>Exodus 11:1</note>; and in Leviticus 13, *the plague of leprosy*. It is written with a *nun segol* <note>A technical reference to Hebrew vowel points and grammar</note>. Both the verb and the noun are found in a single verse in Genesis 12: *But the Lord struck Pharaoh with the greatest plagues*—meaning he plagued or struck him with great blows. For in Greek, according to the Doric dialect, *plaga* <note>original: "plaga"</note> is called a "blow" <note>original: "percussio"</note>, derived from the ancient verb *peplego* in the present tense, which itself comes from *peplega*, the past tense of the verb *plesso* <note>Greek: πλήσσω, meaning to strike or hit</note>, as read in the Greek book of selections by Varinus Camers <note>Favorinus Camertis, a 16th-century scholar and bishop known for his Greek lexicon</note>. [Hebrew: **Nagaf** / To Strike] Impelled, rushed upon, injured, or brought a pestilence. Our translation interprets this as "struck." Exodus 21: *And if someone strikes a pregnant woman.* Soon the translation varies in the same chapter, rendering it as "wounded," as in: *if one man’s ox wounds the ox of another.* Again, in 2 Samuel 12: *And the Lord struck the child.* Similarly, in Exodus 12, it is translated in various ways: *striking the Egyptians*, and shortly after: *to enter your houses and harm.* Onkelos <note>The author of the standard Aramaic translation (Targum) of the Torah</note> translates it in both places as "to strike" in the Chaldean language <note>A common historical term for Aramaic</note>. From this comes the noun with six points <note>referring to Hebrew vowel markings</note>, meaning a pestilence or a slaughter. In the same passage of Exodus: *nor shall there be a plague among you*, which Onkelos turns into "mortality" in Chaldean. Another use of the verb is in Psalm 91: *Lest you strike your foot against a stone*, meaning "injure." You will find another form of the word through the addition of the letters *mem* and *he* at the end of Numbers 25 and the beginning of chapter 26: *Who was struck in the day of the plague for the sacrilege of Peor, after the blood of the guilty was shed.* This last part is placed as: *and it happened after the plague.* All derivatives of this word signify a blow leading to death, or at the very least, near to death.

[Hebrew: **Nagar** / To Flow] Dispersed, poured out, overturned, or flowed down. 2 Samuel 14: *We are like waters slipping away*, which is written as: *like waters flowing down or dispersed upon the earth.* A similar use is in Micah 1: *Like waters that run down a steep place*, that is, like dispersed waters. Jonathan the Chaldean <note>Referring to Targum Jonathan, an Aramaic translation of the Prophets</note> translates this as "deriving" or "flowing down" (specifically *asdin*). And in Lamentations 3: *My eye is afflicted*, where the Hebrew reads: *My eye flows down and pours out.* Likewise, in Micah 1: *And I will pull down its stones into the valley*, that is, I will disperse the stones from the mountains into the valleys in the manner of those wishing to build.

**אנה** <note>Hebrew: *anah*</note> He lamented, wailed, or howled. Micah 2: "He will sing a song," but more correctly the Septuagint <note>The earliest Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> interpreters read: "He will lament a lamentation," just as in Jeremiah 9: "Teach your daughters a lament," and in chapter 30: "A voice was heard on high of lamentation," etc.

**נהג** <note>Hebrew: *nahag*</note> He led or drove. Lamentations 3 <note>The text cites chapter 4, but this refers to 3:1</note>: "He drove me and led me." Psalm 80: "You who lead Joseph like a sheep." Ecclesiastes 2: "And to lead my mind toward wisdom," that is, to accustom my heart to wisdom. From this, the character <term>mores: the customs or behavioral habits of a person</term> and conduct of men are so named from an ingrained habit <note>original: "ab inducta consuetudine"</note>.

**נהל** <note>Hebrew: *nahal*</note> He sustained, bore, or carried. Exodus 15: "You carried them in your strength," and this agrees with the Chaldean translation of Onkelos <note>A famous 2nd-century Aramaic translation of the Torah.</note>. Isaiah 51: "There is no one to sustain her."

**נהם** <note>Hebrew: *naham*</note> He roared or growled. Proverbs 19: "The king’s wrath is like the roaring of a lion," for which the Hebrews read: "The king's wrath roars like lions." And in chapter 28: "A roaring lion." Our translation <note>Referring to the Latin Vulgate used by the Church.</note> reads differently elsewhere, in Proverbs 5: "And you groan at your end," using "groan" <note>original: "gemas"</note> instead of "roar" <note>original: "fremas"</note>.

**נהק** <note>Hebrew: *nahaq*</note> He cried out, shouted, sounded, or brayed. Job 6: "Does the wild donkey roar?" I think the translator intended to say "bray" <note>original: "rudet"</note>, for braying is the natural sound of asses and wild donkeys. Persius <note>A Roman satirical poet.</note> says: "I am split, so that you might say the herds of Arcadia are braying." I am surprised that our translation in another place interpreted this as "to rejoice," in Job 30: "Who rejoiced among such things." But the Hebrews read it this way: "Among the bushes they cry out, under the nettles they are gathered together." All words derived from this signify a roar, just as in Greek *bromasthai* <note>original: "βρωμᾶσθαι" — to roar or snort</note> according to Suidas <note>The author of a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia.</note> and *onkasthai* <note>original: "ὀγκᾶσθαι" — to bray</note>, which are specific to wild donkeys and asses.

**נהר** <note>Hebrew: *nahar*</note> It flowed together or streamed toward; it signifies a course at one's pleasure. Jeremiah 31: "And they shall flow together to the good things of the Lord." Isaiah 60: "Then you shall see and flow together." From this comes the name for a river or stream. Psalm 80: "And its branches even to the river." It is declined as a common gender in the plural: in the masculine, as in Isaiah 33: "A place of rivers, very broad streams," and in the feminine, as in Psalm 24 <note>The text cites 23, but refers to 24:2</note>: "And he prepared it upon the rivers."

# BOOK

...the French Rabbi Solomon <note>The famous commentator Rashi (1040–1105)</note> explains "be enlightened" so that the meaning is "see." This is also how some interpret what was cited above from the sixtieth chapter of Isaiah: "Then you shall see and be radiant." Rabbi David Kimhi <note>A grammarian and commentator known as Radak (1160–1235)</note> holds this opinion in his commentaries. From this comes the word for light or illumination. In the third chapter of Job: "Let it not be enlightened by light." From this also comes what is read in the sixth chapter of Judges: "And they made for themselves dens and caves in the mountains," that is, they made subterranean cracks or fissures like little windows through which light might fall secretly into the pits; for this word suggests such a thing.

**[נוא] <note>The Hebrew root NW'</note>** He deserted. He avoided—a harsh word. He broke, ceased, frustrated, or contradicted. He caused to desert or depart. In the thirtieth chapter of Numbers: "But if immediately as his father hears it, he contradicts her." And in the thirty-second chapter of the same book: "Why do you subvert the minds of the children of Israel?" that is, for what purpose do you break the decisions of the children of Israel? Or rather, "Why do you cause the hearts of the children of Israel to turn away?" Sometimes the letter *aleph* is missing and the *vav* is changed into a *yod*, as in Psalm 141: "But let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head." Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> interprets this as "it shall not defer" or "it shall not avoid my head." Nicholas of Lyra <note>A major Christian biblical scholar (c. 1270–1349)</note>, wishing to imitate him, explains it as "it shall not prohibit my head." Furthermore, "of the sinner" is not translated correctly here; it should be "the oil of the prince" or "of the king." Likewise, from this verb is derived a noun in the fourteenth chapter of Numbers: "And you shall experience my vengeance." This is according to the mind of Onkelos <note>Author of the Aramaic Targum Onkelos</note>, but according to the property of the language, it signifies "desertion" or "departure," as Rabbi Solomon correctly comments in that place.

**[נוא] <note>The Hebrew name No-Amon</note>** Alexandria. In the third chapter of Nahum: "Are you better than the Alexandria of the peoples?" <note>The biblical text refers to "No" (Thebes), which early commentators often identified with Alexandria</note>. There you may see Jerome's commentaries on the Twelve Minor Prophets, and above at the beginning of the letter *nun*.

**[נוב] <note>The Hebrew root NWB</note>** It grew. It bore fruit. It propagated. It germinated. Our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> has "it multiplied." In Psalm 92: "They shall still be multiplied in a fruitful old age," for which Jerome, in his Psalter according to the Hebrew Truth, translates: "They shall still bear fruit in old age." And with the letter *beth* doubled in the ninth chapter of Zechariah: "And wine making the virgins flourish." And see how contrary our translation is in the fourth chapter of Lamentations: "Because these have wasted away, consumed by the sterility of the land," which in Hebrew is: "Because these flow away, pierced through by the fertility of the field." But in the tenth chapter of Proverbs, it is translated as "to bring forth": "The mouth of the righteous shall bring forth wisdom," that is, it shall propagate it. From this comes the noun for "offspring" or "bud" or "shoot" or "branch," which we read as "fruit" in the fifty-seventh chapter of Isaiah.

Lyra says: "they scattered," namely the temple, in which the Jews especially gloried. Whence our translation more truly renders Exodus chapter fifteen: "To your holy habitation." Quiet, tranquil, pleasant, sweet and pleasing, or peaceful. **Numbers 28**: <note>original: "Holocaustum suauissimi odoris atq; incensi est domino id est placidissimi"</note> "A burnt offering of a most sweet aroma and incense to the Lord," that is, most pleasing; where the letter *Heth* is doubled. **נוע** <note>The Hebrew root *Nu*</note> Shook, moved. **Psalm 99**: "Let the earth be moved," for which <term>Jerome</term> <note>The 4th-century translator of the Vulgate</note> reads "let it be shaken."

In the last chapter of **Deuteronomy**: <note>original: "Nec dentes illius moti sunt"</note> "Neither were his teeth moved," for which the Jews more correctly read: "And his natural vigor <note>original: "speciositas," literally beauty or appearance</note> had not fled." From this comes the heavy verb "he caused to flee," that is, "he put to flight." **Exodus 9**: "He made his servants and cattle flee into the houses." From this the name in **Jeremiah 46**: "They fled, stirred up by flight they fled," which undergoes both <term>prothesis</term> <note>The addition of a letter at the beginning of a word</note> and <term>paragoge</term> <note>The addition of a letter at the end of a word</note>. **Isaiah 52**: "Nor shall you go out in haste by flight."

**נוע** <note>The Hebrew root *Nua*</note> Moved, shook. **Amos 9**: "And I will shake the house of Israel among all nations as grain is shaken." And in the passive in **Nahum 3**: "If they be shaken, they shall fall into the mouth of the eater." It is also found through the cutting away of the letter *Vau*. **Amos 4**: "And two and three cities came," that is, they moved or yielded. And **Genesis 4**: "And I shall be a wanderer and a fugitive on the earth." From this are named the **מנענעים** <note>Mena'ane'im</note>, musical instruments made of bronze to which many rattles are attached, named thus from "shaking" and "moving." [נזם] Earring, collar, or nose ornament. [נזר] Bound, separated, abstained, restricted, divided. Word-for-word it is properly: "All the days of his religion, or his abstinence, separation, or monkhood." From this, it is common to say to someone wearing long hair: "Shear your religion" or "shave off your consecration."

[נזר] Crown, diadem. 2 Samuel 1[:10]: "I took the diadem that was on his head." They understand Leviticus 21[:12] in this way: "Because the oil of the holy anointing of his God is upon him," which Onkelos <note>Onkelos was a famous 2nd-century convert and scholar who translated the Torah into Aramaic</note> interprets in the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> language as: "Because the crown <note>original: *dil*, likely a fragment for *dil-taga* or similar</note> of the oil of the majesty of God is upon him." Similarly in Numbers 6[:7]: "Because the consecration of his God is upon his head." And so it is written with five points.

[נחה] He led, he guided. Psalm 77[:20]: "You led your people like sheep." And Psalm 108[:10]: "Who will lead me as far as Edom?" From this comes a transitive verb of the third class, as if he "caused to be led," meaning he sent or let go, as in Exodus 33[:1]: "Let me go."

**נחל** [Nachal] **To inherit.** <note>original: *Hereditavit*</note>. Which our translation <note>The author refers to the Latin Vulgate</note> renders as "possessed." Exodus 32: *And you shall possess it forever.* Likewise Numbers 32: *until the children of Israel possess their inheritance.* This is read word-for-word by the Hebrews as: *until it shall be inherited by the children of Israel, each his own inheritance.* And it follows: *Nor shall we seek anything across the Jordan.* We properly translate it thus: *Since we will not inherit with them.* Likewise Psalm 82: *Since you shall inherit among all the nations.* From this comes the noun **inheritance**. Psalm 93: *and they have afflicted your inheritance.* Similarly, Deuteronomy 30 <note>The author likely intends Deuteronomy 32:9</note>: *Jacob is the cord of his inheritance.* And in the same, chapter 18: *the priests and Levites shall have no part or inheritance with the rest of Israel, for the Lord himself is their inheritance.*

**נחל** [Nachal] **River, stream, torrent, brook.** Joshua 13: *From Aroer, which is situated on the bank of the torrent Arnon.* And also Ecclesiastes 1: *all rivers enter into the sea.* And 2 Samuel 22: *the torrents of Belial <note>A term often used to signify worthlessness, destruction, or the personification of evil</note> terrified me.* It also signifies a **narrow valley** in which a river is diverted, even if it sometimes dries up and becomes parched. **Nasa** [נשא] — To carry, lift, or throw. 
As in Lamentations 3: "Because he has lifted himself above himself." 
And Jonah 1: "Cast me into the sea," meaning "throw me in."

->BOOK TWO<-

Rabbi Moses of Gerona <note>original: "Moyſes gerundenſis"; also known as Nachmanides, a major 13th-century Jewish scholar</note> indicates in his second book on the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible</note>, discussing the compound **theriac** <note>original: "thiriacā"; a famous ancient medical "all-cure" or antidote</note>, how it is made, from what ingredients, and why it is so named, following the subject at length. However, regarding **nataph** <note>original: "nataph"; a biblical perfume ingredient often translated as stacte</note>, which is mentioned here, he says it is a simple, oily resin dripping from the wood of the balsam tree, which we call **opobalsamum** <note>original: "opobalſamū"</note>, that is, the juice of balsam. This is fully described by Dioscorides, the Greek authority on medicine, in book 1, chapter 21. Among the ancient Greeks, every precious liquid was called **stacte** <note>original: "ſtactos"; meaning "drops" or "dripping"</note>. The Greek comic playwright Aristophanes indicates this in his comedy titled *Plutus*, where **Penia** (that is, Poverty) argues that we would have no wealth if everyone abounded in gold and money. Among other things, she says: "For you would not have ointments smelling of stacte" <note>original: "Nec enim habebis ungentis redolere ſtactis"</note>, meaning useful liquids. Stacte was held in such high value that Polybius writes that Antiochus was gifted two hundred pounds of stacte. The word is derived from the verb *stazo* <note>original: "ſtazo"; Greek for "to drip"</note>, which in the future tense is *staxo*, from which come *stagme*, *staxe*, and *stacte*. From this, I think the proper meaning of the word *nataph* is more correctly understood. I have noted these few things so that you may know that even among the most serious authors, there are various and differing opinions on the names of things; for both myrrh and the balsam shrub "sweat" their juice when the bark is cut, as Pliny indicates in book 12 of his *Natural History*, chapters 16 and 34.

[Hebrew: נטר] <term>Natar: He guarded or kept.</term> Song of Songs 1: "I have not kept my own vineyard." <note>original: "Vineam meam non cuſtodiui"</note> Hence the noun, as in the same place: "They made me a keeper <note>original: "cuſtodem"</note> in the vineyards." ->SECOND<-
<note>Likely referring to the second book or section of this volume.</note>

According to the mind of Rabbi David Kimhi <note>original: "rabi Dauidis kimhi"; a famous 12th-13th century Jewish grammarian and biblical commentator from Spain</note>. A servant delicately educated from tender childhood <note>original: "a teneris unguiculis," literally "from his tender little nails," a Latin idiom for early childhood</note> eventually strives to be a *manon* <note>original: "manon"</note>, that is, a "son of the household." This is perhaps a metaphor for the transition from a state of adoption to inheritance, and from inheritance to masterly ownership; however, it is not a standard property of the Hebrew language.

**Suckled / Nourished.** <note>Hebrew root: ינק (YNQ)</note> Exodus 2: "The woman took and nourished the child." Likewise a little earlier: "Take this child and nourish it for me." It is similar to the word for "sucked" mentioned above under the letter *Yod*.

**Grandson.** <note>Hebrew root: נכד (NKD)</note> Isaiah 14: "And the offspring." Genesis 21: "and to my lineage." And according to Rabbi David Kimhi the Spaniard, it is a "son's son." It is written with six points <note>Referring to the Hebrew vowel markings, likely the 'Segol' points</note>. As in Job 18: "He shall have neither seed nor progeny among his people," which is more correctly read as: "He has no son, nor grandson among his people."

**Struck.** <note>Hebrew root: נכה (NKH)</note> Zechariah 9: "And he shall strike her strength in the sea." And through the loss of the letter *Nun* at the start of the word <term>apheresis: the loss of a sound or letter at the beginning of a word</term>, which the *Dagesh* point indicates <note>A dot placed in a Hebrew letter to show it is doubled or that a preceding letter has been omitted</note>. 1 Kings 16: "Zimri, rushing in, struck and killed him." Sometimes letters are missing at both the beginning and the end. As in 1 Kings 19: "But the spear was driven through the empty wound into the wall," which word-for-word is more truly read: "and he struck the spear into the wall." So a little earlier: "he struck them with a great slaughter." And Exodus 9: "I will strike you and your people," where it uses *eche* <note>original: "אכה"</note>, that is, "I will strike," which is defective <note>missing letters</note> at the beginning and the end. For only the letter *Kaph* (כ) is essential; the *Nun* (נ) and *He* (ה) are missing, and the *Aleph* (א) indicates the first-person singular future tense, as is explained more fully in the art of grammar.

**Infirm in the feet.** Lame or gouty. 2 Kings 24 <note>The text cites 3 Kings 24, following the Latin Vulgate numbering</note>: "Pharaoh Necho, king of Egypt, went up," that is, Pharaoh the Lame. Just as we are accustomed to say "Tiberius Claudius" from the word for limping <note>Latin: "claudicando"</note>. This is how the Aramaic translation of Jonathan <note>Targum Jonathan</note> interprets it: "Pharaoh Hagira," meaning "the limping Pharaoh." According to what is read in 2 Kings 9: "The son of Jonathan, weak in his feet." They similarly understand this verse in Psalm 35: "The scourges were gathered over me," meaning ailments of the feet. In these cases, the final letter *He* is often changed into an *Aleph*.

**Beside / Near / Because of / Next to.** <note>Hebrew root: נכח (NKCH)</note> Exodus 26: "And opposite the table the candlestick," meaning near or beside. Elsewhere it is translated as "in the sight of." Exodus 14: "You shall camp in its sight," that is, in its presence. And Genesis 25: "And Isaac prayed to the Lord for his wife," that is, because of his wife. From this root derive nouns and verbs, and it accepts subjoined pronouns and declensions.

# THE BOOK

**נכל** [Nakal] <term>He lay in wait</term>; he devised deceits; and if I may be permitted to say so, he "engineered" them. For so my teacher (may the mercy of God be upon him) Jacob Jehiel—also known as Johannes Loans <note>original: "Iacobus iehiel Ioañs Malachie." Reuchlin is referring to Jacob ben Jehiel Loans, the Jewish physician to Emperor Maximilian I who taught Reuchlin Hebrew. The "Malachie" reference here points to the biblical book of Malachi.</note>—used to speak. That is to say: "Cursed be the deceiver" <note>original: "Maledictus dolosus," a reference to Malachi 1:14, which uses the root נכל (nakal)</note>, according to Rabbi David Kimhi <note>original: "rabi Dauid kimhi," the medieval grammarian known as Radak</note> in his commentaries on the Twelve [Minor Prophets]: "Cursed is the deviser of a fraudulent invention." And in Numbers 25: "Because they also acted as enemies against you and deceived you with snares." This is more correctly read as: "because they are enemies to you in the deceits which they fraudulently laid for you." It is not "by means of an idol," as some faulty books have it, but "by deceit." For the word signifies deceit, snares, fraud, cunning, and a deceptive invention or evil industry. For where the Hebrew has *ormah* <note>meaning craftiness or cunning</note>, Onkelos <note>The famous 2nd-century translator of the Torah into Aramaic</note> in his translation into the Chaldean language <note>Aramaic</note> uses this present word. As in Exodus 21: "If anyone shall kill his neighbor by industry <note>meaning with premeditation or by design</note> and by snares." This is also evident in Psalm 105: "And they dealt craftily with his servants."

**נכס** [Nekas] <term>Substance</term>, riches, family property; goods both movable and "self-moving" <note>original: "se mouentia," a legal term referring to livestock or animals</note>. Joshua 22: "Return with much substance and riches."

**נכר** [Nakar] <term>He recognized</term>. In Lamentations 4: "And they are not recognized in the streets." And Genesis 42: "And yet he, recognizing his brothers, was not recognized by them." And Proverbs 20: "A child is understood by his endeavors." The letter *nun* often disappears <note>A common grammatical shift in Hebrew where the first letter of the root is dropped in certain conjugations</note>, as in other cases. Genesis 27: "And he did not recognize him."

**נכר** [Nakar - *Alternate sense*] <term>He withdrew</term> or alienated himself; he became puffed up or grew proud. Deuteronomy 32: "Lest perhaps their enemies should be proud." Its meaning is found more clearly in Genesis 42: When [Joseph] had recognized them, he spoke more harshly as if to strangers. Word for word it says: "He recognized them and alienated himself toward them." Here, opposite meanings seem to be signaled by the same word. For the previous entry signifies applying one's mind and recognition *to* someone; this one, however, signifies turning one's mind and recognition *away* from someone, and using foreign gestures and a contemptuous will toward anyone, pretending to be like a stranger to them. From this come the nouns "pilgrimage" and "stranger," "foreigner," or "alien." As in Obadiah: "On the day of his pilgrimage." And Exodus 12: "No foreigner shall eat of it." And Psalm 18: "The children of the stranger have lied to me; the children of the stranger have grown old."

**נכר** [Nakar - *Third sense*] <term>He thrust in</term> or shut up. Our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> has "delivered." 1 Samuel 23: "And Saul said, 'The Lord has delivered him into my hands.'"

# SECOND SECTION

**נכאת** <note>Hebrew: *nekot*</note> **Spices.** <note>original: "Aroma"</note> Genesis 37: And their camels were carrying spices, etc. <note>Genesis 37:25</note> Regarding this, Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to Rashi, the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> writes that this word signifies, in a general sense, any mixture prepared from spices. He also places an *aleph* in the position of a *vav* <note>a grammatical note on the spelling of the Hebrew root</note>. Modern Jewish scholars interpret this as **wax**, understanding the cited verse to refer to a wax salve rather than spices. Jonathan the Chaldean <note>The Targum Jonathan, an Aramaic translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, wishing to designate precious things by this word, translated it as **treasure**. Isaiah 39: And he showed them the room of the spices—as if he were saying, the **treasury**.

**נלה** <note>Hebrew: *nalah*</note> **He completed.** He finished, perfected, or ceased. Isaiah 33: When, being weary, you cease to despise, you shall be despised.

**נמל** <note>Hebrew: *namal*</note> **He cut out.** He amputated or circumcised. Genesis 17: And you shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin. In that place, you will find various forms of this word. For it often loses the letter *nun*, as do other words of this type. As in Job 14: He comes forth like a flower and is crushed—that is, he is cut off or pruned.

**נמלה** <note>Hebrew: *nemalah*</note> **Ant.** Proverbs 6: Go to the ant, O sluggard. And in the plural form of the same masculine gender, in chapter 30: The ants are a people not strong.

**נמר** <note>Hebrew: *namer*</note> **The Leopard,** an animal which in Greek is called *pardalis*, having a spotted and variegated skin. Jeremiah 13: Can the leopard change its spots? And in the plural, Habakkuk 1: Its horses are swifter than leopards. And Jeremiah 5: A leopard watches over their cities. Modern scholars say it is named the **leopard**. Hosea 13: And I will be to them like a lioness, and like a leopard on the way of the Assyrians—for so they read it.

**נסס** <note>Hebrew: *nasas*</note> **He exalted.** He lifted up or raised. Isaiah 59: Whom the spirit of the Lord compels—more correctly thus: In whom the breath or spirit of the Lord has raised [a banner]. Nicholas of Lyra <note>A 14th-century Franciscan theologian whose work was a bridge between Jewish and Christian biblical interpretation.</note> explains it as "instigated" or "spurred on." Theodotion <note>A 2nd-century translator of the Bible into Greek.</note> translates it as "he was marked in him"; Aquila <note>A 2nd-century convert to Judaism who produced a literal Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> as "his seal." And this is because in an army, a certain **banner** <note>original: "vexillum"</note> is usually raised, toward which scattered soldiers may flee for refuge; and that lifting up is called a **sign** or **standard**. Lucan, in the first book of the *Civil War*: "Standards facing hostile standards." <note>A reference to the Roman poet Lucan's description of civil strife.</note> Likewise, Isaiah 11: And the Lord shall lift up a sign to the nations. You will understand this more clearly from the verse we read in Zechariah 9: For the holy stones shall be lifted up over his land. Because one truly flees to a sign or banner, therefore this word also means **to flee**.

I have ordained my king. <note>original: "ordinavi regem meum"</note> And that learned master, the man from Burgos <note>Paul of Burgos (c. 1351–1435), a Jewish convert to Christianity and influential biblical scholar</note>, interprets it thus: I have established my king. <note>original: "Et ego constitui regem meum"</note>

**[נסע - To set out]** He has set out. He departed. He went forth. He withdrew. Numbers 11: "A wind going out from the Lord." <note>original: "Ventus autem egrediens a domino"</note> This word is often used in Numbers 33: "They set out therefore from Rameses." Likewise: "From Succoth they came into Etham; and having set out from Marah, they came into Elim." And in Exodus 14: "The angel of the Lord, lifting himself up," <note>original: "Tollensque se angelus domini"</note> that is, the angel of the Lord set out. From this, what we call "stations" <note>referring to the Stations of the Exodus</note> ought to be called the "settings-out" or "progressions" of the children of Israel—specifically when they were withdrawing from their dwelling places. As in Genesis 20: "Abraham set out from there into the southern land." Sometimes it is found as a transitive verb, as in Exodus 15: "Moses took Israel away from the Red Sea," that is, he made Israel depart from the sea. Likewise in 1 Kings 5: <note>The text cites 3 Kings, following the Vulgate numbering</note> "And the king commanded that they should take up great stones."

**[נשק - Weapons]** It signifies weapons of war. Job 41: "Neither spear nor breastplate." <note>original: "Neque hasta neque thorax"</note> Here I believe that either through ignorance or because of the variety of interpreters, our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> left this word untouched.

**[נסק - To ascend]** He climbs. He ascends. Psalm 139: <note>The text cites Psalm 39, likely a shorthand or error for 138 in the Vulgate</note> "If I ascend into heaven, you are there."

**[נעל - To lock]** He bolted, or he sealed with a fastening. Judges 3: "The doors of the upper chamber having been most diligently closed and secured with a bolt." In this same way, the verse in Song of Solomon 4 is to be explained: "A garden enclosed, a fountain sealed." <note>original: "Hortus conclusus fons signatus"</note> All of this signifies to close with a bolt and make secure.

**[נעל - Shoe]** A shoe or sandal. Psalm 60: "Over Edom I will stretch out my shoe." From this comes the word in Ezekiel 16: "And I shod you with violet-colored leather." <note>original: "hyacintho" - often translated as badger skin or fine leather in this context</note>

**[נעם - To be pleasant]** It pleased; or it was sweet, delightful, pleasant, elegant, or lovely. 2 Samuel 1: <note>The text cites 2 Kings, following the Vulgate numbering</note> where we have, "my brother Jonathan, exceeding beautiful," <note>original: "decore nimis"</note> the Hebrew truth <note>term used by scholars to refer to the original Hebrew text</note> reads: "You have been sweet to me," or "you were sweet," or "you have pleased me greatly." To this we add what is read in Ruth 1: "Do not call me Noemi," that is, "beautiful," <note>The author equates Noemi with beauty/sweetness</note> or more correctly "sweet," because it follows: "But call me Mara," that is, "bitter." Likewise that passage in Job 36: "They shall finish their days in good, and their years in glory," that is, in sweetness and delights. And in Proverbs 24: "He who rebukes him shall be praised," <note>original: "Qui arguunt eum laudabitur"</note> but more correctly: "And it shall be sweet to those who rebuke," or "pleasant."

And in Psalm 16: *Delights are at your right hand even unto the end.* <note>original Latin: "Delectationes in dextera tua usq; in finem."</note> For this is how the Church sings it according to the **Septuagint** <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament, often abbreviated as LXX.</note> interpreters, although in this passage the Greek word *terpnotis* would be more correctly translated into Latin as "pleasantness." **Jerome** <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into the Latin Vulgate.</note> translated that in his own psalter as: *Eternal beauties are at your right hand.* Thus you have, in these two quoted verses from **Job** and the **Psalms**, the plural number of this name in a double form, both masculine and feminine.

**Na'aman** <note>Hebrew: נעמן</note> With the last letter doubled through addition, this signifies—according to **Jerome** in the 15th book of his commentaries on **Isaiah**—a very cheap and bitter herb of the worst smell, a name which he himself interpreted as "wild nard." <note>original Latin: "saliunculam." This refers to a low-growing, fragrant but bitter plant.</note> In Isaiah 55: *Instead of the wild nard, the fir tree shall come up.* So writes **Rabbi David Kimhi** <note>A 12th-13th century Hebrew grammarian and exegete.</note> in his *Book of Roots*, stating that it is a kind of lowly shrub. **Rabbi Saadias** says they are very sharp white thorns. **Jonathan**, in the **Chaldaic** <note>Aramaic</note> translation, interpreted not the literal words here but only the sense, saying: *In place of iniquity, righteousness shall be raised up.* **Rabbi Solomon** <note>Commonly known as Rashi.</note> is seen to follow him when he explains: *Power will be taken away from the impious and given to the righteous.*

**Na'ar** <note>Hebrew: נער</note> He cried out. He shouted. He roared. In Jeremiah 51: *they shall shake their manes like lion cubs.* <note>original Latin: "excutiẽt comas ueluti catuli leonum."</note> For which the **Hebrews** interpret: *they shall cry out like lion cubs.* And the Chaldaic translation of **Jonathan** has it thus: *like the sons of lions they shall lift up their voice.* Following this example, **Rabbi Jonah** <note>Ibn Janah, an influential Hebrew grammarian.</note> was accustomed to explain the verse in Zechariah 2, where we read: *Be silent, all flesh, before the face of the Lord, because he has risen up from his holy habitation.* Others also read it: *Because he has roared from his holy habitation.* **Rabbi Joseph the Spaniard**, the father of David, agrees with this explanation; and the son, **Kimhi**, considers this kind of speaking to be similar to what is written in Jeremiah 25: *The Lord shall roar from on high and give his voice from his holy habitation*; or in Joel 3: *The Lord shall roar from Zion.*

**Na'ar** <note>Hebrew: נער</note> He was cast down. Shaken off. Struck or driven out. In Isaiah 33: *And Bashan and Carmel are shaken.* In Psalm 136: *And he shook off Pharaoh and his army into the Red Sea.* And in Psalm 109: *I am shaken off like a locust.*

**Na'ar** <note>Hebrew: נער</note> A boy or a youth. In Jeremiah 1: *Because I am a child.*

In the first book of Kings: *The boy was still a small child.* <note>1 Samuel 1:24. In older Latin Bibles, 1 and 2 Samuel are titled 1 and 2 Kings.</note> In the second chapter of Ruth: *And Boaz said to the young man who was in charge of the reapers.* Because a boy is younger in age, and it is appropriate for him to serve a superior—that is, an elder—the word is therefore also used for a **servant** <term>minister: an attendant or subordinate official</term> of any age or stature. In the forty-first chapter of Genesis: *There was a Hebrew youth there with us, a servant of the same captain of the guard.* And in the thirty-third chapter of Exodus: *His servant Joshua, the son of Nun, a young man.* And in the second book of Kings, chapter five: *Gehazi, the servant of the man of God, said.* From this comes the word for **girl** in the twenty-fourth chapter of Genesis: *A very beautiful girl.* And in the second chapter of Ruth: *Whose girl is this?* From this comes a derivative noun in Psalm 129: *Often they have fought against me from my youth.* Also in another form in the thirty-second chapter of Jeremiah: *Constantly doing evil in my sight from their youth.*

[Hebrew: נָפַח] **To blow, to breathe, to puff out**, and consequently, **to kindle**. In the first chapter of Haggai: *You brought it into the house and I blew it away.* And in the second chapter of Genesis: *And he breathed into his face the breath of life.* And in the twenty-second chapter of Ezekiel: *Fire for melting.* And further down: *And I will kindle you in the fire of my fury,* that is, *I will melt you down.* From this comes the bellows <term>sufflatorium: a tool used to excite a dying fire</term>. In the sixth chapter of Jeremiah: *The bellows failed in the fire.* <note>The author notes a grammatical shift here involving the Hebrew letters Mem and Nun</note>. And in the thirty-seventh chapter of Ezekiel: *And breathe upon these slain, that they may live again.* And in the first chapter of Malachi: *And you puffed at it.*

[Hebrew: נֹפֶךְ] **A precious stone**. Our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> considers it a **carbuncle** <term>carbunculus: a red gemstone, likely a garnet or ruby</term>. In the twenty-eighth and thirty-ninth chapters of Exodus: *In the second row, a carbuncle, a sapphire, and a jasper.* Similarly in the twenty-eighth chapter of Ezekiel: *Sapphire, carbuncle, and emerald.* Others believe this word signifies an **emerald** <note>original: "smaragdus"</note> and they seem to allude to the Aramaic <note>original: "Chaldaic"</note> interpretation. For both Onkelos and Jonathan the Assyrian translated this very word into the Aramaic language as "emerald-like." The Jerusalem Targum has it as "emerald." But Rabbi David Kimhi, in his *Book of Roots*, writes that this signifies a stone of a dark and reddish color. This better fits our common translation of "carbuncle," especially like the one from Arcadia. For Theophrastus, in his book *On Stones*, asserts that the carbuncle brought from Arcadia is somewhat dark, which some people think is called a **ruby**. But concerning these stones, Bishop Epiphanius once dedicated a specific volume to Eusebius Jerome.

# BOOK

**To fall** <note>original Hebrew: נפל (naphal)</note>. He collapsed. He fell. In the twentieth Psalm: **They are bound and have fallen.** And in the fourth chapter of Genesis: **Why has your countenance fallen?** And in the twenty-fifth chapter of the same book: **He died**—meaning he fell—**in the presence of all his brothers.** From this comes the noun for one who is **falling** or **collapsing**. In the forty-fifth Psalm: **The Lord raises up all who fall.** And like other words, it undergoes the loss of the letter *nun* <term>nun: the Hebrew letter 'n'</term> through *aphaeresis* <term>aphaeresis: the loss of a sound at the beginning of a word</term>, as in the thirty-seventh Psalm: **Though he falls, he shall not be crushed.** Furthermore, it takes its various forms. In the ninth chapter of Deuteronomy: **And I lay prostrate before the Lord,** that is, "and I fell before the Lord." It follows: **In which I humbly prayed to him,** that is, "in which I was prostrated, collapsed, or lay down." From this comes the word for "a fall" <note>Latin: casus</note>, and by that name they refer to whatever falls from fruits or from crops as **maphal** <note>original Hebrew: מַפָּל (maphal)</note>, which our translation interprets as **refuse** <note>Latin: quisquilias</note>. For "refuse" is always a plural term and signifies whatever small bits of husk fall from trees, or whatever falls, according to the grammarian Festus <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus, a 2nd-century Roman scholar</note>. Thus in the eighth chapter of Amos: **And let us sell the refuse of the wheat.** From this comes **miscarriage**, a fruit falling before its time. In the sixth chapter of Ecclesiastes: **I declare that a stillborn child is better off than he.** Likewise, the joints of the limbs are so named from "falling." In the forty-first chapter of Job: **The flakes of his flesh are joined together.** In this way, **giants** <note>original Hebrew: Nephilim, which the author derives from 'naphal' (to fall)</note> are also named, because they are so tall in stature that others seem humble and appear to "fall" before them. In the sixth chapter of Genesis: **There were giants on the earth in those days.** Otherwise, in the fourteenth chapter of Job: **A falling mountain crumbles away.**

**To shatter** <note>original Hebrew: נפץ (naphatz)</note>. He overturned. He demolished. He tore apart. He cast down. He separated. He scattered. He departed. He slipped away. In the thirteenth chapter of the First Book of Kings <note>modern 1 Samuel</note>: **Because I saw that the people were slipping away from me.** And in the ninth chapter of Genesis: **And from these the whole human race was spread over the entire earth.** The Hebrews read this word-for-word as: **And from these all the earth was scattered.** From this comes a noun that signifies the **scattering of lightning** from the clouds; it is written with six vowel points <note>referring to the Hebrew niqqud/vowel markings that distinguish the noun form</note>, which our translation renders literally. In the thirtieth chapter of Isaiah: **He will strike with a whirlwind and with hailstones,** perhaps following the Septuagint <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> who, instead of "he will strike," translated it as "he will thunder violently." But in that place, it ought to be a noun and not a verb, as the vowel points indicate. Similarly in the one hundred thirty-seventh Psalm: **And he shall dash his little ones against the rock,** that is, he cast them down or scattered them. Also in the second Psalm: **You shall break them like a potter’s vessel,** that is, you shall scatter or cast them down. From this comes the name for an instrument with which we easily demolish and break...

The first is named <term>mapaz</term> <note>Hebrew: מַפֵּץ, typically meaning a war-club or shatterer</note>. Ezekiel 9: "And every man had a weapon of destruction in his hand," that is, an instrument of destruction.

<term>Nephesh</term> <note>Hebrew: נֶפֶשׁ</note> — Soul, in the sense that it animates. As in Exodus 21: "He shall give life for life." Job 2: "But save his life." It is written with six points <note>referring to the Hebrew vowel markings or niqqud</note> and is of the feminine gender, as in Numbers 15: "If any soul sins through ignorance." Sometimes it signifies a living body or the whole human being, and thus it is also occasionally found in the masculine gender, as in Numbers 31: "One soul out of five hundred, both of the persons and of the cattle." It is declined in the plural in both the masculine and feminine genders. In Ezekiel 13, it is feminine: "To slay the souls that should not die." But in the same chapter below, it is masculine: "And I will let the souls go, the souls that you hunt to make them fly." In this verse, both genders are present. From this comes the verb that means to animate or to refresh, which our translation <note>the Latin Vulgate</note> rendered as "to refresh" <note>original: "refrigerare"</note>, more properly related to the Greek usage of *psyche* <note>original: "psychos"</note>. Exodus 23: "That your ox and your ass may rest, and the son of your handmaid and the stranger may be refreshed."

<term>Netz</term> <note>Hebrew: נֵץ</note> — Hawk. A general name for a bird of prey with hooked claws and an aquiline nose <note>beak</note>. Hence it is said in Leviticus 11: "And the hawk after its kind."

<term>Nitzav</term> <note>Hebrew: נָצַב</note> — He established or erected. 3 Kings 22 <note>modern 1 Kings 22:47</note>: "There was then no king appointed in Edom." From this comes "statue," as in Genesis 19: "She was turned into a statue of salt." From this comes "station" or "garrison" in 1 Chronicles 11: "And the station of the Philistines in Bethlehem," which is found in another form in Isaiah 22: "And I will drive you from your station." From this comes "official" or "prelate" who holds a magistracy, acting as a leader <note>original: "antistes"</note> who stands before others in all labors. 3 Kings 5: "Besides the officials who were over every work." From this, by a grammatical derivation <note>original: "cata paragogē"</note> adding a final *he*, it signifies the lame and the weak, which always stands still and is not raised or lifted up. Zechariah 11: "And that which stands still he shall not feed," which Jerome explains as "the weary he does not support." Hence it is said in Lamentations 2: "He has fixed his right hand like an enemy."

<term>Nazah</term> <note>Hebrew: נָצָה</note> — He flew. In place of this, our translation uses "to quarrel" or "to struggle." Lamentations 4: "For they have quarreled and been moved," for which the Hebrews read "they flew and departed." However, this verb sometimes changes

Because we truly take away, abstract, or despoil that which we cause to escape or deliver, this word also signifies **to take away, to despoil, to remove, or to hide.** **Genesis 31.** "And God has taken away the substance of your father and given it to me." <term>נצר</term> [N-Tz-R] **He guarded. He observed. He preserved.** **Proverbs 22.** "The eyes of the Lord guard knowledge." **Psalm 119**, "Because I have sought your justifications." And **Psalm 34**, "Keep your tongue from evil," that is, guard it.

**נקב** (Naqab) To dig, to pierce. Haggai 1: <note>original: "In sacculum pertusum"</note> "Into a bag with holes," that is, one that has been pierced through. And Habakkuk 3: <note>original: "Maledixisti sceptris eius"</note> "You cursed his scepters," though others translate this as "you pierced through his staff." Hence that passage in Isaiah 44: <note>original: "Et in malleis formauit illud"</note> "And he fashioned it with hammers," which some interpret as <term>drills|terebra</term> with which something is bored through. **נקבה** (Neqebah) A female. Genesis 1: "Male and female He created them."

**נקב** (Naqab) To estimate, to assess, to judge, or to name. Genesis 30: "Appoint your wages which I shall give you," that is, assess them. Amos 6: <note>original: "Optimates capita populorum"</note> "The leaders, the heads of the nations," that is, those who are esteemed and named. **נקד** (Naqad) A point, a mark, or a brand. Song of Songs 1: "We will make you chains of gold inlaid with silver," which is, word for word, "with points of silver" or "with marks." And from this, animals are named that are white with black spots, or similarly, black animals that have white spots. Genesis 30: "The speckled and the spotted." From such livestock, a shepherd or any herdsman is called a **נוקד** (Noqed), as in 2 Kings 3: "Furthermore, Mesha the king of Moab bred many sheep." Word for word, it says: "And Mesha the king of Moab was a herdsman." Mold or anything moldy is also named by this word because of its spots, such as bread that becomes moldy with age. Joshua 9: "Look, this bread which we took hot from our houses to come to you—now it has become dry and," it should be added, "moldy." In place of this, our translation <note>referring to the Latin Vulgate</note> uses a paraphrase: "and broken into pieces by extreme age."

**נקה** (Naqah) To cleanse, to purge, and to judge as innocent. In the last chapter of Joel: "And I will cleanse their blood which I had not cleansed." And in Psalm 19: "And I shall be cleansed from the greatest sin." And in Exodus 34: "And no one is innocent by himself before You." This should be read word for word as: "And the innocent shall not be declared innocent," which means he is not seen as innocent.

<term>Neshek <note>Hebrew: נשך</note></term> — Interest or usury. Exodus 22: "Neither shall you oppress him with usury," or more correctly, "you shall not lay usury upon him." and Psalm 15: "He has not given his money for usury."

<term>Nashal <note>Hebrew: נשל</note></term> — He rooted out, plucked away, or slipped off. <term>Nasham <note>Hebrew: נשם</note></term> — A breathing hole, a blast, panting, breath, or spirit; joined with a final letter <note>referring to the Hebrew letter 'He' forming Neshamah</note>. Isaiah 2: "Cease from man, whose breath is in his nostrils." Also 1 Kings 17: "And the sickness was so severe that no breath remained in him." And Genesis 7: "And all in which the breath of life was within." So too Genesis 2: "And he breathed into his face the breath of life." It adds "of life" so it may be understood as any breath having life within itself; for this word is not used for other winds, spirits, or blasts. And according to Rabbi Abraham ibn Ezra <note>A 12th-century Spanish scholar and grammarian.</note>, it is found used only for humans.

<term>Tinshemet <note>Hebrew: תנשמת</note></term> — A mole, according to Rabbi Solomon, who writes this in his commentaries on the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible.</note>. Leviticus 11: "The lizard and the mole; all these are unclean." It also signifies a bird among the unclean and prohibited birds, which our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate, the standard Catholic Bible.</note> interprets a little earlier in the same chapter as a swan. But Rabbi Solomon writes in the same place that it is a bird that flies at night. Modern scholars <note>Contemporary 16th-century Hebraists.</note> name a small bird this way, similar to an owl, which bird-catchers [identify].

They cite Rabbi Isi <note>Isi ben Judah, a 2nd-century scholar</note>, who said there were two twilights: the twilight of the day when night comes on, and the twilight of the night when day begins. From this, they name whatever is obscure and dark. Jeremiah 13: "And before your feet stumble upon the dark mountains," that is, the cloudy and obscure ones.

This is a prolepsis <term>prolepsis: a figure of speech where a future or resulting state is described as if it already exists</term>. For this reason, some believe this kind of leaning sometimes signifies adoration, just as when mouth is applied to mouth. ...has touched upon, yet following the example of Rabbi Judah <note>Judah ben David Hayyuj (c. 940–1010), a foundational Hebrew grammarian who established the theory of three-letter roots.</note>, I say that each individual instance can, in a certain way, be reduced to a single meaning, as is clear to anyone who considers it well. Genesis 19: "The men of the city surrounded his house." For it ought to have said, "they were turned toward the house."

<term>Saba</term> <note>original: סבא</note> He was intoxicated. He drank. He feasted. He gorged himself on wine. Isaiah 56: "Come, let us take wine and be filled with drunkenness." For which the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> translated more correctly: "and let us be intoxicated." Deuteronomy 21: "He gives himself to gluttony, luxury, and feasting," which is more correctly rendered in two words as: "he is a glutton and a drunkard." In German, this is <term>fressen and sufan</term> <note>original: "freffen und fufan" — modern German "fressen und saufen," meaning to eat like an animal and drink to excess.</note>. Nahum 1: "So is their feast of those drinking together," which others read as: "And like drunkards they are intoxicated." <term>Seba</term> <note>original: סבא</note> This is a royal city of Ethiopia, as Jerome writes in his *Book of Hebrew Places*. Following the example of Eusebius, he writes Seba with the letter <term>Samekh</term> <note>The Hebrew letter 'ס'.</note>. Isaiah 43: "I have given Egypt as your ransom, Ethiopia and Seba for you." It takes its name from Seba, the son of Cush. Genesis 10: "The sons of Cush: Seba, Havilah, and Sabtah." For another word, Sheba, is written with the letter <term>Sin</term> <note>The Hebrew letter 'ש'.</note> and signifies Arabia, named after its founder Sheba, the son of Raamah, as seen in the same tenth chapter of Genesis. From him, they are called Sabæans—not the Ethiopian ones mentioned above, but the Arabian ones. The geographer Strabo writes of these in his sixteenth book, where after speaking much about the Nabataeans, he says: "Next to these is the most blessed land of the Sabæans, which is a very great nation. Among these grow frankincense, myrrh, and cinnamon." Hence, whenever it is found written with the letter <term>Sin</term>, it is translated as Arabia, as in Psalm 72 <note>Psalm 61 in the source's Vulgate numbering.</note>: "And to him shall be given the gold of Arabia." Likewise, a little earlier in the same passage: "The kings of the Arabs and Seba shall bring gifts," where you will find both words in the same verse. Therefore, the unwary are often prone to go astray in this word when they do not look closely at the spelling. I believe this happened to our Jerome by accident rather than on purpose, as in his book *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, he explains the previously cited text of Genesis 10: "The sons of Cush: Seba and Havilah," by adding: "Seba, from whom come the Sabæans, of whom Virgil says: 'The branch of incense belongs to the Sabæans alone.'" <note>A quote from Virgil's *Georgics* (2.117).</note> But soon after, in the subsequent explanation of the verse "The sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan," he returns to the right path.

->BOOK<-

and it shows the difference between the letters *samekh* <note>ס</note> and *sin* <note>ש</note> in those same words, which you should note diligently. For the Sabaeans from *Saba* <note>Sheba</note> are said to be written with the letter *sin*, and not from the Ethiopians. This is clearly indicated by Stephanus of Byzantium in his book *On Cities and Peoples* when he says that Saba is a great city and a region near the Red Sea, from which are named both the Sabaean people and the Sabaean region. Suidas, however, writes that the Erythraean Sea <note>The Red Sea</note> is at the Persian Gulf. And Pliny, in the fifth book of his *Natural History*, chapter 11, teaches that Arabia reaches to the Red Sea—specifically that "Fragrant Arabia," which is wealthy and famous by the surname "the Blessed" <note>original: "felicis"; referring to *Arabia Felix*, modern-day Yemen</note>. Therefore, *Saba* written with a *sin* is the incense-bearing Arabia; but with a *samekh*, it is the Ethiopian one. From this, it is clearly understood that the Queen of Sheba who came to hear Solomon in the First Book of Kings, chapter 10, was not an Ethiopian woman, but the Queen of "Blessed Arabia."

<term>סבך (Sabak)</term> **To entangle; to perplex.** Nahum 1: "For as thorns they are folded together." From this comes the noun for entanglement, perplexity, or an embrace. Genesis 22: "And he saw behind his back a ram caught by its horns in the briars." In the Hebrew, it is read thus: "And Abraham lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, a ram was caught afterwards in an entanglement by its horns." The Chaldean translation <note>The Targum</note> expressed this as "shrubbery," saying that the ram was joined in the shrubbery by its horns. And it is possible that the density of the foliage, entangled among itself like coherent briars, is spoken of in this way metaphorically; hence our translation <note>The Vulgate</note> renders it as "forest" in Psalm 74: "As in a forest of trees with axes." Jerome, in his psalter translated from the "Hebrew Truth" <note>the *Hebraica Veritas*, Jerome's translation directly from Hebrew rather than the Greek Septuagint</note>, translated it as: "In a thicket of wood with axes." Though others explain it as: "In the entanglement of the brushwood with axes." They similarly explain what we read in Job 8: "His roots shall be thick upon a heap of stones," like this: "His roots shall grow leafy over a spring or source," that is, they shall be entangled or entwined with leaves. And if you sometimes find this written with a *sin* in place of a *samekh*, it signifies the same thing: namely, entangled and intricate leaves.

<term>סבל (Sabal)</term> **To bear; to carry.** Lamentations 5: "We have borne their iniquities." And Isaiah 46: "I will carry." And in the same, chapter 53: "And he himself has carried our sorrows." In another form in Ecclesiastes 12, where we read "the locust shall be made fat," others translate it as "the back shall be burdened" or "they shall make the loins carry." From this comes the noun for "burden" or "load." 1 Kings 5: "Seventy thousand of those who carried burdens."

<term>סגד (Sagad)</term> **To bow; to kneel.** Isaiah 44: "He bows down before it and worships."

# SECOND [BOOK]

And according to Onkelos the Chaldean <note>Onkelos was the famous 2nd-century translator of the Torah into Aramaic (the "Chaldean" language); his translations were often used by scholars to clarify difficult Hebrew verbs</note> this word signifies **to worship**. [Hebrew word] <note>Original Hebrew: סגולה (Segullah)</note> **Appropriated**; one's own and peculiar. With the letter *he* added at the end through a grammatical shift <term>cataparagogen</term>, it signifies the same thing as a "personal possession," "private property," or "peculiarity." Exodus 19: *You shall be my personal possession among all peoples.* And 1 Chronicles 29: *From my own personal property I give gold and silver to the temple of my God.* This word signifies whatever I have specifically set aside for myself as a treasure. The Hebrew logicians also use this term for one of the five "predicables" <note>Five categories used in traditional logic to describe how a property relates to its subject</note>, which we also call **proprium** <note>a "property" that is unique to a specific species, like laughter is to humans</note>.

[Hebrew word] <note>Original Hebrew: סגן (Sagan)</note> **Magistrate** and **prelate**. From this, Berosus <note>Berosus was a Babylonian priest; however, the "Book of Chaldean Deflorations" mentioned here was actually a famous 15th-century forgery by Annius of Viterbo used by Renaissance scholars</note> writes in the second book of his *Chaldean History*: *First, therefore, they called Noah "Ogygisan Sagan," which means the illustrious high priest of sacred things.*

[Hebrew word] <note>Original Hebrew: סגר (Sagar)</note> **He closed**. Genesis 19: *And they closed the door.* 1 Samuel 1: *But the Lord had closed her womb.* From this comes the noun for a closure, a cloister, a shutting, a conclusion, or a private chamber. Isaiah 42: *To bring the prisoner out of confinement.* And in the feminine plural, Psalm 18: *And they limped away from their paths,* which was more correctly translated in 2 Samuel 22: *And they shall be constrained in their narrow places.* But more truly thus: *And they shall limp from their chains.* There is also another noun which signifies either a prison, a neck-yoke, or a collar, which our translation interprets as a "cage." Ezekiel 19: *And they put him in a cage.* From this is derived that which binds something and contains it at the same time, like a frame or border. Exodus 25: *And you shall make for it a golden lip all around, and for the lip itself a carved crown four fingers high, and above that another small golden crown.* Which is phrased word-for-word as follows: *And you shall make for it a surrounding embrace or golden margin; and you shall make for it a closure the width of a palm—that is, the measure of a fist—all around; and you shall make a golden periphery or container for the closure itself all around.* Also another significant word in Leviticus 13: *The priest shall shut him up for seven days.*

**סגור** <note>Hebrew: Sagur</note> **Gold that is frequently refined and of the best quality.** It is called in Greek *obrizon* gold, which according to Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedist.</note> is gold frequently tested by fire and very pure. **סגור** <note>Hebrew: Sagur</note> **A weapon of war**, which they call a <term>spatha</term> <note>A broadsword.</note>, a <term>framea</term> <note>A spear or sword.</note>, a <term>mucro</term> <note>A sharp point or blade.</note>, or a sword. **סגריר** <note>Hebrew: Sagrir</note> **A heavy rain or impetuous storm.** Our translation <note>Referring to the Latin Vulgate.</note> translated this as "cold." **סד** <note>Hebrew: Sad</note> **The wood by which the feet of prisoners are bound.** Our translation renders this binding as <term>neruum</term>. <note>Literally "sinew" or "nerve," used historically to mean shackles or stocks.</note> Job 13: "You have put my foot in the stocks."

<note>original: "ram"</note> ...said it signifies a most precious ointment with which the greatest kings used to be anointed. Whence the prophet speaks concerning the Prince of Tyre in **Ezekiel 28**: *“You were the extended and protecting cherub.”* Where the <term>Septuagint</term><note>The earliest Greek translation of the Old Testament, often abbreviated as LXX.</note> translated it as "anointed." And according to the cited **Rabbi Jonah** <note>Jonah ibn Janah, a famous 11th-century Hebrew grammarian.</note>, it should be read thus: *“You are a cherub anointed with the most precious ointment,”* that is, endowed with majesty. This reading is very pleasing to the teachers of the Hebrews, and especially to **Rabbi David Kimhi** in his *Book of Roots*. And for my purpose, according to my teacher **Rabbi Jacob Jehiel**, it signifies a small oil jar in **2 Kings 4**: *“Your handmaid has nothing in my house except a little oil wherewith I may be anointed.”* It is more correctly rendered: *“except a small jar of oil.”* For the woman indicated that a tiny amount remained for her for the necessity of hunger, not for the luxury of anointing. Thus, the phrase “wherewith I may be anointed” is not in the Hebrew text, but should be struck out with an <term>obelisk</term><note>A symbol (†) used by ancient scholars to mark text that appeared in a translation but was missing from the original source.</note>. And so **Jonathan the Chaldean** <note>Referring to the Targum Jonathan, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Bible.</note> interprets it: *“Saul entered to do what was necessary.”* Others derive it from *nasach*; others from *sachach*.

[Hebrew: סוס] **Horse.** **Psalm 32**: *“Do not be like the horse or the mule.”* <note>The text cites Psalm 33, but in modern numbering, this is Psalm 32:9.</note> **Exodus 14**: *“And all the cavalry of Pharaoh.”* It is also used in the feminine gender in **Song of Songs 1**: *“I have compared you to my mare among the chariots of Pharaoh.”*

[Hebrew: סוס] **A species of bird** which authors name differently. For in **Isaiah 38** it is said: *“Like a young swallow.”* But there are two different words there to be distinguished by a mark of <term>hypodiastole</term><note>A punctuation mark used to distinguish between words that might be read together but should remain separate.</note>, so that the sense is: *“Like a swallow and a crane”*—or a heron, or a stork. Others call it a crow. **Symmachus** <note>An early translator of the Old Testament into Greek.</note> did not look at the orthography and therefore erred in translating it as: *“like a trapped swallow.”* In this same word, the letter *Vau* is found changed into a *Yod* in **Jeremiah 8**: *“The turtle-dove, the swallow, and the stork.”* Where Symmachus translated "cicada" instead of "swallow." See how much doubt there is in the names of things, not only in Latin but also in Hebrew.

[Hebrew: *Suph*] <note>סוף</note> Papyrus, reed, or sedge. ## THE SECOND BOOK

More seriously: "Lay aside your old rags." <note>original: "ferius. Pone ueteres pannos." This is a quote from the Roman satirist Persius (Satire 5.92), used here metaphorically to suggest discarding old, worn-out interpretations in favor of fresh scholarship.</note>

**סָחָה** <term>S-H-H: To scrape off or wear away.</term> As seen in **Ezekiel 26**: "And I will scrape her dust from her." From this is derived a noun for filth and excess which is scraped off from any object. In **Lamentations 3**: "You have made me as the offscouring and refuse."

**סָחַב** <term>S-H-B: To rot or decay.</term> As seen in **Jeremiah 46**: "Why has your strong one rotted away?" <note>In modern scholarship, this root usually means "to drag," but the author follows a Latin tradition—likely the Vulgate—interpreting it as decay in this context.</note>

**סָחַר** <term>S-H-R: To turn, revolve, whirl, or go around.</term> As seen in **Jeremiah 14**: "Both the prophet and the priest have gone about," which is to say, they traveled in circles and whirled through the land in the manner of those suffering from vertigo. This means: my heart revolved or whirled like a spinning top, having no rest. For this reason, **Jerome** <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the primary translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> in his translation of the Psalter rendered it as "my heart has fluctuated." Consequently, **Onkelos** <note>The reputed author of the Targum Onkelos, the influential Aramaic translation of the Torah.</note>, wishing to interpret into Aramaic <note>original: "chaldaice"</note> that passage in **Genesis 42** where it is written, "And he turned himself away for a little while"—though it is more correctly read as "he turned away from them and wept"—used this present word.
