# THE BOOK

Of Ezekiel, chapter 24: "Put on the pot, put it on." <note>original: "Pone ollam pone"</note> And in the same book, chapter 11: "This city is the cauldron, and we are the meat." <note>original: "Hęc eft lebes. nos autem carnes"</note> It is declined in the feminine plural, as in Amos, chapter 4: "And your remnants in boiling pots."

**סיר** <term>Sir: A word with two meanings, "pot" and "thorn" or "briar."</term> Nahum, chapter 1: "Like thorns they are folded together." <note>original: "Sicut fpinę fe inuicem complectuntur"</note> Hosea, chapter 2: "I will hedge up your way with thorns."

**סית** <term>Sith: To incite, persuade, or advise.</term> Deuteronomy, chapter 13: "If your brother tries to entice you." And in 1 Samuel, chapter 26: "If the Lord has incited you against me."

**סכך** <term>Sakak: To cover, shelter, hide, or protect.</term> Exodus, chapter 25: "They shall cover [the mercy seat], spreading their wings and covering the oracle." It is sometimes found written with the letter *Shin* <note>the letter ש</note> because of the easy transition of one letter into the other, as they are phonetically similar. <note>original: "ſibi ſymbolicam"</note> Exodus, chapter 33: "And I will cover you with my right hand until I have passed by." It is very often found by <term>apocope</term> <note>the shortening of a word by omitting the final sound</note> as in Lamentations, chapter 3: "You have covered yourself in anger." Also in the same chapter: "You have covered yourself with a cloud," which elsewhere is read—less correctly—as "you have set a cloud against yourself." Also in 1 Kings, chapter 8: "And the cherubim covered the ark and its poles," which should be written with the letter *Kaph* <note>the letter כ</note> and not with a *Beth* as found in some printed editions.

From this word is named every type of covering, tabernacle, hut, or tent. Lamentations, chapter 2: "He has destroyed his booth [tent] as if it were a garden," although there it is written with the letter *Shin*, which has the same value. It also takes the letter *He* at the end for the feminine gender. Isaiah, chapter 4: "And there shall be a tabernacle for a shadow in the daytime from the heat." And in the plural in Leviticus, chapter 23: "The feast of tabernacles shall be for seven days to the Lord." It also takes the letter *Mem* by <term>prosthesis</term> <note>adding a letter to the beginning of a word</note> at the start, as in Psalm 105: "He spread a cloud for their protection."

From this expression is derived the name for a military defense used by those who besiege cities; they place a manufactured roof over themselves so they are not crushed by stones thrown from above. Julius Pollux <note>A 2nd-century Greek grammarian and sophist</note> in his work on the names of armor calls this a *skepasterion*. <note>original Greek: "σχεπαστήριον," meaning a covering or shelter</note> Rabbi David Kimhi <note>A famous medieval Hebrew grammarian and exegete known as the Radak</note> says it is called a "mole," namely because it is used for undermining the walls of cities. Our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> in my opinion, does not correctly translate it as "awning" <note>original: "umbraculum"</note> in Nahum, chapter 2: "They shall quickly climb her walls, and the shelter shall be prepared." The Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translated it better: "and they shall prepare defenses."

**סכך** <term>Sakak (Secondary sense): To mix, to stir up, to gather into one sum, or to cause to run together.</term> Isaiah, chapter 19: "And I will set the Egyptians against the Egyptians."

**סך** <term>Sak: A sum of sums, or a numerical total.</term> Psalm 42, where we read: "For I shall go over into the place of the wonderful tabernacle." The Hebrews explain it as: "I shall go with a certain multitude [sum] of gathered men." Thus the sweetest of Hebrew poets, Joseph Hyssopaeus <note>Joseph Ezobi, a 13th-century Jewish poet from Provence</note> in the introduction of his iambic book which he titled *The Silver Dish*, uses this poem:

# SECOND [BOOK]

סכל <note>Hebrew root: S-K-L</note> **Foolish. stupid. unwise.** Jeremiah 5: *Hear, O foolish people, who have no heart.* From this comes **foolishness, fatuity, lack of wisdom.** Ecclesiastes 2: *And I saw that wisdom exceeds foolishness as much as light differs from darkness.* From this the verb **to be made a fool** is derived. 1 Samuel 13 <note>Original: "i. Regu." In the Latin Vulgate, 1 & 2 Samuel are titled 1 & 2 Kings.</note>: *You have acted foolishly and have not kept the commandments of the Lord.* And 2 Samuel 15: *O Lord, I pray, make the counsel of Ahitophel foolish.* It is sometimes found written with the letter *sin* <note>original: "per sin scriptum"; referring to the Hebrew letter 'ש' when it makes an 's' sound, identical to 'ס'</note>. Ecclesiastes 1: *That I might know prudence and doctrine, and errors and foolishness.* It is also often found in the same book through a transposition of letters <term>metathesis|The grammatical term for when letters in a word switch places</term>.

סכן <note>Hebrew root: S-K-N</note> **To be equal. to be matched. to be comparable.** Job 15: *You argue with words against one who is not your equal.* And in chapter 22: *Can a man be compared to God?* And in chapter 33: *A man will not please God even if he runs with him.* That is, he will not be likened to, or be an equal, or be compared to God.

סכן <note>Hebrew root: S-K-N, second meaning</note> **To foresee. to learn. to explore.** Psalm 139: *And you have foreseen all my ways.* And Job 22: *Even when knowledge shall be perfect,* which Rabbi Abraham ibn Ezra <note>A renowned 12th-century Spanish Jewish scholar and astronomer</note> understands this way: how can a comparison be made between God and man when intelligence stands as a medium between both? So it should be read: *Can a man be compared to God when intelligence is learned between both?*

סכן <note>Hebrew root: S-K-N, third meaning</note> **To be accustomed.** Numbers 22, where we read: *Tell me what similar thing I have ever done to you?* The Hebrews have: *Was I ever accustomed to doing such things to you?* <note>This refers to the story of Balaam’s donkey speaking to its master.</note>

סכן <note>Hebrew root: S-K-N, fourth meaning</note> **Storehouse. repository. cellar. granary. steward and butler.** 2 Chronicles 32: *Also storehouses for grain, wine, and oil.*

מסכן <note>M-S-K-N, a noun derived from the same root</note> **Poor.** Ecclesiastes 4: *Better is a poor and wise youth.* And in chapter 9: *And there was found in it a poor and wise man.* From this comes **poverty** and **want.** Deuteronomy 8: *Where you shall eat your bread without any want.*

סכר <note>Hebrew root: S-K-R</note> **To close. to obstruct. to stop up.** Psalm 63: *Because the mouth of those speaking iniquity is stopped.* Genesis 8: *And the fountains of the deep were closed.* And it is sometimes found written with the letter *sin*, as in Isaiah 19: *All who made ponds to catch fish.* Translated word-for-word, it is: *all making closures of pools for fish-ponds.* It is written with six points <note>original: "sex punctis"; likely a reference to Hebrew vowel marks or a specific scribal notation</note>. Here, "fish" is put in place of "souls," as Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into Latin</note> testifies in his commentaries.

סכר <note>Hebrew root: S-K-R, second meaning</note> **To hand over.** Isaiah 19: *And I will deliver Egypt into the hand of cruel lords.* Although some of the Hebrews also explain it according to the previous meaning, namely: *And I will shut up Egypt in the hand of very harsh lords.* The Targum of Jonathan <note>An ancient Aramaic translation and interpretation of the Hebrew Bible</note> supports this view.

# BOOK

**סכת** [S-K-T] He attended or listened. Deuteronomy 27: "Take heed and listen, Israel." <note>original: "Attende et audi Israel"</note>

**סכות** [S-K-W-T] An idol of a demon. Amos 5: "And you carried the tabernacle of Moloch," <note>The author is quoting the Vulgate translation of Amos 5:26.</note> where it should be read as "the idol of your king."

**סל** [S-L] A basket or hamper. Genesis 40: "And in one basket that was higher," and likewise in the same place: "three baskets are three more days." And this word is found entirely doubled in Jeremiah 6: "Turn back your hand like a grape-gatherer to the basket."

**סלסל** [S-L-S-L] A shoot or a vine-leaf. Our translation <note>The "our translation" refers to the Latin Vulgate used by the Church.</note> translated this as if it were a doubling of the previous word for "basket," as in "like a grape-gatherer to the basket."

**סלה** [S-L-H] **Selah**. "Forever," "always," "continually," or "until." Habakkuk 3: "God will come from the south, and the Holy One from Mount Paran forever." <note>original: "semper"</note> For this is how Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the primary translator of the Latin Vulgate.</note> translated it, although some of our volumes do not have the adverb "always," in place of which the seventy interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> placed *diapsalma* <note>A musical term usually indicating a pause or a change in volume.</note>. However, Jonathan the Chaldean <note>Referring to the Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Bible.</note> translated it as "in the strength of the ages." According to Rabbi Eleazar son of Jacob, in whatever place of Sacred Scripture "Selah" or "Nezah" or "Ad" <note>Three Hebrew words often associated with eternity or persistence.</note> is added, there shall be no end, neither in this age nor in the age of ages. But Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>A celebrated 12th-century Spanish-Jewish scholar and biblical commentator.</note> thinks this word "Selah" means "truly," which is a view that pleases several Hebrew authors. Indeed, it has nothing else to connect to except the musical harmony itself; hence, throughout all Sacred Scripture, it is only found in songs, such as in the book of Psalms and in the song of Habakkuk cited above. Jerome discussed this most extensively after Origen <note>An early Christian scholar (c. 185–253 AD).</note> in his letter to Marcella regarding the *diapsalma*, as did the Bishop of Burgos <note>Paul of Burgos (c. 1351–1435), a Jewish convert to Christianity and influential biblical scholar.</note> in his third addition to Psalm 84: "How lovely are your tabernacles." See his work.

**סלל** [S-L-L] He heaped up with stones or mud. Isaiah 57: "Make a way, prepare a path." Word for word it is: "Heap up, heap up, prepare the way." Similarly in Jeremiah 6: "And pour a mound around Jerusalem." It signifies making something out of mud, wood, or stone higher so that we can enter more easily. From this, a narrow or well-trodden road is named with the addition of the letter *Mem*. 2 Samuel 20: <note>The text cites 2 Kings, following the older naming convention where 1-2 Samuel and 1-2 Kings were called 1-4 Kings.</note> "He moved him from the road into the field." And our translation uses "fortifications" for "mounds" in the same place, 2 Samuel 20: "And they surrounded the city with fortifications." The word is also found through <term>metathesis</term> <note>The transposition of sounds or letters in a word.</note> in Exodus 9: "Still you hold back my people and do not wish to let them go," which according to Onkelos the Chaldean <note>The Targum of Onkelos, the standard Aramaic translation of the Torah.</note> is explained thus: "Still you place an obstacle before my people lest..."

**BOOK**

סלעם <term>Sal’am: A beetle or locust</term>. Our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate, which was the standard Bible for the author</note> renders this as *atthacum* in Leviticus 11. It is also called *atthacus* and *ophimachus* <note>These are Latinized Greek terms for types of wingless grasshoppers or locusts</note>.

סלע <term>Sela: A rock</term>. Numbers 24: "If you place your nest in a rock." And in the same book, chapter 20: "Speak to the rock before them." Also in Psalm 104: "The rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs." From this comes the idea of a fortress built upon a rock, as in 2 Samuel 22: "The Lord is my rock." But it is expressed better in Psalm 18: "The Lord is my firmament," that is, a tower, citadel, or fortress; for Jonathan <note>Referring to the Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation of the Prophets</note> renders it thus in Aramaic: "The Lord is my strength," following the likeness of what is written in Proverbs 18: "The name of the Lord is a very strong tower."

סלף <term>Salaph: To bend back, to twist, to pervert, or to change</term>. Deuteronomy 16: "Gifts blind the eyes of the wise and change the words of the righteous." Onkelos <note>The author of the Targum Onkelos, an ancient Aramaic translation of the Torah</note> agrees in Aramaic, translating it as "and they destroy the words of the righteous." Our translation rendered this as "to supplant" or "to overthrow" in Proverbs 13: "But impiety supplants the sinner." Likewise in Proverbs 19: "The folly of a man supplants his steps." From this comes the noun in Proverbs 11: "The overthrowing of the perverted shall waste them," which means their twisting and iniquity. And in Proverbs 21: "That he may pull down the wicked from evil," that is, that he may turn them back.

סלת <term>Soleth: Fine flour</term>. Leviticus 2: "Fine flour shall be his offering." And a little further below: "A handful full of fine flour."

סמדר <term>Semadar: Immature grapes</term>. Song of Solomon 2: "And the flowering vineyards have given their odor."

סם <term>Sam: Spice or aroma</term>. Exodus 30: "Take for yourself spices." Onkelos translated this with the synonym *bisam*, meaning "fragrant."

סמך <term>Samakh: To join, to add, to place, to lean upon, or to rest</term>. Numbers 27: "And place your hand upon him." And a little lower in the same chapter: "And with hands placed upon his head." And Amos 5: "And he leans his hand upon the wall." This is how we understand what we read in Psalm 145: "The Lord raises up all who fall." Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into Latin</note> translates this more correctly as: "The Lord sustains all who are falling." Not much differently is the verse from Psalm 88 understood: "Your wrath is confirmed upon me." This signifies approaching, drawing near, and surrounding. As in Song of Solomon 2: "Support me with flowers." Likewise in Genesis 27: "I have established him with grain and wine," meaning that grain, wine, and oil should always be accessible to him. Similarly, in Psalm 51: "And confirm me with a principal spirit," meaning let a principal spirit <note>Often understood as a 'generous' or 'noble' spirit</note> approach and draw near.

->## SECOND [BOOK]<-

**I have hated the unjust.** <note>original: "Iniquos odio habui," quoting Psalm 119:113.</note> Rabbi David Kimhi <note>A renowned 12th-13th century Jewish grammarian and commentator from Spain, often called Radak.</note> and Rabbi Jonah <note>Jonah ibn Janah, an influential 11th-century Hebrew grammarian.</note> think that this word is derived from the term immediately preceding it, namely from "wicked thoughts." <note>The Hebrew root *sa'af* (סעף) can refer to branches or divided, ambivalent thoughts.</note>

**סער [Sa'ar]** To swell, to rage, to grow frequent, or to rush in and move like a whirlwind, falling upon something like a storm. Habakkuk 3: "coming like a whirlwind to scatter me." Likewise, 2 Kings 6: "The heart of the king of Syria was troubled," <note>original: "Conturbatum est cor regis syrię."</note> that is, it was moved in the likeness of a whirlwind. And Jonah 1: "the sea went and swelled." From this comes the noun for "tempest" or "whirlwind" in the same chapter of Jonah: "and there was a great tempest in the sea." And 2 Kings 2: "And Elijah ascended by a whirlwind into heaven." It is sometimes found written with the consonant *sin* <note>The Hebrew letter שׁ, which can sound like 's'.</note> and signifies the same thing, as in Nahum 1: "The Lord is in the tempest and the whirlwind is his way." Likewise, Daniel 11: "And the king of the north shall come against him like a tempest." This is also written with a *sin* instead of a *samech*.

**סף [Saf]** A cup, bowl, or chalice... and generally any vessel from which wine is drunk, although our translation <note>Referring to the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> has rendered it "lintel" <note>The horizontal beam over a door.</note>. Zechariah 12: "Behold, I will make Jerusalem a lintel of drunkenness," but it is more correctly: "A cup of staggering" or a "sleep-inducing cup" that brings death. Isaiah alludes to this in chapter 51: "You have drunk to the bottom the cup of sleep," which in another place is interpreted as "compunction." <note>A piercing of the heart or deep regret.</note> Psalm 60: "You have given us wine of compunction to drink." Also Exodus 12: "And dip a bunch of hyssop in the blood which is in the threshold." Behold, above he translated it as "lintel," but now he translates it as "threshold." However, neither fits the context well. Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> wrote that it is a certain type of vessel, and Nicolaus de Lyra <note>A 14th-century Franciscan whose literal interpretations of the Bible were highly influential.</note> says it is a basin—he perhaps means a wash-basin. I would think it should be called a "vial," <term>phiala (vial)</term><note>In this context, a wide, shallow ceremonial bowl rather than a small bottle.</note> so that the sense is: "Dip a bunch of hyssop in the blood that is in the vial," namely a wide, large, silver bowl in which the Passover blood was received. This is how we should understand what we read in 2 Kings 25: "And the three doorkeepers," that is, the three keepers of the vessels. In the ancient Chaldean interpretation <note>The Targum, an Aramaic translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> it is translated thus: "and the three keepers of the treasure over the house of the sanctuary." And in the feminine plural, 1 Kings 7: "And the water-pots, and the flesh-hooks, and the vials." Note there the vowel points <term>hirek</term> and <term>dagesh</term> due to the loss of a doubled letter. Regarding this, Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic translation of the Prophets.</note> in the Chaldean interpretation uses this word *kolaia*. Onkelos the Chaldean <note>Author of the standard Aramaic translation of the Torah.</note> uses the same word in his interpretation, *koltha*, for Rebecca’s water-pot in Genesis 24.

**סף [Saf]** Threshold. Ezekiel 40: "And he measured the threshold of the gate, one reed in width," that is, one threshold. And later: "and the threshold of the gate near the porch."

**שקד** <note>original: "Shaqad"</note> He has protected, or kept watch. **Psalm 84**: *I chose to be cast aside in the house of my God.* <note>The Hebrew verb here is often translated as "to stand at the threshold."</note> Which **Rabbi Solomon** <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), a preeminent medieval Jewish scholar.</note> explains according to the preceding word, that is, to keep watch at the threshold. Some say, however, that it corresponds with the word above and is derived from it.

**מספוא** <note>original: "Mispo"</note> With the preposition *mem*, it signifies all fodder for beasts excluding chaff and straw, which our translation <note>Likely referring to the Latin Vulgate.</note> renders as "hay." **Genesis 24**: *There is plenty of straw and hay with us.* And **Judges 19**: *Having straw and hay for fodder for the donkeys.*

**ספד** <note>original: "Saphad"</note> He mourned or lamented. **1 Kings 14**: *And all Israel shall mourn him.* **Ecclesiastes 3**: *A time to mourn and a time to dance.* And **Zechariah 12**: *And they shall mourn for him with a mourning as if for an only son.* Also its passive form in **Jeremiah 16**: *They shall not be mourned and they shall not be buried.*

**ספה** <note>original: "Saphah"</note> He consumed, killed, destroyed, took away, or put to death. **Jeremiah 12**: *The animal and the bird are consumed.* And **Psalm 40**: *Who seek my soul to take it away.* And **Genesis 18**: *Will you indeed destroy the righteous with the wicked?* And **Deuteronomy 32**: *I will gather evils upon them.* That is: I will consume all the evils of the world upon them.

**ספה** <note>This entry uses the same spelling but refers to a different root meaning.</note> He added, increased, accumulated, or gathered. **Jeremiah 7**: *Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices.* And **Numbers 32**: *That you might increase the fury of the Lord against Israel.* And **Deuteronomy 29**: *That the drunken may take the thirsty.*

**ספח** <note>original: "Saphach"</note> He gathered, joined, or re-collected. **1 Samuel 2**: *And he said, "Dismiss me to one priestly part,"* that is: join me to it. From this comes the noun, as in **Habakkuk 2**: *Pouring out his gall,* that is: joining. And **Job 30**: *And they thought it a delight to be under the brambles,* which should be translated as: *Under the nettles they were gathered.* It is also found written with the letter *Sin* <note>The letters Samekh (ס) and Sin (ש) often made the same sound and were occasionally interchanged in older manuscripts.</note> as in **Isaiah 5**: *And I waited for him to do judgment, and behold, iniquity.* He wishes to say: and behold, a "binding" or an "entanglement," so to speak.

**SECOND**

as if to say: I expected justice, and behold, a small mob. <note>original: "quasi diceret. expectavi iudicium et ecce conventiculum." This is a play on the Latin Vulgate translation of Isaiah 5:7.</note>

**[Aftergrowth]** <note>Hebrew root: ספיח (saphiach)</note> Anything crumbled, tiny, and falling off of its own accord. From this, the sprinkling of rain is so named. Job 14: "And by a flood, the earth is gradually worn away." <note>original: "Et alluvione paulatim terra consumit."</note> More correctly: "Its sprinkling washes away the dust of the earth." This is how it is understood in Leviticus 25: "the ground which produces of its own accord you shall not reap," <note>original: "que spõte gignit humus nõ metes."</note> that is, the fallen fragments of your harvest you shall not reap. For it means to say, according to **Rabbi Solomon**, <note>Rabbi Solomon refers to Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> that even if you have not sown, you still must not reap that which sprouts from the seed that fell to the earth at the time of the harvest.

**[Bowl]** <note>Hebrew root: ספל (sephel)</note> A vial, a shell, or what is commonly called a "cup" <note>original: "tassia," likely related to the French "tasse."</note>; a type of drinking vessel. Judges 5: "And in a bowl of princes she offered butter." And in the sixth chapter of the same book: "He squeezed the fleece and filled the bowl with dew."

**[Ceiling]** <note>Hebrew root: ספן (saphan)</note> A roof, a paneled ceiling, a vault, or an arched roof. Haggai 1: "That you should live in paneled houses." <note>original: "domibus laqueatis."</note> The **Septuagint** <note>The "lxx" refers to the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> interprets this as "hollowed," meaning they intended to say in houses that are arched, vaulted, or domed. Jeremiah 22: "And he makes ceilings of cedar." It would be more correct, if it were permitted to say so: "and he vaulted the house at the summits." And Deuteronomy 33: "in his portion the teacher was placed," that is, "covered," because of the grave that Moses chose in the portion of Gad—though no one ever saw his grave. From this "covering" also comes that which is written a little earlier in the same chapter: "and the hidden treasures of the sands," <note>original: "absconditos thesauros arenarum."</note> that is, the "covered" treasures.

**[Ship]** <note>Hebrew root: ספינה (sephinah)</note> The stern. Jonah 1: "And Jonah went down to the inner parts of the ship."

**[To Strike]** <note>Hebrew root: ספק (saphaq)</note> He struck, he clapped, he struck together. Lamentations 2: "They clapped their hands over you." And Numbers 24: "And Balak was angry against Balaam, and striking his hands together, he said..." And Jeremiah 31: "And after you showed me, I struck my thigh." And Ezekiel 21: "Therefore, strike upon your thigh." And Job 34: "As if he had struck the wicked in a place where people see." And in the same chapter: "In the meantime let it be constrained among us," that is, "clapped together," as if to say "agreed upon" or "contracted," or rather "let it suffice," as will be shown below. It is also sometimes found written with the letter *Sin* [ש], <note>The Hebrew letters Samekh (ס) and Sin (ש) often make the same 's' sound, leading to spelling variations.</note> as in Isaiah 2: "And they have joined with foreign children," that is, "they clapped hands with them," which I found written with a *Sin* in the most ancient **handwritten books**, <note>original: "manu exaratis."</note> but in **printed books** it is written with a *Samekh*. It is written similarly in 1 Kings 20: "If the dust of Samaria shall suffice for the handfuls of all the people who follow me," where this word signifies "enough."

### BOOK

And although in old volumes I have always found this very same expression written with the letter *sin* <note>original: "per sin"; the Hebrew letter Sin (שׂ) often sounds like 'S'</note>, I nevertheless find a certain note in one of my Hebrew books, which was handwritten four hundred years ago, where in the same chapter concerning this word a *scholia* <note>a marginal explanatory note</note> is assigned: namely, "partly with *samech*" <note>original: "partim cum samech"; the letter Samekh (ס) also sounds like 'S'</note>. This means that some books have the letter *samekh*. Similarly, Jonathan the Chaldean <note>Refers to the Targum of Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible</note> also wrote it with a *samech*. You will consider again how easily one moves between letters that share a common phonetic symbol, a point we have often emphasized.

[Hebrew: ספרד] <note>Sepharad</note> **Spain.** Our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> has **Bosphorus** at the end of the Book of Obadiah: *and the exile of Jerusalem which is in the Bosphorus.* Jerome, departing from the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>, says: "We have learned from the Hebrew who instructed us in the Scriptures that it is called Bosphorus." However, I have learned that the common custom of the Hebrews calls it Spain. Therefore, I wonder at Jerome's teacher, since even Jonathan the Chaldean translated it as Spain.

[Hebrew: ספר] <note>Sapar</note> **He numbered** or **he assessed.** In the Second Book of Kings, chapter 24: *After the people were numbered.* It ought to be read: *After he numbered the people.* And in Leviticus 15: *He shall number seven days for his purification.* From this comes the name in Isaiah 34 <note>The author cites Isaiah 34, but the following quote is actually from Isaiah 33:18</note>: *Your heart shall meditate on fear: where is the learned man? where are you weighing the words of the law? where is the teacher of the little ones?* For which the Septuagint has: *Your soul shall meditate on fear: where are the grammarians? where are the counselors? where is he who counts those who nourish the small and great people?*

But according to the Hebrews, the word-for-word translation is: *Your heart shall meditate on terror. Where is the counter? where is the weigher? where is the censor of the towns?* It is as if he were saying: In the time of the Messiah—that is, following his arrival when, according to Isaiah, *your eyes shall see the king in his beauty*—your heart will remember the oppression of the kings of this world, which is unclean. You will remember how formerly, in this age, you were forced to provide tributes, collections, exactions, tax upon tax, forced labor, and even more labor <note>original: "angarias et perangarias"; technical terms for compulsory service or the requisitioning of transport</note>. You will think in your mind of that terror which you then held daily, asking: "Where is the one who counts? Who is the one who weighs?"—that is, the one who assesses us by copper and scale <note>original: "per aes et libram"; a reference to an ancient Roman legal procedure for weighing money/assets</note>. For as our ancestors were accustomed to say, this will be a unique joy for the blessed: to remember past evils. As Virgil says in the first book of the *Aeneid*:

->*You who have approached the rage of Scylla and the deep-sounding*<-
->*rocks, and you who have experienced the stones of the Cyclops:*<-
->*recall your spirits, and dismiss your mournful fear.*<-
->*Perhaps one day it will be a joy to remember even these things.*<- <note>A famous quote from Aeneas to his men (Aeneid 1.198-203), suggesting that past suffering becomes a source of pleasure once overcome.</note>

->### THE SECOND BOOK<-

It will be of help. Thus in the Book of Wisdom we read in chapter 5: *Then the just shall stand with great constancy against those who oppressed them and those who took away their labors.* <note>original Latin: "Tunc stabunt iusti in magna constantia..." from Wisdom of Solomon 5:1</note> You see that these are the "reckoners" and "weighers" of the tyrants of this world. I have dealt with this at length so that you may understand that the *sopher* <term>sopher: a Hebrew word for scribe, from the root meaning to count or record</term> here is the scribe-exactor who records the names for the census and head-tax, and counts and weighs the money exacted, acting as a notary. Jeremiah 36: *That they might seize Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet.* And further down in the same chapter: *And he gave it to Baruch the son of Neriah, the scribe, who wrote upon it.* And Esther 3: *The king’s scribes were called.* From this, that which the scribe or notary writes is called a *sepher* <note>original: "sepher" (ספר), meaning a book, scroll, or document</note> regardless of the vowel points—that is, a "book." Jeremiah 32: *And I wrote in the book and sealed it and summoned witnesses.* And a little lower: *And I gave the book of the purchase to Baruch the son of Neriah, the son of Mahseiah, in the sight of Hanamel my uncle’s son and in the sight of the witnesses who were written in the book.* And Numbers 5: *The priest shall write these curses in a book.* And Joshua 1: *Let not the volume of this law depart from your mouth.* From this, the meaning is extended to "scripture," "letters," or "epistles." As in Isaiah 29: *And the book shall be given to one who does not know letters, and it shall be said to him, "Read," and he will answer, "I do not know letters,"* <note>The author explains this means "I do not know how to read writing."</note> And Esther 3: *And the letters, sealed with his own ring, were sent by couriers.* With a *he* at the end <note>referring to the Hebrew letter 'He' changing the word's morphology</note>, it means "scripture" or "literature." Psalm 71: *Since I have not known literature.* <note>The Vulgate's "literaturam" usually refers to the art of writing or learning.</note> And similarly without the *he* in Daniel 1: *That he might teach them the letters and language of the Chaldeans.*

From this also come "descriptions" and "narrations." Psalm 87: *The Lord shall recount it in the writings of the peoples.* And Psalm 19: *The heavens declare the glory of God.* Hence some interpret that which is written in Genesis 5, *This is the book of the generation of Adam*, in this way: *This is the narration or description of the generation of Adam*, or certainly "the enumeration." To return to the beginning, all these meanings descend from "numbering" and "computation." 1 Kings 3: *Which cannot be numbered or counted for the multitude.* When the consonant *mem* is prefixed, it signifies a "number." Exodus 22: *I will fulfill the number of your days.* Similarly 2 Chronicles 12: *Nor was there any numbering of the common people.* It is also found without the *mem* to signify a number or a counting. 2 Chronicles 2: *After the census which David his father had conducted.*

**Sapphire** <note>Hebrew: ספיר, *Sappir*</note>. Exodus 28: *In the second row, a carbuncle, a sapphire, and a jasper.* Rabbi Abraham ibn Ezra <note>A celebrated 12th-century Spanish Jewish scholar</note> writes that it is a certain red gem. Gaon <note>Likely Saadia Gaon, a major 10th-century philosopher and exegete</note>, however, writes that it is a small white stone which they call crystal. Our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note>, however, always has "sapphire." Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation</note> does not specify the type.

Similarly, in Jeremiah 46: "Put on your breastplates," I found an old <term>scholium</term> <note>An explanatory note or comment inserted into the margin of a manuscript.</note> noting: "some [write it] with Samekh," as if to say some books have it written with Samekh. Thus <term>Jonathan the Chaldean</term> <note>Refers to the *Targum Jonathan*, the traditional Aramaic translation of the Biblical Books of the Prophets.</note> writes it everywhere with a Samekh.

**סרח** <note>Hebrew root: *Sarach*</note> **It overflowed; it remained; it transcended; it was prominent; it hung down more than enough; it exceeded; it lived luxuriously; or it played wantonly.** <note>original Latin: *Superfluxit. ſuperfuit. tranſcendit. ſupereminuit. plus ſatis dependit. exceſſit. luxuriauit. uel laſciuiuit.*</note> Exodus 26: "But that which remains of the curtains prepared for the roof," that is, the one curtain that is extra. In Hebrew: "the remainder of the curtain exceeding." Also in the same place: "That which is more in the length of the curtains." And Amos 6: "And you lounge wantonly upon your couches," which in Hebrew is placed in the third person; it should be understood thus: "And they exceed, they overflow, and the long and wide curtains or coverings hang down more than is sufficient upon their couches." And further down in the same: "And the faction of the wanton shall be taken away." In Hebrew: "And the joy of the excessive ones shall cease."

# SECOND

...their wisdom has been [corrupted], that is, it has deteriorated. <note>original: "cta est sapientia eorum idest deteriorata est." This is likely the end of an entry for a word meaning 'to turn aside' or 'decay'.</note>

**סרן** [Seren] Satrap or prince; see 1 Samuel 29: <note>The source cites "Kings 29" following the older Vulgate numbering where 1 & 2 Samuel were called 1 & 2 Kings.</note> *“But you do not please the satraps.”* It is worth noting that a "satrap" is a title of dignity, as the Greek <term>satrapes</term> <note>original: "satrapes," a title for a provincial governor in the Persian Empire.</note> is written by Suidas <note>Suidas refers to the Suda, a massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia.</note>; it designates the leadership in Judges 16: *“And the princes of the Philistines came to her.”*

**סרן** [Seren] Plate or board. Our translation <note>Refers to the Latin Vulgate.</note> renders this as "axle" in 1 Kings 7: *“And the bronze axles.”*

**סריס** [Saris] <term>Eunuch</term>. Isaiah 56: *“And let not the eunuch say, behold, I am a dry tree.”* Also in Jeremiah 38: *“Now Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, a eunuch who was in the king’s house, heard...”* Such men are usually the keepers of the bedchambers in royal houses—chamberlains—to remove any suspicion regarding the queens and the virgins of the harem. They are named from their duty of "caring for the beds" <note>The author derives the word "eunuch" from the Greek "eune" (bed) and "echein" (to keep/have).</note>, almost like room-wardens. Hence, Potiphar was a "eunuch" in title only—that is, a royal official—because he had a wife, as seen in Genesis 39. For this reason, Onkelos <note>The author of the Targum Onkelos, an influential Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Torah.</note> translated it into Aramaic as <term>Raba</term>, meaning a high official or magistrate. Likewise, in Genesis 40, where it says "two eunuchs," Onkelos translates it into Aramaic as <term>rabraban</term>, meaning officials, prefects, or masters of offices.

**סרעף** [Sar'af] A grove, a thought, or a branch. Ezekiel 31: *“And its branches were multiplied.”* <note>The author is likely conflating the word for 'branches' with 'thoughts' (sar’appim), which share a similar root in Hebrew.</note>

**סרד** [Sarad] With the preposition *mem*, this signifies a mother’s brother, whom we call a maternal uncle. Amos 6: *“And his kinsman shall take him up, and he who burns him [mesarfo], to bring the bones out of the house.”* In this passage, the word *dod* precedes it—which means a father’s brother, or a paternal uncle—and this word follows, meaning the mother’s brother or maternal uncle. Therefore, the text should be read: *“And his paternal uncle and his maternal uncle shall take him up to carry the bones out of the house.”* However, because some manuscripts have this word written with the letter <term>sin</term> <note>The letter Sin (ש) and Samekh (ס) often make the same "s" sound, leading to linguistic debates about whether words are related.</note>, they think it comes from the word for "burning." For this reason, they translated it as *“and he shall burn him.”* But you have heard from me very often about the symbolic exchange between *sin* and *samekh*, where the meaning does not change. Therefore, it is more likely explained as "uncle" than as "one who burns." For who would burn a human body in such a way that the bones remain unharmed?

**סרפד** [Sirpad] This signifies briars or small thorns. Our translation has "nettle." Isaiah 55: *“Instead of the briar [or nettle] shall come up the myrtle tree.”*

**סתו** [Stav] Winter time, when the days shorten. It is called <term>bruma</term> <note>A Latin term for the winter solstice, derived from "brevissima dies" (the shortest day).</note>, specifically from the sign of Libra to Capricorn, where the winter solstice occurs. Song of Solomon 2: *“For lo, the winter is past; the rain is over and gone.”*

**BOOK**

->it is more correctly read thus:<-

For behold, the winter solstice <note>original: "bruma"</note> has passed; the winter rain has changed and gone away. However, "himber" <note>rain-storm</note> is the same as "hyems" <note>winter</note>, which is derived from the Greek word for rain; for "hyo" means "I rain." From "himber" comes "hibernus" <note>winter-like</note> by the removal of the letter "m," just as "paternus" comes from "pater" <note>father</note>. He means to say, therefore, that both the winter solstice and the winter—that is, the entire time from the autumnal equinox to the spring equinox—has passed, changed, and gone.

[Hebrew: סתם] <term>Satam: to stop up, to block, to dull, or to close.</term> 2 Chronicles 32: "It was Hezekiah who blocked the upper outlet of the waters of Gihon." And Lamentations 3: "He has shut out my prayer." Although this is written with the letter "sin," it signifies the same thing. And Psalm 51: "You have manifested to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom." For this, Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate Bible</note> writes: "You have manifested to me the concealed and secret things of your wisdom." But Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the famous 11th-century Jewish commentator</note> explains it as: "In the heart which is dull and blocked up, you have made me to know wisdom." Thus the verse would stand: "In the dullness and the blockage, you have shown me wisdom." Daniel 12: "Because the words are closed and sealed until the preordained time."

[Hebrew: סתר] <term>Satar: to hide, to conceal, to protect, or to turn away.</term> Genesis 4: "And from your face I shall be hidden." And Psalm 19: "Nor is there anyone who can hide himself from its heat." And 1 Samuel 5: "And their protruding secret parts rotted." According to the Hebrew teachers, it is more correctly read this way: "And the 'figs' <note>a historical term for hemorrhoids or tumors</note> which they had in the anus were hidden from them." I find the letter "sin" written here, but it is placed in the stead of "samech," as appears in ancient notes. Likewise, Psalm 31: "You shall hide them in the secret of your face." And Psalm 91: "He who dwells in the help of the Most High," <margin>He who dwells in the secret place of the Most High</margin> which, according to the "Hebrew Truth" <note>a term used by scholars like Jerome to refer to the original Hebrew text</note>, ought to be read: "He who sits in the secret place of the Most High." And by metathesis <note>the rearrangement of letters in a word</note> in the title of Psalm 54: "Has not David hidden himself among us?" And the name has five points <note>referring to Hebrew vowel markings</note>. Psalm 81: "I heard you in the hidden place of the storm." It also takes the letter "he" at the end for the feminine gender. Deuteronomy 32: "And let them protect you in your necessity." In Hebrew, it is: "Let there be a protection over you." Thus, sometimes through a simple paragoge <note>the addition of a letter to the end of a word</note>, it takes the "he" aspiration without changing the meaning. Deuteronomy 32: "I will hide my face from them."

->SECOND<-

<margin>עב ענן עב כל מנקר <note>original Hebrew: "Cloud, thick cloud, cloud, all that pierces." The scribe is listing synonyms and related terms for 'cloud'.</note></margin>
**עב**
**Clouds.** Isaiah 19: "Behold, the Lord shall ascend upon a light **cloud**." And in the same book, chapter 14: "I will ascend above the height of the **clouds**," that is, "cloud" in the singular and in the plural. Judges 5: "The heavens and the **clouds** dropped with water." And Proverbs 16: "As the latter rain," that is, like a **cloud** of the latter rain. Our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> sometimes turns this into "mist" or "gloom," as in Exodus 19: "Now I will come to you in the gloom of a **cloud**," that is, in a dense **cloud**.

**עבד** **He served. He worked. He ministered.** Numbers 18: "Only the sons of Levi [shall] serve me in the Tabernacle." In Hebrew, word for word, it is: "And he, Levi, shall serve in the ministry of the Tabernacle of the Covenant." And in the plural, Genesis 14: "For twelve years they served Chedorlaomer." And in the same book, chapter 29: "I will **serve** you for Rachel your daughter." And in the same: "Jacob therefore **served** for Rachel seven years." From this comes "works," "servitude," and "ministry." In the same book: "And I will give this one to you also for the **work** by which you shall serve me another seven years." From this comes "servant" <term>Ebed <note>The Hebrew word for servant.</note></term>, which is written with six points <note>A reference to the Hebrew vowel points, or 'nikkud'. The word 'Ebed' uses two Segol vowels, which look like three dots each, totaling six.</note>. Exodus 21: "If you buy a Hebrew **servant**." This is also where the word signifies "to farm" and "agriculture." Genesis 3: "To **work** the earth from which he was taken." And in the passive voice, Deuteronomy 21: "Which has not drawn the yoke nor split the earth with a plow." From the Hebrew truth <note>The original Hebrew text as opposed to later translations.</note> it is translated thus: "Which has not been **farmed**, which has not drawn the yoke." And in the same place: "Which was never plowed nor received seed." In Hebrew thus: "In which one shall not **farm** and shall not sow." It also signifies "to sacrifice." Deuteronomy 6: "You shall fear the Lord your God and **serve** Him." And 2 Kings 16: "And he **served** Baal and worshipped him." Similarly, it refers to divine sacrifice. 2 Chronicles 12: "That they may know the difference between my **service** and the **service** of the kingdoms of the lands." Because of this, those ignorant of languages—the magicians, or rather the <term>sophists <note>Here used as a pejorative for pseudo-scholars or those who use clever but false arguments.</note></term> of our time—variously name the book concerning the sacrifices of the Egyptians which <term>Ibn Wahshiyya <note>A 9th-century author famous for translating "The Nabataean Agriculture" into Arabic.</note></term> translated into Arabic. Although its title is *Avodath Egyptim* <note>The Service of the Egyptians</note>, some call the book "Concerning the Agriculture of the Egyptians," others "Concerning the Service of the Egyptians." However, it is better titled "Concerning the Sacrifice of the Egyptians," and in my opinion, best of all: "Concerning the Ritual Actions of the Egyptians." This is very much in the Latin style, for among our ancestors "to make" (*facere*) signified the same thing as "to sacrifice." Hence "action" (*factio*) means sacrifice. Virgil in the third eclogue of his *Bucolics* says: "When I make [offering] with a heifer for the fruits, you yourself come," that is, "when I shall sacrifice."

**עבה** **He made thick. He condensed. He enlarged.** Deuteronomy 32: "**Grown thick**, fat, and broad." From this comes the noun for "dense" or "thick." 1 Kings 12.

->**BOOK**<-

"My little finger is thicker than my father's back." <note>original: *Minimus digitus meus grossior est dorso patris mei*</note> The Hebrews read "my small one," meaning the pinky finger is thicker than my father's loins. Jonathan <note>referring to the Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation</note> translated it from the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> like this: "My weakness is more robust than my father's virility." And in Jeremiah 52: "Furthermore, its thickness was four fingers." And through apheresis <note>a linguistic term for dropping a sound at the start of a word</note> in Habakkuk 2: "And he heaps up thick clay against himself."

**[Hebrew: עבט — To pledge]** He took a pledge. Deuteronomy 24: "You shall not enter his house to carry away a pledge." And because one borrows against pledges, it also signifies "to borrow." In the same book, chapter 15: "And you shall give him a loan for whatever he is seen to need."

**[Hebrew: עבט — To swerve]** He turned aside. Joel 2: "And they shall not swerve from their paths." This specific meaning is found nowhere else.

**[Hebrew: עבטיט — Thick clay]** A single word that is nevertheless explained as if it were two words: namely, "thick clay." Habakkuk 2: "He heaps up thick clay against himself."

**[Hebrew: עבר — To pass over]** He transgressed; he passed by; he crossed over; he moved forward. Genesis 33: "And he himself, moving forward, bowed down." In the Hebrew it is: "And he himself proceeded before them and bowed down." Exodus 12: "And I will pass through the land of Egypt that night." Deuteronomy 17: "That they may transgress his covenant." 2 Chronicles 23: "Why do you transgress the commandment of the Lord?"

From this comes the expression for one who <term>purifies (lustrat)|The Latin 'lustrare' refers to a ritual purification, often involving a procession or passing through something.</term> people through fire. Deuteronomy 18: "Let there not be found among you anyone who purifies his son or daughter by leading them through the fire." Here the translator explains himself when he says "leading through the fire," meaning "causing them to pass through." For in another place, namely 2 Chronicles 28, when it says "he purified his sons in the fire," it is either a metathesis <note>a switching of the order of letters in a word</note> or another word that means "to burn up."

It is correctly read in 2 Kings 12 <note>Modern 2 Samuel 12:31</note>: "And he passed them through the brick-mold." The Hebrews say there was a place where they burned bricks, and there he "purified" them—that is, he burned them. It also means to cross the sea, to transport by ship, or to wade across. As in 2 Kings 19 <note>Modern 2 Samuel 19:18</note>: "They crossed the fords to bring over the king’s household." This is understood word-for-word as: "And the ferry-boat <note>original: *scapha*</note> waded across to bring over the king’s household." Thus, the name for a ferry-boat is derived from "crossing the river," as used there.

With the addition of the letter *Mem* <note>The Hebrew letter מ</note> at the beginning, it signifies a "ford." Genesis 32: "He crossed the ford of Jabbok." It takes the letter *He* <note>The Hebrew letter ה</note> at the end for the feminine gender. Isaiah 10: "They have passed over the crossing"—that is, the ford. And in the feminine plural in Judges 3: "And they occupied the fords of the Jordan." And it is used figuratively...

->SECOND<-

concerning current money and that which is given and taken here and there. Genesis 23.
"Four hundred shekels of silver of approved public money," <note>original: "probatę monetę publicę"</note> that is, of money passing between merchants. It also signifies to surpass or to prevail, as if to "pass over." Jeremiah 23: "And like a man soaked with wine." More correctly: "Like a man whom wine has overcome" <note>original: "superavit"</note>.

עבר <note>Hebrew: 'avar'</note> Beyond. Isaiah 9: "Beyond the Jordan of Galilee." And it receives a preposition just like many other <term>syncategoremata</term> <note>A logical term for words like "all," "and," or "beyond" that have no meaning on their own but modify other words.</note>. Isaiah 18: "Which is beyond the river of Ethiopia." For it signifies a part, place, or side opposite in view. As in Joshua 1: "Which Moses delivered to you beyond the Jordan," that is, on the other side of the Jordan.

עבר <note>Hebrew: 'avar'</note> He barred/bolted. 3 Kings 6 <note>Modern 1 Kings 6:21</note>: "And he fastened the plates with golden nails," which is read in Hebrew as: "And he barred it <note>original: "repagulavit"</note> with golden bolts before the oracle."

עבר <note>Hebrew: 'avar'</note> He was incensed or angry. Psalm 89: "You have put off your Christ" <note>In this context, 'anointed one'</note>, for which Jerome, in his *Psalter according to the Hebrew Truth*, more correctly has: "You were angry against your Christ." So in Proverbs 14: "A wise man fears and turns away from evil; the fool passes over <note>original: "transilit"</note> and is confident," where he uses "passes over" according to the first meaning of the verb. But the Hebrews read it as: "the fool is angry and confident." So in Psalm 78: "God heard and was provoked," that is, he was angry. Similarly below in the same: "and he provoked his inheritance," that is, he was angry against his inheritance. From this comes "wrath," "indignation," or "fury." Zephaniah 1: "That day is a day of wrath." And Isaiah 10: "And against the people of my fury I will command him." Indeed, you will recognize three meanings of the same origin in a single usage in Deuteronomy 3: "I will cross over <note>Meaning 1: to pass through</note> therefore and see this excellent land beyond <note>Meaning 2: the opposite side</note> the Jordan; but the Lord was angry <note>Meaning 3: to be incensed</note> with me." Behold the verb "I shall cross over," the word "beyond," and the verb "he was angry."

עבור <note>Hebrew: 'avur'</note> Grain or produce. Joshua 5: "And they ate of the produce of the land." Likewise in the same: "And the manna ceased after they ate of the produce of the land." And some say it is called this from the "past year," <note>i.e., grain that has 'passed' from the previous season</note> for the produce of the current year is called something else (as seen under the letter B before V).

<meta>This page continues a Hebrew-Latin lexicon, likely from a 16th-century Christian Hebraist work, providing Latin-speaking scholars with the etymology and biblical usage of Hebrew roots. This page covers roots beginning with the letters Ayin-Bet through Ayin-Gimel.</meta>

# BOOK

**For the sake of** <note>original Hebrew: *avur*</note>. With the letter *Beth* prefixed, it signifies "on account of." Psalm 132: *For the sake of David your servant, do not turn away the face of your anointed one.* It also sometimes signifies "because," as in Micah 2: *Because of its uncleanness, it shall be destroyed,* which should be read as: *because it has become putrid, it shall be destroyed.*

**To rot** <note>original Hebrew: *abash*</note>. To decay. Joel 1: *The beasts have rotted in their dung.* The Hebrew reads: *The grains of seed have rotted in the dust,* meaning they are unable to sprout. It is pronounced as if it were *abash* <note>the text notes a phonetic shift from 'p' to 'b'</note> because, as Rabbi David Kimhi <note>A famous medieval grammarian and biblical commentator (c. 1160–1235) often cited by Christian scholars</note> writes in his commentaries on the Twelve <note>The "Twelve" refers to the Minor Prophets of the Old Testament</note>, the letter 'p' is often exchanged for 'b'.

**Coherence** <note>original Hebrew: *avot*</note>. A bond, or intricate and tangled or thick branches; it can also mean a *braid* <note>Latin: *tricha*</note> or the entanglement of any things. Leviticus 23: *And the branches of a tree of thick foliage.* And in the masculine plural in Psalm 118: *Establish the feast day with thick branches.* Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate</note>, in his translation of the Psalter, puts it this way: *among the leafy branches.* Similarly, it appears in the feminine plural in Exodus 28: *Two little chains of purest gold, joined to one another.* From this sense of entanglement and weaving, the word is used for snares or ropes woven from three strands, according to Rabbi Joseph (the father of David Kimhi), who explains Micah 7—*And they have troubled it*—as *And they have tripled it,* based on the fact that three people are mentioned in that passage: the prince, the judge, and the great man.

**Lusted** <note>original Hebrew: *agab*</note>. He went mad with love, or was burning. Ezekiel 23: *And she doted upon her lovers.* And further on: *She doted upon them with the lust of her eyes.*

**Organ** <note>original Hebrew: *ugav*</note>. A musical instrument. In the last Psalm: *Praise him with strings and the organ.* <note>In this historical context, "organ" refers to a reed pipe or flute rather than the large keyboard instrument used in churches today.</note> Genesis 4: *He was the father of those who sing with the harp and organ.* Job 30: *And my organ into the voice of those who weep.*

**Abandoned** <note>original Hebrew: *agun*</note>. Left behind or remained. Ruth 1: *If you wish to wait for them until they grow up and reach the age of puberty, you will be old women before you marry.* In place of this long paraphrase and digression <note>The author is criticizing the Latin Vulgate's wordy translation of a single Hebrew concept</note>, the Hebrew text more accurately has: *Would you wait until they grow up? Would you be abandoned or remained, even if they were to be your future husbands?* From this, the Hebrew teachers call a woman who remains without a husband an *abandoned woman* <term>agunah</term>. <note>In Jewish law, an *Agunah* is a woman "chained" to a marriage because her husband is missing or refuses to grant a divorce.</note>

**Round** <note>original Hebrew: *agol*</note>. Circular. 2 Chronicles 4: *From brim to brim.*

...from man even to beast, as well as the creeping things and the birds of the heavens. And it receives at the beginning the letter *Beth* <note>The second letter of the Hebrew alphabet, here discussed as a prefix meaning 'in,' 'with,' or 'for'</note> which signifies "for," "before," "in front of," or "through," and "because of." 
**Genesis 7**: "And the Lord shut him in from the outside." <note>original: *Et inclusit eum dominus deforis*</note> In Hebrew it is thus: "And the Lord closed [the door] **for him** or **before him**." So also in **Exodus 8**: "Pray **for me**." And **Genesis 26**: "Abimelech, king of the Philistines, looking out **through** the window." And just as the word "forever" <note>original: *usque*</note> among the Latins signifies continuity as an adverb, so also this expression signifies eternity and perpetuity: "into the age," "everlasting." **Isaiah 57**: "The high and lofty One who inhabits eternity." It signifies "the age of ages," which our translation <note>Likely referring to the Latin Vulgate</note> renders as "beyond," as in **Exodus 15**: "The Lord shall reign forever and **beyond**."

<term>Rags</term> <note>Hebrew: עדים (*iddim*)</note> Shreds or cast-off cloths. And **Psalm 147**: "The Lord taking up the gentle." Rabbi Joseph Kimhi <note>A 12th-century Hebrew grammarian and teacher from Spain</note> the Spaniard wants this word to signify "help," "support," and "sustenance."

<term>He adorned</term> <note>Hebrew: עדה (*’adah*)</note> **Hosea 2**: "And she was adorned with her earring." From this comes the noun "ornament," "glory," "beauty," "necklace," or "jewel." **Psalm 80**, in the title which our books have: "To the victory over the lilies, a testimony of Asaph, a psalm." The Hebrews read it thus: "To the victory regarding the roses, the **beauty** of Asaph, a psalm." It is as if it were said, according to David Kimhi <note>The son of Joseph Kimhi and a highly influential medieval biblical commentator</note>, that this psalm is a glory and a beauty to Asaph himself. Also, the noun in another form in **Ezekiel 7**: "And they set the beauty of their ornaments as a matter of pride."

<term>He went away</term> <note>Hebrew: עדה (*’adah*)</note> He passed by, he ceased, he crossed through. **Job 28**: "Neither did the lioness pass through it." And the transitive use of the same in the second part of **Job 25**, where we read: "Behold, even the moon does not shine." Our translation omitted this word of ours; wherefore it is read thus in Hebrew: "Behold, He makes the moon **pass away** and it will not shine," which they explain thus: "Behold, He puts away or takes away the light of the moon and it will not shine."

<term>Assembly</term> <note>Hebrew: עדה (*’edah*)</note> A swarm, a synagogue <note>in the sense of a gathering</note>, a crowd, a council. **Psalm 1**: "Nor [shall] sinners [stand]..."

And there are those who say he did not tremble in the least, but approached with delight, and considered it a luxury to exchange life for death. Others explain it as: "And Agag came to him with chains," <note>Latin: *ligaturis*</note> for both bindings and combinations are called by this name. Job 38: "Will you be able to join together the shining stars, the Pleiades?"—that is, will you bind the groupings of the stars?

**עדף** [ʿadap] **Overflowing. Surviving. Exceeding.** Exodus 26: "That which remains over in the curtains." And Numbers 3: "Those who exceed the number of the Levites." Likewise below: "the price of those who are over and above." Also: "the money of those who were more numerous." From this comes the weighty word in Exodus 16: "Neither had he who gathered more any extra, nor did he who had prepared less find less." In Hebrew it is thus: "And it did not exceed more, and the less did not fail."

**עדר** [ʿadar] **Lacked. Deprived. Diminished. Was absent.** 1 Samuel 30: "Nor was anyone missing from the small even unto the great."

**עדר** [ʿadar] **Prepared the battle line. Arranged. Ordered. Disposed.** 1 Chronicles 12: "Equipped for battle with a perfect heart," <note>Original: *corde perfecto*</note> that is, instructors of the apparatus of war. And a little above: "To help, not with a double heart." In Hebrew it is thus: "And for the purpose of arranging, not with a heart and a heart." <note>This refers to the Hebrew idiom for sincerity versus hypocrisy.</note>

**עדר** [ʿeder] **Flock.** Song of Solomon 6: "Like a flock of goats." And Genesis 29: "Also three flocks of sheep." And below: "And the custom was that when all the sheep were gathered, they would roll away the stone." For which the Hebrew reads: "And all the flocks were gathered there, and they rolled the stone from the mouth <note>Latin: *artificio*; likely a transcription error for *ore* (mouth) or referring to the "structure" of the well</note> of the well."

**עדר** [ʿadar] **Dug. Hoed. Harrowed.** Isaiah 5: "It shall not be pruned and it shall not be dug." And in the same, chapter 7: "And all the mountains that shall be hoed with a hoe." It is said especially of vineyards, whence comes the Hebrew proverb: "dig with me and I will dig with you." <note>A phrase implying mutual labor or cooperation.</note>

**עדש** [ʿadaš] **Lentil.** Ezekiel 4: "And you, take for yourself wheat and barley and beans and lentils." And Genesis 25: "Having accepted bread and a pottage of lentils."

**עוג** [ʿug] **Baked among the coals. Roasted. Scorched under a lid.** Ezekiel 4.

# THE SECOND BOOK

"And with the dung that comes out of a man, you shall cover it in their sight." <note>original: "Et stercore quod egreditur de homine operies illud in oculis eorum." This refers to Ezekiel 4:12.</note> Regarding this passage, the Hebrew scholars—according to the testimony of Nicholas of Lyra <note>A celebrated 14th-century Franciscan scholar known for his literal interpretations of the Bible.</note>—read it more accurately as: "And in the dung that comes out of man, you shall **bake** it in their sight." From this comes "tile-baked bread" or "ash-baked bread": a tart, a toast, a flat-cake, a spiral, or a spherical loaf cooked under a tile and among the coals, as mentioned above. "And you shall eat it like a barley cake baked in the ashes." And in Hosea 7: "Ephraim has become a cake baked in the ashes that is not turned." And in 1 Kings 19: "And behold, at his head was a cake baked on the coals." 

For this reason, some understand this verse of Psalm 35—"They mocked me with mocking"—as referring to food and drink, translating it as: "Among the flatterers who bake food." Our Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the primary translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> does not greatly disagree with them in his *Psalter according to the Hebrew Truth*, translating it as "in the simulation of false words." And Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Shlomo Yitzhaki, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator on the Torah and Talmud.</note> explains it this way: "By way of flattery, so that they might receive food and drink from Saul; as long as he feeds them and gives them drink, they gnashed their teeth against me." He says that **maog** <note>original: "maog"</note> means <term>food</term>. Others explain it as: "those who flatter the ones who knead and prepare the common bread." Still others do not derive the quoted verse from this word, but from <insert>Hebrew word</insert> which signifies something ridiculous, fickle, or empty.

<insert>Hebrew word</insert> **He plundered.** He snatched, spoiled, or kidnapped. Psalm 119: "The ropes of sinners have surrounded me," or according to Jerome, "have entangled me." In place of this, Rabbi Solomon and the other Hebrew scholars read: "The bands or companies of sinners have robbed or plundered me." From this comes the common noun for <term>spoil</term>, <term>plunder</term>, or <term>prey</term>. Genesis 49: "In the morning he shall eat the prey." And Zephaniah 3: "Therefore wait for me, says the Lord, in the day of my resurrection in the future," which the Hebrews read as: "In the day of my rising up to the **prey** or **spoil**." Where the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> translated this as "for a testimony," Jerome writes in his commentaries that a certain Hebrew who had taught him the Scriptures asserted that <unclear>laad</unclear> in this passage should be understood more as "in the future." Rabbi David Kimhi <note>A medieval rabbi and grammarian (c. 1160–1235) known for his Hebrew dictionary and commentaries.</note> wishes it to be understood as the day of Gog and Magog <note>Biblical figures representing the enemies of God's people in apocalyptic prophecy.</note>, whom God will cause to rise up for plunder.

<insert>Hebrew word</insert> **Still.** Further, beyond. Amos 4: "When there were still three months remaining until the harvest." Genesis 25: "My father is still living." And Isaiah 5: "What is there that I ought to have done further for my vineyard?" It signifies a limit or an end. It also takes pronominal additions, as in Genesis 25: "While he was still living." And Exodus 9: "Still you hold back the people."

**[Hebrew: עָוָה]** <term>To do evil</term>; to sin; and, if it were permitted to say, <term>to iniquitate</term>. <note>The author coins the Latin verb "iniquavit" to capture the specific Hebrew sense of committing iniquity.</note> Esther 1: *Queen Vashti did wrong not only the king, but also all the princes.* The Hebrews read it this way: *Not against the king alone did Queen Vashti sin, but against all the princes.* However, according to others, it is derived from another word. The letter *lamed* is doubled, as in Psalm 8: *Out of the mouth of infants and sucklings,* that is, little ones and those who nurse. BOOK

...the letter *yod* following *ayin*. Concerning this meaning, Rabbi Judah <note>Likely Judah ben David Hayyuj, a pioneer of Hebrew grammar around the year 1000.</note> thinks that it refers to what is read in Zechariah 5: "A flying scroll."

**עיפת** <term>Caligavit</term> <note>Latin: "It grew dark."</note> He darkened or obscured. Job 11: "You will rise like the morning star." This is what the Hebrews read as: "if you are obscured," or—if it were permitted to say—"if you are 'twilighted,'" then you will be like the morning. Rabbi Solomon <note>Known as Rashi, the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> explains it as a noun in this way: "The darkness that is in you and your gloom shall be like the morning." Hence that passage in Amos 4: "The one who makes the morning mist," which others, through the use of an article or by a grammatical shift, render as: "The one who makes the dawn and the darkness." Similarly, Job 11: "A land of misery and darkness." The Hebrews say this is a synonymous expression because the two words signify the same thing; they mean to say a land that is dark and gloomy, or shadowy. And what follows in the Latin Job—"but an eternal horror dwelling there"—is not read in the Hebrew, but rather: "and it is darkened like gloom." The meaning of these words is obscurity and darkness. 

There are some who, on the contrary, want a sudden movement, a sudden illumination, a brightening, a vibration, a flash, or a lightning bolt to be signified by that word. Ezekiel 32: "When my sword begins to fly over their faces." It is more correctly translated: "In my brandishing of my sword," that is, when I cause my sword to flash or glit. For it is a transitive verb. And Isaiah 11: "And they shall fly upon the shoulders of the Philistines," meaning they shall suddenly move or flash. And Job 3: "Neither let it be enlightened with light." The letter *pe* is doubled in the same passage: "neither the rising of the surging dawn," which in Hebrew is read: "And he shall not see the flashes of the dawn." Rabbi Solomon interprets these as "splendors."

**עפעף** <term>Palpebra</term> <note>Latin: "Eyelid."</note> Eyelid. In Psalm 10 <note>Psalm 11 in modern numbering.</note>: "And his eyelids try the children of men." And Jeremiah 9: "And let our eyelids flow with waters." Jonathan the Chaldean <note>Refers to the Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Bible.</note> interprets these as the orbits of the eyes themselves.

**עיף** <term>Defecit</term> <note>Latin: "He failed" or "he grew faint."</note> He failed or grew faint. In 2 Samuel 21: "But David grew faint." And Jeremiah 4: "Because my soul has failed on account of those who were slain." Similarly, what is read in Judges 4 should be understood: "Joining sleep with death, he failed and died." <note>This describes the death of the Canaanite general Sisera.</note> It is written with a *patah* point <note>A Hebrew vowel mark indicating an 'a' sound.</note> to differentiate it from another word similar to it but with a different meaning, as mentioned above. Moreover, we often grow faint because of thirst; therefore, the word is found written for one who is thirsty, as in Psalm 142 <note>Psalm 143 in modern numbering.</note>: "Like a land without water to you," which Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate.</note> more accurately translated as: "Like a thirsty land toward you." Isaiah 29: *The weary one still thirsts.* <note>original: "Lassus adhuc sitit"</note> For below you will see "weary" signified by the letter *Ayin* followed by *Yod*; and above by the letter *Yod* followed by *Ayin*. <note>The author is explaining how slight changes in Hebrew spelling (between letters like Ayin and Yod) change the meaning of words that look similar.</note>

**עור [‘WR]** He awakened or stirred up. Job 41: *I will not stir him up as if I were cruel.* <note>original: "Non quasi crudelis suscitabo eum"</note> This is the **active transitive** form; however, it is also found as a **neutral** <note>meaning an intransitive verb where the subject performs the action on themselves</note> and has the same value as "I wake up." Psalm 57: *Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp. I will arise at dawn.* And in Judges 5: *Awake, awake, Deborah; awake, awake, and speak a song.* It is as if saying "wake up, wake up," as in Psalm 44: *Arise, why do you sleep, Lord?* And so it is used metaphorically for "to be vigilant." Song of Solomon 5: *I sleep, but my heart watches.* The **passive** verb is read in Zechariah 2: *Because he rose up from his holy dwelling,* or more accurately, *because he was awakened.* The last letter is also found doubled in Song of Solomon 2: *Do not stir up nor awaken my beloved.* And in Psalm 80: *Stir up your power and come.* And with doubled syllables in Psalm 102: *He regarded the prayer of the humble,* meaning the prayer of one who has been awakened, or rather, of one who awakens—for God looks upon the prayers of those who continually awaken their own prayer. From this is derived the term **עור [‘WR]** for a "master" or "teacher" <note>original: "magister"</note> who awakens the mind of the disciple to learning. Malachi 2: *The master and the disciple from the tabernacle of Jacob,* that is, the "awakener," whom we call the "arguer" <note>original: "arguentem"</note> in formal debates, and the "responder." Hence the masters of the Hebrews say: "the arguer among the wise, the responder among the disciples."

**עור [‘WR]** Foe, enemy, or hater. Micah 5: *And I will destroy your cities.* The Hebrews read this as *your enemies*, an interpretation which the <term>Chaldean translation</term> <note>This refers to the Targum, an Aramaic translation and exposition of the Hebrew Bible.</note> of Jonathan also alludes to.

**עור [‘WR]** Naked or nakedness. Habakkuk 2: *That he may look upon his nakedness.* And in chapter 3 of the same book: *Stirring, you will stir up your bow,* meaning *your bow shall be revealed naked.*

**עור [‘WR]** Skin. Genesis 3: *The Lord God also made for Adam and his wife tunics of skins,* that is, tunics made of skin—a grammatical construction of placement. And Job 2: *Skin for skin.* And in the plural feminine form in Exodus 36: *He also made a covering for the tabernacle from the skins of rams.* And in the masculine form in Lamentations 5: *Our skins were burned as if in an oven.*

**עור [‘WR]** He blinded. 2 Kings 25: *And he dug out his eyes,* or more correctly, *And the eyes...*

...blinded Zedekiah. From this comes the masculine adjective **blind** <note>original: "caecus"</note> in the fourth chapter of Exodus: "The seeing or the blind." It also appears in the feminine gender in Leviticus 22: "If it be blind or broken."

**עוש** <note>transliteration: 'ush</note> It met, came together, or clustered. In the third chapter of Joel: "Burst forth and come," for which the seventy translators <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> more accurately wrote, "be gathered and enter." From this is derived **עיש** <note>transliteration: 'Ayish</note>, the entire constellation of the Dragon and the Bears around the arctic pole, so named from the clustering and collection of many stars. Our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> calls this "Arcturus" in Job 9: "Who makes Arcturus and Orion." It is the constellation that follows the aforementioned cluster of stars known as the Wagon and the Seven Oxen <note>The Big Dipper</note>. Regarding this, Virgil writes in the first book of the *Georgics*: "Here the great Snake glides out with a winding fold, like a river around and through the two Bears." Thus it follows: "they shall perish forever." It also takes an additional "yod" <note>a Hebrew letter</note> by epenthesis <note>an added sound/letter in the middle of a word</note> in chapter 38: "Or can you scatter the circuit of Arcturus?"

**עות** <note>transliteration: 'avat</note> He did evil, sinned, or acted unjustly; as in Esther 1: "The queen has wronged the King." From this comes the transitive verb of the "third form" <note>the Piel or causative stem in Hebrew grammar</note>, meaning to cause to sin, as in Lamentations 3: "To subvert a man in his judgment." This was seen above under the root **עוה** <note>transliteration: 'avah</note> and it signifies to curve or bend. Indeed, the "iniquitous" is that which is "curved" because it is not made "straight." Thus in Ecclesiastes 7: "that no one can correct whom he has despised." Word for word, it is: "Who can straighten what he has made crooked?" In another form in Ecclesiastes 12: "And the strongest men shall falter," which means they shall be bent over.

**עז** <note>transliteration: 'ez</note> A female goat. Genesis 15: "And a three-year-old female goat." And in the plural in 1 Samuel 25: "Three thousand sheep and a thousand goats." In compound form, it signifies the **scapegoat** <note>original: "caprum emissarium"</note> in Leviticus 16: "And the other for the scapegoat." It is composed of **עז** <note>goat</note> and **אזל** <note>he went away</note>. Onkelos <note>author of a famous Aramaic translation of the Torah</note> interprets it this way. Also in Psalm 31: "In your hands are my lots." I do not know why they translated it this way, for it is written "in your hand" <note>singular</note> and not "in your hands." Furthermore, there is no word in the verse that signifies "lots" or "fortunes." Therefore, Jerome, in his Psalter, correctly translated it according to the Hebrew truth as: "In your hand are my times." Rabbi Solomon [says]...

**עזז** <note>Root: Azaz</note> He grew strong. He comforted. He strengthened. He made firm. He fortified. **Ecclesiastes 7**: "Wisdom strengthened the wise man." And **Judges 6**: for that which we read as, "And they were greatly oppressed by them," the truth <note>The author uses "the truth" (veritas) to refer to the original Hebrew text.</note> has: "and the hand of Midian prevailed." From this is derived the substantive noun for strength, fortitude, or power. **Psalm 29**: "The Lord will give strength to his people." It is written with a *cholam* or *chatef-kametz* <note>Technical names for Hebrew vowel markings.</note>. **Psalm 118**: "The Lord is my strength and my praise." It is also written sometimes with a *shurek* or *kibbutz* <note>Alternative Hebrew vowel marks.</note>, as in the **last Psalm**: "Praise him in the firmament of his power." The letter *zain* is also found doubled according to the nature of the primitive form, as in **Psalm 145**: "And they shall speak of the strength of your terrible acts." It also receives the letter *mem* as a prefix <note>forming the word 'ma’oz'</note>. **Isaiah 30**: "Hoping for help in the strength of Pharaoh." From this comes the adjective in **Isaiah 19**: "and a strong king shall rule over them"; and in the plural in **Psalm 59**: "The strong have rushed upon me." And the adjective according to the form of the primitive in **Psalm 24**: "The Lord strong and mighty." From this is named a certain bird among the unclean and forbidden birds, which others call a griffin, but our translation calls a <term>sea-eagle</term> <note>The Hebrew word 'ozniyyah'.</note>. **Leviticus 11**: "The griffin and the sea-eagle." The sea-eagle is a marine eagle and the five-syllable word <note>original: "haliaetus"</note> is written with the diphthong 'ae' in the third syllable. I say this so that Latin books may be corrected in the place cited. It is called thus in Hebrew from "strength," but in Greek from "the sea" and "fishing."

**עזב** <note>Root: Azav</note> He left behind or forsook. As in **Psalm 22**: "God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?" which is sung in Hebrew during the Passion of the Lord: *Eli eli lama asabtani* <note>original: "Eli eli lama azabtani"</note>. That is, word for word: "My God, my God, for what [reason] have you forsaken me?" wherein it is observed that "look upon me" is not part of the [original Hebrew] text. And **Genesis 2**: "Wherefore a man shall leave his father."

**עזר** <note>Root: Azar</note> He fortified. He increased. He strengthened. He helped. **Nehemiah 3**: "And they abandoned Jerusalem as far as the wall of the broader street." <term>Nicholas of Lyra</term> <note>A 14th-century biblical commentator known for his focus on the literal Hebrew sense.</note> explains this more correctly thus: "And they extended its wall." <term>Rabbi Solomon</term> <note>Rashi, the famous medieval Jewish commentator.</note> explains this word as "he fortified." **Deuteronomy 32**, where we read: "And the enclosed also have failed and the remainder are consumed." The truth [the Hebrew] simply has: "And the preserved and the fortified shall fail."

In his eighth book *On Architecture*, where he writes about columns, it seems to me that he correctly names the **base** <term>propodium: the projecting base or foot of a structure</term> and the **ledge** <term>crepidinem: a base, pedestal, or projecting foundation</term>. [Hebrew: עט] **Stylus.** Our translation <note>The "Common" or Vulgate Latin translation</note> interprets this as "reed." [Hebrew: עטה] **To turn, look back, depart, divert, wander, or decline.** 1 Samuel 15: "But you have **turned** to the prey." But our translation interprets it differently in the Song of Songs 1: "Lest I begin to **wander** after the flocks of your companions." Origen, in his first homily on the Song of Songs, translated it according to the former meaning: "Lest I become like one **covered** over the flocks of your companions." It is better translated: "as if **turning** or **departing** toward the flocks of your companions." Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the famous 11th-century Jewish scholar</note> seems to agree with Origen; for this reason he cites the verse from Leviticus 13: "The head bare, the mouth covered with a garment," although there "averted lips" <note>original: "labra uulgo auersa"</note> could be understood.
