[Hebrew: עטלף] **Bat.** Leviticus 11: "The **bat** and the hoopoe also."

[Hebrew: עטין] **A milking vessel** in which milk is collected. As Virgil says in the *Eclogues*: "He comes twice to the **milking pail**." <note>original: "Bis uenit ad mulctram."</note> However, I do not know why our translation interprets this as "innards." Therefore, the "Hebrew Truth" reads: "His **milk pails** are filled with milk."

**עיב** <term>Ayiv: To darken.</term> Lamentations 2: "How he has covered with darkness." Some think it is derived from the word for "cloud," as if "to becloud."

**עי** <term>Ai: A desert, a wasteland, a pit, a scattering of stones, or a heap.</term> Micah 1: "And I will make Samaria like a heap of stones," that is, in devastation.

...desolation and ruin. The Chaldean translation <note>original: "chaldaica translatio" — referring to the Targum, an ancient Aramaic paraphrase and commentary on the Hebrew Bible</note> indicates this through a term signifying heaps of stones and the scattering of pebbles. For Jonathan the Chaldean <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel, the traditional author of the Aramaic Targum of the Prophets</note> uses the same interpretation here as he does in the book of Jeremiah: *And Babylon shall become heaps.* Likewise in Job 30: *But you do not stretch out your hand to their destruction.* Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, 1040–1105), the most influential medieval Jewish commentator</note> explains: "A judge does not usually stretch out his hand—that is, his power—into a tomb, sepulcher, ditch, or pit." And in the plural in Psalm 79: *They have laid Jerusalem as a storehouse for fruit,* where the "Seventy" <note>The Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>, wishing to show that Jerusalem was overturned and destroyed, indicated that mere huts were placed where the most eminent palaces of the city of Jerusalem once stood. For so it is usually read in Greek: *they placed Jerusalem like an oporophylacium* <note>original: "oporophylacium" — a Greek term for a hut or lodge for a watchman in a fruit garden, implying total desolation</note>, which is a small house for gardeners. 

But in Hebrew, it is read in the plural, which according to Paul, Bishop of Burgos <note>Paulus de Santa Maria (c. 1351–1435), a Jewish convert to Christianity who became a bishop and wrote influential critiques of earlier biblical commentaries</note>, is rightly translated as "ditches" or "pits"; for when these are dug, the stones from them are usually piled into a heap. Thus, Jerome’s translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> from the "Hebraic truth" <note>original: "hebraica ueritate" — a term used by St. Jerome to emphasize the authority of the original Hebrew text over the Greek translation</note> could stand together with this, as he translated: *they laid Jerusalem into heaps of stones.* And in Isaiah 17: *And it shall be like a heap of stones in a ruin.* I would prefer to call them "quarries," for nothing here concerns fruit. My teacher, Jacob Jehiel Loans <note>A Jewish physician and scholar who famously taught Hebrew to the Christian humanist Johannes Reuchlin</note>, a Jewish doctor, said this word signifies "solitude."

<term>עָרָה ('arah)</term> He heaped up; he gathered; he accumulated. Exodus 9: *Send therefore now and gather your cattle.* Onkelos <note>The reputed author of the standard Aramaic translation of the Torah</note> translated it this way in Chaldean [Aramaic]. But our translation <note>The Vulgate</note> reads differently in Jeremiah 5: *Strengthen yourselves, children of Benjamin, in the midst of Jerusalem,* believing the word to be <term>עָרָה ('arah)</term> <note>in the sense of "to uncover" or "to make bare"</note> which we spoke of above. But Rabbi Joseph Kimhi <note>A 12th-century Hebrew grammarian and father of the famous David Kimhi</note> explains it in his commentaries as "gather yourselves together," a view the Hebrew school follows. He similarly interprets Jeremiah 4: *Strengthen yourselves, do not stand still,* meaning "gather together and flee to the stronghold of Zion," the highest fortress. Likewise in Isaiah 10: *The inhabitants of Gebim, strengthen yourselves*—he should have said "gather yourselves together."

<term>עַיִט ('ayit)</term> Bird; winged creature; a flock of birds. Isaiah 18: *And they shall be left together for the birds of the mountains,* and further: *And the winged creatures shall be upon it all summer.* And Genesis 15: *And the birds descended upon the carcasses.* And Isaiah 46: *Calling a bird from the east,* where some interpret this as "counselor." From this noun is derived a verb signifying to rush upon, to make a noise, to rebuke, and to be suddenly moved, just as when a multitude of birds [shout] together in a field...

Jeremiah 6: "Let them gather the remnants of Israel like grapes in a vineyard." This is a "sense-for-sense" <note>an interpretation that captures the meaning rather than following the literal grammar</note> translation. The Septuagint <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> renders it this way: "Gleaning, let them glean the remnants of Israel as if in a vineyard." But it is more accurately translated word-for-word as: "By harvesting, they shall harvest the remnant of Israel like a vine." This term is used for crops where the final leftovers are eventually gathered. Deuteronomy 24: "You shall not gather the remaining clusters, but they shall be for the use of the stranger, the orphan, and the widow."

**Yoke** <note>original: Hebrew *‘ol* (עול)</note>. 1 Kings 6 <note>modern 1 Samuel 6:7</note>: "Two nursing cows upon which no yoke has been placed." Translated word-for-word: "Because a yoke has not gone up over them." And Deuteronomy 28: "And he will place an iron yoke upon your neck."

**Stammerer** <note>original: Hebrew *‘illeg* (עלג)</note>. Isaiah 32: "And the tongue of the stammerers shall speak quickly and plainly"—that is, eloquently, purely, and clearly. And through **metathesis** <term>the transposition or rearranging of letters within a word</term> it becomes *la‘ag*—that is, "he mocked." Isaiah 37.

### SECOND [PART]

**Leaf** <note>Hebrew: *Aleh*</note>. A leaf of a tree. Genesis 8: Carrying an olive branch with green leaves in its mouth. The Hebrew truth <note>original: *veritas hebraica*; a term used by scholars to refer to the original Hebrew text</note> has it thus: "and the dove came to him at the time of evening, and behold, a plucked olive leaf was in its mouth." Likewise, Psalm 1: "And its leaf shall not wither." And Genesis 3: "And they sewed fig leaves." Our translation <note>referring to the Latin Vulgate</note> often interprets this as foliage and branches, as in Nehemiah 8: "Bring olive branches and branches of the most beautiful wood and myrtle branches and palm branches, etc."

**Supreme** <note>Hebrew: *Elyon*</note>. Highest, most high. Psalm 91: "He who dwells in the help of the Most High." And Ezekiel 41: "And so from the lower parts one ascended to the higher and into the middle," that is, from the lowest to the highest.

**Exulted** <note>Hebrew: *Alatz*</note>. He was glad and rejoiced. Psalm 149: "The saints shall exult in glory." And the Psalm: "The fields shall rejoice and all things that are in them." And Zephaniah 3: "Be glad and exult with all your heart."

**Dark Gloom** <note>Hebrew: *Alatah*</note>. A shadowy darkness. Genesis 15: "When the sun had gone down, a dark gloom occurred." And Ezekiel 12: "In the darkness he shall go out."

**He Hid** <note>Hebrew: *Alam*</note>. The passive form of which is read in Leviticus 5: "And it was forgotten," which would more truly be read as: "And it was hidden from him." For Onkelos the Chaldean <note>Onkelos was a famous translator of the Torah into Aramaic</note> interprets it as "and it was covered from him," that is, it was concealed from him. So Job 28: "It is hidden from the eyes of all living things." And Psalm 26: "And with those who act iniquity I will not enter." Although this translation is not word-for-word, it nonetheless fits the sense better than how Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Bible into Latin</note> translates it: "and with the proud I will not enter." For the proud wish to be in the open, but those who act iniquity desire to be in hiding and flee the light. But the Hebrew truth reads: "And with the hidden ones I will not walk." Which Rabbi Solomon <note>referring to Rashi, the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator</note> explains as those who hold secret meetings in the dark to perpetrate their acts in the shadows. And Job 6: "Those who fear the frost, the snow shall rush upon them." The Hebrews read: "Obscured by the frost, the snow shall hide them." And Psalm 44: "For he knows the hidden things of the heart." From this, some refer the title of Psalm 9 to "for the hidden things." <note>the Hebrew title *al-mut* is debated among scholars</note> And although Burgos <note>Paul of Burgos, a 14th-century Jewish convert and bishop</note> explains it as "youth," Rabbi David Kimhi <note>a famous medieval grammarian known as Radak</note> understands it as referring to the hidden melodies and mysteries of the song. See Nicholas of Lyra <note>a prominent Franciscan biblical exegete</note> and Paul of Burgos in the additions there.

**Boy** <note>Hebrew: *Elem*</note>. Youth, young man. 1 Samuel 17: "Ask whose son this boy is," speaking of David when he killed the Philistine giant. Likewise, the term for youth is <note>Hebrew: *alum*</note>, as in Job 33: "Let him return to the days of his youth." And Job 20: "His bones..."

**עלמה** <term>Almah</term> <note>A Hebrew word for a young woman</note>. Girl. Young woman. Maiden. Virgin. Genesis 24: "And the **virgin** who comes out to draw water will hear from me," where Onkelos <note>The author of Targum Onkelos, a famous 2nd-century Aramaic translation of the Torah</note> translated it into Aramaic as "girl" or "young woman." And Exodus 2: "The **girl** went and called the mother of the boy." And Isaiah 7: "Behold, a **virgin** <note>original: "virgo"</note> shall conceive and bear a son," where Jonathan the Chaldean <note>referring to Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation of the Prophets</note> uses the same word that Onkelos used for Rebecca. And Psalm 68: "In the midst of **young women** playing tambourines." This word is derived from the masculine form by changing it to the feminine, just as "boy" becomes "girl."

**עולם** <term>Olam</term> <note>A Hebrew word usually meaning eternity, an age, or the world</note>. Eternity. Eternal. An age. Exodus 15: "The Lord shall reign **forever** and beyond." Isaiah 45: "Israel is saved in the Lord with an **eternal** salvation," where the plural number is used as if saying "with the salvation of the ages," meaning both the present and the future age. Hence in Psalm 41 it is said: "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel from **age** to **age**, amen, amen." However, it does not always signify something infinite, but sometimes a determined period or a long time. As in Exodus 21: "And he shall be his servant **forever** <note>In this legal context, "forever" likely means until the next Jubilee year</note>." And Psalm 119: "I will **never** forget your justifications," meaning as long as I live. Finally, it should be understood that this word signifies duration according to the subject matter. Ecclesiastes 1: "For it has already passed in the **ages** that were before us." Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Shlomo Yitzhaki, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the most famous medieval Jewish commentator</note> explains this as "in the ages that passed before us," and thus they have ended.

**עלס** <term>Alas</term> <note>A Hebrew root for rejoicing</note>. He rejoiced. He was glad. He exulted. Job 20: "According to the multitude of his inventions, so shall he endure," where Rabbi Solomon writes that this word signifies joy by the conversion of the letter *zayin* into *samekh* <note>a linguistic explanation of how similar-sounding Hebrew letters can sometimes be interchanged in different dialects or words</note>, so that the meaning is: "according to the riches of his exchange, he shall **not rejoice**."

**עלף** <term>Alaph</term> <note>A Hebrew root for fainting or being overcome</note>. He failed. He fainted. He was weary. Jonah 4: "And the sun struck the head of Jonah and he **grew faint**." The LXX <note>The Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> translated it more correctly thus: "and he was distressed," but it is better as: "and he failed." So in Amos 8: "In that day the beautiful virgins and young men shall **fail** from thirst."

**עלף** <term>Alaph</term> <note>The same root as above, but here meaning to cover or overlay</note>. He covered. He veiled. Song of Songs 5: "His belly is as ivory **overlaid** with sapphires," which is better as "covered" or "veiled," others say "wrapped around." And Genesis...

עמוד <note>Amud</note> **Column.** Jeremiah 1: "And into an iron column." And Judges 16: "Let me touch the columns on which the whole house rests." And in its likeness it is called a "column of cloud." Exodus 13: "By day in a column of cloud and by night in a column of fire."

עמל <note>Amal</note> **Exercised, fatigued, or labored.** Jonah 4: "On which you did not labor." And Proverbs 16: "The soul of the laborer labors for himself." עמס <note>Amas</note> **Burdened or imposed a load.** Genesis 44: "With the donkeys having been loaded again." In Hebrew it is written: "and each one loaded his donkey." And in the plural in Proverbs 20: "Like deep waters, so is counsel in the heart of a man." It is written with a <term>dagesh</term> <note>a grammatical dot in Hebrew used to indicate emphasis or a double consonant</note>. From this comes the heavy transitive verb in Isaiah 29: "Woe to you who are deep of heart," that is, very deep. From this "depth" a valley is named, and it is written with five points <note>referring to Hebrew vowel markings</note> in Psalm 84: "In the valley of tears." And in the plural in the third book of Kings, chapter 20 <note>In modern Bibles, this is 1 Kings 20</note>: "And he is not the God of the valleys." From the verb is derived the noun "depth." Proverbs 25: "The heavens above and the earth below." In Hebrew it is: "The heavens for height and the earth for depth." and it receives the prefix <term>mem</term> <note>the Hebrew letter 'm'</note> at the beginning in Psalm 130: "Out of the depths I have cried to you, O Lord."

עמר <note>Amar</note> **Offered for sale, sold, or prostituted for sale or hired out.** Deuteronomy 21: "Neither shall you be able to sell her for money, nor oppress her by power," in place of "nor prostitute or hire her out."

...rams. And Ecclesiastes 3:4: "A time to mourn and a time to dance." And the somber word of Isaiah 13:21: "The shaggy goats shall dance there for you." <note>The author is finishing the entry for the Hebrew root *Raqad*, meaning to leap or dance.</note>

**רקח** <term>Raqach: He seasoned, prepared spices, or cooked.</term> He mixed them in the manner of ointment-makers, or composed them as pharmacists are accustomed to do. Exodus 30:33: "Whosoever shall compose the like." From this comes the noun used in the same place: "an ointment composed by the work of the ointment-maker." Likewise, incense "composed by the work of the ointment-maker." And Song of Solomon 5:13: "Banks of perfumes" <note>original: *Confitę a pigmentariis*</note>. All these derivatives signify aromatic seasonings used by doctors or apothecaries.

**רקם** <term>Raqam: He embroidered, wove with images, or worked in many colors.</term> If I might use the expression, he "weave-painted" <note>original: *texipixit* — a creative Latin coinage by the author combining the words for weaving and painting to describe embroidery</note>. Psalms <note>Psalm 139:15</note>: "And my substance in the lower parts of the earth." Jerome translates this as: "I was imaged in the lowest parts of the earth." He meant to say: "I was woven together in the lower parts of the earth," that is, in the womb. And Exodus 26:1: "With violet, purple, and twice-dyed scarlet, and fine twisted linen, the work of an embroiderer" <note>original: *opere plumario*</note>; more correctly: "by the work of a needle-painter or weaver." From this comes a garment interwoven with images, or a garment of diverse colors and many threads, as in Ezekiel 16:10: "And I clothed you with diverse colors," and further on: "And you took your many-colored garments." Judges 5:30: "Garments of diverse colors are delivered to Sisera as spoil," and various furniture is gathered to adorn the necks—a rhetorical interpretation.

**רקע** <term>Raqa: He expanded, he extended.</term> Isaiah 44:24: "Establishing the earth, and no one was with me while expanding or enlarging it." And 2 Samuel 22:43: "I will crush them and break them," in the sense of "I will stretch them out and thin them by treading upon them." From this comes the noun for expansion or extension, which we call the firmament. Genesis 1:6: "Let there be a firmament." So too in Numbers 16:38: "And let him beat them out into plates," and further on: "and he beat them into plates," that is, enlarging and extending them by striking with a hammer. However, that which is read in Ezekiel 6:11: "And strike with your foot," can be explained as "tread with your foot," specifically by extending or spreading the dust or mud that is under the foot.

**רשש** <term>Rashash: He perished, was impoverished, or was reduced to the height of misery.</term> Used in a middle-passive sense in Malachi 1:4: "If Edom should say, 'We are destroyed,'" which according to David Kimhi <note>A famous 12th-century Jewish rabbi and grammarian, often cited by Renaissance scholars</note> in his commentaries means "we are poor and miserable." From this we understand what is read in Jeremiah 5:17: "And he shall crush your fortified cities," that is, he will impoverish and destroy them. It has another meaning when there is a prefix *tav* and a *hirek* vowel at the end: a precious stone which our translation calls a hyacinth <note>The author refers to the word *Tarshish*, which shares the same root letters but adds a 'T' prefix</note>. Song of Solomon 5:14: "Full of hyacinths..."

499

<summary>This page defines Hebrew roots beginning with the letter Resh, specifically focusing on terms for mixing ointments, the art of embroidery, the act of physical expansion, and the state of being impoverished.</summary>
<keywords>Raqach, Raqam, Raqa, Rashash, embroidery, firmament, David Kimhi, biblical philology, Hebrew grammar</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the Hebrew lexicon, beginning with the conclusion of an entry likely concerning the word "Tarshish" (associated with precious stones and distant lands), and then proceeding through several roots beginning with the letter Resh (ר), including terms for "wickedness," "burning coals," and "nets."</meta>

# BOOK [unclear]

...Tarshish <note>original: *this*; completing the word *Tharsis* from the previous page</note>. In another place it is translated as chrysolite <note>a yellow-green gemstone</note>. Daniel 10:6: "And his body was like chrysolite." It also signifies a certain island called Tarshish far away; for example, "That he might flee to Tarshish" <note>Jonah 1:3</note>. From this word are derived "poor" and "poverty," and other terms derived by apocope <note>the loss of one or more sounds or letters from the end of a word</note>.

**רשיון** <term>Rishyon: A command or mandate.</term> Our translation <note>the Latin Vulgate</note> renders it as "command," and correctly so. Ezra 3:7: "According to what Cyrus the king of the Persians had commanded them."

**רשם** <term>Rasham: He signified, noted, suggested, or intimated.</term> Daniel 10:21: "I will tell you what is set forth in the scripture of truth," because it should be read as "that which is signified or noted."

**רשע** <term>Rasha: He sinned, acted wickedly, or behaved impiously.</term> Psalm 18:21: "Nor have I behaved impiously toward my God." And Ecclesiastes 7:17: "Do not act too impiously." And in another form in Daniel 9:5: "We have sinned, we have committed iniquity, we have acted wickedly." The noun form means "wicked," "impious," or "sinner." Proverbs 11:18: "The wicked man does an unstable work." And Psalm 50:16: "But to the sinner God has said." And the first form, marked with a *segol* <note>a Hebrew vowel mark indicating an 'e' sound</note>, means "sin" or "impiety." Ecclesiastes 8:8: "Neither shall impiety save the impious man." To this, the letter *He* (ה) is often added at the end for the feminine gender. Zechariah 5:8: "This is impiety."

**רשף** <term>Reshef: A burning coal, a torch, or a lamp.</term> Song of Solomon 8:6: "Its lamps are like lamps of fire and flames." The Hebrews interpret this as "coals," but it is sometimes understood as a burning demon. Habakkuk 3:5: "The devil <note>original: *diabolus*; often translated in modern Bibles as 'pestilence' or 'plague'</note> shall go forth before his feet." Others translate it as a pestilence which kills with its heat; others as an intense fever, which is the same thing. Another meaning is the sharp iron at the head of an arrow, but Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the primary translator of the Latin Vulgate</note> considers them to be the feathers on the back part of the arrows, which he calls "flying things" <note>original: *uolatilia*</note>. Psalm 76:3: "There he broke the powers of the bow," for which Jerome has: "There he broke the flying things [arrows] of the bow." But the Hebrews have: "There he broke the points of the bow."

**רשת** <term>Reshet: Properly a net; by others it is called a snare or trap.</term> Job 18:8: "For he has thrust his feet into a net." And Psalm 57:6: "They have prepared a snare for my feet." Hosea 7:12: "And when they have set out, I will spread my net over them." And Exodus 27:4: "And a bronze grate in the manner of a net."

**רתת** <term>Retet: Trembling.</term> Hosea 13:1: "When Ephraim spoke, horror <note>or trembling</note> seized Israel."
**רתח** <term>Ratach: It boiled, seethed, or cooked by boiling up.</term> Ezekiel 24:5.

fourthly. Its cooking has boiled over.

**רתם** <term>Rethem: A juniper tree, or the act of binding.</term> 1 Kings 19:4: "And he sat under a juniper tree" <note>original: *iuniperum*</note>. Some interpret this as a broom plant <note>original: *genestam*; a flowering shrub common in Mediterranean regions</note>. It has another meaning: "to bind." Micah 1:13: "You... of the chariot"; more correctly: "Bind the chariot" <note>the Hebrew root refers to harnessing animals to a vehicle</note>.

**רתק** <term>Rathaq: An enclosure, a chain, or a conclusion.</term> Ezekiel 7:23: "Make a chain" <note>original: *conclusionem*; in the Latin Vulgate, this word can mean a conclusion or a physical binding like a chain</note>. Also, regarding the passage in Ecclesiastes 12:6: "Before the silver cord be broken," others read it as: "Until the cord shall be chained." Similarly in Nahum 3:10: "And all her nobles were bound in fetters," which means they were chained or shut up.

<meta>This page begins Book 3 of the lexicon, continuing the alphabetical exploration of Hebrew roots. It transitions from the final entries of the previous book into the letter Shin (ש), focusing on terms related to materials, colors, and natural actions.</meta>

# BOOK 3

**שֵׁשׁ** <term>Shesh: Fine linen or silk.</term> Exodus 25: "And fine linen and goats' hair." And in Chapter 28 of the same book: "and of twisted fine linen." Also Genesis 41: "he clothed him in a robe of fine linen" <note>original Latin: *byssus*. This refers to a high-quality, costly fabric used for the garments of priests and royalty.</note>.

**שָׁשָׁה** <term>Shashah: To divide into six parts.</term> As if one were permitted to say "he sexted" <note>original: *sextavit*</note>, just as we say "he tithed" <note>original: *decimavit*, to take a tenth</note>. Ezekiel 45: "And a sixth part of an ephah from a kor of barley." Word for word it says: "and you shall 'sext' the ephah from the measure of barley." It sometimes undergoes an epenthesis <note>the addition of a letter in the middle of a word</note> of the letter *aleph*. It is also the noun for "six." Exodus 16: "Six days you shall gather," and its derivatives as found in grammar.

**שׁוֹשָׁן** <term>Shoshan: A lily, violet, or rose.</term> Song of Songs 2: "I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys." And in the same place: "as a lily among thorns." Just as the name *Rhodus* comes from "rose" and *Florentia* from "flower," so **Susa** <note>Shushan</note> is a royal and chosen city. Esther 2: "There was a Jewish man in the city of Susa."

**שָׁשַׁר** <term>Shashar: A bright red color.</term> A brilliant red pigment made from reddish earth. The ancients used it for splendor, and it is suitable for a painter's brush. It is called *sinopis* after the city of **Sinope** where it is mined, as **Pliny** writes in his *Natural History*, Book 34, Chapter 6. According to **Stephanus of Byzantium** in his work *On Cities*, Sinope is a most splendid city of the Pontus <note>the Black Sea region</note>, founded by Macritius of Cos. He writes that the first syllable of *sinopis* is spelled with an *iota* and the penultimate syllable is long. **Jeremiah** speaks of this color in Chapter 22: "He makes cedar paneling and paints it with red ochre <note>original: *sinopide*</note>." **Rabbi David Kimhi** <note>a famous 12th-13th century grammarian and scholar</note> in his *Book of Roots* says it signifies vermilion <note>original: *minium*</note>.

**שָׁאַב** <term>Sha’av: To draw water.</term> Isaiah 12: "You shall draw waters with joy." And Genesis 24: "That she might draw water, and having drawn it, she gave it to all the camels."

**שָׁאַג** <term>Sha’ag: To roar.</term> Amos 3: "The lion has roared, who will not fear?" and a little further above: "Will a lion roar in the forest?" And Psalm 36 <note>Modern Psalm 38:8</note>: "I roared from the groaning of my heart."

**שָׁאָה** <term>Sha’ah: To be desolated, devastated, or astonished.</term> Isaiah 6: "Until the cities be desolated without inhabitant." From this comes the noun for "devastation," "calamity," or "desolation." Psalm 35: "Let a snare come upon him which he knows not," which **Jerome** <note>the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate</note> more correctly renders as: "Let calamity come upon him." The word appears in another form in Genesis 24: "But he himself was contemplating," or more correctly: "And the man was dismayed because of her." This form uses a metathesis <note>a transposition of letters</note> of the *tav* and *shin*.

<meta>The previous page introduced roots starting with the letter Shin (ש), specifically regarding linen and colors. This page continues the lexical entries for the letter Shin, moving through words associated with noise, questioning, and various physical actions like breathing or trampling. Note: although the previous page mentioned Book 3, this page is headed "SECOND," likely referring to the second section of the letter Shin or a subdivision of the volume.</meta>

->SECOND<-

...of letters, as in grammar <note>the author is likely continuing a discussion from a previous page regarding the grammatical function or pronunciation of certain letters</note>. Another meaning is tumult, noise, sound, or roaring. Isaiah 17: "And the tumult of the crowds, like the sound of many waters, shall sound; people shall sound like the noise of flooding waters." All these signify a roaring.

**שָׁאַט** <term>Sha’at: To despise or treat with contempt.</term> He despised, rejected, or reproached. Our translation <note>the Latin Vulgate</note> renders it as "ambition" <note>original Latin: *ambitionem*</note>. Ezekiel 16: "The daughters of the Philistines who surround you with ambition." However, **Theodotion** <note>a prominent 2nd-century translator of the Hebrew Bible into Greek</note> translated it slightly better as: "who loathe you." The Hebrew text reads: "shamefully despising you."

**שָׁאַל** <term>Sha’al: To ask, seek, or the grave (Sheol).</term> He sought, requested, or questioned. Genesis 43: "The man questioned us," and Isaiah 7: "Ask a sign for yourself from God." From this comes "petition," which is a gift, an interrogation, or a question, as in 1 Kings 2: "I beg one small petition." Sometimes the letter *aleph* <note>the second letter of the Hebrew root</note> vanishes and is not written, as in 1 Kings 1: "May the God of Israel grant you your petition." It has another meaning: a pit, the grave, or hell. Proverbs 30: "Hell and the mouth of the womb," that is, the grave or death. As in Genesis 42: "You will bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to the grave."

**שָׁאַן** <term>Sha’an: To be at ease or prosperous.</term> He sat quiet and peaceful. It is found only with the final letter *nun* doubled; it means wealthy, fertile, or overflowing. Jeremiah 48: "Moab has been fertile from his youth." Isaiah 32: "And in wealthy rest," and a little earlier, "Rise up, you wealthy women." In the masculine, Amos 6: "Woe to you who are wealthy in Zion," meaning you are at peace.

**שָׁאַף** <term>Sha’af: To pant, swallow, or trample.</term> He swallowed up, gulped down, or drew in as a breath or air; he sighed or panted. Jeremiah 2: "In the desire of her soul she drew in the wind of her love," and Isaiah 42: "I will destroy and swallow up at once." Likewise, Psalm 119: "I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit." Jeremiah 14: "They drew in the wind like dragons." Another meaning is to trample. Psalm 56: "Have mercy on me, O God, for man has trampled me." Some Hebrew scholars also interpret this as "swallowed up." Another meaning is to desire. Job 7: "As a deer desires the shade." Others, however, follow the first meaning: "as a deer sighs for the shade." Likewise, Ecclesiastes 1: "The sun rises and sets and returns to its place, being born again there," which they interpret as: "And the sun rises and the sun sets, and panting toward its place, it is about to rise there."

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical dictionary of Hebrew roots beginning with the letter Shin (ש). The previous page concluded with a discussion of the word "Sheol" (the grave or underworld). This page moves forward into words concerning remnants, flesh, physical swellings, and the act of taking captives.</meta>

BOOK

**שָׁאַר** <term>Sha’ar: To remain, be left over, or flesh/kinship.</term> It remains; he was left over. 1 Samuel 16: "There remains yet the youngest, and behold, he is tending the sheep." From this comes the passive verb in 2 Samuel 14: "So that my husband may have no name or remnant left on the earth." And Isaiah 4: "And it shall come to pass that everyone who remains in Zion." Derivatives of this appear in Zephaniah 3: "The remnant of Israel will not do iniquity." Often the letter *aleph* is missing, as in 1 Chronicles 12: "But even all the rest of Israel were of one heart." Another meaning (when the last syllable has a *zere* vowel) is flesh, meat, or food—which our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> renders as "table" in Psalm 78: "Or can he provide a table for his people?" The Hebrews read this as "flesh," and **Saint Jerome** <note>the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate</note> does as well; **Rabbi Solomon** <note>Rashi, the famous 11th-century French rabbi and commentator</note> also explains it this way. This is confirmed a little further down in the same Psalm: "And he rained flesh upon them like dust." Another meaning is a blood relative, kinsman, or neighbor, as in Leviticus 18: "No man shall approach his close relative." It can also mean nourishment or sustenance, as in Exodus 21: "If he takes another wife for himself, he shall provide for the girl’s marriage, her clothing, and her marital rights." Word for word, it says: "If he takes another for himself, he shall not diminish her food, clothing, and her time of duty." It signifies all manner of food. Deuteronomy 28: "And blessed is your remnant," which the Hebrew masters interpret as "kneaded dough." Another meaning is leaven or ferment, as in Exodus 12: "On the first day there shall be no leaven in your houses." In this case, the last syllable is written with a *cholam* vowel.

**שְׂאֵת** <term>Se’et: A swelling, elevation, or skin lesion.</term> Swollen, elevated, puffed up, or bumpy; it is a type of *morphea* <note>a historical term for skin diseases like leprosy or localized scleroderma</note>. Leviticus 13: "A man in whose skin and flesh a different color has appeared." It seems to be derived from another verb, namely *nasa* <note>meaning "to lift up"</note>; see above.

**שָׁבָב** <term>Shabab: Fragments, sparks, or to turn back.</term> Fragments of wood. Our translation <note>The Vulgate</note> renders this as "spider webs" in Hosea 8: "For the calf of Samaria shall be as spider webs." Others translate it as "sparks," as in Job 18: "Neither shall the flame of his fire shine," meaning a spark. Another meaning is to turn or to bring around, as in Ezekiel 38: "I will turn you about and put a bridle in your jaws," and later: "To the land that returned from the sword." And Micah 2: "When he returns to divide our regions."

**שָׁבָה** <term>Shabah: To plunder or take captive.</term> He plundered, seized, or captured. Jeremiah 41: "All the people whom Ishmael had captured." Sometimes it loses the final letter *he*, as in Numbers 21: "And being victorious, he led away plunder from it," where a *yod* is placed in the name instead of a *he*. Likewise, "captive" (male or female), as in Isaiah 52: "Captive..."

<meta>This page continues the dictionary for the letter Shin (ש), specifically focusing on the roots Sheva (seven/oath/fullness), Shabats (gold-weaving), and Shavar (breaking/grain/hoping). It follows the previous entries for Shevet (rod/tribe).</meta>

->BOOK<-

**שבע** <term>Sheva: The number seven, or to swear, or to be satisfied.</term> **Seven.** <note>original: "Septem"</note> Leviticus 23: "Seven weeks," and below: "You shall offer with the seven breads of the unblemished lambs." From this is derived a usage found in grammar and the frequent reading of the Hebrew Bible meaning **to swear.** Genesis 25: "Esau swore to him." Deuteronomy 6: "And you shall swear by His name." From this comes the word for **oath.** <note>original: "iuramentum"</note> Judges 21: "For they had bound themselves with a great oath." And **to adjure.** Genesis 24: "That I may adjure you by the God of heaven." It has another meaning: **to satisfy** or **to fill.** <note>original: "saturare et satiare"</note> Deuteronomy 8: "Lest when you have eaten and are satisfied, you bless the Lord your God." And 1 Chronicles 23: "Therefore David was old and full of days," that is, satisfied with his days. Likewise in 2 Chronicles 24: "But Jehoiada grew old, full of days," that is, satisfied with age. From this comes **satiety** and **fullness**, and other related words.

**שבץ** <term>Shabats: To bind or weave with gold.</term> **He bound with gold,** or tightened, or constricted. Exodus 28: "And you shall tighten the tunic with fine linen," and above, "a straight linen tunic," and further below, "they shall be enclosed in gold," as if constricted by little golden settings, which were translated as "hooks" or "clasps" a little earlier: "You shall also make hooks of gold."

**שבר** <term>Shavar: To break, or grain/provisions.</term> **He broke,** crushed, ruined, or destroyed. Isaiah 14: "The Lord has crushed the staff of the wicked, the rod of the rulers." Jeremiah 19: "And you shall crush the flask in the eyes of the men," and below: "So will I crush this people and this city, just as a potter's vessel is crushed." It is also used metaphorically for **tribulation** and **distress.** <note>original: "consternatione"</note> Psalm 51: "A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit," meaning a broken and distressed mind. Similarly, it is used metaphorically of a man who takes a virgin's maidenhead, breaking the enclosures so that she may bear children. Isaiah 66: "Shall I, who make others give birth, not give birth myself?" And thus the **matrix** or **womb** of a laboring woman is named for its "opening" or "breaking." Hosea 13: "For now he shall not stay in the crushing of children," which word for word reads: "Because the time shall not stay in the matrix or womb of children." 

Another meaning for this root is **grain,** or the harvest of food and provisions in general, or victuals, distinguished by six vowel points. Genesis 42: "And Jacob, hearing that food was being sold in Egypt." It is also used as a gerund in Genesis 41: "That they might buy food," meaning for the purpose of nourishment. Thus it signifies both **to buy** and **to sell.**

**שבר** <term>Sibar: To hope or wait.</term> **He hoped,** expected, or sustained. Isaiah 38: "Those who go down into the pit shall not expect your truth." And Psalm 1...

<meta>This page continues the dictionary for the letter Shin (ש). It begins with the conclusion of the entry for Shavar (שבר) from the previous page, specifically discussing the meaning of "looking" or "hoping," before moving into the roots Shavat (rest), Shagag (error), Shaga (growth), Shagav (exaltation), and Shagah (ignorance).</meta>

->BOOK TWO<-

...145th. The eyes of all hope in you, O Lord. <note>original: "Oculi omnium in te sperant domine." This is the conclusion of the previous entry for the root Shavar (שבר), which can mean "to hope" or "wait."</note>

**שבת** <term>Shavat: To rest, cease, or finish.</term> **He finished, was empty, rested, was idle, kept the Sabbath, or ceased.** <note>original: "Finiuit. uacauit. quieuit. ociatus est. sabatizauit. cessauit."</note> Lamentations 5: "The joy of our heart has failed," meaning it has **ceased.** Genesis 2: "And he rested on the seventh day from all the work he had done." From this comes the word **Sabbath,** <note>original: "sabatum"</note> derived from "rest." Isaiah 66: "And it shall be month after month and Sabbath after Sabbath." From this also comes "Sabbath of Sabbaths" and other derived terms.

**שגג** <term>Shagag: To err unintentionally or sin through ignorance.</term> **He failed unintentionally, sinned ignorantly, or erred without premeditation.** <note>original: "Deliquit non dedita opera. peccauit ignoranter. impræmeditate deliquit."</note> Leviticus 5: "Who shall pray for him because he acted unknowingly." From this comes the word for a **delict** or fault committed not by design. It also appears with an added letter "h" <note>original: "per paragogen he"</note>; similarly it means **sin through ignorance.** Leviticus 4: "The soul that shall sin through ignorance," etc. From this comes the usage in Job 19: "Surely if I have been ignorant, my ignorance will be with me," that is, if I have slipped through imprudence, my imprudence and simplicity shall dwell with me.

**שגא** <term>Shaga: To grow great, increase, or multiply.</term> **He was magnified, grew up, was increased, or was multiplied.** Job 8: "Can the papyrus grow without water?" and in Job 37: "We cannot find him out; he is great in strength." And Job 12: "He who multiplies nations and destroys them." It is also found written with the letter *He* [ה] in place of *Aleph* [א], as in Job 8: "And your latter end may increase greatly." In modern manuscripts, this is written with *Aleph*, but in the oldest and most corrected copies, it is written with *He* instead of *Aleph*. It is also found in a doubled form.

**שגב** <term>Shagav: To exalt, lift up, or protect.</term> **He exalted, raised up, lifted up, or relieved.** <note>original: "Exaltauit. extulit. eleuauit. releuauit."</note> Deuteronomy 2: "There was no village nor city that escaped our hands." <note>The author notes that "escaped" is a rhetorical interpretation rather than a literal grammatical one.</note> Word for word, it reads: "there was no city that raised itself above us" or "against us." Isaiah 9: "And the Lord shall lift up the enemies of Rezin over him." And in the passive form in Isaiah 33: "The Lord is magnified," that is, **exalted.** Our translations often interpret this as **protection,** as in Psalm 91: "I will protect him because he knows my name." However, Jerome more correctly translates it as: "I will exalt him."

**שגה** <term>Shagah: To err or be ignorant.</term> **He erred or was ignorant.** Job 6: "And if I have perhaps been ignorant, instruct me." And Leviticus 4: "If the whole congregation of the children of Israel shall be ignorant." Sometimes the *He* [ה] is changed to *Aleph* [א]. Psalm 19: "Who understands errors?" <note>original: "Delicta quis intelligit."</note> Jerome more correctly renders this as "errors." <note>original: "errores"</note> This is also the view of Aquila, Symmachus, and Jerome. <note>Aquila and Symmachus were famous 2nd-century translators of the Old Testament into Greek.</note>

<summary>This page defines Hebrew roots related to rest (Shavat), unintentional error (Shagag), growth (Shaga), and exaltation (Shagav), providing biblical citations and linguistic nuances.</summary>
<keywords>Sabbath, rest, ignorance, sin, growth, exaltation, Jerome, biblical Hebrew, linguistics</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dictionary of Hebrew roots beginning with the letter Shin (ש). It concludes the discussion of the root Shagah (to ignore or wander) before moving through the roots Shagach, Shagal, Shaga, Shagar, Shad, and Shadad.</meta>

->BOOK TWO<-

The title of Psalm 7 they translated as "for ignorance." <note>original: "ignoratione." This refers to the Hebrew word *Shiggaion*, which the author links to the root *Shagah* (שגה).</note> All terms derived from it signify thick ignorance, or according to others, even care and labor. As in Proverbs 20: "Whoever is delighted by it will not be wise," <note>original: "Quicumqʒ ijs delectatur non erit sapiens." Usually referring to the intoxicating effects of wine.</note> meaning whoever labors in it, or is preoccupied and busied with it. Hence "one who causes to wander." Job 24: <note>original: "Iob.xxviij." The text cites chapter 28, but the verse "Who deceives the just in an evil way" is typically associated with the concept of leading astray.</note> "He who deceives the just in an evil way." And Deuteronomy 27: "Cursed be he who makes the blind wander on the journey." It can take another meaning as "to overtake." Deuteronomy 28: "And they shall overtake you."

**שגח** <term>Shagach: To gaze or look.</term> **He beheld, looked forth, or looked back.** Song of Songs 2: "Beholding through the windows."

**שגל** <term>Shagal: To violate or lie with.</term> **He violated or lay with.** Zechariah 14: "And the women shall be violated." From this comes **wife, spouse, or woman.** Psalm 45: "The queen stood at your right hand," which Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate.</note> more correctly translates as: "The **spouse** stood at your right hand." And Deuteronomy 28: <note>original: "Deutero. viij." The text likely contains a typo, as this occurs in chapter 28.</note> "You shall take a wife and another man shall sleep with her," that is, he shall lie with her.

**שגע** <term>Shaga: To be mad or frenzied.</term> **He raged, was out of his mind, was incensed, astonished, or stunned.** Deuteronomy 28: "And you shall be stunned at the terror of those things which your eyes shall see." From this comes another noun a little earlier in the same chapter: "May the Lord strike you with **madness** and blindness." From this also comes "furious" and "maniac."

**שגר** <term>Shagar: Offspring of livestock.</term> **A recently born animal, or the fruit of the cattle.** Exodus 13: "And that which is the firstborn among your cattle." And Deuteronomy 7: "And the herds and flocks of your sheep."

**שד** <term>Shad: Breast.</term> **Breast or teat.** Lamentations 4: "But even the sea monsters <note>original: "lamiae." This refers to mythical creatures or nocturnal spirits, here used for jackals or whales in some translations.</note> bared the breast." And in the plural, Genesis 49: "With the blessings of the breasts and of the womb." And Song of Songs 1: "He shall dwell between my breasts." It has another meaning when voweled with *tsere*, <note>Referring to the Hebrew vowel mark for "e".</note> meaning **demon.** Exodus 32: <note>Likely Deuteronomy 32:17.</note> "They sacrificed to demons and not to God."

**שדד** <term>Shadad: To devastate or destroy.</term> **He devastated or depopulated.** Ezekiel 32: "And they shall devastate the pride of the Egyptians." It is found as both an active and passive participle. Isaiah 33: "Woe to you who plunder, shall you not also be plundered?" Word for word it is: "This one devastating, and you not devastated." There is also the noun **vastness** or **depopulation.** Amos 5: "He brings vastness upon the strong, and depopulation upon the powerful." It has another meaning, **Shaddai:** strong, great, or almighty. Genesis 17: "I am God Almighty." From that sense of honor, they understand the verse in Ecclesiastes 2: "Cups and pitchers in the service for pouring wine." <note>The author is connecting the word for "chests" or "cups" (*shiddah*) to this root.</note>

->508<-

<summary>This page lists Hebrew roots beginning with the letter Shin, providing Latin definitions and Biblical examples for terms related to ignorance, gazing, marriage/violation, madness, livestock, and destruction. It notably discusses the divine name Shaddai as a derivative of the root for strength or devastation.</summary>

--- Page 511 ---
<meta>This page continues the dictionary of Hebrew roots, concluding the discussion on the root Shad (field/power) and its variants before moving into Shadmah (field/valley), Shadaf (to wither), and Shadar (planking).</meta>

->**BOOK SECOND**<-

...they explain and translate as **honor** and **magnificence.** For the phrase regarding "the pouring out of wine" is not in the original text and should therefore be removed with an obelisk. <note>original: "obelisco effodiendū." An obelisk was a symbol used by ancient scholars to mark a passage in a manuscript that appeared to be spurious or out of place.</note> It has another agricultural meaning. Hosea 10: "Jacob shall break his furrows for himself." <note>original: "Confringet sibi sulcos Iacob."</note> From this comes **field** or **plain.** Genesis 4: "And when they were in the field." And likewise **region, wasteland,** or **level place.** In this sense, it loses one *daleth* and takes a *he* at the end, signifying **land** or **earth.**

**שדמה** <term>Shadmah: An uncultivated or scorched field.</term> Following the addition of the feminine letter *he*, it signifies **uncultivated** and **parched.** Isaiah 37: "And the grass of the housetops which withered before it matured." <note>original: "Et herba tectorum quę exaruit antequā maturefceret."</note> And in the plural, Deuteronomy 32: "From the vineyard of Sodom, and their wine is from the suburbs of Gomorrah," used to mean the **wild and uncultivated fields** of Gomorrah. It has another meaning of **valley.** 2 Kings 23: "Outside Jerusalem in the valley of Kidron." <note>original: "conualle cedron."</note> And because a torrent flows through that valley, it is often used for the **torrent** itself, as the Targum <note>An ancient Aramaic translation or paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> indicates. So also in Jeremiah 31: "The whole region of death as far as the torrent Kidron." Here, Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into the Latin Vulgate.</note> divided this word into two, but it is one word which the Seventy <note>The Septuagint (LXX), the oldest Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> left untouched, writing it as *Assaremoth*. This is how it is read in certain ancient Hebrew manuscripts, although I have found a notation there indicating that it should be read not as *Saremoch* but as *Sademoth*. Now, **Kidron** (which is called *Kidron* in Hebrew) is the name of a once-obscure valley near Jerusalem, named for its **obscurity and darkness.** Through it flows a torrent that sometimes appears dark and sometimes is dry and parched. Indeed, in the aforementioned passage of Jeremiah, Jerome interprets *Kidron* as **darkness** in his commentaries. Hence, those who explain the Passion of Christ as taking place "across the torrent of the Cedars" <note>Referring to the Greek name *Kedron*, which sounds like the word for cedar trees (*kedros*).</note> seem to be in error. For although *Kedron* in Greek signifies <margin>The valley of Kidron</margin> **of the cedars** in Latin, it is not so in Hebrew, where *Kidron* is the proper name of the valley.

**שדף** <term>Shadaf: To wither or dry up.</term> **He withered or was dried up.** 2 Kings 19: "The grass of the housetops which was dried up before it came to maturity." From this comes **aridity**, which our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate.</note> interprets as **blighted air.** Deuteronomy 28: "With blighted air and mildew." <note>original: "Et aere corrupto et rubigine."</note>

**שדר** <term>Shadar: Paneling or ceiling.</term> **A story or planking.** Our translation renders it as **coffered ceiling.** 1 Kings 6: "He also covered the house with cedar panels."

**שדה** <term>Seh/Sadeh: Cattle or livestock.</term> **Livestock.** Ezekiel 34: "Behold, I myself judge between the fat cattle..." <note>The author uses the Hebrew word for "field" (Sadeh) but cites a verse from Ezekiel where the Hebrew word is actually "Seh" (sheep/cattle), likely discussing a variant reading or a phonetic similarity.</note>

<meta>This page continues the dictionary of Hebrew roots, concluding a discussion on sheep/livestock (Seh) before moving through roots beginning with the letters Shin-He, including witness (Shahad), onyx (Shoham), ornaments (Sahar), vanity/noise (Shav), return/dwell (Shuv), and plastering (Shuach).</meta>

**SECOND BOOK**

...and lean. But our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate, the standard Bible translation used during the Renaissance.</note> has transferred this word to mean **sacrifice** or **victim.** Genesis 22: "Where is the victim for the burnt offering?" and further down: "God will provide for himself the victim for the burnt offering, my son." Here it refers to a beast for sacrifice. It is of common gender because it is a general term and is used as a substitute for all other types of small livestock.

**שהד** <term>Shahad: Witness or confidant.</term> Job 16: "My witness and my confidant is in the heavens." <note>original: "testis meus et cōscius meus ī excelsis."</note>

**שהם** <term>Shoham: Onyx or an onyx-colored stone.</term> Genesis 2: "And there is found bdellium and the onyx stone." <note>The text mistakenly cites "Genesis 1" but refers to the description of the Garden of Eden in chapter 2.</note>

**שהר** <term>Sahar: Ornaments for horses or camels.</term> These are what people call **crescents** or **little moons**; for in the Chaldean language <note>A term often used by older scholars to refer to Aramaic.</note>, the moon is called *sehara*. Judges 8: "And he took the ornaments and the studs from the necks of the camels."

**שוא** <term>Shav: A clamor, roar, or something empty.</term> Zechariah 4: "And he shall make equal the grace of his grace." More correctly thus: "And he shall bring forth the capstone with shouts of 'Grace, grace' to it." Or similarly: "A roar and a clamorous shout of 'Grace, grace' to him." It has another meaning of **empty, vain, useless,** or **frustrating.** Job 7: "So also I have had empty months." And Exodus 20: "You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain."

**שוב** <term>Shuv: To turn, return, or convert.</term> This is used in an absolute sense. Isaiah 6: "And let him be converted and I shall heal him." And Song of Solomon 6: "Return, return, O Shulammite." Note it is not "Sunammite," but *Shulammite*, which means **complete** and **perfect.** And Ecclesiastes 1: "And it returns to its circuits." From this come the "heavy" and transitive forms of the verb <note>Referring to the Hebrew causative verb stems like Hiphil.</note> which signify **to cause to return,** that is, **to restore, to give back,** or **to respond** and similar actions. Psalm 51: "Restore to me the joy of your salvation." Sometimes it appears with a doubled second letter. Psalm 23: "He shall restore my soul." And Jeremiah 8: "And he who has turned away shall not return. Why then has this people in Jerusalem turned away with a stubborn turning?" It has another meaning of **to reside, to rest,** or **to dwell,** as in the Psalm already cited: "and that I may dwell in the house of the Lord." Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century biblical scholar.</note> renders it thus: "And I shall dwell in the house of the Lord." From this comes the word for **sitting, residence, a seat,** or **a chair.** Psalm 1: "And in the chair of pestilence he did not sit," which means "and in the seat of mockers he did not dwell." It has another meaning: **to be decrepit** or **gray-haired.** 1 Samuel 12: "I however have grown old and gray."

**שוח** <term>Shuach: To smear or cover with lime or plaster.</term> Deuteronomy 27: "And you shall smooth them with lime." And shortly before: "You shall set up great stones..."

<meta>This page continues the dictionary of Hebrew roots beginning with the letter Shin. The previous page ended mid-sentence discussing the word for "empty" or "vain" (Shav).</meta>

->**SECOND BOOK**<-

...and you shall level them with lime; others think **ashes** are signified. <note>The author is discussing the root *Sid*, meaning lime or plaster, and comparing it to the word for ashes.</note> Isaiah 33: "And the peoples shall be as the ashes of a fire." Furthermore, the letter *samech* is often written in place of *shin*.

**שוה** <term>Shavah: To make equal, level, or comparable.</term> Isaiah 28: "Does he not, when he has leveled its surface?" and in the fortieth chapter of the same book: "To whom have you likened me and made me equal? says the Holy One." From this comes **equal, peer,** and **even** or **pleasant.**
It has another meaning: **to effect, make,** or **place.** Psalm 89: "I have placed help upon one who is mighty." And Psalm 16: "I foresaw the Lord in my sight always." More correctly, however, Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Bible into Latin.</note> translates it: "I have set the Lord." All its derivatives signify "to place."

**שוח** <term>Shuach: To bow down, bend, or break.</term> Proverbs 2: "Her house is bowed down toward death." From this, a **pit** is named, into which something bows or falls. Jeremiah 18: "They have dug a pit for my soul." And likewise a **tomb** for the body.

**שוח** <term>Shuach (Siyach): To speak or converse.</term> <note>While spelled the same as the previous entry in this text's orthography, this refers to the root for speech or meditation.</note> Psalm 69: "They who sat in the gate spoke against me." And Psalm 119: "I will meditate on your commandments," that is, I will speak a meditated prayer. And Psalm 144: "I will meditate on the works of your hands," that is, I will bring forth and speak every concept of my mind; for this is the specific property of this word. As in Isaiah 53: "Who shall declare his generation?" that is, who shall speak it with premeditation and composition according to the concept of his mind? So in the title of Psalm 102: "And he pours out his prayer before the Lord." More correctly, Jerome translates: "He would pour out his eloquence." But it was also heard above that it signifies **meditation, contrivance,** and some **hidden practice** of a man.

**שוט** <term>Shut: To stroll or go around.</term> Numbers 11: "And the people went around and, collecting it, ground it in a mill." And used transitively in Jeremiah 5: "Go around the streets of Jerusalem." And in this sense, the letter *teth* is doubled.
Another meaning is the **crack of a driver's whip.** Nahum 3: "The sound of the whip and the sound of the rushing wheel." This refers to the business of a chariot driver, and thus it means **whip, staff,** or **rod.**
Another meaning is **pitch wood.** Exodus 25: "Shittim wood." <note>original: "Ligna setim."</note> With the addition of the letter *he* and an inserted *iod* in place of *vau*, it refers to a genus of bush which is called *acanthus*, and by us the **thorn.** Isaiah 41: "The cedar and the thorn and the myrtle."

**שוך** <term>Shukh: To hedge in.</term> To wall something off with briars, thorns, and intertwined branches. Hosea 2: "Behold, I will hedge your way with thorns."

<meta>This page continues the Hebrew dictionary for the letter Shin, moving from the root Shuach (to speak or meditate) to roots beginning with Shul, Sum, Shua, Shuf, and Shuq.</meta>

->**BOOK**<-

**שׁוּל** <term>Shul: Hem, fringe, or the edge of a garment.</term> This is what our translation describes in a roundabout way in Exodus 28: "And downward toward the feet of the same tunic all around." <note>original: "Deorsum vero ad pedes eiusdem tunicæ per circuitum"</note> All of this is read in Hebrew as: "upon the fringe."

**שׂוּם** <term>Sum: To put, place, set, make, or pay attention.</term> Exodus 4: "Who made the mouth of man? Or who fashioned the mute and the deaf?" And Haggai 2: "Before a stone was placed upon a stone in the temple of the Lord." And 4 Kings 9: <note>In modern Bibles, this is 2 Kings 9:30.</note> "She painted her eyes with antimony." <note>original: "Depinxit oculos stibio"</note> Word for word, it reads: "And he put his eyes in paint," a construction which the grammarians translate as: "And he put paint on his eyes." It has another meaning, **garlic.** Numbers 11: "Leeks and onions and garlic."

**שׁוּעַ** <term>Shua: To cry out or call for help.</term> Psalm 18: "They cried out and there was no one who could save them." It is also a noun, as in Jeremiah 8: "Behold the voice of the cry of the daughter of my people." It is also translated as **wailing** in 1 Kings 5: <note>Modern 1 Samuel 5.</note> "And the wailing of each one ascended to heaven." It has another meaning: **to smear, anoint, or make smooth.** Isaiah 6: "And close his eyes," by "smearing" them. According to this, Rabbi Joseph, the father of David Kimhi, <note>A significant family of medieval Jewish grammarians and biblical commentators.</note> explains the verse in Ezekiel 16 where we read: "And you were not washed with water for health." <note>original: "Et aqua non es lota in salutem"</note> Alternatively: "And you were not washed with water for smoothness," that is, so that you might be smooth like a hairless person and as if anointed. It has another meaning: **rich, honored, or powerful.** Ezekiel 23: "The mobile tyrants and princes." He wants to say, word for word: "The prefect, the rich, and the powerful." Likewise, Job 34: "Nor did he acknowledge the tyrant when he argued against the poor man," in place of "and the rich man was not recognized before the poor," or "rather than the poor."

**שׁוּף** <term>Shuf: To crush, strike, bruise, or trample.</term> Genesis 3: "She shall crush your head and you shall lie in wait for her heel." <note>The author uses the feminine "ipsa" (she), following the Vulgate's traditional messianic interpretation of the "woman" crushing the serpent's head.</note> It has another meaning: **to darken or overshadow.** Psalm 139: "And I said, perhaps the darkness shall trample me," where the interpretation follows the first meaning. But Jerome later more correctly wrote in his Psalter: "Perhaps the darkness shall cover me," <note>original: "forsitan tenebræ operient me"</note> instead of "shall darken me."

**שׁוּק** <term>Shuq: To desire, long for, or covet.</term> Psalm 65: "You have visited the earth and watered it," <note>original: "inebriasti eam"</note> for which they read: "And you have caused it to long," that is, so that it might be satisfied. Likewise, Genesis 3, instead of what we read: "And you shall be under the power of the husband," the Hebrew truth <note>A common term for the original Hebrew text among Renaissance scholars.</note> has: "And toward your husband shall be your desire or longing." Similarly in the fourth chapter of the same book: "Under you shall be [his desire]."

<meta>This page continues the entry for the root Shuq (to overflow or desire) and proceeds through the roots Shir (to sing or behold), Shur (to rule or measure), Sus (to rejoice), and Shit (to place or set).</meta>

->**SECOND [PART]**<-

...its desire. Another meaning is **to crackle**, **to grate**, or **to resound** in the manner of a thing heavily burdened and shaken. As in Joel 2: "And the wine vats shall overflow <note>original: "redundabunt"</note> with wine and oil." Another meaning is **street**. Ecclesiastes 12: "And the mourners shall go about in the street." Likewise a little earlier: "And they shall shut the doors in the street." Another meaning is **leg**. Song of Songs 5: "His legs are marble columns." And this is transferred to the **shoulder** of a beast. Exodus 29: "And the right shoulder." And from the first meaning, a common verb is derived. Nahum 2: "They collided in the streets," meaning they creaked or resounded with a crashing noise. <note>The author is connecting the "clattering" of chariots in the street to the root Shuq.</note>

**שִׁיר** <term>Shir: To sing or chant.</term> As in the title of Psalm 7: "Concerning the ignorance of David, who sang to the Lord." <note>The Latin "ignorantia" reflects an old interpretation of the Hebrew "Shiggaion."</note> From this comes the noun in Ecclesiastes 2: "I provided for myself male and female singers." Likewise, the basic verb in Exodus 15: "Then Moses and the children of Israel sang this song to the Lord." And the title of Solomon: "The Song of Songs." Another meaning is **to look at** or **to behold**. Numbers 24: "I shall behold him, but not near." And Song of Songs 4: "You shall be crowned from the head of Amana," but it is more correctly: "Look forth from the peak of Amana," etc. Another meaning is **to offer** or **to give**. 1 Kings 9: <note>Modern 1 Samuel 9:7.</note> "And we have no basket to give to the man of God." More correctly, word for word, it is: "And there is no offering to offer to the man of God." Another meaning is **wall**. Genesis 49: "The daughters ran over the wall." And Psalm 18: "In my God I shall leap over a wall." Another is **ox** or **bull**. Leviticus 22: "An ox, a sheep, or a goat."

**שׁוּר** <term>Shur: To dominate, to lead, or to reign.</term> Judges 9: "And so Abimelech reigned over Israel for three years." From this comes the noun in Joshua 5: "I am the prince <note>original: "princeps"</note> of the army of the Lord." Another meaning, formed with the prefix *mem* and the suffix *he*, is **measure**. Leviticus 19: "In weight and in measure." <note>The Hebrew "mishrah" comes from this root.</note>

**שׂוּשׂ** <term>Sus: To exult, to be glad, or to rejoice.</term> Deuteronomy 28: "And just as the Lord previously rejoiced over you by doing you good, so he will rejoice in destroying you." And the basic verb in Psalm 70: "Let them exult and be glad in you." From this comes the noun in Psalm 51: "To my hearing you give joy and gladness."

**שִׁית** <term>Shit: To locate, to place, or to found.</term> Genesis 4: "And she called his name Seth, saying: God has set for me another seed." And the Psalm: <note>Psalm 73:28.</note> "To place my hope in my God," or more correctly, "I have placed." And in the same Psalm: "They have set [their mouth] against heaven..."

--- Page 516 ---
<meta>This page continues the definitions of Hebrew roots beginning with the letter Shin. It concludes the entry for the root Shit (to set or place) and proceeds through Shazaph (to gaze), Shazar (to twist), Shachah (to bow), Shochad (to bribe), Sachah (to swim), and Shachat (to slaughter or hammer).</meta>

BOOK

...his mouth. <note>original: "os suum"</note> In another way it is interpreted in the seventeenth Psalm <note>Modern Psalm 17:11.</note>: "And they have set their eyes to bow down to the earth." Jerome translates: "They have placed their eyes to decline." And indeed, it correctly means **to fix**, **to establish**, and **to compose**. In the seventh chapter of Proverbs: "In a harlot's attire." It is more correctly: "**Establishing** [the look of] a harlot."

**שָׁזַף** <term>Shazaph: He looked upon or gazed.</term> Job chapter twenty-eight: "The eye of the vulture hath not seen it." And in the first chapter of the Song of Songs: "Because the sun has discolored me." More correctly: "Because the sun has **looked** upon me."

**שָׁזַר** <term>Shazar: Twisted and doubled,</term> just as two threads are usually doubled together into a rope. Exodus chapter twenty-seven: "Of fine **twisted** linen."

**שָׁחָה** <term>Shachah: He humbled, bent, or bowed down;</term> used in an absolute sense. Job chapter nine: "And under whom they are **bent**." And in the second chapter of Isaiah: "And all the loftiness of men shall be **bowed down**." And in the sixth chapter of Micah: "And your **humiliation** is in the midst of you." From this comes the verb in the *hithpael* form <note>The reflexive form of a Hebrew verb.</note> **to adore**, **to genuflect**, or **to bow**. Genesis chapter thirty-three: "And he, going forward, **adored** prostrate upon the ground seven times," that is, he bowed. From this come nouns and other derivatives of the same meaning.

**שֹׁחַד** <term>Shochad: A present or a gift.</term> Psalm fifteen: "And he has not accepted a **gift** against the innocent." And in the eighth chapter of first Kings <note>Modern 1 Samuel 8:3.</note>: "They took **bribes** and perverted judgment."

**שָׂחָה** <term>Sachah: He swam.</term> Isaiah chapter twenty-five: "As a swimmer extends [his hands] **to swim**." And in the forty-seventh chapter of Ezekiel: "The waters of the torrent had swollen, which cannot be **waded through**." From this is derived the words for "oar" and "rower."

**שָׁחַט** <term>Shachat: He killed, sacrificed, or slit the throat.</term> Leviticus chapter one: "And he **sacrificed** the calf before the Lord." Likewise in the thirtieth chapter of the second [book of] Chronicles: "And they **sacrificed** the Passover." And below: "The Levites **sacrificed** the Passover for those who had not occurred to be sanctified to the Lord." More correctly, word for word, it is: "And the Levites [were] over the **killing** or **slaughtering** of the Passover offerings for everyone who was not clean." It has another meaning: **to work metal** and **to treat with a hammer**. From this comes **to hammer out** or **to draw out**, and thus it signifies **ductile** or **malleable metal**. In the tenth chapter of Kings: "And King Solomon made two hundred shields of the purest gold." More correctly: "of **ductile** and hammered gold."

<meta>This page continues the Hebrew lexicon, focusing on roots beginning with the letter Shin. It picks up alphabetically with Shachal (lion/asp) and follows through Shachar (dawn/blackness). The translator notes a significant historical event—the "plague" of 1497—within the entry for "boils."</meta>

->SECOND [BOOK]<-

**שַׁחַל** <term>Shachal: A lion.</term> Others think it refers to a leopard. Our translation <note>The Vulgate, the standard Latin Bible used in the author's time.</note> renders it as an **asp** <note>original: "aspidem," a venomous snake</note> in Psalm 91 <note>original: "ps. lxxi," likely a numbering error in the source or referencing an older psalter; the verse is Psalm 91:13.</note>: "You shall walk upon the **asp** and the basilisk." Likewise in Job chapter 4: "The roaring of the **lion** and the voice of the lioness." In the language of the masters <note>The Rabbis/Jewish scholars.</note>, it is a species of owl, but that has nothing to do with this passage.

**שְׁחִין** <term>Shachin: A pustule, scab, ulcer, or skin eruption.</term> Exodus chapter 9: "For there shall be **boils** and swelling blisters upon men and beasts in all the land of Egypt."
<note>The following is a personal observation by the 16th-century author.</note> Note the plague with which God has struck our land from the year of our Lord 1497 until this day, and there is no end yet. <note>This likely refers to the Great Pox or Syphilis epidemic that ravaged Europe starting in the late 1490s.</note>

**שָׁחִיס** <term>Shachis: That which first sprouts from a root.</term> It occurs by the switching of the letters *Samech* and *Shin*. As in 2 Kings chapter 19: "In the second year, eat those things which grow **of their own accord**."

**שַׁחַף** <term>Shachaph: A swelling.</term> Our translation renders it as **poverty** <note>original: "egestas"; in modern Bibles often translated as "consumption" or a wasting disease</note>. Deuteronomy chapter 28: "May the Lord strike you with **poverty**." Another meaning is a type of bird which our translation calls a **gull** <note>original: "larum"</note>. Leviticus chapter 11: "The **gull** and the hawk." Certain Hebrew scholars name it the heron.

**שַׁחַץ** <term>Shachatz: Proud or pride.</term> Job chapter 41: "He is king over all the children of **pride**."

**שָׁחַק** <term>Shachaq: He crushed or ground.</term> Exodus chapter 30: "And when you have **ground** it all into the finest powder." Another meaning is **clouds**. Psalm 89: "Who in the **clouds** shall be compared to the Lord?" Another meaning is **he laughed at, played, mocked, or was playful**. Lamentations chapter 1: "And they **laughed** at her Sabbaths." And in Ecclesiastes chapter 2: "I considered **laughter** an error." And in the same book, chapter 10: "In **laughter** they make bread." And in Judges chapter 16: "That Samson might be called and **play** before them."

**שָׁחַר** <term>Shachar: It was blackening, darkened, or obscured.</term> Job chapter 30: "My skin has **blackened** upon me." From this comes the noun in Leviticus chapter 13: "And **black** hair." And in the first chapter of the Song of Songs: "**Black** am I but beautiful." And sometimes the last syllable is doubled <note>The Hebrew form "Shacharchoreth."</note>, as in the same book: "Do not gaze upon me because I am **dark-skinned**." From this word, craftsmen name **vitriol** <note>A metallic sulfate used in making black ink and dyes.</note>. Another meaning is **dawn, the morning star, the goddess of morning, or early morning**. Genesis chapter 32: "Behold, a man wrestled with him until **morning**." And further down: "For the **dawn** has now risen." From this, **youth** or **childhood** is named, because just as the dawn is for all living things at their rising, so is old age at their setting. Ecclesiastes chapter 11: "For **youth** and pleasure..."

The author notably links the biblical "boil" to the syphilis epidemic of his own time (starting in 1497).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Hebrew lexicon under the letter Shin. It concludes the entry for Shachar (seeking/dawn) from the previous page and proceeds through the roots Shachat (destroy), Shatah (turn aside), Shatach (spread), Shatam (hate), and Shatan (oppose/Satan).</meta>

# BOOK [II]

...are vanity. Regarding "childhood and youth," <note>Referring to Ecclesiastes 11:10, discussing the fleeting nature of life.</note> look for another meaning: to investigate or inquire. Proverbs chapter 11: "He who seeks good things rises early." <note>original: "Bene consurgit diluculo qui quęrit bona"</note> The Hebrew version says: "He who seeks good seeks what is desirable." Likewise in Job chapter 7: "And if you seek me in the morning, I shall not remain." <note>original: "non subsistam"</note>

**שׁחת** <term>Shachat: To corrupt, rot, scatter, subvert, or destroy.</term> Genesis chapter 6: "The earth was **corrupted** before God." And again: "When God saw that the earth was corrupted, for all flesh had **corrupted** its way." Also Genesis 18: "I will not blot out," that is, I will not destroy or subvert. And in chapter 19 of the same book: "For the Lord will **destroy** this city." And above: "For we will **destroy** this place." It also signifies an instrument for breaking or tearing down a building. Ezekiel chapter 9: "And each man has a **weapon of slaughter** <note>original: "uas interfectionis"</note> in his hand," used here to mean each has a tool of destruction, etc. Another meaning is a "pit." Psalm 94: "Until a **pit** be dug for the sinner." But this was noted above in the section ending before the letter *Vav*. Another meaning is a "snare." Lamentations chapter 4: "He was captured in our sins," used in place of "our **snares**."

**שטה** <term>Shatah: To turn away or turn aside.</term> Numbers chapter 5: "A man whose wife has **gone astray**," meaning she has turned aside. And further: "Departed from her husband's bed." This is a rhetorical interpretation rather than a strictly grammatical one, as is the author's usual custom. So in Proverbs chapter 7: "Let not your mind be **drawn away** in your ways." Word for word it reads: "Let not your heart **turn aside** to her ways." From this root, they believe the word for "foolish" <note>original: "stultum"</note> is derived.

**שטח** <term>Shatach: To extend, expand, or scatter.</term> Jeremiah chapter 8: "And they shall **spread** them out to the sun and the moon." And Numbers chapter 11: "And they **dried** them round about the camp." Regarding this, Nicholas of Lyra <note>A 14th-century Franciscan scholar whose literal commentaries on the Bible were highly influential for later translators.</note> says more correctly: "and they **spread** them out." In the Hebrew it is also read this way: "And they spread out for themselves a spreading around the camp." Likewise in Psalm 88: "I have **stretched out** my hands to you."

**שטם** <term>Shatam: To hate or hold in hatred.</term> Genesis chapter 27: "But Esau **hated** Jacob." Also in chapter 49 of the same book: "And those having arrows envied him," which stands for "**hated** him."

**שטן** <term>Shatan: To impede, oppose, pull back, or disparage.</term> Zechariah chapter 3: "And **Satan** stood at his right hand to **oppose** him." From this comes "detractor" in Latin, "diabolus" <note>the devil</note> in Greek, and "Satan" in Hebrew. Psalm 109: "In return for my love, they **slandered** me." <note>original: "detrahebant mihi," literally "they were pulling me down" or detracting.</note>

<meta>This page continues the Hebrew lexicon, moving from the root "Shatah" (to turn aside) to "Rachatz" (to wash), "Shoter" (official), "Shay" (gift), "Siach" (meditation or shrub), and "Shiloh" (Messiah).</meta>

# BOOK TWO

**רחץ** <term>Rachatz: To wash.</term> Leviticus chapter 15. Used of someone who has not washed their hands beforehand. In the Hebrew text: "He did not wash his hands with water." Also in 1 Kings chapter 22: <note>original: "tertio Regum uicesimosecundo." The Vulgate counts 1 and 2 Samuel as 1 and 2 Kings, making our 1 Kings their 3 Kings.</note> "And they washed his chariot in the pool of Samaria." From this also comes the word for "overflow," indicated by six points <note>likely referring to specific Hebrew vowel points or grammatical markings</note> in Nahum chapter 1: "And in a passing flood."

**שוטר** <term>Shoter: An attendant, herald, executor, officer, or messenger.</term> Deuteronomy chapter 16: "You shall appoint judges and masters in all your gates." For which a more accurate reading is: "Judges and messengers," or "lictors" <note>An ancient Roman term for officers who carried rods (fasces) to clear the way for magistrates</note> who carry rods or staffs.

**שי** <term>Shay: A tribute or gift.</term> Psalm 68: "Kings shall offer gifts to you."

**שיח** <term>Siach: An occupation or business.</term> 1 Kings chapter 18: <note>original: "tertio Regum decimooctauo"</note> "Perhaps he is speaking or is in an inn." <note>A reference to Elijah's taunts against the prophets of Baal.</note> This replaces "either he is meditating or he is doing business."

**שיח** <term>Siach: A shrub, thicket, or bush.</term> Genesis chapter 2: "And every shrub of the field." Also in Genesis chapter 21: "She cast the boy under a tree." <note>Referring to Hagar placing her son Ishmael under a bush to shield him from the sun.</note>

**שילה** <term>Shiloh: The Messiah.</term> This is how the word is interpreted. <note>Refers to the messianic prophecy in Genesis 49:10 regarding the scepter of Judah.</note>

<summary>This page defines Hebrew roots related to purification (washing), civic authority (officers and messengers), and various meanings of 'Siach,' ending with the messianic title 'Shiloh.'</summary>
