<meta>This page continues the Hebrew lexicon, transitioning from the entry for "Shiloh" (the Messiah) to the root "Shachav" (to lie down), "Sakah" (to imagine), "Shachach" (to forget), "Shakal" (to be bereaved), and "Sakal" (to act prudently).</meta>

**BOOK TWO**

**שכב** <term>Shachav: To lie down, to cohabit, or to sleep.</term> Genesis 47: "But I will sleep with my fathers." And in Ecclesiastes 4: "If two sleep together, they shall warm each other," meaning they have cohabited. And in the second chapter of the same book: "Neither does his mind rest at night." From this comes the word for a bed or couch where one lies. Psalm 4: "Be sorry upon your beds." And in Song of Solomon 3: "In my bed by night I sought him." It is also used metaphorically for "to level" or "to make equal," specifically when one makes something lie down in comparison to another. Thus in 2 Samuel 8 <note>original: "secundo Regum octauo." In the Vulgate, the books of Samuel and Kings are numbered 1–4 Kings.</note>: "Leveling them with the ground." Also in Exodus 16: "In the morning, the dew lay all around the camp." All its derivatives signify lying down or descending; hence a small pitcher <note>original: "urceolus"</note> is so named because water descends from it to wash the hands.

**שׂכה** <term>Sakah: To imagine, to fashion, to mark with a sign, or to entitle.</term> Leviticus 26: "Neither shall you set up a marked stone in your land." And in the plural in Numbers 33: "Break their titles," meaning to overthrow the carved signs and displays fashioned in stone. From the idea of "imagination," the human heart is named this way, as it fashions, thinks, and imagines. Job 38: "Who has given understanding to the heart?" <note>Referring to the Hebrew word *sekhvi*.</note> In another sense, it is the name for a rooster; the Hebrew masters call it such, according to the testimony of Rabbi Simeon, son of Lakisch.

**שכח** <term>Shachach: To forget.</term> Psalm 77: "Will God forget to show mercy?" And in Isaiah 49: "Can a woman forget her infant, etc.? Even if she should forget, I will not forget you."

**שכל** <term>Shakal: To be bereaved, to be without children, or to be sterile.</term> Genesis 42: "But I shall be as one bereaved and without children." And in chapter 43 of the same book: "You have made me childless." And Genesis 31: "Your sheep and your goats have not been sterile." Another meaning, when the letter Aleph is placed before it <note>forming the word *eshkol*</note>, is a cluster of grapes. Micah 7: "There is no cluster to eat." And in the plural in Song of Solomon 7: "Your breasts are like clusters."

**שׂכל** <term>Sakal: To be diligent, to act prudently, or to understand.</term> 1 Samuel 18 <note>original: "i. Regum xviij."</note>: "He behaved more prudently than all the men of Saul." From this comes a weighty command. Psalm 2: "And now, O kings, understand," that is, become prudent. And again in 1 Samuel 18: "And so Saul saw that he was exceedingly prudent." And a little earlier: "In all his ways David acted prudently." Some explain this as "he prospered," because one who is prudent and foresighted acts successfully. From this comes the name by six... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence at the bottom of the page.</note>

<meta>This page continues the Hebrew lexicon, specifically concluding the discussion on the root "Sakal" (to understand) before moving through the roots "Shacham" (to rise early/shoulder), "Shachan" (to dwell), "Sakkin" (knife), and "Shakar" (to be drunk or to hire for wages).</meta>

->**BOOK TWO**<-

...by points and sometimes by fives, as in Psalm 111 <note>Psalm 111:10; in the Vulgate, this is Psalm 110.</note>: "A good **understanding** to all who do them." And "one who understands" in Psalm 41: "Blessed is he who **understands**."

**שכם** <term>Shacham: To rise early in the morning.</term> In 2 Samuel 15 <note>original: "secundo Regum decimoquinto." The Vulgate titles the books of Samuel and Kings as 1–4 Kings.</note>: "Absalom, **rising early** in the morning, stood at the entrance of the gate." And that "morning" which is included in the meaning of the verb is sometimes also expressly connected to it, as in 1 Samuel 1: "And they **rose early in the morning** and worshipped before the Lord." Another meaning is the **shoulder** or shoulder blade. Genesis 9: "They laid a cloak upon their **shoulders**." And in chapter 24 of the same book: "With the pitcher she carried on her **shoulder**." Another is the proper name of the place, **Shechem**. Genesis 12: "As far as the place of **Shechem**." Another meaning is a **part**, **portion**, or **side**. Genesis 48: "I give to you one **portion** above your brothers."

**שכן** <term>Shachan: To stay or dwell.</term> Exodus 25: "And I will **dwell** in the midst of them." And in Psalm 15, for that which we read as "Or who shall **rest** in your holy mountain?", the Hebrew truth <note>original: "hebraica ueritas." A common Renaissance term for the original Hebrew text of the Bible as opposed to translations.</note> has it thus: "And who shall **dwell** in your holy mountain?" Jerome interprets it this way as well. And in Leviticus 16: "In the midst of the uncleanness of their **dwelling**." From this comes the **tabernacle** in which one dwells. Psalm 74 <note>original: "psalmo lxxiij."</note>: "The **tabernacle** of your name." From this also comes **neighbor**, one who dwells nearby. Proverbs 27: "Better is a **neighbor** who is near." Another meaning is **to bury**. Nahum 3: "Your princes shall be **buried**." And in Psalm 7: "And let him bring down my glory into the dust," in place of "**let him bury**."

**שכין** <term>Sakkin: A knife.</term> Proverbs 23: "And set a **knife** to your throat."

**שכר** <term>Shakar: To be intoxicated.</term> Isaiah 29: "Be **drunk**, but not with wine." And Genesis 9: "Drinking the wine, he was **drunk**." From this is named every drink that can intoxicate, **strong drink** <note>original: "sicera," from the Hebrew *shekhar*.</note>. Leviticus 10 <note>original: "Leuitici.ix."</note>: "**Wine and everything that can intoxicate** you shall not drink." Deuteronomy 29: "Wine and **strong drink** you have not drunk." Another meaning, formed with the prefix *aleph*, is a **tribute** or **gift**. Psalm 72: "The kings of Sheba and the Arabs shall bring **gifts**."

**שכר** <term>Shakar: To hire for wages.</term> Deuteronomy 23: "Because they **hired** against you Balaam the son of Beor." From this comes **wages**, **hireling**, and **stipendiary**. Genesis 15: "I am your exceeding great **reward**." Also in Malachi 3: "And those who cheat the **hireling** of his **wages**."

<meta>This page continues the Hebrew lexicon, moving into roots beginning with the letters "Shin-Lamed." It follows the previous page's discussion on "Shachan" (to dwell) and "Sakkin" (knife).</meta>

**BOOK**

**שלל** <term>Shalal: To seize, despoil, or plunder.</term> Ezekiel 29 <note>Ezekiel 29:19</note>: "He will **plunder** with his hands and **seize its spoils**, and it will be wages for his army." And in Habakkuk 2 <note>Habakkuk 2:8</note>: "Because you have **plundered** many nations."

**שלוב** <term>Shaluv: A joint or connection.</term> Exodus 26 <note>Exodus 26:17</note>: "**Joints** shall be made by which one board may be **connected** to another." Elsewhere, the translator rendered this from "braiding" as "plaits" or "joints." 1 Kings 7 <note>1 Kings 7:28–29; original: "iij.Regũ.vij." Following the Vulgate numbering where 1–2 Samuel and 1–2 Kings are 1–4 Kings.</note>: "Between the **joints** and between the small crowns and **plaits**." The Hebrew masters <note>The author refers here to the "magistri," likely the medieval Jewish grammarians like Kimhi or Rashi.</note> say this noun refers to the steps of a ladder.

**שלג** <term>Sheleg: Snow.</term> Jeremiah 18 <note>Jeremiah 18:14</note>: "**Snow** of Lebanon." And in Psalm 51 <note>Psalm 51:7; Vulgate: Psalm 50.</note>: "I shall be made whiter than **snow**." From this root also arises a verb, as if one were permitted to say "to snow" from the word "snow." In Psalm 68 <note>Psalm 68:14; Vulgate: Psalm 67.</note>: "I shall be made white with **snow** in Zalmon."

**שלו** <term>Shalu: To be made happy, to prosper, or to be fortunate.</term> Jeremiah 12 <note>Jeremiah 12:1</note>: "It is well for all who transgress and act iniquitously," meaning all who are **fortunate** or **prosper**. From this comes the noun in Job 21 <note>Job 21:23</note>: "**Rich** and **happy**." Another meaning is rashness, error, or imprudence. 2 Samuel 6 <note>2 Samuel 6:7; original: "secundo Regum.vi."</note>: "And he struck him because of his **rashness**."

**שלו** <term>Selav: A quail.</term> Psalm 105 <note>Psalm 105:40; Vulgate: Psalm 104.</note>: "They asked, and the **quail** came." And in the plural in Numbers 11 <note>Numbers 11:31</note>: "He gave **quails** caught from across the sea."

**שלח** <term>Shalach: To send.</term> Psalm 105 <note>Psalm 105:17; Vulgate: Psalm 104.</note>: "He **sent** a man before them." You will find this verb used extensively in Exodus 3 and 4, and in Ezekiel 2 <note>Ezekiel 2:3, 9</note>: "I **send** you," and later, "Behold, a hand **sent** to me." From this comes the word for a gift or gifts. Micah 1 <note>Micah 1:14</note>: "He will give **messengers** <note>original: "emissarios."</note> over the inheritance of Gath." Others interpret this as "donations" or "dowries." Likewise, in Exodus 18 <note>Exodus 18:2</note>: "He took Zipporah, the wife of Moses, whom he had **sent back**," along with her two sons. The Hebrew reads: "And Jethro, the father-in-law of Moses, took Zipporah, the wife of Moses, after her **dowries** <note>original: "post dotes eius." The author notes a variant where the word for "sending away" is read as "gifts/dowry."</note> and also her two sons." In another sense, Psalm 78 <note>Psalm 78:49; Vulgate: Psalm 77.</note>: "**Sent** through evil angels," meaning a plague. Another meaning is shoots or branches. Isaiah 16 <note>Isaiah 16:8</note>: "Its **shoots** are left." From these is named a planted garden, because the branches are artistically stretched here and there. Song of Songs 4 <note>Song of Songs 4:13</note>: "Your **shoots** are a paradise of pomegranates," meaning your "plantings." And I believe that from the watering of the garden plantings near Jerusalem, the water was named **Siloam** <note>original: "Siloah."</note>, as in Nehemiah 3 <note>Nehemiah 3:15</note>: "And the walls of the pool of **Siloam** into the garden."

The author provides etymological links between the verb "to send" and related concepts like dowries, plant shoots, and the Pool of Siloam.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Hebrew lexicon, specifically focusing on roots beginning with the letters "Shin-Lamed." It picks up from a discussion of the root "Shalach" (to send or cast) and its various applications in biblical prophecy and law.</meta>

->**BOOK SECOND**<-

...the king. and in Isaiah 8 <note>Isaiah 8:6</note>: "This people has **cast away** the waters of Shiloah that flow with silence." Another meaning is **sword**. Job 33 <note>Job 33:18</note>: "That he might not pass into the **sword**." Another meaning, derived by adding the letter *nun* <note>original: "cata paragogen nun literę"; this refers to a linguistic process where a letter is added to the end of a root to form a new word</note>, is **table**. Psalm 23 <note>Psalm 23:5; Vulgate numbering Psalm 22</note>: "You have prepared a **table** in my sight."

**שלט** <term>Shalat: To dominate, exercise power, or preside.</term> Ecclesiastes 8 <note>Ecclesiastes 8:9</note>: "Man **dominates** man to his own harm." In that passage, you will often find "dominion" and "power" derived from this word, including in the feminine form. Ezekiel 16 <note>Ezekiel 16:30</note>: "The work of a harlot and **bold** woman," used there in the sense of a woman who is a "harlot" but also "powerful" and a "mistress." Another meaning is **shield** or **armor**. Song of Solomon 4 <note>Song of Solomon 4:4</note>: "A thousand **shields** hang from it, all the **armor** of the strong." Another meaning is to **strip off**. Joshua 5 <note>Joshua 5:15</note>: "**Take off** the shoes from your feet."

**שלך** <term>Shalach: To throw, cast away, or hurl.</term> Lamentations 2 <note>Lamentations 2:1</note>: "He **cast down** the earth from heaven." And in Genesis 21 <note>Genesis 21:15</note>: "She **cast away** the boy." From this comes a "heavy" verb form <note>Referring to the *Piel* or intensive grammatical stem in Hebrew</note> from which many derivatives with the same meaning arise. Another meaning is a bird which our translation calls a **cormorant** <note>original: "mergulum"</note>. Leviticus 11 <note>Leviticus 11:17</note>: "The **cormorant** and the ibis." It is also the name of a certain gate in the house of the sanctuary <note>The Temple in Jerusalem</note>, which our translation calls the "Gate of the Ascent," though somewhat improperly. 1 Chronicles 26 <note>1 Chronicles 26:16</note>: It is better rendered as the **Gate of Casting Forth** <note>The Shallecheth Gate; the author argues the name comes from the root "to throw," perhaps where refuse was cast out</note>.

**שלם** <term>Shalam: To return, repay, or restore.</term> Exodus 22 <note>Exodus 22:1</note>: "He shall **restore** five oxen for one ox." And in Psalm 35 <note>Psalm 35:12</note>: "They **repaid** me evil for good." And in Micah 7 <note>Micah 7:3</note>: "And the judge is in **repayment**." Also as a noun in Psalm 91 <note>Psalm 91:8; Vulgate 90</note>: "And you shall see the **retribution** of sinners." Another meaning is to **complete**, **perfect**, or **finish**. Genesis 15 <note>Genesis 15:16</note>: "For the iniquities of the Amorites are not yet **complete** up to the present time." Another meaning is **whole** and **upright**. Genesis 33 <note>Genesis 33:18</note>: "These men are **peaceful**"—it is more correctly rendered as: "They are **whole** and **upright**." Another meaning is to be **well**, **safe**, or **healthy**. Genesis 43 <note>Genesis 43:27</note>: "Is your elderly father **well**?" Another meaning is **peace**. Isaiah 57 <note>Isaiah 57:19</note>: "**Peace, peace** to him who is far and to him who is near." And in Psalm 38 <note>Psalm 38:3; Vulgate 37</note>: "There is no **peace** in my bones." From this comes the "heavy" verb form and from that "to make peace," "to pacify," and so on. Leviticus 3 <note>Leviticus 3:1</note>: "Sacrifice of **peace offerings**." From this we read in Song of Solomon 6 <note>Song of Solomon 6:13; Vulgate 6:12</note>: "Return, return, <margin>Shulammite / the peaceful one / not a name</margin> **Shulammite**," that is, the "pacified one." It is not "Sunammite" as faulty manuscripts have it.

<meta>This page continues the Hebrew lexicon, focusing on roots beginning with the letter "Shin." It follows the previous discussion of "Shalach" (to throw) and "Shalat" (to dominate), continuing alphabetically through the "Shin-Lamed" and "Shin-Mem" sequences.</meta>

->**BOOK**<-

**שמלה** <term>Simlah: A garment or clothing.</term> Exodus 22 <note>Exodus 22:27</note>: "And in the sheep and the **garment**." It involves a transposition of letters <note>original: "metathesis literarum"</note>, for it is found with the same meaning when the letters *Lamed* and *Mem* are swapped <note>forming "Salmah" instead of "Simlah"</note>. Deuteronomy 8 <note>Deuteronomy 8:4</note>: "Your **garment** did not grow old through age." Other instances are marked with an obelisk <note>a symbol used by scholars to indicate a noteworthy or questionable passage</note>.

**שלף** <term>Shalaph: He drew out, unsheathed, or went out.</term> Judges 9 <note>Judges 9:54</note>: "**Draw** your sword and kill me." And Ruth 4 <note>Ruth 4:7</note>: "A man **drew off** his shoe." The Jerusalem Targum <note>an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary</note> explains this as "to prepare" or "to expedite."

**שלש** <term>Shalash: Three.</term> Exodus 23 <note>Exodus 23:14</note>: "**Three** times each year you shall celebrate festivals for me." Many derivatives come from this word, including both cardinal and ordinal numbers. See below in the section on the art of grammar regarding numerical nouns.

**שם** <term>Shem: A name.</term> Genesis 2 <note>Genesis 2:11</note>: "The **name** of the first is Pishon." It has another meaning: **there**, **thither**, or **where**. Ecclesiastes 1 <note>Ecclesiastes 1:7</note>: "And to its place it returns **there**." Under these same letters, the **heavens** or **heaven** is also signified by another noun <note>referring to "Shamayim"</note>. Genesis 1 <note>Genesis 1:1</note>: "In the beginning God created the **heaven** and the earth." It is not found in the singular number.

**שמם** <term>Shamam: He destroyed, devastated, desolated, or abandoned.</term> Lamentations 5 <note>Lamentations 5:18</note>: "Because of Mount Zion, because it is **destroyed**." And in the same book, chapter 1 <note>Lamentations 1:16</note>: "My children are **lost** <note>or 'desolate'</note>." And further in chapter 3 <note>Lamentations 3:11</note>: "He has made me **desolate**." Often one *Mem* is dropped. Jeremiah 2 <note>Jeremiah 2:12</note>: "Be **appalled**, O heavens, at this," used in the sense of "be desolated" or "perish." And again with the *Mem* doubled, Ezekiel 12 <note>Ezekiel 12:19</note>: "The land shall be **desolate**." From this comes the noun in Joel 3 <note>Joel 3:19</note>: "Egypt shall be a **desolation**." And in the plural, Daniel 9 <note>Daniel 9:26</note>: "And after the end of the war, **desolations** are decreed." Sometimes a *Mem* is added at the beginning <note>original: "per mem cata prothesin," a Greek term for a prefix</note>. When you find this same word with this meaning, you will see it marked with a *dagesh* <note>a grammatical dot</note> in the "belly" of the *Mem* to indicate the absence of the other *Mem*.

**שממית** <term>Semamit: A lizard or gecko.</term> Proverbs 30 <note>Proverbs 30:28</note>: "The **lizard** grasps with its hands." Rabbi Jonah <note>Abu al-Walid Marwan ibn Janah, a medieval Hebrew grammarian</note> thinks it is a **swallow** that nests in the houses of kings; our Hebrew scholars call it a **spider**, and this is how it is used in the speech of the masters <note>referring to the Talmudic and Rabbinic tradition</note>.

**שמד** <term>Shamad: He scattered, deleted, ground down, or crushed.</term> Ezekiel 32 <note>Ezekiel 32:12</note>: "And they shall **scatter**..."

<meta>This page continues the Hebrew lexicon, moving through the roots beginning with the letter "Shin." It transitions from the end of the entry for "Shamad" (to destroy) into "Samach" (to rejoice) and "Shamat" (to release or turn aside), concluding with "Semol" (the left side). The author continues to compare the "Hebrew truth" of the original text against the Latin Vulgate translation.</meta>

->**SECOND PART**<-

...his multitude will be destroyed. Proverbs 14 <note>Proverbs 14:11</note>: "The house of the wicked shall be destroyed." And Isaiah 48 <note>Isaiah 48:19</note>: "His name would not have been cut off <note>original: "attritum"</note> from my face." From this comes the grave word of Ezekiel 14 <note>Ezekiel 14:8</note>: "And I will destroy him from the midst of my people Israel."

**שָׂמַח** <term>Samach: He rejoiced or was glad.</term> Psalm 105 <note>Psalm 105:38</note>: "Egypt was **glad** at their departure." And Proverbs 11 <note>This is actually Ecclesiastes 11:9</note>: "**Rejoice**, young man, in your youth." From this comes the noun in Isaiah 55 <note>Isaiah 55:12</note>: "In **joy** you shall go out."

**שָׁמַט** <term>Shamat: He released, let drop, or turned aside.</term> 2 Samuel 6 <note>original: "ij Regum vi"</note>: "The oxen kicked and **turned it [the ark] aside**." In Hebrew it is thus: "Because the oxen turned aside or released it." And Psalm 141 <note>Psalm 141:6</note>: "Their judges were swallowed up joined to the rock." I do not know what this translation is babbling <note>original: "blacterat"</note>, but the Hebrew truth <note>original: "hebraica ueritas," a term used by scholars to argue for the authority of the Hebrew original over the Latin translation</note> holds it thus: "Because their judges **turned aside** on account of the rock." Certain Hebrew masters understand this to refer to Moses and Aaron, the judges of the children of Israel, who "turned aside" from faith because of the rock <note>a reference to the incident at Meribah</note>. Blessed Augustine, however, understanding this verse to refer to Aristotle—moved by I know not what dream—writes that he [Aristotle] trembles in the underworld. But you, remember the words of God in Exodus 33 <note>Exodus 33:19</note>:

**וְחַנֹּתִי אֶת אֲשֶׁר אָחֹן וְרִחַמְתִּי אֶת אֲשֶׁר אֲרַחֵם**
<note>original Hebrew: "And I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and will show mercy on whom I will show mercy."</note>

The word-for-word translation is: "I will show mercy to whom I will show mercy, and I will forgive whom I will forgive." According to our translation <note>the Latin Vulgate</note>: "And I will show mercy to whom I will, and I will be merciful to whom it shall please me." From this word is derived "remission" or "release." Deuteronomy 15 <note>Deuteronomy 15:1</note>: "In the seventh year you shall make a **remission**."

**שְׂמִיכָה** <term>Semichah: A covering or rug.</term> Our translation renders it as a **cloak**. Judges 4 <note>Judges 4:18</note>: "And he was covered by her with a **cloak**."

**שְׂמֹאל** <term>Semol: The left side or the left hand.</term> Through an insertion <note>original: "epenthesis"</note> of the letter *Aleph* in place of *Vav*. Job 23 <note>Job 23:9</note>: "If he works on the **left**, I shall not grasp him." Likewise, 2 Samuel 16 <note>2 Samuel 16:6</note>: "On his right and on his **left**." It is also found without the *Aleph*. 2 Samuel 14 <note>2 Samuel 14:19</note>: "My lord king, neither to the right nor to the **left**." And although some printed books have the *Aleph*, the oldest written manuscripts show a lack of the *Aleph*, just as the Masorah <note>the traditional notes on the Hebrew biblical text</note> indicates; and Rabbi David Kimhi <note>a famous 12th-century Jewish grammarian</note> confirms it as the standard in that place. It has another meaning, formed by adding the letter *He* at the end, signifying a **garment** or clothing through a switching of the letters <note>original: "metathefin"</note> *Lamed* and *Mem*, about which we wrote just above.

**שֶׁמֶן** <term>Shemen: Fatness, oil, or ointment.</term> Leviticus 24 <note>Leviticus 24:2</note>: "That they bring to you **oil** from the purest olives." **שָׁמַר** <term>Shamar: He kept, guarded, or observed.</term> Genesis 37 <note>Genesis 37:11</note>: "But his father **considered** <note>original: "confyderabat," in the sense of keeping or guarding in his mind</note> the matter in silence." From this comes a noun in Isaiah 21 <note>Isaiah 21:11</note>: "**Watchman**, what of the night? **Watchman**, what of the night? The **watchman** said." Isaiah 7 <note>Isaiah 7:4</note>: "See that you be silent," that is, **beware**. It has another meaning: **adamant** or **emery** <note>original: "smerillus"</note> with which precious stones and gems are perforated. Zechariah 7 <note>Zechariah 7:12</note>: "And they made their heart as an **adamant** <note>or diamond</note>." It has another meaning: **dregs** <note>the sediment of wine</note>. Jeremiah 48 <note>Jeremiah 48:11</note>: "And he rested on his **dregs**." It has another meaning: **thorn**, that is, a certain kind of thorn. Isaiah 7 <note>Isaiah 7:23</note>: "And they shall be in **thorns** and briers."

...conjunction, but a point <note>likely referring to a grammatical dagesh</note> serves as an article, thus: "Sun and moon stood still" <note>Habakkuk 3:11</note>. Another meaning is a window through which the sun illuminates the house; our translation <note>the Latin Vulgate</note> has "battlement." Isaiah 54 <note>Isaiah 54:12</note>: "And I will make your **battlements** of jasper."

**שן** <term>Shen: A tooth.</term> Exodus 21 <note>Exodus 21:24</note>: "**A tooth** for a tooth." And Song of Songs 4 <note>Song of Songs 4:2</note>: "Your **teeth** are like flocks of shorn sheep." From this, "teeth of elephants" are named; thus, ivory. 1 Kings 10 <note>original: "tertio Regum decimo"</note>: "A great throne of **ivory**." It has another meaning: a reddish and scarlet color, commonly called crimson. Exodus 39 <note>Exodus 39:1</note>: "Purple and **scarlet** twice-dyed," where the final *yod* is redundant. But it takes the plural *im*. Isaiah 1 <note>Isaiah 1:18</note>: "If your sins be as **scarlet**."

**שנהבים** <term>Shenhabbim: Ivory or elephant teeth.</term> 1 Kings 10 <note>1 Kings 10:22</note>.

Deuteronomy 6 <note>Deuteronomy 6:7</note>: "And you shall **tell** <note>or teach/repeat</note> them to your children."

**שנא** <term>Sane: To hate.</term> Genesis 26 <note>Genesis 26:27</note>: "To a man whom you **hated**." And Psalm 43 <note>Psalm 44:7 in modern numbering</note>: "And you have confounded those who **hate** us." From this comes the noun in Psalm 24 <note>Psalm 25:19</note>: "And they have **hated** me with an unjust hatred." Similarly in Proverbs 8 <note>Proverbs 8:13</note>: "The fear of God **hates** evil," for "the hatred of evil."

**שנב** With the preposition <note>or prefix</note> *aleph*: a folding door, a window. Our translation renders it "upper room" <note>original: "cœnaculum"</note>. Judges 5 <note>Judges 5:28</note>: "Looking out through the **window**, the mother wailed and spoke from the **upper room**."

**שנה** <term>Shanah: To change, alter, or repeat.</term> Used absolutely in Malachi 3 <note>Malachi 3:6</note>: "I am the Lord and I **change** not." And an *aleph* is sometimes found in place of a *he*, as in Lamentations 4 <note>Lamentations 4:1</note>: "The finest color is **changed**." And note that *Shin* is written here with a dot on the right. For the previous word <note>likely "Sane" (to hate)</note> is written with a *Sin* dotted on the left. Likewise, it is used transitively in 2 Kings 25 <note>original: "quarto Regum uicesimoquinto"</note>: "And he **changed** his garments." Another meaning is **second** or another. Genesis 1 <note>Genesis 1:8</note>: "The **second** day." Likewise, used adverbially for "a second time." Genesis 22 <note>Genesis 22:15</note>: "And the Lord called to Abraham a **second** time."

...and the angel of the Lord called to Abraham a second time <note>Genesis 22:15; original: "secundo"</note>. Likewise: two, both, or each of two.

"Cut for yourself **two** tables [of stone]." It also takes a plural ending.
Deuteronomy 17 <note>Deuteronomy 17:6</note>: "At the mouth of **two** or three [witnesses]." It also
signifies "twice." Esther 2 <note>Esther 2:14</note>: "And she who entered in the evening departed
in the morning, and from there they were led into the **second** house." A more
accurate word-for-word translation would be: "In the evening she went, and in the morning she returned to the house of the women **twice**."
From this comes "another" or "double." Genesis 43 <note>Genesis 43:12</note>: "And take **double** 
money with you." Another meaning is "year." Numbers 14 <note>Numbers 14:34</note>:
"A day for a **year**, a day for a **year** it shall be." It is perhaps named from the previous [concept of repetition] because
the course of the sun is repeated as before. The final *he* <note>the Hebrew letter ה</note> is changed into a *thau* <note>the Hebrew letter ת</note> even in the
absolute construction, as in Daniel 1 <note>Daniel 1:21</note>: "And Daniel continued even until the

genitive construction <note>known in Hebrew grammar as the "construct state," indicating "year of..."</note>, as in Isaiah 34 <note>Isaiah 34:8</note>: "**The year** of recompenses for the judgment of Zion."
It also declines in both genders. In the masculine: Genesis 29 <note>Genesis 29:20</note>: "Jacob [served]

Sarah." In the feminine, however, in Psalm 90 <note>Psalm 90:15</note>: "According to the **years** in which we have seen
evil." And in the same [Psalm]: "The days of our **years** in them are seventy **years**."
Another meaning is to double, to repeat, or to do a second time. 1 Kings 18 <note>original: "tertio Regum decimooctauo"</note>:
"Do it a **second** time," and when they had done it a **second** time...
word for word it is: "And he said: **Repeat**, and they **repeated**."

in place of a *samech* <note>ס</note>. Look for the rest [of the details elsewhere].

<meta>This page continues the catalog of Hebrew roots beginning with the letter "Shin." The previous page concluded the entry for "Shanah" (year/repetition) and began the root "Shasa" (to split/cleave). This page explores further definitions of "Shasa," moves through "Sha'ah" (to gaze/meditate/dim), and covers "Sha'atah" (stamping), "Sha'atnez" (mixed fabrics), "Sha'al" (fist/fox), and "Sha'an" (to lean).</meta>

# BOOK TWO

...splits the hoof into parts. And in the first chapter of Leviticus <note>Leviticus 1:17</note>: "And he shall split its wings" <note>original: "Confringetque afcellas [axillas] eius"</note>. In Hebrew it is: "And he shall split it in its wings or feathers," which is to say, he splits the feathers at their very tips.

**שסע** <note>Shasa</note> To cut into pieces. 1 Samuel 15 <note>1 Samuel 15:33; the text cites "1 Kings 15" following the older naming convention where 1 & 2 Samuel were 1 & 2 Kings</note>: "And Samuel cut him into pieces."

**שעה** <note>Sha'ah</note> To look upon or to gaze at. Genesis 4 <note>Genesis 4:4-5</note>: "And the Lord looked upon Abel and his gifts, but toward Cain and his gifts He did not look." Another meaning is to turn, to pay attention, or to notice. Isaiah 17 <note>Isaiah 17:7</note>: "In that day a man shall bow down toward his Maker, and shall not bow down to the altars which his hands have made." This is used in place of "a man shall turn himself toward God and not toward the altars." And in Exodus 5 <note>Exodus 5:9</note>: "And let them not listen to lying words," meaning they should not pay attention to words of falsehood. Another meaning is to grow dim, to be covered in darkness, or to be blind. Isaiah 32 <note>Isaiah 32:3</note>: "The eyes of those who see shall not grow dim." Many understand the verse in Isaiah 6 <note>Isaiah 6:10</note> as coming from this word: "And close his eyes, lest perhaps he see with his eyes." Another meaning is to narrate, to describe, or to count. Our translation <note>the Latin Vulgate</note> renders it as "to meditate" in Psalm 119 <note>Psalm 119:117</note>: "And I will meditate on Your justifications always." Through the doubling of the word in the same psalm <note>Psalm 119:24</note>: "And Your law is my meditation." Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century biblical translator</note> translates it as "delight," thus: "I will delight in Your justifications." This is the *hithpaal* form <note>a Hebrew verb pattern often expressing reflexive or intensive action</note>. Another meaning is "hour." Daniel 4 <note>Daniel 4:19</note>: "He began to think silently within himself for about one hour."

**שעטה** <note>Sha'atah</note> A walking, a step, or a treading. Jeremiah 47 <note>Jeremiah 47:3</note>: "From the noise of the procession of years" <note>original: "pompę annorum"</note>. It is more correctly: "From the sound of the treading of the hooves of his horses."

**שעטנז** <note>Sha'atnez</note> A garment of wool and linen. Deuteronomy 22 <note>Deuteronomy 22:11</note>: "In a garment which is woven from wool and linen."

**שעל** <note>Sha'al</note> A handful or a fist. Isaiah 40 <note>Isaiah 40:12</note>: "Who has measured the waters in his fist?" Another meaning is "fox." Psalm 63 <note>Psalm 63:10</note>: "They shall be the portions of foxes." And in the second chapter of the Song of Songs <note>Song of Solomon 2:15</note>: "Catch for us the foxes, the little foxes."

**שען** <note>Sha'an</note> He lay down, he supported, he leaned, or he was propped up. Numbers 21 <note>Numbers 21:15</note>: "And they would lie down in the borders of the Moabites." And Isaiah 50 <note>Isaiah 50:10</note>: "And let him lean upon his God," which is to say, let him rest in God. From this comes the expression in Isaiah 3 <note>Isaiah 3:1</note>: "Every strong and powerful support of bread and every support of water," which means a prop, a sustaining, or a stay.

<meta>This page continues the Hebrew dictionary for the letter "Shin." The previous page concluded the entry for "Sha'an" (to lean) and began "Shasa" (to split). This page introduces the roots "Sa'af" (thought/horror) and the multi-faceted root "Sha'ar," which covers meanings ranging from measurements and gates to hair, fear, and demons.</meta>

# BOOK TWO

**שעף** <note>Sa'af</note> A hidden scheme or a thought. Our translation <note>the Latin Vulgate</note> renders this as "horror." Job 4 <note>Job 4:13</note>: "In the horror of a night vision," which is to say, in secret thought. From this comes the idea of one who is pensive or a deviser of evil. Psalm 119 <note>Psalm 119:113</note>: "I have hated the wicked" <note>original: "Iniquos odio habui"</note>. Jerome <note>the 4th-century biblical scholar</note> translates this as "the tumultuous," while Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the famous 11th-century commentator</note> defines them as "the pensive," whom the Greeks call *kenembatous* <note>original: κενεμβατους; likely referring to "those who walk in vanity" or "empty-minded"</note>, that is, dissemblers.

**שער** <note>Sha'ar - Entry 1</note> A *modius* <note>a Roman grain measure, roughly 2 gallons</note> or a general measure. Genesis 26 <note>Genesis 26:12</note>: "And Isaac sowed in that land and found in that same year a hundredfold," meaning a hundred *modii* or *coros* <note>a larger measure, roughly 60 gallons</note>. Another meaning is "vileness," an evil mind, a malicious spirit, or a depraved thought. Jeremiah 23 <note>Jeremiah 23:14</note>: "And in the prophets of Jerusalem I have seen the likeness of adulterers," though according to Nicholas of Lyra <note>a prominent 14th-century Franciscan exegete</note>, it is more correctly "the vileness of adultery." Another meaning is "gate." 2 Kings 7 <note>2 Kings 7:1, cited as 4 Kings</note>: "By the entrance of the gate." And in the plural in Psalm 87 <note>Psalm 87:2</note>: "The Lord loves the gates of Zion," which also refers to towns. Another meaning is "barley." Exodus 9 <note>Exodus 9:31</note>: "Because the barley was [in the ear]." And in the masculine plural, 2 Kings 7 <note>2 Kings 7:1</note>: "Two measures of barley for one shekel."

**שער** <note>Sha'ar/Sa'ar - Entry 2</note> To fear, to worship, or to revere. Deuteronomy 32 <note>Deuteronomy 32:17</note>: "Whom their fathers did not worship." And Ezekiel 2 <note>likely Ezekiel 27:35</note>: "And their kings shall dread with great horror over you." Another meaning is a "he-goat." Leviticus 4 <note>Leviticus 4:23</note>: "An immaculate he-goat from the goats." Another meaning is "hair" or a "single hair." Song of Songs 6 <note>Song of Songs 6:5</note>: "Your hair is like a flock of goats." Isaiah 7 <note>Isaiah 7:20</note>: "The head and the hair of the feet." And Psalm 68 <note>Psalm 68:21</note>: "The hairy crown." And 2 Kings 1 <note>2 Kings 1:8</note>: "A hairy man," or more accurately, "a man possessing hair." From this comes "hairy," "bristly," or "shaggy." When the last syllable is marked with *hirek* <note>the Hebrew vowel "i"</note>, it appears in Genesis 27 <note>Genesis 27:11</note>: "You know that my brother Esau is a hairy man." 

Another meaning is "demons," "fauns," "satyrs," or "fools." Isaiah 13 <note>Isaiah 13:21</note>: "And the hairy ones <note>original: pilosi</note> shall dance there." As Jerome testifies in his commentaries, this is understood to refer to demons. Rabbi Abraham <note>Ibn Ezra, the 12th-century scholar</note> says they are called "demons" because they cause men’s hair to stand on end <note>original: horripilare</note> through the phantoms they create, and they even appear hairy to those who see them. Regarding these creatures, the most philosophical Kabbalists <note>Jewish mystics</note> have written sincerely in the "Tree of the Ten Numerations" <note>the Sephirot</note>. Furthermore, that exceedingly learned man Rabbi Moses of Gerona <note>Nachmanides, the 13th-century scholar</note> recorded this in his memory of the verse in Leviticus 17 <note>Leviticus 17:7</note>: "And they shall no longer sacrifice their victims to demons," where this very word is used. From this also comes the meaning "portent" or "monster." Jeremiah...

<summary>This page defines the Hebrew roots Sa'af and Sha'ar, detailing their various meanings in the Bible including secret thoughts, physical measurements (like the modius), gates, and barley. It also explores the linguistic connection between "hair," "fear," and "demons," citing both Christian scholars like Jerome and Jewish authorities like Rashi and Nachmanides.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the entries for the Hebrew letter "Shin." The previous page concluded the entry for the root "Sha'ar," which discussed gates, measures, and hair. This page moves into roots beginning with "She-" and "Sha-," specifically focusing on terms for animals, physical features like lips, and social concepts like judgment and humility.</meta>

-># SECOND BOOK<-

Horror and wonders have been performed in the land. <note>original: "v. Stupor et mirabilia facta sunt in terra." quoting Jeremiah 5:30</note>

**שפיפן** <note>Shefifon</note> A serpent or a horned viper. Genesis 49 <note>Genesis 49:17</note>: "A horned viper <note>original: "cerastes"</note> in the path."

**שפה** <note>Shafah</note> He hastened. Numbers 22 <note>Numbers 22:22</note>: "And when he had gone quickly." Another meaning is to lift up or elevate. Isaiah 13 <note>Isaiah 13:2</note>: "Upon a dark mountain lift up a signal," meaning an elevated mountain. Likewise in Isaiah 41 <note>Isaiah 41:18</note>: "I will open rivers on the bare hills," <note>original: "in supinis collibus"</note> referring to high and elevated places. It also signifies to set a pot upon a tripod.

**שפה** <note>Safah</note> A lip. Zephaniah 3 <note>Zephaniah 3:9</note>: "Because then I will restore to the people a chosen lip." It also signifies an extremity, edge, or border. 1 Kings 7 <note>1 Kings 7:23, cited as 3 Kings</note>: "From brim to brim it was round all about." Likewise a bank or a shore. Genesis 41 <note>Genesis 41:3</note>: "On the very bank of the river." It is also used as a metaphor for language, as in Genesis 11 <note>Genesis 11:1</note>: "The whole earth was of one lip" <note>meaning one language</note>.

**שפחה** <note>Shifchah</note> To serve as a handmaid. Psalm 123 <note>Psalm 123:2</note>: "As the eyes of a handmaid are on the hands of her mistress." And in the plural in Joel 2 <note>Joel 2:29</note>: "But also upon my servants and my handmaids." From this comes lineage and family. Leviticus 25 <note>Leviticus 25:10</note>: "Each shall return to his former family." Genesis 4 <note>Genesis 4:18</note>: "From my kindred and from my father’s house." In this way, it also signifies a nation. Zechariah 14 <note>Zechariah 14:17, cited as 15</note>: "From the families of the earth to Jerusalem." Another meaning is to make bald. Isaiah 3 <note>Isaiah 3:17</note>: "The Lord will make bald the crown of the daughters of Zion." This is sometimes written with the letter *Samech* <note>ס</note>.

**שפט** <note>Shafat</note> He judged. 2 Samuel 18 <note>2 Samuel 18:31, cited as 2 Kings</note>: "For the Lord has judged for you today." From this comes judgment. Deuteronomy 27 <note>Deuteronomy 27:19</note>: "Cursed is he who perverts judgment." It also signifies an exemplar, form, figure, rule, manner, or character. Exodus 26 <note>Exodus 26:30</note>: "According to the exemplar shown to you on the mountain." And in 2 Kings 1 <note>2 Kings 1:7, cited as 4 Kings</note>: "Of what figure and habit was the man?"

**שפך** <note>Shafakh</note> He overturned, poured out, or shed. 2 Kings 21 <note>2 Kings 21:16, cited as 4 Kings</note>: "He shed innocent blood." And Genesis 9 <note>Genesis 9:6</note>: "Whosoever shall shed human blood, his blood shall be shed."

**שפל** <note>Shafal</note> He let down or humbled. Psalm 75 <note>Psalm 75:7</note>: "He humbles this one and exalts that one." And Psalm 18 <note>Psalm 18:27</note>: "And you will humble the eyes of the proud." From this comes the noun. 2 Samuel 6 <note>2 Samuel 6:22</note>: "And I will be humble in my own eyes."

<meta>This page continues the Hebrew dictionary for the letter "Shin," following the previous page's discussion of the roots related to service and family. This section focuses on roots starting with שפ (Sh-P) and שק (Sh-Q), covering terms for physical anatomy, animals, abundance, and musical instruments.</meta>

**BOOK**

**שפם** <note>Shafam</note> The upper jaw or the upper lip. Ezekiel 24 <note>Ezekiel 24:17</note>: "Neither shall you cover your face with a cloth." Word for word from the Hebrew, it says: "And you shall not wrap [a cloth] over the upper lip."

**שפן** <note>Shafan</note> A rock badger, a sea urchin, or a hedgehog. Leviticus 11 <note>Leviticus 11:5</note>: "The rock badger <note>original: "choerogylius"</note> that chews the cud." Faulty manuscripts of the Bible often have "cyrogrillus" <note>a medieval error likely confusing a rabbit or a mythical creature</note> here. Also in Psalm 104 <note>Psalm 104:18, cited as 103</note>: "The rocks are a refuge for the hedgehogs."

**שפע** <note>Shefa</note> Abundance, a multitude, or plenty. Deuteronomy 33 <note>Deuteronomy 33:19</note>: "Because they shall suck the abundance of the sea like milk."

**שפק** <note>Shafak</note> It sufficed, or it was enough. 1 Kings 20 <note>1 Kings 20:10, cited as 3 Kings</note>: "If the dust of Samaria shall suffice." This is often found written with the letter <term>Samech <gloss>ס</gloss></term> instead of <term>Shin <gloss>ש</gloss></term>.

**שפר** <note>Shafar</note> Beautiful, handsome, or excellent. Psalm 16 <note>Psalm 16:6</note>: "For my inheritance is excellent to me." Another meaning is a trumpet or a horn. Psalm 47 <note>Psalm 47:5</note>: "The Lord with the sound of the trumpet." And Psalm 98 <note>Psalm 98:6, cited as 97</note>: "With trumpets of drawn metal and the sound of the horn." It is also found to signify a piece of meat when the letter <term>Aleph <gloss>א</gloss></term> is prefixed <note>referring to the word 'Eshpar'</note>.

**שפת** <note>Shafat</note> He placed, set down, or increased. Isaiah 26 <note>Isaiah 26:12</note>: "Lord, you will give peace to us," or according to the <term>Septuagint <gloss>the Greek Old Testament</term></term>, "give peace to us," meaning "increase our peace." Also in Psalm 22 <note>Psalm 22:15</note>: "And you have brought me down into the dust of death," meaning "you have set me down and made me sit there." Saint Jerome, however, translated it as "you have dragged me down," but this does not suit the specific nature of the language, as is proved in Ezekiel 24 <note>Ezekiel 24:3</note>: "Set on the pot, set it on, I say." From this idea of "placing," boundaries are also named. Psalm 68 <note>Psalm 68:13</note>: "If you sleep among the middle of the lots." Jerome translates this as "boundaries," while the Hebrew scholars understand it as limits or marks.

**שצף** <note>Shetsef</note> A moment, sudden, or brief. Isaiah 54 <note>Isaiah 54:8</note>: "In a moment of indignation I hid my face from you." This has the same meaning as the word preceding it in the verse, and in the study of rhetoric this is called a <term>tautology <gloss>original: ταυτολογια, repeating the same idea in different words</term></term>.

**שק** <note>Sak</note> A sack or sackcloth <note>a rough fabric made of hair</note>. 2 Kings 19 <note>2 Kings 19:1, cited as 4 Kings</note>: "And he was covered with sackcloth." And Isaiah 3 <note>Isaiah 3:24</note>: "Instead of a fine robe, a wrapping of sackcloth." And Genesis 42 <note>Genesis 42:27</note>: "And as one of them opened his sack."

**שקק** <note>Shakak</note> He growled or roared. Proverbs 28 <note>Proverbs 28:15</note>: "A roaring lion and a hungry bear." Others explain it as to wander, to pace, or to be a vagabond. Joel 2 <note>Joel 2:9</note>: "They shall enter the city." Others interpret it as to be hungry and empty; others as being fierce and greedy.

It includes scholarly debates on translation, specifically comparing Jerome's Latin Vulgate with the original Hebrew grammar.</summary>
<keywords>Hebrew etymology, rock badger, shofar, sackcloth, Jerome, philology, biblical translation, anatomy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the Hebrew dictionary for the letter "Shin," moving from the previous entry "Shafat" to the roots beginning with "Shaq" (Sh-Q). It explores the double meaning of "watching" and "almonds," as well as roots related to watering and resting.</meta>

**SECOND BOOK**

**שקד** <note>Shaqad</note> To care for or to be vigilant. Psalm 127 <note>Psalm 127:1</note>: "Unless the Lord keeps the city, he who guards it watches in vain." A word-for-word translation from the Hebrew is as follows: <note>original: "In uanum uigilauit custos"</note> "In vain has the guardian been vigilant." Another meaning is an almond tree. Ecclesiastes 12 <note>Ecclesiastes 12:5</note>: "The almond tree shall flourish." And in the plural in Numbers 17 <note>Numbers 17:8</note>: "Those which, with their leaves spread out, were formed into almonds."

**שקד** <note>Shaqad</note> To mark, to puncture, to enjoin, or to ascribe. Our translation <note>referring to the standard Latin Vulgate Bible</note> interprets this root according to the preceding word, "to be vigilant." Lamentations 1 <note>Lamentations 1:14</note>: "The yoke of my iniquities has watched." <note>Historical note: modern scholars often translate this specific instance as "bound" or "knit together" rather than "watched."</note>

**שקה** <note>Shaqah</note> To water or to give a drink. Joel 3 <note>Joel 3:18</note>: "And it shall water the valley of thorns." <note>The Hebrew "Shittim" is here translated from the Latin "spinarum," meaning thorns.</note> And in the same book, chapter 2 <note>Joel 2:24</note>: "And the winepresses shall overflow with wine and oil." And Genesis 24 <note>Genesis 24:19</note>: "For I will also draw water for your camels." And in the same chapter: "And he gave him a drink." From this comes the word for a cupbearer. Genesis 41 <note>Genesis 41:9</note>: "The chief of the cupbearers."

**שקט** <note>Shaqat</note> To rest, to be silent, or to be at leisure. Isaiah 14 <note>Isaiah 14:7</note>: "The whole earth has rested and is silent." And Joshua 11 <note>Joshua 11:23</note>: "And the land rested from wars." Ezekiel 16 <note>Ezekiel 16:42</note>: "And I will rest."

<summary>This page defines Hebrew roots beginning with Sh-Q, notably "Shaqad," which refers both to vigilance and the almond tree, and "Shaqah," the root for watering and the office of a cupbearer.</summary>
<keywords>Shaqad, Shaqah, Shaqat, almond tree, vigilance, cupbearer, tranquility, biblical Hebrew roots</keywords>

--- Page 534 ---
<meta>This page continues the Hebrew dictionary for the letter "Shin." The previous page ended with "Shaqat" (to rest). This page transitions into "Shaqatz" (abomination) and explores roots related to falsehood, anatomy, leadership, and botanical growth.</meta>

# BOOK

[To be] abominable or detestable. Leviticus 11 <note>Leviticus 11:10</note>: "It shall be an abomination to you."

**שקר** <note>Shaqar</note> He lied or denied. Isaiah 63 <note>Isaiah 63:8</note>: "Children who do not lie." From this comes the noun for a lie or falsehood. Proverbs 18 <note>Proverbs 18:8; though the author may be referring to 19:5</note>: "A deceitful witness utters lies." And Exodus 20 <note>Exodus 20:16</note>: "Do not speak false witness against your neighbor." And Psalm 7 <note>Psalm 7:14</note>: "And he brought forth iniquity." And Psalm 120 <note>Psalm 120:2</note>: "O Lord, deliver my soul from wicked lips," that is, from false and lying lips. It also signifies "freely," "in vain," or "to no purpose." 1 Kings 25 <note>1 Samuel 25:21</note>: "Truly in vain have I kept all that this fellow had in the wilderness."

**שקר** <note>Shaqar</note> With hanging letters added <note>original: "literis appensilibus," likely referring to specific scribal marks or vowel points</note>, it signifies gestures, nods, figments, or fabrications. Isaiah 3 <note>Isaiah 3:16</note>: "And they walked with winking eyes."

**שר** <note>Shar</note> The navel. Song of Songs 7 <note>Song of Songs 7:2</note>: "Your navel is like a rounded bowl." And Ezekiel 16 <note>Ezekiel 16:4</note>: "Your navel cord was not cut." Here, the letter *Resh* receives a *dagesh* <term>dagesh: a dot in a Hebrew letter indicating it is doubled or emphasized</term> because of the absence of a second *Resh*. Another form appears in Job 40 <note>Job 40:16</note>: "And his power is in the navel <note>often translated as "sinews" or "muscles" in this context</note> of his belly." Another meaning is one who is depraved, a plotter of evil, or an injurer. Deuteronomy 29 <note>Deuteronomy 29:19</note>: "And I shall walk in the stubbornness <note>or wickedness</note> of my heart." And Jeremiah 3 <note>Jeremiah 3:17</note>: "Following after the stubbornness of their own evil heart."

**שרר** <note>Sharar</note> To rule, to preside over, or to lead. Numbers 16 <note>Numbers 16:13</note>: "Unless you also make yourself a prince over us." From this comes the word for prince, master, or prefect. 4 Kings 1 <note>2 Kings 1:9</note>: "And he sent a captain of fifty." And Genesis 41 <note>Genesis 41:9</note>: "The chief of the cupbearers." Also "chief of the bakers" and "captain of the guard." This occurs through an <term>apocope: the loss of a sound or letter at the end of a word</term> of the final letter *Resh*. From this root comes the name **Sarah**, because she is a "lady" or "mistress."

**שרב** <note>Sharav</note> Arid, dry, desert, or heat. Isaiah 49 <note>Isaiah 49:10</note>: "Neither the heat nor the sun shall strike them." And in chapter 35 of the same book <note>Isaiah 35:7</note>: "And the parched ground shall become a pool."

**שרביט** <note>Sharvit</note> A scepter, staff, or rod. Esther 4 <note>Esther 4:11</note>: "The king extended the golden rod to him."

**שרג** <note>Sharag</note> To be perplexed or entangled. Job 40 <note>Job 40:17</note>: "The sinews of his thighs are knit together." And because vines entwine with shoots, the shoots themselves are named from this root. Genesis 40 <note>Genesis 40:10</note>: "A vine in which there were three branches."

<meta>This page continues the Hebrew dictionary for the letter "Shin," moving into roots beginning with "Shin-Resh." The previous page discussed "Shar" (navel) and depravity. This page focuses on roots involving survival, conflict, physical cutting, and fire.</meta>

### SECOND [SECTION]

**שרד** <note>original Hebrew: *Sharad*</note> He survived. He was a remnant. Joshua 10 <note>original: "Iosue. xij." though likely referring to Joshua 10:20</note>: Those of Israel who were able to flee entered the fortified cities. Word for word, it reads: "And the survivors had remained of them and they came into the fortified cities." And in the same book, chapter 8 <note>Joshua 8:22</note>: So that none of such a great multitude would be saved. Word for word, it reads: "So that there should not remain a survivor or an escapee."

**שרה** <note>original Hebrew: *Sharoh*</note> He satisfied or sated. Jeremiah 15 <note>Jeremiah 15:11</note>: "If your remnants are not for good." Rabbi Joseph Kimhi <note>A famous 12th-century Spanish Hebrew grammarian and teacher</note> explains this as: "If I have not satisfied you with good things." Although it could be derived from the word above which signifies remnants, as we wrote under the section for *Shin* before *Aleph*. Another meaning: a field, a plain, or the countryside. Song of Songs 2 <note>Song of Songs 2:1</note>: "I am the flower of the field." Another meaning: a breastplate. 1 Samuel 17 <note>original: "i. Regũ. xvij."</note>: "He was clothed in a scale breastplate" <note>original: "lorica hamata," referring to armor made of interlocking rings or scales</note>.

**שרה** <note>original Hebrew: *Sarah*</note> He joined hand [in battle]. He struggled or conflicted. Genesis 32 <note>Genesis 32:28</note>: "If you have been strong against God," that is, you have struggled with God. Likewise Hosea 12 <note>Hosea 12:3</note>: "And in his strength he was directed with the angel," used in place of "he struggled."

**שרט** <note>original Hebrew: *Sarat*</note> He lacerated. He cut up, tore, or incised. Zechariah 12 <note>Zechariah 12:3</note>: "They shall lacerate with a cutting." And Leviticus 19 <note>Leviticus 19:28</note>: "You shall not make incisions in your flesh for the dead." Literally "you shall give an incision." For it is written with six points <note>likely a reference to specific Hebrew vowel markings or a grammatical form</note> in that place. And the same book, chapter 21 <note>Leviticus 21:5</note>: "Neither shall they make incisions in their flesh."

**שרו** <note>original Hebrew: *Serok*</note> A strap or thong. Genesis 14 <note>Genesis 14:23</note>: "Even to a shoe-latchet" <note>the strap of a sandal</note>. And Isaiah 5 <note>Isaiah 5:27</note>: "Neither shall the strap of his sandal be broken."

**שרע** <note>original Hebrew: *Shara*</note> A monstrous limb, larger than is right <note>referring to a physical deformity or an unnaturally extended limb</note>. Leviticus 21 <note>Leviticus 21:18</note>: "Whether with a small or a large [deformed] limb."

**שרף** <note>original Hebrew: *Saraph*</note> He ignited. He burned, consumed by fire, or caused to burn. 2 Kings 23 <note>original: "iiij. Regũ. xxiij."</note>: "He also burned the grove." And below: "And he burned them upon the altar." And from "burning" is named the bronze serpent which Moses made in the desert. Numbers 21 <note>Numbers 21:8</note>: "Make a bronze serpent." And a little earlier: "The Lord sent fiery serpents among the people." Likewise, "burning" angels, whom we call *Seraphim* <term>Seraphim: literally "the burning ones," a high order of angels in celestial hierarchy</term>, are signified by this word.

**שרע** <note>original Hebrew: *Sar'aph*</note> Thought and the purpose of the mind. Psalm 139 <note>Psalm 139:23</note>: "And know my thoughts..."

--- Page 536 ---
<meta>This page continues the Hebrew dictionary for the letter "Shin," following the root "Sharat" (to cut). The text concludes a previous entry regarding "thoughts" or "scrutiny" before moving into biological movement, agricultural terms, and domestic actions.</meta>

BOOK <unclear>HEBREW LEXICON</unclear>

...my thoughts. <note>The text begins mid-sentence, likely completing a verse about God searching the heart or mind.</note> Saint Jerome <note>The 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into the Latin Vulgate</note> translates this more correctly: *And with a shield [he protected] my thoughts.*

**שרץ** <note>Hebrew root: *Sharatz*</note> To move, or to set living creatures in motion. Genesis 1 <note>Genesis 1:20–21</note>: *The living and moving soul which the waters had produced,* instead of "which the waters moved." Likewise in the same place: *Let the waters produce creeping things,* instead of "let the waters cause creeping things to move."

**שרק** <note>Hebrew root: *Sharak*</note> He whistled or hissed. Isaiah 5 <note>Isaiah 5:26</note>: *And he will whistle for him from the ends of the earth.* And Lamentations 2 <note>Lamentations 2:15</note>: *They hissed and wagged their heads.* And Isaiah 7 <note>Isaiah 7:18</note>: *The Lord will whistle for the fly.*

**שרק** <note>Hebrew root: *Shoreq*</note> A vine-shoot or tendril. Our translation <note>Referring to the Latin Vulgate</note> renders this as "vineyard" in Jeremiah 2 <note>Jeremiah 2:21</note>: *But I planted you as a choice vineyard.* And Genesis 49 <note>Genesis 49:11</note>: *Binding his foal to the vineyard and his donkey to the vine, O my son,* instead of "binding his foal to the vine and his donkey to the vine-shoot." Another meaning refers to a sorrel or reddish-brown color. Zechariah 1 <note>Zechariah 1:8</note>: *Horses that were red, speckled, and white.*

**שרש** <note>Hebrew root: *Shoresh*</note> A root. Isaiah 53 <note>Isaiah 53:2</note>: *And like a root out of dry ground.* From this comes the verb "to take root." Jeremiah 12 <note>Jeremiah 12:2</note>: *You planted them and they sent out roots,* instead of "they took root." And in Psalm 80 <note>Psalm 80:9</note>: *You planted its roots;* more accurately, "you caused its roots to take root." By contrast, it also signifies to uproot, extirpate, or destroy. Judges 5 <note>Judges 5:14</note>: *From Ephraim he destroyed [uprooted] them.*

**שרשרות** <note>Hebrew root: *Sharsharot*</note> Chains. Exodus 28 <note>Exodus 28:14</note>: *Chains linked together with one another.*

**שרת** <note>Hebrew root: *Sharat*</note> He served or ministered. Numbers 8 <note>Numbers 8:26</note>: *And they shall be ministers to their brothers.* And 1 Samuel 2 <note>1 Kings 2:18 in the older numbering</note>: *But Samuel ministered before the face of the Lord.* When written with the dot on the left side of the letter *Shin* <note>Technically the letter *Sin*, though visually identical in many early manuscripts</note>, it signifies a frying pan.

**שת** <note>Hebrew root: *Shet*</note> The back or rear. Our translation uses the word "buttocks." 2 Samuel 10 <note>2 Samuel 10:4</note>: *Their garments were cut in the middle, even to the buttocks.*

**שתה** <note>Hebrew root: *Shatah*</note> He drank. Exodus 34 <note>Exodus 34:28</note>: *He did not eat bread and did not drink water.* This word often loses its final letter, *He*. For example, in Genesis 9 <note>Genesis 9:21</note>: *And drinking wine he became drunk,* instead of "and he drank wine." From this comes the idea of a symposium, a drinking party, or a banquet. Esther 1 <note>Esther 1:3</note>: *He had made a great feast for his princes.* It has another meaning: the warp <note>The vertical threads in a loom</note>. Leviticus 13 <note>Leviticus 13:48</note>: *In the warp and the woof.*

**שתל** <note>Hebrew root: *Shatal*</note> He planted. Ezekiel 17 <note>Ezekiel 17:23</note>: *And I will plant upon a high mountain—*

->. 534 .<-

## SECOND [BOOK]

...I have [rooted]. *On the high mountain of Israel I will plant it* <note>original Latin: "In monte sublimi Israel plantabo illud"; from Ezekiel 17:23</note>; and it appears in the passive voice in the first Psalm: *Like a tree that is planted.* <note>Psalm 1:3</note> From this root come the words for "planting," "a plant," and "a shoot," etc.

**שתם** <note>Hebrew root: *Shatam*</note> Open. Numbers 24 <note>Numbers 24:3</note>: *The man whose eye was shut has said,* <note>original Latin: "Dixit homo cui obturatus est oculus"</note> which Rabbi David Kimhi <note>A famous 12th-century Hebrew grammarian and philosopher from France/Spain, often called Radak</note> and Rabbi Solomon <note>Known as Rashi, the preeminent 11th-century commentator on the Bible and Talmud</note> explain as "with an open eye."

**שתן** <note>Hebrew root: *Shatan*</note> To urinate. First Kings 25 <note>In modern Bibles, this is 1 Samuel 25:22. The author uses the Vulgate naming convention where 1 & 2 Samuel and 1 & 2 Kings were grouped as the four Books of Kings.</note>: *If I leave anything that belongs to him until the morning, even one who urinates against the wall.* <note>original Latin: "mingentem ad parietem"; a biblical idiom referring to a male.</note>

**שתק** <note>Hebrew root: *Shataq*</note> It grew quiet, subsided, was calmed, was pacified, or was restrained. Jonah 1 <note>Jonah 1:11</note>: *What shall we do to you, that the sea may be calm for us?*

<meta>This page transitions from the end of the letter "Shin" into the start of a new section or "Book" (Liber), beginning with the Hebrew letter "Tav." **BOOK**

**תא** <note>Hebrew root: *Ta*</note> <gloss>Handwritten Hebrew and Latin notes: *ta* that is, a small cell</gloss>
The inner chamber of buildings; a porch or vestibule. Ezekiel 40 <note>Ezekiel 40:7</note>: *And the chamber was one reed long and one reed wide, and between the chambers were five cubits.* <note>original Latin: "Et thalamum uno calamo in longum et uno calamo in latum. et inter thalamos quinq; cubitos"</note>

**תאב** <note>Hebrew root: *Ta'av*</note> He longed for, desired, or craved. Psalm 119 <note>Psalm 119:40</note>: *Behold, I have craved your commandments;* and in the same Psalm <note>Psalm 119:20</note>: *My soul has longed to desire your justifications.* It can also signify the opposite: to detest or abominate. Amos 6 <note>Amos 6:8</note>: *I detest the pride of Jacob.*

**תאה** <note>Hebrew root: *Ta'ah*</note> He circumscribed, led around, or marked the limits. Numbers 34 <note>Numbers 34:7-8</note>: *From the great sea the borders begin, reaching to the highest mountain.* The word-for-word translation is: *From the great sea you shall mark the limit of this mountain for yourselves.* And further down: *From there the borders shall be measured,* <note>original Latin: "metabuntur fines"</note> standing in for "you shall cause the borders to be circumscribed or limited." It has another meaning if the letter *He* [ה] is changed to a *Vav* [ו]: an oryx <note>a large antelope</note>. Deuteronomy 14 <note>Deuteronomy 14:5</note>: *The oryx and the giraffe.* <note>The author uses "camelopardalim," the Latin term for giraffe.</note>

**תאם** <note>Hebrew root: *Ta'am*</note> A twin. Genesis 38 <note>Genesis 38:27</note>: *Twins appeared in the womb.* And Song of Songs 4 <note>Song of Songs 4:5</note>: *Like two twin fawns of a gazelle.* From this comes the verb as used in the same place: *All with twin offspring,* <note>Song of Songs 4:2</note> meaning "all being doubled" or "paired."
Therefore, some who are not sufficiently literate wrongly assert <margin>Thomas in Hebrew and Greek</margin> that the apostle Thomas is called "Didymus" <note>the Greek word for twin</note> because they want to claim he was "unbelieving" [doubting]. For Thomas <margin>Didymos, that is, twin</margin> in Hebrew and *Didymos* in Greek is the same as *geminus* [twin] in Latin. However, an error arises among the Germans because we use the same Germanic word for "unbelieving" [doubter] and "twin"—*zuifling*. <note>The author is noting a linguistic confusion in German between *Zweifel* (doubt) and *Zwilling* (twin).</note>

**תאן** <note>Hebrew root: *Ta'an*</note> A fig tree. Jeremiah 8 <note>Jeremiah 8:13</note>: *And there are no figs on the fig tree.* And Joel 1 <note>Joel 1:7</note>: *And he has stripped my fig tree.*

**תאר** <note>Hebrew root: *Ta'ar*</note> Species, form, figure, or quality. Isaiah 53 <note>The text says 54, but refers to Isaiah 53:2</note>: *He has no form nor beauty.* And Genesis 39 <note>Genesis 39:6</note>: *Joseph was of a beautiful face,* meaning "beautiful in appearance."

**תבה** <note>Hebrew root: *Tevah*</note> An ark. Genesis 8 <note>Genesis 8:16</note>: *Go out from the ark.* And Genesis 6 <note>Genesis 6:14</note>: *Make yourself an ark of planed wood.*

**תבל** <note>Hebrew root: *Tevel*</note> The world or globe. Job 34 <note>Job 34:13</note>: *Or who set him over the world which he fashi[oned]...*

**SECOND**

[...was born as a twin]. And in Psalm 98 <note>Psalm 98:9</note>: *He shall judge the world in righteousness.* <note>original Latin: "Iudicabit orbem in iusticia"</note>

**תבן** <note>Hebrew root: *Teven*</note> Chaff or straw. Genesis 24 <note>Genesis 24:25</note>: *There is plenty of both straw and hay with us.*

**תהו** <note>Hebrew root: *Tohu*</note> In this word, a *Vav* [ו] is used in place of a final *He* [ה]. It signifies a void, chaos, or a raw and unorganized mass. Genesis 1 <note>Genesis 1:2</note>: *The earth was void and empty.* <note>original Latin: "Terra autem erat inanis et uacua"</note>

**תהום** <note>Hebrew root: *Tehom*</note> Abyss or the deep. Genesis 1 <note>Genesis 1:2</note>: *And darkness was over the face of the abyss.* Ezekiel 31 <note>Ezekiel 31:4</note>: *The abyss exalted him;* and Psalm 42 <note>Psalm 42:7</note>: *Deep calls unto deep.* It is declined as a feminine noun.

**תו** <note>Hebrew root: *Tav*</note> He marked or signed. Ezekiel 9 <note>Ezekiel 9:4</note>: *Mark a 'tau'* <note>the letter T, which in ancient script was shaped like a cross</note> *upon the foreheads of the men.*

**תוך** <note>Hebrew root: *Tavekh*</note> Between or in the middle. Exodus 14 <note>Exodus 14:29</note>: *But the children of Israel proceeded through the middle of the dry sea.* Exodus 3 <note>Exodus 3:4</note>: *He called him out of the middle of the bush;* and Psalm 22 <note>Psalm 22:14</note>: *In the middle of my belly.* From this root comes: to halve, to divide, to split, or to pass through. Exodus 26 <note>Exodus 26:28</note>: *Which shall be sent through the middle of the boards,* meaning that which passes through or is innermost. It has another meaning: usury, fraud, or iniquity. Psalm 72 <note>Psalm 72:14</note>: *He shall redeem their souls from usury and iniquity.* From this also comes "peacock." 1 Kings 10 <note>1 Kings 10:22</note>: *Apes and peacocks.*

**תור** <note>Hebrew root: *Tur*</note> He explored, thought, investigated, or contemplated. Ecclesiastes 2 <note>Ecclesiastes 2:3</note>: *I thought in my heart to withdraw from wine.* It has another meaning: turtle-dove. Leviticus 5 <note>Leviticus 5:7</note>: *He shall offer two turtle-doves.* It has another meaning: a determined time. Esther 2 <note>Esther 2:12</note>: *But when the time for each girl had come in order.* It has another meaning by adding a final *He* <note>term: cata paragoge he; a grammatical addition of the letter He</note>: law or institution. Psalm 19 <note>Psalm 19:7</note>: *The law of the Lord is immaculate.* It has another meaning: order and features. Song of Songs 1 <note>Song of Songs 1:10</note>: *Your cheeks are beautiful like a turtle-dove's;* though it is more correctly rendered: *Your cheeks in the order of their features.*

**תזז** <note>Hebrew root: *Tazaz*</note> He cut off. Isaiah 18 <note>Isaiah 18:5</note>: *And those things which are left shall be cut off.*

**תתח** <note>Hebrew root: *Totakh*</note> A general name for missiles and javelins, which others translate as "razor." Our translation <note>referring to the Latin Vulgate</note> interprets it as "hammer." Job 41 <note>Job 41:29</note>: *He shall esteem a hammer as straw.* Rabbi David Kimhi <note>a renowned 12th-13th century Hebrew grammarian and commentator</note> says that it generally signifies missiles of every kind.

**BOOK**

**תחרא** <note>Hebrew root: *Tachara*</note> A woven collar or neckband. Exodus 28 <note>Exodus 28:32</note>: *As is usually done at the edges of garments so they do not easily tear,* where this word is used to describe the binding.

**תחרה** <note>Hebrew root: *Tachrah*</note> He emulated, was zealous, or envied. Psalm 36 <note>Psalm 37:7 in modern Bibles</note>: *Do not emulate him who prospers in his way.* <note>original Latin: "Noli emulari in eo qui prosperatur in uia sua"</note> Some believe this is derived from the word *charah* [חרה], which was discussed above under the letter *Cheth* [ח] before *Resh* [ר].

**תחש** <note>Hebrew root: *Tachash*</note> The name of an animal that is called a badger <note>original Latin: "taxus"</note>. The ancient translators Aquila and Symmachus translated it as "violet-colored," while Theodotion and Jerome rendered it as "hyacinth-blue." Ezekiel 16 <note>Ezekiel 16:10</note>: *And I shod you with hyacinth-blue leather;* and in the plural in Exodus 25 <note>Exodus 25:5</note>: *And hyacinth-colored skins,* standing for the skins of badgers. <note>The author includes the word "thaśont," likely a variation of the German word "Dachs," meaning badger.</note>

**תחת** <note>Hebrew root: *Tachat*</note> For, below, under, or beneath. Exodus 21 <note>Exodus 21:24</note>: *An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth.* Although it is a preposition, it can take all the suffixes usually attached to nouns and verbs. In the first person, it inserts the letter *nun* [נ] to prevent a gap between vowels <note>a grammatical feature called the "nun epenthetic"</note>, as in Psalm 18 <note>Psalm 18:36</note>: *You have broadened my steps beneath me,* and so with others. From this comes the word for lower or lowest. Psalm 86 <note>Psalm 86:13</note>: *And you have rescued my soul from the lower hell.* <margin>**תחתיה** <note>Hebrew: *Tachtiyyah* (lower)</note></margin> And Psalm 63 <note>Psalm 63:9</note>: *They shall enter the lower parts of the earth.* Similarly, in Ezekiel 41 <note>Ezekiel 41:7</note>: *From the lower parts one ascended to the upper and middle parts.*

**תיש** <note>Hebrew root: *Tayish*</note> A wild ram or male goat. Proverbs 30 <note>Proverbs 30:31</note>: *A rooster with girded loins, and a ram.*

**תכר** <note>Hebrew root: *Tekhar*</note> Interest or usury. Proverbs 29 <note>Proverbs 29:13</note>: *The poor man and the creditor have met each other;* more accurately: *The poor man and the man of usury.* We have written about this word above under the entry for *Tav* [ת] before *Vav* [ו].

**תכו** <note>Hebrew root: *Tukku*</note> He adhered, attacked, or approached. Deuteronomy 33 <note>Deuteronomy 33:3</note>: *And those who approach his feet.*

**תכלת** <note>Hebrew root: *Tekhelet*</note> The color hyacinth <note>likely a blue or violet dye derived from a Mediterranean snail</note>. Exodus 28 <note>Exodus 28:37</note>: *And you shall bind it with a hyacinth-colored ribbon.*

**תכן** <note>Hebrew root: *Takhan*</note> He effected, made, fashioned, or prepared. Our translation renders it as "confirm..."

<meta>This page continues the Hebrew dictionary for the letter Tav [ת]. The previous page ended with a discussion on the root for "below" or "under." This page begins with the conclusion of a previous entry (likely *Kun* or a related root) before moving into alphabetical order.</meta>

->**BOOK TWO**<-

...established. In Psalm 75 <note>Psalm 75:3</note>: *I have established its pillars.* <note>original Latin: "Ego cōfirmaui columnas eius"</note> And as if hesitating, the wording always varies. In Isaiah 40 <note>Isaiah 40:12</note>: *And he weighed the heavens with a span;* earlier it said "established," and now it says "weighed." Likewise in the same chapter <note>Isaiah 40:13</note>: *Who helped the spirit of the Lord?* Behold, here it says "helped." Also in Proverbs 16 <note>Proverbs 16:2</note>: *The Lord is the weigher of spirits,* in place of "the Lord made the winds." But it is more correctly found in Psalm 65 <note>Psalm 65:9</note>: *You have prepared their food, for such is his preparation.*

**תלל** <note>Hebrew root: *Talal*</note> He heaped up, accumulated, or piled up. Jeremiah 49 <note>Jeremiah 49:2</note>: *And it shall be scattered into a mound.* Deuteronomy 13 <note>Deuteronomy 13:16</note>: *And it shall be an everlasting mound.* And Ezekiel 3 <note>Ezekiel 3:15, referring to the place Tel-Abib</note>: *To the mound of new fruits.* In this root, the letter *Tav* receives a *dagesh* <note>a dot in the letter indicating it is "hardened" or doubled</note> because of the shortening <note>apocope</note> of the letter *Lamed*, and the letter is doubled, as in Song of Songs 4 <note>Song of Songs 5:11</note>: *His hair is like the branches of palms.*

**תלה** <note>Hebrew root: *Talah*</note> He hung or suspended. Genesis 40 <note>Genesis 40:19</note>: *And he will hang you on a cross* <note>original Latin: "cruce," though the Hebrew refers more generally to a stake or gallows</note>. Deuteronomy 21 <note>Deuteronomy 21:23</note>: *He who hangs on a tree is cursed by God.* Word for word, it reads: *The curse of God is the suspended one,* where "is" is understood. Sometimes it receives the letter *Aleph* [א] through an insertion <note>epenthesis</note>.

**תלם** <note>Hebrew root: *Telem*</note> A furrow. Job 31 <note>Job 31:38</note>: *And its furrows weep with it.* And Psalm 65 <note>Psalm 65:10</note>: *Drench its channels;* more correctly, "its furrows."

**תלע** <note>Hebrew root: *Tola*</note> A worm. Job 25 <note>Job 25:6</note>: *And the son of man a worm.* And Isaiah 14 <note>Isaiah 14:11</note>: *And worms shall be your covering.* And in the plural תּוֹלָעִים <note>Hebrew: *Tola'im*</note> in Exodus 16 <note>Exodus 16:20</note>: *And it began to swarm with worms.* It has another meaning: scarlet. Exodus 26 <note>Exodus 26:1</note>: *With purple and scarlet twice-dyed.* From this comes the verb "to be dressed in purple" or "to be dressed in scarlet," that is, clothed in scarlet garments. Nahum 2 <note>Nahum 2:3</note>: *The men of the army in scarlet.*

**תמם** <note>Hebrew root: *Tamam*</note> It fell, it was consumed, it was overthrown, or it failed. Genesis 47 <note>Genesis 47:15</note>: *When money failed the buyers,* and in the same: *as money failed, the cattle also failed,* but the translation is complicated <note>The author notes that the Latin Vulgate translation is "intricata," or convoluted, in this passage</note>. And Deuteronomy 2 <note>Deuteronomy 2:14</note>: *Until the whole assembly of the men of war was consumed.* Likewise, Numbers 32 <note>Numbers 32:13</note>: *Until the entire generation that had done evil was consumed.* It has another meaning: perfect, complete, proven, or innocent. Our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> has "immaculate." Psalm 119 <note>Psalm 119:1</note>: *Blessed are the immaculate in the way.* And Psalm 18 <note>Psalm 18:25</note>: *And with the innocent you shall be innocent.* And Song of Songs 5 <note>Song of Songs 5:2</note>: *My dove, my immaculate one.* From this comes integrity, health, and so on. Just as we use the word "to be well" <note>Latin: *ualere*</note>, so among the Hebrews this root is used in a good sense, and sometimes in a bad sense.

<meta>This page continues the Hebrew dictionary for the letter Tav [ת]. The previous page discussed the roots *Talal* (to heap up) and *Talah* (to hang). This page continues alphabetically with roots beginning with the sequence Tav-Mem [תמ].</meta>

# BOOK

**תמיד** <note>Hebrew root: *Tamid*</note> **Perpetual, continuous.** In Leviticus 6 <note>Leviticus 6:13</note>: *The perpetual fire which shall never fail on the altar.* <note>original Latin: "Ignis perpetuus qui nunquam deficiet in altari"</note>

**תמה** <note>Hebrew root: *Tamah*</note> **He was stunned, or he marveled.** In Psalm 48 <note>Psalm 48:5</note>: *When they saw it, they were so amazed.* <note>original Latin: "Ipsi videntes sic admirati sunt"</note> From this comes admiration, stupor, and so on.

**תמוז** <note>Hebrew root: *Tammuz*</note> **An idol or image.** In Ezekiel 8 <note>Ezekiel 8:14</note>: *Women sitting and weeping for Adonis,* <note>The author identifies the Hebrew "Tammuz" with the Greek deity Adonis, described here as "the idol of the suitor of Venus."</note> the idol.

**תמך** <note>Hebrew root: *Tamakh*</note> **He took up or sustained.** In Exodus 17 <note>Exodus 17:12, describing Aaron and Hur assisting Moses</note>: *They sustained his hands on either side.* And in Isaiah 41 <note>Isaiah 41:10</note>: *The right hand of my just one has taken you up.*

**תמול** <note>Hebrew root: *Temol*</note> **Recently, yesterday, or the day before yesterday and beyond.** In Exodus 4 <note>Exodus 4:10</note>: *I have not been eloquent since yesterday or the day before.* <note>original Latin: "nudiustertius," a specific term for the day before yesterday</note> And in 2 Samuel 15 <note>2 Samuel 15:20, cited as 2 Kings</note>: *You came but yesterday, and today you are compelled to go out with us.* And in 1 Samuel 21 <note>1 Samuel 21:5, cited as 1 Kings</note>: *We have been kept from women since yesterday and the day before.* Sometimes it takes an <term>aleph</term> at the beginning by <term>prothesis</term> <note>the addition of a letter to the beginning of a word without changing its meaning</note>, as in Micah 2 <note>Micah 2:8</note>: *And on the contrary, my people have risen up as an adversary,* that is, from before. However, some learned Hebrews believe this word is composed of the particle **את** <note>et</note> and **מול** <note>mul</note>, meaning "opposite." Our translation seems to agree with this, as it is interpreted as "from the opposite" or "on the contrary."

**תמר** <note>Hebrew root: *Tamar*</note> **A palm, the tree that bears dates.** In Song of Songs 7 <note>Song of Songs 7:7</note>: *Your stature is likened to a palm tree.* And in Joel 1 <note>Joel 1:12</note>: *The pomegranate and the palm and the apple.* And in the plural in Numbers 33 <note>Numbers 33:9</note>: *Twelve springs and seventy palms.* It also signifies the smoke arising from bundles of aromatics <note>Likening the tall, spreading shape of a smoke column to a palm tree</note> in Song of Songs 3 <note>Song of Songs 3:6</note>: *Like a little pillar of smoke.*

**תנין** <note>Hebrew root: *Tanin*</note> **A dragon, a serpent, or a snake.** In Exodus 7 <note>Exodus 7:9</note>: *And let it be turned into a serpent.* And further down: *Which was turned into a serpent... and they each threw down their rods, which were turned into dragons.* And sometimes the letter **nun** [נ] is changed into **mem** [מ], as in Ezekiel 29 <note>Ezekiel 29:3, where the word is written as "Tannim"</note>: *The great dragon who lies in the midst of your rivers.* It is also found with another meaning: "to read often" or "to recount." <note>This refers to the root *Tanah*, which is related to the oral tradition or repetition.</note>

->540<-
