<meta>This page continues the Hebrew dictionary for the letter Tav [ת]. The previous page ended with the root *Temol* (yesterday). This section continues with roots beginning with Tav-Nun [תנ], Tav-Ayin [תע], and Tav-Pe [תפ].</meta>

# THE SECOND [PART]

**תנה** <note>Hebrew root: *Tanah*</note> **He gave a reward, he hired, or he valued.** In Hosea 8 <note>Hosea 8:9-10</note>: *They gave gifts to their lovers,* or more correctly: *They hired lovers.* <note>original Latin: "Munera dederunt amatoribus... Conduxerunt amatores"</note> The noun receives an <term>aleph</term> at the beginning by <term>prothesis</term> <note>The addition of a letter to the beginning of a word.</note>. In Hosea 2 <note>Hosea 2:12</note>: *These are my rewards,* meaning "this is my wage." Also, by <term>paragoge</term> <note>The addition of a letter to the end of a word.</note> of the letter <term>nun</term>, or rather by the changing of <term>he</term> into <term>nun</term>, it is also called a "wage." In Deuteronomy 23 <note>Deuteronomy 23:18</note>: *You shall not offer the hire of a harlot.* <note>original Latin: "mercedem prostibuli"</note> It sometimes figuratively signifies retribution; you will find other derived forms as you read.

**תנוך** <note>Hebrew root: *Tanukh*</note> **Cartilage, or the ear lobe.** In Exodus 29 <note>Exodus 29:20</note>: *Upon the tip of the right ear.* <note>original Latin: "Super extremum auriculæ dexteræ"</note>

**תנור** <note>Hebrew root: *Tanur*</note> **An oven, a stove, or a furnace.** In Leviticus 11 <note>Leviticus 11:35</note>: *Whether ovens or fire-pots, they shall be destroyed.* <note>original Latin: "Siue clibani siue chitropodes destruentur"</note>

**תעתע** <note>Hebrew root: *Ta'ata'*</note> **He mocked or deceived.** In Genesis 27 <note>Genesis 27:12</note>: *I fear lest he think I wished to mock him.* <note>original Latin: "Timeo ne putet sibi me uoluisse illudere"</note>

**תעב** <note>Hebrew root: *Ta'ab*</note> **He detested or abominated.** In Amos 5 <note>Amos 5:10</note>: *And they detested him who speaks perfectly.* In Psalm 107 <note>Psalm 107:18</note>: *Their soul loathed all manner of meat.* From this comes "abomination" and other derivatives. In Isaiah 1 <note>Isaiah 1:13</note>: *Incense is an abomination to me.*

**תעה** <note>Hebrew root: *Ta'ah*</note> **He wandered or erred.** In Psalm 119 <note>Psalm 119:176</note>: *I have gone astray like a sheep that is lost.* And in Isaiah 19 <note>Isaiah 19:14</note>: *And they have caused Egypt to err in all its work, as a drunkard staggers.* From this comes "wandering," "error," and so on.

**תער** <note>Hebrew root: *Ta'ar*</note> **A razor.** In Numbers 6 <note>Numbers 6:5</note>: *During the whole time of his separation, no razor shall pass over his head.* And in Isaiah 7 <note>Isaiah 7:20</note>: *The Lord shall shave with a hired razor.* It has another meaning through the addition of the letter <term>he</term>: **a scabbard or sheath.** In Jeremiah 47 <note>Jeremiah 47:6</note>: *Enter into your scabbard.*

**תף** <note>Hebrew root: *Toph*</note> **A drum or timbrel.** In Isaiah 5 <note>Isaiah 5:12</note>: *The lyre and the harp, the drum and the flute, and wine are in your feasts.* And in Job 21 <note>Job 21:12</note>: *They take up the timbrel and the harp.* In these cases, it loses one of its doubled letters, but it retains it in Psalm 68 <note>Psalm 68:25</note>: *In the midst of young women playing timbrels.* <note>original Latin: "tympanistriarum"</note>

**תפוח** <note>Hebrew root: *Tappuach*</note> **An apple, or fruit; both the tree and the fruit.** In Song of Solomon 2 <note>Song of Solomon 2:3</note>: *As the apple tree among the trees of the wood.* And later <note>Song of Solomon 2:5</note>: *Stay me with apples.*

By the best right, thanks are given to our King, the greatest Messiah. # THE THIRD BOOK
### OF THE *FUNDAMENTALS OF HEBREW* BY JOHANNES REUCHLIN OF PFORZHEIM, DOCTOR OF LAWS, TO HIS BROTHER DIONYSIUS, HIS GERMAN KINSMAN.

<margin>a</margin> Dearest brother, you have seen what has been done so far regarding Hebrew letters, syllables, and words—especially the "primitives" <term>the foundational root words from which other words are derived</term>. These were, I hope, sweet to you, but perhaps they will seem bitter to others who have been "nourished on honey and milk" <note>A metaphor for readers accustomed only to elegant, easy literature</note> because of my unpolished style of writing. Yet, if such people consider that all speech must be adapted to the listeners, they will not find fault with me for speaking plainly to my fellow countrymen. For how can those who are unlearned be easily taught through an unfamiliar way of speaking, or through a style prepared at home and labored over by lamplight? Such students would need to pay more attention to the teacher's eloquence—as if deciphering the riddles of the Sphinx—than to the actual rules he is teaching.

<margin>small circle</margin> In my judgment, Aristotle felt much more correctly when he said that in the sciences, a teacher ought to proceed through the most common habits of speech and through those things most familiar to us. Therefore, I have intentionally and often used "solecisms" <note>grammatical mistakes</note> and "barbarisms" <note>unrefined language</note> to explain the specific properties of certain words. To this, one must add that both old age and daily conversation with unrefined people not only dull the tongue but also blunt one's writing style. This follows the sentiment of the tragic poet Euripides, who said: "I have become a barbarian, through being a long time among barbarians" <note>original Greek: βεβαρβαρωσαι' χρονιος ων εν βαρβαροις</note>.

For I am alone, hiding away all day in this "tub of Diogenes" <note>A reference to the ancient philosopher who lived in a large ceramic jar to demonstrate his rejection of worldly comforts</note>. No one lives with me who prizes elegance of words or the study of eloquence. Instead, there are only farmers and lowly priests, or those who approach me (as happens daily) to consult me—not about the "layers of walls" <note>original: muri legulis</note> or "crown gold" <note>a specific type of legal tribute</note>, but about sewers, marshes, timber, rights of way, or other common disputes, whether they be handled in the governor's court or civil court. In answering these people regarding the law, as is my profession, I must observe the local speech of the Swabians <note>A Germanic people from Reuchlin's home region</note> rather than that of the Romans.

You should not wonder any further, my brother, that after walking through green meadows, I am now treading upon rough paths. This was one of the reasons of no small weight why I thought my individual works would be rejected by more polished men of letters; they would see in them no "flower," no charm, but only things that are trivial and unrefined. However, when I recall ancient memories, I find that our ancestors were also greatly delighted by foreign or "barbaric" ways of speaking. For the Greek Aristophanes, in the comedy titled *The Acharnians*, has a character speak in Persian like this: *Iactarman exarxan apissonosatra* <note>This is a string of nonsensical, foreign-sounding syllables used for comedic effect in the play</note>. Such "barbarism" has often brought joy to many and moved them to laughter. Among the Romans...

# BOOK THREE

Truly, who ever despised Marcus Cato the Elder because in his writings *On Agriculture* he speaks "barbarously" in this way: *Haut haut haut ista pista fista, ardannabon damiabo damauftra* <note>original: "Haut haut haut..." These are nonsensical magic words or "charms" found in Cato's *De Agri Cultura*, used here by Reuchlin to show that even great Roman authors used strange, non-standard language when the subject required it</note>? Who threw away the play *The Little Carthaginian* by Plautus on account of the Punic language <note>The play *Poenulus* contains passages in the extinct Phoenician/Carthaginian language</note>? I shall console myself by their example, so that I may hope to find those who are led by wonder to read a subject never heard of before. 

I think this one thing will happen, however: that Agamemnon will not lack his Thersites <note>A character from the *Iliad* known for being a shrill, vulgar critic of leaders</note>, nor Homer his Zoilus <note>An ancient grammarian famous for his harsh criticism of Homer</note>, nor Socrates his "Cloud" <note>A reference to Aristophanes' play *The Clouds*, which mocked Socrates</note>. I expect that eventually certain fanatical whisperers will come forth against me; men who, having been gripped by an old and long-standing laziness toward study, consider it more glorious to criticize many things than to learn a few. They hope to become famous through their contempt and insults toward dedicated scholars.

For they will say that I could not have reached such a height of Hebrew reading in my senior years without a teacher—no matter how hard I tried—such that my studies could benefit others. To them, I will immediately hold up Origen, Saint Jerome, and that Nicholas of Lyra <note>Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349) was a Franciscan teacher whose Hebrew knowledge was essential for later biblical scholars</note>, all of whom are proven to have first studied Hebrew as old age approached. Indeed, almost no one since the Apostles has enlightened the orthodox Church with Hebrew literature who did not begin to learn it in advanced age—except for that distinguished teacher, Bishop Paul of Burgos <note>A Jewish rabbi (Solomon ha-Levi) who converted to Christianity in the 14th century and became a high-ranking bishop and scholar</note>, once the most learned among the Jews. His late conversion was the salvation of many men, and I am not ashamed to "give him the grass" <note>original: "herbā dare" — A Roman military idiom meaning to admit defeat or acknowledge someone as superior</note> while setting aside the rest.

Awaken then, young men! And you, my blood brother, shake off dullness from your mind by imitating such great men. For if such excellent men, even in their advanced years, realized they lacked the noble opportunity for the highest and most pleasant contemplation and thus devoted such great and intense study—however late—to Hebrew, it was so that their labor might overflow onto us. Why should you yourself, and through you other young men endowed with great talent, not hope to reach such perfection through tireless reading and daily exercise, even without a teacher? 

As for my own teachers (so that those barking at me do not insult me), I offer this account: I was never ashamed at any time to scrape together from any Jew whatever little bits might lead to some knowledge of Hebrew books. For just as I did not learn Greek in Ionia or in any part of Greece, but first in Basle from Andronicus Contoblacas, then in Paris from George Hermonymus of Sparta, later in Rome from Argyropylus of Byzantium (while Sixtus IV was Pope and publicly reading Thucydides in the Vatican), and finally in Florence from Me...

-># BOOK THREE<-

[And in Milan] from Demetrius Chalcondyles <note>Demetrius Chalcondyles (1423–1511) was a leading Greek scholar who taught in Italy and helped spread Greek learning during the Renaissance</note>, I received the Greek language in small portions and, as it were, like crumbs falling from the master's table. I would also count among them Hermolaus Barbarus <note>Hermolaus Barbarus (1454–1493) was an Italian humanist and diplomat known for his translations of Aristotle</note>, a distinguished man and very fond of me, except that I drew more Latinity than Greek from him while in Rome. In this same way, I also "fished out" the Hebrew and holy language, not in Jerusalem nor in the public synagogues of the Jews, but from the most learned Hebrews: specifically, with Jacob ben Jehiel Loans <note>A Jewish physician to Emperor Maximilian I who served as Reuchlin's first Hebrew teacher</note> among the Caetii, and in Latium <note>The region of Italy surrounding Rome</note> with Obadiah of Cesena <note>Obadiah ben Jacob Sforno (c. 1475–1550), a famous Jewish commentator and physician who taught Reuchlin in Rome</note>, and elsewhere from various individuals, one thing at a time.

But the envious will, I believe, rise up more heavily against our dictionary, in which the interpretations of many previous writers are frequently criticized. "Oh, what a crime!" they will shout. "Nothing is more unworthy of the memory of the Fathers, nothing more cruelly committed, than that this most audacious man should strive to undermine so many and such holy men who were inspired by the divine spirit!" They will argue that the scripture of the most blessed Jerome was received into the Church on the testimony of Pope Gelasius, and that the venerable father Nicholas of Lyra <note>Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349) was a Franciscan whose literal commentary on the Bible was the standard for centuries</note>, the ordinary interpreter of the Bible and a man of the highest integrity, is approved by all the faithful of Christ. They will cry that "now, at last, some little puff of smoke has arisen to suggest that in many places those great men translated unskillfully."

To their looming shouts, I offer these few responses: that I am permitted to do what was permitted to those same most illustrious lights of the Church. Jerome, a holy man, plucked at the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The "Seventy" (LXX), the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> translators not once, twice, or thrice, but very many times. At times he says they erred by a clear mistake; at other times that they were deceived by ignorance; then that they disagree with the <term>Hebrew Truth</term> <note>Latin: *Hebraica Veritas*. This was the humanist principle that the original Hebrew text was more authoritative than later translations</note>; then that they were misled by the similarity of certain letters; and then that they deliberately concealed or omitted certain things so as not to reveal the sacred mysteries. And yet, Ptolemy, the King of Alexandria, believed they had translated by divine power, and as Justin—philosopher and martyr—writes in his *Exhortation* to them, "he recognized them as men beloved of God" <note>original Greek: ως θεοφιλης ανδρας διεγνω</note>.

Likewise, Nicholas of Lyra shows that Saint Jerome himself was censurable in his translation. He does this in many places, such as in the Psalm numbered 47 in our Church’s count <note>Reuchlin notes that the Catholic/Vulgate numbering of the Psalms (Psalm 47) differs from the Hebrew numbering (Psalm 48). The text in question begins "Great is the Lord"</note>, where at the end he says: "Jerome, however, seems to speak less than well, because in all the Hebrew Bibles I have seen, *almuth* <note>original Hebrew: עלמות. A musical term of uncertain meaning in the header of Psalm 48</note> is one word here and not two." See how he accuses that most blessed man of error and negligence! Indeed, so that Nicholas might suffer the same measure he gave, he was forced to endure similar treatment from the Reverend Bishop of Burgos <note>Paul of Burgos (c. 1351–1435), a Jewish convert to Christianity who wrote "Additions" to Lyra's work, often correcting him</note> through frequent notes, despite the resistance of a certain Brother Doering <note>Matthias Doering (c. 1400–1469), a Franciscan who wrote a defense of Lyra against the corrections of the Bishop of Burgos</note>.

But what need is there for more examples? That same Saint Jerome confesses in his own translation that he himself erred. In his commentaries on Isaiah, chapter nineteen, he says: "I think it better to rebuke my own error than, while I blush [to admit it]..."

### BOOK THREE

...to confess ignorance [rather than] to persist in error in what I have translated. [For example:] "And the land of Judah shall be a joy to Egypt." <note>original: "Et erit terra Iuda ægypto in festiuitatem." Reuchlin is citing Isaiah 19:17, where Saint Jerome famously admitted his initial translation was incorrect compared to the Hebrew truth</note> I could otherwise bring forward many more verses, and the fact that he [Jerome] did not consider it a cause for shame to admit that, even to this day, he was ignorant of the meaning of a certain word in the sixth chapter of Jeremiah; and that he noted the Apostle’s <note>Referring to Saint Paul</note> lack of skill in the grammatical art in the second-to-last question of his letter to Hedibia <note>St. Jerome's Letter 120, where he discusses the difficulty of Paul's Greek style</note>; and that he wrote that the same Apostle used verses from the Psalms differently than they are found in the Hebrew, as in his commentaries on Psalm 13. 

Why, therefore, in those matters which pertain to the method of interpretation, the grammatical art, and the truth of the original language <note>original: "ueritatem idiomatis"</note>, should it not also be fitting for me to bring to light what I have concluded alongside the most learned Hebrews? <margin>—</margin> For indeed, it is to them that one must flee—by the testimony of that same Jerome—whenever a controversy arises regarding the Old Testament. For although I venerate Saint Jerome as an angel and honor Lyra <note>Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349), a Franciscan scholar whose literal commentary on the Bible was a primary source for later Hebraists</note> as a master, yet I worship truth as God. 

And I certainly do not defend our dictionary as being entirely free from every exception. First, because it does not embrace every single thing (for it is not possible to include everything by count, nor is there any vocabulary in all of human life, however immense in size, made or imagined, that could embrace every word of any language). Second, because in explaining words, it frequently varies, although this happens according to the opinion of each individual translator. For we have left nothing, or very little, to our own judgment, but have shown the judgment of each translator. 

It remains only for you to remember that in the preceding two books, I have collected only Hebrew <term>primitive roots</term> <note>The basic three-letter stems that form the foundation of the Hebrew language</note>, and not Talmudic <note>Post-biblical Jewish legal and civil codes</note> or Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> words. Finally, [remember] that I have cited the Psalms according to the Hebrew numbering and not according to the notation of our Church <note>The Hebrew Bible and the Latin Vulgate use different numbering systems for the Psalms; for example, Psalm 23 in English/Hebrew is Psalm 22 in the Vulgate</note>, for the sake of those who will attempt to prudently hunt for our teaching from the Hebrew Bible. 

Now, in this third book, we hasten toward the grammatical art, so that those who already correctly grasp the method of reading and the meanings of Hebrew words from the earlier books may learn from what follows to skillfully explain speech constructed from its parts. The labor is on a slight matter, but the glory is not slight. <note>original: "In tenui labor. at tenuis non gloria" — a quote from Virgil's Georgics (4.6), suggesting that even the study of small things like grammar leads to great honor</note> Therefore, if you love me, you will take great care that your intelligence becomes a helper to our industry. I shall give you brief and light rules, and clear ones at the same time, which no one else has done before me. You, however, take care that I do not find you weary of the labor.

### BOOK THREE
### ON SPEECH AND ITS PARTS

A phrase <note>original: "Ratio"</note> is a distinct combination of Hebrew words expressing a thought of the mind. That combination is sometimes drawn out to a great length and sometimes compressed into a few words; for this reason, there is a need for "distinctions" <note>This refers to punctuation or pauses in delivery</note>. It is customary for these distinctions to be marked by specific points according to the completeness or incompleteness of the thought. This is done in four ways: by the **minor pause**, the **major pause**, the **clause**, and the **conclusion**. I will first demonstrate this in Latin as follows: In the first book of the *Aeneid*, [Virgil] sings: *After the first quiet came to the feast* <note>original: "Postquam prima quies epulis"</note>—here is a brief suspension of the thought which is called a **minor pause** <term>subdistinctio: a minor break in a sentence</term>. There follows: *and the tables were removed*—this is more complete, and therefore it is a **major pause** <term>distinctio: a stronger mark of separation</term>. Yet the sense still hangs. Therefore, this is also added: *They set out the great bowls*—now a fitting part of the thought comes to rest, and it is called a **clause** <term>membrum: a constituent part of a sentence</term>. Afterwards: *and they crown the wine*—this is the **conclusion** of the entire speech, and it takes its name from that fact.

We find a similar practice in frequent use among the Hebrews. They mark the **minor pause** with a single dot shaped above the word of the first suspension, yet in such a way that no one should mistake it for a *Cholem* <note>A Hebrew vowel mark that also appears as a dot above a letter</note>. It is called **Revia** <gloss>רְבִיעַ</gloss>. 

The **major pause**, likewise consisting of two dots placed one above the other over the word of the second suspension, is called **Zakef Katan** <gloss>זָקֵף קָטָן</gloss>. 

The **clause** is recognized by a semicircle shaped like a rainbow placed below the word of the third suspension; it is called **Atnahta** <gloss>אֶתְנַחְתָּא</gloss>. 

The **conclusion**, however, indicated by a small vertical line placed below the word after the clause, shows the completed sense of the entire speech; it is called **Pasek** <gloss>פָּסֵק</gloss> <note>While the author calls this "Pasek," the description of a vertical line marking the end of a verse more commonly refers to the "Silluk" or "Sof Pasuk" in Hebrew grammar</note>. All of this will be made clear to you by this example from the first book of Kings, chapter 18 <note>In modern Bibles, this is 1 Samuel 18:18</note>:

And David said to Saul: "Who am I, and what is my life,
the family of my father in Israel, that I should be son-in-law to the king?"

In Latin <note>meaning, an English translation of the Latin structure provided in the text</note> it is thus: *And David said to Saul*—here is the **Revia**—*who am I and what is my life*—here is the **Zakef Katan**—*the kindred of my father in Israel*—here is the **Atnahta**—*that I should become the king’s son-in-law*—here is the **Pasek**. 

Therefore, let this be the first law in speech: so that you, who until now only knew how to read, may now also be able to read with proper distinction. The second concern in reading will be that you do not pronounce the harder syllables softly, nor the softer ones [harshly]...

For whenever a word precedes and ends in one of these four vowel-letters [Hebrew: אהוי] <term>Quiescent letters: Aleph, He, Vav, and Yod, which often function as markers for vowel sounds rather than acting as full consonants</term>, and it governs the following word which begins with one of the six consonants mentioned above, then that consonant normally takes a **Raphe** <term>Raphe: a grammatical mark indicating a "soft" or "weakened" pronunciation of a letter</term>, and that syllable is pronounced gently, smoothly, or with a soft lisp.

Likewise: *For you will bless the righteous* <note>original Latin: "Item tu benedices iusto"</note>. Also: *You will destroy those who speak lies* <note>original Latin: "item perdes qui loquuntur mendacium"</note>.

# OF THE NOUN AND ITS GENDERS

All Hebrew nouns—whether they are proper or common, substantive, adjective, verbal, **denominative** <term>Denominative: a word, usually a verb, derived from a noun or adjective</term>, abstract, concrete, simple, compound, or of any other kind—are found to be of the masculine gender, the feminine, or both. For the Hebrews attribute a double sex to them according to nature, and they call them **male and female** <note>original Hebrew: זכר ונקבה (*zakar ve-nekevah*)</note>. Genesis 5: *Male and female he created them.*

They recognize the genders of nouns in the singular number—not always, but frequently—either from the terminal letter, or from the addition of adjectives, or from the addition of verbs (to which, according to the Hebrews, gender also applies), or from numerical inflection. Feminine nouns often end in **Aleph** [א], **He** [ה], or **Tav** [ת]. However, feminine adjectives do not end in **Aleph**, but in **He** or **Tav**. If these are added to nouns with other endings, they reveal their gender. As seen in Genesis 3: **"The woman, she gave [it] to me"** <note>original Hebrew: האשה היא נתנה לי; original Latin: Mulier ipsa dedit mihi</note>.

**Tzaba** <note>original Hebrew: צבא (*tzaba*)</note>—that is, "army"—is of the feminine gender. This is known from the fact that it takes the ending **-ot** in the plural number, as in **Tzabaot** [צבאות], which we are accustomed to read as **Sabaoth** <note>The term often appears in the phrase "Lord of Sabaoth" or "Lord of Hosts." The author is explaining that despite its meaning, the grammatical form is feminine</note>. Isaiah 6: *Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God of Sabaoth.* <note>original Latin: *Sanctus sanctus sanctus dominus deus zebaoth*</note>

These are the two inflections <note>referring to the plural endings *-im* for masculine and *-ot* for feminine</note> by which we recognize gender. However, the rule sometimes fails us; for it is not always and everywhere true that a word whose plural ends in **-im** is necessarily of the masculine gender. For **yonim** [יונים, "doves"] ends in the plural with **-im**, as seen in Song of Songs 1: *Your eyes are those of doves.* <note>original Latin: *Oculi tui columbarum*</note> And yet its singular form is of the feminine gender, as in Genesis 8: *He sent out the dove, which did not return,* where the verb applied to it is of the feminine gender <note>In Hebrew, verbs change their form to match the gender of the noun. Here, the verb "return" (*shavah*) would be in its feminine form, proving the "dove" is grammatically feminine despite the masculine-sounding plural</note>. Similarly, the ending of the word **yonah** [יונה] indicates the feminine gender.

Thus, you will find many other words that end in **-im** in the plural, even though their singular nominative forms are exceptions to the rule, such as those that follow:

However, all these forms are subject to exceptions. Regarding the ending **he** [ה], we find **Moshe** <note>Hebrew: מֹשֶׁה</note>, which is Moses. Regarding the ending **tav** [ת], we find **Kohelet** <note>Hebrew: קֹהֶלֶת</note>, that is, Ecclesiastes. Regarding the ending **aleph** [א], we find **Ezra** <note>Hebrew: עֶזְרָא</note>, which is Ezra. And so it is with similar cases; all of these are of the masculine gender despite their endings, and thus they go against the general rule.

Genders are also recognized when nouns are shifted from one gender to another. For example, **gever** <note>Hebrew: גֶּבֶר</note> means a "man" or "lord," while **gevirat** <note>Hebrew: גְּבִירַת</note> or even **geveret** <note>Hebrew: גְּבֶרֶת</note> means a "matron" or "lady." 

And although the meanings of certain nouns may shift from masculine to feminine, the nouns themselves often do not change their form. For instance, although we say **adon** <note>Hebrew: אָדוֹן</note>—that is, "lord"—we do not typically say **adonah** <note>Hebrew: אדונה</note> <note>The author notes that while one might expect a feminine version of "lord" to follow the rules of grammar, it was not standard usage in his time</note>, even though in Latin we could easily translate this as *domina* [lady].

Therefore, you must not always follow grammatical analogy. 

Store this primarily in a mindful memory: remember that I have diligently instructed you not to follow your own inventions of analogy when composing Hebrew sentences without the express authority of the Sacred Scriptures. You may only do so in the active and passive forms of the verb or in common, minor constructions. Otherwise, you will easily sin against the proper nature of the language, and your errors will be obvious to everyone.

Finally, there are nouns found to be of "either gender"—that is, both masculine and feminine. These are mostly names of animal species or classes, such as bird, winged creature, camel, and everything of the raven kind, as well as other bipeds or quadrupeds. Many of these are read in Leviticus 11: *The kite and the vulture according to its kind, and every raven kind after its likeness.* <note>The author is quoting the Latin Vulgate translation of Leviticus 11:14-15</note> Similarly, in Deuteronomy 14: *The camel, the hare, and the rock badger <note>original: "choerogryllium"</note>, because they chew the cud and do not divide the hoof, they shall be unclean to you.* And in the same chapter: *Every clean bird you shall eat*, where "bird" takes a masculine form, and the adjective...

## ON DECLENSION

Every inflection of Hebrew <note>original: "Iudaicorum," literally "Jewish"</note> nouns is made through numbers alone—singular and plural—and not through <term>cases</term> <note>Unlike Latin or Greek, Hebrew nouns do not change their endings to indicate if they are the subject or object.</note>. Therefore, you will see no <term>oblique case</term> <note>Any case other than the nominative (subject), such as the genitive or accusative.</note> except that which either a particle demonstrates, or which the sense of the spoken word requires. And although we will treat these particles fully below in the section on pronouns, we merely list them here in passing so far as is necessary to show declension. Namely, they are these: **ה ל את מ** <note>These represent the prefixes for the definite article and various prepositions often used to indicate case-like relationships.</note>. 

For the **nominative**, a particle is not needed. There follow the **genitive**, **dative**, **accusative**, and **ablative**. For the **vocative** imitates the nominative. These take place in both the singular and the plural number. Therefore, individual nouns are declined by the inflection of the ending from the singular number to the plural number, of whatever gender they may be. 

From this, you understand that there are only two declensions for the Hebrews: 

1.  **The first declension** follows the form of masculines, which inflects from the nominative singular into the nominative plural simply by adding **im** [-ים]. For example: **davar** [דָּבָר, "word"] becomes **devarim** [דְּבָרִים, "words"].
2.  **The second declension** follows the form of feminines, which—ending in the singular in **he** [ה] or **tav** [ת] with the vowels *patah* or *qamets*, or being otherwise of the feminine gender—inflects into the nominative plural only by changing the **he** or **tav** into **oth** [-וֹת]. For example: **chayah** [חַיָּה, "living soul/beast"] becomes **chayot** [חַיּוֹת, "beasts"].

Instruction must first be given on the first declension, which can be done no more concisely than through examples.

<meta>This page continues the grammatical study of Hebrew nouns. Having previously discussed gender, the author now transitions into the rules of declension, focusing on how vowel sounds and consonant strengths change when words are pluralized or placed in the "construct state" (where one noun belongs to another).</meta>

# BOOK

Concerning declension, it is necessary to know that some polysyllabic nouns ending in *l* or *n* with the <term>qamets<note>A Hebrew vowel mark usually indicating a long "a" sound, like "father".</note></term> vowel strengthen their liquid consonants by using a <term>dagesh<note>A dot placed inside a Hebrew letter to indicate it is doubled or "strengthened."</note></term> point. For example, גָּמָל <note>original: "gāmāl"</note> גְּמַלִּים <note>original: "gemallīm"</note>, which means "camel" and "camels." Likewise, קָטָן <note>original: "qāṭān"</note> קְטַנִּים <note>original: "qeṭannīm"</note>, meaning "small" (singular and plural). In these cases, they change the <term>qamets</term> into a <term>pataḥ<note>A Hebrew vowel mark for a short "a" sound.</note></term>.

However, those nouns whose ending sounds like a clear "e" do not change at all, whether in the plural, in the <term>construct state<note>Latin: "regimine". This refers to the form a noun takes when it "governs" a following noun, often translated as "of...".</note></term>, or even with <term>affixes<note>Grammatical endings added to words to indicate possession, such as "my" or "his".</note></term>. An example is זְאֵב <note>original: "ze’ēv"</note>, meaning "wolf," as seen in Genesis 49; and in the plural in Ezekiel 22, זְאֵבִים <note>original: "ze’ēvīm"</note>, meaning "wolves." This remains the same in the construct state and with affixes.

In a similar way, those nouns whose ending sounds like "o" or "u" do not change in the plural, the construct state, or with affixes. For example: אָדֹם <note>red</note> אֲדֹמִים <note>red (plural)</note>, and נָקוּד <note>speckled</note> נְקֻדִּים <note>speckled (plural)</note>.

To help you understand what I mean by the construct state and affixes, you must consider the two-fold state of each grammatical number. One is the **absolute state**, and the other is the **construct state**. Let us take the singular number of the noun דָּבָר <note>word</note> as an example.

When such nouns are in the **absolute state**, they are written and pronounced in the singular with two—or at least a final—<term>qamets</term>. Examples include זָקֵן <note>old man</note>, עָנָן <note>cloud</note>, and חָכָם <note>wise man</note>, and others which you will find in our dictionary.

If, however, the noun is found in the **construct state** in the singular—that is, it governs another noun following it—then it changes the first <term>qamets</term> into a <term>sheva<note>A Hebrew mark indicating a very short vowel or a vocal "stop."</note></term> and the second <term>qamets</term> into a <term>pataḥ</term>. For instance, in Jeremiah 2: דְּבַר יְהוָה <note>original: "devar Yahweh"</note>, meaning "the word of the Lord." But before certain suffixes, the <term>qamets</term> remains.

For those nouns ending in "i", such as קָצִיר <note>meaning harvest</note>, they change the first <term>qamets</term> into a <term>sheva</term> while the <term>hireq<note>A Hebrew vowel mark for the "i" sound.</note></term> remains. As in Genesis 30: קְצִיר חִטִּים <note>original: "qetsīr ḥiṭṭīm"</note>, meaning "the harvest of wheat."

Now consider the **plural number**. There you will likewise find a two-fold state. If the noun remains in the **absolute state**, then the suffix *im* is simply added to the singular form to make it plural; however, the first syllable is then pronounced with a <term>sheva</term>. Exceptions are made for <term>irregular nouns<note>Latin: "heterodita". Nouns that do not follow the standard rules of declension.</note></term>, which will be mentioned later. Thus we say:

דָּבָר <note>word</note> דְּבָרִים <note>words</note>
זָכָר <note>male</note> זְכָרִים <note>males</note>
שְׁאָר <note>remnant</note> שְׁאָרִים <note>remnants</note>
אַבִּיר <note>strong</note> אַבִּירִים <note>strong ones</note>
אֵזוֹב <note>hyssop</note> אֵזוֹבִים <note>hyssops</note>
אֵבוּס <note>manger</note> אֵבוּסִים <note>mangers</note>
עִבְרִי <note>Hebrew</note> עִבְרִיִּים <note>Hebrews</note>

But if the plural noun is found in the construct state—

### THIRD
# BOOK

...of the possessive forms <note>Latin: "genitiuorum." This refers to the plural construct state in Hebrew.</note>. In these cases, the noun drops the final *mem* <note>The letter ם, which marks the masculine plural.</note> and the first syllable is pronounced with a <term>hiriq<note>A Hebrew vowel mark indicating a short "i" sound.</note></term>, and the final *hiriq* is changed into a <term>tsere<note>A Hebrew vowel mark indicating a long "e" sound.</note></term>—that is, the "i" sound changes to an "e" at the end of the word—as we have already shown above. An exception is חכמי <note>original: "ḥakhme" (wise men of)</note>, which keeps the <term>pataḥ<note>A short "a" sound.</note></term>, along with similar words.

But if it is constructed with subjective pronouns and <term>affixes<note>Suffixes added to nouns to indicate "my," "your," "his," etc.</note></term>, which we will teach you about hereafter, then it changes the final *hiriq* into a *tsere* only in the second and third persons of the plural number, while the *hiriq* of the first syllable keeps its sound. Truly, "iambic" words <note>This refers to a specific rhythmic pattern of vowels in the Hebrew word structure.</note> change the <term>qamets<note>A long "a" sound.</note></term> into a *tsere*. We shall speak of these more extensively below, God willing. We mention these brief points only because they are highly necessary for the first declension, so that you may know how to decline words according to all their forms.

Therefore, I repeat the frequently mentioned noun as an example:

| word | the word of the Lord | my word | your word | his word | words |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| דֶּבַר | יְהוָה דְּבַר | דְּבָרִי | דְּבָרְךָ | דְּבָרוֹ | דְּבָרִים |

| words of | of the days | my words | your words | his words |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| דִּבְרֵי | יָמִים | דְּבָרַי | דְּבָרֶיךָ | דְּבָרָיו |
| <note>of them (m.)</note> דִּבְרֵיהֶם | <note>of them (f.)</note> דִּבְרֵיהֶן | <note>of you (m. pl.)</note> דִּבְרֵיכֶם | <note>of you (f. pl.)</note> דִּבְרֵיכֶן |

You now have a model for the changes of the first declension in the masculine form. I have decided to attach certain <term>heteroclite<note>Irregular words that do not follow the standard rules of declension.</note></term> nouns to this, so that you may know what is regular and what is an exception to the rule.

Heteroclites are those nouns that do not simply add the ending *-im* to the singular nominative, but do so with something added or taken away. For example, יָדַיִם <note>original: "yadayim"</note>, which means "hands." For if it were inflected regularly, then by simply adding *-im* it would become יָדִים <note>original: "yadim"</note>, a two-syllable word. But it is not spoken that way; rather it is the three-syllable יָדַיִם. Since a *pataḥ* is added which creates another syllable, we rightly say that this word is heteroclite. The same is true of several others, some of which we have noted here.

| eye | nostrils / face | feet | palm / sole |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| עַיִן עֵינַיִם | אַף אַפַּיִם | רֶגֶל רַגְלַיִם | כַּף כַּפַּיִם |

| ear | door | loin | way |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| אֹזֶן אָזְנַיִם | דֶּלֶת דְּלָתַיִם | חָלָץ חֲלָצַיִם | דֶּרֶךְ דְּרָכַיִם |

[Right side] the fruit of justice
In the **Genitive** case <note>The case indicating possession: "of justice."</note>: **justice**. Amos 6: <note>original Hebrew: וּפְרִי צְדָקָה (*u-p'ri tzedakah*), "and the fruit of righteousness."</note>

If they do not "govern" a following case, then the second-to-last syllable is frequently pronounced with a <term>qamets<note>A Hebrew vowel mark indicating a long "a" sound.</note></term> and the first with a <term>sheva<note>A Hebrew vowel mark indicating a very short, neutral breath sound.</note></term>. ### BOOK [III]

->poverty — height — lack — abundance — history<-
<note>original Latin: *inopia, summitas, defectus, abundantia, historia*</note>

[These] end in *on*. For example:
->needy — most high — failing — gain — remembrance<-
<note>original Hebrew: *evyon* (אֶבְיוֹן), *elyon* (עֶלְיוֹן), *hisron* (חֶסְרוֹן), *yitron* (יִתְרוֹן), *zikhron* (זִכְרוֹן)</note>

->palace — drought — window — pomegranate — priority<-
<note>original Latin: *palatium, siccitas, fenestra, malo granatum, prioritas*</note>
->palace — drought — window — pomegranate — first<-
<note>original Hebrew: *armon* (ארמון), *haravon* (חרבון), *חלון* (halon), *rimon* (רמון), *rishon* (ראשון)</note>

Those which simply add the feminine plural termination **-ot** <note>original: *oth*</note> are declined [in that manner]. As in Esther 6: "the **records** <note>original Hebrew: *zikhronot* (זִכְרוֹןֹת)</note> and annals." Only this noun, **palace** <note>original Hebrew: *armon* (ארמון)</note>, changes the <term>holam<note>The "o" vowel mark.</note></term> into a <term>sheva<note>A vowel mark indicating a very short "e" or no vowel sound at all.</note></term> and becomes **palaces** <note>original Hebrew: *armonot* (ארמנות)</note>, as in Amos 1: "And it shall devour the houses <note>The Hebrew text here refers to the "palaces" or strongholds of Ben-Hadad.</note> of Ben-Hadad." There are some which end in *an* and add **-ot** in the plural, such as:

->gift — table — goad<-
<note>original Latin: *donarium, mensa, stimulus*</note>
->offering — table — goad<-
<note>original Hebrew: *korban* (קרבן), *shulhan* (שלחן), *dorban* (דרבן)</note>
->offerings — tables — goads<-
<note>original Hebrew: *korbanot* (קרבנות), *shulhanot* (שלחנות), *dorbanot* (דרבנות)</note>

But be careful, because there are many masculine nouns ending in *an* which do not end their plural in **-ot**, but in **-im**. As in **garden** to **gardens** <note>original Hebrew: *gan* (בגן), *ganim* (בגנים); the OCR includes a prefix *bet*, likely meaning "in a garden."</note>. In this declination, only those ending in the letter **he** (ה), when they are in the <term>construct state<note>original Latin: *statu regiminis*; a grammatical state where a noun is "possessed" by the following word, e.g., "Table of the King."</note></term> or have suffixes, change the **he** into a **tav** (ת). For example: **lily** <note>original Hebrew: *shoshannah* (שושנה)</note> is in the absolute state in the second chapter of the Song of Solomon: "As a **lily** among thorns." But in the construct state, as seen a little earlier in the same place: "**lily of** the valleys" <note>original Hebrew: *shoshanat ha-amakim* (שושנת העמקים)</note>; however, common custom uses these forms interchangeably.

In the Hebrew text, the word for "three" here is *sheloshah*, which ends in the letter *he*.</note>. But when they are joined to other numbers, they then lack the letter *he*, as is demonstrated in the examples [above].

If, however, the same number is placed in the <term>construct state<note>The form a noun or number takes when it "governs" or is linked to the following word (e.g., "ten of..."). Original Latin: *statu regiminis*.</note></term>, so that it governs the word following it, then that final letter *he* is changed into a *tav* <note>original Latin: *thau*; the Hebrew letter ת.</note>. An example is found in Exodus 34: **the ten words** <note>original Hebrew: *aseret ha-devarim* (עשרת הדברים); refers to the Ten Commandments. Here, "ten" (*aseret*) ends in *tav* because it is linked to "words".</note>, as if one were to say "the ten, namely, of the words." This is just as it is with other words ending in *he*. For example, in Joshua 17: "And the third part of the city of Napheth" <note>original Latin: *Et tertia pars urbis Napheth*; a reference to the regions of Naphoth-dor.</note>.

# BOOK THREE

The same judgment must be held regarding the letter **vav** in the middle of a word; its place is often filled by the *cholam* or *kibbutz* <note>vowel marks representing "o" and "u" sounds</note>. Hey there, Dionysius, my dear brother, you have seen the forms of certain defective words; now listen to how some nouns experience "abundance" <note>the addition of non-root letters</note> at the beginning, the middle, or the end. I say that everything "abounds" which is not contained in the root <term>root: the "primitive" three-letter core of a Hebrew word</term>. All "accidental" letters <term>accidental letters: letters added to a root to change its meaning, such as for tense or person</term> are of this kind, which you will remember I mentioned to you in the first book.

Specifically, at the head of words, the letters contained in this mnemonic phrase are prefixed: **he-emanti** <note>original Hebrew: הֶאֱמַנְתִּי. This word contains the letters He (ה), Aleph (א), Mem (מ), Nun (נ), Tav (ת), and Yod (י), which are the primary letters added to the beginning of roots</note>. With these, frequent derivations of nouns—both those coming from verbs and those coming from other nouns—are properly formed.

An example of **he**: such as **Hosea** <note>original Hebrew: הוֹשֵׁעַ</note>, the prophet. He is named for "saving," according to Jerome in the first chapter of his commentary. His root is written with a **yod** at the beginning; therefore, the **he** is "appended" <note>added as a prefix</note>.

An example of **aleph**: **Achzib** <note>original Hebrew: אַכְזִיב</note>. The Hebrew commentators say it was a city of Judea, as Rabbi David Kimhi testifies in his commentaries on the Tenth <note>likely referring to the Book of Chronicles, often called the "Words of the Days" or "The Tenth" in some traditional lists</note>. Although our translation <note>the Latin Vulgate</note> explains it differently in Micah 1:14 as **Houses of a lie** <note>original Latin: *Domos mendacij*</note>, and the Septuagint <note>the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> as **vain houses**. Its root is read without the **aleph** in Genesis 38, where I do not know what our translation was dreaming when it says: "She ceased to bear after his birth." Concerning this, Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, a famous medieval commentator</note> wrote that it is a proper name of a city, so that the word-for-word reading stands thus: "And he was in **Chesib** (namely, that city) when she bore him."

Regarding **mem**: such as **war** or **battle** <note>original Hebrew: מִלְחָמָה, *milchamah*</note>. Its root is **he fought** <note>original Hebrew: לָחַם, *lacham*</note>. Likewise, **messenger** or **angel** <note>original Hebrew: מַלְאָךְ, *mal’akh*</note>; its root is **he sent a message** <note>original Hebrew: לָאַךְ, *la’akh*</note>. And so it is for many others.

Regarding **nun**: **broken** <note>original Hebrew: נִשְׁבָּר, *nishbar*</note>, as in Psalm 51, "A broken heart." Its root is **he broke** <note>original Hebrew: שָׁבַר, *shabar*</note>.

Regarding **tav**: such as **Talmud** <note>original Hebrew: תַּלְמוּד, literally "study" or "instruction"</note>, whose root is **he learned** or **he taught** <note>original Hebrew: לָמַד, *lamad*</note>.

Regarding **yod**: such as **Jacob** <note>original Hebrew: יַעֲקֹב, *Ya'akov*</note>, whose root is **heel** or **sole** <note>original Hebrew: עָקֵב, *akev*</note>, or **he supplanted** <note>original Hebrew: עָקַב, *akav*</note>. And thus for many other words which you can find more clearly in our dictionary.

In the middle [of a word], "abundance" occurs when a **yod** or **vav** is added, as in **bent down** <note>original Hebrew: כָּפוּף, *kafuf*</note>. In Psalm 145: "He raises up all who are bowed down." For its root is **to bend** <note>original Hebrew: כָּפַף, *kafaf*</note>.

At the end of words, various letters "abound" <note>are added redundantly</note>, such as the **yod** in **milifnei** <note>original Hebrew: מִלִּפְנֵי</note> in Psalm 114: "The earth trembled at the presence of the Lord." In that passage, Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the preeminent 11th-century Jewish commentator</note> wrote that the **yod** is redundant, just as it is in the word **hamagbihi** <note>original Hebrew: הַמַּגְבִּיהִי</note> in Psalm 113: "Who dwells on high." It is the same in the following word, **hamashpili** <note>original Hebrew: הַמַּשְׁפִּילִי, meaning "who humbles Himself"</note>, and in many other words you will find in that same psalm. 

Likewise, the letter **aleph** in the word for ten thousand, **ribo** <note>original Hebrew: רִבּוֹא</note>, is redundant, for the word means the same thing even without the **aleph**. You will find many similar examples while reading the Bible; let this brief mention of them suffice for you as the first steps of your basic training.

Furthermore, since we have touched upon the subject of "irregularity" <note>the author uses the term "exorbitantia" to describe words that deviate from standard grammatical rules</note>, I will not neglect to inform you that often the same meaning is signified even when letters or syllables are transposed. For example: **keves** and **keshev** <note>original Hebrew: כֶּבֶשׂ and כֶּשֶׂב; both mean "lamb"</note>, **gema** and **agam** <note>original Hebrew: גֹּמֶא (papyrus/reed) and אֲגַם (marsh/pool)</note>, **shachis** and **sachish** <note>original Hebrew: שָׁחִיס and סָחִישׁ; grain that grows of its own accord</note>, and **salmah** and **simlah** <note>original Hebrew: שַׂלְמָה and שִׂמְלָה; "garment" or "cloak"</note>, as well as **ga’ar** and **raga** <note>original Hebrew: גָּעַר (to rebuke) and רָגַע (to be at rest/undisturbed)</note>. 

There are other nouns which, with a single sound, signify different things depending on their gender. For instance, **Koheleth** <note>original Hebrew: קֹהֶלֶת</note> in the feminine is the same as "an assembly" <note>Latin: concio</note>, but in the masculine it refers to "Ecclesiastes" or "the Preacher." Likewise, **Knesset** <note>original Hebrew: כְּנֶסֶת</note>, when it signifies a gathering of people or a council, is read as masculine; however, when it refers to any other type of heap or collection, it is read as feminine. And what of this? That a single thing can be named by different words of different genders, just as in Latin we have *vestis* and *vestimentum* [both meaning "garment"], so in Hebrew we have **simlah** and **beged** <note>original Hebrew: שִׂמְלָה (feminine) and בֶּגֶד (masculine)</note>.

Since we have touched upon a few "defective" forms, we must certainly not omit this: the Hebrew language "lacks" the comparative and superlative degrees <note>Hebrew does not have specific word endings like the English "-er" and "-est"</note>, in such a way that they cannot express them with a single word. Instead, they form the comparative thus: they join the adverb **yoter** <note>original Hebrew: יוֹתֵר</note>—which means "plus" or "more"—to an adjective. For example, if I wished to say "John is more righteous than his neighbor," I would take the adjective "righteous," **tzaddik** <note>original Hebrew: צַדִּיק</note>, and follow it with the adverb **yoter**, which governs...

### BOOK THREE

...John is **more righteous than his neighbor** <note>original Latin: "suo proximo plus iustus"; original Hebrew: יוחנן צדיק יותר מרעהו (Yochanan tzaddik yoter mere'ehu)</note>. In this phrasing, the substantive verb—namely, "is"—is missing. This is a common property in the frequent usage of the Hebrew language: the verb "to be" is often omitted, just as we sometimes omit certain categories of words in our own speech. Therefore, the Latin reader must mentally supply the word "is." 

Take care not to forget this. I wish to give you a command to remember forever, and you should always have this verse by Alexander <note>Alexander de Villa Dei, a 13th-century grammarian whose "Doctrinale" was a standard medieval textbook</note> on your lips: *"You must often seek the substantive verb from outside,"* for this is very much the case in this specific language. 

The **superlative** <note>the "most" or "greatest" form of an adjective</note> is constructed in two ways:

First, by adding the word "exceedingly" or "very," namely **me’od** <note>original Hebrew: מאד</note>, to the adjective. If I wish to say "the most" or "very many," I speak thus: **rav me’od** <note>original Hebrew: רב מאד</note>, as seen in Joshua 11: "Exceedingly many." Likewise, "the best" is **tov me’od** <note>original Hebrew: טוב מאד</note> in Genesis 1. Jerome <note>The 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible</note> approves of this in Numbers 12, where he correctly translated **anav me’od** <note>original Hebrew: ענו מאד</note> as "the most humble" <note>original Latin: "mitissimus"</note>. In this form, it similarly governs a comparison using a prefixed particle, as in the place already cited.

Secondly, where Holy Scripture **doubles** the same adjective, it intends to indicate the excellence of the superlative. For example, in Jeremiah 24: "Good, very good; and bad, very bad" <note>original Latin: "Bonas bonas ualde et malas malas ualde"</note>. It is as if the author were saying "the very best," if it were permitted for us—as it is for the Greeks—to form a superlative from another superlative. 

However, the **doubling of a noun** <note>original Latin: "nomen substantiuum"</note> signifies individual items, specific types, or "each and every one." For example, **matteh matteh** <note>original Hebrew: מטה מטה</note> in Numbers 17 means "each individual rod." And in Leviticus 17, where we find **ish ish** <note>original Hebrew: איש איש</note>, our standard translation renders it simply as "a man," but it is more accurately translated as "each man" or "everyone." Indeed, a little further down in the text, it is translated as "any man whatsoever."

Furthermore, the **doubling of verbs** signifies the intensity of the action, as is clear to anyone reading the Hebrew Bible. However, some words are not merely doubled but are composite, such as **sachsach** or **sas’ah** <note>original Hebrew: סכסך and סאסאה</note>, whose simple forms are **sa’ah** and **sach**. 

Because the **participle** among the Hebrews is included within the category of the "noun" (as we said above, it is essentially not a separate part of speech), we must ask: what is a participle but a <term>verbal noun</term>? We give you this rule regarding the participle: understand that everything taught regarding the noun applies equally to the participle. You could indeed include that part of speech under the "verb," following the opinion of the grammarian of Caesarea <note>Priscian, the influential 6th-century Latin grammarian</note>. For Priscian says in his fifteenth book: "What is a participle but a verb that can be declined with cases?" Therefore, when we reach that section, we will teach what is necessary regarding it, provided my memory serves. In the meantime, it will be enough for you to know the partici...

**BOOK THREE**

...[partici]ple <note>original Latin: "pium" (likely the end of "participium")</note>, according to its genders and declensions, is treated no differently than the noun. 

It remains now that we should not refuse to briefly interpose a few points concerning the **pronoun** <note>original Latin: "pnomine"</note>, which is a part of speech we have chosen to include under the category of the noun itself. Therefore, some pronouns are **demonstrative** <note>pointing words, such as "this" or "that"</note> and some are **relative** <note>words that refer back to something already mentioned, such as "who" or "which"</note>. 

Do not let our presentation of this primary division lead you into amazement; for we cannot always imitate the Latin grammarians, just as the Latins cannot always imitate the Greeks. Since I find that not even the Hebrews themselves have treated this specific matter, it will nevertheless be necessary to show the unlearned <note>original Latin: "rudibus," referring to beginners or students</note> the way in which they can understand such expressions and constructions in the Hebrew tongue <note>original Latin: "sermone iudaico"</note>.

Now I return to the matter at hand. Of the demonstratives, some are demonstratives and articles simultaneously, such as those which only indicate the cases of words. Others are demonstratives alone, which point to the actual person of things. We must write concerning the former in the first place. 

The **articles**, which I also partially mentioned above, are five for the Hebrews: 

**He, Shin, Lamed, Et, Mem** <note>original Hebrew: ה ש ל את מ</note>.

<meta>This page continues the grammatical analysis of Hebrew articles, specifically focusing on the five prefix letters that function as case markers, following the previous discussion on the nature of pronouns as a subset of nouns.</meta>

->**BOOK THREE**<-

**The first article is He** <note>original Hebrew: ה</note> in the vocative case <note>used for addressing someone</note>. Deuteronomy 32: "Give ear, O heavens" <note>original Hebrew: הַאֲזִינוּ הַשָּׁמַיִם</note>. Also: "and the earth" <note>original Hebrew: אֶת הָאָרֶץ</note>. 

"Hear, O heavens." <note>original Latin: "audite cęli"</note> In the ablative <note>indicating 'from' or 'in'</note>, as in Genesis 2: "On the seventh day" <note>original Hebrew: בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי</note>, that is, "In the seventh day." 

We use this article quite frequently to explain the genitive case <note>indicating possession, like 'of'</note> because the nominative case <note>the subject</note> often lacks an article. **The second article is Shin** <note>original Hebrew: שֶׁ</note> as in the Song of Songs: "Tell me, [you whom] my soul [loves]" <note>original Latin: "Indica mihi dilectionis anima mea," literally: the strength and sinews of my love</note>. Our translation <note>referring to the Latin Vulgate bible</note> reads: "Tell me, whom my soul loveth." But sometimes it is an article and sometimes a relative pronoun signifying "what," "who," or "which," as seen below. 

**The third article is Lamed** <note>original Hebrew: ל</note>, and it serves the dative case <note>indicating 'to' or 'for'</note>. Ecclesiastes 3: "God gave to the sons of men." Since even among the Latins the dative often signifies the place toward which or into which something is destined. Virgil in the *Aeneid* says: "The spear flies through both temples of Tagus" <note>original Latin: "Volat hasta tago per tempus utrumque"</note>, which Priscian in Book 18 explains as *tago* being used for "to" or "into" Tagus. Therefore, it also sometimes signifies "to," as when we read Psalm 54: "Turn back the evils to my enemies," where the article **Lamed** is placed before the word "enemies." It would be more correctly read as: "Turn back the evils *to* my enemies," because it follows: "and in your truth destroy them." The Hebrews use it in superscriptions, titles, epitaphs, and the calculation of the years of the world in place of the genitive, such as "A Psalm of David" <note>original Latin: "ipsius Dauid," meaning belonging to David</note>. 

**The fourth article is Et** <note>original Hebrew: אֶת</note>, which, it seems to me, was sufficiently explained above in the first book of our dictionary.

**The fifth article is the letter Mem** <note>original Hebrew: מ</note>, and it is joined to the ablative case alone, having the same force as "from" or "by." Although it may appear to be a preposition, we nevertheless use it in the place of an article. This is similar to the letter **Bet** <note>original Hebrew: בְּ</note>, which is sometimes a preposition of place, as in Genesis 3: "Walking in paradise," and sometimes it only indicates the seventh case <note>the ablative</note> and nothing else, as in Exodus 13: "For with a strong hand he led you out." For this, it would be more correctly said: "With a strong hand he led you out." Regarding this case, Servius and Priscian <note>noted Roman grammarians</note> disagree with each other; whatever the truth may be, you would more correctly say "I struck you with a staff" than "I struck you *in* a staff." 

That **Mem** is sometimes written with a *tsere* <note>a Hebrew vowel mark indicating an 'e' sound</note>, as in Ecclesiastes 3: "From the head" <note>original Hebrew: מֵרֹאשׁ</note>, which we read as "from the beginning even to the end." At other times, however, it is written with a *hirik* <note>a vowel mark for the 'i' sound</note>, and then it seems to be derived from the word *min* <note>original Hebrew: מִן</note>, which signifies the same thing; it would thus be an apocope <note>the loss of a sound at the end of a word</note>. Look for this in the dictionary. After the articles which demonstrate the cases of nouns, I will show you the pronouns which demonstrate the persons of things. Therefore, the demonstratives of the first person singular follow.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of Hebrew relative pronouns (words like "who," "which," or "that") and begins a new section on "affixes"—what we would today call possessive suffixes (like "his," "my," or "your") attached to the ends of words.</meta>

**BOOK**

<note>original: "quarto"</note> fourth chapter: "all with twin offspring" <note>referring to Song of Songs 4:2</note>; and in the fifth chapter of the same: "My head is filled with dew" <note>Song of Songs 5:2</note>. Likewise, it is placed before and after articles. In the first chapter of the Song of Songs: "My own vineyard I have not kept" <note>Song of Songs 1:6</note>, where it is placed before a dative <note>the 'to/for' case</note>. Similarly in the third chapter of the same: "Behold the couch of Solomon" <note>Song of Songs 3:7</note>. It is placed after in the same chapter: "I will seek him whom my soul loves" <note>Song of Songs 3:2</note>. 

Just as among the Greeks the article "the" <note>original: ὁ (ho)</note> and the conjunction "that" <note>original: ὅτι (hoti)</note>, and among the Latins the word "that" <note>original: quod</note> are equal in meaning, so the <term>relative particle</term> <note>the Hebrew prefix שׁ־ (She-)</note> sometimes signifies "that," "because," "since," "when," "at which time," or "by which." In the third chapter of the Song of Songs: "When I had passed a little" <note>Song of Songs 3:4</note>. In the first chapter: "That I am dark" <note>Song of Songs 1:5</note>, and in the same place: "Because the sun has discolored me" <note>Song of Songs 1:6</note>. 

And it agrees closely with the word <term>Asher</term> <note>Hebrew: אֲשֶׁר, the standard word for 'who' or 'which'</note>, as in the fourth chapter of the Song of Songs: "Like the flocks of shorn sheep which come up from the washing" <note>Song of Songs 4:2</note>. It is also joined to other connecting words both before and after, as in the fifth chapter: "For you have so adjured us" <note>Song of Songs 5:9</note>, and in the third: "Until she herself wills" <note>Song of Songs 3:5</note>, meaning "until when." It also receives prefixes <note>original: cata prothesin</note> such as B, V, and K <note>Hebrew: בוכ</note>. Indeed, the word "which" <note>Hebrew: אֲשֶׁר (Asher)</note> is joined in the same way to those same three letters and to all articles, for which examples are not needed, because this is common and everyday in the Holy Scriptures.

Now let us move on to the **affixes**. Although these are relatives, they nevertheless seem to signify a certain possession. For they recall the memory of that which we spoke of a little while ago, and they nonetheless indicate that something belongs to that same person we mentioned. For example, when the Lord God speaks to the people in Leviticus 18: "I am the Lord your God; keep my laws." You must remember: whose laws? Surely the laws of him who spoke: "I am the Lord." So in Psalm 2: "The Lord said to me, you are my son," that is, the son of him who said this to you. 

For if someone were simply to write on a wall: "Hear my words," or "This land shall be yours," or "He lost what was his," it would be as if nothing were written at all, because no one understands who is being written about. This is because the person to whom these pronouns—"my," "your," "his"—refer is missing. Therefore, so that I do not create more categories than is necessary, I have included those words which the Latins call "possessives" under the "relatives," and I have named them **affixes**. 

To stay with an example familiar to you, take the word **His word** <note>Hebrew: דברו (Devaro)</note> before your eyes. Remember that the Jews count in a way opposite to us: first the third person, second the second person, and third the first person, in both pronouns and verbs. 

**His word** <note>Hebrew: דברו (Devaro)</note>: see how the added letter *vav* <note>the 'o' sound at the end of the Hebrew word</note> signifies the third person of whom we speak—namely "his," "of him," or "of that one." And in this kind of speaking, it sometimes happens that the letter *vav* is changed into—

->**BOOK THREE**<-

**Ezekiel 12**: "And all who are around him, his aid and his troops," where for **his aid** <note>original: עזרך (*ezrecha*); the author is noting a variation where the usual suffix for "his" is replaced</note> is found **his aid** <note>original: עזרתה (*ezratah*)</note>, meaning his help and protection. In such a phrasing, the letter <term>he</term> <note>the Hebrew letter ה</note> is often placed before <term>vau</term> <note>the Hebrew letter ו</note> to signify the same thing. **Job 25**: "And upon whom shall his light not rise?" where for **his light** <note>original: אורו (*oro*)</note>, **his light** <note>original: אורהו (*orahu*)</note> is used.

**Your word** <note>original: דברך (*Debarcha*)</note>. Note that the final letter <term>kaph</term> <note>the Hebrew letter ך</note> with the vowel <term>qamets</term> <note>a vowel mark sounding like 'ah'</note> signifies the second person, the one to whom we are speaking. Generally, when this is placed at the end of a sentence, the vowel <term>segol</term> <note>a vowel mark sounding like 'eh'</note> is written in the second-to-last syllable: **your word** <note>original: דברך (*debe-recha*)</note>. However, this is sometimes not observed, as in **Psalm 119**: "You have done good with your servant." Sometimes the breathing sound of the letter <term>he</term> is added after the <term>kaph</term> at the end. **Exodus 13**: "And it shall be as a sign upon your hand," where **your hand** <note>original: ידכה (*yadchah*)</note> is used.

**My word** <note>original: דברי (*Debari*)</note>. Consider that the final letter <term>yod</term> <note>the Hebrew letter י</note> signifies the first person, specifically the one who is speaking. Sometimes the letter <term>nun</term> <note>the Hebrew letter נ</note> is placed before that final <term>yod</term>. For example, in **2 Samuel 22**: "You have bowed down those resisting me under me," where **under me** <note>original: תחתי (*tachti*)</note> is used, which in **Psalm 18** is read as **under me** <note>original: תחתני (*tachtani*)</note> with the <term>nun</term> added.

We have now dispatched the suffixes of the masculine gender in the singular number; let us now approach the suffixes of the masculine gender in the plural number.

**Their word** <note>original: דברם (*Debaram*)</note>. Here, the final <term>mem</term> <note>the Hebrew letter ם</note> signifies several people of whom we are speaking, even though the word itself is a single thing we are discussing. Sometimes the breathing sound of the letter <term>he</term> precedes the final <term>mem</term> and signifies the same thing, as in **Jeremiah 12**: "You are near to **their mouth**" <note>original: פיהם (*pihem*)</note>. But even when that breathing sound is omitted, we often find the letter <term>vau</term> following the <term>mem</term> at the end. An example of this same word for "mouth" is found in **Psalm 59**: "The sin of **their mouth** in the speech of their lips," and **Psalm 17**: "**Their mouth** has spoken pride," where **their mouth** <note>original: פיהמו (*pihemo*)</note> is used.

**Your [plural] word** <note>original: דברכם (*Debarchem*)</note>. In this way, when <term>kaph</term> and <term>mem</term> are attached to words, they signify the second person plural (the ones to whom we are speaking) in the masculine gender. This suffix also accepts articles, such as **you** <note>original: אתכם (*etchem*)</note> in **Song of Songs 8**: "I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem."

**Our word** <note>original: דברנו (*Debarenu*)</note>. Here, the letters <term>nun</term> and <term>vau</term> signify the first person plural (those who are speaking) of the masculine gender, even if the thing they are speaking about is a single item.

Thus far, we have covered the attached pronouns which are called masculine suffixes.

**His warriors** <note>Hebrew: גִּבּוֹרָיו (*gibborav*)</note>, which is read as "the shield of his mighty men" <note>original Latin: *clypeus fortium eius*; a reference to the biblical book of Nahum 2:3</note>. This holds true for both the masculine and feminine gender regarding the <term>affixes</term> <note>suffixes added to the end of a word to indicate possession</note>; however, regarding the noun itself, there will be a different rule. Now we prepare ourselves for the plural number: **their words** <note>Hebrew: דְּבָרֵיהֶם (*debareihem*)</note>.

It is customary, however, for a breathy <term>he</term> <note>the letter ה</note> to sometimes follow after a <term>final mem</term> <note>the letter ם, the form of 'm' used only at the end of a word</note>. As in **Ezekiel, chapter 40**: "In their chambers and in their vestibules" <note>original Latin: *In thalamis et in frontibus eorum*</note>, where **unto them** <note>Hebrew: אֲלֵיהֵמָּה (*aleihemah*)</note> is used in place of that which regularly ought to be said, **unto them** <note>Hebrew: אֲלֵיהֶם (*aleihem*)</note>.

**Your words** <note>Hebrew: דְּבָרֵיכֶם (*debareichem*)</note>, as you were able to see in the previous parts.

**Our words** <note>Hebrew: דְּבָרֵינוּ (*debareinu*)</note>, which the feminine form also matches. 

In the feminine gender of affixes, however, when the suffixes themselves are singular but the preceding noun is plural, take this as your example: **her words** <note>Hebrew: דְּבָרֶיהָ (*debareiha*)</note>, that is to say, belonging to a wom[an]...

...are verbal and denominative nouns, which we mentioned a little earlier in this third book when we were writing about the abundance of letters. 1. First, composition <note>when two words are joined together</note>.
2. Second, the article <note>including prefixes like "the" or "in"</note>.
3. Third, the derivational appendage. 
4. Fourth, gender. 
5. Fifth, declension. 
6. Sixth, <term>epenthesis</term> and <term>paragoge</term> <note>original: *epenthesin et paragogen*; these are technical terms for inserting a letter into the middle of a word or adding one to the end for the sake of sound or emphasis</note>.

This word has six letters, of which only three are those that constitute the <term>primitive body</term> <note>original: *corpus primitiui*; the fundamental three-letter root that carries the primary meaning of the word</note>. First, the letter *beth* <note>the letter ב</note>, which serves as a <term>consignificative preposition</term> <note>a preposition that is attached directly to the start of a word; here it means "in"</note>, must be rejected according to the rule about articles/prefixes placed in the fifth section. The letter *resh* <note>the letter ר</note>, however, is a substantial letter, and therefore cannot be rejected...

**BOOK THREE**

...it can, as was shown a little above. The letters *Yod* and *Tav* form the feminine gender ending for ordinal numbers <note>numbers indicating position in a series, such as "first" or "second"</note> whose masculine forms end in *Yod*, as discussed above regarding ordinal nouns of the second declension. Therefore, the ending [תּי] <note>Hebrew: *-ti*</note> must be discarded. Because we have reached the substantial letter <note>referring to the *Resh* (ר) identified on the previous page as part of the core root</note> that remained intact before all others, we still need two more letters so that the <term>trinity of the primitive</term> <note>original: *ternarius primitiui*; the standard three-letter Hebrew root structure</note> may be completed. We shall leave the letters *Aleph* [א] and *Shin* [ש] entirely untouched. Thus, [ראשׁ] <note>Hebrew: *Rosh*, meaning "head" or "beginning"</note> will remain as the primitive root of this word *Bereshit*. Look for this root diligently in our dictionary according to the alphabetical order, and you will find its meaning.

Now, choose another word for yourself. Perhaps you would like one from the Psalms—namely, [וּבְתוֹרָתוֹ] <note>Hebrew: *u-ve-torato*</note>, which means "and in his law." First, the letter *Vav* [ו], meaning "and," is a <term>consignificative particle</term> <note>a prefix that adds meaning but is not part of the root</note> and must therefore be discarded. Second, the letter *Beth* [ב], meaning "in," is handled in the same way. Third, the first *Tav* [ת] makes this a verbal noun, for we should read it as "and in his instruction" rather than simply "and in his law." Since it is a <term>Heemantic letter</term> <note>original: *litera heamanthi*; a mnemonic for the specific Hebrew letters (ה, א, מ, נ, ת, י) used as prefixes or suffixes to form nouns and verbs from a root</note> in this context, it must also be discarded.

Fourth, the second *Tav* [ת] has been substituted for the letter *He* [ה] because of the <term>construct state</term> <note>original: *statum regiminis*; a grammatical state where a noun is linked to the following word, often causing its ending to change, such as "law" becoming "law of..."</note>, as we taught above. Fifth, the final *Vav* [ו] is an <term>affix</term> <note>a suffix meaning "his"</note> and must therefore be discarded. However, the letter *Resh* [ר] is one of the substantial letters and must remain.

If we wish to preserve three letters for the root, nothing remains but *Vav*, *Resh*, and *He* [ו ר ה]. However, it is clear from the dictionary how rarely the letter *Vav* can begin a word, and it certainly cannot do so here. What then? You must remember that there is an easy and symbolic transition between the letters *Tav* and *He*. Therefore, set down [הרה] <note>Hebrew: *Yarah*, the root of *Torah*, meaning to instruct or shoot</note> as its primitive root (noting that the vowel *Cholem* replaces the *Vav*). Then, seek its meaning in the dictionary. Act similarly with other words.

Exercise your diligence vigorously, for this will help you understand almost every noun in the Hebrew Bible. Do not let the weariness of repeated labor discourage you if, at first, you dismantle a word in vain or fail to correctly "strip" a root that is hidden beneath many grammatical layers. You will tire yourself with constant searching in our dictionary until, at last, you emerge victorious in a great triumph. But now, let us move on to the second part of speech.

# THE THIRD [BOOK]

## ON THE VERB

Of Hebrew verbs, some are **perfect** and others are **imperfect**. 
Those are called **perfect** which contain three <term>substantial letters</term> <note>the fundamental letters that make up the core meaning of a root</note>, such as [פעל] <note>Hebrew: *Pa’al*, the traditional paradigm for "to do" or "to act"</note>. **Imperfect** verbs are those which either lack some of the substantial letters or have an excess of them. 

Those which have an excess we call **heavy**, or, because of the number of letters, **quadrate** <note>four-lettered roots</note>, such as [רומם] <note>Hebrew: *Romem*, meaning "to exalt"</note>. Those which lack letters are called **defective**. 

Furthermore, among the imperfect verbs, some are **compounds** and some are **simple**. **Compounds** are those whose parts were [originally] distinct verbs, such as [בלבל] <note>Hebrew: *Bilbel*, "to confuse/confound"</note> and [סכסך] <note>Hebrew: *Sikhsekh*, "to stir up/interweave"</note>. 

Finally, among the **simple** verbs, some are **defective in letters**, such as [את] <note>Hebrew: *At*, "to come"</note> and [בא] <note>Hebrew: *Ba*, "to enter"</note>. Others are **defective in sound** <note>original: *uocū* (vocum); referring to irregularities in pronunciation or vowel changes</note>, such as [שוא] <note>Hebrew: *Shav*, "to return"</note> and [ירא] <note>Hebrew: *Yara*, "to fear"</note>. 

The <term>accidents</term> <note>grammatical properties such as person, number, and tense</note> of verbs are numerous and have been treated with great skill by both the Greeks and the Latins. We omit a large part of these in this book of *Rudiments* <note>a basic introductory textbook</note> not out of any laziness, but because we have included only what is necessary for the Hebrew language, providing the basics for those beginning their education. 

To the verb, therefore, belong **three persons**, which we shall list according to the custom of the Hebrews...
