# BOOK [THE THIRD]

Observe how I cause the act of writing to pass into you, and yet it does not rest in you, but passes further into a third thing—namely, the letters being written. This is called the "transitive of the third." From this, you can learn the three offices of the transitive verb, which will be of the greatest benefit to you regarding the conjugations and their meanings. 

The conjugations of verbs are four:
1. First: **Pa’al** <note>Hebrew: פָּעַל; the simple or "light" active form, now commonly called Qal</note>
2. Second: **Pi’el** <note>Hebrew: פִּעֵל; the intensive active form</note>
3. Third: **Hif’il** <note>Hebrew: הִפְעִיל; the causative active form</note>
4. Fourth: **Hitpa’el** <note>Hebrew: הִתְפַּעֵל; the reflexive form</note>

We shall first speak of the first conjugation in general. It has three endings: **a**, **e**, and **o**, while the <term>qamets</term> <note>original: *camez*; a long "a" vowel sound represented by a small T-shaped mark under a letter</note> always remains in the first syllable, as in:
*   *shakan* <note>Hebrew: שָׁכַן, "he dwelt"</note>
*   *male* <note>Hebrew: מָלֵא, "he was full"</note>
*   *yakhol* <note>Hebrew: יָכֹל, "he was able"</note>

If you wish to commit these to memory, you can do so clearly with this single verse read in the fortieth chapter of Exodus: "And Moses was not able to enter the tent of the covenant, for the cloud covered all things, and the majesty of the Lord was shining, which had filled all things." In this passage, these three examples are written in Hebrew. 

This conjugation is rightly called "light" <note>Latin: *levis*; a translation of the Hebrew term *Qal*</note> because it is not increased by any luxury <note>i.e., it lacks the heavy doubling or prefixing of other forms</note>. It does not delight in a surplus of letters, and it accepts nothing external to the primitive root; rather, it only allows those letters to be joined which are necessarily added to identify persons, genders, and numbers. These are the foundations of conjugation, and therefore we shall use them in the present work as the foundation of all verbs in this manner:

->**OF THE PAST TENSE**<-
->**MASCULINE GENDER**<-

| We did | You (pl.) did | They did | I did | You (sing.) did | He did |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| פָּעַלְנוּ | פְּעַלְתֶּם | פָּעֲלוּ | פָּעַלְתִּי | פָּעַלְתָּ | פָּעַל |
| <note>pa-al-nu</note> | <note>pe-al-tem</note> | <note>pa-a-lu</note> | <note>pa-al-ti</note> | <note>pa-al-ta</note> | <note>pa-al</note> |

->**FEMININE GENDER**<-

| You (pl.) did | You (sing.) did | She did |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| פְּעַלְתֶּן | פָּעַלְתְּ | פָּעֲלָה |
| <note>pe-al-ten</note> | <note>pa-alt</note> | <note>pa-a-lah</note> |

**RULE:** In every conjugation of the past tense, the first person and the third person of both numbers are of common gender, as you see here, because they are applied to both a man and a woman. 

**Another Rule:** At a distinction, a member, or a boundary <note>referring to "pausal" positions at the end of a phrase or verse</note>, the <term>pathach</term> <note>a short "a" vowel</note> of this conjugation is changed into a <term>qamets</term> <note>a long "a" vowel</note>. 

As in Genesis 21: "The Lord visited Sarah as he had promised." Likewise in Psalm 1: "And in the seat..." <note>Original Latin: *Visitauit aut dominus Saram sicut promiserat* (Gen 21:1) and *Et in cathedra* (Ps 1:1)</note>

**The Third Rule.** The first termination of this conjugation keeps the *pathach* in the second syllable for the second person and thereafter. The accent falls on that same syllable, and it marks the letter *taw* <note>original: *thau*</note>—which contains a *dagesh* <note>A dot indicating the letter is "doubled" or hardened.</note>—with a *qamets* point. The third person of the plural number keeps the *qamets* in the first syllable and the *pathach* in the second-to-last, except in cases of "distinction, member, and term" <note>Referring to "pausal forms" where the rhythm of the sentence at a break or end changes the vowel sounds.</note>, where it changes the *pathach* to a *qamets*. # BOOK THREE

The second person plural number marks the first [letter] with a *sheva* <note>original: *pūcto seua*; a very short, neutral vowel sound</note>, the middle with a *pathach* <note>original: *patha*; a short "a" sound</note>, and the last—that is, the letter *taw* <note>original: *thau*</note>—with a *segol* <note>a short "e" sound</note>. However, a *hiriq* <note>original: *hirik*; an "ee" sound</note> is sometimes found in place of the *pathach*, and occasionally a *segol* or *tzere* <note>original: *zere*; a long "e" sound</note>. But this is not the regular rule. The accent is always and without distinction on the last syllable, whether a *vav* <note>original: *vau*</note> is prefixed or not.

I move now to the future tense of the indicative mood, which changes its persons according to a certain mnemonic name that contains four letters. ...are resolved by the same. As in Lamentations 3: "I will remember with memory" <note>original Latin: *Memoria memor ero*</note>. More accurately: "By remembering, you shall remember" <note>original Latin: *Recordando recordaberis*</note>.

Because gerunds <term>Gerund: a verb form that functions as a noun, like the "-ing" in "running"</term> are called "participial verbs," they are often interpreted as participles. For example, Psalm 118 says: "The Lord has chastened me by chastening" <note>original Latin: *Castigans castigavit me dominus*</note>, which could be translated as "by chastening" <note>original Latin: *castigando*</note>.

They are also frequently used as infinitives <term>Infinitive: the basic form of a verb, usually preceded by "to" in English, like "to eat"</term>, as in Micah 6: "To do justice and to walk with your God."

However, more commonly, to indicate the infinitive, the letter *lamed* <note>the Hebrew letter ל, which often functions like the English word "to"</note> is placed before it, as was noted above regarding the *Bachlem* <note>a mnemonic for the Hebrew prefix letters: Bet, Caph, Lamed, and Mem</note>, even though other letters also mark the infinitive and the supine <term>Supine: a verbal noun used in specific Latin and Hebrew grammatical constructions</term>. For instance, Ecclesiastes 1: "The eye is not satisfied by seeing, nor the ear filled by hearing," meaning "the eye is not satisfied *to see*, nor the ear *to hear*."

Regarding that same word "to walk" which I mentioned above without the *lamed*, an example is found in that same chapter of Ecclesiastes 1 using the *lamed* prefix: "to the place from which the rivers go out, they return so that they may flow again"—or more accurately, "they return by flowing." Thus, the Hebrew language uses gerunds interchangeably.

# BOOK

You should be told that a neuter or absolute verb <note>original: "uerbum neutrum siue absolutum," referring to intransitive verbs that do not take a direct object</note> does not form a passive conjugation from itself, especially in this "light" conjugation <term>Qal: the basic, most common form of the Hebrew verb, often called "light" because it has no added prefixes or doubled letters to change its meaning</term> of verbs. It ends in either a *patha*, a *camez*, or a *holem* <note>Hebrew vowel sounds: 'a', 'ah', and 'oh'</note> and is regulated according to the active form from which it is derived; if it is not at the end of a sentence, it keeps the *patha* at the end. 

If a verb begins with one of the guttural letters <note>original: "uocalibus אחהע" (Aleph, He, Het, Ayin)</note>, then the prefixed letter *nun* <note>the letter נ used to indicate the passive form</note> widens the mouth and is marked by a *segol* <note>an 'eh' sound</note> or sometimes by a *patha*, because the original vowel is shortened and marked with either a *seua* <note>a very short 'e' or a stop</note> or a *hateph* <note>a "hurried" reduced vowel</note>. If that same vowel is silenced entirely, then the *nun* of the first syllable can be found marked with a *holem* <note>the 'o' sound</note>.

Many things will occur that seem irregular to you, but these are not regulated according to this "light" conjugation, but are organized according to the "doubled" <term>Dagesh: a dot placed inside a letter to emphasize it or double its sound</term> or other conjugations. **However, while you are still a little one <note>a beginner in the language</note>, learn as a little one does.** In the remaining inflections of the verb—such as the future, the imperative, and the gerunds—when the letters *he* or *aleph* repel the *nun* of the passive meaning, the first letter receives a *dagesh* to show the missing letter *nun*.

Thus far, we have spoken of the general form of conjugating as much as you can bear; now we shall proceed to each specific conjugation in order.

The last syllable sometimes ends in a <term>Pathah: a short 'a' vowel sound, written as a horizontal line under a letter</term>. ### THIRD
to be visited
The Infinitive <note>original Hebrew: הִפָּקֵד (hippaqed)</note> sometimes drops the letter *he* (ה); specifically, when a *beth* (ב) is prefixed, it drives out the *he*. Sometimes an *aleph* (א) is placed instead of the *he*.

### SECOND CONJUGATION
<note>original Hebrew: פִּקֵּד (piqqed)</note> A "heavy verb" <term>heavy verb: In Latin "Verbum grave," referring to the Piel conjugation, which is "heavy" because the middle root letter is doubled.</term> in the third person, singular number, masculine gender; in the past tense, indicative mood, with an active meaning. It is a second transitive form belonging to the "dageshed" conjugation <term>dageshed: referring to the dagesh forte, a dot placed in a letter to double its sound, a hallmark of this verb group.</term>, which is conjugated as follows:

->he visited | she visited | you (masc.) visited | you (fem.) visited | I visited | they visited | you (masc. pl.) visited | you (fem. pl.) visited | we visited<-
-><note>original Hebrew: פִּקֵּד פִּקְּדָה פִּקַּדְתָּ פִּקַּדְתְּ פִּקַּדְתִּי פִּקְּדוּ פִּקַּדְתֶּם פִּקַּדְתֶּן פִּקַּדְנוּ</note><-

->she visited | you (fem. sing.) visited | you (fem. plural) visited<-
-><note>original Hebrew: פִּקְּדָה פִּקַּדְתְּ פִּקַּדְתָּן</note><-

The third person singular masculine receives the endings *tsere* and *pathach* <term>tsere and pathach: Hebrew vowel marks indicating "e" and "a" sounds respectively.</term> and the first letter is pronounced with a *hiriq* <term>hiriq: a Hebrew vowel mark for the "i" sound.</term>. The middle letter is always "dageshed" <note>pronounced with a doubled or strengthened sound</note> unless it is a vowel-like letter <note>a guttural</note> or the letter *resh* (ר).

### THIRD CONJUGATION
<note>original Hebrew: הִפְקִיד (hiphqid)</note> A "heavy verb" <term>heavy verb: In this context, "Verbum grave" refers to the Hiphil conjugation, which is "heavy" because it adds extra letters to the root to change the meaning to a causative action (e.g., "to cause to visit").</term> in the third person, singular number, masculine gender; in the past tense, indicative mood, with an active meaning. ->he caused to visit | she caused to visit | you (masc.) caused to visit | you (fem.) caused to visit | I caused to visit<-

It is called "heavy" because it adds something external to the inflection of the root—namely, a *he* (ה) at the beginning and a *yod* (י) in the final syllable. I would also like you to learn this diligently: when a vowel-like letter <note>a guttural</note> follows the *he*, such as <note>original Hebrew: א ה ח ע ר</note>, then in this conjugation the *he* is marked with a *segol* <term>segol: a Hebrew vowel mark for an "e" sound.</term>, as in <note>original Hebrew: הֶעֱמִיד (he’emid, meaning "he stationed")</note>.
In the present tense: <note>original Hebrew: מַפְקִיד (maphqid)</note>
->causing to visit (masc. sing.) | causing to visit (fem. sing.) | causing to visit (masc. pl.) | causing to visit (fem. pl.)<-

The adjectival verb <note>original Hebrew: מַפְקִיד (maphqid)</note>.

The Imperative: <note>original Hebrew: הַפְקֵד הַפְקִידוּ הַפְקִידִי הַפְקֵדְנָה (haphqed, haphqidu, haphqidi, haphqednah)</note>
->Assign! (masc. sing.) | Assign! (masc. pl.) | Assign! (fem. sing.) | Assign! (fem. pl.)<-

The masculine singular is also pronounced with both *tsere* and *patach*; and in a pause <term>pause: a formal stop in the liturgical reading of the text that often changes vowel sounds.</term>, a *qamets* <term>qamets: a long "a" vowel.</term> is used instead of a *patach*.

The Infinitive is <note>original Hebrew: הַפְקִיד (haphqid)</note> and according to the general rule <term>general rule: translating the Greek 'catapthesin', referring to the standard grammatical form.</term> for all of them, there is a *yod* with a *chiriq* <term>chiriq: a vowel mark for the "i" sound.</term> in the last syllable.

In this conjugation, you shall note—and do not let it slip from memory—that there are three conditions for this verb type. First, it can sometimes be found as a neutral, intransitive, and absolute verb; this happens when there is no corresponding simple verb in the first conjugation <term>first conjugation: the Qal, or simple active form of the verb.</term>. For example: <note>original Hebrew: הֶחֱרִישׁ (hecherish)</note> "he was silent," as in 2 Kings 18: "The people were silent."
Second, it can be found as a transitive verb acting upon a second party; this occurs when it derives from a primitive, simple verb that is neutral or absolute. For example: <note>original Hebrew: הֵקִים (heqim)</note> "he raised up" (something). This comes from the first conjugation of the absolute verb <note>original Hebrew: קָם (qam)</note>, which means "to rise."
Finally, it can be transitive acting upon a third party; this occurs when it is derived from a simple verb that is already transitive in itself. For example: <note>original Hebrew: הִזְכִּיר (hizkir)</note> "he caused to remember." In Exodus 20: "In every place where there shall be a memory of my name, I will come to you and bless you." This, however, has not been translated according to the proper character of the Hebrew language. Indeed, it would be contrary to what our Christ spoke in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 7, when he says: "Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord," etc. Rather, it ought to be interpreted thus: "In every place where **I shall cause my name to be remembered**, I will come to you."
<margin>unless my Father draws him</margin> And here is the "drawing" of the Father of which he speaks: "Unless my Father draws him." For in the text it is written <note>original Hebrew: אַזְכִּיר (azkir)</note>, that is: "I will cause to be remembered" or "I will cause to record."

<note>original Hebrew: הָפְקַד (hophqad)</note> The verb of the passive voice (deponental) <term>deponental: a Latin grammatical term used here to describe a verb that is passive in form but indicates an action where the specific doer is not the focus.</term> whose agent is not expressed is conjugated thus:
<note>original Hebrew: הָפְקַד הָפְקְדָה הָפְקַדְתָּ הָפְקַדְתְּ הָפְקַדְתִּי הָפְקְדוּ הָפְקַדְתֶּם (hophqad, hophqedah, hophqadta, hophqadt, hophqadti, hophqedu, hophqadtem)</note>
->He was assigned | She was assigned | You (m.) were assigned | You (f.) were assigned | I was assigned | They were assigned | You (pl.) were assigned<-

# THIRD BOOK

### The Squared Conjugation
Regarding the verb to which a *vav* <term>vav: the Hebrew letter ו, here acting as a vowel marker</term> is assigned near the beginning, you should know that this occurs because of the conjugation of "perfect" verbs that double their letters, or those that absorb their middle radical letter. This is called the "squared" conjugation because of its four letters. Among the perfect verbs, we will give you this example, whether the last syllable uses a *tsere* <term>tsere: a Hebrew vowel making an "ay" or "eh" sound</term> or a *patah* <term>patah: a Hebrew vowel making an "ah" sound</term>.

**Past Indicative**
| | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| *shofat* <note>He was judged</note> | *shofatta* <note>You (m) were judged</note> | *shofatti* <note>I was judged</note> |
| *shofetu* <note>They were judged</note> | *shofetah* <note>She was judged</note> | *shofatten* <note>You (f.pl) were judged</note> |
| *shofattem* <note>You (m.pl) were judged</note> | *shofatnu* <note>We were judged</note> | *shofattan* <note>They (f) were judged</note> |

**Present**
| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| *meshofat* <note>Singular Masculine</note> | *meshofatah* <note>Singular Feminine</note> |
| *meshofatim* <note>Plural Masculine</note> | *meshofatot* <note>Plural Feminine</note> |

**Verbal Adjective (Participle)**
| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| *meshofat* <note>Singular Masculine</note> | *meshofatah* <note>Singular Feminine</note> |
| *meshofatim* <note>Plural Masculine</note> | *meshofatot* <note>Plural Feminine</note> |

**Future**
| | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| *ashofat* <note>I will be judged</note> | *tishofat* <note>You (m) will be judged</note> | *tishofeti* <note>You (f) will be judged</note> |
| *yeshofat* <note>He will be judged</note> | *yeshofetu* <note>They will be judged</note> | *tishofatnah* <note>They (f) will be judged</note> |
| *tishofat* <note>She will be judged</note> | *tishofetu* <note>You (pl) will be judged</note> | |

**Imperative**
| | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| *shofat* <note>Judge! (m.sg)</note> | *shofeti* <note>Judge! (f.sg)</note> | *shofetu* <note>Judge! (m.pl)</note> |
| *shofatnah* <note>Judge! (f.pl)</note> | | |

**Infinitive**
*shofat* / *shofatnah*

This ends the "heavy" verbs <note>original Latin: "uerborum grauium"; referring to the intensive conjugations like Piel and Pual</note>. The defective verbs follow.

Brother Dionysius, I believe I have sufficiently explained the conjugations of the perfect verbs in the previous treatise, at least as far as concerns beginners and those who are only just being initiated. It follows that I should now pursue the types of defective verbs, which take their origin from the perfect ones. I wrote in the chapter on verbs that some are "defective" in their letters, and some in their sounds. 

Now I add this for you: some are defective in their first letters, some in their middle letters, and some in their last. Those that are defective in the first letters are verbs whose roots begin with either a *nun* <note>the letter נ</note> or a *lamed* <note>the letter ל</note>.
*   *Nun* as in *nagash* <note>original Hebrew: נָגַשׁ; "he approached"</note>
*   *Lamed* as in *lakach* <note>original Hebrew: לָקַח; "he took"</note>

Let us see how the *nun* or *lamed* goes missing in the first position. In the "light" verb <note>original Latin: "verbum leue"; the Qal or simple conjugation</note>, the past is *nagash* <note>נָגַשׁ</note>, *nagashta* <note>נָגַשְׁתָּ</note>. The present is *niggash* <note>נִגָּשׁ</note>. But the future "absorbs" the letter *nun*: *eggash* <note>אֶגַּשׁ</note>, *yiggash* <note>יִגַּשׁ</note>. And sometimes the last [letter]...

...through the *holam* <term>holam: a Hebrew vowel producing an "o" sound</term> and usually the *sheva* <term>sheva: a Hebrew vowel mark indicating a very short "eh" or no vowel at all</term> changes into a *qamets* <term>qamets: a Hebrew vowel producing an "ah" sound</term> at the end, specifically at a *paseq* <term>paseq: a vertical line used in Hebrew text as a musical or textual separator</term>. It should regularly be said *hingash* <note>original: הִנְגַּשׁ</note> but because the *nun* <term>nun: the Hebrew letter נ</term> is missing, a *dagesh* <term>dagesh: a dot placed inside a Hebrew letter to indicate it is doubled or strengthened</term> point is added to the following letter, the *gimel* <note>original: ג</note>, to show that a letter has been dropped. 

**Imperative:** *negash* <note>original: נְגַשׁ</note> but in the defective <note>A "defective" form is one where a root letter is missing</note> form it is *gash* <note>original: גַּשׁ</note> and *geshu* <note>original: גְּשׁוּ</note>. 

Sometimes it is written with a *tsere* <term>tsere: a Hebrew vowel producing an "ay" or "eh" sound</term>. Occasionally, the letter *he* <note>original: ה</note> is added to the end, and then it is pronounced with a *qamets*. 

**Passive Past:** *nigash* <note>original: נִגַּשׁ</note> and *niggeshu* <note>original: נִגְּשׁוּ</note>. Observe how one *nun* repels the other. For just as I say *nifqad* <note>original: נִפְקַד</note> in the passive, I ought to say *ningash* <note>original: נִנְגַּשׁ</note>; therefore, since one *nun* is missing, a *dagesh* is placed to mark the omission. This rule applies to all that follow, so that we do not need to use many words to explain it. 

**Present:** *niggash* <note>original: נִגָּשׁ</note> 
**Future:** *innagesh* <note>original: אִנָּגֵשׁ</note> and *yinnagesh* <note>original: יִנָּגֵשׁ</note>. Behold, one *nun* repels the other here as well. 
**Imperative:** *hinnagesh* <note>original: הִנָּגֵשׁ</note> and *hinnageshu* <note>original: הִנָּגְשׁוּ</note> 
**Infinitive:** *hinnagesh* <note>original: הִנָּגֵשׁ</note>. This follows the pattern of *hippaqed* <note>original: הִפָּקֵד</note>, which would regularly be pronounced *hinnagesh* but is spoken in this defective way.

**Active Causative Past:** *higgish* <note>original: הִגִּישׁ</note> and *higgishah* <note>original: הִגִּישָׁה</note> 
**Present:** *maggish* <note>original: מַגִּישׁ</note> 
**Verbal Adjective:** *maggish* <note>original: מַגִּשׁ</note> 
**Future:** *aggish* <note>original: אַגִּישׁ</note> and *yaggish* <note>original: יַגִּישׁ</note> 
**Imperative:** *haggesh* <note>original: הַגֵּשׁ</note>, *haggishu* <note>original: הַגִּישׁוּ</note>, or *haggish* <note>original: הַגִּישׁ</note> 
**Infinitive:** *haggesh* <note>original: הַגֵּשׁ</note> 

**Passive Causative Past:** *huggash* <note>original: הֻגַּשׁ</note> and *huggashah* <note>original: הֻגְּשָׁה</note> 
**Future:** *uggash* <note>original: אֻגַּשׁ</note> 
**Infinitive:** *huggash* <note>original: הֻגַּשׁ</note> 

And as it is with the letter *nun*, so it is with the letter *lamed* <note>original: ל</note>.

### When the letter Yod or Aleph is missing at the start
**To Know:** <note>original: יָדַע</note> In the first conjugation, it is conjugated as *yadata* <note>original: יָדַעְתָּ</note> and *yadati* <note>original: יָדַעְתִּי</note>. 

**Present:** *yodea* <note>original: יוֹדֵעַ</note>, *yodeim* <note>original: יוֹדְעִים</note>, and *yoda-at* <note>original: יוֹדַעַת</note> or for the feminine singular *yode-ah* <note>original: יוֹדְעָה</note>. 

If the root does not contain the guttural letters <term>guttural letters: Aleph (א), Het (ח), He (ה), or Ayin (ע), which are pronounced in the throat</term>, then both the final and the second-to-last syllables are pronounced with a *segol* <term>segol: a Hebrew vowel producing an "eh" sound</term>. 

**Verbal Adjective:** *yadu-a* <note>original: יָדוּעַ</note> 
**Future (Defective):** *eda* <note>original: אֵדַע</note> and *yeda* <note>original: יֵדַע</note>, and sometimes with a *hiriq* <term>hiriq: a Hebrew vowel producing an "ee" sound</term>. 
**Imperative:** *da* <note>original: דַּע</note> and in the plural defective form *de-u* <note>original: דְּעוּ</note>. 
**Infinitive:** *da-at* <note>original: דַּעַת</note>. 

Remember that the *dagesh* point marks the missing letter.

And I would like you to remember these things hereafter. Now in the passive <note>Referring to the Niphal stem</note>, *noda* <note>original: נוֹדַע; meaning "he was known"</note>, *nodat* <note>original: נוֹדַעַתְּ; "you were known"</note>, and so on. In these cases, the *vav* <term>vav: the Hebrew letter ו</term> is a substantial letter and is placed in the position of the original *yod* <term>yod: the Hebrew letter י</term>; for the exchange of the letters *Aleph, He, Vav, and Yod* <note>original: אהוי; these are the "weak" letters in Hebrew that frequently swap or disappear</note> is easily done.

**Present:** *noda* <note>original: נוֹדָע</note>, *nodaim* <note>original: נוֹדָעִים</note>. **Future:** *ivvada* <note>original: אִוָּדַע</note>, *yivvada* <note>original: יִוָּדַע</note>. Behold, a four-syllable word. **Imperative:** *hivvada* <note>original: הִוָּדַע</note>, *hivvadu* <note>original: הִוָּדְעוּ</note>. **Infinitive:** *hivvada* <note>original: הִוָּדַע</note>.

In the **third conjugation** <note>The Hiphil stem, which indicates causing an action to happen</note>, the **past tense** is *hodia* <note>original: הוֹדִיעַ; "he informed" or "he made known"</note>, *hodata* <note>original: הוֹדַעְתָּ</note>. **Present:** *modia* <note>original: מוֹדִיעַ</note>. **Adjective:** *moda* <note>original: מוֹדָע; "an acquaintance"</note>. **Future:** *odia* <note>original: אוֹדִיעַ</note>, *todia* <note>original: תּוֹדִיעַ</note>. **Imperative:** *hoda* <note>original: הוֹדַע</note>, *hodiu* <note>original: הוֹדִיעוּ</note>. **Infinitive:** *hodia* <note>original: הוֹדִיעַ</note>.

The **passive of the third conjugation** <note>The Hophal stem</note> is *huda* <note>original: הוּדַע; "he was made known"</note>, *hudata* <note>original: הוּדַעְתָּ</note>. This is similar to that passage in Genesis chapter thirty-nine: *Therefore Joseph was led down into Egypt* <note>Genesis 39:1</note>; that is, Joseph was "made to descend" into Egypt. And here the *shureq* <term>shureq: a Hebrew vowel mark for a "u" sound</term> is often changed into a *holam* <term>holam: a Hebrew vowel mark for an "o" sound</term>. The **future** is *uda* <note>original: אוּדַע</note>, *yuda* <note>original: יוּדַע</note>, and likewise it sometimes uses the *holam*. **Infinitive:** *huda* <note>original: הוּדַע</note>.

In the **fourth conjugation** <note>The Hithpael stem, which is reflexive</note>, some verbs change the *yod* into a *vav*, while others do not. This one changes in the **past indicative**: *hitvadda* <note>original: הִתְוַדַּע; "he made himself known"</note>, *hitvaddata* <note>original: הִתְוַדַּעְתָּ</note>. **Present:** *mitvadda* <note>original: מִתְוַדַּע</note>. **Future:** *etvadda* <note>original: אֶתְוַדַּע</note>, *yitvadda* <note>original: יִתְוַדַּע</note>. **Imperative:** *hitvadda* <note>original: הִתְוַדַּע</note>, *hitvadu* <note>original: הִתְוַדְּעוּ</note>.

#### When the Vav or Yod is missing in the middle positions.

*Bon* <note>original: בּוֹן; to understand or discern</note>. You heard above in the discussion of the "squared" conjugation <note>Referring to the Poel/Pual stems discussed on the previous page</note> that an **epenthesis** <term>epenthesis: the addition of a letter within a word</term> of the letter *vav* occurs when letters are doubled or absorbed. Thus here, when I say *bon*, the letter *vav* has fallen in the middle: *bon* <note>original: בּוֹן</note>. And when the final letter *nun* <note>original: נ</note> is cast away, *bo* <note>original: בּוֹ</note> remains. However, when the *vav* is missing, as it is here, there remains a *bo* that is **dageshed** <term>dageshed: a letter containing a dot (dagesh) to show it is strengthened or doubled</term> with a *qamets* <term>qamets: an "ah" vowel</term> in place of the *holam*. Therefore, because the *vav* is missing in the middle, it belongs under this heading. It is conjugated as follows:

*Understand* <note>original: בּוֹן (bon)</note>, *she understands*, *my understanding ones*, *they understood*, *their understanding*, *our understanding*, *she understands* (repeated), *understanding of*, *his understanding*.

**Present:** *Understand* <note>original: בּוֹן</note>. **Adjective:** *Understanding/Discerning*. **Future:** *I will understand* <note>original: אָבוֹן (avon)</note>, *he will understand* <note>original: יָבוֹן (yavon)</note>.

And note: sometimes the letter *nun* <term>nun: the Hebrew letter נ</term> is doubled. But if it is not doubled, a *dagesh* <term>dagesh: a dot inside a letter indicating it is "strengthened" or doubled</term> is usually placed in the first person plural of the past tense, as well as in the second and third person plural of the feminine gender in the future tense, and in the imperative.

☞ **Imperative:** *Understand* <note>original: בּוֹן (bon)</note>, *understand* (plural), *understand* (feminine singular), *understand* (feminine plural). **Infinitive:** *To understand* <note>original: בּוֹן</note>.

The **Passive of the first conjugation** <note>The Niphal stem</note> in the past tense: *He was prudent* <note>original: נָבוֹן (navon)</note>, *I was prudent* <note>original: נָבוֹנוֹת (navonot)</note>.

**Present:** *Prudent* <note>original: נָבוֹן</note>. In the remaining forms, the *qamets* <term>qamets: a long 'a' vowel mark</term> is changed into a *sheva* <term>sheva: a very short vowel or vowel-less marker</term>. A *shureq* <term>shureq: a 'u' vowel sound written with the letter vav</term> is often placed in the position of a *holam* <term>holam: an 'o' vowel sound</term>. **Future:** *I will be prudent*, *he will be prudent*. And in the case of the letters *Aleph, He, Het, Ayin, and Resh* <note>original: אֶחָחַעַר; the guttural letters that cannot be doubled</note>, a *tsere* <term>tsere: a long 'e' vowel sound</term> is used instead of a *segol* <term>segol: a short 'e' vowel sound</term> without a *dagesh*. **Imperative:** *Be prudent* <note>original: הִבּוֹן (hibbon)</note>. Similarly, the **Infinitive:** *To be prudent*.

The **third conjugation** <note>The Hiphil stem, indicating a causative action</note> in the past tense: *He understood* or *explained* <note>original: הֵבִין (hevin)</note>, *you understood*. The last syllable is sometimes written with a *tsere* or a *pathah* <term>pathah: a short 'a' vowel sound</term>. **Present:** *Understanding/Explaining*. **Adjective:** *Understanding*. And if the *vav* is missing, a *qamets* is placed in its stead in the first letter. **Future:** *I will understand*, and in the second and third person feminine plural: *they/you shall understand* <note>original: תָּבֵנָה (tavenah)</note>. **Imperative:** *Understand* <note>original: הָבֵן (haven)</note>. The **Infinitive** is formed similarly.

In the **passive voice** <note>The Hophal stem</note>: *He was made to understand* <note>original: הוּבַן (huvan)</note>. **Present:** *Being made to understand*. **Future:** *He will be made to understand*, *I will be made to understand*. **Infinitive:** *To be made to understand*.

Now the **four-fold conjugation** <note>The Polel stem, used for certain "hollow" verbs instead of the intensive Piel</note> takes its place; in this form, the letter *vav* is the middle letter of the root's substance, and the final letter is doubled by grammatical rule. **Past tense:** *He observed/considered* <note>original: בּוֹנֵן (bonen)</note>, *you observed*.

**Present:** *Observing* <note>original: מְבוֹנֵן (mevonen)</note>; and afterward the *tsere* changes to a *sheva*. **Adjective:** *Observed* <note>original: מְבוֹנָן (mevonan)</note>, *observed ones* (plural).

**Indicative Future:** *I will observe*, *he will observe*.

**Imperative:** *Observe* <note>original: בּוֹנֵן</note>, *observe* (plural).

**Infinitive:** *To observe*.

### ->THIRD BOOK<-

**Past tense of the fourth conjugation** <note>The Hitpael stem, used here for the root B-V-N, meaning "to consider" or "meditate"</note>: *He considered* <note>original: הִתְבּוֹנֵן (hitbonen)</note>, *you considered* <note>original: הִתְבּוֹנַנְתָּ (hitbonanta)</note>.
**Present:** *Considering* <note>original: מִתְבּוֹנֵן (mitbonen)</note>, *considering* (plural) <note>original: מִתְבּוֹנְנִים (mitbonanim)</note>. **Future:** *I will consider* <note>original: אֶתְבּוֹנֵן (etbonen)</note>.
The remaining forms use the *hiriq* <term>hiriq: the 'i' vowel sound</term>. **Imperative:** *Consider!* <note>original: הִתְבּוֹנֵן</note>, *Consider!* (feminine) <note>original: הִתְבּוֹנְנִי</note>.
**Infinitive:** *To consider* <note>original: הִתְבּוֹנֵן</note>.

Whenever the letter *nun* <term>nun: the Hebrew letter נ</term> is doubled and followed by a final *he* <term>he: the Hebrew letter ה</term>, one *nun* can be removed and the other marked by a *dagesh* <term>dagesh: a dot inside a letter indicating it is "strengthened" or doubled</term>. This conjugation, as well as the previous "squared" conjugation <note>Referring to the Polel stem discussed on the previous page</note>, is also found to end in a *patah* <term>patah: a short 'a' vowel</term>, such as: *He wounded* <note>original: חוֹלֵל (holel)</note>, *you wounded* <note>original: חוֹלַלְתָּ (holalta)</note>.

### When the *aleph* is silent at the end.
*He restrained*, *he filled*, *he found*, *he carried*, *he was wonderful*, *he called*. <note>original roots: כָּלָא, מָלָא, מָצָא, נָשָׂא, פָּלָא, קָרָא</note>

I say a vowel is "missing" not only when it is not written, but also if it is written but not pronounced. What the Hebrews call "resting" <term>quiescere: a letter that is written but has no vowel sound of its own</term>, we call "falling silent." **Past tense:** *He called* <note>original: קָרָא (qara)</note>, *you called*, *I called*, *they called*. <note>Conjugated: קָרָא קָרָאתָ קָרָאתִי קָרְאוּ</note>
*You all (masculine) called*, *you all (feminine) called*, *they called*, *she called*, *you (feminine) called*, *I called*. <note>Conjugated: קְרָאתֶם קְרָאתֶן קָרְאוּ קָרְאָה קָרָאת קָרָאתִי</note>

**Present:** *Calling* <note>original: קוֹרֵא (qore)</note>, *calling* (plural), *calling* (feminine singular), *calling* (feminine plural).
And sometimes in the masculine plural, the letter *aleph* is cast away, and it is said: *Calling* <note>original: קוֹרִים (qorim)</note>.
**Adjective:** *Called* or *Invited* <note>original: קָרוּא (qaru)</note>, *called* (plural), *called* (feminine singular), *called* (feminine plural).

**Imperative:** *Call!*, *Call!* (masculine plural), *Call!* (feminine singular), *Call!* (feminine plural).

And sometimes in the feminine plural, the final *he* is missing, yet the *nun*, even though it is at the end of the word, is nonetheless punctuated in that place with a *qamets* <term>qamets: a long 'a' vowel</term>. As in the Book of Ruth, chapter 1: "*Call* me Mara." <note>Ruth 1:20: קְרֶאןָ (qrena)</note> In this case, the letter *resh* is written with a *tsere* <term>tsere: an 'e' vowel sound</term>. But his brother, Rabbi David [Kimhi], in his book on the *Art of Grammar*, writes it with an *aleph* and says that the letter itself is silent. **Infinitive:** *To call* <note>original: קְרוֹא</note>. **Passive past tense:** *He was called* <note>original: נִקְרָא (niqra)</note>, *you were called* <note>original: נִקְרֵאתָ</note>.
In the first and second person masculine plural and second person feminine plural of this form, the *qamets* is preserved. **Present:** *Being called* <note>original: נִקְרָא</note>, *being called* (plural). **Future:** *I will be called* <note>original: אֶקָּרֵא (eqqare)</note>.

**Past tense of the third conjugation: You taught, I taught, you all taught** <note>original: הוֹרֵיתָ הוֹרֵיתִי הוֹרֵתֶם (horeita, horeiti, horetem). The "Third Conjugation" refers to the Hifil or causative form: "to cause to know" or "to teach"</note>.
**Present: Teaching, teaching (plural)** <note>original: מוֹרֶה מוֹרִים (moreh, morim)</note>. **Adjective: Teacher, teachers** <note>original: מוֹרֶה מוֹרִים (moreh, morim)</note>.
**Future: I will teach, he will teach, she will teach** <note>original: אּוֹרֶה יוֹרֶה תּוֹרֶה (oreh, yoreh, toreh)</note> and with a **missing final *He*: I taught, he taught, she taught** <note>original: אּוֹר יוֹר תּוֹר (or, yor, tor)</note>. **Imperative: Teach! Teach (plural)!** <note>original: הוֹרֵה הוֹרוּ (horeh, horu)</note>
and with a **missing final *He*: Teach!** <note>original: הוֹר (hor)</note>. **Infinitive: To teach** <note>original: הוֹרוֹת (horot)</note>.
**Past tense of the passive voice: We were taught, you were taught, you were taught** <note>original: הוֹרֵינוּ הוֹרֵיתָ הוֹרֵית (horeinu, horeita, horeit). This is the Hofal conjugation</note>.
**Future: I will be taught, he will be taught** <note>original: אּוֹרֶה יוֹרֶה (oreh, yoreh)</note>.
**Infinitive: To be taught** <note>original: הוֹרֵה (horeh)</note>.

->**When the last letters are missing.**<-

**Past tense of the first conjugation: He gave, I gave, we gave** <note>original: נָתַן נָתַתִּי נָתָנוּ (natan, natatti, natanu). From the root N-T-N, one of the most common verbs in the Bible</note>.
Thus it is read with a **missing letter** in **2 Samuel 22** <note>The text says "2 Kings 22," but this quote is from David's song in 2 Samuel 22:41 or Psalm 18:40</note>: **"You have given me the necks of my enemies."** <note>original: תַּתָּה (tattah). This is a highly irregular form where the initial and final 'Nun' of the root N-T-N have disappeared</note>. **Present: Giving, giving (plural), giving (feminine)** <note>original: נוֹתֵן נוֹתְנִים נוֹתֶנֶת (noten, notenim, notenet)</note>.
**Adjective: Given** <note>original: נָתָן (natan)</note>. **Future: I will give, he will give, she will give** <note>original: אֶתֵּן יִתֵּן תִּתֵּן (etten, yitten, titten)</note>.
**Imperative: Give!** <note>original: תֵּן (ten)</note> which is sometimes found with a <term>segol|A Hebrew vowel mark indicating a short "e" sound</term>. As in **Genesis 14**:
**"Give me the persons."** <note>Genesis 14:21: Abraham is told to give the captives to the King of Sodom</note>. **Give!** or **Give!** <note>original: תְּנָה (tenah) or תְּנֶנָּה (tenennah)</note>.
**Passive Past: He was given, you were given, I was given** <note>original: נִתַּן נִתַּתָּ נִתַּתִּי (nittan, nittatta, nittatti)</note>. **Present: Given** <note>original: נִתָּן (nittan)</note>.

**For the sake of** <note>original: לְמַעַן (lema'an)</note>

<meta>This page continues the technical analysis of Hebrew verbs, moving from the root N-T-N (to give) to a discussion of "geminate" or "doubled" verbs—roots where the second and third letters are identical. It provides rules for how these verbs change their vowels or drop letters in different tenses.</meta>

->### THE BOOK<-

**Future: I will give, he will give, you will give** <note>original: אֶתֵּן יִתֵּן תִּתֵּן (etten, yitten, titten). From the root N-T-N. Note how the first 'N' has disappeared into a dot (dagesh) in the second letter</note> **Imperative: Give!** <note>original: תְּנֵן (tenen). This is a lengthened form of the imperative</note>
**Infinitive: To give** or **To be given, my being given** <note>original: תֵּת uel הִנָּתֵן הִנָּתְנִי (tet, hinnaten, hinnaneti). 'Tet' is the common form for 'to give'</note>

#### When doubled letters are missing.
Verbs are called **doubled** <note>technical term: geminate verbs</note> when one of the root letters is placed twice: once in the last position and once in the second-to-last. Examples include: **to despise, to pass away, stripped, to be thin, they showed favor.** <note>original: בּוֹז גּוֹז שׁוֹלֵל רָלַל חַנּוּ (boz, goz, sholel, ralal, channu). In these roots, the second and third letters are the same</note>
These are sometimes read as **complete** <note>meaning all root letters are visible</note>, as in Ecclesiastes chapter one: **"The spirit goes in a circuit."** <note>original Latin: "In circuitu pergit spiritus"; Hebrew root S-B-B (to turn/surround)</note> Sometimes they are **defective** <note>meaning a letter is dropped</note>, as in the Second Book of Kings <note>modern 2 Samuel</note>, chapter fourteen: **"And let him return to his own house."** <note>original Latin: "Et reuertatur in domum suam"; root S-B-B appearing in a shortened form</note>

I give you this rule: those verbs whose middle root letters go silent <note>referring to "hollow" verbs like Q-W-M</note> mark their **past tense** with a **qamets** <note>a long 'a' vowel</note>; however, those verbs where the doubled letters are missing <note>geminate verbs</note> are marked with a **patah** <note>a short 'a' vowel</note>. For example:
**Past tense of the first conjugation:** <note>the Qal, or simple action form</note> **He was complete, you were complete, I was complete, they were complete.** <note>original: תַּם תַּמּוֹתָ תַּמּוֹתִי תַּמּוּ (tam, tammota, tammoti, tammu). Note the short 'a' vowel in 'tam'</note>
**Present tense: Complete, complete (plural).** <note>original: תָּם תַּמִּים (tam, tammim)</note> The singular masculine form takes a **qamets** <note>long 'a'</note> to distinguish it from the past tense. According to **Rabbi Moses Zeiag** <note>likely Moses ben Isaac ibn Ezra, or a similar Sephardic grammarian</note> in the *Book of Good Intellect*, this verb lacks an adjective form because it derives from absolute or neutral verbs <note>verbs that describe a state of being rather than an action</note>. However, according to **Rabbi Moses Kimhi** <note>a famous 12th-century Hebrew grammarian from France</note> in his *Introductory*, it is formed as:
**To be complete, I will be complete, he will be complete, they will be complete, they (feminine) will be complete.** <note>original: תּוֹם אָתוֹם יֵתוֹם יִתּוֹמוּ תִּתַּמְנָה (tom, atom, yetom, yittommu, tittamnah)</note> **Future: Completing (plural).** <note>original: תּוֹםִים (tomim)</note>
**Imperative: Be complete! Be complete (plural)! Be complete (fem. plural)!** <note>original: תּוֹם תַּמּוּ תַּמְנָה (tom, tammu, tamnah)</note> **Infinitive: To be complete.** <note>original: תּוֹם (tom)</note>

**Passive Past:** <note>the Nifal form</note> **He was completed, you were completed, they were completed, we were completed.** <note>original: נָתַם נְתַמּוֹתָ נְתַמּוּ נְתַמּוֹנוּ (natam, netammota, netammu, netammonu)</note>
**You (plural) were completed.** <note>original: נְתַמּוֹת (netammot)</note> This is also found with the first vowel as a **qamets** and the second as a **tsere** <note>an 'e' sound</note>; likewise, with the first as a **hiriq** <note>'i' sound</note> and the second as a **patah** <note>'a' sound</note>, or the first as a **qamets** and the second as a **holam** <note>'o' sound</note>.
**Present: Completed, completed (plural)** <note>original: נָתָם נְתַמִּים (natam, netammim)</note> or with the last vowel as a **tsere**. **Future: I will be completed, he will be completed, she will be completed, they will be completed.** <note>original: אֵתַם יֵתַם תֵּתַם יִתַּמּוּ (etam, yetam, tetam, yittammu)</note> **Imperative: Be completed!** <note>original: הִתַּם (hittam)</note>
**Infinitive: To be completed.** <note>original: הִתָּם (hittam)</note> **To be completed (plural), to be completed (my being), to be completed (feminine).** <note>original: הִתַּמּוּ הִתַּמִּי הִתַּמֶּינָה (hittammu, hittami, hittameinah)</note>

**Past tense of the third conjugation:** <note>the Hifil, or causative form: 'to make complete'</note> **I completed, you completed, he completed, they completed, you all completed, we completed, she completed, to complete.** <note>original: הִתַמּוֹתִי הִתַמּוֹתָ הִתַם הִתַמּוּ הִתַמּוֹתֶם הִתַמּוֹנוּ הִתַמָּה הִתַמּוֹת (hitammoti, hitam-mota, hitam, hitammu, hitam-motem, hitammonu, hammah, hitam-mot)</note>
**His completing.** <note>original: הִתַמּוֹתוֹ (hitammoto)</note> The third person singular is also found with a **tsere** in the first syllable. **Present: Completing, completing (plural).** <note>original: מֵתַם מֵתַמִּים (metam, metammim)</note> Sometimes the first vowel is a **hiriq**.

### THIRD [PART]

**Adjective** <note>In this context, referring to the participle: מָתֹם (matom) and מְתֻמִּים (metummim), meaning 'complete' or 'innocent'</note> **Future: I will be finished, he will be finished** <note>original: אֶתֹּם יִתֹּם (ettom, yittom)</note>

[you masculine and plural]** <note>original: תִּתֹּם תִּתַּמּוּ (tittom, tittammu)</note>. #### Passive Voice

**Past tense:** **He was made complete, they were made complete, I was made complete** <note>original: הֻתַּם הֻתַּמּוּ הֻתַּמּוֹתִי (huttam, huttammu, huttammoti)</note> **Future: I will be made complete, he will be made complete** <note>original: אֻתַּם יֻתַּם (uttam, yuttam)</note> or according to **Rabbi Moses Kimchi** <note>A famous 12th-century Jewish grammarian whose works were highly influential on Christian scholars of this period</note>: **he will be made complete, she will be made complete, they (feminine) will be made complete** <note>original: יֻתַּם תֻּתַּם תֻּתַּמֶּינָה (yuttam, tuttam, tuttammenah)</note>.

### Verbs of many letters.
There are verbs that consist not only of three letters like **complete** <term>triliteral</term> verbs, nor only of **doubled** letters <term>geminate</term> like those mentioned just above, but of four. For example:
**to mix, to gnaw, to be moist/fresh, to spread out, to be weak/wretched,**
**to dig/peer, to be fair/bright, to smear/plaster, to confuse, to purify/clarify, to stir up,**
**to destroy/shout, to sprout/stir, to delude, to sweep, to mock.** <note>These are quadriliteral roots: birbel, kirsem, ritpesh, parshez, imlel, chitrey, shiphrah, tichvah, bilbel, birber, sikser, qirqar, shigsheg, ti'te'a, ti'te, ti'te'a</note>
There are also others that consist of five letters, such as:
**to cause to burn, very perverted, very hot/red, very dizzy/palpitating.** <note>original: לְחַרְחַר, הֲפַכְפַּךְ, חֲמַרְמַר, סְחַרְחַר (lecharachar, hapachpach, chamarmar, sechar-char)</note>
Others have six, such as: **to linger/delay.** <note>original: הִתְמַהְמַהּ (hitmahmah)</note> Let us take one of these as an example.
**Past tense of the second conjugation** <note>likely referring to the intensive Piel-like pattern used for these longer roots</note>: **he delighted** <note>root S-'-S-': to play or take delight</note>
**I delighted, they delighted, you (pl.) delighted, we delighted**
**She delighted, you (f.s.) delighted, you (f.p.) delighted**
**Present: Delighting, delighting (pl.), etc.**
**Adjective-Verb [Passive Participle]: Being delighted, being delighted (pl.), etc.**
**Future: I will delight, he will delight, you will delight, she will delight/you will delight,**
**they (f.p.) will delight.**

<meta>This page continues the grammatical instruction from the previous section, moving from verb conjugations with suffixes to the rules governing how nouns interact with one another (syntax) and how their endings change when they are linked in a phrase.</meta>

### THIRD BOOK

Having seen the construction of suffixes <note>The "affixes" or suffixes attached to words to indicate possession or objects of actions</note> both in nouns and in verbs, it will behoove you to read often and extensively in the Hebrew Bible. From this practice, you may learn other varied constructions. For now, you have heard generally how a masculine plural noun, when it governs a case following it <note>This refers to the "construct state," where two nouns are joined together, often translated with "of"</note>, drops the letter *mem* [ם]. For example, in Ecclesiastes 12: <note>original Hebrew: דִּבְרֵי חֲכָמִים (*divrei chakhamim*)</note> **Words of the wise**. Similarly, in the same place: <note>original Hebrew: דִּבְרֵי אֱמֶת (*divrei emet*)</note> **Words of truth**. This also occurs when two or three nouns follow one another and govern each other, as in Isaiah 19: **The wise counselors of Pharaoh**, where it is written: <note>original Hebrew: חַכְמֵי יוֹעֲצֵי פַרְעֹה (*chakmei yo’atzei Far’oh*)</note>.

However, your mind should take notice that the *mem* is also sometimes dropped even in the absolute state <note>The "absolute state" is the standard form of a noun when it is not linked to another in a "words of..." construction</note>, and the *hireq* sound [i] remains in the word itself. For example, in Psalm 144, where we read: **who subdues my people under me**, it ought to read: **Who subdues the peoples under me**. Jerome follows this in his translation of the Psalter <note>Referring to the *Psalterium iuxta Hebraeos*, Jerome’s translation of the Psalms directly from Hebrew rather than the Greek Septuagint</note>. For <note>Hebrew: עַמִּי (*ammi*, my people)</note> is placed there instead of <note>Hebrew: עַמִּים (*ammim*, peoples)</note>. So too in Isaiah 38: **As a shepherd’s tent**, although some say the letter *he* is placed instead of the *yod*, so that it would mean: **as the tent of a shepherd**.

It is also common for the final *mem* to be dropped while the *yod* remains; when a *pathach* point [a] is joined to it, it is pronounced like a diphthong with the preceding letter. In such cases, the ending *ai* has the same value as *im*. In Jeremiah 22: **Who opens windows for himself**, where <note>Hebrew: חַלּוֹנָי (*challonai*)</note> is used for <note>Hebrew: חַלּוֹנִים (*challonim*)</note>. 

Sometimes the *yod* before the final *mem* is missing in writing, yet the *hireq* [i] is nonetheless pronounced. In Genesis 1: <note>Hebrew: הַתַּנִּינִם (*ha-tanninim*)</note> **The great sea creatures** <note>Traditionally translated as "whales" or "great serpents"</note>. We write similarly: <note>Hebrew: גּוֹיִם (*goyim*)</note> **Nations**, and <note>Hebrew: לְוִיִּם (*leviyim*)</note> **Levites**. 

Occasionally, the letter *nun* [ן] is found to take the place of the final *mem* and is put in its stead. In Ezekiel 4: **Take for yourself wheat and barley**, <note>Hebrew: חִטִּין (*chittin*)</note> is used for **wheat** instead of <note>Hebrew: חִטִּים (*chittim*)</note>, etc. 

Furthermore, I have not neglected to mention above that a feminine noun ending in *he* [ה], when governing a word after it, changes the *he* into a *thau* [ת] and the *qamets* vowel [a] into a *pathach* [short a]. For example, in Ezekiel 32: <note>Hebrew: צִדְקַת הַצַּדִּיק (*tzidqat ha-tzaddiq*)</note> **The righteousness of the righteous**. 

You also know the rules for how an adjective and a substantive <note>A noun</note> must agree, although figuratively it often happens otherwise. Just as Homer says in Greek, <note>Greek: τεκνον φιλε (*teknon phile*)</note>, that is, "dear child," even though he means "dear son" <note>This is an example of "constructio ad sensum," where the grammar agrees with the meaning rather than the strict gender of the word</note>. So in 1 Kings 19: **And a great and strong wind, subverting the mountains**, which in Hebrew is: <note>Hebrew: וְרוּחַ גְּדוֹלָה וְחָזָק (*ve-ruach gedolah ve-chazaq*)</note>.

BOOK

**Breaking** <note>original Hebrew: מְפָרֵק (*m'fareq*)</note>, that is, **and a great and strong wind dividing**. <note>A reference to 1 Kings 19:11</note> In this case, the word **wind** <note>original Hebrew: *ruach*</note> is of the feminine gender, and similarly the first adjective, **great**, is feminine. However, the second adjective and the participle are of the masculine gender. In no different a way, Homer uses a participle in this manner: **But the soul of the Theban Tiresias approached, holding a golden scepter.** <note>original Greek: ηλθε δ' επι ψυχη θηβαιου Τειρεσιαו χρυσεον σκηπτροן εχων (*ēlthe d' epi psychē thēbaiou Teiresiao chryseon skēptron echōn*)</note> Here, **soul** <note>original Greek: *psychē*</note> is of the feminine gender, but the participle **holding** <note>original Greek: *echōn*</note> is masculine. Virgil does the same in Book 8 of the *Aeneid*: **Under Praeneste itself**; and Jeremiah in chapter 8: **Why is this people turned away?** where **people** is of the masculine gender, but the phrase **is turned away** is feminine. You should understand this as a conceptual grouping of masculine and feminine. Genesis 1: **Male and female he created them.**

Furthermore, you are aware that a subject and its predicate ought to agree; yet figuratively, the opposite occurs. For example, in Deuteronomy 32: **Do you thus requite the Lord, O foolish people?** The true Hebrew reading sounds like this: **Do you requite these things to the Lord, O foolish people?** So too in Psalm 62: **Trust in him, all you congregation of the people, etc.** and Virgil in Book 1 of the *Aeneid*: **Part cut into pieces.**

But these features are common to many languages. This, however, is unique to the Hebrew language: in "separate relatives" like **that** <note>original Hebrew: שׁ (*she*) and אֲשֶׁר (*asher*)</note>, it first places the antecedent, second the separate relative, third the verb with its subject (or something equivalent), and fourth the relative pronoun with the article **he, she, it** <note>The author is referring to the Hebrew practice of using a "resumptive pronoun" (e.g., "the man *that* I saw *him*")</note> according to the requirements of the case. For example, in Psalm 146, the Psalmist, wishing to say: **In the son of man, in whom there is no salvation**, says it thus in Hebrew: <note>original Hebrew: בְּבֶן אָדָם שֶׁאֵין לוֹ תְשׁוּעָה (*be-ven adam she-ein lo t'shuah*)</note> which sounds like: **In the son of man, that there is no salvation to him.** Similarly in Isaiah 37: **In the way by which he came**, <note>original Hebrew: בַּדֶּרֶךְ אֲשֶׁר בָּאתָה בָּהּ (*ba-derekh asher bata bah*)</note> which sounds like: **In the way that he came in it.**

Other constructions are clear through the use of articles and signs. For instance, when a verb governs a case after it, a sign <note>The author refers to the Hebrew particle *et* (אֶת), which marks the definite direct object</note> is added, especially when there might be doubt as to who is the agent and who is the recipient. For if I say, "The iron loves the sulfur," you do not know which one does the loving; from this, a double-meaning <note>The term used is "amphibologia," a grammatical ambiguity</note> arises, such as: **I say that you, descendant of Aeacus, the Romans can defeat.** <note>A famous Latin oracle: *Aio te, Aeacida, Romanos vincere posse*. It can mean "You can defeat the Romans" or "The Romans can defeat you."</note> But if I say that "The sulfur is loved by the iron," the sign has now made the construction clear. This is unnecessary if nature itself clearly demonstrates the agent and the recipient, as in Deuteronomy chapter 4: **And God created man.** <note>original Hebrew: וַיִּבְרָא אֱלֹהִים אָדָם (*va-yivra Elohim adam*)</note> Hence these signs are abundant in Genesis 1: **In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.** For it is known even without the signs that God is the creator and the heaven is the creation. Certainly, the matter of construction...

...[constru]ctions <note>The text begins mid-word, likely *constructionum* ("of constructions").</note> is entirely supported by the authority of the most learned Priscian, who in Book 17 says thus: **"Every construction, which the Greeks call *syntaxis*, is to be rendered according to the understanding of the speech. You will not discern it otherwise than from the logical order—that is, by appropriately arranging case with case, gender with gender, number with number, person with person, and tense with tense."** These are his words. Since the third part of speech <note>The "consignificative" or particle.</note> provides the greatest assistance to this matter, we shall next direct our studies toward it.

### ON THE CONSIGNIFICATIVE
<note>The term "consignificative" refers to words or letters that have no independent meaning but change the meaning of the words they are attached to, such as prepositions, conjunctions, or tense markers.</note>

The **consignificative** is an indeclinable part of speech that receives the certainty of its meaning from its construction with a noun or a verb. It has two types: for one is **substantial** and the other is **accidental**. Indeed, there are some things that signify nothing at all by themselves unless they are attached to either a noun or a verb. If you have impressed all our previous lessons into your memory, you were taught by us in the first book that there are certain "accidental letters." **Rabbi Marinus** <note>Jonah ibn Janah (c. 990–1050), a highly influential Jewish grammarian and lexicographer.</note>, a very learned grammarian among the Jews, encompassed them in these words: **"My peace, may it build you"** <note>original Hebrew: שלומ"י אר תבנ"ך (*Sh-L-V-M-Y A-R T-B-N-K*). This is a mnemonic device containing the letters used as prefixes or suffixes in Hebrew.</note>. And the most skillful **Rabbi Abraham Ibn Ezra** <note>A famous 12th-century Spanish-Jewish scholar and grammarian.</note> expressed it thus: **"Set for yourself a father of vinegar"** <note>original Hebrew: שית לך אב חומ"ץ (*Sh-Y-T L-K A-B Ch-V-M-Ts*). Another mnemonic for the same formative letters.</note>.

Therefore, from these same accidental letters, some are **consignificatives of verbs** and some are **consignificatives of nouns**. The verbal consignificatives assist verbs in four ways: namely, twice at the end and twice at the beginning. Those which are attached to the ends of **past tenses** are contained in this mnemonic: **M-N-T H-Y-V** <note>original Hebrew: מנת ה"יו; these letters indicate person and number in the perfect tense.</note>. Those which follow at the ends of the **present and imperative** verbs are remembered by this word: **Y-T-Ch-M-V** <note>original Hebrew: יתחמ"ו</note>. However, those which take the beginning in the **future tense**, we call: **A-Y-T-N** <note>original Hebrew: אית"ן; these are the standard prefixes (Aleph, Yod, Tav, Nun) used to conjugate future/imperfect verbs.</note>.

There are others that serve **gerunds** <note>In this context, the author uses "gerund" to describe infinitive forms with prepositional prefixes.</note> at the beginning, which are called by some: **B-M-L-K** <note>original Hebrew: במל"ך</note>. We, imitating common custom, call them: **B-V-L-M** <note>original Hebrew: בבל"ם</note>. Many add the letter *vau* [and] because it also serves gerunds from the start; therefore, they offer their own mnemonic: **B-V-B-L-M** <note>original Hebrew: בובל"ם</note>. You have seen the meanings of those letters both in the tenses and moods of verbs as well as in the gerunds, which signify **in**, **and**, **according to**, **to**, and **from**. The letter *vau* [and] is also accustomed...

**BOOK [THREE]**

...and the letter *iod* <note>original: "iod", the Hebrew letter י</note> serves for both the past and the future. I shall say nothing of *he* [ה], *thau* [ת], and *nun* [נ] at the beginning, or *iod* [י] in the middle of words which indicate the conjugations; these serve not as integral parts of the word, but as grammatical signs, as can be seen in the final two conjugations and in the passive voices. Let us now turn to nouns. Just as verbs derived from nouns are called **denominative verbs** <note>Verbs that originate from a noun, such as "to salt" from the noun "salt."</note> (as Priscian of Caesarea <note>A famous 6th-century Latin grammarian.</note> writes in the first verse of his book *On the Twelve Verses*), so too are nouns derived from verbs called **verbal nouns**. Their beginnings are formed using the letters in the word **"I have believed"** <note>original: הֶאֱמַנְתִּי (*He’emanti*). This is a mnemonic device: all the letters in this Hebrew word can serve as functional prefixes or suffixes for nouns.</note> as we showed above concerning the noun, and we simultaneously added those letters with which nouns are "doubled" <note>original: "daggeſſantur", referring to the *dagesh* or dot in a letter that can indicate doubling or a change in pronunciation.</note>, namely **"Moses and Caleb"** <note>original: מֹשֶׁה וְכָלֵב (*Mosheh ve-Kalev*). Another mnemonic for the letters that can take a *dagesh* mark.</note>, which I am accustomed to group this way for the sake of memory; but **Rabbi David Kimhi** <note>A seminal 12th-century Jewish grammarian and biblical commentator from Provence.</note> collected them as **"Moses and Caleb."**

In this discipline, it would be best if I did not overlook that point regarding the **accidental final *he*** <note>The letter ה added to the end of a word.</note>. For when it follows a word indicating a location, it then signifies a disposition or movement toward that place. This is similar to the endings used by the Greeks:

<margin>*-ze* [-ζε] and *-de* [-δε]. Such as *athenaze* [αθηναζε], which means "to Athens," and *oikade* [οικαδε], "to home." Likewise, *Horebah* [חֹרֵבָה] means "to Horeb."</margin>

**"to Horeb"** <note>Hebrew: חֹרֵבָה (*Horebah*).</note> in the third chapter of Exodus: *He came to the mountain of God, to Horeb.* There is indeed an "accidental" *he* in that name. Yet in the first chapter of Deuteronomy, it says: *But having set out from Horeb,* where there is no aspiration <note>The "h" sound.</note> at the end. However, the first syllable must always be aspirated because the *heth* <note>The letter ח, which has a harsher "h" sound than ה.</note> is a **substantial letter** <note>Part of the root word itself, not a grammatical addition.</note>. All words that begin with *heth* among the Latin writers must be aspirated and written with an *h*, as **Saint Jerome** <note>The 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into the Latin Vulgate.</note> teaches in his book *Hebrew Questions*, where his words are these: **"Frequently the seventy translators <note>The authors of the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament.</note>, being unable to turn the letter *heth*—which sounds like a double aspiration—into the Greek language, added the Greek letter *chi* [χ] to teach us that such words ought to be aspirated."** Thus he spoke. I return to the rule regarding the **local *he***, such as **"to Egypt"** <note>original: מִצְרַיְמָה (*Mizraimah*)</note> in Genesis thirty-nine: *Joseph was led into Egypt.* Likewise, **"to the land"** <note>original: אַרְצָה (*Arzah*)</note> in Genesis twelve: *Into the land of Canaan.* Sometimes, however, neither the *he* is subjoined nor a preposition added to locatives. Just as in Latin we say *vado domum* <note>original Latin: "I go home."</note>, meaning "to the house," so too in the first chapter of Deuteronomy: *Come...*

<meta>This page continues the classification of Hebrew particles, transitioning from interjections and emotional expressions to conjunctions and logical connectors. It concludes with a significant grammatical observation regarding the "Vav Conversive"—a feature where the prefix "and" changes the tense of a verb—as taught to the author by his Jewish mentor, Jacob ben Jehiel Loans.</meta>

->**BOOK THREE**<-

| Category | Hebrew Equivalents | English Meanings <note>The author uses Latin grammatical terms to explain the logical function of these Hebrew particles.</note> |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **For Disjoining** | אוֹ <note>or</note> וְ <note>and/or</note> | or, or at the beginning of a word. |
| **For Opposing** | אַךְ רַק אֲבָל | however, but, nevertheless <note>original Latin: "tamen, uerutamen"</note> |
| **For Opposing** | עִם כָּל זֶה אַפְעַלְפִּי | although, nevertheless <note>original Latin: "quamuis, tamen"</note> |
| **For Denying** | אִם וְאִם וְאִם | even if, although, unless <note>original Latin: "etsi, etiamfi, nifi"</note> |
| **For Reasoning** | לָכֵן אִם כֵּן | therefore, if it is so |
| **For Questioning** | אִם לָאוּ הַאִם הֲלֹא הֲ | whether, if not, is it not? <note>original Latin: "anne, num, numquid, utrum"</note> |
| **For Lessening** | לְפָחוֹת | at least |

If you desire more, you will "hunt" for them in our dictionary, for I am striving to be brief.

However, I should not omit what my most kind teacher, that excellent doctor Jacob Jehiel Loans (may God’s mercy be upon him), showed me while I was a student among the people of Linz <note>original Latin: "apud Cecios," likely referring to the author’s time in Linz where he studied under Loans</note>. He taught me that when the letter *vau* [ו] marked with a *sheva* [ְ] is placed before a verb in the past tense, it shifts the accent <term>accentum: the melodic and rhythmic stress of the word</term> to the final syllable, and the verb is then changed into the future tense. 

For example: דִּבַּרְתִּי (*dib-BAR-ti*) means "I have spoken." It is a verb in the past tense and has the accent on the second-to-last syllable, according to the third rule of the first conjugation mentioned above. If, however, I place a *vau* [וְ] before it and pronounce it with the accent on the last syllable—וְדִבַּרְתִּי (*ve-dib-bar-TI*)—it will no longer be in the past tense, but in the future, meaning "and I shall speak." But if the accent remains on the second-to-last syllable, the verb remains in the past.

<keywords>Hebrew grammar, conjunctions, Vav Conversive, Jacob ben Jehiel Loans, verb tenses, accentuation, linguistic rules</keywords>

--- Page 623 ---
<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of the "Vav Conversive" in Hebrew grammar before transitioning into a personal and motivational address to the author's student, Dionysius. It bridges the gap between linguistic instruction and the broader Humanist justification for studying sacred languages.</meta>

->**BOOK THREE**<-

[The verb] will remain in its state of the past tense. Similarly, when the letter *vav* [ו] with a *patah* [ַ] <note>a short 'a' vowel</note> is placed before a verb of the future tense, it then converts that future into the past. For example: **וַיְדַבֵּר** (*vayidabber*). This word is [originally] in the future tense, "he will speak," as seen above in the second conjugation. But if the *vav* with a *patah* is prefixed to it, it is interpreted as "he spoke." As in the first chapter of Numbers: "And the Lord **spoke**." However, if the *vav* is pointed not with a *patah*, but with a *sheva* [ְ] or with a vowel sound identical to the following letter, then it will remain in its state of the future tense. For example: **וִידַבֵּר** (*viyidabber*), which means "and he will speak."

<margin>f</margin> **[F]inem** <note>The OCR reads "Inem," but the 'f' in the margin serves as both a printer's signature mark and the initial letter for "Finem."</note> I shall make an end of teaching; you, however, should never make an end of learning, if only you are wise. For since no possession is more honorable than learning, that learning ought to seem most honorable which concerns the highest and most admirable things. Such are these "rudiments" <note>the basics or first principles</note> which, although provided through a childlike method, will offer a path for you—and through you, for all who desire secret philosophy—to the investigation of the deepest sciences. To this, a most weighty witness gives his support: that noble and generous Count of the Roman Empire, **Giovanni Pico della Mirandola**, the philosopher, who says in his *Conclusions*: "He who possesses a profound and radical grasp of the order of the Hebrew language, and knows how to preserve that order proportionally in the sciences, will have the norm and rule for perfectly discovering anything that can be known." And the holy man **Jerome**, writing to Paula Urbica concerning the Hebrew alphabet, says: "What is more sacred than this mystery? What is more pleasant than the delight of this secret? What foods, what honeys are sweeter than to know the wisdom of God and to enter into His hidden places?" Wherefore **Rabbi Moses son of Nahman of Gerona** <note>The medieval scholar Nachmanides</note>, in the beginning of his commentary on Genesis, strives to prove with a long discourse that **King Solomon** drew all the influences of his wisdom from the letters of the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible</note>.

Moved at last by these things, my most beloved **Dionysius**, I did not wish to fail your honor. Years ago, when you were but a boy, I sent you across the Alps from Swabia to Florence—then the nurse of the best literature—along with a tutor, and at no small expense to myself. There, for two years, you were a constant companion at the table and home of that man of extraordinary holiness, **Giorgio Vespucci**, so that you might daily hear **Angelo Poliziano**, **Marsilio Ficino**, **Demetrius Chalcondyles**, and other most learned men, in order to grasp the Greek language. Now, I would not have you lack this further distinction: that you, now a priest, should also learn Hebrew.

<meta>This page concludes Johannes Reuchlin’s seminal work on Hebrew grammar. Having completed the technical instructions, he concludes with a personal justification for sharing these "sacred" linguistic secrets with a Christian audience, acknowledging the contemporary tensions between Jewish and Christian scholars before ending with a traditional scholarly flourish and a prayer.</meta>

# BOOK [THREE]

...especially since our local Jews, led either by envy or ignorance, are unwilling to instruct any Christian in their language. They refuse to do so on the authority of a certain **Rabbi Ammi**, who said thus in the Talmud: <note>original: אמר רבי אמי אין מוסרין דברי תורה לכותים... (Rabbi Ammi said: The words of the Torah are not to be handed over to the heathens...)</note>

"Rabbi Ammi said: The words of the Torah are not to be handed over to the heathens, for it is said: 'He declares His word to Jacob, His statutes and His judgments to Israel. He has not done so for any other nation.'"

The word-for-word translation is as follows: "The words of the Law are not explained to any Gentile, because it is written: *He who announces his words to Jacob, his precepts and his judgments to Israel; he has not done similarly for every nation.*" <note>Psalm 147:19-20. Reuchlin is highlighting a Jewish tradition that restricted the teaching of Hebrew and Torah to non-Jews.</note>

To us, however, in the state of grace, a different command is given in the tenth chapter of Matthew: "What you hear whispered in your ear, preach from the housetops" <note>Matthew 10:27</note>. This is what I am doing, and I shall command you to imitate it. Therefore, for this reason: "Remember me, O God, and spare me according to the multitude of your mercies" <note>Nehemiah 13:22</note>. Amen.

<meta>Following Reuchlin’s conclusion of the technical text, this final page contains a postscript by his associate Georg Simler. It provides historical context regarding the publication process and a stern warning against unauthorized "pirated" editions, followed by the formal publication details (the colophon) and the printer’s mark of Thomas Anshelm.</meta>

Georgius Simler <unclear>wishes all readers</unclear> <unclear>to</unclear>
fare well with learning.

You know, most beloved <unclear>friend</unclear>, what the patron of our province—not so much ours as the patron of all learned men—Johannes Reuchlin, whose name I cannot recall without the highest honor and respect, assigned to us upon his departure regarding the production of this work. He himself titled it *The Rudiments of the Holy Language* <note>original: "rudimentorum linguae sanctae"</note>, and he worked tirelessly, gathering material bit by bit from the vast company of the Sacred Writers <note>the "Hagiographa," or the books of the Hebrew Bible</note>, not neglecting even the smallest details. And so, while we were working together as much as the skill and effort of both could produce a finished work, the renowned author returned to Pforzheim and joyfully (as is his custom) received his long labors back into his hands with great delight. He kissed the work as if it were a newly born little son, for we had spent many sleepless nights laboring to ensure the work did not deviate from its original thread and form. 

And since he wished us to be occupied with another task, I thought of those trifles <note>prefatory poems or songs of praise</note> with which we constantly see the monuments of patrons being decorated by associates and hangers-on from the same school. But our Reuchlin said long ago that he had declared war on such incantations and trifling inducements meant only to push merchandise. Thinking them of no value or merit, he judged that such foolish glosses on this varied labor should be entirely neglected and hissed away into silence. 

He considered this course more advantageous because of the recklessness of certain booksellers who, driven by a most ruinous lust for profit, prey upon the most respected authors. In their hope for gain, they toss together works that are far removed from the original manuscripts. Lest those sycophants—those "paper-monkeys" who sponge off our work—should repeatedly attempt the same, he ordered that there be printed at the end of the book the illustrious coat of arms <note>referring to Reuchlin's noble crest</note> with which he was gifted by the generosity of the Imperial Majesty <note>Emperor Maximilian I</note>. By this, students of the Hebrew beauty may be warned to stay away from copies that are not fortified with these insignias. Such books are spurious, born from the mere greed of moneylenders; they are stolen and inferior works brought forth to the total loss of literature. Farewell.

->[A large printer's mark featuring a circle with a cross and the letter 'B' inside, topped by decorative flourishes.]<- 
<note>This is the printer's device of Thomas Anshelm. The 'B' likely stands for "Badensis," indicating his origin in Baden.</note>

IN PFORZHEIM AT THE HOUSE OF THOMAS
ANSHELM ON THE SIXTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF
APRIL <note>March 27th</note> IN THE YEAR 1506.

<meta>Following the initial identification of the book's sections and its historical ownership by the Zurich Library, this page serves as a pedagogical transition. -># THE END OF THE BOOK<-
<note>original Latin: "FINIS LIBRI." This may seem contradictory at the start of a volume, but Johannes Reuchlin’s *Rudiments of Hebrew* (1506) was printed so that the dictionary section followed the Hebrew direction. Therefore, what a Latin reader considers the "end" of the physical book is actually the beginning of the Hebrew text.</note>

->## THE RULE<-
<note>original Latin: "CANON." In this context, a *canon* is a set of instructions or a guide for the reader to follow.</note>

This book is not to be read like other books;
Hold the front with your left hand and the spine with your right,
And turn whatever pages you find from the left toward the right.
Whatever you see written in Latin,
Read in the Latin fashion; <note>Latin is read from left to right.</note> but if Hebrew words are inserted,
They are to be read from the right toward the left.

<summary>This page contains a "Canon" or instructional poem that teaches the reader how to physically handle and read a book printed in the Hebrew orientation, which opens from the right and progresses toward the left.</summary>
